A gorgeous game that might as well be the spiritual successor of ICO even if made by someone other than Team ICO. The benches, beautiful vistas, and interactions between the bothers most strongly invoke memories of ICO.
It is always a pleasure to find games where the gameplay mechanics can supplement the story in a meaningful way and thus turn a video game's story into more than just words on a page, sounds from a voice, or images from a cinematic video. This is especially evident in the final scenes of the game to really drive home certain points.
While the game is relatively short, it was a very enjoyable experience that never outstayed its welcome while delivering am emotional impact that will linger with you once it is all over.

Brothers – a tale of two sons, is a beautiful-looking puzzle-platformer that tells an emotional, bittersweet story. It is like a fairytale as told by the Brothers Grimm, with an unexpected sting and darkness to offset the blissful bits with butterflies and bunnies. At the start, we see how the younger of two brothers doesn’t manage to save his mother’s life. Then, as his father falls deathly ill, he sets off on a long journey with his older brother to a tree that may well hold a cure. Along the way, they run into various creatures and face obstacles that can only be overcome by working together. As everybody speaks an incomprehensible language, the story is told entirely with images and body language.
The game is blessed with an ingenious, yet simple, control-scheme, which allows you to control both brothers simultaneously. One with your left hand and one with your right. If you are lucky enough to have a gamepad, this means that movement is handled with the two control sticks (one per brother) and that for any context-sensitive action (grabbing something or chatting to a character, for instance) you use the left and right trigger, depending on the brother you’re focused on. Once you get used to it, this scheme works surprisingly well, though I did get confused now and then when the brother I was controlling with the left hand was to the right of his sibling. Apparently my brain was expecting my left hand to always control the brother on the left.
Most of the roadblocks involve pulling levers and turning cranks. Barring a few exceptions – such as when the brothers go on a climbing expedition while tied together with a rope – these aren’t exactly innovative, or intellectually challenging. But because of the way you are controlling the brothers, the execution is still interesting. The big incentive to keep going is not finding the next puzzle to solve but to see how the story turns out. The game is good at making you feel invested in the characters, the great visuals and beautiful soundtrack helping to draw you into this world.
Brothers is very linear, there just being a few places where you can deviate from the path a teensy bit to do something optional – like reuniting a giant turtle with her kids. And there are no collectibles of any kind, which is a major plus in my book. All too often the pacing of a game is disrupted by the feeling that you should be exploring every inch of your surroundings to not miss out on something. Even if that something is actually completely irrelevant to the game proper. Brothers moves at a steady clip, never pausing long enough to bore, and it can be finished in a couple of hours. This is probably a negative for some gamers, but good news for people like me, who tend to be short on time and prefer an awesome short experience to a longer just-okay one.
There is an amazing moment late in the game where a little stunt with the controls nearly brought a tear to my eye. I can’t spoil the context, but suffice to say that this is the first time a simple game mechanic ever had such a direct emotional effect on me. The control itself as the narrative device – that is something rare. Brothers is a game that won’t soon be forgotten.

Early Access Review on 25 June 2016
The concept and gameplay is unique, and so far I'm impressed with this in Early Access. I like the setting (American Civil War era), simple economy system as used in the classic "Drug Dealer" game, and the concept of shares in the company as the main storyline to follow. Brownie points for Mac compatibility, as I was too lazy to get on my PC to play!
So far the only minor issues I've got is that tough bandits appear too early in the game, some jobs created are not scaled correctly (5 day delivery on the starter train set? Whoa...), and finally, the major complaint I have is that the UI (at least in the tutorial) really needs work. The quest log fills up pretty quickly, and it's easy to get lost in the entire list. Perhaps a grouped view (main quest, deliveries, events, etc.) and auto-dismissing completed quests would improve the clutter.
Would be good to color-code jobs/quests based on difficulty level as well.
With that said, I think it looks really promising, and I wish all the best for the developers in creating a "Sid Meier's Pirates!"-esque game...on rails! :)

Charming idea, but I can't exactly recommend it in its current state:
1) Difficulty is rather high. Your train will get robbed very frequently, and early on can either pay up (meaning you lose most of your profits) or reload. You can eventually buy gatling guns which but don't expect the game to tell you that those are considered trade goods (rather than guns bought at a gunstore or train upgrades bought at the train yard)
Further, the "urgent mail" missions tend to be needlessly frustrating because of how deadlines are generated: Missions cannot be handed it before 9am, but you can get an 8am deadline (i.e. you would have to do the maths first to work out if a 5 day deadline is actually only 4 days)
2) Controls are cumbersome - for example, to pick a location you have to first click on every potential passenger to see where they want to go, keep track of the destinations, and then click on them again when you have worked out where you want to go. Seems that spreadsheet technology was sorely lacking in The Old West.
If you are not very familiar with US geography you'll also find yourself switching a lot between map view and city view because you can't check from the city view if a particular city is on your route.
3) Everything in the game appears to be random - when you level up you can pick a random skill. The NPCs you start with are random - you can either get a sniper, or a melee fighter, or a guy who is good with a fire extinguisher. If you want to build a sniper but only roll melee damage skills, too bad - try restarting the game.

Very different from RF1 and 2, which were more traditional story-driven FPS's. RF3 is sandboxy with destructible buildings and an assortment of Saint's Row style missions to choose from (not surprising as RF is kind of SR's distant future sequel) as you gradually liberate territory. First couple of missions take some getting used to, but once you get the hang of it, RF3 is very good stuff. Nanite rifle is one of the cooler weapons I've ever used. Worth buying on sale.

Blowing stuff up is extremely fun and handled better than any other game I've played. Combat is a bit awkward, but gets easier after you learn to use all of your tools and not run around like an idiot. There are way less upgrades than I would've liked, and the collectibles are pretty unimpressive. Getting the jetpack eariler would've made the game a lot more fun,.
Looks a lot like Just Cause 2 and other sandbox games, but is actually much more linear.  You need to complete entire areas to advance a lot of the time (run out of stuff to blow up if you don't), and there's very little to do in areas that you've completed. However, there's a real sense of accomplisment unlike for example Prototype where all enemy bases respawn after a few minutes. Took me almost 20 hours of solid fun, which is good for a modern game. Very nice buy for 10€, recommended without reservation for anything less.
Fun enough.  The combination of good physics, good weapons and (especially) the fully destructable structures keep you playing through the weak story and plastic setting.

Awesome game! Smash stuff, drive through it, explode it, love it.
If I had to pick THE moment I fell in love with this game, it would be this:
Mission is to rescue some hostages, they're in a building at the bottom of a quarry, three hostages, in a half-moon configuration, smash my truck through the wall where there was no hostages, untie everybody, throw charges everywhere, get back in the truck, drive out the front of the building, blow the building, drive away into the sunset.

At its best, Guerilla offers white-knuckle action and ridiculous spectacle on par with Just Cause 2, but with better vehicle handling and cooler weapons. At its worst, it offers a lot of unnecessary sandboxing and nags you about side-missions you have no interest in pursuing.
Guerilla has a lot going for it but would benefit greatly if it ditched the sandboxing for a more heavily curated single-player experience that cuts down on travel times and boring side-mission grinds in favor of the huge spectacular missions it often does well.

As a DC fan and a long time gamer, I found this game really fun, but it definitely could use a lot more work.
Don't get me wrong, I absolutely love this game and I enjoy playing it, but I think the cons outweigh the pros.
First off, as a free to play player the game is very limited. There are certain degrees at which a F2P (free to play) player has access to content and this game is extremely limited. The game constantly expands its benefits to members and its market. At this point F2P players should get a more expansive inventory and less limitations on their bank and mailbox (sending and receiving items).
I cannot play this game for 5 minutes without running into something that is trying to encourage me to spend money. Sure, they're a business and they need to make money, BUT we have seen MANY games that do not do this and still succeed.
I love DC and most of their productions, but I've never seen them successful in video games. DCUO is one exception where I think they have done well, but I think they could do much better with more effort. Maybe all they need is an increase in their budget, but this game can be overhauled to be an even greater success.
Finally,
You should play this game, maybe even put a couple of dollars in it. If you plan to play this game long enough, pay for the membership as well. It's fun, but in my opinion it loses its appeal at level 30 because it becomes extremely repetitive and a grind for levels.
Again, however, the game could use a lot of changing in their F2P framework. F2P users have extremely limited access, moreso than most popular/successful F2P.
F2P friendly, 4/10 (Low-No|High-Yes)
Difficulty, 8/10 (Low-Difficult|High-Easy)
Playability (How many hours can you play the game before it gets boring), 8/10 (Low-few hours|High-several hours)
How high is the paywall, 7/10 (Low-cheap payments|High-expensive payments)
Voice acting,♥♥♥♥♥♥10 (Some characters get good voice acting others get absolute♥♥♥♥♥♥ the dialogue can be dreadful too)
Graphics, 8/10 (They're not great, but they're not bad in such a way that it isn't an eye sore)
Overall, 7/10

I've been meaning to review this game for years, but for some reason I just never got around to it.........but fear not, Dion is here now to provide you all a quality review of this ancient game, lol. Well so, spore is a heart breaking game for me personally, and why you may ask? Because.......its seldom we get a game that takes a gameplay concept so unique and full of so much potential. The whole concept of spore, is that you take control over a species that you have created, and you see  to thier survival from the cell stage, all the way up until they mount a spaceship and leave the rock they evolved on behind. This is a gameplay concept that is just begging to breed one of the most deep, and engaging games to ever be concieved.....that is.........if the game is made properly. Unfortunately, spore is not made properly enough to actually make this concept with such huge potential truly shine. To explain to you why this game fails, I'll have to explain each of the phases that this game takes you though. To play this game, you play it in different stages of your species's development, and I'm gonna explain each one. Basically, it goes from cell stage, to evolution stage, to tribal age, to global age, and finally to the space age. I'll explain each one.
Cell Stage-
This is the first, and probably the most fun you will ever have out of this game honestly. At this stage you have started out as a teeny tiny little single cell organism, and your prime directive, is to eat stuff, grow larger, and mate with other members of your species, and try to avoid being eaten by other, larger cells. This whole section plays out more like a minigame then any other stage does, and honestly, its really fun too at this point. However, the things you add to your organism are pretty limited, theres only like a few things to add overrall, and most of these things will be totally useless to you in the later stages, which means you can do litterally anything at this point, really all your doing is just getting to the next stage of evolution, which is, growing legs (or you can just say to hell with legs and slither around like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ snail, its up to you), but either way, your backside is going to end up on land..........probably the only criticism I have for this section is, the lack of variety for your parts you can add, and also the fact that you cant choose to simply be some sort of aquatic creature, you are forced to go to land at the end no matter what.
Creature Stage-
This is the stage where stuff starts getting weird, and the game begins to fail, but this stage is still rather fun overall. You've walked from the ocean with several members of your species (or slithered) and began to start about the business of mating, mingling with other species already on land, and searching for food. Although its fun, I feel there could have been a lot more to this part than what is there. You evolve your species further too, changing and swapping body parts as needed with traits and features that better suit you. But thats just it.......its just you, running around for food, dancing with other species trying to make them your friends, or they give you the middle finger, and use your corpse as thier next campfire meal. Earlier I also mentioned this is where stuff starts getting weird.........and it does at times. You encounter aliens, you encounter massive legendary creatures, and other various random events. The aliens for the most part wont kidnap you personally, but they will kidnap members of your party, which gets quite annoying. And they usually suprise you too, and thier appearance usually sends everyone running around panicking which is quite hilarious.
Tribal Stage-
Alright this is where the game really starts getting dull and boring. This is also where your control over an individual member of your species is taken away, and you are now controling everyone as if this were a RTS game.....things get a lot less about exploration and such, and it becomes a crappy version of command and conquer. You send tribesmen out to hunt and bring back food............you need food to build buildings in your village, and you need buildings to assign special roles to your tribesmen to carry out various tasks. You also use food to make new tribesmen. You will be defending against other tribes of other species that have reached this level of development and one by one, you tolerate this painfully awful system until you are the last tribe remaining in your area. Its not very fun, its painful to control and manage, and its just a mess. This stage could have been great, but it was implemented poorly.
Global Stage-
At this stage, your species remains the only intelligent life on your planet, and so now your doing the exact same thing you did in the tribal stage, but against different factions of your own species, and with far more advanced weapons.....not to mention this time it is a global conflict. It is basically a world war at this point, and let me tell you, this stage is no better, and actually worse then the tribal stage. The poorly excuted gameplay of this segment is so broken, that you will find it extremely difficult to actually win at this stage since the AI has no problem coordinating massive attacks on you faster then you are able to build things. I honestly quit at this segment after several attempts, and skipped to the final stage just to see what this one is like.
Space Age-
Now this segment is where the game becomes something totally unique from what it had been prior to now. In this stage, things actually become very interesting and the game is now fun once more, as your traveling to other planets now. Up to this point, you only saw your own planet of course, but now your gonna see everything but that, as you search for other planets to colonize, and encounter other species, whether they are on your level of technology or not. If they are of course, you can engage in diplomacy with them, and of course, you might want to be careful because they can actually fight and do harm to you if you♥♥♥♥♥♥them off. Encountering species at any level below space age pretty much means you can fly around laughing and zapping them since your too advanced for them (or you can be boring and peaceful) but yeah, the appeal here though, is that the universe is near infinite, and the sheer magnitude of stuff you can run into at this point of the game.......but again, this stage, like all the others, could have been so much better then what it is, and thus, ultimately, this stage, and the cell stage being the best 2 stages, is not enough to save the game in my opinion.
Overall, I wanted to like spore, but there is no excuse for all the missed opportunity with this game. This game is truly heart breaking to me, and I wish with all my heart that someone took this concept and made something with much more content and substance then this, because after playing spore, I felt as though the game was incomplete and rushed, and missing a ton of features, and had a flawed presentation overall. The game is charming, but it doesnt hide how incomplete I felt with this experience.

Bounty Train is currently in Early Access but I’ve found more than enough content to keep me happy (I want to note that others who I know who have played the game have said they wanted more content which i found a little surprising). The developers seem active with updates coming every few months fixing minor issues usually like bugs or adding small features. I am unsure on just how complete the game is as I have been unable to find a roadmap but there are features they plan to implement that aren’t there yet so I imagine there is still some development due.
The story is rather simple. Your father has died and left you his train and shares in his railway company but the other investors want to change the company. You must embark on a quest to find your siblings and convince them to see things your way as with their shares you are majority shareholder. The story isn’t massively fleshed out but it does it’s job of giving you a reason for the gameplay. I do hope a little more is added to the story or at least the main quest because currently I have very little feeling or care towards anyone i’ve met, even my own family members…
It seems the story is there to act as a tutorial and not too much else.
The gameplay of Bounty Train is absolutely fantastic. You start with a basic steam train and just yourself, from there you must travel from city to city delivering cargo and passengers, helping strangers, importing and smuggling goods hiring crew and making money to build up your train.
Your train starts with the basics a locomotive for travel, a passenger carriage, cargo carriage and crew carriage. You’ll need at least one of each of these even as you customize your train and buy new parts. If you find yourself short of funds you can always leave a nonessential part of your train behind to pick up later or just sell it if you feel you no longer need it. Every part of your train can be replaced or upgraded adding a fantastic amount of customization and allowing you to focus on whatever you feel makes money faster (smuggling goods, transporting passengers, raiding camps).
You travel from city to city along your railway routes paying to unlock new routes as you travel and running into random encounters, new side quests and meeting new factions and groups of people, sometimes traders, sometimes people looking for help and others who need work. Most of the games events are randomized so you never really know what’s coming leading you to always be prepared for anything.
Aside from the side quests you’ll find like taking passengers from city to city or traporting goods you also have the ability to take advantage of the everchanging economy.by utilizing the market. There will often be shortages of various goods in other cities and buying them out of your own pocket and delivering them is a fantastic way to earn money, though often overlooked.
Along your route you’ll find yourself able to earn reputation at the various cities you pass through making trading cheaper there but sometimes opening other opportunities too. Cities are not the only places you can earn reputation though, there are different ‘factions’ you’ll encounter and the way you handle yourself in various situations and quests will define/influence the way you are treated by these people when you encounter them next. Once again this can hugely impact just how successful you are in the game.
Different cities you travel to will have different resources and amenities. Some will have a hospital so injured crew can rest whilst others will have saloons for the more shady quests, or banks so you can deposit money to gain interest like a good little saver! Each town sells different goods at the market and some will even sell guns when guns are prohibited in other cities. Each city depot will also supply different parts of your train so travelling around a lot is highly recommended for the best gameplay experience as every town is a little different to the last.
The graphics are lovely on my desktop and the game runs really smoothly. I love seeing my train coursing along the track, steam billowing from the engines as I outrun the bandits. The towns are clean and rather beautiful to look at, even if there isn’t too much going on.
The sound is great also, you’ll feel like you are really driving your own train which the chuckachuckachucka of your train moving along the tracks, the loud train horn to spook the horses who are chasing you down and the bandits gunfire. The towns and cities are full of people murmuring and going about their everyday life. The sound is just wonderfully immersive. I would appreciate a little more of a soundtrack but that’s personal preference and it doesn’t NEED it at all.
--- Vast train customization and upgrades.
--- Side quests that you can choose and play at your own pace.
--- Historically accurate (for the most part).
--- Randomized events, passengers and side quests allowing for masses of replayability.
--- Different crew members with a nicely refined leveling system.
--- ‘Factions’ and reputation that changes as you play depending on how you interact with people.
--- Lots of control over your train, your staff, where you go and what you do.
--- In game economywith a brilliant trading system.
--- Starting a new game wiped my previous game for some reason. I inadvertently wiped three hours of gameplay whilst trying to show my friend the start of the game.
--- Combat is a little difficult and at times redundant. It’s a lot more fun to avoid combat entirely and if you can’t I advise you pick ‘escape’ over ‘attack’.
--- Randomized events + passengers can make or break your run. If no-one wants to go to a city you’re headed to you’ll go bankrupt very quickly.
--- Repairs + healing take a long time. (Will be fixed in next update)
--- No ability to see the map whilst in town so you cannot plan your routes properly or choose which passengers you want to take without opening and closing your map.
(Another thing that the devs are fixing)
--- DLC on sale before full release. Sorry devs, i’ll always have an issue with this and there’s nothing that’ll change my mind on this negative fact. Don’t sell part of your game, sell it all or don’t bother. I have no issue with soundtrack and artbook being sold seperately, I would have bought them, but if this game is going to be a DLC spawner from the start then this review won’t stay positive for long.
Overall I am loving Bounty Train and I know this will be a game I play to finish over and over. The blending of simulation style games with strategy and implementing some fantastic historical events makes Bounty Train feel like a refreshing addition to Steam. Despite the combat being a tad repetitive every other element of the game holds itself well and the gameplay is ridiculously addictive. There is a lot of content already with the general gameplay feeling mostly complete and very, very fun. The price may be steep for some people but for those who really enjoy this style of gameplay it’s worth every single penny, and if that’s not enough to push your hand, grab it in a sale, you won’t be disappointed.

You’ll feel like you’ve walked into a mid 1800’s train station with historically accurate firing pieces, and the old Iron Horse engines themselves. This game is still in early access, and much is yet to be rolled out, but much fun is already on the line for those who want to get in early on a price that may not remain past ea. I received this game free for review purposes, in exchange for an honest review, but bought the dlc myself after having a look at all Bounty Train has to offer.
The game operates much like many of the pirate sims; with a dual view between the map and the train station. When in the map view, you purchase licenses to unlock sections of the track, click on cities you choose to travel to, and deal with bandits, Native Americans, and soldiers who try to relieve you of everything from your cargo, your money, to your life. You may fight, flee, or pay bribe money to dispatch these rascals.
If you fight, you switch to an actual view of your train on the track, where you may direct your hired hands to discharge the bandits with longarms, pistols, or even explosives. Meanwhile you have to extinguish fires, heal your wounded crew, and protect your train. When your train reaches a town, you have a loading screen into the train station view, and each city has its own unique station, and buildings. You may click on the people standing around the station platform to accept fares for other cities, cargo to carry down the line, or letters, messages, or other missions to carry out for love or money. This requires careful planning, as you have a time limit on delivering from point A to point B. So, choose based on the cities you plan to visit next. Certain aspects couldn’t be deciphered like whether my brother was on board or not. I hadn’t had an empty seat when I met him, then I was unable to complete that mission. This has been addressed in an earlier patch for Sam Archer, though apparently it’s still an issue, just with a different brother, as I had the problem with Robert.

Bounty Train has a bountiful story, with immersive missions that will carry you from your inheritance of this train after your Father’s untimely death, all the way to a face to face with Mr. Lincoln himself. If you choose to start with the tutorial, you are given this info in the first town when you return from Europe. You’re instructed to go to the next town to meet with the Lawyer for further instructions. If you skip the tutorial, you begin in the 2nd city with the lawyer. Either way, you take your thousand dollar starting purse, and travel from city to city in search of your siblings, so you can convince them to pool their influence from your combined 55% of the railroad’s stock to convince the company to take the shorter route and spare the Indians in the process of finishing up this train business faster, so you can take the money and run. There is a Sandbox mode in the menu as well, with the time restraints removed to give you unlimited time to complete missions.
If you love historically accurate gaming, this sim’s for you. Everything from the design of the people, the trains, and the buildings, to the 19th century Civil War music is history. The card art includes the various engines. The emoticons includes cowboy hats, Indian headdresses, and caps for the Northern and the Southern soldiers. Whichever faction you choose to ally with, you will find yourself immersed in a time that is rich in industrial legend.  The graphics are simple, but pleasing because of the historical feel. And, what can I say? There are all the neat train cars of a forgotten time.

*Historical quality
*Trains
*Immersive story quest
*Fun combat
*Day/Night Cycle
*Minor bugs and glitches which are being patched
*Incomplete tutorial teaches (fun) aspect of driving train which you rarely use again for some reason
*DLC is not released yet, except for the extra engine (but it’s a great one)
*Unspecified wait on the art book and sound track, as well

is a game that mixes strategy, simulation, real-time combat and trading elements into a pretty neat package which I believe has never been done like this in any other game. The game akes place in the 19th century during the American Civil War and puts you in charge of a train and its crew, as you make your way down the coast of the USA while trying to make a profit.
Despite the fact that the tutorial is somewhat short, it teachs you, or at least gives you some slight insight, on pretty much all the basic things you should know before you first play the game. You can choose to play the normal sandbox mode or hardcore mode, which doesn’t let you save, meaning there is no going back once you mess up. After completing the tutorial I found that while the tutorial does teach you how to properly control the train, I rarely found myself controlling the train in that very same way as I played the game when completing missions and whatnot. I feel like you don’t have that much of control over your train as I’d hope for.
As you travel through the railroad system, and you need to purchase access to new railroads in order to use them, you’ll eventually come across bandits or other factions which you’ll engage on combat depending on how you decide to approach them. Combat is real-time, with the option to pause, and everytime you’re in combat your objective is to defend your train until you defeat all foes. However, each individual wagon has its own life bar and if one of your wagons keeps getting damaged it will eventually slow you down. That said, during combat not only you have to keep an eye for that, but you also have to make sure that your train doesn’t get on fire, which is done by sending one of your crew members to put the first signs of fire off before it spreads along the train. Controlling your units during combat is pretty basic, just select the unit and then click where you want it to move or attack. Usually they will attack any enemy on their line of sight, but when there are multiple enemies you might want to issue orders yourself and focus on a single target.
One thing that actually bothers me is that when you’re ambushed the objective of the enemy always looks like it is to destroy you not rob you of your cargo as you’d might expect. It would be nice if there were different types of combat encounters which forced you to protect your cargo while bandits try to take it away for example. The game offers some degree of challenge not only in terms of combat, but also in the way that you have to carefully plan what missions you will take, which town you’ll visit next, what wagons will you take and things like that. Failing a mission will make you lose reputation with 1 of the 4 factions or with the city you were doing that mission for, and you’ll also have to play a fee.
Towns play a huge role in the game and as time passes, they will change from one side of the fight to another of the American Civil War conflict and that will affect the prices of various products. In towns you can buy various different goods, which you can sell at other towns for a profit, you can hire new crew members, you can upgrade your train by buying better parts and customize it with different types of wagons (passenger wagons, cargo wagons, etc) while designing your own train the way you want to be, still more wagons will make you go slower and consume more coal so you have to be mindful about it. In towns you can also buy new weapons and sell your old ones, accept quests like getting a certain amount of resources or transporting someone to another city, you can also heal your characters and repair your train but in order to do so you’ll have to wait a few hours (in game). You can also buy turrets for your train and choose different stats for your characters when they level up.

The worst part though is that the time allowed to complete missions gets shorter and shorter until finally it's not even actually possible to complete the missions because the travel time is longer than the mission allowance.
As I said, this game will be fun when it's ready but I can't recommend it in the state it is in now.
I am not giving it a thumbs down however, because the game is in early access and honestly - there's a lot of play in it.
THE POSITIVE
Ok, so you have a train you design and that design has many tactical and strategic implications.  From the obvious - cargo capacity, speed, etc. to the not so obvious such as the sight lines for defensive shooting positions, choice of cars to help keep passengers and crew safe, and arrangement of cars to inhibit boarders or provide better access for your own crew.
There is a genuine feeling of progression.  You start out harassed to the point of endangerment by a handful of angry native americans hell bent on guzzling your fire water, and you emerge a terrifyingly dangerous scar faced crew of stone cold killers capable of levelling military roadblocks complete with cannonry.
Your gun ports open to reveal gatling guns placed in your armored car, and you are the laissez-faire nightmare that made the west wilder.
The game is challenging, and not because of dumb things you will find frustrating, but because your decisions matter - all of them matter.  Do you take 2 cars that hold 3 passengers, or one 4 and one 2?  Why do you do that?  Do you go for bigger and more expensive cargo cars, or smaller ones that are less efficient?  The smaller cars can be left behind to repair if they break down...
I recommend the game if you like a mixture of strategy and tactics.
SUMMARY
This game will be great eventually, but it's in early access so only get it if you can handle your junk breaking, losing save games and occassionally hating life.

The Good: Somewhat refreshing take on a top scrolling RPG. You have some humor in a lot of the dialogue that keeps this game from taking itself too seriously. For the price tag the visuals are slightly above average with a decent soundtrack. This game is not a top shelf game. If it had been released in a store this is the type of game that would be in the $15-$20 bin within a month of the release. If you expect this much you will not be disappointed.
The Bad: The combat system leaves a lot to be desired. I found in my short time playing I could win a fight by just pounding keys 1-6 in order. Often I was pulling extra groups just to enjoy fighting. Each character only has two abilities and once you learn the proper order to put them in based on their cool downs (which isn't very long even on the bigger abilities) you can probably just run your finger back and forth on the number keys. The healing system is also a pain to use. It revolves around a quick heal or a channeled heal but both are based on a cool down timer so you can literally spam heals over and over not to mention with the combat system being as easy as it is you rarely need to. I found my healer often spends most of his time auto attacking because he has no offensive ability. Last but not least the "dungeon crawls" are extremely repetitive. There isn't a wrong path to take or a secret door to enter its just a set map with a few different paths. Often to even get the full reward of playing you might as well clear it all rarely ending up with crafting materials to make the important items. This brings me to the last gripe: The crafting system. Every time I found myself trying to grind to get materials to make an item that same item ended up dropping as loot or something insanely better. I'd wager you could complete this entire game without ever crafting a single thing.
But for $15 or cheaper you really can't go wrong. If this game were $20 I would have not recommended this game.

It goes from well-known laws like freedom of speech/demonstration/religion to tiny aspects you'd never see in a geopolitical simulator; blood toxicity level, driving age, maximum age for school, and speed limits on trunk roads, city roads, and highways. It also has a very realistic atmosphere to it. Setting aside the fact the map and characters look like 90s era games, it gives the game a feel no other geopolitical simulator has given me; realism. It goes from setting meetings with political figures and world leaders, to having small talk and influencing well-known figures in your country to vote for you or support your bill publicly. When a law doesn't pass through, a reform can be made. Adding laws into this reform that is bipartisan will increase the chances of it being passed. More features include asking nations for authorization to build a pipeline through their territory, building pipelines for oil or gas, detailed trade agreements that allow you to set the price, quantity, and duration of the agreement (Example: Russia's Natural Gas Agreement with China that will last for 20 years), the game also allows the construction of various buildings or transportations like oil and gas pipelines, high-speed trains, nuclear power plants, oil rigs, gas and oil fields, and even increasing the number of hospitals, homes, schools, or solar fields. The game also has a very complicated economic system. I have been having trouble with it, but I did have some success as Jordan earlier. Continuing on, the game is very recent. It isn't like SuperPower 2 where it was created just before the NATO expansion or the break-up of Serbia and Montenegro, but it was released in 2013, meaning it has the world's youngest country, South Sudan. The game features terrorist groups in every country, ranging from the Mafia to Total Jihad groups (Al-Quaeda). You have the options to infiltrate the groups if they live in your territory, to funding them with weapons, money, and 2 semi-trucks with rockets and explosives if they are in other countries to help them take down that country's government. But if you do this, you have the chance to be caught red-handed. And this will transfer into the news, and Parliment will impeach you. I suffered that while playing as Russia and funding New Zealand terrorists. The game offers so much detail to their options, like adding more medical staff and adding more police staff. You can also investigate politicians and well-known citizens to reveal a scandal to use against them, to spying on heads-of-state or countries to find evidence that will gain the approval of the United Nations Security Council and allow military action against the country. Which brings me to the Organizations of the game.
The game has made Organizations possible, which bring various or all world organizations into the game including the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, Shanghai Cooperation Organization, Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries, European Union, and North American Free Trade Agreement. It then gives you the option to create your own Organization, allowing an Economic Market (NAFTA), Producing Countries (OPEC), Monetary Union (EU), and Political-Military Organization (NATO). This then allows you to choose members states, the budget, the voting system, the secretary general's holding of the seat, and who the secretary general is. You can then meet to set the prices of the product, make changes, etc. Like with OPEC, you can propose to change the average oil price. You can also launch reelection campaigns, even visiting the Olympics, military barracks, and universities. Instead of a SuperPower 2 style diplomatic relations, there are two types of relations. First is economic. Just because the country does not favor you does not affect trade relations. Second is military, allowing certian permissions like allowing air, ground, and naval bases in your/their country while considering the amount, allowing you to edit this at any time via meetings with head-of-state. Diplomatic relations come with various things, like managing embassies, allowing nationals to enter or leave, and forcing ethnic Israeli's living in Lebanon to return. Lastly, the game makes it perfectly with this.
As all military and geopolitical games have, the feature nuclear weapons. Naturally, this game has them. But for the first time, you need to go through politics when proceeding with a nuclear attack. First, you must authorize the use of nuclear weapons. Second, you must make a meeting with the Chief of the Army. Third, you must ask him to authorize the use of nuclear weapons. Forth, you must ask him for the code for the nuclear weapons. And the game never remembers it, You actually need to write it down. Lastly, enter your code when firing nuclear missiles. But in this game, it features something never seen in any game I have played - Chemical and bacteriological weapons. You can actually use the weapons hated internationally. Though it is almost difficult to use them, you need to have a high standing with the chief of the army. Authorize the use of chemical and bacteriological weapons, ask him to authorize their use, and if he allows it, you can freely launch chemical attacks against anyone. Beware - Using nuclear, chemical, and bacteriological weapons are EXTREMELY frowned upon domestically and internationally. If used, you will be thrown out of office, and if not that, the UNSC will send a resolution to authorize military intervention.
Overall, the game is very fun. So far, I have not run into any major bugs like crashes or gameplay interventions. Only bug I have notices was on the Newspaper where it was supposed to say the President of Russia's name, but showed random lettering or coding. I rate it 8/10. If you love geo-political games and have major interests in politics, this game is perfect. Besides the 90s looking interface, no game has ever gone so in-depth. Many offical reviews say the same.

Controller Companion is an application that allows you to navigate the desktop and other programs using a controller, I’ve only used it with an Xbox 360 controller but I believe it works with other controllers as well. Setting it up is incredibly easy and straightforward thanks to the settings menu accessed via the taskbar icon for Controller Companion, allowing you to do things such as change the mouse acceleration and creating profiles for different programs.
The settings for the application in general are very useful and range from starting Controller Companion upon startup to the deadzone of your controller. One of the particularly useful settings is the ability to turn off the ‘In-App’ status for Steam when using Controller Companion. It might not sound ground-breaking but since Controller Companion is the kind of application you always have running in the background, I feel it would get irritating to constantly appear as though you’re using it.
Controller Companion’s strongest, and main, feature is the ability to create profiles for different programs as I mentioned earlier. You start off with the basic Desktop profile which is used by default for any programs unless you create separate profiles for them. As with all profiles you can change the controller bindings for this profile. The Desktop profile also allows you to change your virtual keyboard bindings which are then used by any profile's with the virtual keyboard is enabled. The virtual keyboard has a spiral design and features punctuation and numbers as well as the alphabet, it is obviously not as efficient to use as a regular keyboard but it’s far easier to use than other virtual keyboards such as the one found on the Xbox. Anyway, back to profiles. Creating profiles for other programs is simple. Just below the Desktop profile settings there’s a section called ‘Process Bindings’. The easiest way to get started is to run the program you want a profile for and then select it from the recently used section of the ‘add a new process profile’ menu. Simple. Once you’ve done that you’ve got the same options as the Desktop profile as well as Mouse settings for the specific profile and general profile settings, e.g. the name of the profile. The next time you start the program you’ve just created a profile for, Controller Companion will automatically switch to the bindings for said program.
Another great thing about Controller Companion is that it supports the Steam Workshop. What does this mean for using the application? Well once you’ve created a profile for a program you can upload it to the workshop (or update an existing workshop item) by exporting the profile. Once it’s up other people can download the profile so they don’t have to create their own for said program.
One last thing to mention is that whenever you launch an application with controller support, such as Steam Big Picture or a game with controller support, the application automatically disables itself to avoid any input duplication. It also does this for fullscreen programs such as other games though there do seem to be some exceptions to this.
I’ve been using this application with Netflix as well as a couple of games without controller support and it’s been great. The ability to just sit back and relax while binge watching Netflix without having to stand up to start the next episode or change the volume is glorious. This simple application is a great thing to own if you often sit at a distance from your PC or you just don’t feel like using the mouse and keyboard from time to time. If you wish to up your laziness game, this application is for you!

I preordered this and downloaded it as soon as I could. I've already beaten the story, though it took me a while, and now I'm on freeplay, which I've been playing for a few days. I have to say, the game's a mixed bag. I'll start with the postives:
A lot of new mechanics have been added to the game, like rune tracing and time manipulation for Dr Strange, gravity mines for Star Lord, hacking minigames for Ms. Marvel, I could go on. They've also adapted a few older mechanics like Captain America's shield switches. It's a refreshing new take on the Lego gameplay, after not really getting anything new in Lego Avengers last year.
A totally revamped Custom Character maker, which gives you the ability to pick and choose your characters abilities, instead of having to use specific faces, hair, etc which could really make your characters look lame. It also means you can make your characters OP with several abilities. And finally, FINALLY, we can add capes to our characters.
A more combat focussed style of gameplay, with boss fights being partly puzzle, mostly beat-em-up, where you just get to whale on the boss instead of use the same, tedious old trick on them four times like in older games. It makes the battles feel a lot more alive. Also enemies have health bars instead of hearts. Oddly, you still have hearts, meaning you die in eight hits.
A working map, with several diverse locations from the Marvel Universe.... And the wild west, Egypt, and medieval England, for some reason...
An original story, with brand new voice lines both in the story, free play and when you're just messing around with characters, and several fun callbacks to previous games.
Here's some sort of in-between stuff:
-New voice cast for pretty much all the characters. Take them or leave them, I'm used to a lot of them now but some were a little annoying to listen to at first.
-The storyline's a little dull and repetitive in places, and not as exciting as the first Lego Marvel Superheroes game in my opinion. But like anime, we all know you don't play these for the plot.
-The free-roam side missions are mostly the same, like getting photos for Jameson, collecting items/animals etc, races (unfortunately, they don't let you use speed characters in races, which is bogus). But they have a few new missions, like asking local NPCs for information and reporting back to the missiom giver.
And now, the negatives:
At the end of level 2, you have to do this boss fight with Vulture and Goblin 2099, where you chase them as Spider-Man, web slinging after them, and once you catch them you have to rapidly press a key to beat them, or they'll knock you out of the sky and fly off. Goblin 2099 was particularly annoying as he also threw pumpkin bombs which had the same effect. A lot of these phases where you have to push a button are annoying, as if you tap too quickly nothing happens. If you tap too slowly, nothing happens. You have to find that right level. I think about twice a second is roughly the right speed. Thankfully, this is the only fight like that in the story, but it can be done again in some free play missions. There are a few other times when button mashing is ineffective, so be aware.
You can't seem to name characters in the character builder. Not sure if it's a glitch or what, but I've tried my keyboard and an Xbox Controller and nothing works.
Oh yeah, don't bother with a keyboard yet. A few mechanics, like Dr Strange's time manipulation and Fix-Its work a LOT better if you have a controller as you can move the joystick. Trust me, it's easier.
If you're doing some kind of minigame like tracing a rune, expect Wasp to come in while you're right in the middle of it with a pop-up hint. It's really annoying, and you can't seem to turn them off. And annoyingly, unless you're still holding the button that triggered the rune game, the minigame will stop and you'll have to reopen it.
The character maker doesn't have parts from the DLC characters, despite rumours saying that it would. Also, you don't get all the DLC in the season pass yet, for now you only have the classic guardians and agnets of atlas packs, which is a little disappointing. Had I known, I wouldn't have pre-ordered the deluxe edition.
All in all, it's a fun game. The glitches have given me no-end of problems, and I've been on the verge of ragequitting a few times because of them (I had to replay the Egypt level 4 times because of a continuity glitch), but I'm sure they'll be patched out eventually. Maybe wait until then, or for a sale, if you're not entirely convinced. But if you like modern Marvel and/or lego games, you'll like this. It's got enough of the same things to feel familiar but enough new things to feel original.

This review is all done after initially playing about 5 hours of said game.
I don't believe I have ever had a more confusing experience. I really wanted to like this game. It's extremely ambitious in design and looks pretty solid in areas. Modes such as Armory are relatively fun and grand in scope; however, playing the game is a frustrating experience.
The controls are very strange and do not come to the player easily. You have to fiddle around with it to get it to your liking, which is easier said than done. Think about most first person shooter games with their controls: now remove aspects of sensitivity and general feeling of control on the weapon. I had a problem on more than one occassion where I died because I could not aim at the enemy at all. After going through the control menu, I selected a lock-on control scheme. The only way I could manage to hit anything is with this mode, and I'm questioning if I am simply stupid or the game is too buggy. Another problem I have is picking up weapons; it's very slow, and causes certain games (DayZ) to be incredulously hard to play because you end up getting caught off guard trying to get a weapon that you can't aim anyway.
There are multiple views (third and first), and first person view is relatively hard on the eyes as the head bob on it is ridiculous (you can set it lower); I find myself more comfortable with the third person view, which gives a bigger picture anyway.
The worst thing I encountered in ArmA II (or any of its other games) is that it simply isn't fun. I never felt like anything was going to plan, that almost everything I did was hindered by the control. Perhaps if I had a controller, the game would respond better. Another big deal is the bugs within the game; they constantly appear, from minor ones as texture problems to really big bugs such as your helicopter flipping over randomly to kill you, lock the screen, and cause you to bring up task manager to get out of the game.
The frustration does not end there for me. I also wanted to get in on the DayZ Mod, which conveniently has a download on Steam. This download is not an updated version however, and is completely and utterly incompatible with 99% of online DayZ servers. So, you have to download a completely separate mod, DayZ Commander, to update all of your ArmA II games/DLC and also download updates to the DayZ mod, and then you can finally play a game. Great, right?
Wrong. Most servers seem to require something called "DayZ Epoch", another mod of a mod that you need to download. An extra 400mb on.
So you get that done, and you're ready. It's too bad that the mod has the exact same flaws as ArmA II that I listed above. I struggle to hit ANYTHING, and if I don't have a weapon, finding one while zombies attack you is next to impossible. The atmosphere is pretty cool, and the immersiveness is great, but it just doesn't seem to work at all for me.
I do note here that the creators of ArmA II did not create the DayZ mod, but I have it here for reference due to the fact a great deal of players buy this game to play this mod.
In conclusion, I do not recommend this game; I dislike it for many reasons. If you feel like you can deal with a lot of frustration and can look past multiple issues within a game, then this is for you. I wanted to love this, as it offers a lot, but my experience with it has been bad and I wish it wasn't.
Wait until your friend gifts you this, or try it out before you spend your money. Don't regret buying a game you cannot refund.

So far I can't recommend it, primarily due to in game pricing.  A newspaper costs as much as whole crates of some goods - and you must have a newspaper to get goods pricing in other towns (small issue, easily remedied).
The big issue (and the main reason I gave up after an hour) is that even IF you shell out the cash to get pricing info, do the market research and buy the goods - you STILL lose money (at least I did).  For example, if "food" is selling in Boston for $10/unit and being bought in Portland (Maine, not Oregon - I'm not NEARLY that far yet, lol) for $15/unit - you should gross $5/unit. Not when I try it. Fill my cargo with food, arrive in Portland, click "sell" and it informs me that I will be selling for a loss.
I know prices fluctuate - however, Portland is one town away from Boston on the map. I am also aware that some goods (like food) spoil. However, Portland is only a few days' journey and "food" in the game supposedly takes a week to spoil.  I have yet to make any money (even simply gross profits, forget about net after deducting my expenses) buying and selling any goods.
Portland and Boston are the only towns I have unlocked thus far, because my capital just keeps decreasing.
Of course, if the economic mechanics change to something slightly less punishing (and less decepetive) I'll return and revise my review.  But I'm putting this frustration simulator aside until the next update.

For an Early Access Game Bounty Train is ridiculously fun.
However i'm not sure it's worth it's current £18.99 price tag, there's just not that much game play in it. I finished the campaign in a little over 8 hours and while it is hard it is not hard in a challenging way. Bad guys get more numerous, are much more expensive to pay off and start throwing grenades like they are going out of fashion. Grenades will set your cargo on fire even if they hit the outside of your armored carriage and this just makes the game tedious in the late game.
Reputation just dosn't seem to work properly, I had a run through where I payed off as many people as possible and got my standings with pretty much everyone north of Philadelphia high enough that they would allow me to pass consistently however this seemed to randomly degrade to everyone hating me in no time at all and this strategy leaves you so poor that you have no hope of completing the game in the allotted time frame.
There is no way to avoid fights you know you can't win, creating a game over before the game is over. The only way to "wait" in a city is to repair a broken part of you train, if your train is full health you can't idle in a town until those bandits pass you have no option but to be confronted by them, lose a bunch of money or fight them. The game would benefit hugely from being able to wait in towns, even for a fee. Twice I got forced into a fight where I knew I would lose and had to restart.
Trading (outside of quests) is pretty much worthless since theres no multiplier for trading distance so you're almost always only trading between stations one stop from each other and the margins are pretty much non existant, anything with a margin above 5 gold weighs so much you can't even consider trading in it until you have an end game locomotive.
Enough negatives because I can't stress enough in text how much I enjoyed Bounty Train I picked it up on a whim and didn't put it down untill I finished it. You can see the incredible potential of this game just from playing it for 30mins. I am already eagerly awaiting updates and am very excited to see Bounty Train as a finished product.

This game is a really well done mixture of a few of my favorite games:
- FTL
- Pirates!
- Railroad Tycoon
- Commandos
- Transarctica: Arctic Baron (the elderly among us may remember)
Mainly there are three modes in this game, not counting the tutorial: storyline, sandbox and hardcore.
As you only have one game at a time with only one autosave you have a nice rogue like atmosphere where decisions count and you'll have to live with the consequences. But you get the option to restart a fight if everything goes down south, which is still buggy sometimes as restarting a fight sometimes does not reset your crew and train health or quest status.
Harcore is as harcore says and you have no option to restart at all.
Unless you choose Sandbox mode with no storyline related quests at all you'll probably stick to the necessary routes to complete your story and you'll never visit places far south as of now you always start way up north in Portland.
Placed in the onset of the American Civil War your goal is to fulfill your fathers' legacy: a transcontinetal railroad. Your inheritance: an old train and some cash. So you start out on January 1st, 1861 and have to be finished until July 1st, 1862 or all you and your father worked so hard for is lost.
However, this is the only storyline so far and it is contrary to the games' description linear, totally. Nevertheless placed in a historical setting with restrospective romantic flair it's quite compelling, as it contains elements of Pirates! (find your familiy and get rich in 10 years) and is still difficult to achieve, but tends to get repetitive even if it weren't for those damned linearity memory effects.

The most important feature for earning cash. But free trade does not work so well, as regular trade routes are scarce and difficult to come by, so you'll be mostly stuck to trade missions, offered in towns you are allied with, to earn serious cash.
As a result the game looses the kind of freedom that Pirates! offered as mission bound as you are, while trying to master the logistical challanges of picking up weapon crates in New York, delivering them to St.Louis, probably picking up a passenger in Philadelphia and dropping him off in Knoxville, after you earned enough cash from your weapons delivery to pay the fee for unlocking the route to Knoxville, as you have to go there as part of your storyline.
Consider it more as a bonus. Where do you want to go? Oh, that's (almost) my direction. Hop along, squeeze yourself in between those crates, don't stand in the way and as long as you're here, you can help put out those nasty fires during an ambush and don't expect me to pay for your injuries on drop off.
Seriously passenger transportation works better if regarded as temporarily stocking up your crew with auxillaries with random skills who can assist you during ambushes.
Steam engines need coal, that's a kind of well known fact, so here's an interessting concept/limitation to enhace the challenges of the early game. The further you go and the heavier your train the slower you travel and the more coal you need.
But what starts out interessting tends to get repetitive micromangement in the middle and end game, as coal is very cheap and the cost to fully load your coal tender are neglectable. Additionally it is still (a bit) bugged and you can only travel long distance routes with high end locomotives almost regardless of the amount of carriages und cargo you carry.
Now this is a feature we all do enjoy. Earn cash, buy better locomotives and carriages to improve your performance and earn more cash. In addition to coal consumption and pullable cargo weight this offers some serious thoughts on how to configure your train. There is a big variety of locomotives and carriages in the game for the player to choose from to configure the train to your needs. But there is also a trade off to what really is usefull concerning afore mentioned limitations and you'll probably never buy certain vehicles.
There are four factions in the game. Union, Confederacy, Indians and Bandits. Improving your factions standing with the Union lowers yours with the Confederacy. Bribing Bandits or paying off Indians improves your standing with them respectively. Failing to fullfill a contract your standing drops. You get the general idea....
In principle it works fine, in reality not. Fending off bandits somehow improved my faction standing with them, leaving me unable to attack them when needed to fulfill my quest. Also my standing with Indians and Bandits seemed to change spontaneously over time. As a matter of fact paying your ambushers is the last and least option you'll ever choose as off now you'll get no reliable long term benfits to count on. But it's good that this options exits as it can save your♥♥♥♥♥
Fruthermore as you always start out in the north you'll probably always get allied to the Union as a result of the story.
This is the FTL/Commandos part of the game but instead of a space ship and nazi soldiers you'll be shooting bandits, indians, KKK members or Confederacy soldiers out of a train. You will get ambushed a lot, really. Ambushing trains must have been some kind of popular sport back in the day. Don't get me wrong as fending off ambushers is great fun and really well done and offers a great feeling of the wild west. Really well done and loads of fun.
But somehow the attackers get carried away and always try to kill you or destroy your train. They never just rob you. Also there are still some minor bugs when attackers don't close in on your train and you have to wait until them timer runs out to continue your journey as it is not possible to reverse your train or exit it. Now those would be two features to really improve the game!
You can hire certain characters to help you defending your train and they have lots of different skills and stats in which they can be leveled. Crew composition is great fun as it can give you the certain edge you need in certain situations. Leveling them however is a random choice between three random perks and you don't fully have control on how to level them. Furthermore crew size is limited to five members, which is enough but some skills need rebalancing as they significantly are more difficult to train and you'll get stuck with low level characters. It's easier to hire certain mid to high level characters, as they don't cost you weekly/monthly wages and are always waiting for you at the same location, once you know where to find them.
Bounty Train runs really well and has only minor issues with stability, bugs or game fluidity which is a big pro. When playing you will come upon certain planed but not yet integrated features like different equipment for your crew members. I can only hope that in the future there will be more scenarios, game modes or additional content to choose from and that the variability of this game will be improved. I would even go so far to claim that I am willing to pay for additional DLCs to come as this game offers a unique and well done integration of different and enjoyable game concepts. And I would really regret to see its' potential wasted as in e.g. Cosmonautica. This game truely has a lot of potential, if improved in matters of content, balancing and variabilty as it hold some key elements to become a game that may even set standards. In its' current state it is really fun to play for about 30 hours play time, after that the replay factor declines rapidly. As off now it's not worth 25 bucks. However, you'll have to choose if you like games like this, if you want to support the developers or wait until completion or for a steam sale.

A fun quirky game thats similar to Torchlight in terms of gameplay.  Its qunitecential Swedish setting, campaign story, voice acting and dialogue is a joy to experience.
Controlling three of four different character types, all with their own core abilities (Healer, Melee guy, Tank and Tech-mage makes combat something different to normal aRPG.  It piqued my interest by offering a slightly different levelling mechanism, one which adds to the overall sense of achievement.
In addition your characters maxlevel is capped and must be purchased to go beyond a certain level.  At each level you open up booster and implant slots which enhance your characters attributes and add to their core abilities.  Which really makes your need to find sellable items and cash that much more urgent than just buying equipment.
The crafting portion is a real joy adding a diverse collection of crafting recipes and ingredients which as you can imagine are accumulated through playing .  The real positive is the combination of alternative story/setting and the tactical group combat which takes this from being an also ran dungeon-crawler to something a little different and ultimately worth a second look.

For months I kept hearing about this game from various sources, all of whom said it was emotional and moving, etc. After putting it off for as long as I could, I finally caved and got it when it was on sale. My expectations were that it would probably be another sweet, simple game that tugs lightly on your heart strings, but ultimately forgettable. This is where I say that I was wrong; Not only was it emotional, but I'm not ashamed to say that it brought me to tears by the end. Which is a surprise for many reasons, but the biggest being that I generally don't shed a tear for anything, especially a work of fiction.
All you need to know about the story is this: There are two brothers that set out on a perilous journey to collect the sap of a magic tree, which they believe can heal their dying father. As the game is rather short, saying more would likely spoil some key moments. There are some surprisingly dark tones and imagery, which at first caught me off guard, but it's clear they are not simply there to be edgy. Everything has a deeper meaning, even the controls (I will never think of the left trigger the same way again). The music is excellent and emotive, and the developers use it at the right times, with the right level of intensity. The main theme, especially the acoutic version heard during the credits, is still swimming around in my head as I write this. And It is worth noting that all dialouge is expressed in a fictional language; You won't understand what they are saying, but the characters use expression so effectively that you will begin to realize that you do.
I don't want to oversell it, but saying that I recommend this game isn't enough; It doesn't give it proper credit. It's titles like this that naysayers are clearly not paying attention to when they argue ignorantly against those of us that believe video games are, or can be, a true form of art.

For me this has pretty much been a staple for general desktop use and for playing some games that otherwise don't offer controller support whenever I'm seeking entertainment from the comfort of my own bed.
I had found it was very easy to start using right away after installation; the keybindings are preset to a very decent general desktop use and are a cinch to change in the settings interface.
While the program's first release originally wasn't entirely meant to provide controller functionality for games that lack it, I was surprised to find that most games play very well with it. I
encountered a game in the past that had issue with recognizing keyboard inputs when coming from the controller (it recognized mouse inputs fine though, oddly), but that game has since become officially controller compatible now anyway (KOTOR II), and I haven't found any other games yet that experience that issue. If there are particular games you are looking forward to using this program with to gain controller functionality, I'd recommend researching other user's experiences. Note that some games may just not play as well with a controller compared to mouse and keyboard, but sometimes you can find a sweet spot in bindings regardless and make it work out decently.
With that in mind, the addition of profile game bindings was a welcome one. Earlier in CC's life, there was only one binding profile for everything; now you can have bindings for each game that needs it, or even basic desktop programs. It is very easy to set up manually. You browse for the exe to set a unique profile to start when that program launches, and you can also create profiles based on recently ran processes.  Steam workshop provides community made profiles for games and programs as well if you would like to see if others have already perfected a control scheme for your desired game (why reinvent the wheel?)
On the topic of wheels, the program provides a keyboard wheel that is by default accessed by depressing the left control stick. I have a love/hate relationship with this; I like the simple design, but it takes a bit of a learning curve to get used to it, and even then your typing speed won't be very fast. In any case, however, controllers simply aren't keyboards. I can't imagine why anyone would expect to write paragraphs with this unless it is in practice of patience or absolute necessity. However, it generally works well for any brief bits of typing I need. Note that most games I've experiened don't jive well with the keyboard wheel, and will either not display it (though might still allow you to type), or minimize you to the desktop, but it's not hard to imagine that it acts like this when it is an overlay originally meant for desktop use.
Remember that this is for XInput devices, namely Xbox 360 controllers, and subsequently any device that can be configured to use XInput, such as with controller emulators.  So generally, if you've got Xbox 360 controllers you wish to use, you're ready to roll. If not, you'll need your controller to emulate XInput. Personally, I've been using a specialized bluetooth stack that connects PS3 controllers and recognizes them as XBox 360 controllers, and it works flawlessly with this.
Finally, note that I don't have many "hours played". I've used this well over 200 hours, I'm sure, but there's a nifty option to not allow the Controller Companion be recognized as "actively played" in Steam, which is useful if you want the actual games you play show accurate hours, and allow your friends to really know if you're actually playing something or not.
Note that I have tried other free programs before, and I can understand and do appreciate the virtues of getting by with cheap-as-free stuff, but it has been worth paying the one-time low price in terms of greatly simplifying the setup process and its overall ease of use. Just recently I reinstalled my OS fresh onto a new drive, reinstalled Controller Companion, and it was up and ready right then; no muss or fuss. Ultimately, there's potential that a person could earn more money working at least minimum wage for one hour and buying this software than spending an hour or more fiddling to get free software to work, but if you're a whiz at setting up the free stuff, it may be in your best interest to stick with that instead. When it comes to price points, it's always important to ask whether something is worth your time.
