Brothers is very much a love letter to folk tales, magic, whimsy and darkness. I can find your due problems with it -- parts that drag, parts where maintaining both brothers becomes exhausting, parts that lack the logic/throughline to have quite the power they need to. But it seems beside the point, almost mean-spirited, to have too many tight little reservations when the game has so much unfettered beauty and strangeness, when single-player co-op becomes a metaphor for family bonds. When there's nothing else quite like it, and its closest interactive cousin's probably Ico, our two lonely kids just clinging to each other. Maybe the brothers only do so much clinging, but they can't bear to be apart from each other. Try to control just one at a time for your own convenience, he'll stop, he'll call out for his brother. This is not a game about stoic independence, pragmatic lonerly questing. And that's what makes it both lovely and heartbreaking.

Phenomenal. Some games are experiences you'll never forget, and this is one of those. But let's go with the weakest part, and go from there.
The puzzles are a bit too simplistic, and as a platformer it's very linear. There's no open world exploration here. But you forget all about that, because of how strong the rest of the game is.
Gameplay: A+. You're controlling two brothers simultaneously with both thumbsticks (and both trigger buttons for actions), a mechanic I've never seen used before, and it feels wonderful. Intuitive, actually, which is doubly impressive for a brand new mechanic. The pacing is equally as impressive; there's never a dull moment in the entire game.
Visuals: A++. This game is *gorgeous*. It starts looking good. Each level you go through gets progressively more epic-looking, to the point where you're getting warm fuzzies every time you turn a corner.
Story: A+++. This game will make you cry. And it does it without a moment of actual voice acting. I can't say anything else for fear of spoiling it. But this is a game you'll want to share with people, and you can't, because it hasn't gotten the attention it's deserved. (I'm writing my first review on Steam, just to convince friends to play it!)
I cannot recommend this game enough.

Honest 10/10, has to be one of the best games ever made.
PROS
- Best TES game in terms or lore, storyline, environment, and immersion, also most challenging by far
- Magic is much more complicated than in the later TES games, you can make your own spells and basically become a God, you can also levitate, which is a lot more fun than running
- There's dozens of hours worth of in-game books, as well as a very well documented UESP section for Morrowind, which can help you on quests, character building, etc.
- The narrative doesn't feel rushed like Oblivion or Skyrim, and you are part of an ancient struggle as opposed to a melodramatic invasion
- The graphics are dated, but with MGE you can mod them to be on par with a game from the late 00s. My  modded game looks almost as good as SSE, although I use a few texture packs.
- Only a few mods can greatly update the graphics and melee combat (use the Morrowind Sound and Graphics Overhaul, or just use MGE and install your own textures like I do, although this is more difficult to someone new to modding)
- The Game doesn't hold your hand and you can't just play on max difficulty the whole time, also most enemies and NPCs are at a static level, meaning you can't kill the main boss at level 10 like in Skyrim.
- The community is still active and makes some pretty dank memes on YouTube.
CONS
- The graphics were good for 2002, but not so much anymore. A few mods can fix this quite easily.
- Combat is outdated, but can be fixed with a small mod.
- The game can be iffy on Windows 10 in my experience, but it's mostly stable (more so than Skyrim for me).
- The game has a bad max resolution (something under 1600x900, which isn't even full HD) which can only be fixed by MGE to my knowledge.
ADVICE:
- Use the Accurate Attack mod to "fix" the vanilla melee. It's an easy fix to the number one issue that turns people away from the game.
- Use the UESP pages to read up on strategies to the game to help you with quests and the like. It's a lot harder to just derp through Morrowind than Skyrim or even Oblivion.
Overall an absolute classical legend of a game. Buy it.

Welcome to my first review.
If you're reading this, then you are considering playing the game, aren't you? I hope I can give you the best overview of it.
You start out as a humanoid figure called Qbee in the tutorial. After finishing it, you will be teleported to the Overworld, the heart of CC game. Then, you are instructed to place your first realm, go to all the mines for the first time, beat your first parkour, etc... and eventually finish all the free quests. From there, you are free to do anything you want (Within the rules). You will make friends, create great things, be admired, and so on. This game has no goal, but it's your job to create your own milestones.
Not much to say here. It's not as good as those AAA games nowadays, but not as bad as many pixel games. It's beautiful, charming and relaxing, but still remains as a cubical game.
In short, there are many things you can do. You can build a dragon, build a castle, create a maze, obstacle courses, temple, anything you want! If you want a bit of a challenge rather than some building plans, you may enter pvp and try to become the last Qbee standing, play and beat the hardest parkours or just be a adventurer and explore many great realms built by both the developers and players. Additionally, you can open a shop, horde cubits, hunt rare artifacts in the mines or colllect all cosmetic items.
The downsides, however, are the grinding part and players' trends.
Grinding is a part in all MMOs, and this one is no exception. If you don't know the right way to grind or don't have the patience to do so, you will end up having no cubits (In-game currency) and thus ruining all of your wishes and plans. Fortunately, there are a few guides about it on the forum and youtube, but most players don't bother to do so. This has also led to a shift in players' trend, which now becomes shopping and collecting. Other fun activities are not abundant, and most of them you will see require you to pay to enter, which might end up becoming a scam. Talking about scams, the developers have applied numerous ways to prevent it, but 90% of the time it's the players' faults that turn them into victims. Be smart when playing, and you won't see this game as a P2W.
Why am I saying "if you're lucky enough"? Many will be there to help you if you need help, but only when you meet the right person. It's a game of chance: You will receive great support, or you will be treated rudely by some one-digit years old kid. The community overall is nice in-game and on the forum, but with some occasional fights arguments, and those annoying kids. Socializing is important in the game, as having some friends to talk to is way better than being alone. Be kind to everyone you see and pick the right friends to play with. (Good english is important)
That's all I can say about the game. There are so many things else to talk about, but it's best to leave it for you to explore. If you need help, you can add me in-game. (Same name as Steam)

Cubic Castles a Massively Multiplayer Sandbox game, using the classic blocky art style. The game had a very unique concept and to be honest it is a very good game. There are 4 regions of land (I forgot their names) and in each region you walk around and can enter different people's realms. There are also places that you can go to and gather materials and blocks to craft items and blocks.
You get a realm for free, and here you can do anything you want. Build a large base, a big parkour track, the limit is your imagination. A lot of people opened up shops to earn cubits. With cubits you can go to people's shops and purchase wands, cosmetic items such as hats, and blocks or materials. The freedom that is given to you in this game is cool. Of course, the grinding you need to do is very time-consuming, but if you really wanted to build an awesome world, you'd go for it.
I just built whatever popped into my mind. I had a large cotton farm, a crafting area, a parkour area, storage, etc. I built planes in the sky. I had so much. And that's where this game failed me. That's where my imagination went to♥♥♥♥♥♥ After 150+ hours of grinding and building in my world, a hacker came along and completely obliterated my land. No one was allowed to build in my realm except me, so the only way it happened was a hacker. All of my blocks were broken, all my loot taken, everything gone and the only thing left was dirt blocks flying in the air and random mountains of dirt. This was heart-breaking and I quit after trying to salvage what little was left.
I had heard stories of hackers destorying realms from people but I never thought it would happen to me. The game has ♥♥♥♥♥♥ anti-cheat if it even has any cheating prevention. I've logged in every once in a while just to see people's amazing realm. The population has died a lot from since I last played, but there are still some new players every now and then, and some veterans still play.
Don't get me wrong, Cubic Castles is a great game, trying to be a family-friendly sandbox game with non-violent gameplay. I'm not sure if a new anti-cheat system has been implemented, as the last time I played was about a year ago just to look around. The game still gets updates, and a lot of content has been added since I last played. If you want to try it give it a shot. Hopefully you won't have the same experience I did.

Ibb and Obb is a minimalist treasure. It is masterfully crafted to be simultaneously forgiving enough to retain novice players and challenging enough to keep those with more experience.
It's a fantastic game for couples to play. There's something quite intimate about working together to learn the mechanics and solve the puzzles of the game.
There's nothing like the satisfaction that you enjoy after tenderly guiding your lover out of a frustrating situation when you've seen a solution that they haven't, although of course it's up to you to avoid coming across as a condescending♥♥♥♥♥♥ Master this, and your sweetheart is sure to express his or her gratitude with an endless flow of sexual favours.
I suppose there is scope for the puzzles to end in bitter conflict between the players, but the worst that I have experienced is an exasperated sigh directed at the game.
The sound design beautifully facilitates this calm atmosphere. The music is a peaceful lover's caress and the wizards behind the game beautifully use this to lull the players.
I don't think of myself as someone who enjoys puzzle games, because the frustration makes me feel stupid, which in turn makes me more frustrated. The designers seem to have anticipated this, as evidenced by the calming gestalt of the visuals, the feel of the controls, and the audio.
I'm finding it difficult to think of any drawbacks. Perhaps the fact that the game requires exactly two players; no more, no fewer. But this game is focused on the dynamic of the couple. Any fewer players and it wouldn't make sense, and more and it would feel crowded.
If you have a sweetheart who is cautious about getting into co-op games, this is the one for you.

Personally, I can relate to the people who love this game, as a person who played FlyFF almost a decade ago for a couple thousand hours. It's the community and the memories that I'll forever keep close to myself, as they were an integral part to me getting through my teen years.
As well, I realize that this is another one of those games similar to those that wanted to capitalize on the "golden age of RO", when there were tons of MMORPGs similar to it (And that's in North America. There were a dime a dozen in Hong Kong and South Korea). And while it was released a few years ago, it's now on Steam, and has to compare to what we've got here in 2016. And unfortunately, it hasn't aged well.
If you want to play a free MMO, you're in luck because as of writing this in February of 2016, you're bound to find a hundred other free MMOs that far surpass this one in overall quality.
But if you're curious and wants to see what old 3D Korean Grindfests were like, feel free to jump in. It's free, after all. Unfortunately, expect the following:
- A grindfest
- A community that's close-knit, so it'll be difficult to get in on already-established ones.

This game is the same as it has always been except with updated graphics; naturally. This doesn't hurt the game as the Modern Warfare Trilogy has always been the best Call of Duty games in my opinion. If you played the original it is pretty much guarenteed you will like this since it is the same game. All in all for the new comers:
Story: The story for the campaign is solid and is very enjoyable. I became connected with the characters and really enjoyed playing as them. My biggest complaint since playing the original version is that the campaign is only about 3 hours long, so it is really short.
Gameplay: Plays like any other Call of Duty or FPS really so there aren't really any leaps and bounds making the way this game plays. Weapons are pretty standard modern day weapons. Nothing futuristic or anything like that. Controls are solid and easy to learn. If you play FPS games alot, then you will pretty much already know what does what.
Graphics: Again, this is the version of the game and the main difference of this version over the original. The graphics have been updated and look much sharper than the original. If graphics are important to you, then this is the version of this game that you will want to play. If you already own the original and graphics aren't a big deal to you, there is really no need to get this version.
Con: The only negative thing about this game and isn't due to the game it self is that you can only get it by getting Call of Duty Infinite Warfare (see my review for that game). This really should be sold as a seperate game which is really the only reason I ended up getting Infinite Warfare was to get this version of Modern Warfare since I didn't have the original on PC already. And even still, people who already own the original should just get this one for free as many other developers/publishers have done with other remasters. Why Activision feels the need to bundle this game and not sell it on its own is beyond me because they would make more money selling this on its own. Their loss I guess.
Conclusion: If you already plan on getting Infinite Warfare, then get the version that nets you this game as well. If you already own the original of this game and graphics aren't a big deal to you, then don't bother spending the extra money to get this copy.

Dustbowl is a fantastic little indie game,  that is very reminiscent of the first two Fallout games. Questlines and dialogue are well though out. Combat is turn based and solidly done, I do wish there was a point where you could see enemy HP, but overall not a big deal. It also sports a crafting system to make all that junk you find in the Waste useful. Could not recommend this more to people who like the original Fallout games or just an all round good RPG.

Dustbowl is a postapocalyptic game driven by RNG mechanics while trying to tell a classical RPG story. The art design is actually quite nice, but the actual mechanics of the exploration, crafting and especially the combat system are severely lackluster, making it a game of chance more often than not. The difficulty curve is high, but the options to develop one's character are severely limited, as is crafting, as is the amount of different enemies.
While Dustbowl isn't a complete failure, there are far too many other games doing a far better job at being an indie-survival title than Dustbowl to be able to recommend it.

I bought this game for $2.50 during one of the steam sales.  I don't think it is worth the normal price of $10 but if you can get it on sale, it is a fun little game.
There are some issues as described in other reviews.  The biggest one being the resolution issue (even in fullscreen, it is still difficult to see things).  The poor resolution is because of the artwork which is nice looking for a pixel game.  I like how there are pixel items placed in the game to find and pick up, but sometimes you'll encounter pixel art which isn't interactable (ie. a bottle on a shelf) despite the previous room where the exact same art was interactable.  These inconsistencies seem few and far between, but it is still annoying when they do appear.
The combat system is lackluster and isn't exciting in any way but the game excels in other game mechanics.  There is a food/water/rest system that requires you to find food/water (which isn't easy to come by) to maintain a healthy character.  Thus you are always considering if you want to buy more food/water or ammo/utility.  The story is fine but sometimes feels like a chore (running back and forth between the same locations).  The soundtrack is really nice but the sound effects get annoying after a while since characters don't talk.  I mute the in-game sound and play the soundtrack in the background using my media player.
While I don't see this as occuring, it would be nice if the dev added modding to the game.  This game could become really amazing if players could contribute art/mechanics/items/etc to the world.  The UI could use some improvement and a map would help a lot, but it isn't needed since the map/rooms aren't too complex to navigate.
Overall, I'd give the game a 7/10 for fun/enjoyability.  If you enjoy post-apocalyptic stories and pixel art, you'll enjoy this game for about 15 hours.

Bounty Train is pretty much a spiritual successor of 1993s game "Transartica". The idea of a "base on rails", which you can upgrade and customise is still a novel an interesting idea. The narrative is interesting enough to keep you hooked, but most people will (or will not) enjoy it due to its gameplay. As a European, not very interested in American history, I find this part the most unappealing. However, the game keeps a realistic, non-comical, tone, which makes it easier to take in.
The announced features are mostly there and working. However, beware that the difficulty in the first hours is still brutal, and the tutorial is insufficient. Additionally, the interface lacks descriptions for many core concepts. Therefore, the learning curve is pretty steep and the game requires a lot of exploration by trial and error at the time of writing. The game is functional and looks polished, but is not very accessible at the moment (not as bad as "Towns" in case you ever played that)
However, if you like trains and "rouge likes" (ergo some challenge), you'll enjoy this game.

This is a VERY long review: I played this game for a long time :D The TL:DR version is:
Yeah, its ok, its free, you can P2play it and save some time, its the kinda game you play for a couple of hours every now and then.
Long version:
I played this game before it was on Steam, so I have more hours than those recorded here.
I give H&G a VERY catious Recommend, because it has very fun moments. a WW2 version of BF P4F almost.
Pros:
Re-enact the 1939 Tour De France cycle race.
Reasonable selection of pointed and blunt weapons to apply to your enemies face. Would like more.
Get an infrantryman, use your wits, get better guns, pick your favorite, upgrade and finetune it to your personal style. Buy a Bazooka! Buy a jeep, get promoted, chose to be a Tank crewman, paratrooper, recon sniper, fighterbomber pilot (each with its selection of weapons and vehicles), or just stick it out on the ground. If you grind enough ingame credits, you can swap between the different military arms at will. Stay as G.I. Joe, buy a shiney halftrack and truck all your mates around in style (Comes with a nice siren to warn cyclists off the road).
Stealing an enemy jeep/kubelwagon and roaring up to your mates in a firefight, tooting the horn and yelling "Get in losers, we're invading/liberating Poland" (depends who you fight for).
Buy some stickey bombs and hunt players' tanks. Or better buy a nice hefty wrench and sneak up behind that tank, knock on the door with wrench, and when the cheeky bugger inside sticks his head out to see who is banging on his tincan you bang on his head with the wrench, result: FREE TANK.
Sneak up behind enemy armoured vehicles and climb on top. Ride them into battle, or shoot the driver in the face when he takes a look out of his view slit/hatch/door. Steal his car and show off to all your mates.
There are 3 factions and I have seen battles where all 3 are on the field, just as you secure the point you've taken from one lot when you get smashed from the side by another whole army :D
Then once you make it to officer you can recruit and move units of troops around the War map, a map of the EU from the UK to Russia, with the goal of winning the war for your faction.
Lots of fun run and gun to be had. Lots of stuff to see and do.
CONS:
Can be grindy if you aren't doing well. That's not noob bashing or something: until you figure how YOU are gonna get your XP, then it can be long. Capping points gives a fair chunk. Blowing up tanks gives a fair chunk. Being a half track driver gives a chunk (halftracks are forward spawning points in this). Defending a point against crazy odds gives a chunk. Every player needs to find their own niche to get promoted really and it doesn't tell you that anywhere.
Balance. Even when you pick balanced battles (cause on a War battle a faction can be fighting vs crazy odds, depends what units have been sent into the battle) sometimes you will spawn into a battle (labelled as Balanced) and it will be a couple of infantry squads being pinned/spawncamped by half a dozen tanks. Can't blame the tanks: they are trying to cap that point, it's their objective to capture, but some kind of balance would be nice, not that one team shouldn't have tanks, but give them to the other team also :D
Sniper Pros. LOTS of them. They aren't so hard to deal with but it takes TIME. Again, can't blame them, if you are trying to stop enemy advance and you have a bolt action rifle, you want to bang away from 500-600 yards for as long as you can because that's how a rifle works. Just that these punish noobs very hard, means always you are alone cause every idiot who tries to push with you gets shot before he gets far and you have to go kill the guy who did it or hes gonna do it to you aswell. Makes for a very "RUSH LIKE MAD TO BUILDINGS THEN HIDE!" strategy to many guys who aren't using rifles. Sneaking does work very well in this game btw, theres plentyful foliage etc on most flanks.
Airfield Maps. It's an MMO, but it doesn't feel like one.  That's the biggest thing in a nutshell.  MMOs generally have that vibe about them that says, "Here's a skill bar, pick some powers and use them as needed."  But Defiance doesn't do that.  It's more, "Here's a gun, go kill some stuff."  I love that.  Borderlands of course comes to mind, but it's not really an MMO.  The closest thing I can think of that even got close was
, and that game sucked.  But why did it suck?  Why does Defiance not suck?  The difference was that Hellgate gave you guns, sniper rifles, and so on, but accuracy didn't matter.  If you shot the enemy right in the face, it still did it's calculation vs. your accuracy level to see if you made the hit.  That drove me berserk to no end.  Defiance isn't like that AT ALL.  If you have the skill, if you can hit a target, YOU HIT YOUR TARGET.  This single feature above everything else defies anything bad about the game.  It is truly a single player feeling game on a multiplayer environment.  Never once have a shot a bullet and lag caused me to miss.  NEVER.  This is why Defiance is the best shooter MMO that has ever been released, that defies the rules of MMO bringing people who hate the traditional MMO experience back into the fold.  Like me.

Ok to start I will say that I expected very little, as the game is from the late 2000s, and assumed that it would be a intersting game to play through every year or so, I expected dated graphics, some minor memory leaks causing crashes and perhaps some bordom in the space stage, as I gathered from reading reviews. What came out of this more than anything, impulse buy was a game that I will enjoy for some time to come. So I bought the game, got angry at the cryptic way to activate the online mode, gave up trying to do so, and then played the game. At this point my expectations were so low I was preparing for one of the most unfinished, boring and awful games ever and preparing a refund request. then I played a bit enjoyed it apart from requiring to use two mouse buttons to proceed in the camera tutorials for ... certain stages (I use a trackpad so I had to go get a proper mouse), saved occasionaly, and got to space. then I tried to log off, and my game crashed and I lost my save data for the most recent save, but thankfuly I had saved in the civilization stage last, so I again swept through that (Crushing all under my mighty armies), and then decided to try the space stage again. then I discovered a work-around for the save deletion (save twice before quitting out of the game) and continued. I came out pleased with this game, having enjoyed the expirence of leading a group of aliens to victory against all who opposed me (and allied with some orwellian ducks along the way), the game lacks polish and difficulty in some places (I'm looking at you civilization stage), but is by-and-large, an amazing game, as long as you have a computer that can handle old, yet graphic intensive games (if yours doesn't try running in compatibility mode). I would give it a strong reccomendation at 8/10 and am impressed by how good the graphics are for a 2008 title even if there are other games with better graphics now. I would even say its one of the best games I have played, even above many FPS games and many other sandbox style games, but thats just my opinion, as i don't like most FPS games. to summerise,
8/10, don't regret my purchase, don't bother trying to make online mode work, buy if you like sandbox like gameplay, and orwellian ducks are in it so why not buy it.
I certainly think its one of the better older games out there and I hope many others continue to find the enjoyment  I find whenever I take out a epic or rogue, or destroy my competitor's nests, villages, cities, and planets while cackling manaicly.

A serious contestant for the best game of 2016. Lucent Heart is better than Half-Life 3 would've been.

Lucent Heart, what can I say.
First off, I'm one of the dedicated players who've been playing this for years and I am happy to see it on Steam. However, it didn't went on here without its struggles. Yes, it doesn't have the best graphics, best storyline or the best anything, but this is pretty old. And if you're like me, chances are, you love this game as much as the other player that you invested over thousands of hours into it. Which I did. I would say Lucent Heart is one of those games you played in your childhood and you simply fell in love with it, like Zelda or FF7, Lucent Heart gives off the same vibe and that's one of the charms of this game.
Lucent Heart is a classic anime MMORPG developed by a Taiwanese company called 'Playcoo' and it is staggeringly popular in Japan and other Asian countries, while it is not as popular in the West, it is alive and well through these years thanks to a hardcore fanbase and Subagames who've been running it. Lucent Heart not only offers such a unique storyline and visual design but is bundled with features. Unfortunately, not all of them are out yet because Lucent Heart is currently version 10.0, but regardless, it still have plenty to offer for the time being.
Many people have found their true love through this game, though i like to think it's not a dating game, the theme of this game suggest so. (Note: This game is not dedicated to romance stuff.) But people have met and even marry in RL. Good for them, but what about you, the reader? Well if you are interested, Lucent Heart have a system called Soulmate where you can sign up with Cupid NPC and find your, well, soulmate. And if you feel she/he's the right one for you, then you can marry in-game. And yes, you can marry same-sex user, hurray for equality! (In later version, you may able to create and raise a child regardless of your gender.)

I'm sure you know what these stand for. You can't have MMORPG without a little rivalry. And boy oh boy, you better be careful playing in these matches, it's pretty brutal. In GvG, guilds are challenged randomly by opponent guild according to the system and the Guilds' strength. And you play to win by most points from killing enemies or destroying their flags. Depending how the battle plays out, GvG has 3 rounds and occurs on Friday, Saturday and Sunday. Very exciting. However, if you're in a mood for PvP, there is a channel 'Underworld - PvP' where you can freely kill players outside of the towns. Scary.

While I wouldn't say it's the best feature, you are given an house at lv25 and able to decorate your own place. And if you're brave enough, you can invade people's homes in acquire special items and points, as well as rating their home decoration.

Transports is a must because Lucent Heart is big, pretty big. If you don't like walking all the way to your destination then you can always hop onto the Airship, there are five airships available to different stops and require no fees. Pretty sweet. But if you prefer riding mounts, keep on reading.

Lucent got unicorns, carriage, lions, motorbikes, rhinos and even robots for mounts. It's quite a spectacle in the town, you'd be surprise how well they fit in. You also get support from your pets, or um.. *cough*



Of course, this game also offers "pets" handsome guys.

From the start, you may think the character design choices are quite limited, which I agree. However, if you are patient and dive into the game and press B (which opens Item Mall.) You will find quite a lot of clothes, accessories and adjustments to design yourself. Personally, I love the butler set, fits me quite well I would say. But if you descend from the fires of hell, you can buy some flamboyant clothes or if you're a princess from uh- Wateverland, it got plenty of dresses to choose from. Honestly, this game have a few fashion diva and they take it to the max.

Naturally, you start out as a newbie who have yet chosen their class. Classes is consist of 4 classes, 8 advanced jobs, and have three transformations. You start out with a choice of two, Warrior or Mage. Then once you've done your part, the next transformation of class where you given an choice of two more classes and you keep on building up. Depending on the line of class (Check here for a map:
There's also another class called Phantom Warlock, which is a shapeshifter class. Which I don't know much about but hey, it's pretty cool.


You can play Solo, by any means, but it is hard. Lucent Heart is hard. After all, the game is intended for grinding-lovers audience which they spend most of the time in. Strangely enough, it is addictive even if you're playing alone. Lucent Heart is a lot more fun when playing with your friends. You can party up to 6 members and there are plenty of deadly bosses out there to take on. The gameplay isn't exactly amazing but rather nostalgic, in terms of old gaming. Even if you're not in old games, do give this a try. It is a fantastic game, and I enjoy playing it a lot.
Overall, the game is not without its flaws but nevertheless, amazing game and I'm happy to give it a long review. Annnnnd if you made it the end, pat yourself on the back for being a reasonable gamer and join me, to critically acclaimed game in its own era, the adventure of Lucent Heart.

Before I start this review let one thing be clear: I played Skyrim and Oblivion before I started playing Morrowind.
This game was, for it's time, and still is an amazing game.
It's a lot harder in terms of leveling and characterization that's for one thing.
The other thing is that during most quests you need to go to a specific place.
Normally, more like nowadyas, you could fast travel from and to that place.
Back then there was no such thing as fast traveling.
You had to go there on your own and get back on your own.
This makes exploring a majority of the gameplay.
Keep track of the roads and especially your journal.
Oh yeah the journal, that thingy that I used a lot less in Skyrim and Oblivion.
It really makes the game more immersive, like reading a storybook, but that of your own.
After all the hours I put in this game, around 125 at the time I'm writing this, I still haven't finished the main quest.
Exploring new things, learning about different cultures and groups on Vvardenfell and Solstheim is what I mostly did.
The game, getting back at leveling and characterization, is a lot more of a thing like: "What do you want to be?"
In Skyrim it was really ignorable, except for the first couple of levels, because you could always change direction.
In Oblivion it was a lot more present, finding your suitable playstyle could take a couple of character creations.
Till this very day, I have never made a perfect character in Morrowind, even though perfect characters don't really exist.
Character creation in Morrowind is in my opinion the hardest part. One little mistake and boom, your stuck with it for the rest of the game. A very good example is when I made a mage character.
I was like: "Yeah, I have so much magicka and I made 'no mistake' with choosing the minor and major skills or whatsoever. When I leveled up I saw that my health had increased with a amount so low, It wouldn't matter if I got hit with the same attack, it would still do a ton of damage or almost one hit me.
Then I realized that none of my skills would benefit in a way, that my endurance (value of 30), which increased health (with a tenth of the value of endurance) would increase. Basicly, my character would always get three health more.
To come to a short conclusion:
This game is a classic among rpg games, it really reminds you that a good character comes with good thinking and planning. Nothing is written, except in your journal, what you can or have to do. Go explore it yourself, I know I have a lot more to learn and struggle with when it comes to games like this. In the end, the choice is yours.
One last thing before this review is finished: The music is gorgeous and the atmosphere is really unique, to think that this game was released back in 2002 really astonished me when I played it for the first time.

It didn't age that well but it's still playable fine if you're willing to learn.
My personal +'s and -'s
+ Old games have so much charm
+ Can't be hero of everything. And you start at the bottom at most factions. No instant-owner/leader crap.
+ Interesting lore, if you care about Tamriel at all.
+ You can't be good at everything, and it's great to be handicapped. 'Cause that means you excell at other things and choices matter! It's always nice when choices matter.
+/- I think accuracy is pretty cute. Hitting on screen but missing because stats and formulas. It's kinda cute.
- There's walking as slow as a snail, and there's lightly jogging. Jogging costs fatigue. You can jog with no fatigue left, but your HIT CHANCE would drop 25%
- I hate athletics and speed. They're so important but if you specialise in them you'd be lacking in other areas. If you don't specialise in them, thinking you have enough patience; you don't. It's so slow.
All in all, I think it's fine. It's exhausting but it's fine. A fine exhausting game. Just be prepared for slowness. You really do 'fetch the mead' at the start, so to speak.

As others have mentioned, the game plays in a small window with a fixed resolution. So those of us with high resolution screens get stuck staring at a tiny window when we want to play this game. This becomes problematic in a number of places, the first being a door handle in the beginning of the game as you end up slowly searching for what seems like the single pixel that can be interacted with when you need to open it.
I only spent maybe 30 minutes with the game as I attempted to play it in that tiny window before I requested a refund.
Other issues I encountered:
What seemed like a bug where I wasn't given an item as a quest reward. The lack of this item made combat extremely difficult.
Combat uses one of those click twice and land on the sweet spot in order to hit the enemy (you can see this bar in some of the screen captures). Due to the tiny window, this  was somewhat annoying since it was hard to see the moving bar.
As already mentioned, some of the clickable objects seem to have single pixel detection boxes. This seems to be a bug, since other objects that are exactly the same have much larger detection boxes. If this was encountered in the first area of the game, I can only assume this type of issue will be more common further in the game.
Since it has been over a year since this game was last updated, I can only assume the resolution issue will never be fixed.
The game has an interesting concept, but it's held back by too many early on issues for me to attempt to get past the annoyances. If the Dev comes back and revamps these issues I would be willing to check the game out right now, but until then it seems like an interesting idea that was poorly implemented.

Dustbowl is basically [not]Fallout done as a graphic adventure title.  A neat idea in theory.
While not a terrible game, the execution stands in your way at every turn.  Probably 20% of event flags trigger improperly, many objects don't work (several doors that allowed you to click on them just made a noise and did nothing else), the map was changed without NPC dialogue changing ...and I haven't even touched on the frustrating play balance issues.
Also, the only way to walk faster is to boost the "speed" slider in the options... but this increases ALL game speeds, making combat more difficult and the ending occurs too quickly to read.
I played it through with ample save scumming, and was amused by the effort enough that I don't regret paying the $5 I did, but I would not recommend it for others.  Save yourself the aggrivation and just go buy an actual Fallout game.

Dustbowl is a rogue-lite RPG game, set on a post-apocalyptic world. How it got the way it is? Welp, that's the most interesting thing: not in a cliched way (not to me at least).
The game have a very unique combat system (to which some might say lazy). You basically need to hit a bar on the right spot and get the most damage done on your turn. The only problem is: its a little laggy. Yes, lagged. You press for it to stop, it won't for another milisecond. And that's what throws your whole damage into the dirt.
The movement is the same on a point'n click game, you click, the character moves. You will spend a good ammount of time clicking to move your character (you can set the Character Speed for that in the options menu, thank you game devs!). And there is a sort of "survival" thing going on, but later on it just because tiresome instead of "The Sims" like.
Unfortunately, the story-telling is a bit weird. Im 6 hours into the game, have done a TON of quests, and still I don't have a clear answer about the world, only what I read online and got from enemies. Like it is shy to place an NPC with tons of info about the amazing world Dustbowl is set. The writing isn't something amazing either, every character line sounding like they have a maximum of 40 characters on a crazy-Twitter.
The lack of a map also drives me crazy. It can be a poor one like Neo-Scavenger (or a GREATER ONE like Fallout 1-2), just give me something to use! Most of my frustration in this game is due to my incompetence of not being able to go back to where the hell X or Y place were in that world (which is not huge, but the random encounters makes it much more harder to find).
Yes. Yes, you should. If still in doubt, wait for a promo! If you like games such as Kingdom, Fallout 1-2, Neo-Scavenger or look-alikes, this one is for you. The story is interesting enough, the quests are quite interesting (although you do get bombarded with them), and you just want to see what else the game holds.
Im disappointed at how this game isn't well-known. This is a good game, makes me almost nostalgic.

I decided to give this game a try since I happened upon it on the release date and I enjoy simulations like this.  I must say, I'm very impressed so far.
You're given a nice storyline to begin with and continue from there.  The tutorial will get you familiar with the basic aspect of the game, but from there you're on your own and I like it.  This game is definitely challenging right off the bat and that is something I was looking for.
If you enjoy simulations and having to plan out almost every move from the very beginning, you should give this a try.  It looks quite promising for the future assuming the devs can keep providing updates.
Some personal thoughts/experiences:
- I feel as though the combat is almost too difficult at the start.  I found myself struggling even on the first couple of tracks out of the first town.  After a few tries I was able to figure out what needed to be done, but it was very challenging.
- I don't think you are given enough money to begin with and/or aren't rewarded enough for completing missions.  I was struggling for cash to even afford the licenses needed to get to the first few cities.
- Hardcore mode is turned on by default; I think it should be turned off
- Dialog windows could use some work, maybe separate chat boxes instead?
- After you select a target and give it a command, you need to reselect the target.  I think if you select a target it should stay selected until you escape out and/or select somewhere in the field
- Reload times are way too long
- The Perks are an interesting aspect to the game, though I think some of the power-ups need better descriptions (i.e. What does Willpower do?)
I will be playing this game again and look forward to what the devs have in store for the future.  For now, I think maybe turning DOWN the diffuculty of the battles would be a good idea in order to explore more of the game and allow for a bit more income in the early game.

HuniePop is a game that I can label as a guilty pleasure. Call me a Weeaboo all you like, I enjoyed this game for what it is, a puzzle game with girls in it and it really is enjoyble.
HuniePop starts with your character being greeted by a fairy named Kyu, you soon get aquainted with her and she teaches you the basics of dating. It is then your job(?) to go around town and go on dates with the local hotties. There are also secret girls you can find, but they are hard to find if you don't have a walkthrough or have prior exposure of this game.
HuniePop is essentially Candy Crush but handled
better. Much like Candy Crush you need to match tokens on a grid in order to gain points and thus 'win' when you match enough. Two different things to Candy Crush are passion and sentiment tokens. Passion tokens raise your passion meter which determines how many points you earn per token match. Sentiment tokens raise your sentiment which allows you to use gifts which can alter the game significantly.
When not on dates you can interact with the girls you know, you can ask them questions, they can ask you questions and they can quiz you on questions you have already asked (some questions can get really philosophical). Interacting with girls gives you Hunie™, Hunie™ allows you to buy upgrades for dates, tokens have more value, larger passion gauge etc.
- The gameplay keeps you invested for hours on end
- Each girl has their own specific personality, making them both likeable and dislikeable
- The soundtrack is amazing

TES III: Morrowind was the game that brought me into the world of Nirn and its wonderful lore.
Morrowind is a great RPG with a rich world. It has not aged well, but if you can stand the ugly graphics, animations and sounds etc. you will have a great time. Because Morrowind have so much content. Think of Oblivion or Skyrim. Except this game's world is filled with even more content. More weapons, armours, spells, and skills.
This game has a lot of old school rpg elements and I love that. How you build your character will truly define that character. Your stats will matter early and late into the game, because those early choices for which attributes to level up in the beginning will remind you throughout the entire game.
I don't need to mention the flaws of the game really, you know them already but I will mention some things that I think are truly great and which are unique to Morrowind (and earlier titles). Anyway here are some things I think are really worth mentioning when reviewing Morrowind:
-Enchanting gear: It works as you'd expect it to, but what makes enchanting in Morrowind special is that you can enchant a piece of gear and give that piece a spell. So if you equip that gear you will have access to a spell that you in normal cases wouldn't be able to cast. This is a great way of being able to try spells with the help of gear.
-Spellmaking: It is not too difficult to get into, but it's quite mid/end-game before you can really start due to costs. With spellmaking you can pretty much create any spell you want to. The only restriction is pretty much skill requirement, mana cost and gold cost. Morrowind has a lot of spells, so you can really create what you want to and unlike Oblivion the cap of each effect is really high. This means that if you want to make a spell with fortify acrobatics 10000, you can but it will cost a lot etc.
-Gear: Progression in Morrowind is quite good I'd say and as a side note, a lot of uniqe gear are placed in the world, which means if you know where a unique item is you can go get it if you want to, regardless of level. Now to one of my favourite parts of Morrowind. Your armor set can consist of Boots, Legs, Cuirass, Shoulders (left & right), Gloves (left & right) and a helmet. And what makes this more customizable? You can wear clothing beneath the armor and on top of the armor. So as a knight you can have a full armor, clothing under it and also wearing a big robe on top of all that. This again gives great possibilities for enchanting.
I'd say these are the most important aspects to mention for Morrowind. If you like the lore of Elder Scrolls, Morrowind is a great game for learning more. It is filled with lore about the mysterious dwemer, Nirn and the Daedric gods. The story in Morrowind is also quite good, definitely interesting to say the least. Gameplay can be a bit tedious at times because your movement speed is very slow in the early game and it's a big world to explore but it will improve over time. There's no fast travel, and there are no quest markers. Personally I like that, but some dislike this. I like it because you have to read your journal and truly observe your surroundings in order to find what you're looking for.
Overall this is a great game if you can see pass the flaws. Mods also help if you want to change some aspects, make the game run better or simply making it better looking. It's a hard game to get into, but give it an honest try and you will see why TES III: Morrowind is considered to be one of the top RPG's of all time.

When you first login into the world, you'll be welcomed by the rather dated graphics. Since this game was released more than 5+ years ago, this is quite understandable. The day and night cycles are implimented and some monsters were supposedly appear during a certain time (which is a pretty neat feature imo).
The community so far as I've experienced was very friendly and welcoming. Although there were very much afkers hanging around in town, when you asked for help, a lot of people were eager to offer their knowledge of the game which put a smile on my face.
I enjoy playing solo most of the time in MMOs, while sometimes I do find myself participating a few dungeon runs here and there, if the game is possible to tackle alone, I much prefer it that way. That's being said, this game is certainly solo-friendly in the early game, and is very encouraging towards team work later on in game.
This game follows the same MMO formula as the others, the questing system is quite generic with the "go here, kill that, come back and return the quest to this npc" type and would probably be tiresome as this goes on, but since I'm a casual player, this doesn't concern me that much. Especially understanding that most MMOs were designed to be played that way anyways, and this game certainly tries its best to redeem itself with some fun events with mini DDR-like game (It was called Dance Masters, I think. Correct me if I'm wrong.) and possibly upcoming trivia-type event for players to get involved in.
So, overall (as of now) I'm voting "yes" for recommending this game :)

I have over 600 games in my Steam account, and the vast majority of them are still unplayed. So now I'm dedicating an hour to each of these games and writing a series of One Hour Reviews. An hour isn't very long to judge a game on, so think of this as more of a first impression, and take this review in the spirit in which it's given. Be sure to read other reviews from players who have spent more time in the game.
One Hour Reviews #53 - Dustbowl
Dustbowl is an interesting mix of a point-and-click adventure game and an old-school RPG.  I spent my first few minutes exploring my room and picking up various items left lying around.  But the game quickly introduces it's first RPG elements as I encounter people and having conversations.  Conversations are your classic multiple choice, without any fancy branching dialog options that I saw.  It seems like most folks are there to hand out quests, so early on I ended up with quite a few tasks to help out with, on top of the main questline.
The graphics are very retro, which for the most part works just fine.  But you may be disappointed by the complete lack of graphics options, as you are forced to play in a window at a locked resolution.  That didn't really both me, but my main complaint is some of the fonts used in the game are pretty small and hard to read at times.  Thankfully the small font isn't used in conversations, so it's not something you have to deal with frequently.
The interface is fairly basic.  The screen is split into 2 major areas, with the top area rendering your character and surroundings.  In the bottom area, you have 3 tabs that you can switch between your inventory, your characer status, and your list of jobs.  It feels a little clunky but it works.  Sometimes things aren't entirely intuitive.  For instance, I tried to use a medpack by clicking on it, and then clicking on my character.  That didn't work, and I figured out later I had to click on the hand icon to use it.  It may take you a bit to pick up on how to do things.   Also little things you might expect like hitting Escape to bring up the options menu don't work.  Instead you have to click an icon at the top right that doesn't really look like something you'd expect to open a menu.
Combat is turn-based, but rather than using random numbers to determine if you hit or not, instead it plays out as a mini game.  You have 3 zones representing a miss, a hit, or a critical hit.  Depending on the timing of your click, your shot will end up in one of these 3 areas and do damage accordingly.
I wouldn't call the difficulty punishing, but Dustbowl does not do any hand holding for you either.  You have 3 bars that you have to manage, one for health, one for food, and one for drink.  You start out pretty much broke, so it's up to you to scavenge and manage your inventory well.  Also, you don't automatically heal when you aren't in combat.  You do get some health back after sleeping (once you are tired; it doesn't let you just randomly take a nap), but mostly you are relying on items to heal yourself.  When you die, your only option is to reload your last save, which thankfully Dustbowl lets you save pretty much anytime.
I spent most of my first hour running around the starting area before I ended up outside for the first time.  At this point I was presented with an overland map that felt right out of the original Wasteland game.  So I spent the last little bit of my playthrough exploring the surrounding area and getting into a few random encounters (which aren't always fights).
I had fun with Dustbowl and like it for what it is.  Some folks may be turned off by the old school gameplay, but I found it enjoyable and worth the price.

Dustbowl is a fantastic game and I was pleasantly surprised by how good it is,The storyline and to some extent the gameplay is as good as Fallout 1 or 2,
considering this is a indie title I feel that's a good sign straight way (if you liked the older Fallout titles which most people do). I cut the review into segments so you can easily find the information you need.
Story
The story is a straightforward one but it's well written and you get multiple dialogue choices with the many unique characters you meet.
The game features a good amount of main and side content, locations to explore, and some of the side quests are so well made they almost feel like
the main storyline.
Graphics
The game uses an older pixel style graphics than Fallout or some other indie games, The games interface and pixel style remind me of Maniac mansion or other point and click games of that era (although the interface in Dustbowl is easier to navigate).
Characters have well-drawn avatars and their pixel versions have mouths that open and shut (manic mansion style). I didn't like the Overland maps laggy style of movement but I understand why its done like that (most older games were this way like the older Ultimas).
Sound
The sound effects are made to sound similar to games from that time so they aren't the best but they get the job done and you begin to not really notice anything wrong with them.
General
Unfortunately character customization at the start of the game is virtually nonexistant, but you can select from pre-made avatars.
There is a large assortment of dangers, other than monsters, ghouls and other creepy enemies, such as starvations, dehydration and radiation poisoning.
If you are attacked by certain enemies you get a bleeding status effect that requires bandages otherwise you slowly lose health until you die.
There is a large assortment of weapons and equipment, from melee to ranged weaponry. Quests are here in a large abundance, both main and secondary.
Dustbowl is a fantastic game and has a friendly, dedicated developer that hasn't stopped releasing fixes and updates since release in May 2015, and at £5.99, $7.99 (roughly) you couldn't find a game with more content for such a low price, do yourself a favor and buy this now, you won't be disappointed.
Summary
Positive
+ Good graphics
+ Fantasic Story line
+ Unique characters
+ Well-written dialogue
+ Frequently updated
+ Mild survival mechanics
+ Large assortment of quests
+ Dedicated developer
+ Cheap price
Neutral
+/- Not much character customization
+/- Lag on Overland map (personal preference)
+/- Older, unique art style may not appeal to some gamers
+/- Small learning curve
Negative
- Combat system can be difficult to fully learn until later in the game (after much practice)
Overall score: 9/10

I have Multiple Sclerosis and this program has been a lifesaver for me. I can't use M/KB correctly and while even with a perfect setup I won't be playing Heroes of the Storm (or anything that isn't the speed of an RPG or 4x) again anytime soon I can go back and play tons of games and apps that I never thought I'd be able to use.
Specifically my right (dominant) hand has what is known as drop-wrist and no feeling so its effectively paralyzed. I just want to let everyone know that this is a great program not just for daily use but with some patience at setting up the binds or finding the right workshop support, this program will work magic in making basically everything have a unified easy to use control scheme.
An example would be if you are an Xbox player and love Dynasty Warriors, you expect A to be jump, X to be a regular attack, Y to be a strong attack or chain attack; etc etc, could go on but the idea is that every game now can have those general commands. I can always have A be to conform or use something in a game or be left clicking where needed. Once you get use to YOUR control scheme you can pretty much get it working for every game in some way; whether it be a hack and slash, RPG, adventure game; pretty much everyone has their priorities and then people go out of their way to create unique and maybe easier to use Workshop set-ups for games you might find out you like more.
I sincerely write this as my hand is slowly getting better and I go for more MRIs. At some point I will be able to use the M/KB just fine again for the most part but I feel like Controller Companion will always be my preferred way of using certain programs or playing certain games.
You have honestly made someone's life a little bit better with this program and I say that sincerely.
All the best - Dennis

Sorry guys, I'll be a difference on this list of reviews, I just can't bear this game, It's world may be big and countain a lot more content compared to Skyrim and Oblivion, but the system of the game itself, is the problem squared.
To begin with, the character walking speed is slow as f***, It annoys me the fact that the character is that slow, and since I didn't wanted to pay a ride to Balmora since were saving gold, my only option would be to walk, and walking, is painful.
But hey, there is running, you can make your character run by holding Shift, no problem, right? Wrong, beside the fact that the character running in this game moves on around the same speed as the normal movement speed on Oblivion, running here depletes your stamina, which you need for anything else.
The attack on the game, have a chance of missing the hit, when you begin the game and starts attacking anything, you'll be very familar to this, since most of the time you listen the missing sound. I believe that like on Oblivion, it might affect attack damage too, and probably the accuracy aswell.
The gameplay with the bow and arrow is bad, beside the arrow here moves a lot faster than on Oblivion, which is a pro, there is also the chance your attack may miss, and there's the best part, If the enemy is right in front of you, like, near enough to melee attack you, the arrow you shot will pass through the enemy as if It were not in the way! Not only that, but when you are moving, you also have a high chance of missing a shot, higher than being completelly stopped and shot an enemy. Also, once you prepare the shot on a bow, there is no way of sheathing the bow unless you shot the arrow and waste it completelly, what is an annoyance at early game, since the arrows are quite limited.
The first person camera when using a bow sometimes may give you problems to shoot, since the pose the character makes may hide part of the screen due to the character arm being on the way, so the visibility is bad, to at least have the chance of hitting an enemy, I guess you have to shoot when the enemy is around to the left of the crossair, since aiming directly in the middle of the enemy was causing most of my shots to miss.
And the magic gameplay, It's infuriating, even with light armor, yes, light armor, you have a high chance of failing at spell casting, and the magicka, the only way of restoring it is by making using Wait, and no, 1 hour is not enough to restore full mana, once It's fully depleted, at least with "Untill restored" button, my char needs to wait 7 in-game hours to restore it, and the best part, is that you must do that outside of towns, with the risk of being ambushed by either monsters or assassins, yes, assassins, while you wait for the mana to restore, since "Resting in towns is prohibited", they probably wanted to make INNs useful.
The game also seems to punish players who decide to explore the game since the beggining, since you will obviously go to some place that is not from your level, like a dungeon, and get killed miserably.
You saw someone with an axe? Congratulations, you are dead If It touches you.
But leveling shall solve it, right? Well, leveling in this game takes a lot longer than on Oblivion and Skyrim together, during my around 2 hours of gameplay, I only got 2 levels of Acrobatic, and a level of Marksman, and didn't really got near to the level up.
The dialogues of the game can lead one player to get confused, since It shows all kinds of topics you can use on the npc, beside the greeting dialogue of the npc gives you an idea of what kind of topics you can pick, but you'll most likelly keep pressing all tags to the right of the dialogue screen to see what they will result into.
When you first begin your game, the first thing you guess is "Hey, now I need some equipments to begin my adventure", since you didn't got anything from the guards, but some gold you've found on the way, you think "I'll go to an item shop and buy some equipments".
When you go to the item shop, you notice that the door is locked at everytime of the day, until after you decide to investigate, you notice that the entrance to the shop is actually on the back!! Just why the heck the devs though It's a good idea to make a shop entrance be on it's back! Couldn't it have the entrance more visible?!
And the equipments, beside I loved the fact that the game have a good number of equipments and ways of mixing them, you can even equip a robe right above your armor! I really hate the fact that when you get a glove, or even a pauldron, you need to get both left and right sides of the item, or else your character will look weird because have one side of the equipment, but not the other, no idea why they thought would be a good idea to split those equipments into left and right side, but it surelly is weird, and the weirdest fact, is that even with my char wearing full light armor and having armor rate, my character armor was still being counted as 1, what does influentiate on that? Does the armor rate even involve armor point increase?
The game also doesn't show on It's status window some extra informations about your characters, like casting failure chance, the mentioned above armor rate, or even the hit rate you have, you only have the options of checking through the game status which have a vague description of what they do, beside you may not know what part of those bonuses does, and the skills and their levels.
So, basically, this game hates explorers, at least on the early game, didn't got really far to see more of the game, even more since It tested my patience a lot, so I'll give a not recommended to it.
In case you get annoyed by the game systems, you may try to find mods to make it more playable, but at least in my case, I'm done with this.

Summary: Brothers is an engaging, fun, frustrating and immersive afternoon's fun - requiring a pad.
It's a tough thing to talk much about Brothers - A Tale Of Two Sons. The game is compact; so there's little you can draw reference to without spoiling anything, and to ruin this beautiful little tale would do the reader a great disservice. That in itself should serve as a recommendation, though it comes with several caveats.
Firstly, there is only one reason why you would logically ever play Brothers twice, and that's to get achievements. As sad a statement as that is in many games, here it's in the games' favour, as the achievements here take the form of vignettes which occur off Brother's beaten (and entirely linear) path. These brief scenes take a variety of tones and forms, and some are more enjoyable than others (of course). The merit of this approach is that the achievements enhance the game rather than detract from it, and for this Brothers should be applauded. Find all of these asides from the main tale though, and that's it - nothing more to see here.
So, the game itself. Brothers is an isometric overhead adventure, in which you guide the titular big and little brothers (who call one another Naia and Naiee in the game world's language, whatever those words may mean) around various obstacles on their journey to find a cure for their ailing father. As we have come to expect, the game and soundtrack are both beautiful, with a visually realised and aurally rounded world waiting to be explored. The manner of exploration is probably the most talked about and easily discussed mechanic of the game, which to summarily recap, involves simultaneous control of both brothers. On a standard gamepad set-up, the left stick controls the big brother, right stick the little brother, with left and right triggers serving as each character's action/interaction button, and left/right bumper rotating the camera. This control scheme may be both the game's key draw and most off-putting mechanic depend on how you personally handle the remapping of ingrained controller use - the operation is fairly fluid and has a gentle enough curve to allow you to get used to it, and I personally found the system engaging and enjoyable, but I can see the same aspects frustrating and annoying many gamers.
Nonetheless, overcome the fact that you WILL at times be constantly running one brother into a wall while the other calls out to his counterpart for no reason, simply because the little brother is positioned to the left of the big brother and your mind has once again mapped the left stick to the left character and vice-versa, and you have a wonderful ride ahead of you.
And you will need a controller. Yes, the game has keyboard controls. Be aware however that the game itself will warn you that it is designed, specifically, to be controlled with a pad. On a keyboard certain tasks requiring rotation of both thumbsticks simultaneously... do not map well. I can't honestly recommend the game to anyone without a controller.
As to the story, events and specifics of the world - they should all be experienced for oneself. So long as you have some sort of empathy within you, this is a great little journey which will draw you in fully for three to four hours. The puzzles aren't particularly challenging at any part, there's no choices or branching story lines - and you won't mind. It's refreshing how streamlined and conservative Brothers is with it's mechanics, puzzles and set-pieces, and it deserves to be played both for and because of these aspects. The tone, whist initially whimsical, darkens considerably, to the point where I'd advise against playing the game with younger children. To give it a cinematic comparison, it starts off in Jim Henson's Labyrinth, moves into The Never-Ending Story, and ends... not joyfully. However; I wouldn't change a thing about it.
It is also very worth saying that just because you'll see the entire game in one or two play-throughs, it is still extremely re-playable and enjoyable each time. I fired up the game to check out the keyboard controls while writing this review and I felt an urge to play again immediately, which would make a fourth run at the game.
This really is a beautiful, innovative and rollicking yarn which asks for very little from the player and gives a ton back. The only hold-ups are the aforementioned potential control frustrations, and for those to whom it's a factor, the price. Not wishing to seem ♥♥♥♥♥rdly, for your average player, £12 for a three-hour game isn't great. When you take into account what you get for that price of entry, I'd have to say that yes, it is worth it, but I can't say I paid that for it as I picked up a cheap key. At half price this game is an absolute steal and should be purchased without reservation, at full price, give the points raised here a little thought before committing.

Brothers is a very *significant* game. Here is what I mean by this...
It is clearly indie, it is not long, and it is not complex. It is also a seminal artistic work, in that it attempts to use a unique aspect of video games - control - to convey story and impose emotion into the audience. This is, quite possibly, a feat never before attempted, much less achieved.
A number of analysts have also praised this game as effectively conveying a certain sense of melancholy to the user. I adore games that do this - Syberia, for example, is one of my favorites of all time - and eagerly waited for this to happen here. But it did not, and this is due to what, to me, is a fundamental flaw in this game - voice acting. It is, essentially, that of the Sims - the characters convey actual message through gestures, and speak nonsense and names.
Now, it could very persuasively be argued that NOT relying on dialog would be a strength of a narrative - all the more reliance on visuals and controls-actions dependence to convey a message, right? I agree with this; in fact, if there was *no* voice acting at all in this game, to me personally, it would have benefited tremendously. As it was, while the nonsense spoken lines were read quite well (if they were intentionally written, and if not, they were very well-improvised) - but the fact that they were still nonsense was a massive immersion breaker. I can relate to a mute, I can relate to a deaf character with an expressive face... but I cannot relate to a Sim.
This particular aspect of the game drastically reduces its quality for me, although if it does not break immersion for someone else, they will love it even more. However - regardless of quality, the significance of this work is fundamental; it is a shining example of highly flawed and imperfect art... from which, hopefully, future artists will learn to create more perfect and more complete masterpieces. Which I do look forward to seeing - and I urge you to try this game, if only to be informed when those masterpieces to come about.

I picked this up during a Steam sale, and for what I paid ($5, I think) it was fun enough. It's a top down real-time RPG, you can have up to three members in your party and party members are recruited by class (Berserker, Tank, Controller, Healer). The novel twist to this game is the class mods that allow you to tweak how your ability work.
So while each character has only two skills shared between all characters of that class, how they function depends on the class mod you slot into them. So say your controller has a slow field, you can throw in a heal mod to make that slow field slow enemies and heal party members, or a shock mod to make it slow and shock enemies, or a [stat] buff mod to buff team mates. And so on. It's novel. And while the game is original, I found the story to be unengaging. It's relies on a self-depricating Scandinavian sense of humour which seems to be popular (Dungeons of Dredmor anyone?) at the moment. Worth getting if you're bored and it's cheap.

DISCLAIMER: Most of my in-game time was spent a non-Steam version, thus my low hours listed here on Steam.
Color Assembler, developed by Purple Nebula, is a brilliant atmospheric puzzle game that will both calm your senses and sharpen your brain.
As seen in the trailer here on Steam, the gameplay consists of linking together mutliple colored spheres through one of 8 different filter shapes, which all influence the source colors differently. The goal is to match the color of the target shape on the far right side of the screen. What starts as a simple exercise quickly becomes a true mind bender as the player needs to eventually start linking color spheres to multiple filter shapes to arrive at the correct shade.
Although the challenge ramps up quickly, the atmosphere of the game helps the experience to remain a mostly relaxing one. The design and execution are fantastic, and anyone up for an atmospheric yet challenging puzzle experience will feel right at home.

At the time of this review (July 11th, 2015) there are, unfortunately, still a few bugs. The worst ones I've encountered are:
- Radiation sometimes fails to wear off when leaving a radiated area, resulting in inevitable death
- Combat occasionaly freezes with the character readying his weapon, the combat music starting, but no enemy appearing
Both of these are game-breaking. To circumvent these, always save the game before entering a new area, and from time to time when travelling the wastelands. Keep more than one save and rotate them.

If you read the other negative reviews for this game you'll see a bunch of people complaining that you can't run the game fullscreen, or that you can't resize the window, or other things like that. All is untrue, but it's not entirely their fault: you need tomanually run the AGS setup exe in the game's folder to change that stuff. However, once you do so you'll still be disappointed because this game is awful.
Graphically it looks oldschool, but the combat is not oldschool and that's the part that ruins it. Fighting enemies is done by pressing attack, then timing when to press it again so you stop a meter on the right spot. Then the enemy will attack you in turn, which you can't do anything about, and repeat forever. Every enemy is the same, except for amount of health and damage, and every encounter is mindless and boring while at the same time requiring perfect timing on your part in order to always do critical attacks, because if you don't then you'll die. There's not enough healing items to deal with anything but perfect attacks, every time, because you can't mitigate enemy damage through your own skill or anything and it's just an endless damage race. Better hope you don't get lost in a dungeon cause the enemies respawn but health items don't! Infinite fun!
Basically, just go play Fallout or something. This is terrible and not worth your time.

After I put more time into the game I'll update this review, but at first glance...
Dustbowl is a hardcore 2D survival point and click with similarities and throwbacks to classics such as Wasteland/Fallout and Metro 2044. The game is simple, but has a lot of great features such as multiple quests, really great art, a world map to travel and explore, crafting, and dialog choices.
I found the UI layout to be mostly straight forward and after some deductive clicking around I was easily able to understand the inventory management system which was appreciated since the game does not have a formal tutorial (though in the menu there's some poniters for starting off).
Overall, I feel the game is very original and well worth the money as it can really suck you into a time pit.

Regardless I still enjoyed the amount of exploration the game offered, with many more locations available than I would have expected. Even outside of the main quest line you can find loads of other missions and places to search for loot.
To be fair though there are plenty of bugs to be found and your actions don't seem to impact the world very much, aside from what you do during the final part of the game.
Still I enjoyed the game and would like to see more. 8/10

I really want to enjoy this game. This game is basically a different take on Fallout but instead of a turn/grid-based strategy RPG it's more based around point-and-click style wandering and a minigame of a combat system. The game looks great in terms of pixel art. The intro and the characters are interesting. The game is a huge homage to Fallout in my opinion but I Can Not Stand the combat.
The Only problem I have with this game and the Only reason I haven't played more than two hours is the combat system. The entirety of combat is just a slow-paced meter minigame where a line slides across a bar and you have to stop the line as close as possible to the center to get a hit in. And enemies will randomly spawn in rooms that you've already gone through so if want to backtrack to another room because you found a fuse for a generator you have to shoot down new enemies. And it's not like you get experience or anything from killing enemies. All you get is some random drops and the Priviledge to continue playing the game. It's terrible.
If the combat is updated to be quicker or something is changed then Stellar, I'm gonna not stop playing this game. But right now this second I can not recommend this game unless you're an ace at the game's minigame combat system. That's the Only thing wrong with this game.

(Disclosure statement: In the course of playing the game and interacting with them in the forum, I have become friends with the developers and somewhat of a beta tester. Keep that in mind)
The Atmosphere first of all is something that I look for in all my games. Dustbowl has the same mystery that the zone in S.T.A.L.K.E.R. (albeit to a smaller scale).

Combat is simple to learn but difficult to master. It will quickly become second nature to score critical hits, but the true skill comes from heat/heart shots. You will learn that each part of the body may or may not be armored and you should  make certain to take note of that.
Locations on the map will quickly draw you to the extreme edges to find out the secrets of the Dustbowl. It gives a similar feel to when you leave the vault for the first time in Fallout 1 (or the camp in Fallout 2): Pick a direction and start exploring.
The story right now does feel a little condensed, but there are plans to expand and flesh it out in the near future (speaking from late May '15). But the plot and quests that are set in place now are solid.
Dustbowl, to me, is a great game with plenty more to come in the future.
Addendum:
Now that the story has been completed, I've enjoyed the added aspects of the story. I won't spoil anything, but It's worth experiencing the little nooks and crannies now,
