Summary:
Not a complete waste of money for the now drastically reduced price of $10, or $5 on sale. Not so much bad as mediocre, with the scent of developer neglect.
-----------------
Defiance certainly tries to stand out. A third person shooter MMO is enough, but then you have the TV show tie-in. There are no classes to speak of, leaving you to shoot with whatever you pick up. There are no rows of hotkeys to build up. There are dynamic events across the map, albeit a feature they transplanted from Rift.
Unfortunately it all falls apart. The third person shooting is competent, but it gets old fast. The developers failed to turn class-less gameplay into a virtue, instead rendering everyone identical with exception to minor cosmetics. The game might be enhanced if it included more abilities and encouraged specialization in some weapons. Then there are bugs, occuring most commonly when two people try to complete the same quest at the same time.
The real problem though is that there is no sense of achievement. Levels pass by unnoticed, because the only effect you see are some minor improvements in stats. The only gear you can get are guns, so even cosmetics are underwhelming. The only modes of movement are by foot or by car, and since every car is dipped in the same vat of rust, you won't find much appeal there either.
The final nail is that the idea of this as a tie in series is a joke. You take a mostly story based Sci-Fi show and turn it into a shooter MMO, where all the world's ailes can be solved with copious amounts of bullets? That doesn't work.
The developers don't seem much intent on improving the game, but since fixing the problems would require a massive overhaul, I don't blame them. At least they lowered the price to $10 and don't have any subscription fees. That's why I give this a tentative thumbs up. If you watch the show, or need something to fill the time, you might find something to like, despite all my niggles.

Morrowind is one of the best game of its era. The stories told are fresh and original, the world is bizarre and alien - and huge - and the experience is much more immersive than one would expect from a game this old.
Now, not everything about the game has aged too well: the graphics weren't all that impressive even back when the game was released and the combat is archaic with its heavy reliance on random generated hits and misses based on weapon skill. There are also many other things about skills and leveling that us modern folk would call unbalanced and if not broken, at least annoying - for example, one has to grind skills that raise endurance early in the game to get the maximum health bonuses. Also, walking is painfully slow and the constant fog tends to make it hard to navigate.
Most importantly, though, the vanilla game has a tendency to crash and catch fire at the worst of times. Seriously. This is an old school Bethesda game. Friends of the vanilla game can expect random crashes once every few hours or so.
Fortunately, these days there are plenty of mods for fixing literally all of the above issues and making the game appear at least half a decade younger. This is good news, because without mods, I wouldn't recommend this to anyone but the most hardcore vanilla purists.
Fans of the Elder Scrolls franchise, I absolutely recommend this game, but be prepared to spend a lot of time modding if you wish to have the best experience.

I decided that I would write my first (ever!) review on Steam for controller companion. This will be a short one.
TL;DR: 9.9/10 absolutely fantastic, controller users, purchase immediately.
The purpose of this software is to bridge the mouse/controller gap, much like a Steam controller would. And to that end, it works perfectly. This is ideal for 'couch gaming' or for those of us whose computers are within reasonable reach of the bed - you can easily cruise through videos and webpages without ever going to the computer itself. In the past, I had accomplished this with very long mouse+keyboard cords, but I would have to say this is preferable.
Pretty much everything has been thought out here, with shortcuts mapped to logical places and an easily accessible help guide to rectify any misunderstandings that may arise about the controller functions. I might go so far as to call its design 'perfect' in this regard, or in other words: I've been using it for twoish weeks, and am finding new ways to be impressed with it all the time.
The only weakness of controller companion, if you can call it that, is its inability to replace the functions of both the mouse and keyboard. That's not to say that it doesn't try admirably, indeed, it does. And the keyboard popup is beautifully designed, to the point where sometimes I bring it up just to see it. But just due to the physical limitations of the controller, it can't be a keyboard replacement. I don't consider this a flaw because the developers did their absolute best to bridge the gap, and they really did quite a nice job at it, considering.
A final note I'd like to make is that controller companion handles alt+tab beautifully. You might've thought that a software which essentially has to register a connect/disconnect as it shifts the input between 'mouse' and 'controller' modes would have some fudge ups, but I've encountered none. And when I say that, please understand that I'm alt+tabbing like 50-100 times daily if I'm gaming. It has never, ever, had an issue. It's glorious. I've come to really like the USB connect/disconnect sound as I tab around-- it just reminds me of what a great software this is.
For $3, it's a heck of a lot of bang for your buck. Consider all the other things $3 would buy, and then consider that this thing offers far more convenience than any of those things. The only hassle I ever encountered was needing to find a way to be "in-app" long enough to post this review (since it runs in background). This is, of course, not the dev's fault. Do I recommend it? Yes, absolutely I do.

This program works great. I don't use it as a mouse+keyboard replacement but it is competent enough after messing around with some Windows settings to make text more readable.
What I use this program for is playing old games like Blood Omen 2, games that control horribly with mouse+keyboard but don't work well or at all with new controllers.

Sometimes I like playing my games on the couch with a controller, Controller Companion makes the transition from desktop to couch much simpler.  I have it start when Windows boots and run it in the background, so when I want to just kick back with controller in hand there is nothing additional I need to do besides turn on the controller.  There has been a steady stream of updates, and good communication from the developer as well.   It is well worth the full asking price, and I would recommend it to anyone who uses their computer from their couch.

Edit- (Yea, I'm not doing my traditional reviews anymore, takes too long to type out).
I must start out by saying that I probably have upwards of 3,500 hours in this game, maybe more, its just an estimate. But I have been continuously playing this game since it came out in 2008.
Spore - a God Game - comes in 5 major stages throughout its 'story mode' proggression. Each stage gives you a certain card at the end depending on how you played during that stage. Each card gives you a perk for the future stages and decides which of the 9 archetypes (there is a tenth one but it's only for when you start a game on the final stage) you'll be once you reach the final stage.
Now let's talk about:
-
Hell, I've owned the Origin version of this game since the year it came out. And I'm obviously still playing it to this day.
Even when you think you've just gotten tired of Spore, about a month later (at the most) you find yourself with a nostalgia boner about a mile high when you see the slightest reference to this game.
-
Very well made, and perhaps the biggest reason why you'll get that nostalgia boner.
This game ALMOST literally has infinite replay-ability. When you feel you're running out of ideas; look up Parky's "Random Spore". It adds a fun factor in the sense that you have no control over what your creation will look like, or what archtype it'll be.
Spore took the tag "God game" to a new level, while also allowing a feeling of being the creature as well.
The titles says it all. I highly recommend you get BetterSpore, choose whatever part-adding mods to your own desire.
- Crashes occaisonally, which can be extremely frustrating if you don't save often. Of course, that's your solution is just to save fairly often. People are saying that the Steam version crashes more than the Origin version, but it my personal experience it crashes less.
- The game is made by EA. I say that the Base game is worth full price, but you can get it on sale if you want. Creepy&Cute is purely optional but makes for insanely better looking creatures. However, it is not worth an additional $20. I bought it half off and I'd barely say it's worthh that much. Suit yourself though. Now for GA, I've never owned it but it gets mixed reviews. It's up to you again. Just be careful what you buy cause this♥♥♥♥♥♥is all owned by EA.
Spore is an amazing game, I can't even comprehend why you wouldn't buy it. This game you will be with you for life, and the gameplay is insanely fun. On top of that, the minimum graphic requirements for Spore are so low you could run it on a toaster, so never worry about not being able to run it. All in all, this game is a
, even if you somehow get bored with it and only play it for one playthrough. It is an experience that cannot be missed, and actually has very few flaws. It's a solid 9.5/10 for me.

If you play from your couch and don't want to have a mouse lying around, you need this.
I have my PC in the basement but play in the family room upstairs.  Initially I depended on Big Picture to navigate but it has some drawbacks:
- games that first load a launcher and require a mouse to start the game
- when a game crashes to the desktop or Big Picture itself goes awry (which is not often), you're left hanging
- with dual monitor/TV setups and A/V receivers in the middle, the image would often switch to the monitor in the basement unexpectedly for whatever reason
I used all sorts of work-arounds for the problems above but still found myself getting off my butt and going downstairs when something went wrong.
I have PGP which I use for games that don't support controllers, and it has a so-so background Windows profile that can be used to navigate.  However, that had its own problems and I could not count on it reliably.
I decided to try Controller Companion and life is so much easier now.  It all comes down to the level of integration it has right off the box, unobtrusive presence, and usefulness of the commands that are bound to it by default.  I now have it set up to launch with Windows and I never lose control of my computer with my xbox 360 controller.  Incidentally, this is why my play time with this game appears so low.  I no longer launch it through Steam because I always have it on.  I actually had to launch it a few times through Steam to register the minimum 5 minutes required to post a review.
An example of a feature I love is being able to switch screens with a shifted shortcut.  This is extremely useful in my case.  Controller Companion stops emulating your keyboard by default when switching to fullscreen mode so as not to interfere with the game's native control option.  You can override this behavior with a key-press shortcut while in-game, which is handy for the occasional title that requires an alphanumeric entry at the beginning (player name in Skyrim, for example).  You even get an awkward but effective letter entry method for simple naming and such.  To top it all off, even though its default configuration is extremely useful, all inputs are highly configurable.
This has to be the best app you can get to retain control of Windows with your gamepad.  The folks that put this together really did their homework to anticipate what their users would need in such an app.
Highly recommended!
Note:
I would not recommend it as a replacement for PGP or similar software for games without gamepad support because those programs have per-game profiles already established, making them a much more convenient choice.

This program is amazing! Not only can you use in your web browser or on your desktop, it even works for mapping controls in games. It let's you have different control set-ups for individual programs and it automatically switches when you open a program. Mapping buttons (or multiple button combos and mouse movements) is a breeze with the simple interface. Plus, by using the back/select key you enable the second function buttons, an extra 13 buttons that are great for the surplus of controls found in PC games. Also typing is noticeable better with the spiral keyboard than the on-screen keyboard method that you would see on an console (still not the best for long sentances but great for short searchs such as Netflix titles) This program can perform the same funtions of programs like XPadder and Joy2Key for half the price and the convience of being avaliable on Steam as well as working for both Xbox and Play Station controls and most others. It also runs in the backround and pratically uses no CPU or RAM to run.
I would recommend this to people who just want to use controller for their games, want a remote for media apps (Netflix), and can't wait/want a cheaper alternative for the Steam Controller.

"Free to play" is bordering on false advertising here. Most of the content is locked away behind a paywall.  And I don't mean cosmetic items on doo-dads to make you level faster. Most of the actual CONTENT you have to pay for. It's free to play in the same way WoW is free to play... you get to play some beginner content, and then you have to start paying to continue.  If you don't pay them at least $5 to upgrade your account to "premium", you are basically on your own to play a trial. Even if I wanted to give items to new players that are free to play (which I do), I can't, due to the very restrictive limitations on free players, and even premium players.
So, assuming you pay... is it a fun game? It varies mission to mission. Some mission mechanics are downright idiotic, with no fix in sight (Stompa in HH... players will know what I'm talking about... or even Paradox Wave for that matter), while others are reasonably satisfying to run (Desecrated Cathedral is a good 4-man mission).  But the learning curve is STEEP.  There are many ways you can fit your character, but only a handful of correct ways. Many players have been carried all the way up to the latest tier (currently tier 7), only to have to come to terms with their utter lack of understanding of the game, and are now expected to perform. Be prepared to suffer through many unsuccessful raids as you try to progress. And don’t even bother trying to progress a villain character at this point… the villain side is all but dead.  They were going to have cross-faction mission support on the last update, but it was cancelled at the last second… that leads me to the final point…
The biggest issue with the game at the moment is support. Since Daybreak took over from SOE, support is now cut way back, and certain employees maintain clear grudges against players who raise issues that they would rather not deal with.  Both myself and the youtuber “MUD2MMO” encountered this issue with Ted Stone, aka “Mepps”, the Community Manager. When raising awareness for issues with Game Update 47 earlier this year on the DCUO forums, we were both banned.  After a few weeks passed, Mepps admitted to the problems we rose, but never apologized or repealed the bans.
Verdict? Pass, until it's verified support has improved.
***Sept 1,2017 update***
Don't even bother installing. I've uninstalled it today.  Late last year they introduced Time Capsules. Many skill points (a big determinant of your stats) are locked up in these, costing hundreds in real world money to roll the dice at getting, and/or spending tens or hundreds of millions in game to get. That was bad enough to chase off most of my old friends from the game. Then, they tried to "make stats matter" again, and instead made older group content nigh impossible for those leveling up, and even those at end-game, ruining the feeling of being a powerful superhero.  Along with that, the biggest, baddest "OP" items in the game, with the best stats, had their stats flattened to their combat rating, making them nothing special anymore.   Then... and this is the straw the broke the camel's back...they lied about returning back to a 6 month cadence for major releases. Episode 28 was released on June 1. It's only been 3 months, and today they annouced that on the 20th, Episode 29 with be moving the combat rating up again. For those not familiar with the game, there are elite items that give set bonuses, and they take a while to farm. Even if you did not fail to complete the pair of elite raids every two weeks (the most often you can run it without paying for resets), it would take you, with the current episode 28 DLC, almost the entire 6 months to get the full set... and that's very unlikely, as one of the elite raids (in this case, Ultimate Soldier Elite) is harder. That means to get the full set before the next DLC makes it obsolete, you have to spend big bucks on replay tokens.
The time capsules, together with the accelerated schedule, is clear evidence they have given up on catering to all but the biggest addicts in the game.  If you are not prepared to drop $100+ each month above and beyond the subscription fee on Time Capsule stabilizers and replay tokens, this game is not for you.

Everyone might have played turn-based strategy games like XCOM or Disgaea 5. Visuals are different bu,t yes the concept is still the same. Player has to control certain characters and have them do certain actions each turn. Insidia is a similar game developed and published by Bad Seed, and the game is currently available as Beta on Steam.
Insidia is really limited in terms of game modes, as it is still in beta phase, so we don’t know what to expect in the full release. We tested the game with AI as we were not able to find many players to play with online. The game only has either online play against player or against AI.
Insidia starts with player selecting the team of 4 characters, and make sure of what kind of team build player wants, as each character has a different class, either tanker, assassin, specialist and all. Once the player selection is done, the game will start. Player has certain amount of time to make the selection of what they want to do with the champions. All the champions need to be deployed before we can use them, and person can only use one character in one turn. Once the selection is done, there is movement execution turn and in the end it is the combat specific actions which will taken care of.
A person cannot move same character in consecutive turns. The objective of the game is to take over the energy portal. And use the cannons on the center to fire at the enemy base. The champion needs to stand on the specific position to have cannon fire. Any of the structure gets destroyed by the cannon, champion can be made use of that gate specific gate to sabotage the base, and this will cause victory.
Insidia needs to be played strategically and have to use the skill of each champion to win the game. Sometimes the game can be finished faster, sometimes it can even take an hour to finish. The graphics of the game are so far simple and environment feels like Overwatch a bit, with all the textures and color scheme.
The game still has a lot of potential of improvement as it is still in beta phase, some things are missing such as character development and we feel disconnected with a few characters. It is not exactly clear why everything happens at first. After one game of playing through for a long time was able to get an idea of what is going on.
I would rate Insidia as 7.5 stars, as for the beta, because it is still unclear and less game mode to play with, looking at it as beta, I am sure there will be a lot of improvements that the developers will do for the game, and hopefully full release will have a lot of different additions to it.

I enjoyed this game immensely, would recommend it to anyone. The game's one misgiving is easily out shined by the game's over all fun and awesome style. The pixel art is great, and the ambient sounds are generally pretty good. The combat itself is simplistic but not easy, and it has a certain rhythm to it that really works once you get used to it.
The game very much does not hold your hand and early on its easy to wander in the 'wrong' direction and get into trouble. (This isn't a bad thing!) After I was forced to restart I found my second attempt at the game a lot easier, once I knew where things were on the map, but I definitely felt like I had earned it. (It was awesome to make my own map on paper, haven't done that in years.)
That does bring up my only gripe with the game. The developers using a particular engine called AGS, and apparently every time they update it corrupts all previous saves. This isn't really acceptable in my opinion. The developers recommended not updating until you were ready, but like many people, I have steam set to auto-update.
Despite this, I still recommend the game. The game is short enough you should be able to complete it between updates.

Open world... Checked! Science Fiction... Checked! Great graphics... Checked! Fragments of RPG... Checked! Good idea connecting MMO game with TV series... Checked! I could finish here... but i WONT.
Lets see...
Open World: It is open world but to survive i further areas you HAVE to gain some money + exp and the fastest way to do it is to do the Main Plot Missions, which are boring. So the open world... There are some group events, big group events and... huge group events. The small ones are repetable (the arkfalls those small ones). The event can occure even 3 times in 10 minutes in exact same location. The big group events are base defences with several waves of AI foes, each wave "harder" than the previous one. Its not quite like it though. After 3 or 4 waves the place is swarming with players so killing all enemies is a piece of cake even for new players. You stand, you shoot, you reload, you throw granade, you shoot, you reload... And thats it. The huge group events are more rare, they happen once per 1.5 maybe 2 hours. Those are just series of small ones (arkfalls) ended with a boss... And again the boss is no challenge couse the place is swarmed with players. Thruth be said... the game is no challenge at all.
Gread Graphics: The textures are smooth, the terrain is so lovely, you can go sightseeing... Unfortunately it seams that earth is attacked by clones of bandits, hellbugs, and other evil spawn. You can almost feel the Kamino Probes...
Fragments of RPG: This will be fast. The skilltree is so unballanced you can't even imagine. And the "traits" you unlock... I can't tell the difference after adding skillpoints....
Good idea connecting MMO game with TV series: Lets see. Developers said that the TV series will be strictly connected to the events in-game, I even watched whole season of Defiance to check that out. And guess what... The show is awful, and i couldn't see ANY connections between the game and the episodes. The only thing is we meet the poor TV series characters... poorly acted... with poor AI... with frustrating lines and story wich is poor too.
In conclusion this is poor, not challenging, boring, frustrating and VERY over advertised game. I do no recommend it, unless you're a masochist.

The game is short and depends on the main mechanic of controlling 2 characters at the same time.
One with each analog stick and each brother also has one action button.
It's simple. The puzzles aren't that complicated at all, but they are amazingly clever on how they play up the simple nature of the controls. It's mechanics also purposefully serve as a narritive device through the puzzle solving and both characters rely on one another to progress on their journey.
This game also does a superb job of telling a story through the gameplay. No dialogue whatsoever.
Yet it is a powerful and amazing adventure with epic scenes and harrowing moments.

This app was a great idea.  I didn't think a controller would be able to be used effectively as a mouse or keyboard input, but these guys really put some time and thought into their software  The result is a great seamless environment for playing games and interacting with Windows without having to put down the controller or pick up a mouse.  I'd say its a good temporary keyboard replacement too, but only if you have pretty short things to input.  Also, the option to use the controller as a mouse in games is great, especially casual games I like to play from the couch.
Another benefit I'd say is that I don't get any soreness or cramping from continually using a mouse.. the controller I have (Logitech F710) is so much easier on the hands and wrist.  Not that I'd give up the mouse for an FPS or RTS game of course, but it has its uses.
Things I'd love to see implemented:
- Inheriting the base profile settings for all new profiles created.  By this I mean, everytime I reconfigure the base profile, I'd like to see those changes propagated to each individual profile where I hadn't specifically remapped a certain button or back+button combination.  This could be done with some 'inherit' option in the individual profiles
- Remapping XInput controls for games that don't have configuration options.  That would make another selling point for this app, although I'm not sure if its even possible without hooking XInput.
Anyway, great app. The one thing Steam was missing to make couch gameplay a reality. (and I'm saying this while owning a wireless keyboard and mouse!)

I find it hard to put into words what makes this game so special. It isn't a graphically taxing game, but it has amazing visual appeal.  I found myself taking frequent screen captures because the world offers so many "Did you see that?" type of moments.  The soundtrack is fantastic.  This game will take you around 2.5 hours to beat, depending on how many secrets you're looking for. A second playthrough won't offer much unless you're looking to clean up the secrets you missed the first time. Most puzzles are pretty easily solved but good enough to make you think for a minute without being frustrating.
You need a controller to play, and that's really what is so amazing about this game. Without trying to give any spoilers, this game uses its control scheme to set up a tactile feeling of loss that resonates more than anything I've experienced in any other game, film, or piece of music.
Would I buy it for $15?  Probably not.  But at $5-$10 this is completely worthwhile and one of the most unique gameplay experiences ever (and I've been playing console and PC games for 30 years).  If you liked Journey or Shadow of the Colossus, you'll love this game.
Highly, highly recommended.

I should mention, first of all, that I am new to shoot 'em ups, this is my first game in the genre.
It is indeed a fun game. The patterns are exquisitely complex, and they often combine when having more than one enemy type on screen, leading the player to manuever extremely carefully in these scenarios. Obviously, there are some tools to ease survivability. Nevertheless, it provides quite a decent challenge. I still haven't played through the rest of the levels, I've only played through two. I recommend playing on Easy or even Normal for only a couple of levels, then playing the rest of the game (and replaying already completed levels) on Hard, since that's when the game truly tries to stop you in your tracks.
The only downside that I did encounter was the fact that, at first, the game's framerate would be halved (from 60 FPS to 30 FPS) occasionally, something that usually should not be a problem, except for the fact that the enemies and projectiles' velocity is tied to the framerate. Ergo, when the framerate lowered, everything else slows down. This, however, was solved by reducing the resolution and disabling texture smoothing.
Not just that, but I am the only one suffering from this issue. I've been asking around, and low-end desktop and laptop computers can run this game just fine, always at 60 FPS. So that's not a problem.

Defiance is a Third Person Shooter action game with MMO elements. It features some fairly well done combat mechanics (namely, moving and shooting is pretty robust) and a full campaign. I've probably burned around 85 hours on it by now, and have a pretty high level character.
That being said, Defiance has a lot of problems that I can elaborate on.
1. Combat: The game can go from laughably easy to incredibly hard based on the drop of a hat. Wide, open free roaming environments can lead to long range combat to reach an objective, but then upon reaching the objective enemies spawn in point blank.  The shooting elements handle well, the enemy types can be fairly diverse, but with the exception of the very powerful Volge enemy types (think, large metal roboguys who can almost 4 shot you near the beginning of the game) enemies are kind of weak unless in very large numbers. The AI has some predetermined behaviors that are easy to learn and counter for, and occasionally you'll have a lot of fun fighting off multiple enemies at a time. However, the difficulty scales very inconsistently, often going from cakewalk to instant death depending on the location and mission.
2. Single Player Elements: Campaign missions are not consistent in their difficulty nor are they especially interesting after having done one of the four possible types of mission. These types essentially are "Go here and push a button, kill the guys, repeat", "Go here and shoot some guys, grab a thing and come back", "Go here and do this repeatable quest" and "Go here and do a minidungeon". The single player parts also offer a plot involving an "Ark Core" or whatever said plot-driver is and a few characters who are generic and underbuilt. Final boss is a refreshing dose of difficulty, but is both too little and too late to make a huge impact.
3. Multiplayer Elements: Coop and Competitive multiplay exist in Defiance. Coop modes have Dungeons and more Organic repeatable missions that reset periodically in the world. That being said, Coop tends to be incredibly easy for essentially the vast majority of the game's possible playable parts- save for one AND ONLY ONE segment- the Major Ark Fall that is called down by players buying a purchasable item through the Defiance store. This Major Ark Fall event features significant quantities of per-player scaling robobaddies ready to screw you up. That being said, the Major Ark Fall calldown is only difficult for its final boss, which is something of a behemoth of incredibly frustrating AoE attacks and is basically unkillable for the most part (unless, say, an entire clan of orginized players goes after it with a very specific technique). Competitive multiplay is by queued instance only, it seems, although there is a "Shadow War" pvp event which I have never seen in action. Multiplayer has some balance issues due to the weapon generation systems, currently (01.11.2014) there is a sniper rifle that can charge up its shot, and break appart the shot into individual shots (making a sniper with a tight shotgun like spread). This "Surge Bolter" style of rifle is incredibly overpowered at this point, due to a balance patch that made all Semi-Automatic rifles do more damage than previously. I figure this weapon is probably bad for multiplayer just because it can 1 or 2 shot people really frequently and has no accuracy modifier caused by movement/standing/jumping.
4. Logistics: The menus are awful, but navigatable if you learn how they work like I did. That being said, they desperately need some serious revisions especially in the Item Comparison department (which is currently, essentially broken). The modification section of the menus, known as the "Salvage Forge" is used to modify weaponry to make them have extra magazine size, a scope, ect, as well as to reset the "Weapon Mastry" points on a weapon, to make it able to level up player weapon skill despite having been used a lot by the player. The player to player interactions are also somewhat flawed, the "Quick Menu" features multiple types of functions that CANNOT BE ACCESSED ANYWHERE ELSE. This basically means that the radial escape menu and the various player menus regarding character are all disconnected from Adding friends, joining a clan, ect.
5. Overall Opinion: Say, a 1 point game is something like Full Spectrum Warrior (an unworkable piece of garbage), a 5 is say Dead Space 2 (Working, but lacking significantly in some serious aspects regarding player experience) and a 10 is closer to Half Life 2 (arguably one of the best experiences gameplay wise in my opinion); Defiance is a whimpy 4/10 because of many reasons stated above, and some others I haven't gotten to. I really, really love third person shooter games, and this one in particular captured my attention with the decent combat mechanics and the layers of possible depth (unlockables, however, are all that are left by this point), but lost me because of failure to carry through an enjoyable experience. I still had fun with this game, but often only because of shooting a badguy in some kind of impressive way (see: 360 no scope with that overpowered sniper rifle I talked about), or laughing at my friends when we could make the game's party functions work for us. If it goes on sale for 5 bucks, I recommend trying it out if you're really into the Borderlands style of game (respawns, MMO format, active weapon play, decent combat mechanics) but I strongly suggest bringing some FRIENDS or you will probably never be able to justify the ~18gb of this games overall size.

Dustbowl appeared silently on Steam a few days ago. No fanfare, no publicity, one moment silence and the next. *poof* It's here. A little slice of retro-apocalypse goodness. The brainchild of two developers, Dustbowl is set after the visitations of an alien race who covered the land in a biochemical dust that quite literally rendered the surface of the planet unlivable. A toxic, barren wasteland (drawing inspiration from the UFO afterlight storyline) where what remains of humanity gathers together in small underground shelters, away from danger, away from the light.
Technology has fallen apart, and humanity lives precariously on the cusp of extinction, this is very much the death throes of society, with people still struggling to come to terms with what has happened. Worse, your shelter seems to be suffering a major case of the shakes, prompting the leader of the shelter to call two of the most experienced surface scavengers to a meeting, and to plea to them for assistance. One, your father, reluctantly volunteers to see what is causing the tremors, leaving you alone in the shelter to find your way, and find answers.
The world of dustbowl is consistent, and very quickly shows itself to be deep, full of characters suffering and broken by the very events that have driven them underground, the survivors in the HUB feel just like that, survivors by necessity. Some showing clear signs of depression, others panicking and more concerned about their own skin, others yet just getting slam drunk because "who cares, the world is going to hell"
And this is just the first area, once you get out into the game overworld, it's not going to get any more cute and cuddly either, I can assure you of that much. The game overworld is meaty, sporting multiple locations that will require you to either talk, shoot or puzzle your way through them. The game falls somewhere between a Role Playing Game and a point and click adventure, and even borrows some elements from survival sandbox games with thirst, hunger and tiredness being perennial beasts that stalk you every step of the way. In case you're feeling particularly masochistic, the developers even put in a hardcore mode, which yes, will delete your save file when you die. You will die. This game does not pull punches.
If there is one criticism I could, and should level at this game, it's that the game engine (Adventure Game Maker) is almost certainly running at the absolute roof of it's capability here. The developer has crafted a masterpiece in Dustbowl, but make no mistake, AGM is bursting at the seams to contain this world, every trick and optimisation to cram the content in has been done, and you can almost hear the engine screaming in agony in the background as it works tirelessly to make this thing happen.
In a sense this would be akin to the times when games like Driller came out on the spectrum. Yes, you could push polygons and 3D rendering out on a computer with 128K of memory, but the poor thing creaked, and you could -hear- it creaking. People have asked if more content will be added, it might happen, but the engine is really being pushed here, so it'll be a case of hammering it in with a wedge in small chunks at a time I think.
This game almost certainly deserves to be a success beyond the developers most optimistic expectations, such that a sequel can happen, but it needs to happen in the same style, just in an engine that won't beg for mercy when they create this wonderful, vast canvas.
The combat deserves specific mention. I always felt games like Fallout 3 strayed too far towards "real time" combat, Dustbowl strikes a brilliant balance by being turn based with a reaction-ish based timing sequence for determining if you hit, crit, or miss. Weapons have their own distinct damage ranges, and your power in the game is strictly gear dependent (which means that progressing through the story will directly improve your ability to fight and also to defend yourself against the horrible nasty mutant things). The range of weapons is diverse, even at the early stages you'll find a goodly selection of pistols and assorted BB based weaponry, I can only assume it will escalate from there.
The art style is -very- retro. Going right back to VGA style RPG's of yore, but it works, evoking memories of Wasteland (the original, not even the remade original) and of similar games in that era. It's a very consistent art style, and the eye to design has been thoughtful and considered. The Subway (your first 'dungeon' area) is dingy and foreboding, and even though it's never explicitly threatening, there's always that nasty feeling you may be going a little too far from safety.
Dustbowl came literally out of nowhere, and it's possibly been the most pleasant surprise this year to date. It's had no press, and no hype, and that's one of the greatest injustices I could possibly think of, because this is a terrible disservice to what is possibly one of the best RPG's outside of the AAA releases.
Verdict :

If you enjoy old school adventure games I think you can get behind this title. I myself enjoy the retro visual style and throwback interface to older adventure games. The story and writing are ok, nothing spectacular but it’s far from dreadful. The post-apocalyptic setting and story are interesting and different enough from the rest to keep me intrigued on what happens next. The game world and quests are fairly large and so far I have had an abundance of objectives and missions to keep me busy.
My biggest complaint is how combat works and plays out. Most if not all encounters are random and combat is turn based. When you enter combat, it randomly (?) decides who has initiative, to attack you simply hit your attack button, a bar will fly across a multicolored slider bar, and you hit the attack button again to stop it. Based on where it stops and lands, it calculates the damage. It’s not horrible, but more often than not it just feels cheap and cheated.
Despite the combat, this game offers a fairly rich and expansive adventure for the low cost of $9 usd. The old school interface, vfx and pacing will turn off some, but for those who grew up or enjoy that era of gaming, you will love this. You can tell the developers put their heart and soul into it and are influenced by many awesome games and movies like Fallout, Mad Max, Metro 2033, Stalker, Defiance, A Roadside Picnic.....the list goes on and on. I highly recommend it, easily one of my favorite indie titles of this year to date.

As the other reviews say, this is a cute and terrifying adventure game that allows you to build and level up your crew and your plane to take on the Axis enemy. However, there are a few things you need to keep in mind or else this will really ruin your day.  Thinks to keep in mind to enjoy this to its fullest:
1.  This is the biggest thing, there is no Autosave.  This means when you feel like you're on a roll and things are going well, STOP.  Save and Quit.  Then open the game back up and continue.  Twice now I've leveled up my crew past 7, got my plane in very good working order to a spec I was confident in, made a single mistake and lost everything.  When you crash your plane you basically have to start over with low level everything.  If you are a few stages in, that means every single mission will destroy your low level crew and most likely you will start your game over.  I will probably not pick this game back up because:
2.  There is a significant amount of mission grinding to level up and upgrade, which can get repetive fast.  If you try to go onto the next main mission without a significantly leveled and upgraded crew, you will be destroyed.  Then you will have to start over.  Shoot for around level 6 or 7 on your crew before trying the first main mission, and make sure you have belt feed machine guns.
3. There is some training missing.  There are critical details not mentioned that you have to pay attention to.  Details not mentioned are survivability during a crash and how to use equipment in your plane, both of which are really important if you dont have a good game save.
All in all I got about 8hrs of fun enjoyment out of this game, but when I lost all my grinding XP and upgrades (twice) because of a simple mistake (flew too high during heavy fire so navigator couldn't plot a course, ran out of fuel on the way back, lost plane and crew), it is really a bummer.  If you keep a few things in mind mentioned above, this is a great, fun, rewarding game.  If you make the mistakes I made, you will not have a fun time.

Old but Gold in a shellnut, this game is extremely outdated with Bad graphics that can only come from that special era of early polygon modeling, and the combat is incredibly flawed, striking an ugly mix between dice rolling and straight up hitting things.

To conclude, if you can look past it's flaws and old age, Morrowind is great game that no RPG fan should miss

Morrowind was my introduction to the world of Elder Scrolls. I didn't manage to get properly acquainted with the game until several years after its release, I couldn't stop playing it after I did. I don't know if people will find the game as interesting by today's standards, but it still plays great. Different, but great.
Morrowind plays much like an old style action RPG game, where RNG plays a very prominent part. Combat is one of the areas in which this is very noticeable, as enemy and player attacks have a chance of missing for no visually justified reason. Early on, when your skills are low, you are very likely to miss most of your hits, but as your skills start improving, you will slowly see more and more of your hits connecting. For me, it took a little while of getting used to, but now I find it an endearing trait of a bygone era that adds to the unique flair of the game.
The game also encourages a more attentive mentality, as most of the dialogue and quest information is relayed in pure text. There's quite a bit of voice acting, but the vast majority of dialogue requires good ol' reading. There are also no map markers to aid you in where to go next. You have to stay smart and check the journal for your latest entries or ask around towns for more information.
I absolutely recommend this game, it has a certain charm about it that makes me come back to it and replay it every couple years.

I´ll have to start this review by saying i´m not fan of the series, i don´t have any nostalgic memories about Morrowind and actually first TES game which i played was Skyrim back in the 2013, i was not really that impressed about it compared to hype what it caused back in 2011, it was alright casual open world game but♥♥♥♥♥♥poor role playing game, after that i left TES series to rest until now.
Since my childhood i have heard constant praise about Morrowind, when Skyrim was released i heard people were comparing these two and almost everyone agreed that Morrowind was a superior game, it could not be anymore just a nostalgia since so many agreed to it, so after many years my hype for the The Elder Scrolls Morrowind had built up and now finally when i tried it and played the main story through i got to say i´m disappointed.
But was The Elder Scrolls Morrowind bad game? Partly yes, but the roleplay elements were pretty solid but let´s see overall PROS and CONS of the game by my taste.
PROS+
+ The game has limitations to your build, your character can mostly excel on one area compared to Skyrim´s jack of all trades style→(you can basically be good at everything). If you start your build as a melee character you can´t middle way through of the game just make full 180 and start to build in to a mage, or of course you can but it would be waste of levels and experience points which brings me to the next pro.
+ Morrowind allows player to "fail" game has a respect to the players intellectual capacity and lets player kill anyone they want even if those persons are important to the main quest, it allows to build your character "wrong" game does not have artificial limitations, it trusts that the player knows what he/she is doing.
+ Dialogue has a actual meaning, in Morrowind there is not that huge arrow pointing on the direction where to go most of what you get in Morrowind are clues from dialogues or compass points, example North of Caldera go there.
+ Main story is actually pretty well done on the Bethesda standards. Not these recent family issue ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t (Fallout 3&4) or muhahaha i´m evil dragon because i´m evil (Skyrim)
+ Character progression, you start as a no name loser, and end up being a god like being.
+ You simply can´t join every guild possible since some of them are enemies and their ideologys are polar opposites, again comparing to Skyrim Thief´s guild avoids killing at all cost but still allows member of the dark brotherhood to join in the fun.
+ Limited use of fast travel and it costs gold.
Most of these Pros are missing on the modern games since gaming audiences have grown ("Casual gamers") so big game publishers has to act accordingly by dumbing down the game mechanics to make more money, so that even mongoloids could play through the game.
But why i was so disappointed you might ask well here comes my reasons.
CONS-
- The combat and overall gameplay, yes i could not get used to Morrowinds roll of the dice combat, i understood that you had to have high enough skill level to your weapon of choice to hit your target repeatedly but thats not the only thing that was wrong, on my 30 hours of gameplay i never felt that my character hold a real weapon on his hands, i tried long swords, maces, spears, short blades, but in the end every fight atleast with a humanoid enemy felt like 2 guys poking each others with sticks, combat was so underwhelming and really boring.
- And what i mean by overall gameplay? well the most time consuming the traveling jump, jump, jump, jump stop to fight a rat jump, jump, jump and now im out of fatigue so my hits misses almost everytime "SCREE" cliff racer attacks. miss, miss, miss, miss, hit ,miss, miss, miss hit you know the drill by now it´s kinda tedious.
- Quest design mostly is your basic errand-boy fetch quests go here, kill this, get that, report back. Even faction quests fall victim to this simplistic structure, and they don't even give interesting narrative reasons for why you're doing the things you're doing, and i just finished Morrowind when i played through on these past 4 days and there is only 2 quests which i remember you had to bring some poor ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ his pants back, and the final mission.
- Exploration is unrewarding, yes you heard me right after about 18 hours of gameplay i had achieved to become Knight of the Imperial Dragon and won the duel against Varus Vantinius so i got possibly one of the best possible weapons and pieces of armor to my character just under 18 hours, so if i do not enjoy the combat and i already have really good gear what would be my reason to explore? And also most of the exploring would happen on the tombs which almost look the same, some of them has a loot of spoon and 10 gold some of 100 gold why would i care.
- The enemy variety there might be lot of different creatures lurking on the world of Morrowind but the ones you see 80% of the time are Rats, Cliff Racers, Ghosts, Kagoutis and Skeletons not really that bad of a thing but still it gets pretty boring.
So overall is Morrowind a bad game on my opinion? No, is it a good game? Only on roleplay aspects, will i play it ever again? Probably not, since gameplay is pretty important to me on games, if i want just a good story i can read a book, watch a movie,anime or some series so without fun or compelling gameplay games are not really that great.
I can already guess that if some Morrowind fan sees this review they will think me as a casual gamer, but i think this review is more for a people like me without a nostalgic memories of Morrowind, but in the end i can still somewhat recommend this game just don´t fall on that hype, it´s better RPG than Skyrim but overall atleast for me it was not anything that special.

This game feels robust and polished.  I am not in particular a fan of DC, or most MMORPGs for that matter: typically I find the controls clunky and too much reliance on the part of the developers on players having learned what to expect by playing other similar games.  Not in itself a bad thing but it can leave a game feeling rough around the edges.  Not so this game.
The controls are EXCELLENT.  If you usually play games with fine-control of your own actions, you may, like me, find most MMORPGs unresponsive and awkward, even after learning the control systems properly.  This game doesn't feel like those games.  It feels like a 3rd person adventure / shooter game.  WASD + mouse.  Just what you want :)  LMB and RMB are your two default attacks and as you level up you learn to do combos with them - tapping and holding.  So that's just great.  Then there's a hotbar - like almost all MMORPGs - but it's just there, it's not your main source of destructive power - that's still in your mouse.
This game also FEELS excellent.  Although I was initially put off a bit by the cartoonish appearance of some NPCs, I kept going and by day 2 that completely didn't matter.  On top of that there's a really good amount of voice acting, which makes a big difference to me in feeling that I'm playing a game that the devs want me to enjoy at every turn.  The cutscenes are polished, the graphics are really nice, and the game strikes a brilliant balance between a dynamic, responsive control system and the high number of powers, skills, buffs and combos that are the heart of most MMORPGs.

The game had a very rough launch with bugs, Hence the low rating for the game by Meta. But those bugs are all but squashed now and the game is really solid.
It's like a mix of swtor, and borderlands 2. The way the area's are created has a Swtor feel, and your running around shootings things much like Borderlands, or so I hear. (I never actually played either Borderlands, but that's how people are describing it).
With only a few hours of game-play in it, I'm already getting my 10$ worth out of it easy, and the game story will draw you in. The characters personalities seem pretty solid as well, you'll hate them, love them, and get annoyed by the ones your supposed too.
Ontop of that, the customization for your character is pretty legit as well, not only being able to choose which weapon and side arm you want, (which is no limitations, you could go sniper rifle/Assault Weapon Sniper Rifle/Bazooka, Pistol/Energy Gun, or even Shotgun/Shotgun) No limitations in mix and matching weapons.
Just like Swtor you can break down your weapons as well for parts and income, or add accessories and mods to them which will boost their ability, as well as change your characters headgear, and outfit to mix and match.
Definetly worth the 10$ easy.
Cons:
The few Con's I found are not huge, but could be a turn off for some players.
1) The starting area's at least are pretty empty. To me this actually enhances the feel of it being a wasteland. If there were 100's of people running around, wouldn't feel like that, so to me this is actually a plus, but for others may be a turn off. There is a helpful automatic party finder however, which helps to get groups.
2) The Chat system is totally implimented bad. You can never see what anyone is saying around you or in the area. To see it, you have to stop what your doing and press Enter. Which then a Chat screen the size of the entire screen pops up. Which only then can you respond. Terrible chat system for an action game, because half way through responding to what your friend just said your getting shot at, and need to stop.
However if you use VOIP to talk with friends, again, the chat system is of no concern for you really.

is a Top-down, Action-RPG developed and published by fatshark – pushed out of the gate in late-Spring 2012. Its reception was largely mixed – due to bugs, unfinished content and a lack of any sort of co-op mode. But how does it hold up five years down the line?
The game takes place in a post-apocalyptic Sweden after the ‘Untergang.’ You take control over a bunch of mercenaries looking to make their mark on this new world. Their misadventures take to us to Solside – which perilously hangs over the Krater – a seemingly endless abyss that draws those from all over to seek its riches and possibly their demise in the process.
conspires to deliver a smooth and diverse gameplay experience using various Action-RPG mechanics as its base. What differentiates Krater is that you can control up to three mercenaries at once – providing the tools to micro-manage each member quickly and efficiently.
At first, you start with only three mercenaries but you can recruit others at recruitment NPCs on your travels. Mercenaries can be lvl’d up and enhanced through implants, boosters, weapons and gadgets – which provide a host of different possibilities and interesting combinations to tinker and experiment with.
There are a total of four different classes – Bruiser, Regulator, Medikus & Slayer. Each class has a mutant variant which possess radically different models and skills. Mutant variants have to be recruited. There isn’t any way to transform your base class into its mutant variant or vice versa.
The game will propel you forward in the form of both primary and optional quests, slowly opening the large map up for exploration. There are many neat references through various dialogue and item descriptions that will hint at the world pre-apocalypse.
Crafting in
does not sit passively in the background. Recipes – obtained from drops and various receptacles – will grant you the ability to create a host of weapons, implants, boosters and gadgets allowing you to negate much of the gold cost from buying items from NPCs outright. And gold can be scarce for much of the early to mid-game so crafting becomes invaluable.
There are a large of number varying environments – which all conspire to immerse you in the post-apocalyptic setting – from bunkers, swamps, deserts, caves and more. There’s a lot here for the eye to see to keep things fresh.
In-game graphical options are limited – offering a small range of customization. You will notice the occasional flickering texture here and there. It is noticeable but doesn’t occur often enough to cause an annoyance.
’s soundtrack is exceptional in its range in tonality to fit any given moment. You’ll often stop and just sit back to listen to its complexity and ambience. In addition to the sublime OST, you have crisp animation sounds and various spoken commentary given by each mercenary throughout your adventures. For example, if stationary for a period of time, that fact may be noted by a mercenary. There are many different scenarios that’ll prompt a host of comments. The cut scenes that divide chapters are also brilliantly voice acted.
The
co-op portion was a later addition to the base game and comes in the form of three multi-lvl missions – which add new areas, bosses and a good way to get loot. It’s important to note, the standard campaign story cannot be played in co-op.
While the added co-op missions themselves are fun. The net-code is quite buggy and crashes have been known to occur frequently. As of writing this, I strongly recommend playing the co-op missions only in solo-mode which can be done by hosting your own game. The reason for this is that there is a bug present that can reset your characters completely to their base configuration if the host of a co-op game crashes.
The last boss in the co-op mission Electrified!, Electro Bert cannot be killed at this time, due to a crash that always occurs about a minute into the fight.
was initially planned to be the first part of a three part saga. Because of its mixed reception, the two other parts were never completed. The end of the current game ends on a cliff-hanger and the story may never have a proper resolution.

Because of the crash that occurs in the Electrified! co-op mission, there is a single achievement that cannot be attained at this time. For those looking to accrue the other 40 achievements, you’re looking at around a playtime at the bare minimum of around 50-60 hours.
We’ve just eclipsed
’s 5-year anniversary. Despite all of the updates and additions in that time-frame which have been few and far between throughout, what we have is a game that still garners very mixed sentiments from those that experience it. I feel that
will be remembered as a game that could’ve been exceptional but fell short of the mark in the end.

Concept is great, but the encounters in the beginning are far from balanced. Enemies hit with critical hits more than misses, they have armor while you don't, drop almost nothing of use and rob you of more than half your health and with almost no way to heal up. I can understand the prospect of a difficult game, but the risk versus reward for this games combat is awful, and their is almost no chance to avoid or escape it.
Edit: I have complete it, and while the difficulty does go down further on, I would like the option to run from fights. Some battles have no rewards and are just a massive waste of resources.
Storage quickly becomes a problem too, as only 16 slots does not facilitate enough space for everything you may need.
Weight capacity of 35 Kg is not enough if you want a Flamethrower, as .2 Kg of fuel is consumed per use, making both the flamethrower and it's fuel way too heavy for anything practical.
The Maching Parts weight is also too high, being a full Kg, meaning that crafting with them is harder than needs to be.
Basically, there are lots of off balance mechanics that could use tweaking, and make the game a lot more enjoyable, but after the early game hell, the story certianly drew me in, and that was what allowed me to complete the game.
So if your focus is story, then I can recommend this game.

What a wonderful game!
A story telling the journey two brothers undertake to find a cure for their seriously ill father. You control both brothers simultaneously, having to help each other to overcome the many obsticles they encounter.
The puzzles can tax your co-ordination, as you try and maneuver the brothers into position and interacting with the correct one - but don't let this deter you; this game is telling you their story and the puzzles are just there to give you the sense of the struggles they come across.
The sounds in the game are simplistic, but they work perfectly to set the atmosphere - the game doesn't even need dialogue, the actions of the characters and the random noises they make say all that needs saying to let you understand what is going on and what you need to do.
The graphics in the game are beautiful. The art-style I would say is in the same vein as Fable, which again suits it just right, and will leave you wide-eyed at the various environments the brothers must progress through on their journey.
The game may be short, but it is an experience you need in gaming. I highly recommend this!

Best Elder Scrolls game , no comparison even 15+ yrs later, like don't worry about its age it can be a little daunting at first but  I promise you the payoff is huuuuuuuuuuuuuuge. The amount of lore and just juicyyyy detail in this game, like literally they'll hide content most people will never find and that's what I want out of an rpg where like u have to have the skils to levitate and if u levitate in a random cave and check some little corner that has no indication theres anything there, u can find like some godly weapon/artifact bc none of the game is leveled. You'll walk into a cave at level 1 and just get annihiliated by a winged twilight and I love that. I love that there are parts of the game that are just more inherently dangerous, like daedric ruins are completely unapproachable till way later and I loveeeeeeee that. Things are hidden and difficult but they are there waiting for you to just look hard enough, the detail is there, and if you see someplace you think you could fly to and there might be something hidden up there, chances are, something is.
I'll never forget gameinformer giving it a 7-something back in the day bc "its all just walking and talking :'(" bc we were so flush with amazing and deep rpgs back then that all people cared about was flashy combat. The combat is definitely weaker than later entries but like this game rly aint for you if you're looking for stellar and modern combat even though imo the combat is rly fun. I personally like how much micormananging it requires, I like the ritual of gathering all the necessary supplies I need to just clear one cave, I like being restricted in the beginning to where I have no idea what to do or how to proceed bc everything just kicks your♥♥♥♥♥so hard, I like that. I like that there genuinely are other ways to progress in morrowind outside of killing things, like alot of rpgs boast that but you can go full speechcraft build and get puuuurty far just like you can go full mage and not even focus at all in combat magic its aweeeeesome. But even so, I like that in combat I have to be thoughtful about what spells I use and when bc my mana won't regen on its own without sleep or a potion, I like that I can steal a random item and get dragged into a box-dimension where a legendary and unique sword that has a shape thats not in any other elder scrolls game is kept by a rly powerful guardian in a rly obscure tower.
Dreamers will approach you and speak crypticly and make you feel paranoid and unsafe no matter where you are, like you're always being followed and watched. You'll wake up sweating from detailed wall of text nightmares that leave you with a thousand questions. The faces of dreamers hollow and out of that gaping disturbing hole emerge worms.. This is the Elder Scrolls in it's prime and if you value an absurdly detailed plot and lore and world with sci fi undertones (more like overtones tbhhhhh), then this is your game. Bethesda's taken a turn for the worst recently and this masterpiece reminds us all why it's so heartbreaking for those of us who've witnessed the descent and why we expect better and why we have such passion for what can be done with this universe that we all love so much.

Many of my complains might sound vague, because it’s hard not to spoil anything major otherwise, but I think it should be comprehensible enough.
, it’s the over-the-top writing and plot twists that kill the suspension of disbelief very early on. Some plotpoints are simply too much to take them seriously and this was rather easily avoidable, by some changes to the setting or paying more attention to details on the part of the writer.
is the protagonist, who is a “grumpy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥” somewhat typical for VNs, but takes this attitude to new heights, to the point when it stops being in any way relatable or interesting to read. Also, he’s meant to be a genius, but really doesn’t do or say anything that would make the reader feel this way. Through the whole story he acts more like an annoying bum than an actual protagonist, his only agency being in the past or making him even a bigger ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
, it’s how characters react to the most bizarre things happening within the plot, like a shocking confession from the protagonist that gets turned into a joke and is pretty much never referenced again by anyone but himself. I can be pretty patient with such stuff, but when no one acts like a human being, it becomes a serious problem.
, it’s the “true ending”,
I don’t think it’s not allowed to present a sad or even drastic resolutions to a VN plot, but the way it was done here and presenting it to us as the intended message of the story - it’s simply too much.
Other than that, I can’t say it’s a terrible VN in its core. It has decent enough art and writing in some parts of the story is really good. The pacing felt pretty consistent and never got me bored or wanting to skip though any larger parts of the text. Also, it has suprisingly good voice acting, that helps you get immersed in the experience. It doesn’t even do that bad of a job when tackling the obvious philosophical questions coming from the story (although it you want to see them done really well and deeply, try the brilliant
).

Much of what I complain about is subjective to some extent, and the game is cheap and made competently enough to not be a thoroughly bad experience. I simply have too many problems with it to give it a thumbs up.

A great and unique ARPG. You're given control of three characters at a time but don't let the thoughts of micromanaging put you off, as it hardly feels like a chore. Each of your characters has a different class such as tank, ranged damage, healer, and others you can get though playing the game. All of their skills are laid out on your skill bar so there's no need to click each separate character just to use their skills.
Along with that all of your characters abilities are very customizable. The regulator character's slow aura for instance can be altered to also heal allies that stand inside of it, or damage enemies that touch the aura. You can have the bruisers taunt ability give a defense buff to nearby allies.
On top of all that, the game makes use of a wide color pallet. A feature not seen very often in today's video games. With online co-op, plenty of quests, and a giant world map, there's no reason to pass this up if you're a fan of the genre.

"And they lived happily ever after".
Most if not all of us will have heard those words uttered to us at some point in our lives. For me it brings back memories of being a young nipper, tucked up in bed, my grandmother telling some tale of a far away mystical land, full of giants, griffins, ogres, goblins and other mythical creatures such as happy wife's that don't nag.
I loved a good story in my childhood and nothing has changed as a 31 year old man. Its one of the main reasons I love gaming so much. Its a story that you control. Some games are more open so you tell the story to your self as you play and change the direction in which the game is going. Others are far more linear and have a set dialogue and plot that you can change very little.
"Brothers a Tale of Two Sons" is the latter. However don't let this put you off, the story is fantastic and so well told you will be hooked from the moment you take control of them both. Talking of controlling I should mention how the game mechanics work as they are fairly interesting too.
You control both brothers at the same time using the left stick (I used a gamepad) for the older brothers movement and the right stick for the younger brother. Each brother can (and must) interact with the world and that is done by the applicable side of the game pad in the way of the trigger buttons.
Its slightly disorientating at first but you soon get the hang of it, although I found it easier to allocate each brother a side of the screen, dependent upon which half of the controller moved him - otherwise I tended to wonder why the brother I thought I was controlling was wondering off the wrong way.
Each brother has abilities that the other can not do, not as in super powers, you're just two normal boys, but as in the older brother is stronger and can lift heavier objects, jump farther, throw objects (including little bro) whilst the little brother can slip through tight gaps, climb on fragile objects etc.
The brothers must work together to get from their house to go and get a cure for their sick father which is obviously not at the local doctors as that would make for a fairly poor and short story, along the way they encounter all manners of fantasy creatures, although no wifes that don't nag.
The puzzles put in front of you are not so much puzzling as thoroughly enjoyable to do, as is the fantastic unfurling fantasy story ahead of you. I recommend this to anybody, its genuinley a real gem..........the end

This is the game that delivers on the promise of narrative-entwined gameplay that we glimpsed a year ago in Journey. It'll be remembered (and dissected, and copied) for one specific, powerful moment, but the game's true success is the way it uses its 'single-player co-op' gameplay to define the brothers as individuals and a team in the hours leading up to its climax. Even better, the whimsical, often brutal fairy tale design of its Scandinavian-themed world makes it easily one of the year's best-looking games.
In terms of tone, the game is equal parts Ico, Journey and Limbo. There's an innocence and beauty to the world, but an undercurrent of melancholy and danger. It gets dark. The game uses a fictional language and, aside from its very first minutes, features no text or prompts. But you'll never have a problem understanding what's being said, thanks to the expressiveness of the models and voice work. The controls are as minimal as the UI: each brother is tied to one analog stick and one trigger for movement and context-sensitive actions.
The gameplay revolves around solid, but light, platforming and puzzle-solving. The real draw is how well the gameplay serves the story and atmosphere. The role the brothers play in solving physical puzzles or traversing the environment is defined not only by their sizes, but by their personalities. I'd like to give a few examples, but I don't want to spoil much for you. Suffice to say, their interactions with each other, and with the other characters in the world, feel natural.
There's real wonder and fun in this title. Enjoy.

I my opinion, I give this game 9/10.
My first impression of this FPS is a "Tactical Team Base Game”, teamwork is essential for victory.
The game has no cash shop which means it is a "No Pay to Win" weapons, perks, equipment or any other augment enhancements.
The game also offers a "Dedicated Server" program through the Steam\Library\Tools, which is nice if you want to host for LAN parties or to setup a server in your area for better ping gaming.
Depending on ping and the server your on, the game has good hit registry.
The controls have your basic setup, plus some additional keys for leaning left or right, prone position, peeking, healing and reviving down teammates. There is a little learning curve with the additional keys but average FPS player will quickly learn and over come.
The game also features in-game voice so that you can talk to your team and also to be albe talk to the other team too.
The game is also balance in that everybody uses the same 4 type of weapons which gives the players equal footing. There is no high rank OP weapons and gear vs beginning\low rank weapons and gear. It is Skill vs Skill, Team vs Team.
If you don't want to Pay To Play for a game like the Battlefields series or the C.O.D series and gives every player and equal footing on the battle field, this is the game I would suggest.

Mount & Blade: Warband is a 2011 RPG by Taleworlds Entertainment. While other RPGs only pretend to let you tell your own story, Mount & Blade actually does.
In the war-torn world of Calradia, you play as an entirely customizable character.
You can decide to either
a) help one of the six fractions, b) one of the six claimants for each throne,
or you can
c) create your own faction entirely by yourself d) be a peaceful merchant instead.
Most of the time you travel around the poorly presented, yet big, but negligible, map.
You visit various lifeless towns and villages, on the quest of gaining renown and money. You talk with lords and ladies, you capture and sell lords, you fight raiders. You win or lose tournaments, you get rekt by bandits when you simply wanted to visit the horse merchant. You receive a small, yet enormously rich village by your king which you find devastated by an a**hole who somehow managed to teleport across the entire map. You travel with your mates Jeremus and Artimenner who start bi**hing around who is the better doctor. Following a group of soldiers who promise some mighty fine loot, you discover that you have nothing to eat, because the chicken you had bought have rottened.
And at the end of the day, when it's already 3AM you finally manage to turn away your face from the monitor and ask yourself: What have I done? Shouldn't I have spared this group of poor villagers?
Mount & Blade: Warband really isn't a perfect game. It's graphics are short above awful, combats are sometimes deeply frustrating, quests are repetitive, the lords and ladies of Calradia all seem to do the exact same stuff, feasts resemble an exhibition of Gunther Hagens' "Body Worlds"... The list of cons is near infinite.
But at the same time, Mount & Blade is a perfect sandbox. You can do whatever you want to. The story might be non-existant in the game, but inside your head it turns into the best story you have ever seen inside a game.
You write your own story.
Buy this game and regret that you have ever found out about it.

This program is an absolute must-have for anyone that values controller support.  While initially lacking valuable functionality like rebind-able keys on a per-application basis, these features were quickly added making the ridiculously low price all the more worth the purchase.
Awesomely well thought out functionality worth noting includes automatic disabling of mouse-mode when any application invokes full-screen with the option to re-enable mouse control and remember its toggled state on a per-application basis.  Even the virtual keyboard is well thought out, at least for use with an Xbox 360 controller.  While it's still a pain to use as compared to a keyboard, it's far better than Steam's funky input method for games while running Big Screen Mode.
It's even quite well designed with an intuitive and simple to use yet beautifully minimalist interface.  You can definitely tell how much thought and passion went into this product.  The profile creation mode for instance let's you browse for an executable on your computer or choose based on a recently used programs list.  Even going so far as to include the application's icon at an appropriately larger size given most use cases for this program are for users not sitting right in front of their screen.
The bottom line: if you have an Xbox360 controller and want to use it inside Windows for basically anything (except typing more than a few characters) then you want this program.  Enough said.

This game is basically five very small games in completely different genres strung together by a single graphic style and very loose narrative.
Each individual game has very little content or variety and quickly becomes a race to reach the next game and escape from a lack of new things to see or do. This also means that replay value is very limited as the game will proceed in more or less the exact same way every time.
The design of creatures, buildings, vehicles etc has very little effect on their functionality, which is mostly pre-determined by arbritrary rules that are never explained. For instance, an aeroplane cannot have weapons that point down, ie; bombers. You can install such weapons but they will not work.
Despite references to evolution, the game's progression feels very contrived and gimmicky and the way in which a species progresses feels more like creationism given how the environment has no effect at all, and is the same each time. The only driving forces in the 'evolution' of species here are the player's sense of aesthetics and the game occasionally telling you to add a certain part in order to progress.
With no such thing as difficulty or challenge, the game is unlikely to prove engaging except for small children and people who want games to be challenge free.
In short, a grand experiment, but a failed one. It is easy to see and admire the ambitions the game developers had, but the actual product is nowhere near being it. There simply is not enough game in this game to justify the price or indeed even live up to what the store page might reasonably lead you to expect.
