You can lead fifty soldiers versus fifty enemies (how many does, say, Skyrim allow again? Twenty, tops?). Form battle lines, maneuver around the map to get a clean charge, or to avoid enemy volleys. And with a tiny little mod, you can break the unit limit, putting hundreds of soldiers on the battlefield at once. All this time, you're still only playing your own character - no all-knowing top-down perspective here!
Place eighty crossbowmen in a double line on that hill there. Order sixty huscarls to move forwards through the valley, in close formation. Take forty knights around the hill. Lead the charge the enemy's unprotected flank, as they get pinned between the huscarls and the hill. As your enemies start running, find the enemy commander and take him down, so you can imprison him for ransom later, as honour demands.
This is one of the very few games where riding a horse is both easy to do, and actually useful. In some big RPGs (I mean: Skyrim and the Witcher 3), you can ride horses, but you really don't want to - it's clunky, and you don't really get anything out of it. Playing this game, you understand why people go into battle on horses. The added speed and momentum of a thousand pounds on hooves is a game-changer. Couched lances, horse archers, heavily armoured chargers: this is how you win battles (terrain permitting).
The reason is one of my favourite mechanical innovations, in any game, ever. It's so simple you wonder why it's not (as well-implemented) in every game. Basically: you get bonus damage if you are moving towards your target, or if your target is moving towards you. If you are moving very fast (like on a horse), you get a lot of bonus damage. If your opponent is charging you on horseback, you can stick a pike them, and get the same bonus damage. On foot, stepping backwards and forwards is the key to defending and striking. This simple thing makes maneuvering in combat important and useful, it makes horses powerful, it gives the combat system a really realistic feeling, without being clunky or difficult to grasp.
Other upsides: easy to mod, nice little bit of trade/economy sim, nice bit of diplomacy, well-balanced and useful skill system. No magic, no potions, but healing is not a pain - or if it is, you were too reckless, a commander's got to watch themselves, of course.
In general, a very, very good compromise between realistic combat and playable combat.

Before I start, you should know that less than 2% of people who bought this game actually gave it a positive review which means the "overwhelmingly positive" review rating it has is very deceptive. You can see here that Steamspy shows 2.2m people have bought the game:
This is despite how only 39k people who bought the game reportedly reviewed it. Obviously, something's fishy here. It seems that the game has a cult following, and deliberately gives negative reviews bad ratings to make them go away. If it was overwhelmingly positive, then why did only 1.77% of people review it with a 96% approval rating? It seems like a lot of trolls just want more people to buy the game so they can keep on trolling.
In any case, the single player's complicated at first, but too simple after. You get lost initially with what the best backgrounds and skills are to grab and how to approach the landscape, but once you do, you find you're doing the same things over and over to get favor with lords and villages to expand your estate and claim your kingdom. The roleplaying aspect is rather shallow since the quests really just have different names for doing the same things. A lot of the skills are useless as well since they just make things more difficult. For example, there isn't much reason to be a trader in this game since the trade discount for higher trading levels is practically useless. On top of that, you're better off just allying with a faction, and then pillaging enemy villages to take everything they have before selling it. Yea, your relationship with the faction you pillaged will plummet, but it's your enemy anyway so you don't really care. There's also no general reputation in this game or badboy points, so you don't really have to worry about being treated as a warmonger. Just keep pillaging and pillaging until you get enough money to afford a huge army. Once you fight enough battles, your soldiers will level up, and you'll get an elite and unstoppable force to ransack the enemy kingdoms. Then, help expand your kingdom as much as possible before overthrowing the king and you win.
Combat in singleplayer is very easy as well since the computer is a piece of cake. It falls for feints all the time, and doesn't dodge at all. Usually, the computer just rushes you as well. There are no tactics put in place. Just clump up to fend off the enemy first wave of cavalry, use your archers to pick off the infantry, and then charge your cavalry to kill enemy archers.
On the other hand, sieges are ridiculous since there are no catapults, ballista, or battering rams. All you get are towers and ladders to charge at choke points which results in lots of guys randomly trying to breakthrough and often getting slaughtered. On the other hand, defensive archers and crossbowmen are hit or miss. Sometimes, they annihilate the enemy. Other times, they can't shoot at all and get slaughtered too. The lack of destructable environments makes it so you can't knock down defender fortifications either, so it's even more annoying.
There are lots of mods for the game, but they really just change the skins and names. Most don't have functional differences.
The multiplayer on the other hand is very cliquey with many people believing they're good despite how they're really not. Often, the winner of a duel is determined a lot because of having better connections or faster fps such that characters go through animations faster when attacking or won't get hit even when you see weapons go through bodies (or weapons hit even though weapons didn't touch bodies). It kind of reminds you of how pros prefer to play side-scrolling fighter games like Street Fighter offline since even the slightest delay makes all the difference in reaction time.
Also, you often encounter matches where one faction wins or another because of getting more compatible equipment with the terrain at hand. Some factions get better cavalry archers for open terrain, but they have awful shields and swords for urban combat. Some factions get better throwing weapons to attack people who run away, and others get better armor that lets them take more hits. On top of that, people often team up in public games to the point that a winning team is determined by whoever has more people cooperating behind the scenes. There is no random matchmaker to ensure anonymous teamwork and chemistry. Instead, you often end up with one team that watches its others backs while the other team just gets slaughtered from engaging one at a time while teammates abandon each other.
Other problems include how you can't hear footsteps (like in counterstrike), how horse gallops aren't audible at reasonable distances unless you crank up your volume, and how you can jump in a full suit of armor to dismount someone on a horse. As much as the computer is awful at falling for feints and doesn't dodge, people on here play like ballerinas since there's no stamina gauge to keep them in check. The multiplayer game is more like a cartoon than a medieval simulator. This is especially obvious when you're shooting arrows at someone, but someone can turn on a dime in contrast to how your aiming feels like it's wiggling like a whip.
Anyway, don't waste your money. It's a great concept, but there are serious issues with execution. If you want, just wait for the prequel to come out which will have a much updated engine to play on:

-Being able to turn off the controller with the press of a button instead of removing the battery pack

TL:DR  12/10 for Atmosphere/World  14/10 for Class/Race/leveling system, 11/10 for Questlines and Lore. 10/10 for detail. Music 9/10, very fitting.  Nothing can be flawless, but in my mind ES3 comes close.
6/10 for combat system (age plays its toll) and 7/10 for bugs or lack thereoff.  I can't think of anything in this game that could be considered below average. Morrowind is Quality and Quantity.
This game is Rich, its unique, its different every time, it requires thought and has a learning curve.  This game is the reason I preferred XB over PS as a kid & still do.
Although I'm a FPS man though and through, Morrowind is my favorite game. Though the game world may technically be "smaller?" and much dialogue is not voiced, the Game World feels & truly is larger than almost any Map I've ever played in an open-world game, even when I'm jumping through it @ 100mph with enchantments.  There may not be as much voice acting but the game is rich with flavor, humor, and lore for those who are capable of reading.  The Freedom is unmatched, no starting dungeon, learn it yourself.  It never holds your hand. Some quests - "Yea i need this really small specific item from this cave thats, uh, kinda southeast of here" or maybe "go to this dangerous Ruin alllll the way across the map, over the hills, across the water, past the cliff racers, next to tha lava, across from the ghetto"  So I strongly recommend using jump and levitate to navigate the mountainous world easier and faster.
Most importantly, the leveling system is less "everything levels up with you so leveling is nearly pointless" like oblivion, and more "certain places are always dangerous for low level characters from the start & conversely very powerful items can also be obtained @ L1."  This allows players to truly see if they've turned into a force to be reckoned with after some proper leveling/gear aquisition, and makes for a believable world.  The game can be played very quickly but there is a learning curve before a player will know the where and hows of becoming godlike.
I personally consider the class/race/sign combination along with the unique attribute/skill leveling system to be the best Role Playing set ever put in a videogame.  Put simply, skills/traits not chosen as major/minor skills are possibly more important to character builds than skills that are chosen due to governing attributes.  It makes for a relatively complex system that will truly never be the same with any playthrough. Also, all races have different starting dispostiion towards each other depending on their lore (like real life).
As for the chance hitting, either use magic then or practice your chosen martial art until you always hit.  The NPC's that stand around all the time? Hey most of the people I know don't do much more than stand around anyway so its just like IRL besides I got better things to do than hunt for strolling NPCs.   Any other complaints about easily one of the best games ever made?
Actions have consequences, the quests sometimes require intelligence to solve, certain races truly don't like each other, certain guilds truly don't like each other, the fast travel is boats, wizards, and gaint nats, along with marks and recalls.
As for my dislikes, it could be a little less buggy & its slightly too easy to exploit for my purist/vanilla tastes.  Thats it.
Buy this game, it will make any collection rich.

A charming tale which is told by sight and sound rather than traditional scripting.
The two titular sons are brothers who must journey to assist their sick father. A journey that will call upon both of them to work together to overcome the sometimes hostile environment to reach their goal.
The mechanics and premise of the game are beautifully simple and excellently excecuted.
The left thumbstick of your gamepad controls the movement of the older brother with the left trigger handling any of many interactions with the environment and/or the younger brother. The younger of the two is likewise controlled (you guessed it) by the right thumbstick and trigger.
It takes a little bit of getting used to but clicks into place quickly enough and feels really rewarding once you get to grips with it.
The puzzles never seem to get too difficult but require enough thought to not seem contrived and they never infuriate.
Anyone who has ever played Kuri Kuri mix on the PS2 will enjoy this immediately, as well as feeling right at home. The main difference here being the excellent way the developers have made two main characters that you can instantly empathise with.
Ultimately I would recommend this at full price. At the holiday price it is quite simply a steal. Don't miss this one.
Additionally I would like to add that I am playing this game using my motherboards onboard graphics. And it runs fine. It should run really well on older systems.

Very fun, if intense and quite difficult at times. My reccomendations to success are:
1. Prioritise spending on your plane over your crew outfits.
2. Prioritise getting better guns, then armour, then systems. Don't bother spending money on survival items, as that money could have gone towards helping the plane not crash in the first place (plus most survivability comes from your crew outfits).
3. If you can, completely avoid hazards. If you can't, minimise the time you spend in the range of hazards. Use your navigators custom waypoint feature as soon as it's avaliable!
4. There is no downside to activating your engineers lean fuel mixature power. Activate it whenever you can to avoid the chance of running out of fuel if something on your plane breaks and creates fuel eating drag, or if you need to activate boost to get out of a sticky situation.
5. If you run into an ace pilot, turn around and lead them into the channel to fight. It's far easier to take them out by themselves then do the mission, then it is to try and do the mission while they're attacking you.

I can confidently say that after what amounts to 24.8 days of playing time, this is one of my all-time favorite games, and one I still consistently play.
The graphics can at times be left wanting, but the 200 player multiplayer servers that run with acceptable ping even when fyll definitely make up for it. The multiplayer is definitely the ultimate feature of this game, tied with the massive and very active modding community, though the single-player campaign can get repetitive and boring.
The massive amount of decent mods, plus the dozens of masterfully crafted mods that could be, and on two occasions have become, their own DLCs, make this game captivating every time you sign on. However my one major sadness concerning the game is not a fault of the game itself, but its rather small online community that has dwindled over the years. Even the best multiplayer mods can have a handful of servers up at a time, but to remedy that I would definitely recommend joining a community, such as a regiment in the Napoleonic Wars DLC or its several mods, as soon as possible. It shouldn't be very hard, as many are constantly recruiting on public servers.
I hope you all enjoy the game as much as I have.

There really isn't a way for me to recommend this game enough. I played it when it came out on the 360 and had to buy it again on Steam.
The first thing to know about this game is that it's ideally suited to a gampad with two analog sticks. It's possible to play with a mouse and keyboard, but it was specifically designed with a dual analog stick controller in mind.
The gameplay mechanics can take a little getting used to, but after a short time, they feel very fluid and natural. You control one brother with the left stick and left trigger and the other brother with the right stick and right trigger. Those are the only buttons you use. Sounds simple and it is, but it's so unique. I've never played a game like this as far as controlling characters and it's truly a joy to play.
The puzzles are fairly simple, but satisfying. The music is absolutely beautiful. The graphics aren't going to push your graphics card, but they are definitely appealing.
The story is at times funny, hopeful, touching, and incredibly sad. There is no spoken language in the game, but it does an amazing job conveying emotions via the characters gestures and vocalizations.
This is definitely one the most interesting games I've played in a very long time and I highly recommend that you give it a try.

I heard once that there would not be ten games better than Brothers this year. I initially scoffed, particularly after some of the releases at the beginning year. However, after actually playing the game, I am glad to be wrong. Story-telling has never gone so far on such simplistic, yet satisfying and ingenius controls.
Gameplay-
Though the puzzles are often not complex, they serve to develop a bond between the brothers and the character. This bond in turn, constructs an experience unlike any other.
Story-
Though this story contains tropes familiar to the average person, it somehow transforms that into something deeper. Due to the length of the game, it would be difficult to explain further without ruining some of the experience.
Value-
The value in Brothers does not lie in the gameplay. If you are looking for a lengthy game with some "meat" to it, look elsewhere. If you are looking to take explore the emotional depths a platform such as video games can provide, look no further than the "Add to Cart" button.

I don't think I've played a game where an emotional narrative was so well expressed through mechanics or especially though the control scheme. Brothers is a really short yet fun and engaging game. And though it starts with a quite cliché beginning it has some incredible pacing and reveals which affected me a surprising amount.
While the control scheme can take some time to get used to, and can get confusing when the player characters are in certain positions, it is also exploited perfectly numerous times to create small platforming puzzles and at some points hugely emotional payoffs.
What's even more impressive is that the majority of the ingenous mechanics and dynamics that are born from the controls are explored and then left behind when it is time for new ones to be introduced. This combined with a beautiful aesthetic and several well crafted set pieces makes Brothers one of my favourite games.

It's seriously amazing, though I will admit that the Steam Controller has made me use this less frequently. I still recommend it wholeheartedly though.

Despite the cartoony characters and planes, this game will give you hours of fun as the campaign is more than twice as long as the Battlefield 1 campaign for only $15
Pros:
- Death of crew you've spent a lot of time with is actually quite heartbreaking. If you had to give the only first aid kit to another crew, you're out of first aid kits. Seeing one of my best crew die at his post, he really looked like he was suffering even though this game has cartoon bobbleheads for the crew. I zoomed in at him when he was dying, the last first aid was used on the pilot. When his time was up, he slowly closed his eyes in front of my eyes. This game can actually make you emotional, +1
- Very intense, especially when brawling 10 fighters at once, or seeing an ace pilot tear through your armor. Everything is in real-time, so you don't have the option to freeze time. There's a bonus for not  slowing down time. +1
- Realistic manoeuvres such as evading flaks, corkscrew and emergency dives which exist in real life. Lost my best engineer while he was repairing the wing, I had to dive or my plane was going to find a new home in Dusseldorf. +1
- If you get a turret with an ammo feed, you can actually see the ammo feed in the plane. Unsure if it goes down as the turrets fire though. +1
- i can turn my plane into a german bomber by drawing the balkenkreuz on the wing. +10000
Cons:
- Unrealistic aerodynamics:
If half of both your tails are gone, the plane still flies perfectly. The tail is crucial to the plane's survival as it's unable to turn if both of the tails are gone. This isn't shown in Bomber Crew and the plane still flies as if nothing happened. -1
- Sometimes the ace pilot doesn't even hit you. He can do many risky manoeuvres but sometimes he doesn't even hit your plane when going head on with you. -1
- Unrealistic fighter physics:
I understand that this is a cartoony game, but when fighters get too close to you, they can pull up as if it was a toy plane. The amount of time they took to pull up was unrealistically stupid. -1
Overall score: 10001/10

Looks like it plays out like Spelunky or Caveblazers, but is actually more about gathering resources and then managing to survive long enough to actually spend them. Makes for a somehow both relaxing and intense gaming experience when trying to weigh wether or not you risk going just one floor deeper maybe, get just a bit more experience and gold and cristalls or if you want to head to your HQ to spend your shiny in loads of upgrades and classes.
Also you never dive with just one character into the "dungeon", you pick and choose between various team mates to form your squad and then change between them anytime you want. The managing of who to pick is quite fun. A medic and a soldier? Maybe you'll get just a bit further with the medics health packs. But then you can't pick your miner and miss out on tons of loot. Maybe just the miner and the medic? Risky, but fun to experiement with your options. Also there's like 10 of those guys so you got lots of combinations.
Overall I had a pleasant few hours so far. It looks nice, it plays really fun (did I mention you have an unlimited jetpack?) and is good both for extended sessions and a quick run.
Plus bonus points for a dev who will quite literally implement your ideas within like a day or two if its something that's quickly done and an actual good addition.
Oh and it's only 5 bucks. Probably one of the best deals on steam right now. Big thumbs up.

This stirring playable story brings innovative control and gameplay elements by forcing your thumbs to play cooperatively.  "But Mr. review guy my thumbs already play together!"  No they don't, not like this.  Each analog thumbstick controls a brother and you'll need to move them iindependently to progress.  This is why a gamepad is required to play.  While this gameplay is brand new, it can be difficult to pull off.  The game doesn't punish you for this, as the objective is to guide you through the story.
This game clocks in at about 3 hours but like a good movie I never felt like I wasn't getting enough value for my money.  Brothers is made by a filmaker who's trying to convey a story by capitalizing on the medium of games rather than film.  It's a brilliant proof of concept about the strengths of storytelling in an interactive medium.  There's no real dialog, no long cutscenes, no tutorial, no high score list, no online deathmatch, or any of the other stuff we cram into games now a days.
It's said a good writer shows instead of tells.  This game shows us that good gamemaking can be doing instead of showing or telling.  It's time our subpar stories in games get out of the way and let the story come from playing it interactively.  For more on that thought, check out Hitbox Team's blog (the folks behind Dustforce) about designing game narrative.

Brothers is a short but powerful experience that should be played by everyone who enjoys strong storytelling. The gameplay mechanics are analogous to how much both brothers rely on each other to get through their perilous journey, and the developers executes simple and personal storytelling to a high degree. The soundtrack is probably the strongest element in this game with it's majectic and emotional score. My experience with Brothers, especially towards the end, is similar to how I felt about To The Moon, and this game is amongst the few in my library that never overstays its welcome and manages to make me feel intimately with the characters when so little is said. This game still deeply affects me and I wouldn't mind replaying it to see the story unravel again.

Uhm not sure what to write here so just gonna paste a pancake recipe:
Ingredients:
100g plain flour
2 egg
300ml semi-skimmed milk
1 tbsp sunflower oil
or vegetable, plus extra for frying
pinch salt
Method:
Blending in the flour: Put the flour and a pinch of salt into a large mixing bowl and make a well in the centre. Crack the eggs into the middle, then pour in about 50ml milk and 1 tbsp oil. Start whisking from the centre, gradually drawing the flour into the eggs, milk and oil. Once all the flour is incorporated, beat until you have a smooth, thick paste. Add a little more milk if it is too stiff to beat.
Finishing the batter: Add a good splash of milk and whisk to loosen the thick batter. While still whisking, pour in a steady stream of the remaining milk. Continue pouring and whisking until you have a batter that is the consistency of slightly thick single cream. Traditionally, people would say to now leave the batter for 30 mins, to allow the starch in the flour to swell, but there’s no need.
Getting the right thickness: Heat the pan over a moderate heat, then wipe it with oiled kitchen paper. Ladle some batter into the pan, tilting the pan to move the mixture around for a thin and even layer. Quickly pour any excess batter into a jug, return the pan to the heat, then leave to cook, undisturbed, for about 30 secs. Pour the excess batter from the jug back into the mixing bowl. If the pan is the right temperature, the pancake should turn golden underneath after about 30 secs and will be ready to turn.
Flipping pancakes: Hold the pan handle, ease a fish slice under the pancake, then quickly lift and flip it over. Make sure the pancake is lying flat against base of the pan with no folds, then cook for another 30 secs before turning out onto a warm plate. Continue with the rest of the batter, serving them as you cook or stack onto a plate. You can freeze the pancakes for 1 month, wrapped in cling film or make them up to a day ahead.

I think a lot of the other reviews have covered things I like about this game, because all in all this game is really fun, but I have one big complaint:
It's way too easy to accidentally pull your pilot off the controls and crash your plane.
I did it once early on and attributed it to me being new to the game. I played for a while after, and after another couple crashes I got the hang of it. I was having a great series of runs, my crew was gaining some great abilities, I felt like I could really handle some serious challenges. Then while on a low risk mission I missed on a click and instead of selecting another crew member, i pulled my pilot off the controls and set him to walk a few feet away. I caught it within seconds but there was no way to get him back to controls because the plane immediately started nose diving. Boom, there goes my investment in my plane and my well trained crew. Not because I made poor strategic choices, not because I bit off more than I could chew, not because I forgot some essential function, but because I misclicked. Felt like a pretty big punch in the nads.
I'd really like some way to make sure this doesn't happen accidentally, maybe just a quick confirmation before removing your pilot ("do you really want to take your pilot away from the cockpit? (y/n)") because it feels like I have this self destruct button just sitting around on my plane waiting for the mission when I accidentally hit it.

This game is a ton of fun! I think I can best liken it to a compacted FTL. You fly missions with a crew of 7 people (2x Gunners, Bomb aimer, pilot, navigator, radio/radar, & engineer) that you have to micromanage within the bomber all while trying to complete objectives (mostly bombing things). The difficulty can surprise you as one thing going wrong can quickly escalte into chaos (like 3 fighters showing up while your trying to put out an engine fire). In-between missions you can customize your crew's gear (there are decent pre-sets that you can use too), select secondary skills for your crew, and customize your bomber (everything from paint to the guns).
Things I liked:
-Decent amount of customization. Even though some of the upgrades are linear (like radar mk1, radar mk2, ect.), you still have to keep your bomber under the weight limit your engines can support so you end up having to make sacrifices in some areas. You can kit your people and bomber for your playstyle as well with things like thermal gear if you like to fly at high altitudes to avoid hazards like flak or AA and whatever gear you buy for your people is stored so you can swap kits for diffrent missions.
-Freedom. The most important skill IMO is the navigator's "custom heading" skill. Until you get this skill you actually can't complete some of the bonus recon missions and are restricted to the predefined course. Also, in combination with the radio guys "radio for recon" ability you can plot courses around nasty stuff like flak or swing around behind your target so you can come in from the back.
-Not too punishing. I was worried that getting shot down was going to be the end of the game as i'd loose all my customizations and peopple but, the game will give you a new fairly upgraded bomber (equivelent to the campagin level your at I think?) and the recruits you choose from will start off at higher levels as well. So, you only need to take a couple ez missions to get back into fighting shape. I should also mention that you can make emergency landings or jump out of the plane and they have a system for determining if your crew survives or not. PSA Do not try an emergency landing without working engines! You will literaly just turn straight down and dive into the ground (It's a little funny the first time you see it but, more anoying). I have yet to try bailing out as you can't even carry enough parachutes until later in the game.
-Longish. There's only like 10?, I think, campaign missions but, there seems to be an unlimited amount of side missions you can perform with the campaign missions being like difficulty gates. When you complete a campaign mission all the side missions get more difficult. As of this reveiw i'm about 21 hours in and i've only made it to the 5th campaign mission (plus I have the DLC missions to go through as well).
-Smart AI. Some of the enemy fighters are actually quite clever and will do things like pull up under your plane in your gunners blind spots to shoot you. I swear i've seen squads of fighters test which guns I'm operating then attack from my blind sides as well. So make sure you stay aware of where your gunners are and move them around as appropriate (you have 2 gunner mains but, anybody can operate any station).
Things I didn't like:
-Hotkeys. You can ignore the input section of the startup screen as i'm not sure they even have anything to do with the in-game buttons. In-game there's only one crappy screen with the obvious hotkeys on it and none of the useful ones. There should be way more hotkeys then there are and the keyboard is woefully underutilized (although as a positive you can do mostly everything with the mouse if your drinking coffee with your other hand).
-Debrief length. The worst offender for this is the crew screen where you have to wait for it to tell you that each crewmember made it back and THEN it applies their exp and they all level up. At first it's just meh but, after level 7 it just feels like a huge unskippable waste of time. On the plus side i'll give them props for thouroughly explaining all the skills you gain on this screen.
-Jerky Flying phsyics. Granted, i'm not a pilot or anything but, I don't think a bomber can 180 on dime. Also, for some reason emergency landings are THE WORST EVER. As soon as you click it your bomber just nose dives into the ground like wtf. LEARN TO GLIDE BRO. If your out of fuel or have no engines your better off just letting the plane slowly glide into the ground (move everybody into the most armoured or least damaged part of the plane (not the wings!)) or just bailing out but, as I mentioned earlier, you can't even carry enough parachutes for your entire crew until you've upgraded your bomber quite a bit (you can have up to 4 equipment racks on the plane that start off only being able to hold one thing each so that's a max 4 parachutes if you dont take usefull stuff like med kits or fire extiguishers). Also, pro tip: If you don't have enough med kits and one of your crew is dieing you can emergency land before their timer is up and they will most likely survive instead of bleeding out during the flight home (once you get some lvl 2 first-aid guys you don't have to worry about this).
-Ammo wasters. I'm actually not sure if this is un-purpose or not but, sometimes your gunners will just randomly shoot even when they obviously have no angle on their target which wastes your ammo and then they're stuck reloading when they actually do have a shot. Side note, if you want them to just spray all their ammo around the place you can click the defensive button which has varrying success at keeping fighters back.
Overall I'm really enjoying this game and reccomend it for people looking for an FTL-like crew management game. Lots of chaos and quick decision making while trying to spam all your crews abilities. Oh, and the bonus you get for not using the slow time ability is pennies so dont feel bad for using it.

This game lives on.  Sure, the graphics are a little old, but the Morrowind world is still stunningly beautiful and somehow the game is very relaxing.  This is not a game that one "completes" as such.  There is a main quest, but that is not what the game is really about. There is much exploration and many different types of activities that one can and must do in order to succeed.  Like life itself, its not about the destination, but the journey.  It is not a quick game, but one that you can spend hundreds of hours in.  The gameplay is great.  There is so much to do, and so many different ways to do it.
I use Mods.  I dont like mods that alter the character of Morrowind.  E.g. Putting Japanese anime characters into Morrowind would destroy the enchanting look and feel of Morrowind.  The mods I use are OpenMw and Tamriel Rebuilt.
OpenMW is a fan made engine that has better performance and graphics and is more reliable than the original.  It requires better hardware in order to do this, but nothing that would challenge a modern gaming rig.  It runs a different program, but uses all the data from an original Morrowind installation.  You install Morrowind using steam, and then install OpenMw.  It needs to see a legitimate installation of Morrowind as part of its installation.  I play Morrowind on Linux.  The original Morrowind did not run on Linux, but OpenMw does.  Less booting into Windows is good.  To do this, I install on the original Morrowind on Windows and my dual boot Linux has to see the steam installation on my windows partition.
Tamriel Rebuilt have expanded an already huge game and multiplied the land mass by a factor of 5, and increased the number of quests by about a factor 1.5.  You need to use OpenMw in order to use Tamriel rebuilt, because otherwise, expanding the real estate by a factor of 5 causes the map on the original Morrowind engine to malfunction.
The downside of using OpenMw is that Steam does see your gameplay, or make online copies of your saves for you.  I do hope that Steam or Bethesda one day accomodates OpenMw and Tamriel rebuilt, because it is really ready to go.  Steam - meet OpenMw meet Tamriel Rebuilt meet Steam.  It would be that easy.  I would love to pay for a newly revamped version of Morrowind.  If Steam or Bethesda will accept this fan created engine and expansion, then I also hope that the do not ignore other fan created mods giving better looking bodies, grass, water etc.

Spore isn't Maxis's worst work..(SimHealth) but, it ranks amoung the bottom. When you buy Spore, you actually buy five mini games (emphasis on the mini). The five are single cell organism, creature, tribe, city and space.
You have to guide your being trough the five stages adding or, removing traits to make it suprior to the other organisms
-Single cell: This is the shortest stage in the game, but one of the best. You guide your organism trough the water finding food and defending yourself.
-ceature: This stage is wrinse and repeat. You go around finding other organisms and befriending them or, fighting them. You do that for 2 hours straight before advancing.
-Tribe: This is no doubt the worst part of the game. This stage acts as a lazily put togather RTS with no aperent goal.
_city: This stage is like a better version of tribe stage. There is more costomazation and, things to do. But, still isn't worth it.
-Space: It is obvious that your intented to spend most of your time in this stage. This stage is well put togather, and there is plenty to do.
Making a game of mini games but focusing most your effort on the last one is not a great idea. The first four stages are like an obsticle to get past, they're redundent. The last stage could have been a game by itself and it would'nt have been half-bad.
Some might like this type of game, but it isn't for me.

A roguelike platformer in a similar vein to Spelunky/Caveblazers, but set out in space in an asteroid, and you play as a squad of astronauts in bulky exo-suits loaded down with guns and explosives.
The Superfluous is a fair a bit slower paced then the two games mentioned, though. You get to control a squad [one active at a time, but swap out anytime] of spessmens that have varying talents and intended roles. Light weapons, Heavy weapons, Demolitions, Mining, Medic/Support, mix and match your members as you wish and set out to
explore the asteroid's vast cave system at your own pace.
It also has co-op if you have real friends that come over to play games with you. Sounds like a cool feature, I guess.
TL;DR
Play as a group of clumsy spessmans exploring a big rock with guns and explosives. Also, no ghost or penalty for being slow. So explore, mine, and genocide to your hearts content each level.

This title has taken a place on my wishlist very long.

This game takes on a seemingly light view towards the pretty dramatic subject of the poor survival rate bomber crews suffered during the 2nd World War, but actually manages to catch the core idea very very well.....surprisingly much so.

People would appreciate this game much more if they have a bit of background knowledge on the subject of WWII Lancaster bombers and it's rising challenges during the duration of the war dealing with the German forces who were getting better at countering the, for then pretty advanced, British Air Force bombing tactics.
All in all a game that is much more hardcore then it's kiddy style seems to reveal at first, and although pretty intense at times.... as soon as you return to base it's so easy to start a new mission again.

The game plays out very much like a familiar micro-management game that was based in the future and in space.
Yes, I'm talking about
. Bomber Crew isn't entirely like FTL as they have different unique selling points (USP) but share the same roguelike elements.
If you are interested in micro-management games, you would enjoy this but do not go into Bomber Crew with the mentality that it is like FTL as it is missing narrative and story elements to keep you invested in the world that it is Western Europe. It is a great game nonetheless, the music, the calm before the storm and the recovery after the chaos keeps me invested but that may only be me. If is your decision whether to get the game or not but I highly recommend it.
You as the player would take control of a Royal Air Force Avro Lancaster Heavy Bomber during the second world war and attempt to manage her crew while going on dangerous missions. There isn't much narrative in the game but what's interesting that it is quite historically accurate with women aviators and operations that actually took place during WW2. What's not quite historically accurate is that a single bomber is used to undertake those operations. I'm sure there would at least be a few hundred bombers to carpet bomb across Normandy during Operation Overlord and not just a single Lancaster.
I'm not one to know much about Fighters and Bombers at all so please forgive me.
I have yet to lose any of my crew as well as my bomber nor have I needed at any point to make an emergency landing or have my crew bail out. I played an extremely safe route by grinding for money and intel points to further upgrade my crew and bomber to ensure safe trips back and forth from home base (Yes, despite being in the Royal Air Force, you have to earn your own money in order to upgrade your bomber).
What I do know about the roguelike nature of Bomber Crew is that when a crew member gets heavily damaged, they will go into the downed state where they have to be treated by another crew member with a first aid kit. Leaving them in this state for 2 minutes would result in their death and their names will be recorded in the
in the main menu. If your current bomber is destroyed and or lost in the wild, you will be issued a new one which would have the default Mk1 equipment.
Bomber Crew plays very much like FTL in the sense that crew members would not do something until you tell them to do it. For example:
Gunners would sit idly in their Gun Turrets until you've marked enemy fighters using the periscope.
Engineers will not automatically repair malfunctioning systems until you tell them to.
Bomb Operators will not release bombs until you tell them to.
Etc, etc.
Unlike FTL, Bomber Crew's crew members are not exactly jack of all trades. Yes, Gunners can help repair systems but what I'm saying is that them crew members cannot improve in every skill. They are only allowed up to 2 different skill sets. The first skill set is selected through Recruitment. Your crew will have 7 members max and they have to satisfy the roles required for the Bomber to operate fully. You will need a Pilot, an Engineer, a Radio Operator, a Navigator, a Bomb Operator and two Gunners. When these Primary Skillsets reach a certain level, they can be trained to acquire a Secondary Skillset like Bomb Operators can become an Engineer, Gunners can administer first aid, etc.
I recommend having at least 3 crew with First Aid skills as when it maxes out at Lv 4, they can heal other conscious crew without the use of a medkit.
These skillsets are extremely important as you would need them in order to carry out successful critical missions like;
Navigator: Custom Markers placed - To avoid hazards such as Flaks, AA guns and more importantly Radars.
Navigate using Stars - Allow the navigator to still put out markers at High Altitude (Must be night time).
Engineer: Boost / Lean Fuel Mixture - Increase speed and usage rate or decrease speed and usage rate respectively (To better manage fuel as it is a finite resource that constantly decreases).
Ontop of the skillsets of your crew members, you can outfit them with different equipment which can better protect them against damage from gunfire or the cold, survivability on the ground or sea (when your crew bails out or your aircraft crashes). Equipment also affects your crew member's speed and is generally traded out for armour or other stats.
I personally have 2 crew members; Engineer and Bomb Operator to have relatively lightweight equipment as they will be the ones running around the Fuselage repairing systems as they are both Engineers.
The mission objectives are something to take note of as your Lancaster can be outfitted to drop different types of munitions; Supplies, Grand Slam Bombs, Bouncing Bombs, etc.
Learning and knowing how to use them is crucial as some of them are used in missions like dropping a Grand Slam bomb to destroy a Flak Tower or using a Bouncing Bomb to destroy a german hydroelectric plant.
These are pretty simple to undertake as all you need to take note of is the requirements of the Bombs and the use of the Bombsight. Shouldn't be too hard, yeah?
There are also optional missions where you have to take a recon photo using the bombsight. Just fly over the site and snap a pic. Optional missions are pretty awesome as they grant you a stack of cash that is normally more than the regular pay of your main missions.
Sometimes, you can encounter enemy Ace pilots when undertaking missions. Though as a Bomber, you are not suppose to go head to head with an ace, they serve as an additional challenge that you have to pay attention to. Each and every ace pilot has their own unique themes and attack patterns. Some use incendiary ammo, some will fire rockets up your bum. When you meet these aces for the first time, they would arrive and ruin your day for a moment then proceed to retreat. You can choose to chase after them but during the second encounter, they would be more relentless and actually attempt to pull down your pants and twist your♥♥♥♥♥♥until it snaps off.
I'm not very sure what to call the art design of Bomber Crew. It makes everything seem cute and child friendly, that is until you fly across the channel into Dunkirk. It seems very much voxel like as the colours are vibrant and outstanding.
The sound design is also superb with the flak explosions in the distance and hearing enemy fighter engines. I was hoping to hear german Stukas but those aren't fighters, silly me. I could just play Day of Infamy for that.
Music is also very well done. It brings back memories of the older Medal of Honour games. The instruments used are generally symphonic (Confirmed by a friend who have spent years in a classical band) which blends very well with the combat in the game.
Personally, my favourite thing in the game is when your bomber gets shot up, you can see bullet holes in the shell and see into the fuselage. No matter how nice or golden your bomber is, you might as well get used to getting your fuselage shredded and riddled with bullets despite all of the armour you have. Burning engines, exposed fuel tanks can also happen which tells you that the bomber is in bad shape.
Bomber Crew is a breath of fresh air from all the controversy revolving triple A titles. I personally love the game and would play it every now and then in short bursts. Overall with the great sound design and art direction supported by the superb gameplay and connection you have with your bomber and her crew, I give this game an
.

You are the crew of a RAF heavy bomber. Take off, shoot down enemy planes, dodge flak, drop your bombs on the target, and make it home in one piece (more or less). Along the way use your XP and cash to train the crew, improve their gear, and upgrade your plane. Missions range from search and rescue in the English Channel to dropping heavy bombs on Berlin.
Overall, this is a fun game, though the campaign is relatively short. You must jump from station to station in the bomber, making decisions for the crew members at critical times during the missions. The graphics are whimsical, but the action is realistic without being graphic. It is very immersive; the first time you ditch your shot-up bomber in the North Sea you'll find yourself worrying that the crew members survive. Recommended.

NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
Note: The Superfluous is currently in Early Access. The version reviewed was current as of the date of this review (20161203).
The Superfluous is a two-dimensional action platformer with some rogue-like elements from new indie developer Voided Pixels.
The background story is amusing and sets the scene well for your task. You see, there's a large asteroid on a collision course with Earth, but it's not due to hit for a thousand years. You're part of a die-hard group that wants to destroy the asteroid to ensure that it won't cause destruction of the Earth, no matter how far in the future, and the group eventually receives enough funding to warrant a deep space voyage to the asteroid to destroy it. The game even keeps track of how long you have until the Earth is destroyed; it starts at a little over 365 237 days.
Graphics - The Superfluous uses 2D large-pixel graphics exclusively, adorned with coloured dynamic lighting, and it looks pretty darn good. It won't make you swoon or marvel at the graphics while you play it, but the characters are somewhat likeable and the enemies, though rather derivative, are mostly recognisable.
Weapons and explosions look a little boring, and there could definitely be a bit more variety in the scenery, but the game is set on a large asteroid cruising through deep space, so the atmosphere is appropriate.
Graphics settings are limited to windowed or full screen: no detail levels, special effects, or even resolution settings. But that's okay. The game achieves the look for which I assume the developer was striving, and it all works pretty well.
Sound - Sound effects are okay, if nothing special. There are no voiceovers. Music is nice, but fairly limited. I've been playing for a couple of hours and haven't turned it off, so that has to say something.
Gameplay - The game plays like a cross between a twin-stick shooter and a typical action platformer. It has full controller support, or you can use mouse and keyboard, but in either mode you move about with the left hand and control the aiming direction of your weapon with the right.
The stated full controller support is present, but it's awkward and hard to use. For some unexplained reason the developer has chosen some very odd controls that aren't all in keeping with conventions, and they just don't work very well. To begin with, in the menus you have to select items by pressing the right stick. This is only a minor annoyance, but navigation would be so much easier using the 'A' button for selection and 'B' for cancellation, like pretty much every other game with controller support. But worse, the in-game controls then use the 'AXYB' buttons for controlling gun direction/aiming, when it would be so much better to use the right stick, again like pretty much every other game with independent weapon controls. Keyboard controls are a bit better, but I'd prefer to use the mouse for aiming and left and right mouse buttons for shooting my weapons, instead of everything using the keyboard. And the game doesn't seem to allow setting up your own control configurations, either.
Once you manage to overcome the control difficulties, though, the game is quite fun, if rather challenging. You start each level in a cave within the asteroid and need to reach the exit at the bottom, killing aggressive creatures and collecting loot as you go.
Enemies are mostly a bit derivative and some seem a bit out of place. For example, I can't help but wonder why there are crabs on an asteroid in interstellar space, but there they are, regardless. But they do their jobs well enough, most often causing considerable pain frustration on your journey.
Before each level you choose up to two squad members to go on each mission and you can swap between them at will with a key or button press during the game. To begin with you only have three squad members from which to choose, but there are more that can be unlocked, if you can manage to play well enough to beat a level or two. Each character has predefined stats and primary and secondary weapons or abilities. Some primary weapons and explosion-related secondary weapons (e.g. grenades) actually damage the level geometry, allowing you to reach otherwise unreachable places. And never mind about getting stuck: the unlimited jetpack equipped by each character can be used to escape from even the deepest hole.
The touted rogue-like elements include procedural level generation, which works quite well, though enemy types seem very limited; permadeath, requiring you to start again from the beginning when you die (albeit with clones of the same characters available); and unlockables that last across deaths and restarts, such as new characters and character upgrades. There's a notable lack of any cool loot, though, and the game itself tells you that character upgrades aren't effective enough to make a big difference. A bestiary would be nice, though, especially if it lasted across multiple play throughs, and would fit in with the story well enough.
The game includes three worlds ('biomes'), but at this stage only the first one is near completion. I'm not sure how they tie in with the backgound story, but given the rest of the background story, I'd expect there to be at least a tongue-in-cheek reason to be provided for their existence before release.
As far as Early Access issues are concerned, I found The Superfluous to be very stable, with no crashing issues or serious bugs. But the grammar is atrocious, to the point where it really lets the game down. The story is quite clever and could be amusing, but it falls flat with grammar and spelling errors, and a writer who doesn't know the difference between 'then' and 'than' or 'effect' and 'affect'. Hopefully the developer will have the game text professionally edited before release. Oh, and there seems to be no way to quit from in game or the main menu; I had to ALT-TAB and kill the process.
Pros:
+ Good background story with a sense of humour
+ Rogue-like elements are relatively well done
+ Trading Cards
Cons:
- Bad controls, on both keyboard and controller, with no reconfiguration screen.
- Very hard to get into.
- Terrible grammar.
Ultimately, The Superfluous doesn't really offer anything you haven't already seen before, but it does what it does reasonably well. It's overly difficult and a bit clunky in places, and it could definitely do with a rework of the control systems and some editing of the in-game text, but it is still in Early Access, so there's a chance these might happen before release.
If you're into challenging action platformers and enjoy some tongue-in-cheek humour, pick it up and give it a try.

This game is good. REALLY good.
I picked up Morrowind in 2014, and I just really got into it this year (2017). Even though this game is very old, it has everything I want for and RPG. It has my favorite character creation of any game that I've ever played. The simplicity of being able to select your playstyle by chosing the weapons and equipment you're going to be using, backed up with all the statistics and dice-rolls, creates this idea of actually role-playing a character. And being able to do what they're good at, and failing at what they're not good at.
Many dislike the combat in this game, saying the "Pen-and-Paper RPGs don't belong in video games," but it makes sense and feels fair seeing that if you were very well-trained with a sword in your hand, why would you use a bow?
But the best thing about Morrowind has to be the world and the characters in it.
The culture in Morrowind is more fleshed out then any other game I've played. To my surprise I was truely facinated learning about the different Houses in the game, and how their arcitecture changes based off of the enviornment they rule over. I was really eager to meet the Ashlanders, and see how their nomadic lifestyle differed from the citizens on the inhabitable places on Vvardenfell.
There are way more NPCs in Morrowind compared to Skyrim or Oblivion (Granted, in Morrowind they're not voice-acted). Each character talks like a real person. And they don't praise and worship you the second you start (similar to how they do in Skyrim). You have to earn your title as hero.
Even the lore is better than any modern Elder Scrolls game. Each conversation can lead you down a rabbit-hole of backstory and history about the people in Morrowind, and I found myself selecting every dialogue option to learn about the Nerevarine, the history and relationship between the Temple and Imperial Cult, and heratige of the Ashlanders.
Remember, you are not playing as yourself, you are playing as the character you created.
If you go into Morrowind with that mindset, I promise you, it will not let you down.

If enjoy the general gameplay of Bethesda RPGs and the world of Elder Scrolls, then you need to play this game.
Get it, install the Overhaul-mod, and enjoy graphics that will still be good enough for today (including foliage that reacts to the player, something that not even Skyrim had).
It is more "number-mechanics in the background" than the recent ones, especially with character development, but with that comes more freedom for experimentation. Character-choice is more meaningful, not just because of math but general world logic (for example, beast races can't wear boots as they actually walk like digitigrade animals).
Guilds are more realistic as you don't just have a simple quest-line, but have to rank up, including your actual skill (some guild members won't even talk to you beforehand). Besides the basic guilds you can also join political houses and the world reacts accordingly, adding more depth and immersion.
I could go on and on, but basically all the praise and other reviews are right: this game is a milestone, and still holds up more than you'd expect.

For anyone wanting to revolutionize their living room PC gaming, this is well worth the current $2.99 asking price.  Before buying this I had cobbled together a sometimes-working solution for using a gamepad for desktop navigation and control with autohotkey scripts, Joy2Key, and a lot of profanity...  Then I saw this in the store and figured I could spare three bucks to try it out, so I bought it.
Turns out, this just works, so incredibly well.  It disables itself automatically when a program or game goes fullscreen, and you can easily toggle it back on if you need it.  I have slightly modified the default key bindings and added an alt+F4 shortcut using the bumpers so that when I'm in a non-steam, non pc-friendly / controller aware game (or console emulator *cough*), I can easily exit back out and get back to big picture mode.  As an added bonus, this also enables you to use non-steam aware versions of media apps, like the windows 8 netflix or hulu apps, with your controller.
If you want to be able to use this to navigate 'protected' system stuff, like task manager (or the windows 8 on-screen keyboard...go figure), make sure and go find the executable, right-click it and go to properties -> compatibility tab -> then select 'run this program as an administrator' - then you can use your gamepad to kill 'stuck' programs if need be.
To the devs - thank you so much for making this - we've needed something like this for a long time.
To alienware - You guys need to put THIS on your alpha instead of whatever you're using now, this is way better than your 'baked-in' solution, and way less frustrating to deal with (which is why I uninstalled it all almost immediately and went with the AHK / J2K home-grown method).
To Steam - can you add a few more 'yes' buttons for your 'Do you recommend this software' selection?  I need more than just one for this.
To everyone else - buy this.  It's way worth it.

Call me crazy for dropping $3 on a program that does what Xpadder did for free.
See, for the price of a cup of coffee, I got a product that worked 'right out of the box'.
Some features that this program has over the likes of Xpadder:
1. It comes pre-loaded with an intuitive control scheme for the Xbox 360 controller, identical to what I'd set up myself using XPadder. It's worth looking into the settings at first just to be sure of what everything does, but it does pretty much everything you'd expect with buttons to spare.
2. You can change all of the bindings, and this software works from the controller first. In other words: with this you bind your macros to the buttons, whereas with the likes of Xpadder you assign buttons to existing keyboard inputs. It sounds like a small difference, but it means that this software is purpose-built to let you control your computer with a controller.
3. This program sits in the system tray (out of sight) and automatically disables itself when you start playing games. It also has your Xbox button bound to Steam Big Picture. This means that right from the moment you install it, you can launch Big Picture mode and transition seamlessly into and out of controller-enabled games. I'm pretty sure that with some fiddling, you can bind certain button combinations to automatically start Netflix or pull up Google for a quick search.
That's why I was willing to pay for this software, and I think that you should too if you're someone interested in couch gaming. It's much easier to use than the available free software, and it comes with enough functionality to do just about anything you want.

Brothers is an amazing game. I played it a while back and wrote a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥review that didn't really portray how much I enjoyed this game. A few of the generalized points about why I love it:
First, the graphics. The use of the Unreal Engine 3 is really taken advantage of, with some incredible lighting and unbelievable physics. It is a very colorful game that is very immersive.
Second, the controls. The fact that I prefer a controller helped in appreciating the gameplay a lot more. In this game, one controls both brothers - at the same time. That's right, no switching back-and-forth between them. It is why a controller is required (though I've heard of people using keyboards somehow), because you need the two joysticks. When controlling both brothers at the same time, it is noticable that the older brother has assets while the younger brother is weak.
Third, the storyline. There are not many games that are able to choke people up (emotionally). This is one game that was, at the very least, able to choke me up (even if it was just at the end). The story is about a widowed ill father, and about his two sons travelling far and wide to reach a cure. When the characters talk in the game, it is an unknown language. But even when people do not speak the same language, when they feel strongly about something and speak to you anyways, you may just understand what they said.
In the end, this is a very nice game. Personally, having a brother that only shares a mother with me, I couldn't understand the full extent of their emotion.

If you're trying to get this game to work on something with a high DPI (what Apple would call retina) display, it may crash. If it does, make a short-cut to it on your desktop, go into the properties of the short-cut, select the "Compatibility" tab, check the box labeled "Disable display scaling on high DPI settings", and then click OK. If this was your problem, the game will run fine when you use the short-cut and scale itself automatically (I think THQ implemented it with vectorized graphics and text anyway). It would be nice if Steam could do this for folks with older games in which it's necessary, although this may be one of the few.

I bought the "Best Friends Forever Double Pack" for my girlfriend and myself and we absolutely love it. The double pack is an amazing deal, only adding two dollars to the regular price for an extra copy of the game. It's a perfect gift for a girlfriend/boyfriend/bestfriend and so on, at a price that is a real steal. The art style in game is simplistic and beautiful and very cute to say the least. With a pleasant and calming soundtrack and smooth yet challenging level design the game is relaxing while still making you think to progress through it. The levels and "worlds" increase in difficulty, adding twists in each world that add a new layer to the gameplay. Just make sure you and whoever you play with have good communication skills and are up for a challenge, but most of all just enjoy the game. It's much easier to progress with a cool head and by letting the rhythm of the level and the momentum of the moves you use to solve each puzzle advance you forward. I would highly recommend this game to anyone really but especially couples who like a fun challenge.

I have to say I just found this game, and it's what I've been looking for as I love mining/building games.  However, I will say that I don't like most games, so my tastes in games are very different than most people.  Which means, it might not be a game for you.  It's very sand boxy where you build your own realms / spheres / worlds and visit those areas built by others.   It reminds me of Windborne in this manner.  There are only minimal game provided areas - Cubic Town Center, Cubic Lobby, Cubic Learning Center, an Adventure World (tutorial), and multiple Mines (to get resources for building), so you have to rely on the other players to provide entertainment or economy realms.  There are daily quests, where you can earn in game currency for completing them; however, there is not a detailed quest line built per se.  There are some other quests that also act as a bit of a continued tutorial, but there aren't that many quests at this point.
There are a lot of childish players, so you have to be very careful. If you go through the tutorial adventure, go through the learning center and read a bit of the forums you will get plenty of warning about scammers, so be mature and don't fall for them instead of whining about them or saying the game itself is 'scamming' you.  It's not.  Be smart and protect yourself.  Wait to make friends instead of friending everyone right off the bat.  Turn your realm settings to only let yourself build there.  I personally turned off access to my realm until I got it to a point that I was willing to share it.  However, I made sure to not enable others to build in my primary realm, so they can't destroy my creations as there are always griefers in all games. So there are ways to protect yourself in game with the settings which include blocking other players from your realm.  Use those controls!
Prices for the game provided items seem pretty reasonable for the things you can't gather yourself.  Especially since you can mine for in game currency (cubits), so you don't have to pay to play.  You get a cubit for approximately every 20 blocks you mine.  It's not much, but you can slowly earn enough to make a store or from other player purchases via cash registers in game. I eventually see myself building a small store to sell things to make more cubits  If you want it all now, you can purchase cubits, but you don't need to purchase cubits to play the game.  There is also a simple daily quest which provides you 50 cubits if you complete it (do it daily for a month and that's about 1500 free cubits just from the quests).  Apparently they also have a number of game sponsored contests where you can win cubits as well (though they typically require an entry fee of 5000 cubits which you get back at the end of the contest). It seems like a very generous game with ways to get in-game currency.
While their news feeds and blogs seem a bit outdated, it appears that they are still building this game as they are talking about a new release of material this summer.  From this page, it says it is still open beta, so that means it is still in development.  A lot of the game seems to have a volunteer staff (apparently most of the mods are volunteers), so it seems to be on the players rather than the developers to keep up with some of the PR things. While the wiki is a bit outdated, that seems to be on all the players, as anyone can be providing input to a wiki, but I guess people are playing rather than updating the online documentation.  One look at the overworld maps, and you can see the game has an active community, as individual realms are supposed to disappear off the map (they still exist and you don't lose any of your stuff, but you will need to stake out a new location when you return) after at least a week of inactivity.
I will say, it can be a bit confusing at first, and I still have a lot to learn as I've only been playing for a few days; however, this is also the nature of a beta as documentation typically lags behind development.  The list of recipes posted by the game developers seems pretty comprehensive.  However, it can be a bit of a pain to find what you are looking for on the list as some of the recipes are rather complex (which speaks to the depth of the development thus far).  The initial adventure is pretty good as a tutorial, but the player needs to know that it's okay to bale out of it after you get to the mayor portion as it becomes rather advanced at that point (a lot of parkour skills needed, IMO).  It keeps warning you if you try to leave, and I think they need to make it a bit more obvious that after the first part and the 'scamming' lesson, that you have learned the basics and can start to build since you've learned the basic skills (and come back later if you want to finish it and work on those advanced skills).  Also, right now there isn't a good way to figure out the clans, so it's hard to tell which to join due to similar interests / game styles and which to avoid.  Finally, the game camera angle sometimes leaves a bit to be desired as I'd like the option to go more horizontal sometimes.
One of the best guides I found for the game is drewbiscus' Mining Guide here on steam.  Highly recommend reading it BEFORE you start to play and follow the tips as you will start far ahead of the curve as mining is one of the primary skills for this game.  If you are smart and mine down to the base in your realm, you can then start building up.  And if a 17 x 17 space isn't enough room initially, rather than buying a new room or realm, remember the starter realm can be built up to 80 blocks high...so build UP.  You can get at least 3-4 more levels if you build them about 20-25 blocks apart (which is far enough to not block the visual angle when you are on one of the lower levels). You can either craft/build ladders or use clouds or just water to build a way to get to the upper levels ('swimming' up the water is my favorite way to change levels).  You can also purchase portals to move between the layers, but you don't have to do this right away if you don't have the cubits (or are trying to save them for other things).
You really don't HAVE to purchase cubits if you are patient and enjoy the basics of the game - mining, building, decorating, crafting, individual economies.  However, if you enjoy the game, you should, at some point, want to purchase some cubits to support the developers of the game.
In general, the game itself seems pretty solid even if it is beta. Yea, there are immature players and griefers, but you get that in any game, especially free to play games. Don't judge the game itself because of the bad people playing it.  The key is finding other long term, mature, solid players to hang out with, and ignore/don't feed the immature ones.  I am enjoying the game thus far, but I like non-violent, sandboxy, building games.

A thorough tactical FPS game that is uniquely broad in scope encompassing many aspects of other genres such as RTS.
The learning curve may be a little steep for mastery of all of the game's functional characteristics and quirks, but 20 minutes of tutorials will grant sufficient experience for primary gameplay.
This program represents the closest approximation to real-life warfare I have yet encountered - or at least what we can imagine an actual battlefield would be like.
Rather than focusing on raking in points, this game leans toward tactical awareness in vast open-world environments where the main goal is to capture towns in a strategically dynamic environment - cooperatively with other players and non-player-characters.

And old relic of the last generation of PC's gaming titles. While titles like Portal 2 had the subtitle, "Best PC Game in Recent History" and Minecraft with "Most Successful Indie Game", SPORE stands with a very unique title...
"Most Hyped-Up Game in Recent History".
When dev companies built up hype engines for titles like Fable III, Watch_Dogs, and No Man's Sky I always rolled my eyes. Because after SPORE disappointed audiences on such a massive scale... who could be trusted? And, sure, SPORE wasn't the first big promise in gaming history. Don't you worry! I've got my targets set straight on Daikatana one of these days. I'll get to it soon enough. But for now, let's just talk about the little Life Simulator that Thought it Could.
SPORE was supposed to be the next step forward for Maxis and EA. Will Wright, the amazing creator of such smash series as SImCity and The Sims decided to make his latest game the next step forward in simulation gameplay: a game that simulates the history of life in a galaxy. You would be able to create a species and watch them evolve and develop into a civilization. But when it came out... it didn't quite live up to its expectations, as I'm sure most aged PC gamers know.
But that doesn't mean SPORE is a bad game. It's just disappointing.
SPORE is divided into 5 main segments in the development in your fully customizable species: Cell, Creature, Tribe, Civilzation, and Space. Each one is made with a significantly different gameplay style so I'll divide my analyses into little chunks as I did with Sonic Adventure DX. So...
CELL: Kind of boring, but not terrible. It's like a simple game of Pac-Man, but there's no maze and the ghosts are everywhere. You can choose to eat your fellow single-cell organisms to become a carnivore or eat microscopic bits of kelpt and other vegetation to become an herbivore. It's very simple and you evolve through it so quickly that I didn't really get much enjoyment out of it.
CREATURE: Pretty good. You get to control your species as nests of animals and you can choose whether to harmonize with other nests of creatures or devour them whole. The choice is pretty much the same as the last stage, but I can kind of understand. You're still an animal with nothing in mind for morality. That being said, the customization in this section is pretty limited. You can play as the creature you want to make, but the game ranks different parts and if you get a better body part it's often smarter to use that one. So you'll end up evolving with a creature that you made out of practicality, not out of creativity, which irked me somewhat.
TRIBAL: Worst stage in the game, but again... not bad. I hate this stage because it's very easy for your village to get torn down by other tribes and random animals that come by so you can never go to war with your full tribe because some other tribe might come in and destroy it. And, yet again, you can only choose to be civil or destructive. By now that seems like such a traditional moral value... but most tribes weren't that developed, so I'll give SPORE the benefit of the doubt. It's plays like a clunky RTS without too much strategy. Just gather food and attack/communicate with other tribes. It's not that hard.
CIVILIZATION: Pretty good. It's a very simple RTS and the AI is pretty rubbish, but there is some fun to be had. You can now customize buildings, cars, boats, and planes to your heart's desire and slowly building wealth and size as a planetwide empire- which ridiculously easy- is pretty fun. Again, you can choose to be hostile or civil by opening trade routes but NOW... you can violently convert opposing nations to your religion. Honestly, those three choices don't seem intricate enough to justify how societies develop and interact with other societies. It feels too simple, too easy.
SPACE: By far, the best. The game opens up to a massive galaxy and your morality is no longer an issue. You can open trade routes, attack nations, or do both and not worry about any consequences on your further evolved self. The galaxy is a bit repetitve but the joy of seeing your empire slowly grow to an unprecedented size was very unique for me. Also... f*** the Grox. Trying to get to the center of the galaxy was a pain in the a** because of those f***ers, and I personally want to talk to the person who got the achievement of wiping the Grox out, because I seriously think they might have half their brain missing.
The game looks very cartoony and appeals to younger audiences, despite dealing with ideas of the circle of life and you choosing to be violent or not with opposing forces. But the game does look nice. And the soundtrack is pretty great too. The only thing throughout the game that itches me a little is the Create-a-Creature program in the game. Sure, it's very detailed and the amount of things you can make in the game is nearly infinite... but it's still limited (even in creative mode!) You can only have so many parts on your creature and some body parts won't attach to others, such as hands or feet which bothered me a little. It kept me from making some truly grotesque monstrosities I had bubbling in the back of my brain, but oh well.
SPORE is decent in its execution, but it promised something so much more to audiences that the collective sigh of disapproval around the world was pretty well justified. But after nearly ten years of SPORE coming out, is it really that bad? No. It's still a fun look (but not exactly accurate) representation of evolution in a species and a civilization over time. If you want a creative game that'll give you plenty of hours to mess aroung with all of its features, let me just tell you I put in 17 hours in my first playthrough from all the tinkering I did, and I could certainly put in more and I might one day in the future. SPORE is still a good game, it's just not great. It's a fair 7/10.
