I'd compare it to reading a good book, really.
If you're not the type that's able to sit still for long enough to read a good book, you just won't be able to get into this game. The upshot of this delayed gratification (partly by design, partly by just being an old game), is that the enjoyment you can get out of this game is just so much more
The main storyline does a good job at hooking you in after a couple of main quests, and, from then on, creates this really eerie and unsettling atmosphere that blankets the whole world.
It's an experience that's very unique to Morrowind. And, if you are the type of person that appreciates these sort of characteristic atmospheres and rich worlds, you will, of course, love Morrowind.
However, if you are coming to this game from Skyrim, you will not necessarily enjoy Morrowind just because you enjoyed Skyrim. There are a couple of reasons why:
Its gameplay is very different. The combat will take you some getting used to -- swinging a sword in Morrowind is based on your skill level, and, even though you may make contact with the enemy, you will, most of the time, miss. In theory, its supposed to make the combat a little bit more "Dungeons and Dragonsy", but, in practice, it involves just spamming your sword over and over really fast so you can hit your enemy. There are mods to "fix" this, for those who can't tolerate it, but, be warned, those mods really screw up the durability system in the game. (and I'm sure there's a fix for that too, but then that's just a modding hassle). Personally, I don't mind it. You just have to get used to it.
Secondly, you gotta be able to read. Obviously, being an old game, there was less space for having fully voiced characters, so they had to rely on text. This isn't a problem to me. So much of the enjoyment of this game, atleast in my time, has been from just talking to scholars/savants, learning about the world, getting the chills when you uncover some kinda secret about a person, and solving some of the interesting (in my opinion) problems between people-- this is something that you might overlook if you're unable to sit down and just read. There is a lot more that you can get out of this game than just "hack n slash" and "loot grabbing" (that is, of course there to accompany everything else, though)
Let's see, I think that's everything I have to say about this game... Oh, yeah. If you do buy this game, and get bored wandering around, do the main quest. It's not ♥♥♥♥♥♥ (unlike Skyrim, imo). And it really hooks you in. Stay away from spoilers if you can, don't go on wikis and read about stuff obviously haha, that's a mistake I made. But oh well.
I would personally recommend this game to anyone who enjoys characteristic narratives, retro RPG gameplay, and anyone who's on a budget PC and can't run heavier more flashier games
There is a lot of enjoyment you can get out of this game even though its old. Infact, you may even be charmed by it.

I really like this one compared to the later ones in the elder scroll series.
1- No object physics, this means you can do housing properly without worrying about your setup falling apart.
2- No content scaling, meaning that if you know where that deadric sword is and can get to it no matter your level, you have it.
3- You can eat everything! Scrib jelly! Metal bars! Precious stones! Ectoplasms!
4- Spell creation too combine every available effect from other spells.
5- Levitation and jump spells, to go where your heart desire.
6- Extensive guild questlines. Starter quests are mundane and feel like you are working for the guild, you don't get guildmaster so easily! You have to climb up the ranks from doing chores to helping the guild in more meaningful ways.
Things I don't like and got changed later in the series.
1- Negative effect potions are useless since you cannot use them on others.
2- Animal races cannot wear helm and boots.

A couple of funny things that happened to me -
An engine dies and needs repairing. I walk my engineer out onto the wing, but while he's there three bogies pop up. I use evasive movements to avoid their fire TOTALLY forgetting about my poor engineer.

Another - I got shot up REALLY BAD in a mission. There were large chunks out of the side of the plane, but I managed to get it back. A nice little Dungeon adventure/RPG that I am thoroughly enjoying. It has a casual essence, without getting too hardcore, nor too repetitive.

I like roguelikes so I don't mind a challenge. Losing characters after they die for the duration of a dungeon? Fine. Enemy encounters where the odds are stacked against me? Okay. Constantly being screwed over by the RNG? That's just a hazard of the genre.
Calling Dungeon Rushers a roguelike or even a roguelite would be an insult to those genres, however, because it fails to deliver the satisfying feeling of being able to progress after trying and trying again. The climb is just too grindy to be any fun.
If anything, Dungeon Rushers is a linear mobile RPG masquerading as a dungeon crawler. You enter dungeons from the map and, upon beating one, the next one in line will spawn.
You also have access to a store and a forge; the former allows you to purchase equipment, potions, and materials from a very limited list of 10 and the latter allows you to craft items from materials gathered during your dungeon dives. Unfortunately, the selection in the store is crap. It was a good idea to make it so that the selection changed every time you entered a dungeon, but a not so good idea to make it so that you can only purchase one of each item. You'll frequently run out if potions as a result since you can only buy one and a dungeon run will require you to use three or four.
It's a good thing you can craft to supplement that number, right?
Wrong. Crafting suffers from the same issue that the shop does: you never seem to have enough of the materials you need to craft the essentials and going through the same dungeon again and again with the hope of getting more materials typically yields ones you don't need. So, you'll have plenty of accessories and weapons, but your potion stock will continue to dwindle.
This becomes especially problematic because you don't have any healing spells when you start out and the only way to treat status effects like poison and burning--which will constantly be applied to your units by two of the five or six types of skeleton enemies you'll keep seeing--is with beer. Beer is craftable, but if you lack the ingredients--and you will!--then these skills that slowly inflict damage over time will be the death of your party again and again.
The final point in this trifecta of "why this isn't fun" is the dungeons themselves, which isn't great considering you spend the majority of your time in them. Dungeons are a series of panels, covered in the fog of war, that you'll move to by clicking. The fog disperses to show you either empty space, an altar that will give you a random (usually negative) buff, treasure chests, switches that open locked doors, the exit, or more often than not--enemies. You can't run from combat, so if you come to an enemy that out guns you, you lose everything gained during your run and start over. That means whatever garbage materials you found and what little experience you earned is lost--including any potions you used in a futile attempt to save yourself. Talk about insult to injury because now you have to grind for materials in order to get more potions.
Dungeons are the exact same layout every time you run them and that lack of variety is mind numbing considering you're expected to play them again and again. The exp. you get is so low that it's frustrating because you only have basic equipment available to craft and in the store and the only other way to get stronger is to--you guessed it--grind.
The dungeons give you a chance to win some extra exp. by completing challenges, but these often render you so weak (don't use potions AND fight every enemy and other such combinations) that you have no chance of completing all three and getting out in one piece.
It feels like a badly done mobile port: tap, tap, tap/grind, grind, grind. Only, in a mobile game you could probably pay money for materials and avoid the tedious grind. The fact that they're charging 14.99 for this in its current state is ludicrous. Nothing much has changed in the past few months of its Early Access stint.
There’s an online aspect of the game where you can build dungeons and share them with others, but there isn’t much of a community to speak of. Much like the dungeons in the game, you build mazes with enemies and traps and not much else. There’s no exploration and nothing to do other than to try to find the exit before you get killed.
.Pros,
.Cons.
.Bottom Line.
This game isn't challenging--it's frustrating. A lot of the mechanics work together in the worst of ways, screwing you over and making the enemy impossible to beat without an insane amount of grinding.
Avoid until updates revolve around game balance rather than adding skins that they can charge for and adding online game modes for which there is no player base. The last update that worked on balance was January 23rd and it only made the heroes weaker while leaving enemies untouched.

Brothers isn't necessarily an uplifting game; to compare it to a fairytale is to evoke the original meaning of that term, the one designed to scare small children. Some grim things occur in the course of the brothers' quest. But the brothers' commitment to their goal and to each other is so strong, the various parts of this game so superbly crafted and woven together; that it's hard not to feel deeply touched when you finally reach the end of the road and see how deftly this game marries its gameplay to its themes in a way few have before.
If you're the sort of person who thinks video games are capable of not just entertaining us but also making us think and feel, you owe it to yourself to play Brothers.

Simple, elegant, and engaging. Brothers is a fairytale adventure in the tradition of The Neverending Story. If you enjoy games like Ico then this is definitely for you. You control both eponymous brothers in their journey to save their father. Only by leveraging each boy's strengths can you complete the adventure.
Despite the note on the Steam store page for this game, you can play it with your keyboard only but it is quite awkward. A controller is highly recommended. I use an Xbox-style controller and it works beautifully. The left analog stick controls the older brother's movements and the left trigger allows him to interact with objects in the environment. The right analog stick and trigger control the younger brother. And these four simple controls unlock a sweeping, high adventure.
Sit back, dim the lights, and immerse into an elegant, emotional odyssey.

I'm glad games like Brothers are being made. Unfortunately, Brothers doesn't fulfill its promise of heartache and adventure.
Brothers felt too slight to earn any of its emotional moments -- moments I wish I could have loved -- leaving me cold and confused by their failure to inuit purpose in an otherwise charming fantasy world. For a game convinced of its own theatrics and empathy, there was little tacit characterization delivered through its gameplay and broad, if uneventful narrative arch. And its controls, while applied interestingly enough, were troublesome and clumsy, turning moments of real emotional struggle into fighting with the game itself. In short, Brothers is simple, not elegant.
People keep making the argument that Brothers told a "moving story through its controls and level design" (Kotaku). Actually, that would be Journey, a truly epic yet subtle experience. That's the gold standard for games like this, and I don't believe Brothers made the grade.

A challenging, fun game with potentially nerve-wrecking moments but lots of enjoyment in store.
Bomber Crew has a cute and pleasing visual style and excellent pacing. Fairly easy to learn and get used to, without becoming tedious or tiresome.
If I would have any complaint it would be that sometimes a particular mission you thought would be hellish turns out to be a milk run (especially if you play optimally) and other times a mission you were confident you could cruise through becomes an encounter with doom as you find yourself frantically juggling desperate efforts to keep wounded crew members alive, a freezing pilot struggling to evade a hail of bullets and a hydraulic malfunction, all the while you'd be flying blind in a burning, bullet-riddled ruin and-- yupp, those were two of our engines that just straight up fell off into the Atlantic...
...But I'd be lying if I didn't also say that those moments are hilariously fun and exciting.
This game is not for the faint of heart - there are a hundred things happening at the same time and all of them need your immediate attention. In many ways, this is a multitasking simulator and almost a mental test of fortitude under pressure.
There's a thin line between exciting challenge and plain frustration, but I'd say this game manages to fly above that line for the most part - at least until the pilot freezes and the engines just give out and the engineer has to physically climb out onto the wing and repair it while Jerry is coming up with machine gun fire that takes out the navigator...

The art-style is deceptively cute; this game gets INTENSE. Extremely challenging, and I occasionally wonder where I screwed up (managing fuel is a little tricky at times), but it's SO satisfying to just barely make it home after a successful mission.

Hello,

1) When you win a fight, and collect reward, you are often ripped off out of your loot. Rinse and repat through your lineup till you or enemy is dead. Sounds simple right? NOPE. Here is why. Your team is on left on screen, enemies on right. I've played the game for, I think, 1000 hours when I was younger, but on a non-Steam-version. I've never had the DLCs.
Now I bought Spore and all it's DLCs on Steam-Sale and started to play again.
It's such a great game, but also has some flaws. The idea of Spore is AMAZING!
But sadly in some stages, the developers didn't put enough effort in it. I think the most developed stage is the last one, where you can travel the whole galaxy. It's amazing how big the galaxy is and I loved terraforming planets to make them able to be inhabited by creatures or to enlarge my empire. I've also always tried to get friends of the Grox (biggest empire in the Space-stage), or even trying to beat them (I've never beaten them, it's too difficult...)
The second most developed stage is the second one, where you can develop you own creature, communicate with other ones and explore the planet.
The other stages, I have to admit, are a little short, especially the first one, where you are only a cell.
It's so much fun to create species, there are many body-parts and many possibilities to combine and even more with the DLC "Creepy and Cute". But Sometimes you wish for even more body-parts, maybe some more exciting, or that there are other possibilities for putting them on you species. For example, making things bigger, having scarier mouths, and beeing able to put more parts on your species body than you are allowed now.
That's why there are many mods, that make the creating of species much more interesting and sooo great. Go to Youtube and serach for "Spore creations" and you'll know what I mean.
I'd love to see a Spore 2 where all those flaws are fixed and the developers really put effort in. Many people would probably buy this because they had so much fun with the first one.
But sadly after, I think, 9 years, they probably won't develop a Spore 2 and we have to keep playing the fist game.
Even though Spore is not the newest game anymore, you should give it a try, because it really can be fun.

Fantastic!!!  Describing this game as a beautiful marriage between creative game physics and elegant gameplay doesn't really do it justice.  Sure, it has the child-like charm of an other-worldly candyland platformer (Kirby's Dreamland) combined with counter-intuitive game mechanics that constantly challenge your battle-tested gamer reflexes and force you to always play with your cerebral cortex in overdrive (say... Portal?)  But, let's be honest:  It's not like this is the first game to use inverted gravity in a platformer (although the mandatory co-op feature is a cool spin on the idea).  The real genius of this game is in its simple elegance.  The controls are intuitive (even when the physics are not), and the ultra-stripped down minimalist shapes that comprise not only the backgrounds, but even the game's nebulous protagonists could have come off as childish or unambitious, but instead seem to be exactly what the game calls for; a beautiful but unassuming graphical landscape that leaves the brilliant puzzles nothing to hide behind.  I could (and did) get lost in this game for hours, and can't wait to go back for more.
All that for $10?  Buy this game right now.

Morrowind has also the most choices, being able to complete the game's main quest with or without the "essential" npcs living (there are no "downed" npcs in this game! Perma-death for everyone!).

Dated, but still better than Skyrim and WORLDS better than Oblivion.  It's not yet another fantasy europe RPG like most of use have become accustomed to.  It's an alien feeling world where nomadic tribes survive in the ashen wastes surrounding a volcano steeped in unique mythology.  You have the open world feel of the sequels, but with more world building and culture.  You can work for guilds, armies, great houses, earn the right to build your own house, find countless hidden artifacts.  Honestly, I started tracking down a quest line once that I stumbled upon by accident and didn't hit the internet for years after its initial release.  Thats the level of detail that goes into this.  The gameplay will annoy many as most of your actions are most based on rolls and chance than your skill as a player.  Charcter building takes getting used to and can be extremely frustrating to some, but the pay off is endlessly worth it.  My xbox version no longer runs but has well over 400 hours on it.

Writing this review just after I've unlocked 100% of the Steam Achievements. Took me 55 hours to do that.
It is an enjoyable dungeon-crawler game, where each little dungeon can be considered a bit like a rogue-like experience If the whole party dies, you need to attempt the individual dungeon again from scratch (No saving during a dungeon run.)
Following the rogue-like genre, your party grows in experience as each dungeon is bested, and you gain more equipment that stays with you.for later dungeons. The bested dungeons, owned equipment and character ranking are the things that get saved automatically as you progress.
Positives:
Diverse selection of equipment.
Pick and choose armour, weapons, magic items to customise each character.
Crafting items from components.
Grow the party of adventurers over time, and later select which ones go on a dungeon run.
As you traverse the map, the scenery and monsters changes.
Different monsters require different strategies to combat effectively.
Each character has a skill-tree, and you can pick and choose the skills to practice.
Negatives:
** The game becomes fairly same-y and grindy after a few hours play. ** (This is a MAJOR issue.)
Would have liked there to be more strategy within the game play. (i.e. useful strategy rather than just adopting a most efficient way to go forward. Most of the fights play out very similar to one another, once you know what you're doing.)
Characters max out at level 10, even before all the skills have been chosen. No way to complete skill-tree.
It's a good game, a fun game, certainly worth playing for some hours. However, it does lose its appeal fairly quickly. I wouldn't recommend going for it unless you like the dungeon-crawler rogue-like genre, and can stomach a somewhat grindy game-play, with limited strategic possibilities. Would probably suit a more casual gamer, who like to play small chunks of game-play, e.g. 15 minutes here, 30 minutes there.

First off, a huge thank you to the developer for providing me with a promotional copy of this game for review purposes.
I played this game for around 15 hours, both on-stream and offline. It isn't the best game I've ever played, but it's also far from the worst. It does have a few bugs here and there, and quite a few typos in the text, but nothing game-breaking. The main negative I take from the game is that the game is really grindy. Even after playing 15 hours, I still wasn't able to "beat" the game. I got up to Platinum League and started getting wrecked, so I just got tired of the grinding and got bored. The bandits are horribly annoying, especially when starting out, but the option is there to remove them, which is a huge plus. I can agree with others that you only really need one good gladiator to progess.
Another glaring negative is that the tutorial isn't very helpful, and a lot of the game concepts are not explained very well. I had played around 10 hours before I figured out how to upgrade my school and hire extra staff. The tutorial could certainly use work.
I was unable to figure out what the purpose of the beast pen was. I received a couple of beasts as rewards for pit fights, but the only thing I could figure out to do with the beasts was send them into fights, which they lost horribly and died. I can only guess that this feature of the game has not yet been fully implemented.
It does appear that the devs are still updating the game, so this might be one to keep an eye on. Hopefully they wil be able to fix the issues and further polish the game.
All in all, I enjoyed the game and don't regret playing it. I would recommend this game as a sale purchase if you enjoy tycoon or management-style games.

PS: Happy new year.

Clustertruck, like the steam bio says, is a platformer where you jump on trucks in a "the floor is lava" style race to the finish. It took me about four hours.
Let's start off with the mechanics. This game is all about mechanics, and they pull through. The 3D platforming has a frantic feel that is somewhat common in the genre. The controls are pretty smooth, though the speed of the player's motion made it pretty difficult to actually hit the mark with certain platforms sometimes. Other than that, everything worked: jumping on trucks in midair worked better than I expected, and the special abilities really added to gameplay as well.
Of course, there is no story to speak of, but instead of a weakness, I think it makes the game special. Clustertruck knows it's just a silly platformer whose purpose is to entertain us for a few hours. It really gets into the spirit of classic gameplay in that way, for which I have nothing but respect.
Now, the art. The backgrounds (read: none) and the textures (very simple) could probably have been a bit more detailed, but the simplicity of it all lent something to the player's concentration. It's not a weakness, but it's not really a strength either. The designers made a choice to keep things simple and that works for them.
Finally, the music and sounds! I was really impressed with the upbeat, electronic soundtrack throughout the games multiple worlds. Each world had a different song, a slightly different feel, but each song still felt energetic and conveyed that frantic feel that the game needed. And let's not forget the sound for landing on a truck which were satisfyingly solid.
This is definitely a good game. It's absolutely worth the $15, though I got it on sale for less. For sure worth the 4 hours (minimum, without going for challenges and other fun extras) that you get out of it. As my brother said, it's "just a wholesome classic game."

Cute characters, great art, horrible puzzles.
The "Super Mario Galaxy" of traditional Sierra / LucasArts style adventure games has your characters walking around circular planetoids. Unfortunately, the puzzles they encounter are so illogical that a guide is absolutely required to make progress. Some locations even exist purely to confuse the player, and serve no true purpose. It's a real shame.
I judge games by their gameplay, and Tales of Cosmos fails miserably, falling into all the bad habits of the old adventure genre, with bizarre solutions that no human being could ever guess. Even if you intend to randomly try things for hundreds of hours, sometimes you have to try the "thing" on the "thing" multiple times before you get the desired outcome with no feedback. "Try every object on every object, then try it again" is the marching order, and even then you're unlikely to ever make some of the logical leaps. Out of frustration, you will launch your slow spacecraft for another planet to see if you missed something, and watch your characters shuffle in slow motion, like geriatrics, around this beautiful scenery. For some solutions, you have to do the "thing" at the right time. How likely are you to make that leap? To stand in the same room, doing nothing, waiting for an event to happen? Not likely.
The character movement is extremely slow, and flying between planets takes far too long as well. It feels like planets were placed a fair distance away from each other to artificially extend gameplay. Even the old Sierra adventures had game-speed controls.
I would like to recommend it, because it is extremely cute and contains great art and animations (I love it when the little puppy fogs up his space helmet from panting). These characters deserve a better game. If you want to play through a short, cute adventure using a walkthrough (there is a steam community guide, thank god), go for it, but if you like to solve puzzles on your own, this romp through the cosmos will infuriate you.

I ruptured a disc in my neck in 2010 that, obviously, required surgery.  I have suffered with right arm/shoulder/neck pain ever since.  It can get especially bad after spending all day at work on the computer and then coming home for more PC action that evening.  Games like Starcraft 2 have become impossible for me to play because I cannot intensely hunch over a mouse and keyboard for any extended time any more (like more than 10 minutes).  Just surfing the net can be bothersome.  Needless to say, I have been eagerly awaiting the Steam Controller to be released so I can play games and surf the internet from a controller.
At least half of what I want has arrived.  This app is really cool.  I can now search for something to watch on the internet without feeling a bunch of pain.  Getting me away from the mouse/keyboard during internet surfing should actively help to reduce the amount of pain I feel, hopefully allowing me to get back to some more intense mouse/keyboard games at some point.  I highly recommend this app.  I will be using this product every day until the Steam Controller comes out and (hopefully) is even better.

Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is exactly as the title suggests, the story of two boys, connected by the bonds of brotherhood, unified in their quest to find a cure for their dying father (this is relayed to the player in the first minute or so of the game).  From the moment we pick up the controller (more on this later), we too, are tied to these boys.  We guide them forward, facing the adventure that lies ahead.
Brothers is in every way an experience refined to its most vital, leanest, core.  There is no dialogue to read, no complexity or depth to the controls, or even mindblowing technical detail to the environments.  What we have instead is not by many standards an objectively better game, but one which utilizes its design choices to create an incredibly engaging and meaningful experience.
Brothers’ story is “told” to the player through an almost primal but ultimately simple and refined manner.  No English nor any known language is spoken (as far as I know) in the world in which our fated brothers inhabit.  Instead, the intonation of the voice and the expressions displayed by the characters serve as the primary method of narration.  In this way, engaging our senses without having language and words to get in the way, we begin to empathize at a core emotional level with the brothers and the people around them.  Wanting to smile at the sound of their laughter; tensing at moments of stress, tearing at moments of pain.  Without “telling” us anything, Brothers makes us feel.  And that in itself is an achievement.
Upon recommendation, I was told to play Brothers using a controller.  After playing through Brothers, I can understand why such a recommendation was made.  The controller is split in half, one action button, a camera button, and an analog movement stick for each brother.  In this way, each brother feels like an extension of the self.  As you struggle to coordinate the movements of your own hands, you watch as they too, struggle to work together.  As you improve, so do they, traversing the terrain with the ease of a well oiled machine.  In this way, running, tiptoeing, sneaking around, moving in general just feels good in analog, as it should.
And while Brothers is by no means a technically impressive game, it does pull off awe inspiring spectacle.  The terrain is highly varied, puzzles never overstay their welcome, and moments of pure exhilaration and smile inducing giddiness play at odds with true moments of adversity, rounding out the experience as a whole.  In this way, the variance of the environments reflects the range of emotion that occurs in Brothers.  Wrapped in what in hindsight looks like a 2-3 hour rollercoaster ride, but in the moment, felt like days of adventuring, Brothers is an experience worth having.  Not to watch someone else experience, or to even read about, but to have and experience and live yourself.

This is probably one of the best games I've ever played. Yes, there is the nostalgia factor for me, as I used to play Morrowind when it first came out as a kid. But playing it again now, with a much higher tolerance to long paragraphs and an improved ability to grasp more complex plotlines, has proved to me that I didn't just love this game because it was an open world RPG that revolutionized my childhood gaming ecperiences; but because there is so much more to it than what you can gather at first glance.
First and foremost you have to get past the dated graphics, don't be a snob, some of the best games I've ever played wouldn't even challenge a boxy PC running Windows98. Because the value in these games may not be found in their appearance, but instead in the sheer beauty and depth of their stories.
Morrwind is a prime example of this. A hapless prisoner thrown into a world you know nothing about, given only directions to a skooma addicts house and a rough frustrating terrain to traverse. You don't have any other option but to explore this magical land before you, joining guilds, talking to strangers, and conquering the land, and the land has much to offer.
However, the most grasping part of Morrowind for me is the depth of the story and the world around it. This isn't some haphazardly thrown together nonsense, but rather a world with people and traditions and beliefs and culture, all coming together to form the world that you are now a part of.
I don't want to say anything more in fears of stealing the enjoyment of discovery that one might get from this amazing game.
The onlly thing left to say is that I highly recommend you play it, it will provide countless hours of fun and excitement for the whole family.

i'm only going to list the negative game mechanics that the devs have refused to change... because they are targeting a purely casual audience.
for perspective... let's list some fundamental problems here in no particular order... that makes the game such a waste of potential.
- you can sprint or slide while reloading.
- you can fire immediately with basically zero time between swapping primary weapon with interactions like stop bleed, revive, slide, vault, jump, take objective... your weapon is always ready to fire as if you have 4 arms.
- most buildings and areas have open ceilings. and easy/low skill to throw nades in common areas from various safe locations.
- "supported" position is basically no recoil. such skill.
- you see your entire team's icons through walls so you rush around corners without a care. there is no adrenaline factor when coming around corner and holding fire until you identify that it is not a friendly... so redundant since ther is a minimap. basically another major brain substitute.
- minimap shows red markers if an enemy fires his weapon. free intel. brain substitute.
- friendly fire is on but you only do 5% health damage per bullet, even headshots. so that just promotes cod spray through teammates. no big deal.... pointless.
- yeah. the medic's role was gutted. now you can bandage yourself to stop bleed. medics are just there to make the game super forgiving with revives. this series used to be 1 life to live per round... like counter strike. then the medic got revamped in aa3 with secures and revives.. and it was unpopular... but it's here in aapg.
- you can get revived after being shot in the face or killed by grenade. you are immune to damage while waiting for a revive, both bullets and grenades... you can still talk to your team.
- everyone is unable to keep on task (map/mission objective) because the win condition really focuses on revive. everyone wants to be revived.
there is no penalty after being revived.. your run speed is hilarious for someone who was at zero health and brought back for a 2nd chance to steal the win from the rightful victors.
- it is sad that the most often way to win a round is to just rush around and kill off the entire enemy team. ignore the objective because it is so unlikely to be completed. defense has such luxury to ignore objectives...
- the round timers are way too long. the pace of this game is faster than cs, yet the round timers are 4-5 minutes. it is a total joke. no pressure on the clock to do the objective. "take your time and kill all enemies." that's what the mission briefing should read...
- no unique missions. just universal kill all enemies before time runs out. and same loadouts each map. tons of smoke and no tools to counter sniper lanes (need m203/320 to deter/delay defense rushing assault spawn like aa2, smoke doesn't cut it. sprint and reload makes it much worse)... thus no maps are able to stand out as unique missions.

i could list more features that are just implemented without any real though, but what's the point. the devs claim they want our feedback, but we give it and it goes ignored for years. the devs refuse to compromise on certain major issues (casual stuff listed above).  the devs don't appreciate such detailed feedback. the devs just want you to like everything they decide on or GTFO. they don't understand what makes a great game great and they've admitted as much. yet they will ban you from their forums and delete your posts with no good excuse. there is no accountability for their abusive actions. ....just amazingly horrible public relations. and i am a retired US Army Veteran as well as a veteran comp player of the series going back to 2002.

Dungeon Rushers did little to impress me. I had my eye on it because of its aesthetic and only started it after it came out of Early Access. I had high hopes that were not met at all. I expected to be playing a fun game, but all that greeted me was a slow and dull experience. I was disappointed with what I played.
The UI is one of my biggest problems with this game. It’s not meant for a mouse at all, but whipping out my gamepad didn’t have good results either. I don’t know how the game went through a period of Early Access with such severe problems. Selecting skills and clicking on enemies just didn’t feel great at all while on the other hand, navigating the world map was easy. The controller had a better feel for combat situations when it worked, but became very time consuming when doing anything with the overworld. The word I could best use to summarize dealing with the UI is “dysfunctional.”
When touching your gamepad, the game switches to it and cannot switch back to mouse controls without restarting the game. You’ll still have some functionality with the cursor which you’ll need since the gamepad will have an unreliable time executing your commands. I’ve ran into situations where while trying to select an ability, the game somehow though I was also trying to select a utility move (Switch, Defend, Potion) at the same time. This meant I couldn’t do anything except drink until Mr. Mouse Cursor came to the rescue to set things right. I preferred having the gamepad do things since there were no hotkeys of any sort at my disposal. The game felt designed for mobile from the very beginning despite releasing on Steam first. All I need to do is point to the big circular icons, how the dungeons appear on the world map, and how the party moves in the dungeon.
Another gamepad issue involved the frequent occasion of selecting a skill and not being able to select any enemies on the screen. Dungeon Rushers wanted me to use two different methods of input just so I could play the darn thing. Even when you can select enemies, sometimes you can’t select that one enemy that’s at a downward angle. It adds to the game feeling very janky and unresponsive, especially when I’m able to attack enemies during their death animation unintentionally.
The combat is very simple and boring due to the lack of skills available. Each character you acquire will only have three skills that grow in power depending on how you use your skill points. The challenges also make things worse since you need to complete them to unlock the heroic mode for a dungeon. They will often have you limit your already limited options (skills, potion use, etc.), making things extra dull. The problem comes from nothing being interesting. The skills, the items, and the rewards all contributed to the feeling of wasted time/overwhelming despair. That’s a huge problem in a turn-based RPG. You want a good variety of skills and glorious destruction. I saw none of that from this title. Only boredom and grind. And Fog, an enemy encounter buff which lasts for the whole battle and gives a 50% chance to hit the intended target. What in the world?
Anyhoo, the grind. You can expect characters to level up very slowly and having to repeat dungeons to gain more power and crafting materials. Oh right, the crafting has levels to it too for each item category which means crafting things that you don’t care about just to level the category. The only form of healing comes in the shape of health potions which aren’t always available in the shop which tends to refresh after a dungeon rush attempt. Usually a single potion is available for purchase which makes healing a problem. Eventually you get a vampire who can help your party indirectly and there’s a fifth character that I don’t know much about.
The game’s sense of humor didn’t do much for me. The bard seemed annoying and most of the jokes fell flat on their face. There are a couple good ones in there though that might make you chuckle. The shapeshifting text that shrank to fit inside of the box when there was enough of it made reading somewhat annoying. Please don’t move words around when I’m trying to read the dialogue.
The one good thing about Dungeon Rushers is the art style. I enjoyed looking at the character art. There’s a nice mixture of drawn and retro elements that you can see throughout the game. I also appreciate that you can sort items to make things easier since crafting and collecting materials can turn the inventory into a mess. The dungeon skills were an interesting touch. You can think of them as exploring skills or ways to set up an encounter in your favor (revealing tiles or attempting to put enemies to sleep at the start of battle).
Dungeon Rushers feels like a game meant for the mobile arena and it shows. It’s not a game meant for long sessions and it had me easily bored with its uninspiring combat and writing. I’d recommend avoiding it for PC, especially if you run into the number of UI problems I had with selecting things.

I was a big fan of YDKJ back in the day, and was excited when I saw this remake was available. Unfortunately, it disappoints on a few key fronts and I can't wholeheartedly recommend it:
1) 2-player only. Many older YDKJ version offer more players, and console versions of this remake offer 4-player. This is a game where more players = more fun, so the lack of 4-play is disappointing.
2) No net play. While Jack is best face to face, and none of the older Jacks had this either, if I recall... it should be a standard feature on a modern remake like this.
3) No controller support. This is probably the reason for the 2-player limitation. Both players have to huddle around the keyboard, which is a bit lame. I'd like to hook a laptop up to the TV and give each player an xbox360 controller to buzz in with... but no dice. This is another feature available on consoles, by the way.
In summary, this is tha YDKJ you know and love from 1996... which is 2014 is a bit disappointing. The PC version is also surpassed in features by the console version.

My, oh my.  Cookie Masterson and the JellyVision team return.
Is it a reboot?  Sorta yeah.  Is it a remake?  Nah, not really.  Is it the same as it ever was?  Yes and no.
The questions are all new, as is the dialogue and there is a slight change in the key assignments, but Cookie, the interface, Jack Attacks, DisOrDats and screwing should be familiar to any YDKJ veteran.  What is VASTLY improved are the production values.  Not only had YDKJ gone all high-def (‘n stuff), but there's full-screen support for this bad boy (woohoo!).  The addition of the "Wrong Answer of the Game" prizes, Nocturnal Admissions and Who’s the Dummy shake it up a little bit, in a good way.  I am, however, on the fence about the achievements (Getting "mouth breather" is not exactly something I'm proud of).
While I don't exactly miss the "Gibberish Question" portions, I do miss 3-player support (yeah, it was actually a thing on the older games).  Rumor has it, some other versions of this have 3-player support (Don't hold me to that, as I am speaking for the PC/Steam version.  Mostly, though, I REALLY miss the 7 or 15 question selection some of the older YDKJ games had.
Do any of my negatives turn me off to it?  No, absolutely not.  The new YDKJ is like having your best friend over to your house after losing touch for 10 years.  He/she has certainly changed, but they're (likely) still the same person and you can still relate.  In the case of YDKJ, they're the same person, funny and relevant as ever, polished and shiny, and damnit, they look better than I do for having 10+ years go by since I last saw 'em!

Summary:
From the dev team that brought us games like The Darkness, Chronicles of Riddick, and Syndicate, Starbreeze Studios have tried something refreshing and much appreciated. Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons keeps the narrative-driven gaming trend going this year with relateable interactions and development in an unforgettable journey.
The game starts off showing a flashback of the mother of the two sons' death. Whilst reminiscing on that tragic day, the two brothers' father falls ill. After a trip to the local doctor, the brothers are told about the water from the 'tree of life' which appears to be the only way to save their dad, and so their quest begins.
Right off the bat the visuals are phenomenal, making use of the Unreal Engine 3. Vibrant colors shown in various settings such as forests, mountains, dungeons, and small towns, nice cell-shading style, detailed shadows...for an indie-style game, it actually looks on par or even better than some AAA titles. To top it off, the soundtrack sets the tone and brings the world to life, immerseful and always in the back of your mind whilst playing (see video at the top to get an idea).
The controls are unlike any I've played before it. You control two characters simultaneously, and whilst there's very few controls to use (movement for either side of analogs, and one button interaction for each brother), how they integrated and executed the controls is brilliant. It takes some getting used to, and you'd tend to forget a finger on a button here or there whilst trying to keep the brothers on track with their mission, but the game isn't punishing. It's simplistic and overall not too difficult to play. The two brothers rely on one another to move forward, both having significant differences to get through various puzzles. However, playing with a keyboard can prove to be frustrating. Definitely recommend a controller (even the Steam page claims it requires a controller to play, although keyboard controls are available).
There is never a dull moment in this game. The pacing is perfect. For such simple mechanics with the unique twist of controlling two characters at once, each segment, or well, chapter, is different and utilizes the innovative controls in a variety of ways. And the best part about the pacing is, and this is a debatable point, the simple puzzles keep the game from detouring and ruining its experience.
Whilst the gameplay and graphics are integral, very fun parts of the game, what outshines more than anything, what brings all the elements together and shapes it into an extraordinary game, is the growth of the brothers. They have to go through hell and high water in order to save their father, and like any group of siblings stuck together for so long, there's going to be rivalry. Their age and clothing show their typical, rather cliche attitudes well, and we need that to piece their styles together as there's no English in this game. There's voice-acting, but done in a fake language allowing us to detail the characters on our own. The brothers encounter various people and things to interact with, with both reacting their on way to any given situation, further drawing their different personalities to us.
Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons is an emotional ride. It doesn't just stop with the engaging, roller coaster of a story, it is a well-rounded game with fun controls and beautiful graphics to follow suit. It shows us very, very strong bonds as children, as siblings, as a family...life lessons secretly hidden in this title. This, along with Gone Home, have really set a new mark in gaming today, pushing forward for the better of the industry. And now...I urge anyone who stuck around reading this to try it. We need more games like Brothers. These titles are taking risks and evolving the gaming industry, or have the possibility to, so long as they get more exposure. And even without talking about it, the experience itself is worth the price of admission. A general $15 full retail price for a 3-4 hour game, but there's constant sales and even if you don't catch it during a sale it's still very much worth it. Couldn't recommend Brothers enough. Thank you for reading.

You Don't Know Jack is pretty awesome, to say the least.
It still keeps the wackiness of the past installments, only without the other forgettable hosts (YDKJ 2 I'm looking at you). With 70+ episodes to play through, each averaging at about 10 minutes, you've got some serious replayability. Some of the humor falls flat, but the majority of it is pretty clever and funny.
Unlike the older games or its console counterpart, the game doesn't support more than two players. Despite that, it's still perfect for hotseat trivia and parties. Like the older games, it lets players play by themselves, so if you for some reason dont have friends you can still progress through the game.
The only issue that I have with YDKJ is that unlike the past installations, the episodes' questions are static and aren't procedurally asked. This tips the game in favor of people who've played the game before. The quick play option helps out a bit by picking a random episode, but that episode is still the same since you've played it last.
Otherwise, YDKJ is a great trivia game that can be played solo or with friends.

So in Spore you basically create your own little .....sperm looking cell that swims around and eats things. You can make it eat meat, plants or whatever you'd like as you upgrade it, avoid being eaten by bigger looking sperm monsters, and then eventually upgrade to the land stage where you grow legs and take to the land to make friends or eat everyone.
1. Make everyone your friend and be social (you do this by singing, dancing and finding upgrades as you go along)
2. Make some friends and then slaughter whoever you don't like. You don't like frogs? Kill those frog looking people.
3. Don't have time for singing, dancing or being nice? Make the baddest, meanest looking sperm creature the world has ever seen and eat everyone's face off!!!
As you continue to grow your brain gets bigger. Once your brain fully develops you make a tribe. You then can repeat steps 1-3 in the tribe stage. You don't want to be nice, play music and make people like you? Grab some spears, axes or torches and burn down their village. SHOW NO MERCY! Upgrade to the civilization stage and continue forward.
The good part about this game is the ability to customize just about everything. Want to look like a giant green tadpole with a mouth and arms?  Done  Want to look like a giant parrot with a beak and winged feather limbs? Find the parts and DONE  Want to make your creature have 5 foot long arms, flap around and be multicolored and uglier than the in-laws? Done (no offense to anyone in-laws :P )
There are so many options that you can replay through being passive, nice, both, mean, barbaric and eating everyone while laying waste to the entire planet destroying all who would dare to oppose your parrot frog in-law monster!!!
Every step you take though lets you get certain abilities and unlock different achievements so there is a lot to do and once you get to the space age you can then fly around in your own ship and explore the solar system and you have more to do.
1. Camera system is a bit wonky at the Tribe stage+ but once you get used to it then it's not too terribly bad
2. Sometimes your character can look a bit splotchy but the graphics are from a game that's 10 years old, so you can't expect too much, I mean it's not Half-life 3 right?...oh wait...
3. Sometimes the AI acts a bit dumb. You tell them to go eat in tribe mode and they stand there almost starving to death before eating (same for harvesting food at times)
All in all I would recommend this game to anyone especially to those who have frog parrot in-laws and those of you who want to be a deadly sperm alien eating everything in its path. 9/10

Brothers is an adventure game where you play as two Brothers on the search for a remedy for their ailing father.
Brothers was recommended highly to me by colleagues, and I went into it with a fresh mind, knowing nothing about it.
While the game is great on many levels (which I'll come to), I feel that the renound it has is purely based on the gimmicky control system. This isn't me being negative or insulting, it's just fact, the controls of the Brothers is pure gimmick. But, it works quite well! (<exclamation point, doesn't show on Steam reviews :|)
Other than the controls, I didn't really feel the game set itself out as as much of a stupendous game as I'd been led to believe; certainly not Game of the Year, which I heard some had elected it to be.
I fully completed the game within 5 hours and did indeed enjoy the story. The graphics, at times, were mindblowing, and are definitely this title's strongest point. It's weakest feature, however, I feel, is the lack of language from the characters. There's a certain charm listening to the almost Simlish talk from the characters, but ultimately it dissociates you from the characters, being unable to fully understand them, and unable to fully connect with them.
When you do connect, it's on a base level of emotion, and has almost no base in logic or drive, just raw emotion. Which, at times is more than enough to push the game forward, but at others leave you with a feeling of pointless energy, "I guess we just go forward then?" for no real reason.
The game is really fun and definitely something everyone should experience, but it is by no means one of the greatest games I've played. I had a super time with it, and found it very cost-worthy at it's price, and would recommend it to all.

Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons is billed as a single-player co-op game. While this may seem like a contradiction at first, all is made clear once you start playing the game - you control both protagonists at the same time, hence cooperating with yourself in what is essentially a 3D puzzle platformer. The two brothers have different and complementary abilities and the game's puzzles are built around that mechanic. It's a very interesting and well-executed concept, and the game manages to stay just challenging enough throughout its (admittedly short) duration.
Rounding out the package is an emotional rollercoaster of a story set in an absolutely beautiful and gripping fantasy world. I don't think I've ever been moved to tears by a video game before, but Brothers managed to do it, delivering an experience that I won't soon forget. Recommended to everyone (but heed the notice on the Steam store page about this game requiring a controller).

Dungeon Rushers is quite nice dungeon crawler, though definitely closer to coffee break one than hardcore ones like Elminage or Wizardry series. DR is somewhat niche, because it has exploration with top down perspective, and combat with side view, while majority of crawlers have both in first person perspective.
Compared to many crawlers you also don't create your characters in DR, you instead get 10 characters as you progress through story, which in most cases correspond with common rpg classes.  Each one of them has three combat skills (except one who has four) and up to three camp/exploration skills.  Characters are varied, (especially later ones when you get druid who has two forms or mummy mage, which uses hp instead mana for his skills) and each one, maybe except one which is slightly weaker, are useful. Each character has talent tree divided into three branches, and by investing points in them you can get their skills upgraded or stats increased. You have only enough points to buy maybe 2/3 of all upgrades at most, so you need to select what you really want, it also makes different builds of the same character possible. I would say though that are choices are equally useful or strong, in fact some things are rather useless.
Exploration is okay, there is plenty of enemies (there are no random encounters in this game, only set ones), traps, rooms with treasures and shrines which can bless or curse you. Sometimes you need to find switches or keys, the game also supports using passwords to open the doors, but no dungeon in campaign uses this. Fighting is also rather good. You use party of maximum five characters against enemy party of maximum six. Dungeons in game are divided in four large areas: castle with skeletons, mountains with goblins, jungle with amazons and pyramids with mummies. Each arena has about seven different enemies, so enemy pool is not that big - some games like Elminage have more enemy types in one dungeon than DR in entire game. While you have quite plenty of skills, not many of them are that useful, I have mostly used just basic attacks and buffs, offensive attacks are mixed bag - some are good, and some are weak or have occasional use. For example one of the attacks can be upgraded to remove enemy buffs - sounds useful, but there is only one enemy in game which actually gives buffs. Rest of them gain buffs (or rather one buff, critical hit chance increase) by passive skills, and those can't be removed.
You can give some items to your characters, which can be bought, crafted, or looted from fights and treasures. Item selection starts very weak, but later in game there is quite some items to select from. But the fact that you have only few characters, and many ways to get items make both shop and workshop somewhat not very useful. Workshop has levels for every item category, and crafting items yields you exp used for leveling. You need several items crafted to level up, and since you don't need that many items, you will have to craft random things just to get to higher level.  Shop has eight random items or crafting components, and refreshes after completing a dungeon. You will mostly want to just buy components, since first items are rather expansive, and second it's better to craft them and get exp. This makes gold almost useless, it can be used for gambling, from which you can get special potions. Problem is that many dungeons have challenges which restrict you from using potions, and when there are no challenges you can (or should be able to) destroy everything without them. Also plenty of items give increased magical resistance, but there are not many enemies with magical attacks, and the ones who have them, in most cases have also skills that resurrect or summon new enemies, so you will target them first anyway.
Speaking of challenges, each normal dungeon has three, after completing dungeon with them you unlock heroic mode of that dungeon. This is something which is not explained very well in game. You can complete those challenges at any time, and heroic mode is not that harder. It has enemies with increased stats, but also better loot, including some unique items that drop only form that mode, and some of them are way stronger that anything that can be crafted by the time you get them. This too makes shop and workshop inferior to looting.
Game in general has rather rough start, and can be hard for some people in beginning, and later it gets easier. It's mostly because you don't have full party early on, and also because of this game unique approach to healing. There is no classical cleric character in this game, the closest to that is herbalist which you get near the end of second act. The only way early to heal is to use potions, and later vampire character buff. Those potions are somewhat rare, and if you make bad decision you can easily run out of  them, and you will have to grind to get them. There was also certain hard encounter early on, but that was nerfed already.
The game has also function to create your own dungeons, which is quite nice, but this is only addition to dungeon crawling, not game main focus.
Currently the game is in somewhat rough state. There are bugs, there are crashes. Some skills are bugged and don't work, shop is bugged too. Inventory only recently got sane item sort by category, and not by tier. The developer is fixing those bugs through, and that's good. The developer is also making mobile version, so let's hope he will fix pc version alongside it. The game is enjoyable and worth getting, though you might want to get it on sale. Overall it can be rated 6,5-7/10

tl;dr:  one of the least fun games I've bought in the past year
What is the game like?
It's a grindy smartphone game.  You follow a fixed path from dungeon level to dungeon level, stomping the monsters and finding the treasure chest in each one.  There is a challenge for each dungeon along the lines of, "Do it without losing anyone, drinking healing potions, or triggering a trap."  If you win the challenge, you can play it again on "heroic" level.  It has some bugs and runs slowly.
But the graphics are hand-drawn and jaw-dropping, right?
It is "old school" which here means "bad graphics."  It uses tile-based maps and a JRPG combat field.
So... deep character creation?  Customization?
Sorry, nope.  You pick up heroes in dungeons along the fixed game path.  You can add stat points to them when they level up.  You can't even change their name or icon.  Later you have more than 5 guys, but you can only bring 5 at a time, so that means there's some tactical gameplay somewhere.
But I'm sure the combat makes Divinity: Original Sin look simple, because it's deep and strategic, right?
Not especially.  It's turn-based JRPG combat where each piece moves once, using one of three skills that are pre-set for the character.  You can find similar ones on free online games on the internet.
But there's crafting and loot -- so that's awesome, right?
Well... no.  You get a set of about 12 items per region that you can buy or craft.  They are fixed items, with no modifications or options.  By the middle part of that section you'll have all the best items the region can offer, and then you just wait to finish enough dungeons to get to the next part of the map where you get 12 more items.
Is it funny?  Because they say it's funny.  And "off-beat."
Oh lord no.  It's like listening to seven-year-old boys.  "Are you a really a vampire?  But you walk in the sunlight with us!"  "Oh," little-girl giggle, "I wear sunscreen!  Really it's wrinkle cream, so I don't get older!"  "Let's hit our bard because he's annoying!"
So is there anything good about this game?
I kept hoping it would get better, but it didn't.  It would be a decent tablet game for $1.99 if you needed something to kill time on an airplane.  Maybe.  I got bored.  I'm not sure why so many people seem to like it.

Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind is one of those games - perfection. It's hard to put into words. I played this to no end, for years and years before they dropped it on steam. I had the old, non game of the year version which didn't even have a journal for quest keeping. Had to use an actual pen and paper to write down quests and hints. Stressful as hell, but honestly so much fun. Very few games have the ability to send shivers down my spine with their soundtrack, but theres really nothing like charging headfirst into Ghost Gate with 'Call of Magic' blessing your eardrums.
Compared to its more modern counterparts (Oblivion and Skyrim), the combat is aged and clunky, but you very easily get used to it, or you can just circumvent it with combat mods. The weapon, Armor, monster and creature diversity is unmatched and the map is 24 square kilometers of pure, hand crafted beauty. The story is unreal, literally millions of side quests.
The lack of Fast Travel (other than boats and those damn awesome Silt Striders) really forces the game to feel like an actual adventure that cant just be breezed through with fast travels or game mechanics. It feels real. To this day, still my favourite Elder Scrolls of all time.
The RPG elements, leveling up and skills and whatnot is indepth, so indepth you probably need a guidebook or youtube tutorial to explain just how intricate it is. Theres no 'pick this skill when your x level'. It's all practice, the more you do x, the better you get at it, and the more your governing skill increases.
I've got a lot of history with this game, and whether its nostalgia, or a deep appreciation for the masterpiece that Elder Scrolls III is, or both (probably both), this game will go down as not only my favourite Fantasy game or RPG game, but as my favourite game of all time.
Do I recommend this game, abso-♥♥♥♥ing-lutely

EGO Rating is required to have more Perk slots, loadouts, and to upgrade your EGO Power. This, along with leveling up system, makes this a favorite for me.
Leveling up system you say? This games Leveling up system puts you in a square/rectangle, with one of 4 Ego powers in each corner. The rest is filled with perks. You pick one Ego Power in the beginnning of the game, and if you want another one, you need to build across the grid, grabbing perks until you reach the power of your desire.
Lets talk about Arkfalls. Arkfalls are special side missions where you need to do a certain quest. Defeat 3 waves, break a crystal, etc. Then, you get the Arkfall SItes previously mentioned. These put you inside a Arkfall, fighting off enemies. There are 2 Arkfall SItes: Minor and Major. Minor ones send you in, you kill some people and bam! uncommon loot, with a rare chance of rare. However, Major Sites send you into the Arkfall, and going deeper inside to fight a creature. You get much better loot, and a bunch of xp. I have only found 1 Major during my 8 hours of playing, which I consider myself lucky to find. I have, however, particapated in multiple Minor Site raids.
All in all, this game is absolutely amazing. 17000/10. Make sure to buy it during the Winter Sale, as it is only $5 right now.

Have you ever seen someone successfully wield a hand grenade as a melee weapon against a  tank? Play Heroes and Generals, and you will. I will give this game a solid 51% because, if not for infantry play, it would be inferior to War Thunder in every way. Here is what a typical game experience is like:
1. You shoot an infantryman twice with a .50cal machinegun -- which, fyi, is a kind of antiaircraft gun -- and then watch him run away.
2. You chase him until your tank tread grinds to a halt running over a small rock.
3. You stand up to peer out the hatch and figure out how to get unstuck.
4. You spot him, but because the view controls randomly fail to register, you have to hammer the zoom-out key three times to duck back into the hatch, by which time...
4. ..you are swiftly one-shotted by the same soldier, with a .30 cal rifle.
5. Respawn. Overturn your tank by running over a bicycle.
6. Respawn and get exploded by three shots from an anti-tank rifle
Everything about this game reeks of inattention to detail. For example, on one map, a significant layout feature is that it is bisected by a rail line. It is just low enough in some places that you can sort of drive over it. Sometimes. If the phase of the moon is just right, you might not get stuck on it totally at random. Who puts such a feature in a map? Were you non-commital as to its intended purpose? Did you stop and think about whether it should represent a geographic barrier, or were you ambivalent, and just decide "screw it, it looks cool, and I don't care whether it adds or detracts from the gameplay".
Also, as mentioned, the antitank rifle is ridiculous. Not just historically but, above all, from a game balance perspective. The fact that these things hit a tank harder than a machinegun hits a soldier is ridiculous. The trouble here, is that the developers are catering to cheesy spastic players who want to spam tanks like crazy, so they attempt to balance that out by making tank MGs shoot spitwads, and making the antitank weapons absurd. The sensible thing to have done would be to balance this economically by making tanks expensive and AT weapons cheap.
The game's only saving grace, besides infantry, such as it is, is that the unlock progression keeps you in suspense as to what it's like to finally use the horrifically misbalanced weapons which are killing you every two minutes.

Update 5/16/2016
Just when I thought this game was as unbalanced as possible, it has totally outdone itself. It turns out that fighter planes are impervious to .30 cal fire. Not just resistant. So, upon figuring this out, I turned to my 37mm cannon and found that, implausibly, fighters will shrug that off as well. You have to pull multiple hat-trick shots using a cannon intended for ground targets in order to kill a fighter plane. I think, at this point, that the game has entirely parted ways with any pretense at realism or balance, and it is more like a modified game of paintball with bizarre rules. Presumably, fighters are expensive, so the rationale was that they have to be nearly impervious, even in ways that make no sense at all.

I have either been hugely missing out or actually no one until now tried to create a good gladiator school simulation. The setting is interesting, has hardly been explored and holds the potential for deep strategy, as well as brutal action.
First off, like others said before, this game begs for a decent tutorial, Apart from crashes or technical issues, this should be priority number -1. Throwing a player into the game with a "go explore"-attitude might work if this was an adventure game, but for a supposedly complex genre, you at least need to show the player the basics. "How do I tend to the gladiators needs?", "How do I earn money?", stuff like that.
A good strategy game needs a tutorial, and if it doesn't, the game isn't complex enough.
Second, the content. This game is hopefully far from finished, so I have no idea what amount of content is about to come, but for the price tag attached to this at the moment, the content feels lacking, to say the least. If I start a gladiator-school-simulation and get about 8 building options for the school, I wonder where the main focus of this game lies.
Last, but not least, the presentation. I'm not against cartoonish artstyles, and if used correctly, can even benefit a mature setting like this, but this isn't the way to go. This doesn't have to look like Hatred Tycoon, but after all this is a setting where slaves fight for their life and get ripped apart by lions and bears. Gladiator School looks more like a game rated for ages 6 and up.
Worst of all, the game doesn't look simple, but cheap, basiclly like a free-to-play-flash browsergame. And that for a 10-dollar EA-game.
Keep a close eye on this one, it has potential, but at the moment, not much of it is used.

A cute D&D inspired dungeon-crawling RPG with the kind of mildly amusing, quirky humour where you probably wouldn't laugh out loud but instead, at the very most, exhale forcefully through your nose. Maaaybe.
You click around or use your arrow keys to move around a tile-style dungeon, revealing more of the map as you go. Event-tiles scatter throughout the halls somewhat randomly and activate upon contact. There's a bit of a hassle in that when you're moving you can only reveal the tile you're on, and not the tiles around you, so you're often bumping into monsters and traps before you can make plans to evade them. Thankfully your party posseses various skills, which cost stamina, that allow you to reveal certain tiles if you don't feel like running in blind. This can be very useful if you're running low on health and looking to avoid unnecessary confrontations. Battles are turn-based and to be honest, very simple. I haven't felt challenged so far, even when playing the 'Heroic Mode' dungeons, but hopefully that will change as I move further into the game.
You'll find gold, salvage loots, craft gear, as well as level up and unlock skills and abilities. It's all very standard.
There IS a dungeon building aspect to this game, which I touched on very briefly, but not enough to really comment on at this stage. It's very easy to set the tiles and add monsters and traps so at a glance it look pretty solid... You can take that as you will. I haven't even touched the PVP yet though.
By the way, you might be under the impression that you can create and customize your characters to your personal tastes but this is actually not the case. There is a preset story with already-made characters that unlock the further you progress into the game. This isn't inherently a bad thing, rather think of it as a heads up if you happen to have made the same assumptions as I did.
Overall, I don't think you'd find anything new or groundbreaking here but it's still a nifty, little dungeon-crawler. Generally fun for those who are already into this type of game but it probably won't win anyone over. I'd say a 5/10, still recommendable.

Wow, sitting here writing this review the theme/music is playing in the background and I haven't heard it in so long, takes me back to the countless hours I spent ever engrossed in what came next.
This IS my favorite game of all time. It opened up to me the possiblities of what a video game can do. In all honesty this was only the second RPG I had ever played, and from the hauntingly beautiful music, to the ENORMITY of the map, this was a game to truly explore. Explore--as in not only the land, the buildings, the caves, the mausoleums, they added UNDERWATER grottos as well, and each of these were themselves at times huge. In each of these areas you could count on trouble, but, worthwile loot and exp. for your time spent clearing. I'm sitting here with a smile on my face, thinking of when so many times at work I was really in Morrowind. What was I going to do after I got off of work. Where to go. What was the best way to finish a quest, or whatever/wherever I left off the night before. And oh yes, it wasn't the night before but actually the EARLY MORNING before work, and so MANY of them as well.
Now, I realize this is a older game, but, if you love the ESO series, and haven't played Morrowind give it a try--who knows--you too may just find yourself at work red eyed and waiting, wishing for quitting time.

Been playing this since it came out back around '01 or '02. Simplistic in some ways, compared to modern RPGs, but in many ways much deeper than today's open-world first-person games. If you're reading this, do yourself a favor and just buy Brothers - A tale of Two Sons right now.
Brothers, for lack of a better term, is a masterpiece IMHO. Somehow, Brothers delivers an emotional, compassionate story, without a single word of dialogue in the whole game. Charcaters do speak, but their language is Simmilar to Simlish (The Sims) I suppose. Although you cannot understand the language, You will still understand what is going on. You will have to prepare yourself for many emotions throughout the game. I will list a few I've experienced: Sadness, joy, wonder, curiousity, horror, excitement, and despair. Sounds a bit over the top? Well go see for yourself. You may experience emotions you never new existed.
Brothers perfectly marries Story with Game Mechanics. The best way i can explain it is that you play the story. Again, for lack of a better term, Brothers is a Singleplayer Co-op game. If you were not aware, You control two Brothers independently using the joysicks of your controller (Provided you use a controller). Contrary to the Notice above, The game will work with a keyboard, But I would not recommend it. Seperately controlling the two siblings, you traverse the game working together. I would not classify Brothers as a Puzzle Platformer, however. It's simply a journey. Which brings me to the final point.
Brothers took me roughly 3 hours to complete. I would say there is some replayability, but thats only because there are achievements you will miss and areas you may have skipped. So maybe 5 - 6 hours will be all you get out of Brothers, unless you play through games several times. I know that so few hours may not warrant the price for some people, but I promise you'll remember this game for as long as you live. I know I will.

I'll start by saying that this game used to be pretty good. Hell, I loved it a year or two ago, but these days theres no point in even trying to get into this game. The F2P model is trash, restricting you from the best PVE gear and not allowing you to get a single full PVP set. The powers have never really been on par with eachother, so if you're into PVP you have a very small selection of powers, even smaller if you're F2P.  Speaking more on the PVP aspect, don't you hate open world PVP games where theres people in that world to fight? In DCUO that problem is solved with the PVP phase of the game being completly empty! In PVE phase at least, you'll run into a decent amount of people in the lower level areas. Groups for instances have also been found almost immediatly, which would be great if you weren't required to have some higher level carry you through them. If you're okay with being carried, theres almost always someone in your mission to do it, but that just isn't fun gameplay to me.
The real deal-breaker with this game to me is the F2P model. I said I used to love this game, and when I loved this game I had a chance to gear up and be as good as people who sank hundreds into the game. Even if it was slower, it was at least possible. PVP is simply broken now.
Don't worry PVE'rs, the game sucks for you too. Getting to the end game content is just tedious after the first ten levels, and after you get to the end game you have three options. Either subscribe to the game, buy each pack of DLC seperatly, or have nothing to do for the majority of the time. Most instances and raids require you to have bought some DLC for it, and those DLCs are incredibly overpriced for how little they delievered. This game would've been great, if only someone else made it.

Defiance is not that bad but it's also not all that good.
However, it is a decent TPS multiplayer shooter that does provide some enjoyment.
Essentially, this game becomes extremely repetitive in a very short amount of time. Everything about it is mediocre. It really does nothing all that great.
The vast amount of bugs, bad balance, terrible chat, smallest MMO game world I have seen, small amount of content/story, boring grinds, and awful design decisions tends to drag this game down.
Like say....PvP. Worst ever!
However, I do enjoy the PvE MMO aspect since it's fun to mindlessly kill the terrible AI; it takes no skill what so ever +1.
This game is really easy to play which is about it's only saving grace and the reason why I still log on occasionally. Mowing down hordes of enemies with up to 50 players at once is kinda cool which no other current online shooter I know of offers this atm.
The shooting is pretty smooth and fluid so it's quite playable.
Lastly, chasing loot can keep a player going even if the RNG is awfully bad. It is a nasty grind though, so beware.
Problem is, the content in this game is lacking and due to the now bare bones dev team: new content and updates are far and few between + poor in quality/quantity. :(
Recommending Defiance only if you can get it for 5 bucks or less. It's good fun as a PvE game if you want to relax and shoot hapless AI.

Dungeon Rushers is a turn based, dungeon exploring RPG. Tasked with with finding the treasure at the end of each dungeon you enter, and killing monsters and surviving traps along the way. You can't see what's ahead of you on the grid based exploration stage, but character abilities aid you in taking a peek at where some traps and enemies lie, and even just revealing a few squares so you can properly prepare youself. Combat with monsters is turn based as well, with some strategic attacks and abilities to turn the tide of battle in favor of your heroes, nothing RPG fans haven't really seen before.
The real selling point and reason I ended up buying the game was the ability to build your own dungeon, and have other players wander through it in an attempt to beat it in a mode called Arena. While there is a free build mode that lets you upload more creative dungeons to Steam Workshop, you start off very limited in the Arena proper. I don't mind unlocking monsters and more rooms, but I still can't use signs or doors in my game. Still, this building mode is cool and I love games that let you build dungeons other people can go through.
The dungeon builder is also a huge problem too. The game spawns bonuses and secrets itself, you can't place them, and nothing stops players from doing a lot of terrible things. Many player built dungeons are just five traps and a boss you can't use abilities on. No room for the game to even spawn secrets. There's no incentive to make good, creative dungeons in Arena right now, but I'm hoping with some changes it could be so much more.
