This is an impresive game that fulfil it's role perfectly with engaging graphics and adorable bobble head characters.
Every take-off is risky and will lead to an intense mission into wich you risk the lives of your crew members and your plane itself.
You will have to think fast and act cleverly to avoid any stupid mistakes and dangerous situations or else your fly could end up fast and dramatically.
But overall it isn't so difficult even if it could get really intense sometime, there are some smart moove and abilities that could save your crew and your plane if used correctly or at least delay the critical moment to let you recover and repair, you can also decide to abord the mission at any time to give it another try later when you will be more prepared, for so long that you could return and land on your airfield.
It's not so frustrating to loose compared to some other Roguelike, because you can get a new planes and crew that will get few upgrade or levels depending on how much research point you had before loosing your previous crew, wich prevent the boringness of restarting all over from scratch.
There are plenty of upgrade for your planes, you will have to pick them carefully because you have a maximum weight that depend on the engines you choose, and you won't be able to max everything at a time, i think it is a good point that force a little bit of reflection and sacrifice.
There are also variety of equipments to choose for your crew members depending on the role each of them will have, the situation, and the mission you will be playing.
It took me arround 25 hours to finish it, and there are some free contents and paid DLC planned (new plane(s) ) that will improove it's replayability.
The game is basically endless but once you have finished the main campaign it is only about replaying the missions that will randomly spawn on the briefing map, so its life time will depend on you but expect at least 20 hours of intense and fun gameplay.

TL;DR Overall, I really like this game, semi-smooth controls once you get use to them, challenging and fun gameplay, and very interactive dev team. Only issues are frustrating to get into in terms of controls and challenge of the levels, and that it is only 4 hours long to complete for the campaign, which isn't really worth the $15 in my opinion. All in all a fun little game, which I would get if it is on sale, otherwise not really worth the full $15.
In-depth review:
First impressions of the game were not really all that great to be honest. The controls were very frustrating to get used to, and honestly in general the controls are a little clunky. It also didn't really seem like it inovated much, it seemed like I could just stay on one truck and make it through the level. However if you keep playing the controls become smoother, and the levels become actually challenging and a lot of fun. To be honest, the game isn't very long and not all that challenging, I finished the campaign in 4 hours, and I only had the double jump ability. Yeah there were some very difficult levels, but other than those they were mostly pretty easy. It is kind of buggy in the physics of the trucks, so a lot of the time you can abuse them and finish the level fairly quickly.
Other than the easy difficulty, and short levels I don't have  a lot to complain about with this game, A lot of the levels are a lot of fun, and very satisfying finish. The gameplay is very unique to this game, I haven't seen a lot of other games with this spin on platforming. It is really fastpasted and it is generally very fun to play.
While I don't think this game is worth the full $15, I do think that this is a very well made game. I think that if anyone is interested, you should get this while it is on sale.

Steam release review
Pros
+Supports any controller that has Xinput support.
+Plug and play, no setup is required at all.
+Controller keyboard bindings are customizable.
+Software includes a virtual spinning keyboard that can be opened at any time.
+The software is conveniently in the Steam software library so it can be installed on any machine you log into.
+Mouse movement on the controller has stick sensitivity so the mouse will actually accelerate the longer a direction is held.
+Software is disabled as soon as a full screen game is opened. This can be overridden by pressing a combination of buttons at any time.
+Inexpensive software
Cons
-Does not actually support games. It's meant for just controlling a PC without the use of a mouse and keyboard.
-Directinput controllers are not supported. However, there's plenty of ways to emulate Xinput currently.
-No deadzone options which can be really annoying sometimes. Sometimes the mouse or page scrolling will move on its own on controllers with loose sticks.
-Steam will always say your in-app when the software is opened. Games don't seem to override the user's Steam status either.
-Windowed games do not disable the software which can cause problems for games that only support windowed mode.

Pros: Price, Functionality, Easy to Use

Keep in mind: this game is definitely not bad. I have to especially give kudos to them for giving players infinite mining stamina and infinite lives, free of charge. Yes, it SHOULD be standard to begin with, but I've played plenty of F2P games where it is not. Speaking of microtransactions, I was pleasantly surprised by how little they were shoved into my face during my first hour or so playing. In fact, I only saw them when I opened up the in-game store.
The problem with this game is not the paid features, but its mediocrity. It tries to be not only an MMO and a crafting/mining sandbox game, but also a platformer and a single player adventure game (which the creators tried and failed to disguise as a tutorial). These are all types of games I honesly enjoy, but, because it attempts to be so many different types of games at once, it ends up being a jack of all trades and master of none.
The game would also be more enjoyable if it wasn't for the terrible camera. Perhaps I'm just missing something, but I was never able to find anything resembling free camera movement, nor did the game even suggest such existed. Sure, you can rotate the camera, but it would be much more convenient if you could TILT it as well, so it isnt' just pointing at the ground all the time.
UPDATE: I tried playing some more, to give this game a second chance, but, to be perfectly honest, I was bored the whole time. I saw very few players outside of the main lobby, and I had more fun going through the game tips than I did actually playing the game. The overworld makes no sense, and all my time I spent there was stumbling about looking for some sort of direction. Even the adventure mode, which is supposed to be a tutorial, is utterly confusing. Half of the time I spent playing it, I was stumbling about with no idea where to go, what to do, or how to complete an area.
Bottom line: This game is confusing and boring. I won't be recommending it to my friends.

The gameplay, if I had to say what it most reminds me of, is I guess most like Warhammer Quest, in that there are essentially two phases: exploring the dungeon (from an overhead perspective, clicking the adjacent square in the direction you want to move) and handling combat encounters (which - unlike Warhammer Quest - switches to a side view of your party and the enemy, and doesn't involve moving and positioning characters, though you do choose who is on the front line - i.e. your tankier guys - and who is on the rear line - i.e. your squishies). Encounters include dealing with traps, 'events' that play out and feel a little like the curios in Darkest Dungeon (here's a fountain, interact with it or move on? Interact and it might grant healing... or it might poison you), and grabbing your primary goal in each dungeon: the treasure (which can include coin, crafting ingredients, and equipment, some of which is rng-based - i.e. you can find nice rare gear if you're lucky). Some characters have skills that come into play in the 'exploration phase' (such as disarming traps or detecting what is in adjacent squares: whilst disaming traps (mechanically in the case of one character, magically in the case of another) is for sure handy, I do think some of the abilities you can use during exploration are a little lacklustre and probably don't see much use. Many encounters are groups of enemies, which triggers combat.
Combat is handled in a turn-based fashion with characters acting in an order derived from their stats (you can have them defend and wait until after others have acted if it's a good idea - and it sometimes is). There aren't a huge number of different actions you can take; for each character it essentially boils down to picking one of their three available combat actions (or using a potion, or defending/waiting and acting later in the round). The three actions do differ (quite substantially) and are unique for each character, so it isn't as limiting as it might sound. Each character can perform one action per turn, but can only perform actions if they have sufficient mana/stamina to do so (each has a 'standard' action that costs nothing, but the juicier more effective skills do drain mana/stamina). Enemies have resistances to the effects that your character's actions bring to the mix (stunning, bleeding, silencing, etc) which you can check with a right click (you also get a preview of what the currently selected action will do in terms of damage before you commit to it, so that informs your decisions too), so you can tailor your approach according to the enemies and situation. This adds some nuance to the combat and helps prevent it from being oversimplified and repetitive.
It is relatively simple but with enough going on to make it feel like your decisions do matter, and they do; however in the very early game, when some characters and actions aren't available, it can feel a little like you can't make a great deal of tactical choices - but then, I get that this is done to ease the player into the game's mechanics, so just bear with it and as you get further in, it'll begin to feel more rounded. Related to these limitations (characters and actions) in the early game is that the game does allow you to attempt areas and challenges way before you've unlocked sufficient party members and actions/skills to effectively be able to handle them (so with one hand it starts you off with limited characters and actions to ease you in, and with the other grants you a guaranteed lose if you try something beyond your party), and I've read comments in the forum from people frustrated that they can't progress. They actually can progress, just not on the area/heroic challenge that they were attempting before being suitably strong enough to do so. For example, rather than completing each dungeon and then immediately trying to complete the 'heroic' challenge for that dungeon, it is often more viable (and in some cases only really possible) if you tackle the next few dungeons on normal *before* going back to the earlier dungeons and trying them on heroic (to be more skilled up, better geared, to have more characters/actions unlocked, and to know more what you're doing!). A bit of common sense and recognizing when something appears beyond your party goes a long way on this front. You can also repeat dungeons you've already completed to grind up more xp if you need it (I haven't felt the need to do that, but it being possible does grant players finding things a little on the hard side in their latest dungeon a way of getting their party stronger for it whilst also learning more effective strategies).
Characters gain xp from combat and level up, allowing you to select options from upgrade trees that enhance their abilities. Whilst it's nice that each character has their own unique upgrade tree, the trees themselves are not expansive enough to allow for a wide variety of builds like you have in some games. But it does at least give a sense of progression, and it does actually translate into your party being more powerful in combat, as well as you having more ways of dealing with encounters and situations.
You can individually gear up your characters from stuff you've looted or crafted. Crafting is fairly simple and relies upon ingredients you can find or buy from a greedy witch's shop, and for each category of crafting (armour, weapons, jewellery, potions, etc) the crafting character levels up (a la Diablo 3) revealing new recipes for increasingly handy gear (it's well worth crafting stuff you don't need in terms of equiping your party just to level up your crafter).
As you complete dungeons, others are unlocked on the world map to tackle (at first in a very linear way, later with some branching), and you can (and should) also attempt each and every dungeon on heroic mode (no potion use allowed - don't attempt until/unless you've got characters, gear, skills, and sufficient player skill appropriate to the challenge... and if you do, don't whine about dying in the forums... you can always go back and do the heroic challenges for earlier dungeons when you can roflstomp them). Some of them are multi-floor affairs (manors). Completing the first floor of a manor does grant access to the next dungeon, but I recommend you proceed through all floors of each manor first, because you'll be better able to handle the next dungeons if you do so. Oh, and because loot. You can (once you get to a certain point in the game) create your own dungeons via a quite simple in-game editor and share them for others to play, and play dungeons of others - this feature isn't ideally set up at present imo, but may well become more satisfying as it develops.
There's a quite basic storyline that progresses via character dialogue as you progress through dungeons, but if you're the kind of gamer that is all about story it certainly isn't going to blow your socks off. It's a flimsy thing that is more a light-hearted parody of fantasy tropes than a detailed narrative, but it doesn't pretend it's anything more than that. Read a book instead, some of them are awesome!
TL;DR (fair enough, I've written a f****** book here):
Overall, for the price point, I'd recommend this title to anyone that likes either dungeon crawling or turn-based combat (so long as you can tolerate it not being the most complex TB combat ever). If you like both, I'd recommend it more. I wouldn't recommend it to anyone for whom any of the following are vital: a deep storyline, bleeding-edge graphics, AAA values (whatever they are, they appear to be absent in a lot of AAA games lately...) - if you're after those, you should expect to pay a little more than the price of this!

I'm quite a fan of games that let you do what you want. This game is the prime example of that. It doesn't hold your hand and you are plunged right into the middle of a war-torn land with naught but some clothes and a blunt sword.
Warband gives such a sense of accomplishment like when you defend your first castle from 1000 madmen with crossbows and pikes with only a handful of your elite men.
When I say you can do anything, I mean you can become an infamous bandit that everyone hates, including other bandits, you can be a noble and loyal knight or lord, a humble merchant or a godlike king.
Commanding your armies in battle is one of my favourite features. One criticism is that it's too easy to take advantage of the AI though.
The game isn't too hard to pick up, but takes quite a bit of time to master the mechanics to be fully efficient at conquesting through the lands of the filthy swadians.
Did I mention there is multiplayer? If you do happen to find a server with a respectable amount of people, you will die. A lot. Because I'm bad, I keep away from online.
Also, all I've been reviewing is the base game. There are plenty of overhauls that, after 500 hours and counting, I haven't even touched. That should be a hint at how much replayability Warband has (if you manage to stick to one character for long enough).
If you like games, Warband is for you.

With the addition of profiles,
became the top notch keyboard and mouse emulator for controllers! Now you can set profiles to specific programs, either by manually selecting them or picking from a list of recently executed ones. You can also share your profiles with friends and the community by selecting the "export" option! The profile loads automatically as soon as the program is launched and is fully effective! Also possible to set multi-binds and repeatable keys. Aligned with the also recent stick movement rebinding,
is your best friend to emulate those games without any controller support!
______________________________________________
Some time ago I was saying to a friend how practicle it would be to use my XB1 controller to navigate through Netflix. As someone who's mostly in bed with the laptop by my side, a more comfortable alternative to the touchpad (or even Win8's touchscreen capability, which is not as comfortable as it sounds if it's on a laptop) was really necessary. Then came Controller Companion! I didn't hesitate to buy it, seeing all it has to offer for such a low price. While there are other free/shareware programs that do the same, I doubt all of them treat your axis as an
by letting you customize the cursor sensibility or even let you map a total of 32 binds by using the "back" button (on XBox controllers that's the equivalent to PlayStation's "select") as a secondary input. Better yet, you can set commands to the "home" button and for those with an x360 controller, CC lets you turn off the accessory with a simple button press!
Yes, it does have many positive points to it, but it also has negative ones.
the spiral layout might not appeal to everyone. Would be interesting if we had the option to alternate between that and QWERTY. As someone who used virtual QWERTY before, I know it can be easier than learning your way through a new layout.
This can be a pretty cheap alternative to the upcoming Steam Controller if we can have multiple profiles and the possibility to set the left stick to WASD and the right stick to mouse movement. I understand that the idea is to provide an easy way to navigate for those who can't always use their mouse/touchpad and keyboard, but expanding that by giving full customization so we can replace Xpadder and other programs would be even better. Controller Companion is fast, easy to use and offers some neat features that could justify a higher price -- R$6.00 (feel free to make conversions) is a bargain considering the latest build of Xpadder is around R$24.00! Here's hoping the developers aim to make it even better!

Beautiful little game based on the mechanic of having two analogue sticks, one for each brother, and a single action button each.  A good 2-3 hours even on a quick playthrough, of working together to solve puzzles - the little brother can slip between the railings of a gate, the bigger brother can apply his strength and give him a leg-up, and the two of them can thus manoeuvre through the game.
The scenery is wonderful even if the game is a little linear, but there are parts where you can go off the beaten track and get yourself an achievement or two.  The game mechanics works but - warning - though you can play on keyboard, it's DESIGNED to have two analogue control sticks.  It works fine even if they are mapped to the keyboard control, though, as it only supports the XBox controllers natively, but you really need the sticks at some points.  Use XPadder (freeware version) to map, say, an old Playstation controller to the keyboard and you're golden.
Nice enough story to carry it through, and you can't really get lost.  Particularly nice touch at the very end (just think to yourself:  What would I normally have pressed in this situation?).
Crying out for some kind of sequel where greater use it made of the control system they've come up with, though.

The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind is in my honest opinion the single best TES game out of all the franchise, from TES I: Arena, to TES V: Skyrim, and including all the spinoffs.
Morrowind was the jump off point for Bethesda in terms of open worlds, and curiously is done better than all the other games that include open worlds by the Developer, from Oblivion/F3 onwards. It has a beautiful, immersive, living and breathing world that makes you feel small. From the moment you exit the character-creation to the last time you exit the game the world, you will find, will stick with you.
The story, though, is the highlight. As soon as you step of the boat, you get enveloped into a massive power struggle between Great Houses, Forgien powers, Living gods, beings that seek to transcend existence, your previous incranation as a legendary hero, and the lore that drove them each to where they are today. Though, what is really unique, is that the story is deeper than you want it to be. Want to play a generic hero of legend? You can. Want to delve head first into incredible lore to which there is no second in gaming? You can do that, too.
As for the Gameplay, that is paradoxically one of the strongest and weakest aspects of the game. As Morrowind was a first for Bethesda in terms of making a real-time, FPRPG, the gameplay is pretty unpolished and you may find yourself struggling immensely against basic concepts such as hitting enemies with weapons, unless you have a very good idea of what you're doing and how to build your character. The game also has a lot of aspects that tend to garner extremely polarizing opinions - For example, the wayfinding, which isn't done with map arrows to show you exactly where to go, but give you a set of instructions and push you on your way. However, with outlandish bugs, an immense upward potential in terms of character power, and zany items, people have managed to break the game in ways that will be forever cemented into gaming history. The age old hack of using the Enchanting - Smithing - Alchemy trinity in order to great gear that makes a god? The chowing-down-a-buffet-mid-combat to heal yourself? That too.
In short, even if you don't like old RPGs or might find you have an aversion to the "old-timeyness" of Morrowind, you should definitely try it!

The Elder Scrolls games are all known for having an incredible amount of diverse content from weapons and spells to quests and characters. Morrowind throws you into a world with a rich history and it's up to you to decide how to play it. There are no waypoints and no fast travel. Everything is recorded in your journal so you have to figure things out. Sure, the random combat is dated and can be infuriating sometimes ("WHY CAN'T I HIT THIS GUY!") but that also makes leveling up your abilities more rewarding. The graphics are obviously outdated but if that's not super important to you then the game can still look quite nice despite its age. Overall, Morrowind is a pure rpg experience that gives you complete agency to do pretty much anything in a large and detailed environment.

Bomber Crew had been bouncing on and off my wishlist for weeks. This game kept showing up on my 'other games you'd like' lists, and it seems like a game I'd love. I love management, I love military aviation. What's not to like?
Then I'd read the reviews and complaints, consider them valid, and they would talk me out of buying it and I'd remove it from my wishlist until the next time it would show up. Now that I've seen it for myself... yeah, the reviews were right.
There's no sense of management or strategy here whatsoever. It really is about reaction speed and the accuracy of your clicks. You're performing the tasks of every single member of your crew because no-one has the self-motivation to do anything unless you're directly controlling them. Gunners won't shoot at enemy planes. The engineer won't fix things. The bombardier won't bomb. The navigator won't give a heading. Nothing.
You can imagine what this gets like when you're nearing the bomb run, you have switch to the pilot to lower the altitude so that you can see what you're bombing, highlight your target for the navigator, then switch to the bombardier to open the bomb bay doors and drop the bombs.
Don't click the wrong person though! Because when you're dealing with the bombardier, it's easy to accidentally click the pilot or something. You don't want to move your pilot to the bombsight because then no-one will be flying the plane and you'll crash.
So you handle all that. But wait, you're being attacked by 6 fighters and unless you spend 15 seconds targeting them for your gunners, no-one will shoot at them. And oh crap, you've lost your hydraulics and you need to tell the engineer to fix it, otherwise he'll just sit there. You do all that and then get back to the bomb run.
Then your gunners chime in, "Waaaaa we don't have any ammo left! What on Earth do we do now?!?"
So you have to make them get out of their turrets and go get some ammo because those unopposed fighters are shooting you to pieces. And then you get back and you've overflown the target, so now you have to tell the navigator to...
You get the idea. I'm pretty sure that being a bomber crewman during World War 2 was very stressful, but not stressful in the way this game makes it. There's no air of realism or planning in the way the game comes together.
I can see how people would like this. I think if you like puzzle games with a very tight time limit, games that require some dexterity, you'd like this. But if you're like me and you're looking for something that's management related, revolves around strategic planning, or if you're a WW2 history buff, this game isn't for you.

This is a weird one. It’s not quite a racing game per se, more just driving in 1970s Italy while talking to your passenger and hitchhikers, while at times racing or tailing other cars. It can get a bit confusing when you have to read replies and choose from 2 or 3 things to say while simultaneously steering a car in an isometric viewpoint.
I’m not sure I’ve got a firm grasp on what the game actually tries to communicate. I mean there are strong political overtones about how your character and her primary passenger are communists and that some of the people they’re tailing are neo-fascists, but I personally don’t know enough about Italian politics after WWII ended to properly judge it. I know that communism as well as anarchism had a lot to do in how Italy looks today, but I couldn’t tell you any specifics.
The game apparently also has a bunch of different endings, all relaying a variety of further information, alongside an encyclopedia of things that the characters talk about during the events of the game to give players more context to what they’re saying. If that at all sounds interesting to you, I’d recommend it for what it is, but personally, I think I’ve had my fill.

This game is all style and no substance. While it deserves to be applauded for trying something new and experimental, its gameplay and systems are so minimal that it matches more of what may be seen in an old Atari game or experienced via a film, with the very passive gameplay consisting of for the most part veering left and right on a highway as your indestructible car typically will always only need to drive straight ahead, at one of two speeds. At certain moments you can choose to pick up various hitchikers or not, which provide for more dialog exchanges, but beyond that the gameplay consists of all just driving along a highway and selecting dialog responses to your passengers.
The game is more of a somewhat docile, dialog-centric experience, with the enjoyment from the title deriving mostly from how you choose to respond to the other character's dialog and seeing how they react. Despite the weight of some of the game's dialog (abortion, running away from personal problems, etc...) I never found myself caring much about any of the characters. The game's presentation is very unique in that it mostly all takes place via the car rides being depicted and the portraits of the main character and another passenger going back and forth in dialog. The game has
which may lead to some replay value, and I'm guessing these are unlocked by selecting different responses to the dialog, taking characters to where it is they'd like to go, etc.
I enjoyed some of what the game offers, and it has some introspective moments whether through the silence one finds in a car ride or a surprising exchange of dialog with someone you didn't expect to meet, but the game is also just art mimicking reality at that point, and while its illustrative style is appealing and its very limited gameplay is unique, I can only say I'm glad I checked the game out on sale as I've been interested in it, but I don't think I would say others "need" to experience it by any means. I would only recommend this game to people that find its visual style appealing and can tolerate extremely limited, near nonexistent gameplay in the traditional sense. The game will still immerse you in moments it presents, but its default asking price of 9.99 is somewhat high.
I still enjoyed some of what the game presents, its cool visual style, and a chill atmosphere, but I also found it to be pretty pointless as a game, and think it may have been better suited as a film. At only a half an hour for my first playthrough, I may still go through another time to see more of the content/characters/endings, but at the same time I think having already gone through and seeing what it does once it may be a diminishing return of caring to do so.

Cons (in order):
- Price

- Gets old very fast

- Higher level player created dungeons in the arena mode can still contain level 1 creeps -> fighting e.g. 6 stacks full of skeletons is time consuming and the rewards are minimal.
- Badly implemented/slow UI elements. This may cause a creature not to end his turn or the movement on dungeon map is not completed -> in both cases you have to forfeit the run.

Currently the game feels just like a mediocre smartphone port that has been released on PC without giving thought to current or new features that would make it "feel more like a PC game".
If you want to see a proper port check Kingdom Rush or Kingdom Rush Frontiers.

I've played a lot of turn based RPG games in my lifetime and I have to say that this game is probably the most boiled down simplistic out of all of them.
If you haven't ever played a turn based RPG, this game would probably be a good intro into the genre... maybe...
Story and atmosphere (or lack thereof) isn't very interesting.
Extremely linear progression with loads of repetitive fights.
Creating your own dungeons isn't as fun as you might think. I suppose if you have a lot of friends with this game then it may be worth doing it since you can create the dungeons and then have your buddies run through it. However, I don't think it would be a lot of fun since these dungeons aren't that much more different than the single player dungeons.
The difficulty in this game seems to assume that you will be replaying earlier single player missions and/or doing the multiplayer dungeons for loot and experience.  I finally ran into a huge wall when I was breezing past everything and suddenly the creatures were hitting me for the majority of my health each time.
Crafting system is extremely simplistic as well.  Just form a couple of items found either by dungeon diving or purchasing from the store and you have created your new item.  You don't need patterns since new items are "unlocked" when you get to a certain level.
Overall I'm quite disappointed as the game looked to be more in depth than what it really is.  I suppose I have nobody to blame but myself for not reading up more on this game.  C'est la vie!

I picked up this game because I heard it had a great story, saw that it looked beautiful, and liked what they were doing with the single-player-coop gameplay.
After playing it through, I can say that it fully delivered in all three of those aspects, and even exceeded my expectations.
The story itself, although I did find it a slight slight bit predictable, was incredible.  The most important thing to note about it, however, is that this is not a situation where one could argue that "it should have been a movie."  The impact that this game had on me happened because I was the one who was going through the game, not someone that I'm watching.  As the game progresses, this feeling intensifies and near the end it actually manages to get emotionally difficult to play.
I've never had that happen to me in a game before, and it was an eye-opener.
Technically, the game is gorgeous and the graphics meld perfectly with the story and world, and the gameplay is smooth and enjoyable.. even though I had one or two annoying bugs (but they were fairly minor).
Overall, if you like those emotional-roller-coaster games (like To The Moon) this game is a must-play.  So do it.

is a neat little game with great replay value. However, it is best appreciated in small doses. As said by other reviewers, it is much more a narrative-driven experiment than a racing game, but there are some endings and achievements that ask for the player to have good reflexes and race other cars. The dialogue is surprisingly rich and becomes more interesting after having finished three or four playthroughs (which last between 15 and 20 minutes each), as the player begins to put the pieces together and can focus on the characters instead of the road.
may have a particular resonance with Italian or italophile people, but as someone who doesn’t know much about the history of the country, I thoroughly enjoyed learning more about some of the emblematic figures and political struggles of Italy in the 70s. And needless to say, the soundtrack and art are really unique and aesthetically pleasing !
In conclusion, I would recommend this game to people who favour choices and dialogue over reflexes and speed, and advise those who are not convinced by their first playthrough to at least complete several others before giving their final verdict.

TL;DR Wasted potential. Dead development.
Heroes&Generals despite being a good alternative to Battlefield series with a great not too fast/slow pacing (that I enjoy way more than annoying BF chaos) is a giant waste of potential, all thanks to it's devs. The development is dead as clearly unfinished mechanics (very shallow tank/air combat and RTS gamemode) haven't been significantly updated since I started playing (addition of soviet faction in febuary 2015). Reto-Moto is currently milking players by adding more and more camos/skins and overpowerd weapons/vehicles (that in 90% nobody ever really wanted) to buy (price too high for grinding these).
The player-developer communication does. not. exist. The development feedback section on forum is filled with detailed suggestions and constructive criticism. All of this is getting ignored by devs. There are almost no developer responses to these posts. Also devstreams are disappointing and the part dedicated to answering players questions is based on drawing a random question from twitch comment section.
I really want this game to succeed but seeing the current situation I cannot recommend this game for today.

I do not recall ever played something like this ... It is pure poetry , a work of art in all areas . Story, design , music , emotion , adventure , sadness , joy , fun , tied in a lovely and completely original harmony . Every moment in this game is a unique and completely new experience . There wasn't a moment I felt that something is repeated or follows a familiar pattern . Beyond all these, it manages something that only a few modern games manage: to engage the player emotionally from the first scene to the last. Those who think that this is a tale for kids, make a very big mistake . It is a story without age , light and dark at the same time that , as more fairytale becomes, the more real it looks. That's because the creators have managed to shape and mold real characters ! I wouldn't vote any expensive , overadverted game of a giant game developer company as the best game of 2013 (and beyond) , but that. It sounds perhaps too much ... Just play it and you'll understand .
I will not go into more detailes , you don't need them . Ultimately , all you need to know about this game is that you have to "live it" more than any other game that has come out this year .

DR is a fun little game with tongue-in-cheek dialogue, lite rpg-character building (unique skill trees with multiple start choices), and a solid turn-based combat system.
Pros
- Lots of unique dungeon levels, espeically for the price point. At least 58, which doesn't appear to count the 5-in-1 Castle locations.
- Turn-based combat system is clear, and the character gearing options (each character has 8 slots)let the player try meaningfully different strats.
- The majority of dungeons have a set of three challenge conditions which unlock a "Heroic Version" of that dungeon if met. Things like "Max 3 Potions", "No KO", or "100% Map Reveal." Helps keep things fresh.
- No bugs I've noticed. Yay for no bugs!
Neutral
- There is a crafting system where your dwarf gains recipes as his craft xp increases. However, since the subsequent recipes seen to require ingredients only available in level-appropriate zones, it seems to just be a more complicated store. (Maybe more later recipes would reward players who went deep into potion tech or something, I'm not deep enough).
Cons
- There don't appear to be hotkeys for expected things (like "D" for Defense or "Space" for Continue), making for more mouse clicking than I'd expect.  (1-3 work for each characters attack options, however.)
- The first part of the game- until you get your third character- struck me as a little grindy. I wish I had just powered through until I got the third character, I'd have enjoyed it more.
All in all, an easy game to recommend given the apparent lenght of the game, meaningful combat system, distinct character classes, and price point.

Defiance is a game that does a lot of right but the wrongs are very loud. That doesn't mean the game isn't any fun, just that it feels like it's just at its infancy and it depends a bit too much on the show to keep growing. I won't talk about the story of the game here, just know that the main story line is long enough to satisfy most people. Outside of the main story the rest of the gameplay relies on events and like I said, the TV show. With the TV show the game gets episode related content every two weeks. That gives you the opportunity to unlock outfits and/or weapons.
The main attraction here are Arkfalls. After the latest DLC these are even better. They vary in size, from what we call a minor arkfall to the Arkfalls in which you can go inside the ship to loot it or fight an epic boss.
The game has different types of instances that are replayable and enjoyable. For example, the original 7 co-op missions had certain tasks (pursuits) that you needed to accomplish in order to unlock an outfit. Now they have expanded on these co-op missions by adding previously solo missions, including the last game mission. It won't count towards your story progression, but if you're stuck, it's a good way to see what other people do and get some first hand experience before running the mission again. There's also the PvP instances and the gigantic Shadow War, which doesn't throw you in a different instance. You and your team fight against another human controlled team in the map where everyone is playing. People outside the shadow wars can't shoot you, but NPCs can and will. if there's an arkfall where the shadow war is taking place the visuals get impressive.
There are also emergencies which is not so different than other MMOs spawn events and Sieges, which happen at different locations every hour. These are fun "team based" missions, it is smart to wait for more people before you start siege. Think of it as horde mode so you'll want to get a high rank and make it as far as possible within the time limit.
There's a lot to do in Defiance (I don't recommend the PvP though, its probably doing more harm to the game than anything else, they should have just made Shadow Wars the only PvP in the game) and the shooting mechanics are really fun. Driving is also enjoyable and you can play by yourself but you'll never be alone. With the new changes it is easier to notice when a friendly is down so you can revive them.
I hope Trion focuses more on the bst parts of the game (the co-op parts) so this thing can grow into an amazing experience. Red 5 ditched PvP from Firefall 'cause it wasn't working, Trion Worlds should do the same in Defiance.

Back when I was a kid, I really loved the Microprose game "B-17 Flying Fortress". It was an extremely difficult simulator and had a lot of problems, but it also had a killer feature: you could manage your B-17's crew RPG style. When I heard someone was making this feature into a dedicated game, I preordered it on the spot. That turned out to be a great decision.
Bomber Crew is an intense and demanding light strategy / RPG game where you manage the crew of an Avro Lancaster bomber. You fly missions to destroy enemy targets, drop supplies to friendly troops and photograph targets of opportunity. Your crew does the actual flying, shooting and navigation, your job is to send them where they're needed (for instance sending your mechanic to repair some broken hydraulics) and to give them orders.
Your main tool in this job is a kind of all purpose targeting circle, which you use to tag enemy fighters, pick which navigation target to fly towards next and so on. Since the game runs in real time, this can get EXTREMELY hectic. Your plane is on the bombing run, fast approaching the target. The bomb bay doors are open, the bombs are primed and your bomber is sweating over his bomb sight, waiting for you to call out the perfect moment to release the payload. "Enemy fighters on the radar!", calls our your radar officer. Suddenly you have to jump out to tag the fighters so your gunners can open fire on them, but all the while the bombing target is drifting closer and closer...
As your crew gains experience they will learn useful skills which make your life easier. You'll need it all once you start to fly over Germany itself, and suddenly "flak" doesn't just mean a couple of machine guns anymore.
The small dev team has also updated the game several times, adding requested features and fixing small problems. They've also promised to add in more content, including the legendary B-17 bomber, Memphis Belle. A great, very enjoyable game and a dev team who seem to be in it for their genuine love of the subject matter. What more could you ask for? Buy this game!

This is a fun, addictive card game that is easy to learn but difficult to master.
What sets this apart from all the other card games available on Steam? Aside from generally good gameplay mechanics, it takes place in a weird, zany world that is quite apart from the stale, drab poker games we are all used to. In the world of Card City Nights there are talking corporate turnips, magical foxes, and many other fantastical things.
It's a refreshing, innovative attempt to make a card game that is different from anything else you've played.
It is single player only but I found the AI to be a challenging opponent.
As far as the plot, when the game starts out you've just moved to the titular Card City. You quickly run into a large cast of colorful characters in a surreal world. The people of Card City are obsessed with (you guessed it!) a card game. There's a tournament and whoever can collect 8 legendary cards and defeat the Card King wins a big prize. So that is your goal for the game.
After a brief tutorial you starting building up your deck and, in a mostly linear fashion, start challenging tougher opponents.
The card game itself takes place on two 3x3 grids. You and your opponent each have decks of between 20 and 40 cards. You start by drawing 5 cards, and then each turn you play 1 card and draw 1 card. You win if you can reduce your opponent's health to 0 or if your opponent is unable to play another card (his entire 3x3 grid is full). You both start out with 7 health and can go up to 10 health.
There's 4 basic types of cards you can play. Attack cards damage your opponent or disable his cards. Defense cards add to your health. Revive cards bring disabled cards back into play. Neutral cards do nothing by themselves but are useful to facilitate using other kinds of cards.
Each card has from 0 to 8 arrows on it corresponding to the N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW directions. The goal is to play your cards on your grid in such a way that the arrows connect. This will trigger a combo based on what kinds of cards are part of the combo. The cards will then be removed from play.
The whole system is very easy to learn. But as you continue on your journey you run into all sorts of new cards that force you to change and adapt your strategies. When I first started the game I was using a balanced deck with a healthy mix of all the different card types. By the midgame I had an Attack deck that was focusing on dealing as much damage as possible as quickly as possible. By the end game I had a deck that dealt no damage at all but was focused purely on disabling the enemy's cards.
You gain more cards for your deck by challenging particular characters for booster packs. If you win a booster pack you get 5 cards at random from that type of booster. As you progress through the story you will also find a store where you can buy cards for coins (that you get by defeating opponents). You'll also find a chemist who can merge certain cards together to create new cards.
There's 180 cards in all and a huge variety in the sorts of decks you can build and play against. A few examples:
The Apathetic Frog card is useless as it literally does nothing. It has no arrows or effects.  But it can be used with the chemist to create cards that are actually useful.
The Princess Pitch DX is an Attack card that is highly useful. It is easy to trigger and when triggered it removes all cards in play. So basically you use it at the beginning of the game before you've played anything useful to get a cheap shot on your opponent. Or you can play it later in the game if you're losing and need some enemy cards wiped out immediately.
I liked the various soundtracks in this game.
I encountered only one minor bug; sometimes while on the world map I had to click multiple times on a destination to travel there. That's just a minor quibble though.
I also wish there was some way to go back and see what the computer just did. There were a few times the computer played some new card that took me by surprise and I didn't have enough time to read the card text before some devastating combo was used against me. Yes, you can change the overall game speed but here I was really just looking for a one-time way of looking at what cards had just been played.
After finishing the main game there are a number of optional boss fights to try out.
Overall I quite enjoyed Card City Nights. It took me about 23 hours to beat it (including the optional fights). The game is inexpensive too! If you like casual card games check this out!

I wanted to like this game - the music in the trailer is amazing, the setting is a rarely seen one, and the characters seemed unique.
Unfortunately, the in-game music is less remarkable, the dialogue is railroaded so tightly that the characters feel one-dimensional instead of complex, and the branching story paths feel completely arbitrary - it seems at least half of them require you to unceremoniously ditch your passenger. Also, even if you've seen a cutscene before, you can't skip it, or even speed it up - this makes unintentional trips down the same story path boring and frustrating, and there's no real way to tell which turns will and won't uncover new content.
All of that could be forgiven if the gameplay were fun, but... it just isn't. The collision geometries will often have you colliding with invisible hitboxes, the "autopilot" doesn't work well enough for you to rely on it, and the frequently obscured road means you will often rear-end unseen traffic.
The car's velocity occupies the distinct territory of "too fast to stay in the right lane, too slow to pass in the oncoming lane reliably," and there are no brakes. You can stop for passengers, but the controls don't give you any way to slow the car. So if you have three cars in front of you in the right lane and three cars coming at you in the left lane, you're either going to rear-end the car in front of you or sideswipe multiple cars while lane-sharing.
The result is a buggy, unsatisfying game that seems to fail at everything it sets out to do. The setting is interesting, to be sure, but I feel that exploring it isn't worth sinking several hours into such frustrating gameplay.

Wheels of Aurelia is something quite special - I've played it for a little over an hour, having completed it four times with four different endings (apparently there are sixteen) and I still feel driven to play it again, to discover more possibilities, as well as enrich my understanding of the lead character, the driver Lella, and her hitchhiker Olga (there are many passengers whom I can pick up along the way, who are also fascinating, but as the game always starts with Olga accompanying me, I feel the strongest attachment to her).
While the game is, at its heart, a simple driving game set against a beautiful coastal backdrop, the game it reminds me of the most is Papers, Please. While Papers, Please was set in a fictional time and place, it effectively evoked the struggling post-Soviet States of the late 80's-early 90's - its social insights felt non-fiction. With Wheels of Aurelia, which takes place in Italy in the 1970's, you get that same level of social ambience, that feel that the story and characters are caught up in a tide of history. And critically, you'll feel the need to play it repeatedly to uncover more of the story, as Lella interacts with everyone a little differently depending on the person and the vehicle.
Concerning the gameplay: the driving is fun, but simple. Of the cars you can choose from, or win (via illegal street race challenges), each has its own distinctive character. Even though great pains have clearly been made to make driving easy -stopping for anything is accomplished automatically, for instance, and your car always re-aligns itself, unless you're accelerating- it's nice to see that some attention was paid to making the vehicles diverse enough that each lends a different feel to the game.
Gameplay also involves branching dialogue, which plays out simultaneously with driving - you can choose to ignore any conversation, of course, and keep your attention on the road, but that might upset your passenger! Both driving and dialogue are accomplished via the arrow keys, keeping the interface very tight and as undistracting as possible.
If you can't tell, I thought this game was excllent and I hope it gets the attention it deserves. Kudos to the developers for this fresh, stylish and thoughtful game.

Solid writing, gameplay is surprisingly engaging for short bursts if incredibly simple, great soundtrack. I have a few minor quibbles with it here and there, but it succeeded in making me feel like I was a rebellious youth on the streets of late 70s Italy, so I can forgive them.

Discuss feminism and a woman's right to choose, while racing against neo-fascists and listening to 70s-style Italian pop music. Debate papal politics with a priest or talk Juventus F.C. with a hitch-hiker as you zip through pretty towns that dot the Italian coastline. These are not the kinds of conversations you would typically find in a video game, but they feel right at home in this vintage road-trip setting. And to be honest, it is in these conversations that you find the real meat -- and arguably the point -- of this game.
You see, the driving aspect is deliberately simplisitic, but provides a welcome sense of forward momentum. It also sets the stage for the interesting chit-chat. A perfect backdrop, in my mind, which does a good job of emualting the calming, yet distracted feel of conversing while keeping one eye on the road. The conversation mechanics are similarly simple: you either pick from one of two scripted responses/questions, or you choose to stay silent. That's basically all there is to the gameplay, and it results in a fun, fluid, and deceptivley-breezy pick-up-and-play experience.
I say "deceptive" because the topics themselves can be quite heavy. This is a post-dictatorship Italy, struggling with economic and social crisies. There are progressive movements, but they face strong neo-fascist or conservative oppostion. In short, it's hard not to blame the player character for wanting to get the hell out of dodge. But as I've said, it's breezy, so don't expect a deep dive into these topics, either. For me it was just enough to pique my interest so that I began to read about some of the issues elsewhere, and the game injects enough charm and character so as to not weigh the player down at any moment. Breezy.
One thing to note is that each play-through takes somewhere between 15 - 20 mins, but each can branch in different directions depending on player choices and what seems to be a bit of a random element. There are sixteen endings in total, and I'm looking forward to trying to reach them all. Wheels of Aurelia definitely isn't a game for everyone, but if any of the above has you intriguied, you may find it quite essential.
(I originally bought this game in a Humble Bundle last year, which included an earlier version of Wheels of Aurelia and provided a Steam key once it was Greenlit.)

For people who enjoy a great experience and aren't concerned with a playtime:price ratio should certainly check it out.  If you are looking for challenging gameplay or vast amounts of content this might not be for you.
As an experience this game is incredible.  It pulls a "Shadow of the Colossus" and tells a wonderful story with little to no dialogue.  The art is beautiful, with benches to sit the brothers on, set in front of some truly great vistas.  The world is fantastical, yet grounded.
Looking at it as a game, however, leaves some good and bad. The game does contain an interesting control scheme, in which the player uses the left stick and trigger to control one brother and the right stick and trigger to control the other brother.  Clever utilization of this control mechanic is found throughout the game, with a few moments that really stand out.  The puzzle mechanics throughout the game are never truly challenging, often being pretty straight forward.  The game is also pretty short at 4 hours or less.

This must be one of the most visually pleasing and emotionally touching games I have played in recent years. Top that with some very creative controls (though at times confusing) and clever platforming and puzzles and you have the recipe for this game. The only drawback to be found here is the length of the gameplay, which must be considered quite short. But what it lacks in quantity it more than makes up for in quality. It is developed by none other than Starbreeze Studios, the company who brought us games like The Chronicles of Riddick, The Darkness and most recently Payday 2. So it is safe to say that they have had some moderate success already with proven creativity. It is clear to see the Scandinavian influences in this game in the way of backdrop scenery and folklore, and even the folky chants playing in the background.
The key feature in the gameplay is controlling the two Brothers at the same time to solve puzzles. Therefore it is highly recommended to use a XBOX controller while playing this. That was also the intention of the developers, seeing it was first released on XBOX Live. I haven't tried playing it on the keyboard, but I feel that would be a bit awkward. Even on the controller it can be awkward at times, especially when the character you control with the left stick is on the right and vice versa. Something just crashes in the brain when that happens.
It seems to me that this might be the start of something good. There is a lot of uncovered ground here both in the gameplay idea and in the world it is set in, and hopefully Starbreeze will build on this and release an even bigger title in the future. Short or not, I do not think you can play through this game without being awed in one way or another. Definitely recommend this to anyone who loves games in general and love new experiences within their favored media. Starbreeze certainly deserves your money for making an impact on the gaming scene.
I rate this game a solid 9/10!

Dungeon Rushers is fun turn-based rpg focused adapting to different enemies and situations as you progress. While I have been playing I have seen several updates to fix what the game currently offered, was well as new content added in that has made the game even more enjoyable.
While the gameplay can be seen as repetative at first, it does become more interesting as you progress. The gradual addition of enemies as you progress as well as new team members positioned throughout the campaign add a level of fluidity to the combat system so it does not get too dull.
Story
If you are looking for a truelly deep plot then this might not be the best game to go for. Instead the plot follows a band of adventurers that increases as you progress in the search for loot. The interractions that are currently scripted do push the plot forward, but seem to be mostly for the amusement of the players in comedy.
Combat
As I have been doing this in early-access some of the combat has been a little off. For the most part it is a simple turn-based combat with the speed of each member and monster determining the order of combat. Each character in tern seems to be designed to function in a particular role. An example would be the dwarf being a tank while the bard from the trailer is a support/mage. While getting to a full party can be a struggle, it is important to note that there is no permadeath, so as long as the end of the level is reached you can keep progressing.
Multiplayer
I am not a fan of competative multiplayer, but this game has done an amazing job at creating an interesting system. Each player has their own personal multiplayer dungeon that they are free to create. They can then attempt to complete other players in hopes of aquiring materials to upgrade their own. As of right now being conquered has no penalty I've noted. Wins will increase rank, loses when attacking lower your rank, so pretty standard in that regard.
As a side note. Characters still earn experience, money, and items while completing dungeons. So if you get stuck or irritated with the campaign it can be an alternative way to train units at the same time you are advancing your multiplayer rank.
Misc
Recently a gambling system has been implemented to cope with the store. The store only has a set number of items that restock at random after a dungeon has wiped the party or been conquered. The gambling system allows random potions, ingredients, or equipement. The campaign objectives are for those that want to continue to grind or get rare/unique items. When objectives are complete they unlock "Hardcore mode" in which more enemies may appear and potions are unavailable, as well as a changed map on occasion.

Tactical RPG Dungeon-crawler
Medium
9/10
The narrative element is presented during the intro and through banter between party-members and non-player characters during dungeons and through signs in dungeons.
You play as Eliot, a waiter who quits his job in search for a better life as an adventurer.
7/10
The majority of the game is spent in dungeons, which consists of tiles. The party can move only one tile at time. Those tiles can contain either a room, a monster or a trap. Rooms can contain events that can give buffs or debuffs or signs that give hints or lore.There is a wide variety of traps that falls into either magical traps or mechanical traps. There is a huge amount of different monsters of various different races, that each have their own special abilities or strengths.
Combat with monsters is turn-based tactical battles where the turn order is determined by speed. During combat the party can use various items they may have collected in order to help them such as potions or bombs.
All party-members has different map-abilities and combat abilities. Map-abilities range from the ability to locate event rooms, trap rooms or monster rooms, to healing party members, restoring stamina or mana. Likewise, all party-members have some ability to help either avoiding or mitigating traps.
Party-members can level up and gain skill points which can be allotted to provide bonuses that character's prefered map-abilities, trap-abilities or combat-abilities.
The goal of every dungeon is to find the treasure of that dungeon. Every dungeon also have three challenges that can be completed, those give no added benefit, but does provide some replayability. Once a dungeon has been completed in regular difficulty it can attempted in heroic difficulty, where the party will have to defeat monsters in order to get a key required to open the final chest.
The party can also attempt to clear other peoples dungeons in order to earn blueprints, which is required to improve the players own dungeons. The clearing of other peoples dungeons and the creation of the player's own dungeon is done as asynchronous multiplayer.
9/10
Dungeon Rushers has a 16-bit cartoon-style art-style that will be either hit or miss for most people.
7/10
The soundtrack for the game is awesome and very fitting for the game, so is the sound-effects in the game.
8/10
If you are looking for a 16-bit tactical role-playing dungeon-crawler that pokes fun at role-playing stereotypes and tropes, that offers near infinite replayability due to the challenges and steam worshop access, this is the game for you.
I still find this game very enjoyable.

Consider this an "almost good enough" game:
The game runs fine and sadly the eventual staleness of its gameplay sets in, before you're even halfway through.
The procedure is this:
You unlock all five characters and... at this point you've seen it all.
Fight monsters.
Try to get a "perfect" in the dungeon, or don't.
Equip slightly better loot - to be fair there IS some decision making about what your party equips, but again it's not explored deeply enough by the devs.
There is a crafting system which you level (but you don't get higher lvl crafting mats from dungeons so essentially you're tied to your best dungeon - which is the same as getting loot. This is a MAJOR FLAW.
In other words - there is no point in crafting because crafting can only produce you gear which is already dropping anyway.
The solutions for the crafting system are many:
A) Simplify the system's materials so they can create better gear than you find and also will not make the mats from the Skeletons obsolete when you reach the Orcs.
B) Introduce something special - random chance of making the item exceptional quality i.e. with better stats than what you can find.
C) Make crafted items that cannot drop otherwise. Right now there's about four such items, which is obviously not good enough.
Pros:
Customised dungeons other player try to beat.
An ok skill system
Easy and simple little game
Cons:
Potential unrealised.
Repetitiveness sets in very early in the game.
Variations of aquiring better gear are SEVERELY limited.
No key customisation.
Lacking a lot of intuitive hotkeys in general. Can be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥if you're on a laptop.

More and more often I'm told that less is more and games with people pointing to Morrowind as definitive proof of that mind set. It seems that there are many who think that the level of depth Morrowind indulges in is detrimental to the experience. To that I say balogna.
Morrowind was the defining single player gaming expereince for me. It's a game whose story is filled with wonder and nuance that leaves me still finding new and interesting lore with every play through. Its replayability is enough to leave me returning to it and slogging through it's dreadfully slow combat even after sinking several thousands of hours into more satisfying combat experiences like Skyrim.
And why is that? It's the depth of options available. It's how your choices matter. It's how performing actions that would ostracize you from others prevent you from taking certain paths. It's how interacting with NPCs, while extremely limited, feels like something that matters even if it is only the level that they like me that drives it. It is all of this and so very much more.
Morrowind may not be the end all be all best game of the century, but it has its charm. The combat is clunky and tiresome, but the game hits a home run in almost every other sense in ways that few games ever cater toward and that is enough to make it a timeless classic.

TLDR:  This is a solid "don't waste your time" thumbs down.
If you enjoy pixel hunting (the art of finding juuuust the right spot to position your mouse when you click), you'll love this game.
If you enjoy buggy early access or beta games or games with poor design choices used to mimic "increased difficulty", you'll enjoy this game.
If you enjoy micro-management real-time-strategy games in a WWII bomber setting and are willing to put up with bugs, dicey design/coding issues, you will probably enjoy this game.
This game was actually pretty fun, for several hours in my first session playing it.  Well, at least I did righ up until I had my crew decked out in thoughened survival gear, well equiped bomber, on the 3rd stage of the campaign, level 8 pilot, level 6 everyone else except a level 2 bombardier (more on that in a minute).
It was fun right up until my pilot decided he'd get out of his seat and go for a coffee (or whatever the heck he was doing!) while flying at low altitude en enemy territory.  This was triple-frustrating.
First, the things you can click on the screen horribly overlap so that when you position the mouse to that your eyes and the mouse icon are telling you that you have X selected, the incorrect game coding actually thinks you have Y selected.  So, when trying to select crew in tight quarters, it's quite possible to grab the wrong one or to heal or revive the wrong crewman when 2 are "down" close together.
However, even that poor coding shouldn't have made my pilot get out of his seat when my medic started to heal him.  There is a skill that allows you to heal partially wounded crewmates by clicking on them. I had used this on several prior missions.  On this final mission, I click to heal thee pilot and then go about the next set of clicks.  I notice the plane losing altitude, but too late.  The pilot left his seat.  AND...I couldn't get him back in his seat because the medic was standing so close that between the pilot, pilot's seat, and medic all the mouse was targeting was the pilot or medic, not the seat.
So, we crash, my nicely appointed bomber is destroyed and the crew that I'd just decked out in survival gear is all kia.
It's a pixel hunters dream!  I don't like pixel hunting so, I'll call it more of a nightmare (or bad design or bad code).
What makes this the MOST frustrating, is the triple whammy.  The reson I was at low altitude and didn't have more time to hunt for the "pilot seat pixel" was because several missions prior, my pilot (the strange fellow he was) decides to crash on approach to the runway.
We weren't out of fuel, there were no other issues.  He just did a lazy turn and acted as if he was on approach, but very short of the runway.    Since the mission was over, I was just moving the camera around and looking at the plane and bladn terrain/clouds when I notice we're much to low based on our distance from the runway.  Before I can get the landing gear down, my pilot decides he'd rather park in a field than on the runway straight ahead.
The bombardier dies.  This is what leads to the problem that killed my plane, and possibly this game for me.  The replacement bombardier didn't have the skill to take a medium altitude recon photo that my trained bombardier had (crew gain skill after each mission and when they acrue enough they unlock abilties).
So, my pilot killed the bombardier, then, knowing we'd be at low altitude, since the replacement couldn't do recon at medium, he decides to leave his seat when I'm not looking.  So, this is either a bug, very poor design, bad coding, or he was a suicidal German imposter.  Either way, it was terribly unfun to "lose" while I did nothing wrong.
The game feels like early access or beta.  If the developer cleans it up and fixes the bugs or shoddy code, it could be a little gem.  As it is, I'm giving a thumbs down until they put in a "fasten seatbelt" option to lock a crewman in his seat.  There's no valid reason for crew to be moving about the cabin when I didn't tell them to.  I mean, it's a micromanagment game.  If I didn't tell that idiot to leave his seat, he should not have....but he did.  So, put in seatbelts and it's a thumbs up. (When the pilot leaves his seat your plane will crash, no autopilot.)
Also, the skins pack is garbage. Don't even waste $2 on that.  They're mostly plain colors or random, simple designs with little creativity and no historical value (I assumed the latter, which is why I chipped in the extra couple bucks).
Oh, and as a note, I played offline, so steam didn't count the several hours (about 5) that I played in my first sitting.
Aaaaaand, when I reloaded the game online, the replacement pilot managed to crash the plane when I activated an evasive manuevers skill. Come for the weird, surrealist sense of humor, stay because the card game's actually pretty good.
At the end of the day, Card City Nights is a more nuanced adaptation of the card games from Final Fantasy 8 and 9; cards interact with one-another based on whether their arrows link up.  Both players have their own 3x3 grid in which to play.  This grid also serves as an important resource; if you reach the point where you can't play a card (because your grid is full, or because your hand and deck are empty) you lose the round.  Interestingly, if you run out of cards in your deck you still have a couple of turns, as you start taking damage for every card under the hand limit you are, meaning that you can still make a last-ditch attempt to turn the tables.
The simplicity of the core mechanics belies quite a bit of strategic depth; Card Mill and Disruption are all just as viable as the basic Offense and Defense strategies, but the game will require you to have a way of doing at least some of everything.  It's possible to spend a lot of time optimizing combo potential with card utility and there are very few 'wrong' ways of building a deck.
Card City Nights is apparently a massive cross-over game, featuring characters from the studio's other works; of these I'm only familiar with Iji, so most of the crossover appeal is lost on me.  Having said that, the result is a downright bizzare setting in which you'll find giant anthropomorphic vegitables, sentient moai in top hats, demons and the patron diety of explosions all living together in a single city; unfortunately you only get to explore 30-something screens of it, all illustrated but not animated.  There isn't really a story: you have a set of legendary cards you have to track down that serve as the means of stringing you from battle to battle.  All in all the plot and the setting both exist primarily to connect you to your AI opponents, and while i'd be lying if I said it wasn't charming it's not really a reason to go out and buy the game in and of itself (unless you're a diehard fan of Ludosity's library of titles); it certainly works in the game's favor more often than not, but I think they could have gone a bit further with it to make something really memorable here.
At the asking price it's definitely worth picking up.

The biggest let down is really the lack of any multiplayer, which sucks since the game is really fun and would be an absolute blast to play with friends.  Otherwise it is a fantastic single-player CCG with plenty of depth for any fan of the genre to enjoy.

A single-player CCG is a rare sight these days, and
delivers on a lovely sociophobic experience that allows you to have virtual card fun without the lowly need to match yourself against other people's skills. The AI is passable, although I have to admit that I spent most battles executing my own strategy instead of having a back-and-forth against a computer.
The visuals, characters, and humor all range from 'okay' to 'lovely', with the whole plot thing being just unintrusive enough as not to annoy you between battles. The deck management system is nothing to write home about, but it does its job and is, once again, simple enough to work.
is also streamlined and slick enough to play nicely and without any unnecessary clicks.
So in the end it all boils down to whether you'll like the combat mechanics, which are... original. A mixture of CCG and match-3, it offers a 3x3 field and a deck of cards that can be connected via a number of points (sides and corners). Your goal is to create combinations of various card types to achieve great strategic results...
...At least in theory. In practice most fights I've had ended with either me or the opponent not having valid moves (i.e. being unable to place any more cards) instead of killing each other. Perhaps it was the intended strategy—after all, disabling cards and turning them from strategic resources into clunky fodder is a part of the game. But it also made the fights lengthy and monotonous, and just didn't feel fun to me. It felt like a game of attrition.
All in all,
has an inventive system that isn't balanced/utilized properly. Thankfully a sequel seems to be on the horizon, that perhaps improves the game's less successful elements and creates an even better experience!

Time to raid some dungeons, get some loot, and then young adventurer, die a horrible death… wait a minute.
I will add a TL;DR at the end.
This story starts with Elian, a kid who finally decides to start raiding dungeons, get loot, and have an adventure. Along the way he meets friends and uncovers a horrible scandal in the midst.
The gameplay consists of going through levels/dungeons and trying to find the loot and get out. There are optional objectives to unlock a Heroic variation for the level. As you beat more levels and level up, more characters will be available for your dungeon raiding party along with better loot and gear. The game contains a shop and a crafting aspect to buy or create your own equipment and potions. If you do not want to constantly raid to try and get the same piece of equipment or loot all the time for the party you might as well do it yourself.
There is a large world map with multiple levels allowing for hours of playing through the campaign (without the Heroic variations added in). The actual levels consist of a grid of different rooms littered with enemies, traps, events, some small puzzle-like areas, and of course the loot. In the dungeon you will move space by space to find these goodies (or baddies) and of course the loot. Each member of your party will contribute unique dungeon abilities (non-combat within the grid dungeon) and combat abilities. As the story is continued the scenery will change as well since you will be advancing to different areas within the world map adding new looks for dungeons and new types of monsters.
The game’s combat is turn-based and centers around speed for deciding turn orders. Each member of your party will have three different unique possibilities to them when it is their turn. The game contains a very interesting multiplayer aspect where you can create your own dungeons with the multiplayer limitations or make a fully unlimited version for the steam workshop. In multiplayer you have limitations on your dungeon, but those can be upgraded to allow for more freedom as this is the base other players will try to plunder from. When trying to look for multiplayer dungeons you never know how hard (or easy) the dungeon will be.
The world map is designed like an adventurer’s map and it’s well, very pretty to simply look at. Inside the dungeon, as mentioned before, it is a grid map. The graphics within the dungeon are more pixelated, but still refined in look to make it nice to look at. Combat is also quite refined within its art and characters on the battlefield.
The music is relaxing and well composed to fit the atmosphere of adventure and explorations along with the style of combat.
+  Relaxing experience
+ Large amount of possible gameplay time
+ Multiplayer and steam workshop dungeons
+ Interesting story
+ Good replay value
- Early access bugs
- Possibility of getting repetitive later on (not for all, but some)

Though Dungeon Rushers does not sport a decent story, sense of progression, or intricate crafting system that we've become so accustomed to seeing, it's not advertised as including either of those.
The quirkiness is not too much. There's a huge selection of members to choose from. The art-style is cute and charming, and each character has their own appeal. Thorgrim is your grumbling old dwarf who grows increasingly tired of your antics, that vampire chick is obviously high maintenance, and you can't have a proper dungeon travelling party without a musical bard at your side. The game allows you to create your own dungeons. In any game with any amount of drawbacks, a space for player-created content is always a plus.
Most importantly is the fact that the game is still in the very early stages of development. It's — in my opinion — one of the more well-developed games to hit Early Access, and it has room to grow considerably.
How simple the game is designed means developers can freely add content as time permits. While it does little to inspire and offer a completely memorable experience, the game definitely shows promise. That's a huge win as far as I'm concerned.

Casual card game with a bit of story to go along with it. Or a character, anyway. The card game itself is interesting; you have  a 3x3 grid on which to lay cards. Cards have arrows on them; different cards have different amounts of arrows, in different directions, and the object is to lay them out in such a way that the arrows match up. This can add to your defense, damage your opponent, or, in some cases, have a special effect. So it takes a little thought, and some luck, but it's not hard to learn at all. As you play and win matches, you win more cards, and you can build your own decks using your preferred combinations of those cards to either play the way you personally like to play--defensive, aggressive, some of both--or specifically to combat a given opponent who plays a particular way. Definitely recommended for anyone who likes card games.
