4/10
While I appreciate that Card City Nights is trying to create a fresh and interesting take on card games, I can't say it really succeeds. However, the system of connecting one card to another through the arrows on the periphery of the cards has some potential. Some things that might benefit the game include some deck-building statistics in the builder. Let me organize my collection by symbol: for instance, if I click a shield in the deck-builder, only show me cards that include that symbol (including two symbol cards). Additionally, let me organize by arrow: if I click on the left arrow or left upper arrow, only show me cards that feature this. This would greatly benefit players who want to dig into the system that you've created.
The main issue with the game, in my opinion, is the booster feature. Whenever you beat an opponent, you get a booster with random cards from one of the featured sets. Some of the opponents can be played repeatedly to earn extra boosters, but often these are "best of 3" matches and can take some time. But this is a single-player game, this isn't Magic the Gathering. Just give the player certain cards after they beat certain opponents - I don't think it's a wise move to build grinding into your game. Though perhaps certain players feel excited opening boosters, I never used boosters in the entirety of my time playing Magic the Gathering (many, many years). I always bought on secondary markets where I could pick the cards I needed. You can buy individual cards from some of the vendors in the game, but the majority of the cards are underwhelming and overpriced.
The "best of 3" matches take a while, because the majority of the time it seems like the best strategy is to either have your opponent run out of cards or have him be unable to place one on the board. Attacking the opponent would be faster, but this strategy seems less viable to me than the others I mentioned. Opponents begin dropping cards with two symbols quite early in the game, meaning that only two cards are needed to create a combo. Some of the cards that opponents drop are absurdly powerful, and if you don't have an answer immediately you'll be in trouble. One opponent dropped a card that removed one card from my deck every turn - another dropped a card that disabled a random card on the board every turn (this almost always seemed to target my cards). The cards I had access to just seemed uninteresting and underpowered in comparison.
Lastly, this game has a fantastic soundtrack. Skip the game and spend your money on the soundtrack instead.

A spot on Yu-Gi-Oh affectionate parody with a diverse and slightly off kilter cast. This game combines linking cards to form damaging, defensive and dirty combos with a quirky but well-realized world populated with rivals, eccentrics and people who look like Easter Island heads. This thing is as wonderful as it is hard to describe.
That having been said, I'd not recommend it it anyone who hasn't watched the original Yu-Gi-Oh or at least knows what that is. You will not get the jokes. I also warn that if you want a challenge, you won't get it until your about halfway through the game. Thankfully for people like me who have become slightly disillusioned with the whole TGC scene, which I'd imagine is anyone looking at this review, the lack of difficulty is made up for with the ability to just play against characters for fun. Its good to see so many people interested in things like this, things that are genuine, charming and just self-aware enough to look smart without going overboard.
9/10, for simply not being ENOUGH. It needs more card effects, preferrably crazy and more crazy characters to round it out a bit further, preferably before the final boss. The shortness doesn't bother me, because I feel no pressure to finish it quickly, and the lack of multiplayer is more of a nuicance than a real problem. As for the grinding, yeh, you need to do a little bit, but it feels like a side effect of the game genre, and I'd rather do that than pay real life money at least.

Ibb and Obb is a cooperative game meant to be played with a partner. It's a 2D platformer in which you have to complete puzzles together in order to progress. Each person plays as one of the titular characters, and your goal is to complete levels by helping each other get past obstacles through various means.
The game design is simplistic, but elegant. The world is divided into two parts, above and below the ground, and gravity is inverted while you are below, meaning that you will "fall" upwards. The game is simple enough that the lack of a tutorial doesn't really matter; players can intuitively figure out how things work.
My main gripe with this game is how hard it can be for someone who's not used to playing video games. Although the controls are easy enough for just about anyone to grasp, some of the puzzles can be extremely difficult to complete. My partner and I got stuck on an early level because one of the puzzles required her to complete a series of actions precisely, with very little time to spare. She couldn't do it, so I had to do that part for her in order to finish that level.
Currently, we're at a point which requires too much coordination, and we both agreed that it would be next to impossible for us to get through together. Thus, we've simply stopped playing the game, which is sad, considering how much fun we've had playing so far, despite certain bouts of frustration.
Another annoyance is that there is no in-game option to switch characters. Your character is determined based on whether you created or joined a game; if you start a game, you will play as Ibb, the green character, whereas if you are joining a game, you will play as Obb, the red one. I feel like the inability to switch characters is such a big oversight, because depending on which one you play, you will have different obstacles to overcome, and some of them are much more difficult, in my opinion.
In summary, this is a fun little two-player game that is very easy to pick up. It's an especially great game for couples in long distance relationships, as you may sometimes find yourselves yelling at each other, which often leads to laughter. However, I would not recommend this game to those without any prior video game experience. Both players need to have good coordination together to be able to make it further into this game. Overall, this game can be challenging, but it is certainly enjoyable.

Best game I've played this year. No, really. What seems a simple enough idea is actually very involved, during bombing runs and dogfights. I refuse to use the time slowdown option that has been added post-release, because I like how it simulates real aerial combat, with slow periods of flying to and from objectives punctuated by the utter chaos of sudden pitched battle, with fighters strafing you, equipment randomly failing, and flak going off all around. You get surprisingly invested in your crew too, or I do anyway, getting really quite upset when they die in a way reminiscent of X-COM. Unlike X-COM though, you can't just reload a save game to restore a fallen airman. The game uses a single save slot and automatically saves to it every time you exit to the menu. But I quite like that - it adds to the challenge, and the emotional investment. When a character is dead they stay dead, and it makes the game that much more tense.
Very much recommend this to anyone who enjoys tactical simulations, or has any interest in aerial warfare.

I’m about 90% sure this isn’t an accurate representation of bombers in Europe during the World War II, but don’t let that keep you from moving forward with Bomber Crew.  It was sold to me as “WW2 FTL,” which immediately tickled all of my fancies, but it turned out to be just different enough that I was caught off guard – but familiar enough that I can still tell you that this is as close as you can get to playing FTL in a World War 2 bomber.
If there’s one thing that is fundamentally similar between FTL and Bomber Crew, it’s that they’re both really tough games.  You start out putting your crew together in a sort of “pick the best ones” lineup to fill each role.  There aren’t any resources or requirements here and the supply is infinite, but these men and women end up being very important to keep alive as the game moves forward.  Then you have to equip your crew with the ever-growing collection of gear and equipment in a very ‘XCOM-ish’ setup that requires you to use the money that you earn from each successful mission to purchase additional and better gear.  Next, you get the opportunity to address your aircraft – which seems to be modeled after the British Avro Lancaster – by upgrading, adding parts, and of course decorating it as you see fit.  From there you’ll head into the briefing room and pick one of the available missions, determine what difficulty and objectives fit your current situation and skill level, and head on out.
The gameplay itself seems very hands off in the early missions.  You can easily complete the necessary tasks like aiming a special reticle at enemy fighters so your gunners will engage them, sending your crew to repair broken pieces of your plane, and dropping those lovely bombs (or whatever needs dropping) on the targets below.  However, this peaceful simplicity is quickly lost as you head in to tougher missions with a combination of ground fire/flak and many tough and deadly enemy fighters.  Those “survival” stats that you think are useless early on start to become increasingly important as your flying coffin starts to fall out of the sky.  There doesn’t seem to be any sort of long term failure state – as I would have encountered it quickly – but if you fail several missions in a row and keep getting forced to pick fresh crews and throw them in to a poorly upgraded plane, things will get increasingly more difficult.  Difficult enough that you will probably want to restart the whole campaign to break the loop.  It does seem like, as you progress, they give you better starting bombers.  However, it is often the case that they aren’t as good as the one you left in a burning crater somewhere over France.
If there’s one significant issue that I have with Bomber Crew, it’s that I feel like the controls really inhibit the game.  It helps a bit to use hotkeys, but you’re still required to click specific areas in, on, and around your plane in order to do pretty much every task.  This can be a real pain as you move the camera around to get a better an idea of what threats are coming at you from the outside.  I think it would be nice if you could direct your crew from any camera angle rather than the close up side view that you’re required to use.  Perhaps if you could  just turn on or off the roof of the plane so you could manage the crew the same way, but also keep the ability to have a nice view of the bomber’s hull and its damage while heading out to its mission if you want.  It is also a hassle that the ‘aiming’ method you use for targeting new headings or enemy fighters is extremely sensitive compared to other mouse and camera movements.  There is an independent slider for its sensitivity, but it’s one of those cases where it’s so high that determining the sensitivity can easily leave it too fast or make it too slow.  It may be the case that, as I familiarize myself with the hotkeys and can instinctively select the crew members I want at the time I want them, I’ll be able to make up for the times I accidentally send someone out to stand on the wings or click just beside the machine gun instead of on it.   It just seems like with the crowded nature of the inside of a bomber, the developers should have probably taken a little more care to make sure tasks can be easily performed in the complete chaos of bullets ripping your burning hull to pieces.
I really enjoy when I see an indie game that looks like it’s going to be fun and it ends up living up to my expectations.  Not every game is going to be perfect, especially not right after its release, but if this developer sticks with it – we’ll have another classic title out there that carves a little deeper in the mountain of new genres that indie games have started to mine.  I usually don’t pay full price for games that often, usually only when it’s a game I’ve been excited about for a while, but I made an exception here because it appealed to me in a number of my interests in both gaming and aviation.  If you even kind of liked FTL for its gameplay or enjoy hectic management games, this is 100% for you and you should have already bought it before getting to the end of this review.

I've seen several people who played this game on youtube and thought it looked pretty fun so I decided to buy it.  Unfortunately I just can't reccomend it, because it isn't a very good platformer.  After a couple hours of playtime I've gotten halfway through world 6 (out of 9 IIRC) and I have been constantly frustrated by one thing: lack of consistancy.  As you may or may not know, the game is a platformer, challenging you to run through the levels as quickly as possible while avoiding obsticles.  The catch is that you're doing so on the back of moving trucks with slightly wonky physics, and therin lies the problem.  The trucks move in a wild and unpredictable manner, bouncing off each other and off obstacles, stopping and starting on a dime.  This really ruins the "get to the end as quick as possible" goal because you don't know whats going to happen at a given point.  You get a neverending stream of deaths, not due to lack of skill but due to just randomness: a truck you were aiming for hits an obsticle and stops dead, or is freed from a pileup and rockets forward and its just frustrating but not in a good way.  You don't feel satisfied upon completing a level of clustertruck, you just feel relieved because it often feels like I won, not because I was good at the game, but because I was lucky.  Take, for example laser world.  This was one of my favorite worlds because it emphasized jump timing and planning ahead.  But, one level in particular stood out for taking all this and just tossing it out.  Level 4-7 involves dodging lasers while heading through a fairly narrow canyon.  The first half is fine, but about 2/3 of the way through there's a dogleg bend where trucks tend to get stopped.  If you're jumping and keeping up your speed through the first half and the trucks get stuck there?  Good luck not dying.  Pretty much the only way to beat that level is to have the trucks not get stuck, and that just isn't fun.  Its a shame really, because its an interesting concept and one thats fun to watch, but the endless frustrations brought by random elements, occasional physics issues, and other random bugs (for example occasionally spawning way off to the side and instantly dying) pretty much suck any actual fun out.

Ibb and Obb is a cooperative game meant to be played with a partner. It's a 2D platformer in which you have to complete puzzles together in order to progress. Each person plays as one of the titular characters, and your goal is to complete levels by helping each other get past obstacles through various means.
The game design is simplistic, but elegant. The world is divided into two parts, above and below the ground, and gravity is inverted while you are below, meaning that you will "fall" upwards. The game is simple enough that the lack of a tutorial doesn't really matter; players can intuitively figure out how things work.
My main gripe with this game is how hard it can be for someone who's not used to playing video games. Although the controls are easy enough for just about anyone to grasp, some of the puzzles can be extremely difficult to complete. My partner and I got stuck on an early level because one of the puzzles required her to complete a series of actions precisely, with very little time to spare. She couldn't do it, so I had to do that part for her in order to finish that level.
Currently, we're at a point which requires too much coordination, and we both agreed that it would be next to impossible for us to get through together. Thus, we've simply stopped playing the game, which is sad, considering how much fun we've had playing so far, despite certain bouts of frustration.
Another annoyance is that there is no in-game option to switch characters. Your character is determined based on whether you created or joined a game; if you start a game, you will play as Ibb, the green character, whereas if you are joining a game, you will play as Obb, the red one. I feel like the inability to switch characters is such a big oversight, because depending on which one you play, you will have different obstacles to overcome, and some of them are much more difficult, in my opinion.
In summary, this is a fun little two-player game that is very easy to pick up. It's an especially great game for couples in long distance relationships, as you may sometimes find yourselves yelling at each other, which often leads to laughter. However, I would not recommend this game to those without any prior video game experience. Both players need to have good coordination together to be able to make it further into this game. Overall, this game can be challenging, but it is certainly enjoyable.

Dungeon Rushers | Testing Grounds
Here's my review of Dungeon Rushers

+ Very strategic fun gameplay in a traditional turn-based style where you take turns striking, you must carefully plan out how you traverse the dungeon and also be careful which abilities you use on which enemy to be as resourceful as possible.
+ Challenging, you and the enemies both have pretty low HP so you really have to be careful to avoid as much damage as possible, along with traps, and use healing items sparingly as they don't come very often.
+ A variety of abilities that can be upgraded as you level up
+ Great soundtrack and battle music
+ Amusing story and lot of humor in the dialogue
+ Lots of content
+ Crafting, enemies and chests can sometimes drop crafting materials or you can buy them from the shop which you can combine to craft a large variety of weapons, armor, and potions and you can level up crafting professions as well to make better gear later on in the game.
- The "events" seem to give a chance at a blessing, debuff, or item from a chest. The problem with this is that they can really ruin your run if you get debuffs like poison, bleed, or burn damage which will damage your characters pretty severely in battle, while the good buffs don't seem to help that much. (I would have liked to have seen a "HP/Mana restore" buff from one of these events)
- Lacks enemy variety, or more importantly there's not enough bosses which makes it feel like you are fighting the same group of monsters over and over that doesn't feel rewarding.

It may feel like a mobile game sometimes, and a free-to-play game other times - but it somehow manages to just break through that barrier and give you enough control to make it feel like a good game that you've paid for.
It is slow though. Very slow. You have to grind through levels and do a lot of levelling, with features being given to you gradually over a very long period of time. 2 hours in now, and I still haven't gotten the arena or my own dungeon unlocked. I still haven't unlocked enough characters to even make use of the party swap in/swap out feature.
I can tell there's something great here though. A detailed RPG with a really cool art style that will challenge your decision-making skills and allow you to compose your own party of adventurers which will get slaughtered unless you think ahead and use some strategy with your composition.
If anyone has any questions, feel free to either add me or comment on this review, and I will answer them!

I don't normally like card games much, and probably wouldn't have looked at this title twice under normal circumstances. But I had a coupon for 90% off, it looked nice, had mostly positive reviews and promised to be something different from the usual card game. So I purchased this game anyway. And I must say it's one of the better decisions I have ever made, as this game is quite fun to play.
The gameplay is somewhat different from any card game I have ever played before, with each player placing cards on a 3x3 board. Most cards have arrows indicating which directions they can be linked to other cards, and an icon which designates which effect the card will have (attack, defence, revive and coin). The aim is to reduce your opponents defence to zero while preventing them from doing the same to you by chaining cards with a total value of 3 or more icons. Although it's game over when one of the players has filled up their board and cannot place a card at the start of their turn.
Difficulty starts out quite easy, with your opponents mostly killing themselves by filling up their boards before you even have a chance to finish them off properly. But after the first couple of locations are dealt with the AI quickly steps up its game. All the opponents seem to have different strategies, as well as different cards in their decks, so what was a winning strategy for one opponent may fail completely with the next. The game easily allows for different strategies to be employed by giving the user a total of six different card decks, so you could for example have one deck which is primarily an attack deck, another wich focuses on defense, another which quickly discards cards from an opponents deck (I forgot to mention, when a deck reaches zero the player takes 1 point of damage each turn, even if they have a shild activated. And dies when they have no cards left to play.) and another which... well, you get the idea. Although I could find no way to completely remove a deck once created.
The game is beautifully presented in all aspects. The cartoon graphics are first class, the music is pretty good and provides a nice ambiance, and the plot is mildly amusing if perhaps a little ridiculous.
One feature I would have really liked to see in this game, and I feel is a bit of a glaring omission is some kind of online two player mode. I'd really like to test my Card City Nights skills against human opponents, as beating the AI can be a bit too easy once you know what you're up against.
Overall I'd give this game 8.8/10. While it was really quite fun to play there is little to make me want to come back to it after completing the game, 100%-ing the achivements and beaten every opponent at least once. That and a lack of any kind of two-player mode prevents this game from breaking the 9 point barrier.

Simple in concept but not the best execution.
Clustertruck gives you a simple goal, make it the end zone while jumping from truck to truck and touching anything else results in an automatic fail allowing you to restart the level. It's an absurd concept but interesting enough to make a full game out of. The problem is the controls feel incredibly mushy and you feel like squishy ball rather than a person jumping from truck to truck. I'm not sure if this is what it's supposed to feel like. Everything in the game is physics based but on a physics model that seems to be seemingly random as truck paths will drastically change in your different attempts and sometimes leave you in situations where you couldn't have made it even if you were the best player. I've seriously had groups of trucks ahead of me crash and all go off of a cliff leaving me without any options to continue in the level. The random physics also seem to apply to the player but to a lesser extent, sometimes I'll try and jump forward while sprinting to clear a large gap only to get shot up into the sky for no apparent reason. You can sometimes "wallrun" on the sides of trucks and launch yourself but this seems to be due to the game thinking that the slightly tilted truck is a platform but it's so inconsistant it's a major headache.
I only recommend this on sale.

Awesome piece of software. My gaming PC is in the basement, with cabling run for two locations on the first floor: a typical office setup, and the living room TV with wireless Xbox360 controllers.
Previously I had the computer set to duplicate the display full time, and used (the also awesome) Voicemeeter audio driver and software mixer to pump audio to both office and living room simultaneously. This worked fine, but there are horrible tearing issues on secondary displays when cloned and switching primary displays is an extra step I couldn't be bothered with. Typically games aren't affected because Vsync, but we watch a lot of video as well.
Now, with Controller Companion, I'm still able to game in the living room without any stupid prep work on the PC, but I can just switch video output to ONLY the TV, using a button combination on the controller, meaning no tearing issues. I can also control Windows completely, meaning no running back and forth or logging in remotely from my phone to fire up a video or start Steam Big Picture.
Honestly had I seen this two days ago I probably would've saved a few hundred bucks ordering a second (budget) gaming PC for the living room so the kids would stop bothering me, but that's not true at all: It's worth any price to get the kids to stop bothering me. Also this software is just rad for running a living room PC.
Seriously, aside from the first cherry-chocolate malt I had at DQ after the horribly long winter in this god awful wasteland in which I live, this is the best three bucks I've ever spent. I actually gave the guy more cash money on the other site on which it's being sold just because it's that great. You can accomplish the same thing with other software, lots of time, and copious amounts of sadism, or you can buy this.

- Still a great game after nearly a decade
Cons:
- The game is old; in my experience the game is capped at 30 fps with mediocre graphics
- Once you reach the space stage, it will get repetitive quickly
- Creature creator controls is a bit buggy at times
- Needs an Origin account to access online content such as the Sporepedia
You know those games where once you start to play, you can't seem to quit? Spore is one of these games, and I have enjoyed every hour that I've spent playing.
Due to the freedom of choice that you have, you can try out different ways to play; whether you want to be a warmongering dictator, a money-crazed economist, or a friendly peacemaker, the choice is yours I've had multiple saves, each with a different archetype, and I can assure you that the effort spend is worth it.
While on the topic of archetypes, there are 9 total archetypes. Each has their own unique skills and advantages in the space stage. Archetypes are determined by your behaviour in previous stages. For example, if you are aggresive throughout the game, you will get the Warrior archetype which increases you spaceship's health and weapon effectiveness. Note that archetypes are determined after the civilization stage and as you enter the space stage. This means that you can make up a combination of 4 different alignments to determine your archetype. It's hard to explain so just Google it. TL;DR: There are multiple classes which have different skills and advantages.
The game is divided into 5 stages: Cell, Creature, Tribal, Civilization and Space.
The Cell stage acts as a tutorial and foundation to your game. Here, you will decide how you will playstyle in the Creature stage; be it an aggresive carnivore,a sociable herbivore, or be the best of both worlds and become an omnivore.
The Creature stage is where the fun starts. You play as a creature you design and try to evolve to a higher sentience. While doing so, you hunt or befriend other creatures to gain body parts which you could use to alter your appearance and abilities. Here, you finalize your looks and enter the Civilization stage.
If the Cell stage is a baby, and the Creature stage is a child, then the Civilization stage is the pre-adolescent. The game suddently changes to a RTS and therefore management becomes essential to the game. You control your units and try to achieve global domination by claiming other cities through various means. Here, it gets harder as you pave your way to the Space stage.
As I said before, the Space stage is where you will invest the most time in. You explore the universe, meet new species, gain new allies or enemies, and eventually conquer the galaxy. Here, the game's plot starts to develop (although personally it doesn't really matter). This stage requires the most time and focus as the fights get more intense and quests get more complicated and time-consuming. You'll learn more of the business aspects of the game as you trade your resources for money, realizing that some colonies offer more for the same resource. So get money, get better equipment, and start aiming for space domination.
When it first game out, Spore boasts the abillity to be able to create creature that you like. That is true to a certain extent, but it doesn't stop there. When you reach the later stages, you get to design buildings and vehicles. The creation tool is simple and user-friendly and looks crappy at first. But with enough creativity and skill, you can create a lot of unique creations that looks and functions differently.
There's also the Sporepedia, where you get to share yor creations and download others'. Unfortunately, the system is unappealing and frankly, bad. It is horribly crowded and the filters don't really help. It would be better if Steam enabled the Workshop here, although it is unlikely since Spore is owned by EA, and the game pretty much runs through Origin.
For both DLC, the C&C and Galactic Adventures DLC, please refer to their individual reviews on my account.
Spore is a great game if you love to create monsters and let your creativity run wild. It is also a great RTS with a lot of content to explore. The space stage, however, may get repetitive. I usually find myself playing the space stage for a few hours before going to the creature creator to freshen up my mind. Despite its age, Spore is a wonderful classing and remains enjoyable even today.

Brothers is an adventure game that plays like a cinematic experience. While the game only offers about 5 hours of gameplay (with very little replay value), you will discover that it accomplishes more in those 5 hours than most 50 hour games do today. The Swedish game company Starbreeze Studios worked with film director Josef Fares, and I think that a lot of his skills  in telling stories transferred into this project. The camera work is spectacular, never glitching and often used to show off beautiful artwork or colorful characters. The birds eye perspective of the two main characters is completely free of user interface elements, making it feel like 'you are the character' rather than 'you are playing the character'. The graphics are similar to the whimsical characters and environments seen in the more modern Fable games. They aren't realistic by any means, but they are still beautiful to look at.

An interesting and innovative collectible card game with a nice comic book aesthetic and solid story to progress through.
There is the background exploration of the city and its characters and the various silliness going on, but the primary draw is the gameplay of the card game of course - and it plays pretty well, with it being fairly easy to pick up but there is a fair amount of strategic depth in both selecting your deck, and actual play of cards and reacting to what your opponent is doing.
A key feature is that instead of being just another variant of existing card games with different stats used to basically do the same thing, the mechanics of how the game plays is completely different but reasonably easy to pick up. Then on top of that you get the standard variations to the rules added to the cards, but the triple aspects of the cards connections, the card type (attack, defense, etc.) and any special rules or bonuses makes for a lot of ways cards interact with each other, making deck building and gameplay pretty varied and tactical.
Overall this is very easy to recommend for anyone that likes the genre as it combines a well thought out and innovative card game with a well polished wrapper around it.

I used to use xpadder to control my desktop (mouse, volume, scroll wheel etc) but there are several big advantages to this software:
*
*
The companion will stay on in games and apps you still need a mouse for, but will switch off in big picture mode or for controller enabled games. You can even override this with a simple button press and it will remember your preference. Genius!
*
*
Most of the time when couch surfing, I'm typing in simple searches like 'netflix', 'totalbiscuit', or 'PC master race' ;) In that situation, getting up is a pain and a second wireless keyboard seems like overkill, so the keyboard input is really helpful. That's not to say it doesn't work really well; it's probably slick and easy enough to blog or write on and it's leaps ahead of steam's similar big picture feature, but it's not a keyboard rival and wasn't designed to be.
*
*
If you've ever used your analogue stick as a mouse pointer in a desktop situation, you'll really appreciate this. You can be slow and precise, or shoot off to the corner of your screen to quickly reach things.
*
*
No more quickly flicking the top of the battery pack out of your xbox 360 controller and back in, a simple button combo turns it off for you. Hallelujah!

I thought Oblivion was superior to Skyrim, but after playing Morrowind for the first time, I can say it outclasses its successors in almost every conceivable way. Initially I was apprehensive because of Morrowind's antiquated mechanics and lack of fast travel and map markers (handholding, essentially), but these are just obstacles which can be overcome by progression, much like a difficult encounter or level requirement. The sheer amount of content and depth of lore present here evokes lamentation when you think of what Bethesda has become; I truly believe every subsequent release has been a downgrade and recommend any fan of the series, nay, any fan of role-playing games to acquire this immediately. Mods are only recommended if one truly cannot handle the vanilla graphics or interfaces. I s'pose if you stepped off the boat and the first thing you did was try and find or map a sprint key, then some can be installed for convenience, but shouldn't be used at the expense of immersion. Perhaps you may require several guides - especially if you've only played Skyrim - and, well, that's your prerogative, but I implore you don't spend more time on the wiki than you do in-game. Well, this is pretty long-winded... Anyway, just get it and you'll never feel the same way about its successors, even more so when you're levitating across large portions of the map and reminiscing about how you died trying to bludgeon that worm several hours ago.

Morrowind is simply the best the RPG-Genre has to offer, aside from the Fallout games. The game is rich filled with lore, locations, loot, and cliffracers. You first start off as part of the trend of being a prisoner. Now, depending on how you built your character (mostly from picking a class or creating one) you can be as weak as a kitten, strong as a rock or somewhere in between. The main story is roughly 5-8 hours depending on where to go and such, now, speaking of travel, I have to say, it feels like real life, walking is slow, but jogging is slightly faster and there's no run button. But that can be remedied rather easily and quickly by dedicating yourself to the ''speed'' attribute. I'd highly go against this for 3 reasons:
1. By devoting yourself to speed, you're character is going fast, but is weak in almost every aspect.
2. Even without speed, you can easily get around rather easily via silt striders (which act as carriages from Skyrim).
3. There is this one in-game item which you can get from a specific person named ''Boots of blinding speed'', this particular person isn't very far if you take the Seyda Neen siltstrider to Vivec, and taking the Vivec boat to a town named ''Hla Oad''. The person should be somewhere East, not far from Hla Oad.
Now that we've gotten out of the way, I'll tell you this, even if you somehow make a powerful class, it WILL have its disadvantages, whether that disadvantage comes from race, gender, obviously class and how you go through the tutorial.
Off in the start, everything is against you, even the citizens of Morrowind will make your life a nightmare. But that can be remedied (again) through a attribute ''Personality'' which increases the chance of speech successes and starts your conversation with (almost) every with a high or low ''disposition'', again, this is dependant on personality. This game isn't perfect, and I'll list SOME of the hundreds of the major problems that plague this game:
1: ♥♥♥♥♥♥, old engine, the engine Morrowind uses is VERY old (2002 old), as such downloading mods that improve experiences will cause lag and stability issues. Go on Google and search ''Morrowind, OPENMW'' and search up a tutorial on how to download it. What this essentially does is improve UPON of the old engine, as such, it makes it on par with some of the newer, more modern engines.
2: Poor combat. It's not perfect, yes, as even if you use weapons you ARE skilled at, you will still frequently ''miss''. I guess I don't hate it enough to add a mod that improved the combat. Yes, again, if you don't like the combat, add a mod.
3: Crash issues and bugs. Sometimes you may encounter a few pieces of♥♥♥♥♥♥ nasty bugs in the game. Such as getting yourself stuck in a tree or even buildings. That can be resolved with the TCL command in the console (`, above the TAB key).
Also, I highly reccomend a Youtuber that goes by the name ''Zaric Zhakaron'', he is fantastic at the Elder Scrolls games and will help you through videos on how to make the very game, Morrowind, a bit more slice of Heaven.
If you havent played Morrowind, I highly reccomend that you do, and I implore you to do so.

This game is probably my favorite game from 2013.
Brothers is an adventure game that plays like a cinematic experience. While the game only offers about 5 hours of gameplay (with very little replay value), you will discover that it accomplishes more in those 5 hours than most 50 hour games do today. The Swedish game company Starbreeze Studios worked with film director Josef Fares, and I think that a lot of his skills  in telling stories transferred into this project. The camera work is spectacular, never glitching and often used to show off beautiful artwork or colorful characters. The birds eye perspective of the two main characters is completely free of user interface elements, making it feel like 'you are the character' rather than 'you are playing the character'. The graphics are similar to the whimsical characters and environments seen in the more modern Fable games. They aren't realistic by any means, but they are still beautiful to look at.

A Tale of Two Sons probably isn't for everyone and certainly can't be considered serious gaming.
The game is linear, third-person, and difficult only because you control one character with the left stick and the other with the right stick. There isn't much meat in this game with only 12 achivements and 4-6 hours of play time.
There is zip dialog (we'll cure the foreign distribution and language issue by using grunts and gestures while avoiding the expense of voice actors).  There were other aspects of the game that suggested that it was made on the cheap like an invisible NPC, crude graphics in one chapter, limited camera angles, poor proportions for some items, etc.
Achievements really aren't for merit or difficulty.  They seem like an after-thought and more related to finding Easter eggs in the game than showing any skill or working out anything difficult.
There is no plot beyond a quest to get a magic item to save the boys' dad,  After all the trouble, there is a disappointing ending that presumably was to make you feel sad and think that doing good requires sacrifice or some such.
It had some high points like flying a glider, but the mean average is below zero in my oipinion. Basically this game is as flat as a pancake when it comes to excitement.  Not sure I would recommend it to anyone. I'd give it a PPPfffffpppptttthhhh rating.

What an incredible game!
Every aspect of this game is completely elemental, from the gameplay to the storytelling. It is one of those rare games that presents itself to you as-is, without hints or tutorials or even comprehensible dialog, and yet is 100% accessible due to near-perfect design.
The controls are probably the defining element of the game and they are based on the concept of controlling both of the brothers at once. Both in theory and in practice this is an awesome idea, and it works really well.
The visuals are clean and consistent with a stunning sense of grandeur and fantasy.
The story, rather than being confused due to the lack of dialog (characters speak a vaguely nordic language), is very engaging and evocative. The cartoonish, fantasitcal appearance of the game belies an experience that is much more gritty and emotionally impactful than your average adventure game.
Expect to put about 3 hours into the game, with some replay value if you want to experience all of the little side-stories.

I've had this game for a decent amount of time now, and I can say that I do recommend this game. However, it definitely isn't perfect (not saying that it can't be). When the game is good, it is fantastic, the gunplay is great, all of the different roles you can choose from, it truly is a great game, but when it's bad, it's baaaad. Tank gameplay is both underpowered and overpowered, infantry can be sniped from across the map and unless you have anti-tank weapons you really can't do anything about them. At the same time, anti-tank mines and grenades deal an incredible amount of damage in an incredibly small amount of time, the RPG-43 and the Panzerwurfmine are perfect examples. The aircraft (I haven't done a lot of piloting, so this is coming from and infantry perspective) seem to have a large advantage over everything else.  Their bombs can easily take out infantry, jeeps, IFVs, and tanks. For the most part, that's the way it should be, but they aren't balanced properly. Many games I've been recently have the air force on one team, but not the other. The main balancer of planes are other planes, when there is no opposition in the air, they have an absolute field day. The AA guns do help a bit, but you can easily be killed with a bomb or an infantryman before you even get to deal damage. Paratroopers are a lot of fun, but enemy aircraft can shoot down the paraplanes very easily, unless there are friendly fighters protecting it. The recon and infantry classes are, for 90% of the time balanced well, but you occasionally get that one guy who can snipe you from a bush half the map away from you, which isn't really the devs fault, but is VERY annoying. Overall I've found that games that have only infantry (I'm counting paratroopers and recon as infantry too here) have the best gameplay. As I said, when the gameplay is good, there aren't many games that can match Heroes and Generals, but some improvements need to be made. That's all I got.

It's not the most balanced or in-depth CCG, but it oozes a charm that I've come to expect from a Ludosity game.
PROs:
-The cards have personality to them
-The mechanics are fairly innovative. It's not a MTG, Yu-gi-oh, or hearthstone clone.
-The art is stylized and fun
-The dialogue is silly and each NPC feels unique.
-It's only $4
MIX:
-Standard CCG RNG. Can be frustrating, but it's kind of inherent to the genre.
-Most matches are fairly easy
CONs:
-The final opponent of the main story is unfair. Like, it's the point, but it's still annoying.
-Some people might find the music repetitive
-You're not going to be able to have endless new and interesting matches.
Overall, I find this game to be incredibly enjoyable, not for the gameplay, which is fine, but for the heart and effort that went into character design and dialogue. I was motivated to get good at the game so I could see who the next character would be and what cute little jokes they would tell.

I usually don't bother leaving games a review at all, let alone a negative one...
...and, it pains me to leave this game a negative review, because it aims to be something very rare (and something I much desire) in the video game marketplace: an age-neutral co-op game. All the other coop games on the marketplace are shooters with blood and guts and the disemboweled souls of little puppies flying everywhere. I was hoping that the game would be something fun to play with young folk. It was excellent until we reached the little black spikeballs of death that chase you. Despite all our combined inginuity and (not too terrible) platforming skills, we could not progress past a certain scene with spiky deathballs that chase you. Was there a difficulty setting we could turn down? Nope. Were there cheat codes we could use to experience the rest of the game? Nope. Could we just "git gud"? I suppose,  but the goal wasn't to play an intense, twitch-based, control-heavy platformer.. it was to have fun with a friend, and also to solve some cool two-player puzzles (like the gameplay trailer shows.)
The little black monster also neatly brought into focus the game's other failings: the controls are unpleaseantly slippery, which exascerbates the precision needed to engage the puzzles and platforming elements, especially perching on your friend's head. Perching on your friend's head is an element needed to solve many puzzles, but for such a pivotal gameplay element, it relatively difficult to achieve. We always needed two or three tries to accomplish something central.
All-in-all, from what I've seen, the concept is good, and the art is fairly cool, and the mood is cheerful, but the execution was a fail, because the execution kept us from experiencing the rest of the game. I wish I could reccomend this--I really do.

This is my third time attempting to right this review, since when my wireless controller turns off I have to press the xbox/central button to turn it back on, which automatically puts steam in big picture mode and deletes my review progress.
Its too bad that steam doesn't have 'neutral' reviews. This piece of software does exactly what it says on the tin, and works well with my knock-off Xeox wireless gamepad. You can bind essentially any key to any button you want, and can even bind non-standard functions such as opening steam or temporarily disabling controller companion. However, you cannot change the left and right sticks (except when you click the sticks in to act as a button) as they are used exclusively for the mouse cursor and mouse wheel/scrolling, respectively, but you can change how fast the controller moves and scrolls in the settings. The back button also cannot be repurposed, as it is used to activate a secondary function on all buttons when held down, with the exception of the left or right triggers and the start button.
Controller Companion also does not interfere with any games, as it temporarily disables itself when any game is launched in fullscreen. For games that don't launch in fullscreen, you can simply press the back and start button together to disable it manually, so unless you're playing a game where you need to press start and back at the same time, you won't have any problems with it.
The problems I have with this software is the lack of being able to bind more than one key to a button at any time, even though this is a function that free software such as joytokey has natively, which can pose a problem if you want to use basic windows commands. Also, the in-built virtual keyboard, while designed specifically gamepad use as the keyboard is designed in a circle-like manner rather than a traditional layout, is just a bit too twitchy and/or unresponsive, and can put strain on your thumb. Also I've had numerous problems with the xbox/central button. Not only does pressing it bring up an annoying 'click here for help' prompt, but it also, seemingly randomly, forces me into big picture mode regardless of the button settings I have. I don't know if this is because I'm using a knock-off controller, but I doubt there's any way to fix it. Also while you can make a shortcut to turn the controller off it does not work for me, likely due to the same reason.
In conclusion, this software is well-priced for what it is, works quite well and is a good choice if you're a couch-based PC-gamer, but there's also other free software out there that can do basically the same job for free.
EDIT: After some googling I've managed to disable the crappy xbox accesories that was causing a popup every time the guide button was pressed, as well as using a dll file to stop big picture popping up every time the guide button is pressed also. It's still dumb that I had to do stuff like that to get my controller to work right, but that's not the fault of the controller companion software.

If you're a controller freak, look no further than Controller Companion. (tldr...skip to bottom...)
Of all the controller assistant applications that I've tried, none of them have been entirely suitable for couch gaming, they have only ever been keyboard and mouse emulators.
While Controller Companion is another one of those emulators, it manages to seamlessly merge your controller experience with your PC. Other programs break the immersion with overly complicated settings, too many keybindings, and the constant requirement to disable the program every time you want to run a game. Controller Companion manages to solve these hassles with simple user interface for settings, intuitive controls, and most importantly, Big Picture Mode integration.


With the push of one button, Controller Companion can launch Steam in Big Picture Mode, while disabling itself in the process. This allows you to operate the interface using the intended gamepad controls, rather than with the emulated mouse.

Not only does it work with steam, but with any fullscreen application. Say for instance, you happen to use EA Origin for some strange reason (I know, crazy right?), or your Assassin's Creed 4 key was exlusive to the U-Play launcher. When launching any fullscreen title, regardless of DRM, Controller Companion will switch off its mouse/keyboard emulation in order to let you use your controller as the game/application intended.

What? You didn't want it to switch off the mouse? No problem. With a simple button combo of back+start, Controller Companion will reactivate the mouse controls. Other combos will allow you to switch displays, hange the volume,  and even turn off the controller altogether.

Controller Companion also comes with built in media controls, the Y button allows you to pause and play, while the left and right bumpers allow you to change the track. You can even do this in-game by reactivating the program using the Back + Start combo, and then proceed to listen to your  music. I personally use Spotify, and don't know whether it works alongside Steam's music player, but and media program should work.

One other fantasic feature is the keyboard implementation. Other emulators lack functional keyboards, (unless you consider memorizing ten thousand keybindings functional). Conroller Companion allows you to type using a spiral staircase of letters, which is operated with the left thumbstick. In practice, the typing is quite similar to Steam's Daisy Wheel Keyboard. While I prefer Steam's Daisy Wheel for its efficiency, the spiral keyboard system works suprisingly well. Compared to the daisy wheel, I find typing takes a little longer since you have to contantly rotate the stick to find the correct letter, but the spiral is so much fun to use. (also, I waste so much time just spinning the mesmerizing endless vortex of letters)  But given time and practice, anything can be done quickly, and I'm sure I'll be using it regularly.
A quick note on what Controller Companion does NOT do... I have found a few form and review posts stating that they cannont connect their controller, and I would assume that these people have incorrectly assumed that this program allows them to connect their controller to the computer. Controller Companion only serves as a utility for your controller and does not pair the controller to the computer wirelessly in any way, it assumes that you already have a working controller setup. If this is your goal,
I might also add that Controller Companion is not built to replace your keyboard and mouse for keyboard/mouse dependent games. While it could function in an RTS, your keyboard and mouse will be far superior, since you have access to all of your hotkeys. You're better off changing a control sceme in-game to use the default gamepad driver than you are to modify the Controller Companion for a specific game. Though it can be done, most games have controller support anyway. Thought it may not be enabled by default. Some games such as TF2 and CS:GO will require you to turn on controller support in your settings.
In short, Controller Companion wants to be your friend. I'll never go back to those crummy mouse emulators, because this, good sir, is a step above all other offerings. Sure you could settle for a half decent, free program, or even a crummy paid one, but this, this is more than half decent, and it is well worth the three dollars I paid for it. No hassle, seemless integration, easy to use, and gamer friendly. What more could you ask for?
(At the time of writing, I have been unable to get the media controls fully operational. I am able to use the  media controls while the settings window is open, but not while it is minimized to the taskbar or tray. However, based upon previous reviews, I have yet to see anyone else with this problem. All things considered. this is a day one review and I am still very impressed with the program. If this is a common problem, I expect it to be solved in the near future.)

UGH, I want to like this game so much.
It checks a lot of boxes
✓ Crew based gameplay
✓ individual stats and unlockable, worthwhile skills
✓ lengthy singleplayer campagin
✓ lots of customization for your aircraft
✓ strategic, riveting choices.  i.e. do I send my repair guy out to fix the engines or keep him in a turret?
✓ WWII arial combat theme is fun
And then it falls pretty flat after a few missions
✕ The game forces you into clumsy "hands off" gameplay design.  You have to micromanage your crewmembers and literally look at every enemy aircraft for 2-3 seconds each to "tag" it before your gunners will shoot at it.  You can't point and shoot the turrets yourself, and you can't really steer the plain directly yourself, only follow waypoints, select altitudes, and perform certain maneuvers
✕ the grind is real.  Every campaign stage you have the choice between 2-4 rotating missions and then a "final" harder mission that really can't be attempted without serious risk.   The payout and xp your crew gains per mission is relatively minimal, such that it takes several missions to level them up and earn enough money for upgrades.  During such missions, especially the high risk ones, it's likely that you'll lose crewmembers to various battle fatigues, or the whole plane entirely.   Then you're pretty much back to square one.  The crucial unlocked crew skills you come to rely on can quickly be lost.
✕ Permadeath is a concept that has a place in some games, but it's poorly implemented here.  There SHOULD be a bit of a compensating payoff for continuing to grind into the game and avoid the utter disappointment of losing countless hours of progess.
Another game that handles permadeath well is Darkest Dungeon.  Throughout the game you "upgrade" your town/base area to make it easier to recruit and train high skill team members, it's also possible to make the process of buying new upgrades permanently cheaper, which gets you back on track faster in the event of setback.
If this kind of better developed base advancement concept were in bomber crew, the game would be less frustrating

I have been into this game since the early BETA. Yet pretty much all the problems I had back then are still here plus some new ones.
Now straight to what you want to read, I suppose.
-It is a harsh game, it really punishes you for your mistakes. And it takes a while to respawn and to get into the action.
-One shot body shot is there and is quite common on the field, if you deslike that then I cannot recomend you this game.
-The weapons model is quite unusual, realistic maybe, with heavy recoil and high spread.
-The whole "completely open maps" idea sounds great at the beggining but you may eventually get into situations where your spawn point is surrounded, and any other spawn area is surrounded by seasoned players.
-Also you may find yourself in situations where your whole team have no means to defeat a treat - let's say a tank. Or you find yourself with a terrible gun choice for the map you got into.
-Netcode is pretty bad. Enough said.
-Character movement is chunky to say the least
-One sided battles, where your team get turn into swiss cheese while the other side have a nice time happens quite a lot. That said, I've been playing with the germans most of the time.
-Match making will often put you in a team full of people who just got into it versus seasoned players.
-It is a heavy grind to unlock weapons and besides that, you start with a not very precise nor powerful nor fast firing semi-automatic rifle, but the game puts you versus seasoned players with upgraded automatic rifles.
-I cannot describe exactly what is wrong with the aim system, but I just could't get used to it.
-The RPGish stamina systems allows for infinite bunny hopping but limited sprint, it not only doesn't make any sense but also it aggravates the slow game pace you alrady have.
It was quite a frustrating experience. The lack of team oriented gameplay is visible and slow unbalanced gameplay seen in the -not quite balanced- avaliable maps and weapons turns this game into a stress machine.

A competent but very flawed CCG that takes too many missteps for me to recommend it.
The core mechanic of stringing together combos is undercut by several cards like bombs, potions, and barriers that, in a single turn, can invalidate three or more turns' worth of effort. These broken cards are pointed out in a Community Guide.
As a result, few strategies appear to be meaningfully better than simply spamming disables to your opponent's cards and filling their board, so that they can't play a card. Because the game is single-player, there's no "meta" as such, and this strategy works for >95% of the game's opponents.
The lack of real strategy involved makes for a game that is occasionally amusing or satisfying, but largely dull.

Card City Nights is a Trading/Card game set in a Ittle Dew universe with cards from almost every universe of Ludosity if not all.
You are a card gamer that wish to be the champion and to reach your goal you’ll need to obtain all 8 legendary cards to be able to compete in the biggest tournament/competition the city has never held in the past.
The gameplay is easy to learn but you’ll need more than several attempts to have a perfect knowledge of the game. And you’ll mostly need to make different deck to counter or beat some tough opponents with a very specific deck.
You begin each standard match with 10 HP and a number of cards set as well as your opponent. (unless you set a special name, refer to (*) at the end) Each player has their own 3X3 playing field. Each turn the player need to place a card on their field. The aim is to set your opponent health to 0 HP. To do so you need to connect cards together to make a combo. To connect 2 cards you need them to point toward each other with their arrows: like a card on the left will point toward a card on the right with its right arrow and the right card will point toward the left card with its left arrow. To make a combo you need to connect cards together to have 3 or more symbols of the same kind.
There are 4 kinds of symbols: attack (red sword), defend (blue shield), revive (plus shape) and support. (yellow coin) And each card can have one or two symbols on it. The support reduces the number of symbols you need to connect. So if you place a 2-support-symbol card you only need to connect it with another symbol you wish. (attack, defend, revive or even support) If you connect 3 defend symbols you’ll get 3 shield points. If you connect 3 attack symbols, you’ll need to choose if you wish to attack your opponent or your opponent’s cards. If you attack your opponent, you’ll decrease his/hers shield or health points. But if you attack one of his/her cards, this card will be disabled and will stay in the field forever. Unless your opponent revives it by combining 3 or so revive symbols.
So you can win a match by:
-	attacking your opponent until he hasn’t any health point left
-	disabling cards of your opponent to make his/her field full so he lost by forfeit.
-	Drawing your opponent until he has no card left. He will take an increased damage every turn.
When you defeat an opponent (a match can be done in 1, 2 or 3 sets) you earn gold and/or a specific booster pack. You can also earn gold coins by clicking in the scenery. Gold are the currency of the game: with it you can buy extra cards you already own or a skin for your field or fusion cards to make a new one.
And two more main things. Each card has their own rarity and depending of it you can only have a limited number of the same card. You can have 3 same common cards, 2 same rare cards, 1 epic card of each kind and only one legendary for the whole deck. Cards can also have a very specific power that triggers while placing it on the field or doing a combo.
Finally when you talk with people or fight opponent you’ll sometimes learn where is/are the next legendary card(s). You can always see all the cards and skin fields your own, sort the cards and make new decks.
(*):
Thanks to the 1.1 Valentine’s update Gamers and Hardcore-gamers can “enjoy” this game in their way.
Gamer can play this game in a hard way by simply set his/her name to HardPlaya. He/she will begin each match with 4 HP and his/her opponent with 8 HP. Despite the difficulty there is no reward for beating this mode.
Hardcore player can play this game in the very hard way by simply set his/her name as ReallyPlaya. He/she will begin each match with 1 HP and his/her opponent with 10 HP. Despite the tough difficulty there is no reward for beating this mode.

Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons surprised me. It is developed by Starbreeze Studios, who are also behind games like The Darkness, Syndicate (the 2012 FPS, that is) and Payday 2. With a developer that is mainly known for shooters, I was sceptical of all the praise that this game has received, but it turned out that I judged too soon.
It is a singleplayer co-op game, and whilst that sounds a bit like a buzzword to hype up a gimmick, it is actually a legitimately innovative mechanic. You control two brothers at the same time, with the left analog stick and left trigger for the older brother and the right stick and trigger for the younger. It is neat to have a solo co-op experience, although it can get very confusing very quickly to control two characters at the same time, unless you happen to be ambidextrous.
Brothers is an experience. The world design is phenomenal, with many gorgeous setpieces. The snowy landscapes in particular look stunning. The characters also have quite some personality, despite the fact that they all speak in some sort of pseudo-Germanic moonlanguage that is not subtitled. It is an interesting way to tell a story, and I think it was a good decision.
The game has a great story, do not get me wrong, but I personally felt slightly underwhelmed by its conclusion. The climax itself is not earth-shattering, although I will concede that it is told well. Either way, the experience as a whole is sublime. It is a game that has to be completed in a single sitting, and that is not a particularly difficult feat, because the game is very short.
Those who desire a concise and conclusive experience will be pleased to hear that Brothers can very easily be fully experienced in approximately three hours. Besides collecting the game's twelve achievements, there is pretty much nothing else that can be done after completing the story.
Your mileage may vary on whether or not you are willing to pay €14 (or your regional equivalent) for such a short experience, but I personally recommend it. You must experience this. Not just the story, but the game's world as a whole. Wait for it to go on sale if you must, but you are really missing out if you do not get it at some point.

This isn't a Sims/Surviva-Management/Roguelike game, it's Dragon's Lair in a plane. The challenge is battling a clunky UI and control scheme while executing the optimal queue of clicks and keystrokes.

I want to start by saying I am no stranger to trading card games.  I've played Magic the Gathering, Hearthstone, Dragonball Z, Pokémon, Gundam Wing, and others over the years; with that said I highly recommend this game.  It has the perfect balance of simplicity and depth that very few games do successfully and an engaging story that doesn't take itself too seriously to go along with it.  You are a simple card game player hunting for the legendary cards and a grand prize and you meet plenty of people along the way.  It's one of those games that is perfect for playing a couple of games in here and there until you complete the story.
I won't get too detailed on the game play because trying to explain it here probably wouldn't do it justice and I am sure you will get the idea from the screenshots / videos.  The game is about making groups of cards which activate abilities that can help you or hurt your enemies.  For example, you place cards on your board in groups to attack your enemy's life points or block their ability to play cards while they try to do the same.
The only negative about this game is it has very little replay value.  Despite that, the game felt long enough where I was satisfied with the time I had invested when the ride was over.  This is a game I would recommend even at full price; if you have a few extra dollars in your steam wallet and don't know where to spend them, grab this one!

Mount and Blade: Warband hmmm........Well I guess I'll start; Mount and Blade: Warband is a 3rd / 1st person RPG, that allows you to play pretty much as whatever you want, whether you want to be a tyrannical warlord or a paragon of good its all up to how you want to play the game.
Starting the game you choose your character, you can be either a man or a woman you then decide on starting stats that will be determined by choosing various options which can be added to when you level up.
There are two modes to this game an overworld in which you navigate the map and the 3rd / 1st person mode in which you fight, walk around towns, castles and villages; In the overworld map you can move around and find traveling bands of lords and bandits moving around doing there own thing.
The main part of MB Warband is to start out with nothing and raise yourself to greatness this can be achieved by recruiting companions, training troops and starting your own kingdom or perhaps become a vassal of an existing one.
My usual way to play is to join the Kingdom of Nords wait till I have a lot of gold, troops and maybe a castle or two before renouncing my pledge and going on my way to establish my own empire.
The graphics have been said by many to be lacking but given the age of the game and the size of the team that made it, as well as the exceptionally awesome game you can't really hold the graphics against it.
The sounds and music are hit or miss I would have to say, though they do try their best to add to the atmosphere and does its job to complement the game and immerse the player in the world of Mount and Blade: Warband.
Although I have mainly played singleplayer, the multiplayer of Mount and Blade: Warband is where this game truly stands out, I have spent almost a 3rd of my total time on this game playing multiplayer whether playing serious battles fighting for the glory of my team, or stuffing around with a group of people who just want to have some fun there is generally something for everyone.
Overall I will say Mount and Blade: Warband is a fantastic little game that you can easily loose hours and hours of time playing. Expanding your empire or helping a King to expand theres honestly this is a game that needs to be experienced and is one that should be in the library of all gamers.
(Like all my reviews I do not put a score as it is my belief that games like all forms of art are subjective and therefore it is impossible to afix a number to them)

This is my favourite out of all the Elder Scrolls games.
- The combat is pretty weird. It relies on your skill level and agility to land a blow on enemies; so when you start out your weapons are going to miss. A LOT! Spells also have a chance to fail being cast (again, dependent on skill level) and they still consume your magika when attempted. You also do not regenerate magika over time, but via potions and resting/sleeping.
- Pretty much nobody likes you from the very beginning, some more than others. You can join factions and complete important quests to improve your standing, but this can also draw dislike from OTHER factions, too (eg. joining the Fighter's Guild may put you in worse standing with the Thieve's Guild)
- Fast travel is kind of non-existant in this game. I stress the words "kind of" because you can use other methods to get around. The Mage's Guild has a teleport system, there are Stilt Striders and sometimes boats in major cities and you can buy scrolls that teleport you to the closest Imperial Fort or Temple.
- Important note: Sometimes you have the option to deny a quest; and sometimes you'll be unable to change your mind and the quest will be barred from you forever.
- There's also no autosave, so it's important to set a "quicksave" key and use it often to avoid losing progress.
I take all these points NOT as cons, but as challenges. I felt like Oblivion and Skyrim held my hand a little too much with quest markers and the ability to quicktravel from one end of the world the other. It took me time and effort to advance my character to the point where I could explore more dangerous areas, and I felt like that time spent grinding my combat skills on lesser creatures had paid off.
I'm not going to say anothing about the main story (for the sake of spoilers) other than it was amazing. I genuinely wanted to carry on taking the main quest path in this game, whereas in the following two games I felt like I could take it or leave it as I pleased.
Both DLC packs that this came with were very satisfying, though they do require you to be a capable level; otherwise you won't be able to make it very far. Regardless, the DLC is up there with the likes of Shivering Isles and Dawnguard. They gave me a large enough new area to explore and a juicy questline to follow.
This is one of the few games I'd ever give a 10/10. I never felt like I had to compromise or meet a middle ground with this game, which is what every game should aspire to be like.

RaySupreme aims for Silo 2's clean and simple interface approach and expands it with animation, texture painting, Scripting, and NODEs..
Vertice, Face, and Edge selection modes are always listed at the top center of the interface for easy access and above each viewport are the options to work with your models while wireframe only, solid, textured, etc.
Along the left hand side of the interface your basic tools are listed and change in context to which ever mode you are currently working in. More elaborate tools are found under an explorer list on the right hand side.
Most of the sections can be moved around and sized to your preference; accommodating the task you will be using the most.
But most impressive are the tool tips. Every feature, tool and option is defined with a comprehensive explanation either in the explorer window or at the bottom of the screen (Help option in the menu reveals some guides as well).
The elaborate help system makes RaySupreme a meaty animator, painter and modeler for those new and learning.
Also added are Node Graphs and a Scripting section making the small $50 price tag as astonishing as Blender's free offering. As with all premium software, however, RaySupereme streamlines and simplifies the modeling and animation process for those not experienced enough to begin tackling the steep learning curve demanded by Blender.
For long-time hobbyists, RaySupreme is a cheap and fun suite to try out and play around in.
For those beginning to learn 3D modeling and animation; RaySupreme is a MUST have!

I've finished the first chapter / scenario (essentially a tutorial, story intro and chance to get gear) and have saved at the start of the next area to write this. I am enjoying myself. The game is an ode to the old Quest for Glory series, and I think the developer captured the feel quite nicely.
There is a lot of text, all fully voiced; the writing is excellent and the voiceovers adequate, mostly done as narration by the developer (in fact, I'd say the lack of professional voice talent actually adds to the old-school feel). The music is good and nicely complements the atmosphere. The graphics are a mixed bag; many of the 2D backgrounds are quite attractive, while navigation screens are fairly cartoony with a nearly top-down perspective that my brain wants to be more isometric, and the avatar that shows on-screen during navigation is a stiff 2D representation but gets the job done. The game plays in a 4:3 standard perspective, and has black bars on both sides when played on a widescreen monitor. Interfaces aren't completely intuitive but still fairly easy to figure out, with left-click going deeper into the selection and right-click up one level.
I thought the "surprise" during the first area was a nice touch to add some drama and significance to the story, and I find myself wanting to continue to see what happens.
Recommended for Quest for Glory / King's Quest 1-6 fans at the current price point of $3.
