I have a love/hate relationship with this game. Everytime I think I'm done with it over some new change I just come crawling back a few months later. I started out in 2013 when it first came to the PS4. I was hooked, as I had never really devoted myself to an MMO before. That being said, I was a total noob; it took me about a month to reach level 16. Though as time passed I became more and more dedicated to the game, leading it to be the only thing I played for a good while. I eventually stopped playing around the release of Amazon Fury: Part 1. I took a break for a couple months before deciding I wanted to check it out again, but this time I brought some of my friends. They got tired of the game, but I didn't. After being exposed to PC gaming I switched over to here, and I'm in the middle of my bi-annual DCUO craze. I've written quite a few reviews on Steam before about this game but they were all pertaning to a specific issue that had angered me. I think it's time to write an honest, wholehearted review on the game.
Now to start off I want to stress how much I wish I could give this game a "neutral" score. Sadly I'm stuck with a Get/Don't Get option. I guess this is Steam's way of telling me to pick a side already. First, the good. This game has really fun combat for an MMO. (It started out as an action game.) There's a plethora of combos for each weapon style, and beyond that each of these styles has ranged AND melee capabilities. Instead of "classes" in other MMOs, you choose from a list of superpowers. Each power has two "roles" that determine playstyle in group instances. The roles are Tank, (Trying to take the heat of combat on to yourself.) Damage, (Getting in the heavy blows on the enemy.) Healing, (Restoring the health of allies.) and Control. (Keeping the group running smoothly by stunning enemies and restoring their energy pools.) While every power has a damage-dealing role, others are only found in certain powers. But bear in mind, most of the powers today are from DLC so if you're F2P, you're limited to the powers found in the vanilla release. Thankfully, each of the powers feels and looks quite unique. I also want to praise the gamepad support. Not many MMOs are playable with a controller. This game is equally, if not more fun with a PS3 or 360 controller. The higher-level armor styles look VERY cool. A lot of people stick around in this game purely to collect pieces to mix-and-match. Most importantly, if you're a DC Comics fan you're going to have a blast. This game's art was based off the works of Jim Lee, and it features some pretty gorgeous comic-style cutscenes. There's a ton of famous DC stories that make a return here, as well as some pretty captivating new ones. The world is chock-full of fun references to various DC characters, places, and events. Overall this game does a pretty great job of making you feel like a superpowered hero or villain.
Alas, this game has started to deteriorate over the years. This Jauary marks the 5th anniversary. As I mentioned above about the DLC, that is a common problem within the game. If you're a subscriber things really aren't that bad at all, but if you're going into an MMO like this expecting to stick around as a F2P you're going to be disappointed. F2P in this game is essentially a trial edition. This is probably due to the game's decline in popularity, forcing the devs to compensate for the financial loss. I've heard a lot of stories about the devs being complete jerks, although I've never actually encountered anything like that. Quite the opposite, to be honest. But if that possibility turns you off I understand. One of the most infuriating changes recently in my opinion is the mark conversion. You see, there was this currency that existed ("Marks") that was used to buy gear, styles, and other various things. As the power of the item increased, the cost of marks increased. It worked fine. If it ain't broke, don't fix it right? Sadly, they "fixed" it. The previous Marks were changed to a new type. The gimmick this time around is that you only get these marks from missions and instances specific to your gear level. To be fair, this is a good idea on paper. It aims to encourage better teamplay and less reliablility on being carried. But from what I've seen, the AMOUNT of marks you get does not change. Only the level you have to get them at. But the price of gear goes UP, despite your rewards not. Worse yet, Style costs now scale also. Meaning that after someone works hard towards enough marks to buy something, they have to choose between a cosmetic item or a piece of gear that will allow them to progress. Of course they're going to pick the gear! What choice do they have? Please, someone corrrect me if I'm wrong on that. The whole implementation of that system was very confusing to me. PC Sever population is also criminally low, but this problem will soon be remedied after the merge with the Playstation servers later this month. Lastly, one of my biggest problems with the game is something that is probably pretty minor in everyone else's opinion. You can not remove the license for this game from your account. This means that if you "delete" it, it isn't going anywhere. Including those 100+ achievements, which will factor into your game completion average on your profile even if you delete the game files.
TL;DR: If you're interested in the game because you want to be a superhero or villain along with some friends and explore the DC Universe, this is definitely your best bet. Just go in knowing that you're going to have to subscribe at some point. If you're looking for the next great MMO (or a nice game completion rate) you're probably going to have to look elsewhere.

Gameplay? 9/10, one of a kind
Story? 6/10, straightforward, occasional funny dialogue
Replayability? 5/10, depends on person
It's a unique TCG game, I'd say it's a puzzle + TCG mix - it's not something that you would play absent-mindedly imo. You collect cards that have arrows on it and you line up the arrows to combo into different actions (attack/revive/defense). It sounds simple, but the game pulls it off really well and makes you consider if placing a certain card down into a certain position is the right thing to do. I'd say the level of difficulty really depends on the player, but I'd give it a medium difficulty. It's the uniqueness of this game that makes me recommend it, I can't think of any other TCG game currently that utilizes this style of gameplay. The storyline is average/straightforward, not particulary interesting but fun enough with humorous dialogue here and there. I wouldn't say this game is incredibly replayable - there aren't any "random" opponents to play that have really new strategies every single time, you'd be playing the same characters over and over again if you wanted to keep playing after defeating everyone. The AIs will stick to their playstyle - defensive, offensive, etc. I guess it really depends on if you *really* get sucked into the gameplay. For me, this is probably the only time I will be playing it through unless if new content was added. It was really compelling to finish the game and I found the experience thoroughly enjoyable; and here I am, writing a review days after buying the game and "completing" it - after completing it though, I just don't feel the urge to keep on playing and rebattling the revamped opponents (the game kicks up the difficulty a notch once you complete the storyline).
It took me around ~15 hours to achieve 100% but I'd say 2-3 of those hours I spent idle/afk, also, I could probably get another hour or two of new gameplay in if I went ahead and challenged the "revamped" characters.

This game is well worth the money regardless if it's on sale or not. Give it a try.

Just finished the campaign of M&B Warband Native, and it has been an amazing adventure. Warband is the kind of game that takes a very long time to complete and lots of dedication. While the game isn't perfect (then again, what game is?) it has many upsides such as the epic battles you engage in to either follow your dreams of uniting Calradia under your control, or helping one of the Kings of an existing faction to bring Calradia together. You also have to care for your troops, which means you have to be careful with money early on and consider if your army size is necessary, because if it's too small then you may get steamrolled, but if it's too big, you might not be able to pay everyone and your troops will leave. Warband is a very unique game on the market as a Sandbox Medieval Simulator which basically means it's not a copy of a different game (that I know of). You will have great times on your adventure such as getting your first fief or winning your first tournament, and have bad times such as running into a horde of Sea Raiders or being taken prisoner while most of the time, enemy lords somehow escape your party of 100+ after a battle. All in all, this game is worth buying or at least trying out the demo, and I can't wait for Bannerlord to come out :D

Particularly in conjunction with one of the major graphics extension mods (MGO, MGE, etc.), this is one of the best RPG games of all time.
Progressing in the game isn't as easy as later installments of the Elder Scrolls series, but it's much more rewarding. You don't start the game good at everything, and have to build your skills before you can accomplish mission tasks with competency. Not even basic swordfighting, or in-character athleticism are guaranteed. You can and will miss hits with your weapons if you're not skilled, and an unpracticed runner won't be able to jog long distances while still maintaining the stamina necessary for a swordfight. Quests require a little bit of thought to complete, and either require money for travel expenses or time and effort to trek long distances in pursuit of a quest objective.
Luckily, unless you use a third-party service to disable the DLC, infinite weak dark brotherhood assassins will randomly attack you when you try to rest due to the Tribunal DLC. This continues until you complete the relevant questline. While rather annoying if you're ill-prepared, if you outfit even a level one player with half-decent weapons and armor you can kill the assassins for easy access to high-value armor (which you can wear if you want to be overpowered), and from then on you'll have a steady source of income by selling the high value armor of the never-ending assassins. Kind of an exploit, since it can speed up the otherwise slow progression in game, but it still feels fair in my opinion since the game has plot-driven reasons to be sending assassins your way and it's not the only example in the game of being able to make large chunks of money at once with some diligent looting and mercantilism.
Where this game really shines, aside from its brilliant and (in my opinion) realistic gameplay mechanics, is in the detail and scope of its cities and environments. Massive and mostly open cities such as Vivec make you feel like you're actually visiting a real civilization and learning its culture. They can inspire a sense of reverence that one usually only feels when visiting other cultures in real life.
A genuinely interesting world awaits the competent and disciplined player with this title!

Try to ignore the nostalgia fan boys in the other reviews, here is an unbiased review of the game;
1. Do NOT play this game without mods, you will regret the disgustingly outdated graphics and gameplay nuances.
2. Take your time during character creation, look up a couple YouTube guides on the way Morrowind character building works, because if you make a mistake during character creation, you ae done for. It is much more unforgiving than future Elder Scrolls titles.
3. There are no quest markers, so if you rely heavily on those and get frustrated trying to complete quests based on the occasionally vague quest descriptions, just bare that in mind.

If you like WWII British Airforce aesthetic and the micromanagey panic of FTL, or just fascinated by WWII bombers, you should check this one out.

I generally enjoyed this game, but the big takeaways: It's hard, it's short, and it's a whole big mess of fun.
PROS:
* I've never played FTL so to me, the gameplay was very original (other reviewers talk about FTL a bunch)
* The gameplay is very addictive
* Missions are quite fun... most of them
* The music has very much a Fallout vibe (seeing as how it's the 1940's and all) which I of course love
* Seeing your bomber riddled with holes is oddly fulfilling
* The game is instense in all the right ways and slow where you want it to be slow. The pacing in general is phenomenal.
CONS:
* VERY short campaign. I beat it in 20 hours
* No multiplayer. This game (or some alternative version of it) would be fantastic with players assuming various roles onboard the bomber crew
* The difficulty goes from moderate to absurd in the blink of an eye. Jet fighters are ridiculously prevalent in the late game. If Nazi Germany had half as many jet fighters as this game presents we'd all be living in a "Man From The High Castle" world today.
* Missions do get repetitive. I'd like to see some more variety
* The enemy ace fighter pilots aren't scaled to your skill level and tear you to shreds in the early game
* Lots of balancing is needed
Generally I like this game. I'm glad I bought it and I'm looking forward to starting a new game here in a few minutes. I recommend it, but with the caveats of the cons listed above; it's a good game, and could become a *great* game if they expand on it a ton and work on its balancing issues. Broadly speaking I'm glad I picked it up and I recommend it to anyone who wants a fun WWII time management bomber sim-lite.

I bought Card City Nights in May of 2014 for 99 cents and almost two years to the date, finally started and finished the game after around 13 hours.  I only used my mouse and didn't try the other control methods, or was even aware there were any.
True to its name, Card City Nights is a collectible card game with a strong focus on combat.  As a new arrival to the island, you quickly learn about the game and how everyone is positively bonkers about it.  The plot is fairly basic--find the eight Legendary cards and face the Card King in combat for the million-coin prize.  The protagonist resists at first, but they have a free deck of cards and there are plenty of people to face, so why not?
The tutorial gave a pretty easy overview of the rules.  You and your opponent each have a 3x3 board, a coin is flipped to determine who goes first, and you both draw five cards to form your hand.  Then it's a matter of linking your cards' arrows together in order to attack, defend, and recover.  You lose if your life hits zero, if you fill your board and can't place a card, or if you completely run out of cards to play.  Matches are played in best of 1/3/5 format, and there didn't seem to be a penalty for losing other than having to start that fight over from the beginning.  Several cards have a variety of effects, such as one reviving a random downed card and then disappearing off board, or moving to an open space every time you start your turn, or having an additional effect depending on what kind of combo it's a part of.
And like most other card games, most of the game takes place outside of battle where you try to put together a deck that can't be beat.  You have to build a deck of 25 to 40 cards, and you're allowed five dupes of common cards, three of uncommon, only one rare, and only one total Legendary per deck, so there's a lot of options.  My interest in the game kinda waned until I woke up and just made a deck from scratch, paying attention to arrows and effects I wanted.  Everyone in the game uses a different deck though they only stick to one, so you could honestly tailor a deck around destroying specifically everyone as you play.  In battle, you're at the mercy of RNG on your draws as well as what the opponent feels like using on you, but outside of perceived biases, the game felt fair about random targets.  Kinda hard to say that when victory is snatched from you with a convenient draw for your opponent, though.
I was kinda surprised at how much dialog there is.  You can talk with several people at each location and everyone has quite a few things to say, especially if you can fight them since they'll have different things then.  Of course this is entirely optional, but it's kinda neat.  Characters have things to say about other people, or you, or other things.  One NPC in the mall had what felt like 100 things to say, though thankfully that wasn't the norm.  That all of the characters come from prior Ludosity/Daniel Remar games might be a treat to some, seeing familiar faces in different roles (and on the cards), but this was my first so I'll be facing retroactive recognition whenever I go back for Ittle Dew and pick up some of the others.
As for things I didn't like...I initially didn't like that you couldn't outright buy new cards.  When the shop unlocks early in the story, you're only able to buy extra copies of the non-Legendary cards you have already.  To get new cards, you have to fight certain NPCs for their boosters (or trade them in later on), so you're at the mercy of RNG for what cards you receive, but each booster NPC provides only one specific pack and each card is tied to a specific booster.  You can keep fighting them to eventually get the cards you want, but my only other complaint is that there's no card catalog to fill out.  It'd have been especially helpful to at least see what cards you have/have seen/haven't seen so as to know how to get that amazing card you saw your opponent use and to scratch that completionist's itch, but I guess the guides on Steam have you covered there if you want to do some cross-referencing.
Overall, I liked CCN and I think it's definitely worth the buck I gave for it.  If you're into card collecting or deck building or whatnot, you'd probably like it too.  Difficulty is kinda hard to pin down since each person has their own deck setup, so you can go from being stonewalled to being locked down to being blitzed to being drained of cards.  You'll probably have to lose your first fights with everyone so you can learn their decks and how to counter them, so that might turn some people off.  But as someone who seems to have interest in card games but rarely plays them, this was not a waste of time at all.

Card City Nights is an altered version of the 9-square mini-game from Final Fantasy VIII, except that in Card City Nights, it's the entire core of the game.  Childish humor fills the game, as the main character goes on a quest to collect all 8 legendary cards from a variety of card masters.  Defeating associates and assistants to the card masters in best of 3 or best of 5 collectible card matches,  you collect enough cards by winning battles until you have an almost unbeatable deck.  Cash dropped by these thugs give you money to buy more cards and more 9-square boards, until you have enough rare cards to absolutely mow these people down.
The mechanics of this game design are well thought-out.  Excess cards can be recycled into card packs, preventing the player from collecting 10-20 of each common card in a never-ending quest to collect enough rares (cough Pokemon TCG for Nintendo's Gameboy cough.) In addition, there's a minor alchemy system to process cards that may not be affordable from the game's card store in the mall.
All an all, a moderate-speed economy system gets this game going.  The delightful humor prevents the game from getting dull, and this is a must-play for card genre fanatics or older children. 5/5 stars.

1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

At first, you wouldn't bet a dime on Brothers : A game made by Starbreeze who made that ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Syndicate FPS (and two very good Riddick games), written and directed by a movie director (do you feel the nasty Heavy Rain interactive movie vibes ? yeah...) and that lasts 2-3 hours.
But that game is a surprise, a really good surprise. Despite their experience as FPS designers, Starbreeze manage to make an excellent puzzle/adventure game with a funny twist : indeed, you play both brothers with a single controller (don't try to play with a keybord, you'll die. A lot). A "single player cooperative game" if you like. The learning curve on that game is great : the first puzzles help you to manage the tricky part about moving two characters at the same time and to prepare you for the more difficult ones along the journey. And if you like, you can also enjoy the funny animations along the road as the brothers interact differently with their environment, or enjoy a nice rest on a bench while admiring the gorgeous backgrounds.
The good part about getting a movie director is that they understand how to tell a story without words : indeed, people in this world speak some sort of Sims' language and everithing is told through directing and sometimes through the gameplay.
It helps that the story is pretty simple. Not to spoil anything, you control two brothers who, after losing their mother, discover that their dad is sick and that they have to go on a journey to find some healing potion. But as the game progresses, the game is getting a little bit more emotional. Let me tell you something : eventhough I've been shaken by a few games or movies, I never cried in front of a video game until the epilogue of Brothers.
So because of its breathtaking visuals, the amazing way to tell a story and the inventive way to play it, for the future of video games and to tell the industry that this is what we want, you have to play Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons, to tell your friends and your family, to offer it (with all the sales going on, that game can be pretty cheap).
And when you'll do it, play it in one run (the game is short so it won't be hard), and you will see why I think this is the best game of the year.

Ah Morrowind, the game people will constantly say is better than Skyrim in every way.  After playing and loving Skyrim for over a year I decided it was time to expand my horizions.  Being a huge nerd and lore lover, I wanted to play more elder scolls games.  They seemed fun enough, I could mod them to look better, and since they were so old they would be cheap.  So when the steam summer sale came around I picked up Morrowind and Oblivion.  After installing MSGO Tamriel Rebuilt and some various visual enhancing mods I was ready to go.  Around 100 hours of gameplay later I have defeated two gods and about a million cliff racers.

I arranged a marriage for a ashlander chief, tricking him into believing his wife was a princess when really she was a slave I had bought.  I had found a wizard wearing a dress and a fur hat, locked up by the creatures he summoned.  I killed a maniac nord who put drugs in candy, and so much more.  I still haven't even started the Tribunal DLC, or explored much of the mainland added in by the spectacular Tamriel Rebuilt.  I have almost 100,000 gold, a full set of ebony and glass armor, a daedric artifact, lots of daedric loot, and a house full of artifacts I don't want to get rid of.
I hope to one day finish the tribunal DLC, to defeat a third god, to get over 100,000 gold, to maybe even fill in the entire map.  The last week I have not played Morrowind due to my modded Skyrim setup working for once.  I have realized that I have barely played Oblivion, besides testing a mod loadout, Morrowind has totally taken away any desire to play it.
Some day it shall be Oblivion's turn, but until then I shall be dreaming of the beautiful mushrooms, the moan of a silt strider, the quests I can't remember what to do because the journal entries are buried behind hours of achievements, I am the Nevar reborn, I hope to some day have the power to defeat the living god Vivec, when that happens, I shall know my questing is over.  Whether I replay this game or not I am unsure of, probably, maybe, maybe after giving Oblivion a shot, maybe later.  So I can relive this wonderful adventure again.

Please ignore the 11 hour statistic of my playtime, as I have owned this glorious gem in multiple incarnations of my life, starting with a PC copy my stepdad brought when he moved in, along with TES IV and Fallout 3.  I can tell you with great certainty that, even then, as an 8 year old child who had very little experience with Role Playing Games, Morrowind was the favorite of those 3 games, and for good reason, of which I wish to explain to you now.
Morrowind does not hold your hand.
Morrowind is not an art mueseum with a handful of forked paths.  Morrowind is a Thousand-Kilometer wide sandbox that has the depth of the deep blue with undiscovered fossils at the bottom for those who become skilled at its numbers, subtleties, and secrets.
Morrowind gives you an amount of freedom currently unmatched by the thousands of games that have come after it, even in its own series.
Player Agency - a term used by developers to describe the interplay between a player's desired action to take inside the game, and the resulting malleability of that game world.  Simply put, if the player desires to do X, does the game let them do it?  If so, does it give them a Y?
Yes, yes it does.
I was only level 7, but I really wanted to fly to the peak of a Dwemer Ruin named Arkngthand.  So I took, what stood in my head, as the neccessary steps to accomplish this.  I became a trusted member of the Mages Guild in Balmora, until I took up a quest that required me to replace another member's soul gem with a fake one.  However, instead of finishing the quest, I took that soul gem, and many others on the desk, with me.
I then tried to use that very soul gem in the Mage's Guild and have one of the mages enchant levitation on a pair of Robes for me - Partially attempting to mock the game's stupidity.
The game mocked me back.
The enchanter noticed that the soul gem was, in fact, stolen.  What was a simple prospect to fly like a bird became a bloodthirsty manhunt by Balmora's guard force.  I escaped, but at a great cost.  I was a wanted man (Or Mer, I should say) , and I had been banished from the Mages Guild, requiring a great deal of work to get back into their good graces.
I soon made it a goal to be able to fly, and become the most powerful mage in the lands.  I'll show them!
The next 100 hours of gameplay that followed was a mission of revenge, filled with maniacle schemes of gaining power and political influence not only in the Empire, but the Telvanni Wizards.  I got my flying robes.  But also much more.  A surplus of enchanted Throwing Stars.  I would rain doom upon Balmora and the Hlaalu guards protecting it.  I would blast fire into the faces of warmth, defense, and the hospitable.  Vvardenfell would become a cold husk of death and disease - It's own powers of poison and illness that foreshadow's the game's main plot being used against itself.
And The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind happily abliged.  It was one of the most empowering acts of player agency I had ever experienced.
The final act of my inquisition of doom was to murder a pillar of the Tribunal, a God-King of Morrowind:  Vivec.  After a long week of excersizing my powers and preparations, I had completed my task.  I was even able to trap his soul and use it to enchant a pair of gloves with a constant "Restore Fatigure and Health" effect - Ultimately making my character immortal.
At that point, I had reached the end of my own main plot.  I never even spoke to Caius Cosades to research the Nerevarine Prophecy, or in ending the blight's grip around Vvardenfell.  But I still had a story to tell.  I made it my own, and mine only.
If my personal anecdote is not enough to convince you to buy this game, then I'm afraid that you, perhaps, don't yet understand the true potential of games that give you the agency to do whatever you desire, in a world just as rich in detail as the one you currently inhabit.

Gorgeous looking puzzle adventure game featuring a robot out to save the city and his grilfriend from three big, bad, mean bully robots. Addictive music accompanies challenging puzzles. Strongly recommended, definitely worth the full price.
In this game, you play a cute little robot that, at the start of the game, seems to be a bit down on his luck. First, you must re-assemble yourself by finding your missing bodyparts. This serves as a little tutorial on what your robot can do: you can stretch out your body to become longer, thus being able to reach higher places, but walking becomes more clunky. Or, you can shorten your body, which allows you to get into small spaces and which gives you longer arms to reach things beyond your regular reach.
The goal of the game is to get back into the robot city and save the city and your girlfriend from three bad robots. Along the way, you encounter a wide variety of other robots in the city, most of which need help in one way or another. Progression requires a combination of getting items and solving puzzles. The game quickly becomes semi-openworld-ish, by which I mean that at most times, you'll be working on more than one puzzle / quest at the same time, and you're walking up and down the city, although it's not completely "open world" either (you need to finish some puzzles in order to be able to access certain new areas). The puzzles and quests can be quite challenging at times, and they are incorporated into the story very nicely (as opposed to other games, where puzzles sometimes feel completely out of place or jerk you away out of your immersion).
It's very satisfying to progress through the story; it feels good to solve the puzzles and dig in deeper into the visually very appealing world. The music is very original and really fits the game perfectly. Instead of a continuous, repetitive background music throughout the entire game, every screen has its own song that really fits the situation. The sound effects are great too (I can especially recommend listening to the robot band, once you've helped them out!).
All in all, I really enjoyed this game!
+ great artstyle
+ great music to accompany the game and story (after you've helped the band, stay a while, and listen :))
+ challenging puzzles
+ cute story
+ loveable characters
+ easy, intuitive gameplay
- the game is rather short, I would've loved to walk around in this world more!

用龙骑士统一了一次，然而并没有任何提示胜利的信息。。P社好歹还有一个框。
这游戏虽然好像可以有很复杂的操作，但那个秘制UI的操作玩过教程之后我就只记得怎么切换近战远程编队和选择自动/手动/Hold模式了。几乎从来就没手按过技能，基本就是开战后调整一下相对位置，集中援军（或者坐等盟军先去消耗）之类后马上切自动的。唯一有次微操是一次攻城，攻破城门后立刻后撤等敌人自己出来，要在狭窄的通道上打就会输。然后再冲。唯一需要单个单位微操就是攻Crime首都时候让两个龙骑士单独飞过去放技能，不过也只调了位置为她们自己打因为我根本忘了怎么手动放技能。。
某种意义上说调整位置和各个击破还挺重要的，经常是全灭和很小损失的区别。如果真搞清楚怎么微操估计可以打出很少特殊部队横扫全图的打法。不过除了前期龙骑士这种3人1地的小势力或者自建势力还要精打细算一下，中后期基本就是横扫速度的区别。偶尔可能会碰到很imba的NPC也可以堆精锐强突过去，而且损失不会太大。
消灭势力领袖（包饺子让其无法撤退下野）可以立即消灭一个势力，可以利用这个快速取胜。有次我碰到个imba NPC导致反复测试各种有效率打法起码一小时，然而发现那回合我在另一个区域已经可以歼灭对方领袖立即消灭这个势力了。。。
小屏体验不佳，右边立绘只能显示一半。。

不过看着小（zhi）人（pian）们对打，喊着各种中二的口号厮（zhuan）杀（jin），还有带感的bgm还是很有趣的。而且这种无论是UI还是Sprites的“简陋”感觉反而可使其与战国史一样很适合做mod，要出个编辑器和工坊卖2倍价格也值。

Okay, so Lost Technology is in a very strange situation but the game itself is pretty solid and I'd absolutely reccomend this game with a few caveats.  So its like a turn-based tactical RPG made real time with a lot more troops and an overmap where you engage in diplomacy and move/recruit troops; its fantastic! And the story very well done from what little I've seen of it. Although that brings me to the localization.
One thing I do have to say is unless you speak japanese your not going to get the full game, at least for now.
You see the thing is the game is being localized in pieces and based upon people buying the game. Of the time of the review only 3 (supposedly another batch is coming) of the 12(?) main stories have been translated and a handful modes have not been brought over (although 3 of which are freeplay modes so I'm not really sure what thats all about since they have the same map and factions but another seems to be senarios or something to that effect). Also the way the developers decided to handle having non translated stories is to simply say "the story hasn't been translated your in freeplay mode" rather than just warn you that this story hasn't been translated here it is in japanese which maybe I'm in the minority on but moving on.
The localization itself is not amazing as there have been times where I suddenly get a string of kanji thrown at me when I hover over abilities or even item names in dungeon master mode. Although that is an exception rather than the norm. Overall I'd say what is localized was done very compitently the characters' personallity don't feel lost in translation as can happen.
Anyways enough whinging on the localization I honestly adore this game. I'll continue to update this review as things move along.
TLDR: The games great, localization not so much

A delightful, but hectic little game with a lot of character.  If you're in to the FTL style "management of chaos" games, this is in that vein.  Run your WWII Lancaster into the heart of Germany in semi-historic missions, whilst fending off roving fighter squadrons, which only get more crafty as the war progresses.  The loss of a crew is always disappointing, but there is a sense each time that there was something you could've done better, or would have been able to prepare for.  It's a little forgiving though, as the next plane you're given will be fitted with some similar tier upgrades that your last one was.
[Updated with some additional impressions] One thing that stood out to me when playing this, was the great sense of empathy you felt with your crews. Unlike a standard flight-sim, you're much more intimitely a part of the crew's experiences.  You see them when they're wounded and giving aid to eachother (or sometimes unable to); taking over for a mate who's out of action; desparately fixing broken systems under heavy fire...  Although the artstyle and theme is humourous and light-hearted, I greatly enjoyed that Bomber Crew can - in at least some small way - put you in their shoes, and maybe get a sense of what these people went through.

This game comes across as a high-school project - and if you think of it that way, it deserves an A.
The game's main issue is difficulty. It seems to be a very short and simple game, so to compensate for its lack of content it has a high difficulty level to keep you playing the same few levels over and over. But unlike other games that are difficult due to level design, this game's difficulty could have been adjustable in the menu, as what make it hard is the short time limits and your limited health bar.
Except that there's no menu. The "return to menu" option when you die actually just means "forget any checkpoints you reached and start over".
There appear to be only two checkpoints before you reach the final "boss" (one after each of the two other simple "boss" creatures), but it's quite difficult to reach each checkpoint, so losing progress because you went to the nonexistent menu is annoying.
Other irritations:
- If you run out of time, instead of having to play the level again, or going back a level, or losing a health point, you lose instantly. Needlessly harsh.
- There is no warning (blinking or chime) to let you know you're almost out of time.
- If you finish the level by killing the last enemy right when the time runs out, it doesn't count: you just lose. This happened to me twice in my 45 minutes of playtime.
- Level transitions are too quick. You're not given any rest after passing a level and no time to prepare for the newly spawned enemies.
- Having to aim your "sword" with the mouse is a bit irritating, since the mouse cursor is a bit hard to see and I think I'd rather just aim in the style of the Mass Effect conversation bubble (i.e. aiming with no cursor)
- Um... $CDN7.79? Hell no! This is firmly in the 99-cent category.

Shapes of Gray is a top-down arcade-style game and is what would happen if Binding of Isaac and WarioWare had a baby.  You’re confined to a single room per level with the objective of defeating the surrounding enemies within a set time.  The characters and environments are all different shades of gray (hence the title) and while the environment is the same each level with minor change for the boss levels, the characters are all uniquely designed in both looks and attacks.
There are 49 levels initially plus two more gameplay styles to unlock upon first completion.  These both add more character types to encounter and while one is a ‘Second Quest’ style game the other brings a coin-collection mode for added difficulty.
I was given a key-code for the download of the Steam version for review but I had previously purchased the Wii U version upon its initial release.  The Steam version fixes the frame rate issue that a couple levels (Level 3 in particular) faced and also adds in a trail effect for all characters and weapons.  This comes in handy for catching bullet trajectories and is just a cool affect in general.
Each boss acts as a checkpoint which is very welcome but seeing as there are only two checkpoints then, I do wish there were one additional checkpoint after Boss 2 or a way to recover one heart at least.  This is due to both the time mechanic in each level and the random enemy layout.  The quick levels make the game a fun and easy way to kill some time and random enemy layouts keep you on your toes so you are not memorizing their patterns.  However, with both the time mechanic and some achievements being for fastest completion, it becomes difficult to complete some later levels without losing a much-needed heart.  The split-second it takes to relocate all enemy locations means their attacks have begun and you can’t proceed with the shortest route anymore for their defeat.
This does become frustrating but once the final boss is defeated, the feeling is very rewarding and I dug right into the next sections.  Definitely grab this game and see if you can unlock everything.

It's a collectible card game, without any microtransactions. Yeah this game is a game that you buy and thats it, nothing in the game is locked behind microtransactions or any of the other shady crap other card games do. Its also got a really charming art style and its a lot of fun. Pretty much you should buy it right now if you like TCG games.
Lemme tell you how the game works, each player has a 3 x 3 grid that they place cards down onto and each card has arrows on the sides or corners. And by lining up 3 or more cards with the arrows touching you activate the cards based on the proportion of cards used to make the match. 3 attack cards will attack the enemy for 3 damage, 3 defense cards will heal you for 3. Lining up 2 defense cards with 2 attack cards and you can make a choice to either attack or defend for 2.
And then there are other mechanics like flipping cards, disabling cards, cards that have effects based on the combo they were used in. All in all this is a VERY solid purchase for the price.

This is a simple, one-player videogame version of card games like Pokemon or MTG, with a little storyline thrown in to guide you through increasing levels of difficulty. I never really got into any physical card games, but I really enjoy Card City Nights! Pros and cons from my experience:
Pros:
- No significant learning curve: The rules are easy to pick up and you're playing in minutes.
- A fun variety of cards to work with, allowing you to build (up to six) different decks to experiment with different strategies.
- AI players use different style decks and strategies, requiring you to adjust your own style and decks to beat them.
- Some of the battles are tough, but not so tough you get frustrated.
- Suitable for kids or adults, and a good introduction to strategy card games of all types.
Cons:
- Some bugs in the Windows version, particularly an annoying 10-15 second lag that often occurs at the end of a match.
- You earn coins from some matches which can be used for buying cards or backgrounds, but as far as I can tell there's no real reason to use them since you already get plenty of cards from boosters and the backgrounds are just the ones that the AI already uses.
- A multiplayer option would have been nice.
All in all a good buy at regular price and a steal on sale.

The game mechanics are fun but the problem with the game is in the card collection and deckbuilding.  My favorite part of trading card games is being able to put together fun and creative decks.  This game, especially as a single player game, takes far too long to start getting any interesting cards, and even then you usually only will get singles of cards.  Deck building is extremely limited because of this and essentially you will just toss together whatever cards you have at the time, rather than try to build a deck with any intentional strategy.  Overall I became bored with Card City Nights because of these limitations and lost the interest to keep playing.

I had a lot of fun with card city nights. It was all the fun of a good yu-gi-oh game but more streamlined with simpler rules.
The artstyle and colour choices are pleasing to the eye and there are some very interesting character designs. This bizarre world you play in seems to operate on its own rules and give you the feeling that you're just in a part of a crazy city that is obsessed with this card game. Purple people and sentient turnips are great to play against, strangely enough.
The music is surprisingly catchy. At first I didn't think much of it, but after a couple hours the tunes started to grow on me. There were times where I would catch my foot tapping to the beat. Good music helps me think as well, so it was very welcome in a strategy/card game.
There were enough cards to make you want build your collection, but not enough that having a goal of getting them all would be too annoying. The strategies that you can come up with vary quite a bit and everyone who plays this game will have a different strategy.
Multiplayer would be a cool feature to add if there are enough people interested. I would love to try out my hyper snake deck on real people since the AI in this game is a bit easy.

I bought this game on CD when I was in my early teens. After hearing so many good things about, that it was a legendary must-play game, I just had to pick it up. Sadly, the game didn't grip me how I hoped it would back then.
Every few years since then, I would give the game another go to see if my mind would change on it. The first three times I tried to play Morrowind, I couldn't get into it. This fourth time, though, I think it finally clicked with me. Normally I prefer playing hack-and-slash ARPGs over the slower paced, more traditional role playing games. That's why I enjoyed Skyrim so much, and why it took me so long to finally come around to Morrowind.
The role playing mechanics here are very, very solid, giving the player all the right tools to experience the game however they want. You can be quite literally any kind of character that you want to be here, and it is easily the game's strongest point.
Another thing that the game absolutely nails is the exploration. The world in Morrowind is big, and the restrictions on fast travel make walking from place to place a must in order to get the full experience. Younger me hated this, but adult me thinks this is fantastic. There are numerous opportunities to tread off the beaten path whilst walking between Point A and Point B, and there's always something new to discover around just about every corner. The lack of loading screens is also a huge plus, as it increases the immersion factor and really makes you feel like you are a part of this world.
However, there is one lingering problem that I have with this game that still manages to greatly frustrate me, and that's the combat. Yeah, I get that this is a role playing game, not an ARPG, and that the combat is meant to be focused around your character's fighting skills rather than your own arcade skills. But man, real-time first-person combat mixed with dice rolls and hit percentages just doesn't work for me. My brain just refuses to accept it. To be fair, the combat becomes more bearable once your skills have had time to develop (or you can just mod the game to make it work the way you want it to) but I can easily see this combat system driving off new players who may not have the patience to bring their skills up. After all, that's what happened to me.
All in all, though, Morrowind is a classic. I wouldn't say it's my favorite Elder Scrolls game, because that's Skyrim (I like my hack-and-slash ARPGs), but I'm glad that I picked it up again and was able to finally get absorbed into its world like so many others before me.

Most of Brothers isn't challenging and at points isn't even all that engaging.  A lot of it seems to be designed to just let you enjoy the experience, much like Journey (though even Journey had a bit more in the way of mechanics).  The story follows 2 brothers (whoa, spoiler!) who are on a quest to obtain a magical elixir to cure their ailing father.  There are 4 controls in the game - left stick + left trigger are the move/interact buttons for big brother, and right stick + right trigger are the same for little brother.  At various points during the journey, they will have to interact with various bits in the world to progress in what amount to simple but neat puzzles.  The biggest challenge in the game comes from having to use both sticks at the same time to control 2 different characters.
It has many varied locales with a bit of a mythical edge to them; you encounter strange creatures very early and then it just keeps getting more interesting.  The game is a fun little diversion, and then you get to the last 20 minutes.  You know how in some games there is that moment where you see how you will have to implement the mechanics, but you don't want to do it?  I struggle to think of a comparison, but Brothers has that.
The achievements are easy to get, but not story based; at various points along the path you will encounter people, creatures, or events that you can investigate or ignore and approach how you see fit.  The game never tells you how to do anything after the initial control map, which I appreciated.  It's really never difficult to figure out what needs to be done, but the lack of text prompting was welcome.
Ultimately, it's a few hours of whimsy, peppered with just enough "game" to keep it interesting.  I never got bored or frustrated, and by the end I was sufficiently invested that I let the credits roll without stopping them.  Worth a play.
Oh, and check out the benches.  Neat views.

Now let me follow that up by saying that this game is excellent, and is definitely worth your $15. It's more akin to an adventure game than a puzzle game, and it manages to fit a lot of emotion into a short time slot. The soundtrack is amazing, and really adds a lot to the game as a whole. The characters are believable. And it's amazing how they manage to make something as simple as the button you press to do something an emotional experience (you'll know what I mean when you play it). Overall, an excellent use of 3 hours of your life. It's really too bad they aren't selling the soundtrack, because I would absolutely buy it.
Edit: As it turns out they ARE selling the soundtrack, and it is awesome.

I decided to buy Machinarium because it looked like a charming puzzle game that would make me think. I was not dissapointed.
The puzzles are all very unique and solving them can take anywhere from 30 seconds to twenty minutes. The best part is that not everything is a simple point-and-click puzzle, which helps the game stay fresh throughout. I never wanted to stop playing Machinarium during my first playthrough. The puzzles that I couldn't solve made me restless and were like an itch that I couldn't scratch. I was very tempted to look at a guide whenever I got stuck, but decided not to because what would the point be? This game is all about the satisfaction of solving difficult puzzles. That moment of your brain's light bulb dinging is an amazing feeling.
If I had any gripes about Machinarium it would be how there is little replay value. Sadly there is only one difficulty to the game, which means that once you beat it, you already know what to do the next time. I wish that the developers made a hard mode which increased the complexity of the puzzles, like Shadowgate did.
That small complaint aside, Machinarium was a joy to play and I'm happy to support indie devs that make unique and charming games. I only paid $2.50 for this game because it was on sale, but I wouldn't have been mad paying full price.

For Doom 2 there were two official level packs released: 1) No Rest For The Living and 2) Master Levels. The former is unavailable as a separate title here on Steam but it is part of the Doom 3 BFG Edition. I think it's always a good idea to include smaller titles in various editions of games; I wonder why Master Levels was left out.
Master Levels consists of 20 levels (a secret, 21st level can be accessed through one of them) that can all be run under a DoxBox menu (which is quite ugly). There is another expansion available on Steam for Doom titled Final Doom. However, the levels here are part of two chapters (or storylines, if you will). So, all the stages in Master Levels look different as they were made by different people. This includes Tim Willits, the lead designer of many id Software titles.
This I recommend only for hardcore Doom fans. 15 EUR is way too much for 20 WAD files - Final Doom is way more challenging and has consistency in its levels and only costs 5 EUR. I believe all can be found in various id Software packs and receive a discount regularly.

DOOM is often credited as the best game ever made. This is true. But, true on a deeper level than usually discussed. DOOM itself was a groundbreaking game in its day. If nothing more was done than releasing the game, that alone would have forever secured it in the pages of computer gaming history forever.
What is less often noted in reviews of DOOM is that it’s so much more than just a single game. ID Software intended DOOM to be able to be modded from the beginning. That’s why it’s WAD files are designed as they are. So that resources could be replaced and the game could be ever-expanded.
More than that, once the commercial viability of DOOM had ran its course, the source code to the engine itself was liberated under the GNU GPL; making it Free Software. Everyone who knew how to code could now tare into the very heart and soul of the software that brought DOOM to life and make it into whatever they wanted it to be.
In doing this, ID Software had made DOOM eternal. More than just swapping out map layouts, audio, and visuals; people could mod the very engine itself; as well as eventually write mods for the engine to run within the game. This was made possible because people could mod the engine. They were able to implement a scripting language within DOOM that modders could then use to add things like new enemies, weapons, and much, much more.
What this all means is that when you step into the esteemed halls of DOOM, you’re not just getting a game. You’re getting so much more. You’re getting full access to an entire engine. Couple that with the Free Software programs that have been made to edit DOOM; and you have a full software development suit.
The DOOM modding community is alive and well. It creates amazing game after game. Note I said games, not just levels or mere mods. All sorts of games. It’s been nearly twenty four years and I am still finding entire games people have created for the DOOM engine. Some new, some old; all fun.
There are people who have made it their passion to mod DOOM. They try every idea imaginable for the first person shooter genre and beyond. It is a development platform that has a massive array and tools and community support. Never have I seen a more accessible entry into making your own game in 3D space.
And, if you used only your own content, the game is yours; as the license does give you that. GPL work can be sold for a profit legally. (Note, the original DOOM wad files can not be used in this way. You have to make your own stuff or start off with the FREEDOOM wad files.)
All that said, DOOM is more than a game. It is a platform of limitless potential to the budding map maker, coder, and modder. It is the definition of ease of access, yet the very wellspring of the experimental in gaming.
Time and time again, I have seen DOOM mods that I have enjoyed more than AAA releases. I have also seen DOOM mods that have re-made AAA releases with better game play.
I will describe just a small smattering of what can be done with DOOM.
Want to play something new forever? Why not try Oblige? It’s a Free Software program that uses procedural generation to create new levels for DOOM. With this program, you’ll always have more maps to play.
Try Slade and Doom Builder to create your own maps manually. They are detailed level design tools that allow for editing in 2D and 3D. Slade can edit far more than just maps.
Want to explore deep learning? There is a DOOM engine plugin for creating Bots to play DOOM. There is even a competition that you can enter; both are called ViZDoom.
Want a great arcade shooter? Try Reelism Gold. Every game is a slot machine that rolls three mods and you try to get the most points before you die.
Want to play a bloody gory DOOM with new weapons, vehicles, and new demon attacks? Try BRUTAL DOOM.
This is the value of liberating a game engine under the GNU GPL. It allows the community to rally behind the game and make it into so much more than just one game. It allows people to make the software their own and truly make new, revolutionary, and fun things with it.
I often wonder why more of the game industry hasn’t fallowed the ID Software model. Proprietary first, then Free Software once the commercial value of the engine has ran its course. It’s the ethical thing to do. It wasn’t just the technological leaps forward that made these engines and these games so valuable to the public. It was that ID Software gave these innovations to the public. In so doing, they changed the way the public saw the software they gamed with. Software was no longer a black box that just made the game work. Software was now an open door to creativity that a community could bond together over. That’s what made ID Software games so special; more than anything else.
I also wait, in hope, that ID Software itself will continue to fallow this model. We’re still waiting for the ID Tech 5 release under the GNU GPL.
That said, ID Software has no one there that originally started the company; and Carmack was known for really pushing for the source code releases under the GNU GPL. Many have told me that with him gone; we’ll likely never see another source code release from ID. I don’t want to agree with them too quickly. But, I think they’re likely right. Were the source code releases ID’s tradition, or Carmack’s tradition? Only time will tell.
I hope ID keeps this tradition. I also hope other software development companions fallow this model. That said, we’ll always have DOOM. The original DOOM. Which, twenty four years later, is still alive and well with its modding community. A truly infinite game that is forever growing.

Man oh man… After finally beating the game, I’ll share some of my thoughts about this short, but fun and really challenging game.
Shapes of Gray is a fast-paced arcade-style top-down “shooter”, although most of the time you aren’t shooting, but wielding a sword. Your objective is to destroy all the other gray shapes in order to proceed to the next stage.
Presentation-wise, this game lives up to its name. The whole game is presented in shades of gray, while the main character and enemies are all gray shapes. The minimalistic aesthetic gives the game a nice retro look, which works fairly well along with the game’s arcade gameplay. The music, while not particularly spectacular, does its job well-enough with the game’s style. What I really want to talk about is its interesting gameplay mechanics.
The game’s stages are limited by a very short timer (think WarioWare’s microgames), which forces you to play aggressively. However, you also have a very limited number of lives, which encourages the player to be careful. This system really puts the players in a very stressful situation: confident players will see themselves rapidly losing their precious lives (which do not regenerate between stages) against the various gray-colored enemies; meanwhile, doubtful players will see their runs be ended because they couldn’t defeat all the enemies in time.
And this system is the most prominent reason for this game’s difficulty. The game starts off easy enough to get used to the simple mechanics, but by the end of the game, it gets really hard. In order to succeed (especially in later levels), one has to find the balance between aggression and carefulness. And I must say, it’s very hard to find. I was stuck for several days on the last stages of the game because I was either too careless, or too slow. I must admit, it made me very frustrated at times, and it honestly made me angry, not at the game, but at myself. I lost a lot, but it never felt it was the game’s fault, as it doesn’t rely on artificial difficulty or cheap mechanics.
The enemies are designed in such a way that the player needs to adapt their playstyle in order to defeat each and every one of them. And they must do so quickly, as the enemies are ruthless and very aggressive. Each stage has a specific set of different enemies, and it is quite interesting discovering how each enemy type interacts with each other. Fighting each different enemy requires different strategies, which get more and more complicated when you are facing different types of enemies at once.  Some enemies can destroy other enemies and help you or harm you in the process. Others are immune to the rest of the enemies’ attacks; and others are immune to your attacks.
The very high difficulty really punishes the player for small mistakes, which forces the player to perform near flawlessly in each stage. This is a completely personal preference, but I feel this tight margin of error works a bit against the game’s overall enjoyment and fun aspect. I’m not much of a fan of extremely difficult games, as they result more in frustration than fun. However, anyone who’s looking for a challenge, this game’s the solution, without a doubt.
The game increases its replay-value by adding an Arcade Mode after finishing the first campaign. This mode adds coins and achievements into the game’s main mode. Players will surely have to try several times in order to obtain all the achievements, as they increase the difficulty of the already hard main campaign.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Now, I’d like to talk about some stuff I feel would make for a much better experience while playing the game. Of course, all of this is just personal preference, and I hope the talented people at Secret Tunnel Entertainment take these bits of advice in consideration for a sequel, an update, or a future game if applicable:
-	In terms of difficulty and overall enjoyment, I’d say the game would benefit a lot from more health-recovery items.  They do not automatically make the game easier, as sometimes attempting to get the extra lives is riskier than ignoring them, but they do allow the player to mend previous small mistakes, and it gives them much more to think about while playing. They rarely appear in the game, though.
-	The replay-value and overall enjoyment of the game would benefit a lot from a character or weapon selection, letting the player choose at the start of the run according to their playstyle. Maybe a bigger sword that swings slower, or a quick but shorter one. Or a weapon that shoots bullets that take two or three shots to take out each enemy.
-	I don’t ignore the fact that the game has power-ups that change the way the player tackles each challenge, but I felt they were underused, considering they always show up in the same spot and they stay in the player’s possession for a very short period of time. Maybe adding more power-ups and/or allowing them to appear at random would make for a better experience.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Of course, reviewing this game for what it doesn’t have would be unfair and a huge disservice to what this game actually delivers. Everything listed previously is just feedback for Secret Tunnel Entertainment, and it should not negatively influence your decision to get this game. What this game offers is quite enough for me to consider this game as money well-spent. It satisfied my desire to feel accomplished and challenged, and it got some pleasant surprises and smiles out of me several times. Especially during the ending, which really surprised me in a good way. It was so unexpected and funny it honestly made me chuckle a few times.
All in all, I recommend this game if you are mildly interested by it. If you are looking for a challenge and a humble but solid game, you’ve found it.

Described by the developer Secret Tunnel Entertainment as “WarioWare meets Hotline Miami”, Shapes of Gray had some pretty impressive shoes to fill. I  happy to report that with its tight controls and frantic timed battles, it lives up to it’s description.
In Shapes of Gray you play as a little gray blob with three lives and a sword in a top down circular arena.  The game controls like a simplified Hotline Miami: one stick to move, one to turn and a trigger to swing your sword. The level count starts at 50 and your little gray blob descends the tower, floor by floor. Each stage gives you only seconds to take in your surroundings, defeat the new enemies set forth to destroy you and proceed to the next level.
There are three bosses within the tower (at levels 35, 20, 1). Each one feels unique and takes some time to figure out the trick to defeating them. I particularly liked the 3 stage style of the boss at level 1 and found its classic “video game boss” feel very charming. A defeated boss acts as a checkpoint, and you will start at the level immediately after the boss if you die, or fail to complete the level within the time frame.
Both bosses and minions are highlights in Shapes of Gray. Some enemies will shoot at you, some will charge, some will even bounce around the stage, all with the intention to deplete your 3 Lives to zero before you reach the end of your 50 level gauntlet to the end. There are many systems in the game to use enemies against each other, and use their attacks against them, but I will let you discover those for yourself.
OK. I lied.
Those moments were some of my favorite in the game. I have to tell you about the time I batted an exploding enemy into another enemy a second before my time expired. AND the time I found a ninja star power up and went on to ninja the crap out of the next couple stages till I ran out of bad♥♥♥♥♥ninja powers. AND THE TIME.. no no.. YOU need to discover these things. The sense of discovery in a circular arena was a surprising plus.
It took me about 2 hours to clear the first 50 stages in order to open up the rest of the game. But that isn’t because the stages were long or boring. Quite the opposite. The stages are quick and brutal, but take skill and understanding of the in game systems to conquer. Don’t get me wrong, I wanted to throw the controller many times, but I also wanted to kill that stupid bullet spraying star shaped thing into submission and prove my gladiatorial prowess. ARE YOU NOT ENTERTAINED!! It is safe to say I intend to sink many more hours into Shapes of Gray.
After completing the initial 50 stages you unlock the main menu as well as a whole new 50 stages to defeat. While the first level set, or tower as I have begun to describe it, feels defensive the second set is very offensive. This change, along with its completely new enemies types force you to charge at your enemies and brave into battle. A random thing I love in the second set of 50 stages besides the utter difference in strategy is the fun sound the new bomb-like guys make. It’s this “Booommmmmshsshshshshsssssssshhhhh” sound that I can’t write, but believe me it’s super fun.
You also unlock an arcade mode for the first tower (and the second tower once you conquer its 50 levels). The arcade mode adds a score system and coin grabbing mechanic to the game which adds even more randomness to each level and drive to play again and again. There is also this other little gray dude that heat seeks toward you that you can continue to bat away to multiply your score. He follows you through the levels until you inevitably screw up and let him finally commit suicide on your body. It’s not as gruesome as it sounds. An impressive debut for Secret Tunnel.
The technical issues for the WiiU version are gone in the PC release, but even those were quite minor when you consider that this game was built a one-man development studio. The head of Secret Tunnel Entertainment is Trent Steen, a game game jam winner and GDC 2015 Platinum Award winning writer.  After you play Shapes of Gray, or while you eagerly wait to get home from work to boot it up, head to
. There you can read his Narrative Analysis of Metal Gear (metal….. gear?) or check out his other projects (Like Candy Poop Butt Game). You should also listen to my interview with him on The Cardboard Box Podcast where he discusses indie game development and working with Nintendo.
Shapes of Gray is difficult–but never cheap. “WarioWare meets Hotline Miami”? Shapes is as addicting as its spiritual parents. This is a great first game and has cool and interesting game systems that keep me coming back for more. I also want to just hear that bomb guy’s sound some more. I look forward to the next title from Secret Tunnel Entertainment, but will continue to enjoy this one until that day inevitably comes. This game deserves your attention.
A copy of this game was provided to CBxCasts by Secret Tunnel Entertainment.

Shapes of Gray is a top down action game. Each level lasts several seconds and gets increasingly difficult. I found myself frustrated at some of the later levels, but it compelled me enough to push through it. The concept is simple, and that isn't a bad thing. The game is based around mastering simple mechanics, and it executes on that well, introducing new ways to use the core mechanic every few levels. The most interesting part to me is the ways you can get enemies to intereact with each other, using one enemy's abilities to destroy another. Sadly I never did finish the game as it doesn't save your progress in between play sessions. I'd say pick it up if it goes on sale.

Shapes of Grey is a fast paced arcade game warioware mashup that will always keep you on your edge. You play as a nameless circle with a melee weapon as your only line of defense against numerous other shapes each with their attacks and patterns. The bulk of the game is found in the two quests, each of which is a gaunlet challenge of clearing 50 floors (while only having 10 seconds per floor to clear it) It is important to note that you only have three hit points so you have little room for error adding to the difficulty.
The gameplay I am happy to say is very responsive and I can recommend both mouse and game controllers as working very well. When you die (and trust me when I say you will die a lot) it always feels like it is your own fault and not something that was out of your control.
Clearing the quests on their own provides a fair challenge, but for those that seek something more difficult will find that in the arcade runs. After completing a quest for the first time you will be able to play that quest again this time in the arcade mode. In arcade mode is basiclly score attack where you try to get the highest score possible. Each floor has coins that you can collect that increase your score multiplier and you get points based on how quickly you complete a floor. Getting a high score is certainly not easy and the pressure only builds as you get towards the end of a run desperately trying to hold onto your hit points.
In summary, it's fun, challenging, and best played in short bursts.

Defiance is definitely an interesting game.  The storyline starts off well, but I felt somewhat cut off from what exactly was going on.  I progressed, I participated in collective, massive battles of 50-100 people, I participated in the instance levels that came with the game.  It is definitely an TPS and it works well for the shooting part.
However, if you haven't watched the show this is based upon, then you will definitely lose out.  I have not watched the show, and I barely knew what exactly was going on.  The military was involved somehow, and the sidequests made very little sense.  Some of the missions were super difficult for 1 player in story mode.  And I was armed to the teeth with grenades and assault rifles.  What really ticked me off is that I would kill enemies in my story instance, use up all my grenades doing so, one person survives and kills me off.  What happens?  The story instance restarts with all the enemies coming back alive to full health and ammo.  Except I have no grenades and no ammo.  Every time I had to restart, the story instance would restart and I would not.  This happened many times, and eventually I was spending an hour on a simple mission, because I had to kill every enemy all over with next to no ammo and grenades.
The massive battles were interesting, but there were no rewards other than shared xp (amongst a hundred people).  Also turns out I can explore the whole map at any level, and there is literally nothing that interested me landmark wise.  Everything is almost the same everywhere.  The skills were decently thought out, and the skills as well as the lack of lag and graphical distortion were really the only positives for me.
Don't get me wrong, if you enjoy TPS and you have a few other friends who like 'em and you wanna just fool around in an MMO with guns, then maybe this could be a game to do so in.  But it loses it's fun very fast.  In my personal opinion, it was not worth the buy.
