For a while I've been looking for a game like Spore, where you can be creative with your character in so many ways. As soon as I got this game, I immediately loved it.
My favorite levels (From Top to bottom):
-1. Creature:
You get to be up close and personal with the creature you make. I prefer games where you get to be a single character that you can actually see as he/she moves around. I don't have the Galactic Adventures expansion pack at the time I posted this review, but I'm looking forward to it.
-2. Space:
You get to explore space, fight/befriend other empires. And the Grox. Even though I wish there was a "Final Boss" and an "Ending" somewhere in the game, I still like the idea behind the Grox. Before I knew they existed, I didn't think there were any true "villains" in Spore and that the only main villain was you if you wanted to be. (Or, one of the enemy empires if you wanted to pretend they were the main villains of your story).
-3. Civilization:
Same reason I like the Space level. You get to choose which nations are your friends and which nations are your enemies. I had a lot of fun with it because when I was ready to take on the last enemy nation, I sent my whole military after them.
-4. Tribal:
While it still has the same "choose your friends/enemies" concept (As, does pretty much the entire game), for some reason it just didn't stick with me. I'm not saying I dislike the Tribal level, but it was somewhat forgettable.
-5. Cell:
I feel like the cell stage was the most boring part of Spore. That doesn't mean I think it's bad or anything. It just seems like it needs something more.
Complaints aside, I love Spore. It's absolute fun, especially if you've ever had an idea for a creature/monster that you just want to bring to life. I recommend this game for anyone who wants to create playable characters from complete scratch.

Update! Got Spore to work with Steam now. So ignore hours played here. I've well over 600+ hours with this game since it's release quite some time ago.
So Spore is a God game of sorts, which would be ironic considering it focuses mostly on evolution for what should be the meat of the game. Depending on how you play however, it can still be a good chunk. Starting off from a tiny organism in the primordial soup, you work your way up through the food chain by consuming matter and gaining points to evolve new parts to make you more dangerous, defensive or the alpha being in the micro world. Eventually you gain the ability to have the very basic instincts of a sentient creature, growing legs and walking onto land where you proceed to evolve as before in a much larger world. From there you eventually gain a higher thought process and begin displaying the ability to form a cohesive society capable of thinking. From there you move through what's something of a crude cross between an RTS and several janky game mechanics to befriend or defeat other tribes which appear in the world. Eventually moving on to be the dominant species and begin warring with other nations which spring up. You've several ways to dominate the planet, truth be told, the mechanics behind conquering the world are the same for any path really.
And then onto the true meat of the game. Space exploration, terraforming new worlds, meeting new space empires and either kill, conquer or buy worlds from them. And then, the steam for this game begins to die down and the fun train slows substantially. Sure, at first exploring the stars is fun, but after awhile it can begin to become more of a chore to hop around space, meeting certain goals and milestones to improve your ship and empire and defending against aggressive or downright hostile space beings. I will say though, it took a long time, but your ultimate goal is to reach the center of the galaxy. I won't say what you find of course, so the truly curious will have to find their way there or just look it up online like a panzy.
Now as for the different stages of evolving a creature, a bit more in depth.
Just to note, as you progress through the stages you can choose different paths such as herbivore and carnivore which then translate into other catagories later in the game such as industrious, warlord or peaceful. All of which give some special abilities in the tribal, civilization and space stages and also effect how your creatures evolve in what parts are available in evolution.
The first two stages, cell and creature, are fairly similar in mechanics in terms of gaining DNA to evolve. The cell stage is very simple, depending on your difficulty, but typically isn't hard to get through at all. Then the creature stage which uses the same mechanics of the cell stage, but on land and much more three dimensional. The game is a bit silly in how to befriend other creatures, using silly but amusing mechanics. Combat is essentially two animals clawing at each other until one or the other is dead. This is where you begin really planning your creatures evolution a bit more. You can shape it's torso, head and any other appendage to your liking, making everything from humanoid bipedal creatures or a giant♥♥♥♥♥♥♥hopping around. Whatever floats your boat or finds your lost remote, weirdo.
When it comes to interacting with the world, whether it's combat or communication, it functions quite a bit like an MMO actually. You click where you want to go or use the typical WSAD keys to move around. Hotkeys, 1234 and such will perform actions depending on what you're doing with small cooldown timers. When moving on after you've gotten enough DNA, the camera mechanics and interactions perform roughly the same for the Tribal stage. This is probably the shortest stage there is. You can easily and quickly defeat or befriend other tribes and chances are it'll take about thirty or forty minutes. Operates the same with hotkeys and movement, but more like a badly formed RTS where you can move units around to collect resources and the such.
Next is the Civilization stage which is pretty bland to tell the truth. You can design your own land, water and air vehicles in just about whatever fashion you see fit. In terms of conquering, they're all pretty much the same except for trade which allows you to peacefully buy other civilizations land, but to some extent works on the same mechanics. Then you get to the true meat of the game. SPACE. And at first it's pretty amazing with how massive of a galaxy you have to explore. You'll meet a handful of different species near you, explore different planets and stars that you've seen in the sky since you first crawled onto land.
Terraforming, now there's a thing. At first it's pretty neat, slowly shaping a world to sustain life, plopping plants and animals to create a stable ecosystem so you can build colonies to populate new worlds. Along with colonizing you can collect a substance found on many planets called Spice. In this time, the most precious substance in the universe is the spice. The spice extends life. The spice expands conciousness. The spice is vital to space travel. Actually, no it's just a valuable trading commodity of different colors and rarity. You can trade spices between different systems and eventually, in most cases, be able to buy the system and aquire new planets to claim as your own.
Now things start to sort of fall apart when it comes to advancing. For a bit all these things are a bit of fun and in short bursts, it can be. However after awhile the game becomes tedious and more of a task. The expansion for the game, Galactic Adventures, does add a fairly decent amount to do, but comes across as excessively cheesy and hokey, though I imagine the target audience was a bit younger than most of the people actually playing the game or somebody at Maxis and/or EA was smoking the dank and watching far to many kids shows on Saturday morning. But a fair amount, if not almost half of other missions aren't so bad and involve a combat system which reflects what you would have experience back in the creature stage. Just with lasers and such. It does make for a less tedious but slower method to obtain Sporebucks, though you eventually reach the point where expanding your civilization, which requires massive amounts of Sporebucks to upgrade your ship. Keep it up though and this grind isn't to bad, but then you're left with even less goals to pursue as you look forward to the tedious journey to the center of the galaxy.
Oh right, your ship. Almost forgot. So you get to design a space ship of any design at the beginning of the Space stage. It doesn't matter what parts you put on it, as your ships abilities, defences and other functions are unlocked in other ways. So the design is purely aesthetic. Controls are the WSAD setup with your cursor acting as a point of aiming. Combat is usually fairly simple and becomes somewhat routine after awhile. Once you upgrade your ship enough though, combat becomes hardly a challenge and becomes more of a management thing in simply making sure your ship stays fueled and powered up.
There's not much else to say here. I will note, I remember this game being hyped up beyond belief and being a great letdown to a lot of people. I didn't feel all that disapointed, but felt there was a much greater goal this game could have accomplished rather than slowly fizzling out in its gameplay late game. I'm sure some people find the tasks entertaining for a long time, but I've found it's better in short bursts in the late game, as just about everything else can be done in a matter of six to ten hours.
So is this game with the expansions worth $40(USD)? That's a shaky yes. But if you're not willing, wait for a sale. With that, I am about to hit the maximum amount of characters available to write a rev--

A very innovative card game. I've seen nothing like it. 99% of the trading card games out there all share the same mechanics like the play area, card costs, attacks phases, etc. Card City Nights is unique in this respect in that its mechanics require a lot of thought into dueling and deck building, even when using the most basic of cards. Synergy is the only key in this game. A deck full of powerful cards that don't synergize is pretty much unplayable.
Absolutely worth it for its price.

If you like card games or board games, this is a fun quirky single player entry that has great deck building. It would never work as a multipler game, but finding ways to do broken things against the computer and using the multiple ways to win each match was a lot of fun.

For CDN$2.24(on sale right now), I would highly recommend Card City Nights if you want to get a fun card game. (For the record, I haven't played a card game since yugioh like 10 years ago, so my opinion about card games may not be that informed)
Like other card games, you will need to gather cards(by beating enemies, buying from stores, combining unwanted cards, you can get a special card by beating each boss) and build your decks. To beat the enemy in a match, you either have to reduce his hp to 0, make the table full of cards so the enemy cannot place any more cards or make the enemy use up all his deck.
Based on these different winning conditions, you can design your deck accordingly. For example, if you want to play aggressively, you can put many attack cards that can easily combo(the cards have directions, you need to connect cards of the same type(attack/heal/revive/neutral) to combo) in your deck. You can also pick many cards with disable/rotate effects. If the enemies do not have revive cards, they will get stuck with too many cards(either disabled or in wrong directions) on the table. Alternatively you can build a large deck with lots of healing cards and try to outlive the enemy. This works well when the enemy has a small deck(there are also cards that let you directly remove the enemy's cards).
Different AI enemies will use different strategies. There is enough variety. In particular, bosses will have special cards that have powerful effects, like hp regen every round, attack card that can be reused indefinitely, shield that prevent any damage to the owner's hp(but you can disable or remove the card). The bosses are appropriately challenging(tho I don't feel that they are cheating). You will have to use the correct tactics to beat them.
The graphic of this game is ok(you can see screenshots on steam). The story is not very serious. The dialogues sometimes can be pretty silly but funny. Anyway I think the focus of this game is the gameplay. For someone like me who doesn't usually play card games, I have lots of fun playing this game. It even makes me want to try out other card games. For 2 bucks, I think it is really worth. The only complaint I have is that there is no multiplayer mode.

If you enjoy an easy-going yet skill-based game, or if you enjoy the elements of both puzzles and trading card battles, I highly recommend 'Card City Nights.'
In 'Card City Nights', you fast travel through an island city with a chill, evening atmosphere, talking to comical NPCs, and battling them in a TCG for booster packs. In the card game proper, each player has a 3x3 card grid, and seven Defense Points. The goal is either to fill up your opponent's grid with occupied space, or decrease their Defense Points to zero.
Cards have three main categories: ATTACK, which can disable opponent cards, or damage your opponent's Defense Points; DEFENSE, which can increase your own Defense Points; and REVIVE, which can bring your disabled cards back into play.
The challenge of the game is that cards must be played in combos. Each card has a specific set of arrows which tell you where on the grid it can be placed for maximum efficiency, and cards in a combo must point to each other in order to be played. While some cards have multiple arrows, others only have one (some trick cards have none). They can also have additional effects such as rotation, teleportation, or extra damage, making gameplay interesting, unpredictable, and especially fun.
The game works in an almost Rock-Paper-Scissors type of balance, where a specific strategy you use for your deck to counter that of your opponent's will expose you to another vulnerability. Having the freedom to make your own deck allows you to explore and create your own combos. Each NPC uses a consistent strategy, making training accessible, but not simple-minded, since the variability of play is kept intact by the limited number of cards you're allowed to use at once. This could actually be printed as a physical card game, and I would invest in it without hesitation.
Personally, this game meets all my standards for a perfect single player game: completely replayable, expansive but not overwhelming, customizable, encouraging of practice, and a smooth, approachable mood shown through the art style, music and NPCs (I once spent a quarter hour just reading the funny lines of the gossiper at the city mall).
An online multiplayer mode would send my love for this game over the top, like a rocket that shoots through the sky and explodes, scattering its awesome rocket parts over the world. Seriously, game designers, if you're reading this: give 'Card City Nights' an online multiplayer mode, or the aforementioned physical card game.

Master Levels of Doom II is somewhat of an expansion to Doom 2 in that it contains 20 PWADs with 20+1 levels to play (one of which is a secret level in one of the wads). Master Levels consist of high quality levels for their time with the intention of being challenging and difficulty. Of course the difficult is easy compared to the Final Doom IWADs, Plutonia and TNT, and modern WADs pretty much make all the levels pretty much puts the levels to shame. Considering that 1994 WADs aren't known for their quality and seeing that we're paying for what is basically community map pack of WADs, well they must be good, right? For the most part, yes actually, and seeing that this comes for free if you buy Doom 2, I really can't complain since it's not like you'll pay much for it. Doom 2 is already enough of a great game and having more Doom to play is welcoming.
As for the levels themselves, they are for the most part solid and enjoyable, albeit some are a bit sloppy. Only level I do not like is the secret level, and to spoil it, it's just a room full of Cyberdemons with nothing else to it. So much for wanting to play a secret level. Other than that, I can't say a whole lot other than that it's free for buying Doom 2, you can run the WADs on any source port these days (don't complain about my lack of playtime), and of course, you don't need to launch it through Steam as the original Doom is DRM free.
I should say this, if you want to make playing the levels more convenient and a 20+1 level episode instead of multiple PWADs that almost all replace MAP01: Entryway, try out this tool, it bundles all the WADs in one WAD file and you can launch it with DOOM2.wad with the episodes Hell on Earth and Master showing up, Master being the Master Levels. The tool is linked here.
Download for Master Levels Patch:
Last thing to say about the Master Levels is that it comes with Maximum Doom, which can be summarized as WAD Shovelware with 1,830 amaetur PWADs, which includes 191 PWADs for Doom 1/Ultimate Doom, 1629 Doom 2 PWADs, and surprisingly, 10 PWADs for Heretic. May seem great with all those WADs to play, right? Well no, it's not anything worth checking out as the amount of low quality WADs is astounding. Sure we have more WADs now than then, but seriously, to think Maximum Doom is officially licensed shovelware and pretty much forgotten since no one really wants to mention it. Yes, back then the internet wasn't all that great so having a disc full of WADs sounds great in theory. But even back then the quality is just horrific, and it's even worse now seeing that it's mind-boggling to think people can make some of the stupidest mistakes possible. HOMs everywhere, texture problems, poorly designed levels that aren't even playtested by the looks of it, and simple mistakes breaking whole maps (How can you mess up a square room?!). The quality speaks for itself when one of the maps is a room with the letter G. Yeah, let's praise G the map. Doesn't help many of the Doom 2 levels are Doom 1 levels poorly converted over to Doom 2, which means more texture issues, perhaps even missing textures if I can recall. Also most maps seem to be made with deathmatch in mind, but who wants to play deathmatch with god awful maps like these, especially when they don't even play right on single-player as it is. Maximum Doom only exists to go talk back at D!Zone, but really, neither are good and Maximum Doom being officially licensed means nothing as the quality of the WADs remains poor.
I don't recommend checking out Maximum Doom but if you really want to see what it is, well there is an archive of all the Maximum Doom levels for you to play, all 3,943 levels with some copyrighted music and sounds here and there (from the SImpsons and Monty Python for example). Funny enough, some of the level designers involved with the Master Levels did not got there levels in the package, but they got it in Maximum Doom instead. Whether they're good or not, I wouldn't know since I have not gone through more than 50 levels of Maximum Doom. Anyways, play the 20+1 levels of the Master Levels, they are worth your time to play. Maximum Doom, just skip it unless you are really bored or just want to experience some abysmal WADs, but that is your choice after all. I should note that the Heretic levels are not in this download but not like you really want to play 10 crappy PWADs, especially on a game like Heretic, why would you.
Maximum Doom Download:

Woof, this one is tricky enough to get running in a source port that I just ended up skipping it after touring some of the content in the included DOSBox emulator. That said, if you're desperate for a little more DOOM II, there are better ways to play the Master Levels than this.

Contrary to popular belief DC universe online is actually a fun and very playable MMO for the PC and playstation 3. The game has without a doubt been very rapidly depopularized over the course of time it has been on the market and the pvp server is almost completely dead now if it isn't already which is kind of a complaint. Some of my best memories of this game are from random raids on the hero and villain bases. The gameplay is utilizing a fighting engine which has without a doubt been used more over the years. The fighting mechanics are actually quite interesting and blend with the gameplay smoothly and actually enhance the experience. Some problems however can occur within the very beginning of the game, even in creating your character. For one the game has a naming system that will not allow copyrighted material or trademarked material of any type which would be ok if it didn't restrict anything that could be considered copyright as well which could at times disregard an entire unique name because it may have certain phrases or terms in it. Another issue with the naming is that Most of the good names have already been taken so you have very slim odds of getting the name you want on the first try. You can also add onto the fact that it will completely overide your name if it has any grammar errors, puncuation marks, or even one to many spaces. Some of the bigger problems are actually from level 1-9 and then level 30 and up, the best moments of the game are generally had after you get through level 9 but an issue is that once you get to level 30 you have basically done everything so you have no real point anymore. You could replay old missions which can be repetitive and quite boring but a fun thing to do was to raid the villain base and have a great time. Of course that is no longer an option due to a dead pvp server. Overall despite the faults the game is still great, especially for a free game and It has to be a solid 8/10. Long download but it's worth it.

Lost Technology is a Doujin (japanese indie) RTS which focuses on territory control and squadron management.
Gameplay
The game allows you to choose one of several factions and manage your squadrons, income and diplomacy in order to control more territories and expand. When engaged in battle, you are allowed to control your units like in many games in the genere, however, units have special skills which tie into their respective playstyle, which in turn, is determined by the units they are allowed to control and the terrain they start at. For instance, elves, as residents of the forest, and primarily bow-centered, require more guerrilla-type tactics, while the Lizard-men rely in rush tactics and sheer numbers. During battle, you are slso able to control Vaguard and Backline units and assign a specific role during the battle. The ability to pause all movement in order to position your camera and make adjustments is also included. The game also allows you to form alliances with other factions, so long as you have the money for it, however, there is also the risk that an ally quckly decides to trminate all relations in order to pursue their own goals. Enemy turns are surprisingly fast, so it can be somewhat difficult to grasp the overall status of the campaign and see the state of diplomatic stances. However, turns are brief and decisions (whether good or bad) are resolved quickly, avoiding tedium.
Controls
The control is almost exclusively tied to mouse and keyboard. The only way to move the camera arround the field is to move the cursor to the edge of the screen, which in my experience, has causd me to panic and click all over the place, oftentimes exiting the game into the desktop. Unfortunately, at this time, there is no option to re-bind keys. However, anyone who has had experience with an RTS should have no problem adjusting to the control scheme. The menus are window-based, and for the most part, they work fine. The ability to manage squads and send them from city to city is a very nice touch.
Sound and Art design
The game uses hand-drawn sprites to indicate characters and faction leaders, and there are dozens of them. Each character is extremely different and surprisingly fleshed out, going so far as to being partially voiced. Though dialogue in significant story cutscenes is text and sprite based all characters have their own battle quips, which, for a title made by a single person (or a small group of people) is trully commendable. Sound effects are mostly stock-level, but fit the action on screen well and are not intrusive or distracting. The real stand-out, however, is a surprisingly well-composed soundtrack which is mostly orchestral, save for battles , which go for a mixture of hard rock and orchestral arrangements. A small gripe I might have with the art design is that Leader or Hero type units are somewhat hard to distinguish at first, but with enough time and patience, you learn to tell them appart and this issue doesn's tarnish the experience. However, the art of all the characters is incredibly well thought out, and the lore that goes into each one of them is charming and detailed enough to make you care for them, whether friend or foe in the ongoing war.
Final words
Due to the lack of a very in-depth tutorial, new or inexperienced players (such as myself) might have a hard time managing all that happens arround them in such a short time. However, the addition of a pause button that allows you to make adjustments to your strategy as well as the ability to assing behaviours to specific squadrons is not only appreciated, but essential in order to achieve victory. Once you understand the mechanics, as well as your factions strengths and weaknesses, the game can become nail-bitingly exiting, and managing to defend a territory against an imposing invading force, as well as watching as factions rise and fall during the course of the war is extremely entertaining. Sadly, the game isn't complete due to the fact that localizing all the scenarios and campaigns has proven a monummental task for the development and publishing team, however, what we have is a surprisingly deep and lovingly-crafted RTS with an allouring cast of characters and beautiful soundtrack, all for a verry low asking price. If the idea of playing a part in this high fantasy, grand scale conflict appeals to you, then Lost Technology is a great choice. Verry highly recomended.

I've been playing this game since the first in it's series was in its beta phase in 2006.  That's a long development cycle, but the game started as a two-person operation between Armagan and his wife.  Since then, the graphical presentation has improved slightly, while the models have remained somewhat behind the curve.
Nonetheless, I consider this game the game of my last decade, with gameplay that is second to none.  This is the game that inspired the entire medieval combat simulator genre.  In addition to addictive multiplayer arena-style matches, this game also has a robust single-player campaign that is open-ended and not story driven.  You make your own story in Warband.
The graphics, while not really pretty or even the best optimized, are good enough to carry the gameplay, which is where this game's strengths lie.  There's no other game in the rpg genre that does mounted combat, and melee combat better.  It's rare to find a game where you can be the single warrior, among hundreds and in some cases (if you have a strong enough system to support them and capability to mod the game) thousands of troops on the same map, duking it out and cutting down their opposing ragdolls.
I don't know what else to say, I've been playing this game for so long that there's probably a ton in here that I'm taking for granted and not mentioning here.  The best advice I can give to anyone who is on the fence, is to try the demo first, that should put you over the fence on whether or not to buy it.

Honestly, this is one of my favorite games of the year right here (I just found out about it this year so that's why). As someone who loved Yu-Gi-Oh! and dabbled in Magic The Gathering, I thought I'd give this a shot since it was only $2. When you start the game, you're thrown into a tutorial and it teaches you the unique way to battle. The way this game is different in how you battle is that not only do the cards matter, but where you place them matters even more. Each card has its own unique layout of arrows that you have to connect with other arrows on other cards, as well as matching the different card types (Attack, Defense, and Neutral). Using this, you go through the town and battle different unique and quirky people and work your way to the top.
The only thing I'm not that fond of in this game is there's really only one dominant strategy, and it's offense offense offense. I wish there were different ways to beat enemies, like milling or a defense-type thing. But even then, there is strategy in building your deck on how you should be offensive.
But all in all, the battle system is unique and the characters are fun to talk to and battle. Seriously, buy this game. Buy it for full price, because it's worth it. And if it's on sale, that's even more reason to buy it!
P.S. If you go on the "Dollar per Hour of Gameplay" motto, I got it for $2 and it took me 8 to beat the game once and an additional 2 to do some of the post-game stuff.

Morrowind is without a doubt my favorite game of all time. I say this as a person who is not simply operating on nostalgia, but as a person who has a little bit of perspective. I was only 5 when Morrowind came out. My first real experience with an Elder Scrolls game was playing Oblivion in middle school, and I loved it. I then decided to go back and play Morrowind, and I was completely blown away. This is a game that will not disappoint you. It is an experience, and one with endless possibilities (it's been over 8 years since I first played Morrowind, and I still play it today, as a sophomore in college). This game gives doesn't just tell an incredibly meaningful and nuanced story (although it does that), it doesn't just create multi-dimensional characters with real personality (it does that too), but it completely puts you in a world of wonder, a foreign land with culture and politics unique to itself, and depth unlike any other game I have ever played. There are so many positives to this game, it is impossible to list them all, but I will try to list some highlights. The major one is the story and lore. The story of this game is a complexly woven story, and one that is entertaining from beginning to end. The characters for the most part are interesting and modereatley fleshed out (of course there are exceptions, but the shortcoming are made up for with characters like Crassius Curio). The game world feels alive, with its internal politics and multiple factions, and of course all the scores of books to read. Another great thing about Morrowind is the fact that actions really have consequences. Joining certain factions can cause other factions to dislike you more, etc. There are dozens upon dozens of weapons, and limitless spells - inlcuding levitiation and teleportation spells. The open world the size is pretty dang large, and it helps that it is filled to the brim with towns, dungeons and quests. It is completely non-linear, and you can completely ignore the main quest if you want (although it's great so I would recommend doing it). The game world is not leveled, meaning that there are some areas that will have really tough enemies that you just can't fight until you are a higher level, so you have to be careful at first. I love this, it makes the world feel more real and mysteriously dangerous to explore. Finally, one of the best things about Morrowind is the incredible score! The music is phenomenal, and really sets the tone of the world. However, all these positives don't mean that Morrowind is without negatives as well.
There are a few downsides, the primary being combat. The combat is largely based on Dungeons and Dragons style dice rolls, meaning that it can be frustrating. At early levels you are highly likely to miss enemies, even when you're directly in front of them. This improves once you are past about level 7 or 8, but at early levels it can be difficult. The graphics are obviously a bit dated, but this can be fixed easily with free mods (and graphics don't make or break a game for me anyway). The final downside is that there is a lack of voice acting, as most of the dialogue is text - meaning you have to read. This is also not too bad, it means that characters can say a lot more for less disk space, but it can take away from immersion at times.
All in all, Morrowind is an incredible game, full of possibility and entertainment, and will be one of the best purchases of your life. I have logged thousands of hours into this game (not on Steam, I spent most of my life playing the disk version). Play this game! 10/10.

Lost Technology:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~
The Reinald Empire has been ruling the world for the last forty seven years. Before the rise of this Empire, relentless wars between the twelve factions who co-habit this world had an incredible impact, especially on technologies. And the result was devastating, as all valuable technologies that each of the factions had created were destroyed. Unfortunately the beloved Emperor has passed away from illness. The Prince (his successor) died suddenly and the next family member to take the throne is Agnes, the granddaughter who is only fourteen years old. The empress doesn’t know a thing about politics, military or anything within her empire. To make it even more dangerous, her prime minister, with whom she has direct contact, is a warmonger and only interested in his own fortune. Will it be the end of the Reinald Empire?
Lost Technology is a strategy / anime game set in a fantasy world where humans are the largest faction.
The first thing you must do is to go through the small tutorial. It will tell you how to recruit units, move them through the world and show you how to attack locations. The reason I am writing this is that I consider myself a pretty good gamer when it comes to strategy games. Therefore I have a tendency to jump straight into the thick of it and usually don’t have any issues. In this case, I had a bit of trouble and got a bit frustrated. So, to avoid the frustration do go through the tutorial because it is an interesting game.
On the main menu, you can choose between four levels of difficulties. Then you have to select which faction out of twelve you would like to play.
The map has seventy-six locations and most of them will be divided between all the twelve factions. Depending on who you choose, you’ll start with three or four sites. There is an exception; one of the factions will start with a whopper ten locations! In this game, you basically have to conquer your enemies. There are two phases per turn, the first being the recruitment of units and moving them to a specific location. In this phase, you need to look at how many squads you can have in each of the specific locations (it varies between six and twenty squads) and which unit you can recruit. To touch on this quickly, you have a large number of units to choose from but some of them can only be recruited by a specific hero. For example a mage can only recruit mages, a religious hero can only recruit priests and clerics, and so on and so forth. You can only command one action per squad in this phase. If you need to recruit to fill up a damage squad, you’ll not be available to move it to another location until the next turn. Even worst, you can’t send it as a reinforcement to a province who is under attack.
The second phase is the real time battles. This is setup in a pixel graphic style and it is very cool. You can select formations, and some of your units will move faster than others. As I mentioned above, there are plenty of units (over one hundreds), from mages, lizards, priests, frogs, werewolf, demons, knights, soldiers and many more. During the battle, a picture of your hero (anime) will be put up and text will be displayed with their thoughts, as well as a Japanese voice over. Now, here is a whinge on my behalf . . . most German, Russian and French games have text and voice acting in English.so why do a larger number of Japanese games only make an effort on the text side of the equation? In this game, pictures of the heroes will pop up during the battle and say something in Japanese, but I don’t understand it and the English text will disappear quickly. Look, it is purely a whinge here because I feel that I’m missing the impact a hero has in the battle. For me it would have taken this game to bigger heights!
Graphically the game looks good and I really enjoy the pixel battle setup. The price point is stunning and this game will give you plenty of re-playability.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Nice graphics
-	12 factions to choose from and stacks of units to recruit
-	Fun real time battle
-	Trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	No English voice over
-	Interface could have been better
-	No achievements
Lost Technology is a really nice package for the price they are asking. Plenty of re-playability and a fun strategy game when you get used to the interface.
7/10

Well frankly this game has a lot of potential, but its got a few major problems too. It seems vaugely inspired by the old Koei games like Gemfire and such, but its alot faster paced and free map movement instead of turn based.
Good Things
* Lots of unique factions
* Decent world map with nice choke points for holding off enemies
* Fun concept
* Obviously dedicated creator and fan base
* Tactical landscape useage in combat
Bad Things
* Overwhelmingly unbalanced, to the point some factions can NOT win against others even with overwhelming numbers, so you can be winning and have conqured a huge chunk of the map, but then suddenly your at war with the one faction your group cannot beat and you just basically have to hope another computer faction takes them out or ... you can just suck it cause your gonna loose
* Unbalanced heros, some heros are really cool and useful, while others litterally are just a slightly tougher generic troop
* AI issues during castle battles
* Poorly designed castles, theres a reason castles dont have fully exposed sides, and the game demonstrates this well by having the ability to simply walk around some castles walls or you attacking from the non walled side if your behind where the game expects you to start
* The ease of getting gold means that its super fast and constant each turn in the world map, meaning unless your lucky and factions your not fighting with next to you are allied, you basically cant do anything cause you get attacked non stop and your units are exhausted from helping other regions, leaving you basically unable to ever act at times for multiple turns in a row
* The break neck speed at which is the games pace, means that tactical movement of troops is all but useless unless your a race with cavelry, and your units will just ignore you and charge if an enemy gets near anyways
* However out of everything, the thing i find most annoying is the fact that you cannot recruit units from areas you conqure, if you beat an area with magic frogs, you cant hire them, if you beat an area with giant troll looking things, you cant hire them, but it will still show them in your recruitment tab, for ... just no reason at all. Also wandering heros you cant hire will constantly walk around in your territory being pointless.

Shapes of Gray is an old school retro arcade style challenge game. It is designed for short play sessions. You will play the game, get into it and complete some challenges, and exit the game having been rewarded for your playtime as you gradually improve each time you play. Therefore do not expect longer, more than an hour, sessions to be as rewarding.
Where Trent Steen, the one man rock band of Secret Tunnel Entertainment succeeds the most is in the tight controls. The gameplay mechanics are fantastic. The game is challenging and if you’re not careful you can easily lose your three lives. However, the game never feels as though it is cheating you of those lives. You’ll quickly know the why and the how of how you died and with a little practice come to comfortably beat the levels that you found yourself losing to. You are a little blob and your objective is to destroy the enemies in the tower. Each enemy does different things and most levels have multiple different enemies that you need to clear in order to progress. One of the tricks to eliminate enemies is to use their power against one another, for example if one collides into another they both may be eliminated. This is my favorite aspect of the game because it feels as though you’ve outwitted the clever AI. The game requires a twin stick controller to work most effectively (note: I have not tried playing with anything other than my trusty Xbox One controller) as you use the left stick to move, the right stick to aim and the trigger to use your weapon.
The game features three boss levels – 35, 20 and 1 (you start from the highest level moving down though the game does get harder as normal) – and each acts as a checkpoint. They all feel like traditional end level bosses as each is more uniquely powerful than anything preceding it. Game over status comes after you’ve been hit three times – you have three hearts – or if you run out of time on an individual level.  Completing the first 50 levels opens up the rest of the game but that requires a lot of challenge. Admittedly, I left my play session for the time being having beaten the first fifty levels. I look forward to playing more of it in time.
Shapes of Gray is a fantastic game that deserves greater attention than what it has currently received. It’s one of those quick play titles that will remain in your memory banks in a similar way to Super Hexagon and others of its ilk. At $7 at full price and $3.49 for the remainder of the Steam sale it is very much worth picking up.

Shapes of Gray is an experience akin to Nintendo's WarioWare series of games, particularly to that series' microgames. Every stage involves you trying to complete a task (in this case, killing every enemy on the screen) within a short amount of time without any sort of direction. Considering that your character and most enemies die in a single hit, learning enemies' weaknesses and how to exploit them without hurting yourself provides an interesting challenge. What sets this challenge apart from the microgames of WarioWare is what happens if you do die. Once you lose your allotted three hearts, you have to continue either from the beginning of the game or from the stage immediately following a boss fight. In either case, the orientation of the stages sometimes changes, which keeps the game feeling fresh even though you are redoing stages you have already completed.
Even though I have not completed it at the time of this review, the inclusion of a "second quest" is my favorite part of the game. Rather than simply being a more difficult version of the first quest, it includes entirely new enemies, which means new behaviors and weaknesses to learn and exploit. It's almost like having two games in one, which is great without even taking into consideration the game's affordability. Shapes of Gray isn't the most intense game on the market, but it is one of the most enjoyable I have come across in recent memory, and while I can't guarantee you'll feel the same, I can guarantee that the time spent playing won't feel like a waste.

Each of the classic doom games comes with level files (PWADs) and the engine to run them. While the levels are authentic, fun, and challenging, you should note that the engine that comes with this game is abysmal. It has terrible controls and a low resolution (320 x 200 pixels) that cannot be changed. It is completely unplayable, in my opinion.
Your only real option is to buy this (for the level files) and then download a free and open-source port (ZDoom, GZDoom, etc.) to run them. These source ports will allow you to customize the resolution, controls, and graphics quality. Some ports will allow you add dynamic lighting, anti-aliasing, z-dimentionality, various automap additions, high-quality sprites, particle effects, etc. If this sounds like too much work, then you probably shouldn't buy this game. If you try to run it through Steam, you'll be very disappointed.
As far as the levels themselves are concerned, they're great! I am having a blast playing through them!

First off, the actual "port" Steam gives you is horrible. I would never, ever buy this at full price (this game's a steal during sales anyway).
This makes the process of playing all the levels without loading up a WAD each time much, MUCH easier (just make the WAD and run a port through ZDL as the other DOOM games):
If you don't know what the hell "run a port through ZDL" means, here (I keep spamming this around, but only because it's so simple and effective):
This may seem like a lot of work but in my opinion it's worth putting in these few minutes (and it really shouldn't take more than 10mins tops if you're slow) to get a really good experience.
Now then, I didn't really get into Ultimate DOOM because everyone and their Minecraft-playing 8-year-old brother knows about it, but this might be something that people aren't that familiar with.
These levels were mostly unreleased DOOM II maps, and they were meant to be played one by one (although there are maps that you can group together according to who made them). For the most part, I think they warrant the name "Master Levels" because they feature either very challenging shooting, intricate puzzles or even both. The majority are really good and some are just cheap (lots of Revenant spamming or similar), but I'd say the amount of good maps outweighs the bad ones by quite a wide margin.
As someone who played DOOM back in the day, but lived in a craphole country where getting DOOM alone was a challenge, yet alone an official map pack, this was a nice breath of fresh air. If you're an old DOOM fan tired of ploughing through Ultimate DOOM for the n-th time, I'd definitely recommend this. If you're a new DOOM player and you liked the crazier moments of Ultimate DOOM (looking at you, Thy Flesh Consumed) or DOOM II, well, there's lots of that and more, so also a "recommend" from me.

The game plays like a beautiful fantasy adventure movie, the sort that sticks in your mind from your childhood. The scenery alone may be enough to make it worth a playthough, but the story is also touching, if somewhat predictable. I never quite got the hang of controlling the brothers using each respective control stick (Xbox controller required), but the game never requires precision or precise timing for travel or puzzle solving. Though the game is brief (3-4 hours, a one-sitting game), count this as one worth experiencing at least (and probably only) once.

Story:
"Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons" puts you and two Brothers into a fantastic world filled with Giants, Trolls and Giffins. The father of the two gets very sick and only water from a special tree can heal him, so the brothers begin their journey to save their father. Since the game is roughly 2 1/2 hours long, any more information would spoil the experience.
Controls and Gameplay: The controls of "Brothers" are different to what I was used too. With the left stick you control the older brother, with the right stick the younger one and with LT and RT you interact with the world correspondent to the sticks. The skillset of the two brothers is narrow but quite different to one another. The older brother is very strong and can lift his little brother, help him to get accross water (the little brother is scared of water) or turn big levers and the younger brother is small, so he can fit trough almost everything. With that setup you have to solve riddles (mostly by climbing and jumping) or fight against trolls (with your magnificent brain of course). Because of the very unusual controls, "Brothers" will demand a good Hand-Eye-Coordination, especially since when you get familiar with the controls, the game is pretty much over.
Graphics and Design: The Unreal-Engine, mixed together with beautiful painted backgrounds and art-design, makes this one of the most beautiful games I've played this year. Not because of its technology, but for its design and the changing scenery "Brothers" delivers. You'll vist dark forests, snowy mountains, a Giant-Castle above a bottomless pit and some other beautiful places.
Bottom Line:
"Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons" is a good game. I have payed six Euros for a 2 1/2 hour experience. Under normal circumstances I would have been mad for paying more than double in Euros than I got hours in Playtime back. But "Brothers" is different; The beautiful art-design, the soundtrack and the nice idea of the separate controls fit so nicely together and make such a great experience, that I can bear the low playtime.
8.5 / 10

Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is a good game that you should try if you really hate your fingers.
It does a great job communicating its narrative though its mechanics rather than textboxes or Voiceovers. The whole experience is tightly crafted, giving you rarely a dull moment in the 2,5-3 hours it takes to complete. The art stlye gracefully jumps from light-hearted, medieval charm to dark, uncanny and unnerving. It feels very much like a old Grimm Brothers Fairytale with a healty dose of nordic mythology thrown in for good measure.
While the core gameplay is nothing to write home about, the story certainly is. This is a very emotional game, if you allow yourself to get invested in the world and its characters and the payoff at the end is enormous. This, however, also highlights the biggest weakness "Brothers" has: It moves way too fast. It's not too short, in my opinion, it just gives very little breating room between one set piece moment and the next.
Still, I very much enjoyed the experience. It may not be the smoothest ride out there but oh boy, is it a ride.

Picked this game up for about $4 on sale and I must say, I've definitely got my money's worth from it with about 114 hours worth of gameplay at the time of writing this review.
This game plays out very much like an online Borderlands, for better or for worst. The game play is a pretty straight forward with a basic run and gun core gameplay. There are a wide variety of weapon types to choose from, allowing players the ability to customize their character exactly how they like them with no real restrictions as to what weapons can be used by which class or race. There are also a host of abilities that can be used to aid in breaking up the monotony of the run and gun format, much like Borderlands, but often times I have found that they are not essential to game progression. The world is large and feels adequately inhabited, with a number of random missions going on at all corners of the map at any given time. The map itself is gorgeous, with a fair amount of variety from region to region. There are also a number of different gamemodes available to offer a little variety with the world. Everything from time trials on ATV, to special events where you battle progressively more challenging enemies, to multiplayer PVP.
And now for the drawbacks. Because the game has the same gameplay mechanics as Borderlands, it can get very monotonous. For the most part, this is counterbalanced by a wide variety of weapons which offer different challenges when fighting enemies, but still the format of running around shooting enemies over and over can get boring. While there are a number of different random missions that crop up all across the map, giving you the opportunity to get additional money, the missions fall into only a few different categories and after a few hours of gameplay, will become less interesting and more of an annoyance due to the lack of variety. Another disappointing aspect is that while the weapon types are varied, the number of available weapons of each type are not so much. There is no real variety to the weapons themselves, unlike Borderlands. In Borderlands, if you found a specific weapon you liked, you could search for additional variants of the same type that offer additional perks or slightly varied stats. In Defiance, once you find a weapon you like, you're pretty much stuck with that same weapon. The only possible choices you have is to find some mods to give it a few additional stat bumps or find the same exact weapon in a more rare version for a few tacked on perks. There's no real variety and aside from personal preference, no obvious reason to choose on weapon over another. Finally, my last gripe is with the PVP... PVP can be a bit glitchy at times. Sometimes when you go to join PVP, its supposed to teleport you to the area where the PVP is going on, but it doesn't, leaving you to commit suicide to fast travel to PVP since often times its a few kilometers away. I've also seen the respawn screen glitch and not allow you to respawn. I waited nearly 10 minutes, with the sounds of the battle continuing in the background. The buttons would respond on mouse over and when clicked, but it would not allow me to respawn. I ended up having to restart the game to clear this fault.
Overall, for a pretty fun casual Borderland-esque game, I feel that it is worth the money, especially if you pick it up during a sale, but be warned that a lack of variety can make this game feel a little monotonous, especially on longer play sessions. Also, I hear that the game is a lot more fun if you drag along a few friends... I'd rate this game a solid 4.5 out of 5, since really only a few minor tweaks to the game could definitely improve the overall play value...

Ludosity has probably one of the most unique if overlooked voices in the independent gaming community, and Card City Nights is a hallmark of their own brand of weird on a classic trope; trading cards. Be it combat with an executive turnip person or duelings with a ghost or three, there are few digital card games that outright wants to have fun, in both execution and style. It never had me laughing out loud but the cartoonish surrealism and genuinely well crafted card play brought me back again and again.
The card play itself has more of a boardgame feel to it, with a 3x3 board both you and your opponent have free reign of placing down cards on. These opposing boards basically demand that you have preplanned combos in your deck, as the only person that really can determine if you're going to have the upper hand or not is you. While the decks are randomized, luck isn't really as much of a factor as it is a gameplan, which you'll probably have to change up often as you go into new battles with different variety of foes. "Matching" cards is done through connecting the arrows each card possesses. There are eight points of contact in all; the angles and the sides. The majority of cards you collect will only have two or three arrows each, where special silver, gold, or platinum cards can vary from all 8 to just 1. Having cards that line up with each other is crucial, and demands a certain kind of forethought that you will build over the course of the game. It's far more complex than it sounds, and a variety of special abilities and different ways you can win makes the game an utterly fascinating breakaway from the usual fare.
Is there bull**** moves that even the computer abuses? Yes. Yes there are. Matches can go on forever, and when it follows a 2/3 game style, not knowing if your hardfought victory is going to happen twice is a horrible feeling, especially when what you fear comes true. While this does garuntee that even the easiest matches still demand some thought, the over all repetition can eat away at you near the end like it did me. I do love this game for what it is, but at the end the final couple fights feel downright unfair, and that's where the 2/3 deal often works at its worst. The experience as a whole was absolutely worth it, but who knows, you may grasp the rules better and stand a greater chance by the end of it.
While I haven't checked out Little Dew yet, I'm probably going to have to make that as one of my next stops. For the insanely cheap asking price of two bucks, CCN is of such insane quality that anyone would be hard pressed not to pick this bad boy up. Also, the soundtrack is wonderfully funky and fits the game perfectly. Don't miss out on this one if you can, and if you ever see this on sale? You have no excuse. Absolutely worth the buy.

Alright, my last review was a bit harsh, but the glitches and crashing has been covered in other reviews. I wish there was a middleground between reccomending and not recomending the game, Because that's what I would say.
Spore is great for two kinds of people, those who like building expansive empires, furocious creatures, little stories and plots, and for the people who like making things that look like d***s, it works well for either.
You go through 5 stages, cell, creature, tribal, civilization and space, progressing through each stage somewhat too fast. The cell stage is fun, and helps introduce new players to the concepts of evolving their creature, getting DNA points and progressing to the next stage, the creature stage.
The creature stage is definetly the most notable and popular, as well as the favorite among many, it tends to be the longest stage (other than the space stage) but after a few playthroughs, you can typically get through it in an hour to 45 minutes, which is again, kind of short, but it's still quite fun.
Then we come to the tribal stage, which is, in my opinion the weakest stage of them all. You can get through it in about 30-45 minutes, depending on how you decided to play. It can become uninteresting after 4-5 playthroughs (I've gone through about 12 times now) but it's quick enough to ignore. My main complaint is that it's undynamic, other tribes don't fight eachother, they all seem to simultaniously hate your tribe, and never fight over resources, land, or anything else.
After getting through the tribal stage, you reach the civilization stage. I've heard lots of complaints about it, but I find it interesting, especially playing as an economic race, setting up trade routes, avoiding conflict with less friendly civilizations and becoming allies with the superpowers of your starting world, i've seen many complaints about it, and from what I've seen it's really up to personal opinion and interests.
And finally, the longest stage in the game, I haven't seen much about the space stage, it's basically the civilization stage, but over the galaxy, where your ultimate goal is to eventually enter the black hole at the center of the galaxy, but I've never been hooked enough to get close, as it's too much of a repeat of the civilzation stage. don't get me wrong, conqurieng solar system and expanding my intergalactic empire feels awesome, either through trade, religion or military might. But interest is lost once you get bored, and decide to start a new creature.
Overall, I reccomend, but don't reccomend spore. It definetly becomes boring if your not like me and make up little stories and a whole lore behind each species, developing imaginary links between each (and then getting to the space stage and anihilating your previous creations).

I honestly hate to say it but this game is a failed amazing idea.
To put it simply the complete lack of any significant single player content simply murders this game. The quests are bog standard, repetitive and dull. (Deliver message, kill bandit lair repeat ad nausem.) The noble interaction is a complete grind. About as bad as the Oblivion wheel where you basically just have to do the same tasks over and over again in order to get some count in the middle of nowhere to like and support you. It's dumb, not fun, and grinding to the highest degree. Has no excuse not to be improved.
The combat here is this game's saving grace. It's simple and fun, and the feeling of cutting through flesh with steel is satisfying and something I throughly enjoyed. But you must realize you are not doing that at least 70% of your single player game time. You are grinding something. Training your troops, relations, trading. It is a chore to get to do anything significant in this game. You start at the bottom of the barrel, and must work your way up. How do you get money? Grind. How do you train troops? Grind. How do you increase relations? You can guess.
In the single player. (Which I am primarily reviewing this game for, since most people probably play this game for it.) the combat like I said is fine, but the A.I is simply atrocious. It's one strategy is to zombie like rush you. If you are fighting 50 to 50, they will rush. 25-90, they will rush. 200-1, they will rush with that one little peasant. The individual combat with the A.I is just as much as a let down. They simply try and hug you, rushing into your chest and swinging wildly. There is no grace or cool swordplay. No clashing against swords as you are parrying difficult blows. It is a screaming half naked man charging you with an axe, and all his friends are just the same, charging completely mindlessly. This will get you killed, and often. And everytime it is simply frustrating and annoying.  A neat feature I noticed is when enemies rush you, and the one in front has a single sword, but the one behind has a sword and shield. The one behind the sword enemy can actually block attacks aiming for the sword guy, the hitboxes mesh horribly togeter and make it a impenetrable wall of flesh that pretty much beats you to death.
You might argue up above is that you simply need a better army, or that the better trained troops use skill. No. A majestic Swadian Knight unhorsed will charge just as mindlessly as some Forest Bandit, it is simply unforgivable in a game like this. You fight armies of zombies with your own army of zombies. And since the process of getting troops trained is a death march grind, you'll probably cry when you see your elite Vaegir Knight get taken out by a bandit. That's two more hours of grinding for you!
The single player is 70% of the time a dull chore with no highpoints and a constant format of boredom. It's you taking your small party across the wartorn nation of Caldaria to deliver the epic message to Lord #453 so that way your little green bar with him will go up with him by one so you hope for ♥♥♥♥'s sake you can do something fun at some point.
In order to get to any semblance of fun with this game you have to climb a mountain of dullness to get a single cool battle of your zombie army against the others.
PROTIP: 40 well trained infantry troops on a hill can pretty much kill any party in this game. That's how garbage this A.I is.
This is a mindless grind at it's worst, only backed up by great and fun combat, which the game seems to try and do it's best into making not fun. This game would be 100x better as a series of battles or a campaign, not this aborted mess of a empty sandbox. Mods might save it, so if you must play this game I highly recommened Floris Mod, or you should probably just play Napleonic Wars since it is much, much better in all regards.
And there's a mutiplayer too as well. That about sums up the mutiplayer really, it's there, it's nice and you can play with your friends. But public matches are really messy. You're better off with Napleonic wars.
TL:DR you'll watch hours of your life waste away as you grind to get to some sort of fun spot in this game. I ♥♥♥♥ing hate it. And i'm going to play it again because I desperately want to get to that fun spot. I advise you stay far away and heed this lesson of dangerous addiction.

The "Master Levels for DOOM II" is an officially licensed, fan-made expansion (of sorts) for "DOOM II". It is a loose collection of .WAD files created by DOOM fans and hand-picked by the developers at id Software.
The collection itself is a kind of hodgepodge with no real continuity between levels, and is navigated via a custom menu screen created specifically for the expansion. Most of the levels in here are great, many of which are devilishly hard or contain complex puzzles and intriguing design elements. There are, however, a few I found to be woefully short or overly simplistic. But frankly, by the end of this 20 .WAD phantasmagoria of evil, you'll be thankful to have had those brief reprieves.
The only downside to the "Master Levels" is that the Steam release operates through a DOS Box emulation, so it looks and plays terribly. I recommend just running the .WAD files individually through a source port like “GZDOOM” and use the idclev## cheat code to jump around to the desired level. There are ways to have your own menu to navigate the .WADs more easily, but if you’re too lazy to make it work like me, then a simple .txt file to keep track of which levels you’ve mastered should suffice.

Labyrinth, The Dark Crystal, Legend, The Neverending Story, these are all small glimpses into wildly imaginative worlds, worlds that seem to overflow with the opportunity of adventure and the idea that around every corner lies something new and amazing (and possibly life threatening).
Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is the closest thing I've experienced to the awe inspiring, imagination bending feeling that I had watching those films as a child. You continually feel like you're playing witness to just one story that takes place in a much bigger whole. The environment and the creatures and charcters within it all play a role in creating the illusion of a much larger world, ripe with mystery and adventure.
The gameplay, pacing and storytelling all feel like a modern reimagining of the stylings of games like Heart of Darkness and Out of This World but in a much more forgiving way. There's no leveling, no loot, no collectibles, no health, no powers, there's nothing to take away from the excellent gameplay, pacing and story.
As of the time of this review Brothers is on sale for $7.49 but even at its standart retail price of $14.99 this is an easy to recommend game that should absolutely be experienced.
As a final note I feel that I should mention that if you have a partner you've been trying to get into gaming this is a great game to do it with. Each brother is controlled by one stick on the controller so if you snuggle up on the couch and share the controller you can both play. The story is excellent and has wide appeal and the gameplay is simple enough that it would be easy for the inexperienced to pick up and play.
Can't recommend this enough.

I cannot recommend this game in good conscience to anyone. There are broken promises abound, incredibly poor quality updates, and a fundamental lack of understanding at both developer and management level about the game. Between cheating in PvP not being addressed, the shallow content updates, delayed update schedule, and fumblings of even the most basic systems... the game just does not have much going for it.
I have hundreds of hours logged into the game because of the old PvP community that has since disappeared. The final straw for me was when 100% damage mitigation was declared a legitimate tactic by the development team, even though it was abusing a very obscure game bug to achieve it.
Some other issues with the game, as I perceive them:
PvE Content: Overall you are looking at maybe 10-20 hours of story quests, maybe 5-10 hours of races and challenges, and perhaps 5-10 hours of instances.
* The main story isn't too bad - mostly your standard MMOG quests. There's some interesting ones here and there, but overall it's an average experience. The final boss fight was actually mildly engaging, but that's probably the only difficulty people will ever face with the game.
* Instanced dungeons were fun, but the game encourages repetitious grinding of them. This leads to the limited amount of them becoming stale in short order.
* Challenges can be fun, they're probably one of the more enjoyable pieces of content in the game.
PvP Content: Used to be okay, now completely intolerable. Due to a damage resistance bug, specific players have an unfair advantage the developers have said they are unwilling to stop. Therefore, players are not on even footing.
* PvP queues were altered to allow Shadow Wars ("open world" PvP) to start faster. This had the consequence of making the instanced PvP maps completely dead, they do not start anymore.
* Shadow Wars take place in the open world, which was not designed for PvP. There's a serious lack of cover, dull terrain and paths, poor objective spacing, and are just overwhelmingly disappointing.
* The first DLC update came with a new PvP map, which has serious graphical glitches (lighting breaks and makes your screen black), invisible walls that look passable, and a few other issues. Since that map never has enough people in queue, it was never fixed.
Updates: Overall very slow to come out due to console restrictions, and sparse on fixes or changes. DLC is slow, vaguely outlined, and often fails to deliver your money's worth in content.
* The "Season Pass" was supposed to be a one-year, 5 DLC package. As of the time of this review (November 25), only one has been released since April. There is no way all five will come out in a year's time.
* The only DLC released was abysmally poor in both quality and quantity. The paid update was supposed to be a multiplayer horde-style arena, but was turned into a 5-wave single player instance. The leaderboards are bugged and constantly reset, making competition pointless. A truck with a mounted turret was scrapped due to technical limitations.
* There's a fundamental lack of understanding of how the game works at the developer level. Patches often come in that do not address player concerns, but do the complete opposite of what is requested.
* Weapons like the FRC SAW were nerfed due to AI not pressuring players enough, making them the leading weapon for PvE content completion. They were marginal in PvP, and became useless post-patch.
Verdict: The game has a great third person shooter mechanics, and that's about all it has going for it. Content is sparse and shallow, with updates not adding enough to sustain interest. Developers seem disinterested and not engaged with what the community wants, which leads to very poor content updates. The PvP is no longer competitive, due to the bugs being abused and general lack of care on the studio's part.
I would not recommend purchasing Defiance. If you do decide to buy it against this advice, then I would highly recommend avoiding the Season Pass.

For gameplay I think it's actually really good.
Looking at PvE it reminds me of Tabula Rasa which I miss SO much, and other third person MMOs like Global Agenda, there hasn't really been an MMO third person shooter with a big persistent world like this since Tabula Rasa.
Games like Destiny, Borderlands and others don't have that. So if you like overworlds, that's a plus on this game vs the others.
This being pretty much the only one out like that, if you liked the two MMOs I mentioned, you'll like this.
It's also similar to Borderlands in terms of getting a constant stream of weapons and how the shooting mechanics work, but Borderlands isn't really an MMO so the similarities end there.
The tie-in with the show is superficial at best right now. Season 2 seems to be the same as well, though the new Silicon Valley content links storyline, oddly enough, from the
website
The shooting mechanics are good, the powers are good, though more variety of abilities would be nice in the future.
You gain "levels" by increasing your EGO rating through achievement-like objectives and just getting "levels". Due to DLC5 making weapon damage scale to EGO rating now, it's a lot more traditional than it was. However, you can still do all content regardless of EGO rated, and you do get boosted if the difficulty level is higher than you can naturally handle.
There is a decent variety of things to do now, with arkfalls, sieges, side quests, story quests, and emergencies.
The driving is fun. Just going around the world jumping around on your vehicle, running over enemies can be enjoyable. I really hate the races though, the mechanics are horrible when confined in races.
I think the storyline is good, not great, though the cliffhanger is a bit lame.
The games chat works more or less like a traditional chat in an MMO now.
However, this game also has a pathetically low amount of social interaction compared to other MMOs.
No AH or mail system either.
For PvP howerver, I would look elsewhere.
It's been my stance that any MMO with a PvE overworld and instanced PvP will just never have good PvP. It's impossible to balance, and never will be.
If they had just stuck with Shadow Wars (which is fun) and open world PvP, it would've been a lot better, but since it has instanced PvP, there's better games. TF2 is one I can think of off the top of my head and it's free.
There is an in-game shop. Most of the stuff is vanity. Overpriced vanity at that.
Also in the shop is lock-boxes that can get you weapons and mods, but you don't really need to buy them with cash (they are REALLY overpriced anyways, like $5 a box).
You can also get most of the lockboxes in-game with the games currency.
There's bag space, I suppose that might be needed for some, but it's not pay to win.
However I think the biggest selling point is it's F2P. It's hard not to recommend at least trying it at that price. Especially with no monthly fee and nothing from the overpriced in-game shop item being "necessary", you can definitely get your moneys worth, and it's also easy to go back to if you stop playing for a long period of time.
I can't really recommend the DLC Season Pass (unless it's on sale for $20, then get it) or packs though, unless you really enjoy the game and want to throw a bit more money at the developer.
Not because I think the DLC is bad per say, but that I'm not a fan of the season pass system in this industry.
DLC1 Review: DLC1 includes a small quest chain and 5 arenas, in which you go instead and basically just shoot a bunch of mobs for gear and rep.
The reputation vendors sells a series of "charge" weapons, which are weapons you hold the shot button to charge up, and an energy sword which are basically lightsabers.
You can also co-op the arenas now, so if you like doing instances with friends, it might be worth it.
DLC2 Review: is far superior to DLC1. The arkbreaks you can call down are pretty fun to do, and there's always people doing them (though recently, it's died down a little due to loot reward issues).
Even if you don't own the DLC, which would prohibit you from using the new weapons, it's still a good update.
You also get daily/weekly rewards which includes money, resources and a "battery" that you use to call down the arkbreak arkfalls.
There's also a small quest chain that explains the new stims and boost systems, as well as a small story quest that gets into the arkbreak system.
It also lets you equip all the new weapons that drop within arkbreaks. Non-DLC owners can't use them.
I'd say DLC2 is worth buying.
DLC3 Review: Pass.
What you receive for owning this is a samurai outfit, two new blue weapons (a sniper and shotgun) and a title.
You also get access to a new vendor and daily/weekly contracts for a new faction.
That's it. There's no quests and everything else with the update you can get for free.
It's the worst DLC of the five, so you really aren't missing much if you don't get it.
The incursion event weapons are tied to this DLC FYI.
DLC4: I think it was pretty good. There's no new faction but a new lockbox tied to an already existing reputation.
There's a bunch of new story missions which I find good enough, considering how starved this game is for new story.
There's 9 new arenas, which can be done co-op, which are okay. I can see them being fun, but I personally don't care for them
Owning the DLC gets you access to the new quests, one of the new lockboxes and a title. I think this is slightly better than DLC2, so it is the best so far.
DLC5: Get it if you want some Arkforge for altering gear. You get 1k and some other stuff, so worth it if you want that.
With the F2P transition, some of the new TV/Game tie-in missions have had the voice actors for the some of the NPCs change. It's by no means horrible, but you will notice and it is pretty jarring, though the updates are free so I can't complain that much.
In terms of how the store works, it's basically the same as it was when it was B2P. The game takes Rifts model as opposed to say LOTRO or Secret World where content updates cost money. All Defiance content updates will be free.
There is, what I find funny, a "subscription" option now in the shop. Which gives you various passive boosts to things like XP/Skill etc, as well as a 10% discount in the store.
I find it funny because the game was B2P with no sub option prior to F2P. It's the first F2P transition I'm aware of where a sub option gets added to the game.
Is the patron status worth it? That's up to you. Like Rift, it's nice but nowhere near being a "necessity"

I'm a huge Adventure Time fan, but generally not into this sort of game.
They have the voice actors from the show which is nice. The art style is nice (but unfortunately let down by the graphical fidelity). It runs fine too. That's about it.
Ignoring the fact that this used to be a free browser game
and hasn't changed drastically since that iteration, this game is boring, repetitive, lazy and cheap. It looks like crap, controls like crap, feels like crap and sounds like crap. This game sort of feels like it was made by people who do really care about the show, and wanted to make something that does it justice, but there simply wasn't enough money or talent to do so.
While the art style is good, the graphical quality is terrible and there are "jaggies" everywhere you look. Each stage has a single, static, unfathomably low resolution backdrop.
The levels from each world look very similar, and there are not many landmarks to help you remember where you are. This isn't helped by the lack of a mini-map.
The controls are fairly responsive, but the animations don't flow well into each other, which along with other things, results in really bad game-feel. Running around and fighting does not feel fun. I find myself actively avoiding enemies just because they simply aren't fun to kill. The camera nauseatingly jerking back and forth as you change directions, and vibrating slightly when you run in diagonals does not help the cause. Nothing in this game feels fun; the only enjoyment you get comes from completing tasks and advancing through the stages.
The sound design was put together in an obvious rush. Sound effects cut abruptly in and out, play at seemingly random volumes and sound like they were pulled straight from a stock library with little to no afterthought. Although the voice actors do a decent job, the dialogue during cutscenes is riddled with pops and clicks.
