This game…..This game is truly one of a kind in overall presentation and style.  Yes there are some games like Mount and Blade but nothing comes quite close to Mount and Blade (or MB for short), or at least none that I know of.  It is too bad I got into this game seemingly towards the end of its popularity lifespan in the multiplayer stage as Bannerlord is soon to be released and I have a notion this game will be not forgotten, but much less frequented once it does.   Let me first say that Mount and Blade does multiplayer VERY well…very well…  Taleworlds got the formula down for simulated ‘sword and shield’ combat on a quasi-ARMA/Total War series style map very well (some of you may or may not agree with that analogy).  The mechanics in this game are second to none in terms of uniqueness and originality.  But be warned…The learning curve for multiplayer is very steep, but very fun and rewarding once you get ‘kind of’ good ( some of you may know what I mean by getting at least ‘kind of’ good in multiplayer).  And in addition, the multiplayer may be highly addictive once you get into it, it is that good!
The singleplayer gameplay is very nice too, think of the Total War series meets FPS/RPG with a 3rd person perspective ARMA medieval style twist, although kind of generic in terms of overall execution and ‘diplomacy’, but don’t let that deter you this is quite an experience the first, second, and maybe even third or fourth (or even more) time(s) around.  The overall style of this game is something to be remembered for a long time if not forever.
And lastly, the character face editor ooh boy, the character editor is something of a beautiful novelty.  Some of the custom faces you’ll see in multiplayer are downright hilarious!  The custom face poser is possibly the worst/best thing I’ve ever seen done this way!  NO GAME has done face poser quite like MB….no game!
Below is my list of pro/cons:
Pros:
-Multiplayer is like no other and the custom faces and characters add a lot of individuality to it.
-face poser (hilarious mechanic…you should see other players faces in multiplayer laughing is half the enjoyment in some aspects!).
-Single player is also like no other in terms of overall execution and style.
-difficult and unique, but very fun and rewarding realistic style ‘sword and shield’ melee combat as well as archery and various thrown weapons you would expect from the medieval period this game seems to be roughly based around in terms of time and technology.
-many, many different character builds, weapons, and a good mix of factions to choose from ( factions seem to represent the middle ages in  Western Europe, Eastern Europe/Russia, Asia, Middle East, and ‘Scandinavia’ pretty well, albeit in a generic fashion).
-Endless options for character customization and playstyle builds.
-The campaign is very much at ‘your own pace’ it’s basically a big sandbox with various things to accomplish and do…all at your own pace and choosing, do whatever you want, however you want adding to the games originality.
Cons:
-The diplomacy in the singleplayer game can seem very across the board generic at times.
-There are some fairly minor bugs in both MP and SP where you will get ‘code errors’ (like option to host a feast at your castle once you become married to one of the vassals’ relatives).
-The swing mechanic and combat whilst very good and very intuitive can be very hard and confusing to learn at first to some.
-Some of the SP factions seem to be overpowering at times (Nords, Swadia), although this is arguable.
My rating breakdown:
-.05 minor bugs that can be annoying to some
-.05 sometimes seemingly unbalanced factions and generic diplomacy with somewhat scant options in terms of directives
My final rating is 9/10 (1.00 = 10 = 9/10)
I highly recommend this game to you if you like sword and shield style melee combat and, if you like the middle-ages time frame, pick up this novelty!

This is a great game and a great addition to the Atelier series.
I'm actually doing this review because I picked it for a Steam Award, as it's one of my personnal favorites.
There are many reviews already, so I will skip the general points and instead talk about the main mechanic and selling point of the game: the synthesis system (also know as crafting).
In short, it's a JRPG with a heavy focus on crafting. But that sentence doesn't really do it justice.
The crafting involves a complex system (puzzle), called Synthesis, that allows you to change several aspects of the item you are creating through player skill, experimentation and planning. To make better items, not only will you have to increase your proficiency with the crafting of that item, but also with others that may serve as materials in the process. You need to consider the materials' types, quality, sizes, shapes and transferable properties in order to create the best ones. In the end of all that, it's the player's knowledge of the materials and crafting system and skill in working with those that will determine how good those crafted products will end up like. The better your items, the easier the fights will be, and trust me, unless you are overleveled for a challenge you are going to need the best you can craft.
There's not much of a point in dwelling in the details of the system in a text targetted at people who haven't played the game yet. The system was designed to be learned through experimentation, which I think fits perfectly with the alchemy motif. The game walks you through the basics, but there are many advanced concepts hidden in the Synthesis system that one must grasp in order to truly master it. There are several guides you can look up on those. I made one myself, actually, about activating item properties during synthesis, which can be found in the guides section of the game here in Steam. If you want a more visual insight on how it works, check out some gameplay videos, I assure there are more than enough of those.
Finally, if like me you like crafting but feels like the average crafting systems are made too simple (for a good reason, because it's usually meant as a sub-system) and wants a game that makes you feel like an artisan and actually crafting things, than this is the kind of game you need.

Here's what you've probably heard about "Brothers": It's a quirky little indie title with an offbeat "one character per stick"  control scheme tha's got a cool ending and employs some mind-blowing narrative techniques.
All of this stuff is correct. The control scheme does a fine job of throwing the right and left brain for a loop, and makes the "single player co-op" experience deep and rewarding. There's a unique joy to be taken from mastering the intricacies of the controls, and the gameplay+storybook art style combo are enough to warrant a purchase. What's nice is that the storytelling is also great -- while the game only takes about three to four hours to beat, there are some spectacular sights to be caught along the way, and it's nice to see that the idiosyncrasies of the gameplay actually translate into effective new methods of storytelling.
The problem here, as with other short one-and-done titles that are becoming increasingly popular (e.g. Gone Home), is that once it's over, it's over. It's a sweet and fun and memorable experience, but there's not much else to catch on a second playthrough. Ultimately, it's a question of value. I can reasonably justify a price tag of up to 15 dollars for Brothers, which is about the same as I'd pay for a 3d movie ticket. But if you'd like to wait, don't worry: this is a Steam game after all, so there's no doubting you can pick it up for a nice discount at a later date.

In the rising sea of indie games, it can be difficult to choose something to play. There are plenty of games that aren't very good, some that are average, but then there are those gems, those works of art that shine above the others. Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is a well-told tale about two brothers going on an exciting and intense adventure. It features unique gameplay and an outstanding way of storytelling that makes it a very memorable experience. This is a game that simply cannot be overlooked, because to do so would be to miss a truly unique experience. While the game itself is only several hours long, it is well worth the money.
The controls are very unique, as they require the player to essentially control two characters at the same time. PC gamers wondering why a controller is so important to experience this game can rest assured that there is a good reason for this: each player can be moved around independently with separate thumbsticks, and actions can also be performed with separate buttons for each player. While this is an experience that one needs to get used to at first, it works very well and really demonstrates some creativity on the part of the developer. A mouse and keyboard really wouldn't work as well for this game, so a controller is quite useful.
The game features beatiful, detailed graphics creating an incredible setting for the journey. The player is frequently given the opportunity to sit back and admire the view and become completely immersed in the experience. This is a game that lets the you experience virtually every emotion out there: happiness, sadness, anger, fear, you name it. And it does so in an amazing way that really makes this one of the most memorable games out there.
The journey of the two brothers is quite linear, but this works well for this game and really gives the player a good idea of progression. There are also many puzzles to solve, and none of them felt exceedingly difficult, nor too easy either.  The game manages to stay fresh and avoids getting too repetitive. The puzzles are designed so that both brothers are needed, with each brother only being able to complete certain tasks, forcing the player to use teamwork as much as possible. For example, the big brother is more capable of lifting heavy objects, while the little brother is more capable of fitting into smaller spaces. And there are plenty of other examples like this.
Perhaps most impressive is the ability of the game to tell a story without any actual discernible dialogue. The brothers (and everyone they meet) communicate in a fictional language, but the story is still told through body language in a very clear way.
The game gives you the opportunity to explore and to interact with everything you meet. Each brother has his own unique way of doing so, producing different results. It's definitely worth to talk to th
The Steam achievements are very interesting and are based on exploration and performing certain tasks that may not be obvious at first. You will definitely need more than one playthrough to get all the achievements. However the tasks themselves are not very difficult nor tedious, and enhance the experience by letting you witness hidden features that would have otherwise been overlooked.
If you have any intention of trying it out, do not look at too much gameplay footage beforehand. The game is heavily story-based, and spoilers are easy to run into. This is one of those situations where you don't want the game spoiled in advance.

I recently wrapped up a 2 hour playthrough of Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons. I give the developers full credit for creating some astonishingly beautiful visuals, which truly enable the fairy tale world of the game to come to life. I was swept away by breathtaking vistas of misty valleys and snow-capped mountains, as well as some of the most gorgeous water effects I've ever seen in a video game.
That being said, I didn't find any other aspect of this title to be particularly noteworthy or enjoyable. The puzzles are extremely simplistic and I was never, even for a moment, at loss as to how to proceed. This simplicity might lead one to think that this could be a good game for kids, but the grim tone and surprisingly gruesome middle section quickly put that idea to rest.
I question the decision to implement a made up "language" for the characters to use to express themselves. I think it badly detracts from the seriousness of the story. I would have preferred either no dialog at all (pantomime would probably have been sufficient) or some concise dialog/narration in a real language. Perhaps something written in a fairy tale style would have fit the mood of the game perfectly.
Finally, I have to take major issue with the ending. I think the developers were going for grand operatic tragedy, but because of the complete lack of characterization things fall totally flat. The shrill and melodramatic music that underscores "big" moments makes the lack of true drama all the more obvious and jarring.
I'm sure many people will enjoy Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons, but based on my own taste in games and art in general I don't find anything to recommend here.

My wife's Uncle Ken was a navigator in a Liberator bomber with the 8th Airforce, so this game has an oddly personal feeling to it.  It looks cute, at first, and during the training missions, it feels a touch cartoony - though that does not detract like it does in Civ VI.  This cartoon bobblehead gives you the illusion of security - even when your gunners first give Jerry what-for.
That illusion is dispelled when you really head out over the Channel.  The Sweaty Betty's first mission was easy enough - bomb stuff.  But the second quickly went FUBAR - though not SNAFU - because I know the name of who, ahem screwed up.  First I dropped all my bombs on a single target - there were two bombing sites - then I didnt tag the enemy fighters fast enough, didnt dispatch my mechanic to repair the engines quickly enough - I was loosing the four fast enough that it was damn near a count-down.  I finally said "bugger it" - lets see if Steam catches that one - and told the pilot to take us back to Ol' Blighty.  Which, I suppose, he successfully did.  Unfortunatly, a Lancaster doesnt maintain altitude very well on a single engine, so as soon as we found England, we promptly landed.  Face first.  Which I do not recommend as a landing proceedure.  Two of my crew lived to see the Sweaty Betty II.
This is a hard, unforgiving multi-tasking game.  I'm looking forward to more of 1942, though hopefully I've seen the last of roman numerals.  Wishful thinking, which, incidentally, was the name of my training bomber.

The combat here is this game's saving grace. It's simple and fun, and the feeling of cutting through flesh with steel is satisfying and something I throughly enjoyed. But you must realize you are not doing that at least 70% of your single player game time. You are grinding something. Training your troops, relations, trading. It is a chore to get to do anything significant in this game. You start at the bottom of the barrel, and must work your way up. How do you get money? Grind. How do you train troops? Grind. How do you increase relations? You can guess.
In the single player. (Which I am primarily reviewing this game for, since most people probably play this game for it.) the combat like I said is fine, but the A.I is simply atrocious. It's one strategy is to zombie like rush you. If you are fighting 50 to 50, they will rush. 25-90, they will rush. 200-1, they will rush with that one little peasant. The individual combat with the A.I is just as much as a let down. They simply try and hug you, rushing into your chest and swinging wildly. There is no grace or cool swordplay. No clashing against swords as you are parrying difficult blows. It is a screaming half naked man charging you with an axe, and all his friends are just the same, charging completely mindlessly. This will get you killed, and often. And everytime it is simply frustrating and annoying.  A neat feature I noticed is when enemies rush you, and the one in front has a single sword, but the one behind has a sword and shield. The one behind the sword enemy can actually block attacks aiming for the sword guy, the hitboxes mesh horribly togeter and make it a impenetrable wall of flesh that pretty much beats you to death.
You might argue up above is that you simply need a better army, or that the better trained troops use skill. No. A majestic Swadian Knight unhorsed will charge just as mindlessly as some Forest Bandit, it is simply unforgivable in a game like this. You fight armies of zombies with your own army of zombies. And since the process of getting troops trained is a death march grind, you'll probably cry when you see your elite Vaegir Knight get taken out by a bandit. That's two more hours of grinding for you!
The single player is 70% of the time a dull chore with no highpoints and a constant format of boredom. It's you taking your small party across the wartorn nation of Caldaria to deliver the epic message to Lord #453 so that way your little green bar with him will go up with him by one so you hope for ♥♥♥♥'s sake you can do something fun at some point.
In order to get to any semblance of fun with this game you have to climb a mountain of dullness to get a single cool battle of your zombie army against the others.
PROTIP: 40 well trained infantry troops on a hill can pretty much kill any party in this game. That's how garbage this A.I is.
This is a mindless grind at it's worst, only backed up by great and fun combat, which the game seems to try and do it's best into making not fun. This game would be 100x better as a series of battles or a campaign, not this aborted mess of a empty sandbox. Mods might save it, so if you must play this game I highly recommened Floris Mod, or you should probably just play Napleonic Wars since it is much, much better in all regards.
And there's a mutiplayer too as well. That about sums up the mutiplayer really, it's there, it's nice and you can play with your friends. But public matches are really messy. You're better off with Napleonic wars.
TL:DR you'll watch hours of your life waste away as you grind to get to some sort of fun spot in this game. I ♥♥♥♥ing hate it. And i'm going to play it again because I desperately want to get to that fun spot. I advise you stay far away and heed this lesson of dangerous addiction.

A real bargain at it's selling price, this is a bit of a gem.
+ A involving set of game mechanics that suck you in and keep you playing for just one more turn
+ A surprising level of depth, polish and care has been taken, reflected in the level of detail such as a whole roster of characters and their associated artwork and backstories
+ Original variation on the total war type game formula with a rich set of factions each with their own unit rosters.
- Still some rough edges to be polished after launch - a few windows untranslated and options missing, but nothing game breaking
- The gameplay could do with a slow down option, both on the battlefields but especially on the campaign map where it's sometimes impossible to read messages and the outcomes of battles they scroll by so fast. A pity since you can miss the great level of detail and following your heroes in a battle can become a bit of a challenge.
+/- The ai on campaign level seems decent, making treaties and invading, the battle ai is basic but will still keep it's archers behind infantry, etc. Seems to struggle a little with sieges both defending and attacking, but since total war still has this issue it's seems unfair to level much blame here.
+/- There is a learning curve  (though I found the tutorial gave me what I needed to start me off), could do with a being a bit clearer about what certain abilities do and being able to view enemy stats and abilities would be useful as well.
Overall really impressed with the quality of this, it's surprisingly fun and addictive and you can see there's a lot of heart and passion that's gone into creating it. For the price it's at (£1.99 at this time) it's an absolute bargain in my opinion.

An incredibly fun RTS that revolves around recruiting wandering mercenaries and completing hidden quests in your journey to unite (or destroy) the world.

The soundtrack is wonderful, and fast paced, even though the songs repeat they're never annoying.
The artstyle is fantastic, every character portrait is detailed.
It encourages thoughtful usage of your men, since you're limited to 24 groups of units on a field at one time. Do you put heavy focus on your front line, using sheer power to break into the enemy lines? Do you put focus on your backline, giving you the ability to disrupt and wittle down the charging enemies? Do you send a group of swordsmen to take out the enemy backliners (Oh who am I kidding, always do this)
That being said, holy moly does that tutorial and various systems need worked on.
It doesn't tell you that pausing is possible.
It doesn't explain how important the trust mechanic is.
It doesn't explain much really.
My first playthrough, atleast 10 hours, came to a grinding stop because I realized a bunch of these things way too late.
Many of the systems also don't make sense, the trust mechanic being one. Why does attacking an ally make your men more likely to run away from a fight?
Why are certain enemies able to spam pushback skills, drawing out fights as your men race fail to reach them, adding minutes onto a fight?
Why are you unable to mold squads together, instead of having to individually drag characters from one squad to another when you just want to move your units around.
All those gripes though, can be avoided if you merely read the FAQ ahead of time.

I really like this game. One of my favorite World War 2 era shooters. But it has its ups and downs
Pros:
- Realistic gameplay including vehicles, guns, character movement, maps, etc.
- It's fun as well as serious. You can do fun/funny things to dead bodies or characters that will make you and others laugh
- Customization in this game is amazing, you get to make whatever kind of soldier you want ranging from a sniper, medic, Machinegunner, paratrooper, tank driver and many more
- Guns are great in Heroes and Generals. They feel realistic and almost as though you're actually shooting someone when you shoot someone. It gets rid of one gun being overall better than the other one by balancing out the stats of the guns and the required skills to shoot the guns. Also giving each gun a purpose, no longer will you be able to hit a target at longs range with an SMG.
- World War era. This is my favorite part about H&G. It would be one thing that it's realistic and fun but another thing that it's set in an era that most series abandoned (Call of Duty, Battlefield and Medal of Honor to be specific). Most people are used to the future or modern day warfare type games and unless you were alive and playing video games back in 2003-2008 then you wouldn't know the feeling of playing a World War game.
- The interface in Heroes and Generals is great. It isn't filled up with useless things like the chat, bullets, HP, Compass, Mini-Map, stance, toggle buttons etc. Instead it's just showing the only things necessary in a realistic way.
- The graphics on this game are pretty good for the most part (unless playing on low) and it's pretty good for a game that is in beta. If you have low standards for graphics in a game or you don't mind graphics (Example saying TES V: Skyrim looks good) then you wont care. If you're one of those people who have a high expectation for graphics then you wont be dissapointed.
Cons
-Money. The money in this game is so bad! Everything is very expensive and you have to play constantly if you want to get anywhere. OR! You could use real money to get in game currency so you can buy the things that should be offered to you automatically. This is kind of a pay to win game
- Progression. Yes I know that it's realistic to have ranking up be hard and not being able to reach the rank of staff sergeant in one day. But the progression to the next weapon is really rediculous. It took me forever to get the grease gun!
- Gun unlocks. The fact that you have to unlock guns via progression and buying them isn't really that good. If the game were realistic then it would allow you to play with whatever gun you want. Especially since most of everybodies favorite guns are the type of guns you have to unlock later in the game. And, I know, this is to give it more of a video game feel so you want to play but seriously though
- The community in H&G is pretty bad. Lots of people don't play with you strategically or sometimes you will see people arguing in the chat and you will rarely see people go Call of Duty fanboy mode and start raging that they died and you took their kill. But much like Chivalry: Medieval Warfare, the community and fanbase highly immature. No offense to anyone who enjoys this game and is mature. You're the reason I still come back btw
So, overall, what do I think of this game? Great game. Totally recommended and it's free so why not? If  I had to make a verdict for this game it would be an 7.5/10 at the most since it is only in Beta and when the game is finished no doubt it will be a 10/10.

Alright, first off, I'm biased about the series. I did post-game(?), went 100% with the items, CGs, events, played only on normal, etc. Here are my thoughts for this game (no spoilers). Look at the bottom for the non-boring part
Graphics/Performance
- Port is kind of mixed as mentioned countless times related to shadows
- Performance is good except in foresty areas and cuts the FPS in half if it's raining/foggy in that area. Otherwise, most areas run great
- Character 3D models felt like a downgrade compared to Sophie. You could probably notice some details like shadows, the facial animations, and the overall character animation is stiff
- Firis' character art looks great, it feels like it didn't translate well to a 3D model though
Sounds
- It's Atelier music. Great as always as they still managed to keep the feel of series' music. Most the BGM is done by the guys who mostly did the music from Totori onwards and a few tracks by the original creators
- Did encounter some weird instances of two BGMs playing together which is noticeable when you immediately enter or leave an area
- Do read the music commentaries after you finish the game. They're always fun to read (and the VA bonus voices)
Story/Character
- It's a variety of slice of life kind of story, ie. don't expect too much. I understand that can turn off a lot of people who aren't really into slice of life
- It's nothing special, Firis is just a simple girl who wants to experience the world (hence the "Journey" for the second "Mysterious" title)
- On the way though, you do get to see a bunch of characters and your party members' side of stories and life
- I feel like the characters in this game are weak. Why? Not much character development or more scenes to show then who they are and there's too many "important" (the not-typical NPC kind) characters that aren't really given much screentime
- However, I do appreciate how some them tie to each other, the previous installment's characters, and well, the rest of the people in the game. Like how some character's stories are resolved at the end. That really warms the heart.
- I'm a huge sucker for item descriptions in games and this does not disappoint. Item descriptions can tell a lot about their everyday life and world and this game tells descriptions in a way how Firis and her sister are talking about said item (though only in text).
World
- First part of the game has a time limit. Let's not discuss why the alchemy exam as the reason for the time limit is stupid because we're talking about a game where a burger pops out of a cauldron by just putting the ingredients in an unsanitary cauldron
- I'm a fan of the time limits since the first game of this series and the first part of this game has it. The limit for this game is so lenient, you could get at your destination and have everything prepared in 1/3 of the time limit (and it's completely doable even without relying on a DLC item that reduces the time passage). I can understand the time limit isn't for everyone, they may feel uncomfortable about it.
- Instead of the traditional Atelier where you have either one or a few hubs to rest at, this one you travel and look for camp spots to go to your Atelier. Okay, so you still have a hub but you go with it and you can only go in it at certain places
- It really does feel like you're on a journey with how the areas are so vast (and empty) and so many areas that you have to travel in-between.
- In which the vast areas can be a problem when you just want your♥♥♥♥♥♥to get done. And the quick travel becomes accessible once you get to a certain part of the post-game and that one doesn't even let you travel anywhere.
Gameplay
- Other than the usual crafting mechanics, what's different from this one is that each items you craft now have their own kind of "mastery" in which you can't just immediately craft the most powerful item the first time you sythesize it. You have to keep on crafting it to unlock perks for it. This actually gives you the illusion that Firis' way of alchemy is different.
- They actually balanced the battles for this one in that you don't feel that powerful early in the game and post-game. Enemies can take a beating so your items aren't the usual one hit KO to enemies.
- Though battles can still feel easy. You have four alchemists at your disposal meaning you can abuse them with their items since there are only specific items that alchemists can use. Course, that could be a balance problem in that they're all paper which can easily be cut so maybe put a tank or two in your party
- I only played on normal since I already find it difficult (and tedious) with common mobs with the same or higher level as yours. Post-game bosses that aren't story related? Now those are the challenge.
tldr; I like the Atelier series, I like this particular game even with flaws as it felt like they went one step ahead but two steps backwards. You should play it if you're a fan of the series, you should think about playing this if you just want to play a cute JRPG, and you should avoid this if you can't tolerate a subpar port or anything with anime tropes. There is not much to this one. Card City Nights is an indie trading card game from Ludosity. Let’s get rocking.
The Good
Once you figure out that the strategy of crippling the cards your opponent has on the board is the only viable strategy, you’ve found your golden ticket to finishing the game.
The store system was easy to use and it’s always nice to be able to supplement your deck with better cards sans a booster pack. (The booster packs were usually alright though).
To it’s credit, there are no in game transactions for real money in CCN, a problem that plagues games of this nature nowadays.
The Bad

In 1998, the point-and-click adventure game was declared dead, and with good reason.
had just been released to critical acclaim, but dismal sales.  If
can't make money, the industry reasoned, then
adventure game can make money.
Thankfully, word that point-and-click adventures were unmarketable didn't make it to the Czech Republic, because after a decade nearly devoid of the point-and-click genre, seven Czech developers self-funded
and reintroduced the world to the fun of point-and-click problem-solving.
The big strength of
was that it brought some novelty to an old genre.  It didn't feel like a cheap knock-off of
or a similar big-name title.  It just had a subtle humour, a subdued melancholy, and an endearing, wordless story about a little robot.  The visual design was very good, and the sound supported it well.  The puzzles were challenging, but fair -- frequently problems that could seem insurmountable at first glance, but would resolve themselves in a moment of sudden insight.
This little game has a timeless character that protects it from appearing dated or obsolete.  It's as playable and enjoyable now as it was on the day it was launched.  It's a worthy purchase.

TLDR: A blast from the past that, if you like DOOM and happen to see this in your library, play it; it's worth a whirl.
A series of WADs plucked out by id to put into the retail market in a time when illegal WAD packs were finding themselves on store shelves on a regular basis, D!Zone being such a pack. Originally shipped with a large collection of PWADs, named Maximum Doom, Master Levels was chopped from the collection to resell on Steam with the DOOM Classic Complete pack.
Now here's the big question: Does it hold up? The answer: pretty much.
The levels in it's packaged form are played through DOOM-it on DOSbox, but can be selected individually through most any source port such as Zandronum and GZDoom. The levels are intuitive and quite difficult, especially if played through a pistol start via vanilla means, though this can be remidied by packaging it into a MegaWAD using certain programs and methods. Every level does play well, with the liberal use of tricks and traps we've learned to expect from DOOM II, plus some daring ones that can kick your a.s.s. Definately worth playing these levels one way or another, with some edge of the seat fun for both newbies and veterans.

I first played the Master Levels on the Playstation version of Final Doom. I highly recommend this expansion to Doom II as the levels in it are challenging and fun. Master Levels for Doom II, the maps that I've played (not many of them) are very basic in design but still have the same charm that the originals have.
I like all things DOOM (yes even DOOM 3), but I absolutelly hate everything about the way this item is packaged, I already had The Ultimate DOOM, DOOM II and Final DOOM before buying this bundle specifically for the Master Levels...
Not to mention that the game's levels are in a haphazard array of separate PWADs instead of a single IWAD, which must have been the way it was originally packaged.
The DOSBOX prompt that I receive when I launch the game is nothing short of broken, after I select which level I wish to play and hit enter to start it the game freezes on a black screen that has a series of black bars at the top, who the hell keeps allowing these old broken DOSBOX engines into Steam rereleases of older games?
Not everyone has the same problem with DOSBOX as me but the reason I bought this bundle in the first place was so that I could insert what I thought would be an IWAD into GZDoom and launch it through that instead...
For those who don't know there are two separate types of WAD files, IWADs and PWADs.
An IWAD is a standalone game like DOOM or any other game that runs on the same engine.
A PWAD is a patch that replaces peices of data from the IWAD that it runs alongside, which in the case of the Master Levels would be the levels themselves.
I actually created a single PWAD for the Master Levels using DOOMBUILDER 2, so that I wouldn't have to restart the game EVERY time I completed a level, the only problem being that it is still in PWAD format and will not run without a DOOM II IWAD since the PWAD does not contain anything other than the map data.
Also more than half of the levels are listed as Map01, which is a problem that I corrected by renumbering them.
I don't think most people would wish to endure the absolute pain in the♥♥♥♥♥it was for me to convert all the individual PWADs into a single file.
I say get the bundle on sale, assuming that you are capable of fixing the broken game you recieve.

There are some extremely minor things that I find wrong:
- The super heroes/villains that accompany you on missions are extremely weak, except in the beginning, which is when you really need the help. Some missions are really hard to complete as a controller, so if that's the way you choose to go be prepared to have to search for a group.
- The superspeed glitch that makes you fall through the ground.
- The falling player base.
- The locked stuff, and the super high prices. If the game was $20 to unlock everything, then maybe we'd be talking, but it costs $60 to unlock mostly everything (not including all the extra episodes) and then a subscription to get everything else.
- How the game limits you to 1500 in game money (not a lot, especially at higher levels) and then puts the rest in an inaccessible bank unless you buy the game.
Ultimately, this is probably the best game I've ever played. Many people have started leaving because DayBreak, whoever that is, ruined something- I have no idea what it is, I just started playing -- but the game is AMAZING, and I can't even tell what they messed up.

There is something strangely unique about this game, something that can only be summed up in one word... "Alien"
When you look at Morrowind compared to the recent Elder Scrolls titles, Skyrim took inspiration from Germanic paganism and Nordic culture. Oblivion, taking place in Cyrodiil, was modelled after medieval Europe. But Morrowind, it travelled in areas unknown, with a hint of Mongolian architecture every now and then.
Morrowind is dangerous and beautiful, it's like a parent telling you "you're responsible to make your own descisions, but be careful"
There are no quest markers and no fast travel, so planning ahead and reading is very important to stop you from getting backtracked.
Whilst I appreciate how far TES has come at fixing problems and refining the series, something was really lost. Morrowind has some kind of charm to it. Being able to level up acrobatics by enduring fall damage and being able to superman jump if you dedicated enough time to it, making custom spells including levitation, faction notoriety and infamy.
If you're wondering on wether or not to get the game due to it's age, I'd would say yes, and this is coming from someone who started from Skyrim and worked their way down.
There's also the work of OpenMW, a standalone version of morrowind running on a more stable engine that has a fully working multiplayer and many bug fixes. So even more of a reason to get this game.

This game…..This game is truly one of a kind in overall presentation and style.  Yes there are some games like Mount and Blade but nothing comes quite close to Mount and Blade (or MB for short), or at least none that I know of.  It is too bad I got into this game seemingly towards the end of its popularity lifespan in the multiplayer stage as Bannerlord is soon to be released and I have a notion this game will be not forgotten, but much less frequented once it does.   Let me first say that Mount and Blade does multiplayer VERY well…very well…  Taleworlds got the formula down for simulated ‘sword and shield’ combat on a quasi-ARMA/Total War series style map very well (some of you may or may not agree with that analogy).  The mechanics in this game are second to none in terms of uniqueness and originality.  But be warned…The learning curve for multiplayer is very steep, but very fun and rewarding once you get ‘kind of’ good ( some of you may know what I mean by getting at least ‘kind of’ good in multiplayer).  And in addition, the multiplayer may be highly addictive once you get into it, it is that good!
The singleplayer gameplay is very nice too, think of the Total War series meets FPS/RPG with a 3rd person perspective ARMA medieval style twist, although kind of generic in terms of overall execution and ‘diplomacy’, but don’t let that deter you this is quite an experience the first, second, and maybe even third or fourth (or even more) time(s) around.  The overall style of this game is something to be remembered for a long time if not forever.
And lastly, the character face editor ooh boy, the character editor is something of a beautiful novelty.  Some of the custom faces you’ll see in multiplayer are downright hilarious!  The custom face poser is possibly the worst/best thing I’ve ever seen done this way!  NO GAME has done face poser quite like MB….no game!
Below is my list of pro/cons:
Pros:
-Multiplayer is like no other and the custom faces and characters add a lot of individuality to it.
-face poser (hilarious mechanic…you should see other players faces in multiplayer laughing is half the enjoyment in some aspects!).
-Single player is also like no other in terms of overall execution and style.
-difficult and unique, but very fun and rewarding realistic style ‘sword and shield’ melee combat as well as archery and various thrown weapons you would expect from the medieval period this game seems to be roughly based around in terms of time and technology.
-many, many different character builds, weapons, and a good mix of factions to choose from ( factions seem to represent the middle ages in  Western Europe, Eastern Europe/Russia, Asia, Middle East, and ‘Scandinavia’ pretty well, albeit in a generic fashion).
-Endless options for character customization and playstyle builds.
-The campaign is very much at ‘your own pace’ it’s basically a big sandbox with various things to accomplish and do…all at your own pace and choosing, do whatever you want, however you want adding to the games originality.
Cons:
-The diplomacy in the singleplayer game can seem very across the board generic at times.
-There are some fairly minor bugs in both MP and SP where you will get ‘code errors’ (like option to host a feast at your castle once you become married to one of the vassals’ relatives).
-The swing mechanic and combat whilst very good and very intuitive can be very hard and confusing to learn at first to some.
-Some of the SP factions seem to be overpowering at times (Nords, Swadia), although this is arguable.
My rating breakdown:
-.05 minor bugs that can be annoying to some
-.05 sometimes seemingly unbalanced factions and generic diplomacy with somewhat scant options in terms of directives
My final rating is 9/10 (1.00 = 10 = 9/10)
I highly recommend this game to you if you like sword and shield style melee combat and, if you like the middle-ages time frame, pick up this novelty!

I don't even know what to think about this one. Let's break it down so there's no confusion:
- As a game I think this is REALLY interesting and deep. In a way it reminds me of Dominions 4 with how units seem to have a lot of stats and skills to them.
- The world and lore seems really interesting with a ton of varied races that manage to deviate a bit from the typical fantasyt tropes.
- Graphically battles are fun to watch and the style is appealing, despite the game not running too well and the UI being plain, awkward and at times confusing.
- If we go by the developer's word then there's a ton of content in the game as is.
Why the negative review then? Cause the game's distribution is kind of a confusing mess.
As of the time of writing there's only 3 translated campaigns and the rest of the races have had their story mode pulled out of the game (still playable, just without plot). The reasoning for this is that the translation job is a very big task and so they want to see how the games does before commiting to it, with plans to release the rest of the races' plotline as DLC.
This by itself sounds ok, considering the game is so cheap, but... there's just no information at all about the process and there's even some confusion about what IS actually in the game. How much could this DLC be? How long could a translation take? Will the game get patches aside from that? Will they finish working on the manual (which is as of yet untranslated)? Is there or is there not mod support? Because some info says there is but then some other posts say they had to take it out for "copyright reasons" which is... yeah. I've even had a couple windows come up with gibberish so out there somewhere there's still a couple UI bits that have not been translated.
I'm just not sure what to think nor if I want to keep the game without seeing where it goes. As a game it seems like it has a lot of promise but the release leaves a lot to be desired and is frankly a pretty bizarre way to put something on the store. With any luck the developer will see this, they seem pretty active here, and can address some stuff that could potentially bring this into a recommendation.
For now I recommend that you at least try it if you want a deep strategy game but be aware that the game could potentially never be fully localized.

This is the most frustrating game I'll ever recommend. Gameplay is difficult, made more so by the amount of stuff that you need to know which the tutorials don't address. The single player campaign requires tremendous amounts of grinding, because your overall strength is limited by how much cash you make, and that's limited by what levels you can play on in what difficulties, so there's a fairly linear grind that has you replaying these same, circular little levels that do nothing and go nowhere (the singleplayer experience of this game), as you try desperately to keep the number of creeps below 100 (the unstated lose condition for the game, though you figure it out quick; there's also a nice visual effect that makes it clear you're boned as the creep number climbs up).
But it's a lot of fun. Seriously, give it a try. Funstrating. There are deep mechanics to this simple looking game. It's compelling to try to get further. Levels are unforgiving, even brutal, as a lot of the difficulty ends up being down to not allowing exponential increases in the enemies on screen... Balance seems to be 1. good, and 2. absent, in that 1. you'll find levels get progressively harder and you'll enjoy being challenged, but 2. there is no real effort made to ensure the player progresses at any given speed - you just slam into a brick wall of unsurpassable difficulty, or the level is easy and you can do it fine. Either you're over the hump and can do more damage than the enemies can take hit points, or you're not and you have to replay earlier levels more.
There are a number of improvements possible for this game, but it's already a quixotic, charming, maddening, enjoyable title. Hopefully the designers will continue to improve it. But I can recommend it as an enjoyable and even somewhat innovative Tower Defense title right now, as long as you're willing to lose quite a lot if you're trying to progress through the levels too quickly, and don't mind a total lack of hand-holding past a few basic tutorials.

Not every Early Access title has to have the most glamorous hopes and dreams or the desired budget to make a blockbuster game that otherwise wouldn’t be possible. Meet Unterrainer Informatik OG a small but experienced team of three software developers led by Psilo, the company’s lead programmer, software engineer. They have a well developed philosophy that in today’s age of sandbox games and user generated content that there is still time for old fashioned games. They believe in the fundamentals of gaming that are being thrown out of the window in favor of glitz and glamour. Those fundamentals being that a ‘game, above all other things, needs to be based on a good idea and needs an interesting story. I agree with this appraisal. This is of vital importance because if you are lacking in these things then it is impossible to create something that people want to play for an extended period of time. Even in today’s pick up and throw away world you still need these fundamental things.
So what exactly is Throbax TD? That’s an easy one to answer. It’s a tower defense game in which you, the player, have to survive waves of enemies otherwise your planet is destroyed and thus the game over. But it’s not your standard tower defense game. That would be too simple and although the production isn’t glamorous what it does offer is something fresh and challenging. As the Steam description aptly states there are two phases of gameplay involved. The first phase is an RTS where you use your strategic thinking in building your defense systems in order to avoid the incoming onslaught. The game then transitions into what would be considered a typical tower defense game. These two phases work wonderfully well together. You can clearly see where the developers draw their inspiration for the game from – which they unabashedly state is the tower-defense map in Frozen Throne, one of the most popular maps in gaming history. They have big shoes to fill if they intend on living up to their aspirations but thus far the development choices have been intelligent.
Arguably the most fascinating aspect of the project is that there is multiplayer. Unfortunately, in my time with the game before going to print I never got involved in that component of the game. However, people that I have discussed the game with me advise that the current status of the multiplayer is weak but there is more than sufficient grounds to believe that the multiplayer as it is developed will likely become the lifeblood of the game.
The graphics and sound are not going to blow you away. The team have concentrated on giving the best playing experience possible. The team have not offered any of the bells and whistles that you have come to expect from modern gaming. This would work against everything that the team stands for. If you’re looking for your smoke and mirrors then you’re best to look away.
Throbax TD is definitely a throw back to an older age in gaming but it’s a delightful visit and one that is highly recommended. At $2.99 it’s a cheap investment into a promising title.

Atelier Firis is a story about finding your own way in life, discovering who – and what, exactly you are – and helping those you meet along the way do the same. It is a game about fulfilling dreams and potential, with a strong message of “it isn’t the destination, it’s the journey” tied in for good measure.
The gameplay matches that aesthetic. From the very first step outside of your small, isolated town as Firis Mistlud, the world seems massive, daunting and full of wonder. But just like your little alchemic companion, you aren’t afraid – the game places you in the first level and essentially forces you to take in all its breadth.

A good game, a fun game, yet it cannot compare to her big sister Atelier Sophie.
Unlike Sophie this game has a timer again, which made me feel rushed. Despite the fact that i did have ample time i just didn't put as much time into side activities as i did with Sophie as i was worried i might unexpectedly run out the clock. After the main story the "post-game" is a continuation without a time limit, as such its not like i really missed out to much by sort of rushing through the main story.
Now i can casually focus my time on unlocking recipes, doing side quests, visiting areas i skipped and companion story.
The alchemy game is once again an enjoyable little mini-game, yet it feels like it lacks some depth that Sophie did have. I'm also not a big fan of how they moved alchemy performance from the tools to experience with items. In Sophie a good cauldron and high Alchemy skill let you make good items, you could even make items that were to high level at the cost of a penalty. In Firis you just need to spam an item over and over untill you're good enough to unlock features in the puzzle mini-game which then only apply to the leveld recipes. Also no more crafting items when your alchemy level is to low for them.
This results in the first items you make of something you just learned are pretty much always terrible, and you need to spam them over and over before you can start making them decently. Only to unlock a new recipe and have to start spamming that again.
Where Sophie had excellent pacing with introdicing new mechanics and spread these out across the game to keep things interesting, with Firis it often feels like a new mechanics arrives (way) late and then you get several in a short time. Especially the stuff to help you move around the map should've been way sooner.
Something new in Firis is that it has an open-world. No more selecting a map from a world map and going there, no, you walk everywhere yourself. Which is quite a lot of fun and adds an exploration element. Drawback is that its much harder to find ingredients you need and can involve having to spend a significant time running back through previous areas. In addition it basicly means you can almost mad dash towards the finish line of the main story with only one real hurdle in your path. So nothing is really inviting the player to take it easy and focus on side-activities.
Finally the game is just not a good port, again unlike Sophie which was an excellent port.
The game is still fun, the characters are nice, and you are getting a lovely gooey-sweet wholesome story for that feel-good experience. With plenty to do post-game! Really, the main story is quite short and you are suppose to keep playing. The music has its usual Atelier charm, the voice acting is decent, and the combat system is basicly alright.
There are a lot of recurrent characters from Atelier Sophie as well so you should really play that one first, if only to enjoy Firis more but also because Sophie is just a bit better in almost every way.

I know, I know, I know...
God, how do I review this without sounding incredibly b****y?
Well, I like DOOM. I like DOOM II. Both are fun, fast, and incredibly addicting games. I'd recommend them to anyone in a heartbeat, they're that fun. So, when I got DOOM II, and saw I had the Master Levels for free, I was more than excited to get back into the action and blast some more demons, but I was oh so wrong.
Master Levels for DOOM II is a collection of levels with no relation to each other (similar to DOOM I and II's levels), that you select in a DOS menu, and play. And then you quit the game. And then you pick a new game in the DOS menu. And then you play another level. And that immediately is one of my aching problems with id's care for these games that I might as well bring up now.
See, 3D Realms was caring enough to re-released Duke Nukem 3D with modern controls, and an easy menu to select the main game and the DLC packs along with it. But id just seems to have slapped everything together. The crappy mouse controls are the same, the aiming is the same, and there's not even a menu to just access DOOM II or Master Levels, so all you have is the DOS menu, which I don't hate, but I see it as lazy programming that could've been easily fixed, if they had the two games packaged together.
That wouldn't stop me from hating how cheap Master Levels is, though.
I believe these levels are ideas the creators didn't use for DOOM II, and they're left as some sort of second-helping for those who wanted more DOOM to satisfy their sadistic hearts. I wouldn't mind playing through these levels, though, if there was some actual polish or good level mechanics. So many times, the game expected me to do something that was never established in the previous levels, like walking across a wall to get to another ledge or shooting a door to open it instead of hitting "space", which got incredibly aggravating at times.
There were good levels that I enjoyed, but they were so overshadowed by poorly-designed and infuriating ones, that it felt more like a chore to play this game. Hell, I logged more hours on this than DOOM I or II.
I know, it's free, grow up, whatever. I'm just saying I didn't enjoy it. If you already bought DOOM II, you probably don't care what this guy is saying about you free extra levels that came with it. But I won't be satisfied until I voice my opinions and my verdict for this game is... a 6/10. It's just not as fast-paced or enjoyable as the first two games, for clunky level designs and weird gameplay mechanics. But when it's good, it's as fast paced as its predecessors, so I believe there's some value for fun there.

EDIT: Original review below. I no longer recommend this game, due to changes that have rendered the game completely unplayable. Whether it's because of something that was introduced in a patch, or Trion simply moving the game's servers to a closet in their office, I was unable to play without outrageous amounts of lag. Unless you love rubberbanding, please avoid.
Contrary to my initial impressions when I heard that Trion was developing a game in conjunction with a SYFY ORIGINAL SERIES™, Defiance is almost shockingly competent.
Taking tips from Borderlands in the form of colored loot and bizarre weapons, and the open world events they've spent so long tweaking and refining in Rift, Defiance is less an MMORPG and more of an open-world shooter, vehicles and all. The reason that Defiance is _shockingly_ competent is that both the shooting and the driving handle extremely well, better than some MMO shooters that I can think of (*cough* Global Agenda *cough*) which can often make you forget that it's an MMORPG at all, seeing as just blasting robots and giant bugs can be fun.
Rather than a traditional leveling system, the game uses a seemingly nonsensical "EGO level" which is sort of an overall game completion score, seemingly culled from many different factors, including player XP, the completion of side events and achievements, discovering new locations, et cetera. I can't say this for sure, as the system is never explained and its number just seems to rise whenever I do things. The important thing, however, is that while you do get access to multiple perks and one of four primary active abilities, your EGO level hardly affects your character's relative power, and has no bearing on mission or event rewards, meaning that Defiance does what many modern MMORPGs fail to do: allow you to easily group up with your friends and play the game together.
The bottom line is, Defiance is a GOOD GAME. I'm really enjoying the time that I'm spending with it, and the game doesn't have to use a carrot and stick to encourage me.

There's a tl;dr at the bottom.
This isn't the best game you're ever going to play, but it's pretty f**king sweet. A one time buy gets you in the game, with no monthly fees after the purchase. It's a third person shooter, and its mechanics are well done.
Defiance is best described as Borderlands' style of loot drops, with more of Saints Row gameplay. As you level up, you'll find better loop drops (different grenade launchers, rockets, pistols, magnums, different variatons of shotguns, snipers, grenades, shields... so pretty much the same as Borderlands) as well as mods you can apply to the guns. Mods you can buy or find dropped, typically after boss encounters.
Arkfall/Siege events are randomly generated, as well as mini "survive the waves" missions will pop up on the map and you can participate or skip as you please.
Arkfall events are typically the same survive the waves type event, where more and more mutants will burrow up from the ground and attempt to wipe you, and any other random players that wander into the zone, out. This can vary, as sometimes you may need to shoot the Arkfall (it's a giant crystal) while avoiding the mutants trying to take you out.
Siege events are almost the same thing, but replace the mutants with nasty superior alien beasts named the Volge. They are decked in armor and only immune to headshots, some can teleport, and others can toss dozens of explosives at you at once. They spawn in packs and are just as fast as you, and you must hold them back while you keep the generators in the area going. As you progress into higher waves more Volge will drop, and it will slowly start to remove the easy level Volge in place of the higher tier aliens. It can get very tense, especially when you've got three Viscera teleporting around you.
So aside from the randomly generated events, there is also the main storyline the game follows. This is mostly a single player affair, although you can group up with players and play through most of the missions with them. The cutscenes that take place only have your character regardless of party, and the NPC's in game only refer to you. So while you may have a friend along to play the story, the main storyline feels very much like a singleplayer game.
There's also PVP arenas and instanced dungeons, though I have played neither.
There's a Season Pass available that is supposed to release more missions, I assume these missions are filler content between each season of the TV show. Considering much of the team was laid off a few months ago, and only 2 of the 5 packs are released, it may not be a good idea to buy the season pass. Not unless you really enjoy the base game.
Oh, and you do NOT need to know anything about the TV show to play the game. Though if you're inclined, give it a shot. It's not bad. The most it ties in to the show is the tutorial, and an audio log or two makes a brief mention of the main characters of the TV series.
As for the community... this may make or break the purchase for you, but I love the community. There are always people playing. Not a lot, but you'll always find a decent amount of players exploring the world. And they don't communicate. Sometimes a player will jump in to a mission to help you out if you're being overwhelmed, but it's a wordless initiative and the player will leave once the mission has wrapped up and you're safe, with neither of you sharing words. In twelve hours of play, I have only seen four chat messages pop up on screen.
I personally love how peaceful it is.
tl;dr -- Borderlands style loot system, no monthly fee, third person shooter with solid mechanics. Community doesn't talk much but is active and will help you with missions. Storyline feels like a single player affair but most missions can be played with a group. Worth playing if you like third person shooters, IMO. Do not need to watch the TV show to understand the game.

While it's called Adventure Time, this game doesn't really benefit from having AT title.
First off, if you're buying this game because it is an adventure time game, you're not buying it for the right reason. It has characters from adventure time, and that's about it. The story isn't gone into too deeply. You find yourself thrust into a videogame world. You try to find bmo. All explained in the opening sequence that's pretty much it.
The main premise of a world is 6 levels and a boss. You hack and slash (kind of button mashy at times) through enemies, collecting various enchiridion pages that offer powers. It's worth mentioning that the game will be very easy unless played on the harder difficulty setting. The pages themselves are plentiful, so you can almost never run out.
I feel that this game might have benefited more from a rogue-like procedural generation level structure, rather than having fixed levels. It would have made it more challenging, and it would have given the game a lot of replay value. As it is, the static levels don't do the game any favours.
This game can be played with both controller or a K&M setup. The controls cannot be customized through the menu, but thre are a few "presets" to choose from. Peronally, I found using a controller to be the more logical way to play this, as there are not many keys to be used.
Thr graphics are very good during gameplay, but when you are shown close-ups during cutscenes, the models look very odd. The cutscenes might have benefited from being animated and pre-rendered. There is a fair amont of variance throughout each of the worlds, which is good.
The voice acting in this is limited to that of finn & jakes's cutscenes and some BMO is thrown in there too. Oddly, none of the bosses were given voice acting, despite the fact that they speak in the show. I found this rather odd. The background music for this game is very good. It has a sort of retro gaming feel to it, but it's not fully 8-bit in style.
There are some bugs in this game, but none I found to be game breaking in any way. The game devs included a "return to start" option in the menu, which helps if you get stuck on a floating island in the middle of nowhere. Fun fact: You can actually use this option at any time, even if it is "greyed out".
In short, don't buy this game just because the adventure time label is slapped on it. It is a fun game for a single playthrough, but beyond that it has no replay value, as far as i'm concerned. If you're a fan of roguelikes you probably won't be interested, but it might appeal more to people who want to get in to roguelikes, as this game is about half way there already, if a bit button mashy at times.

So, ibb and obb...with a name like that I'm not that surprised that some people were like "Meh, it looks trippy, I don't wanna play it." But for the people who played the game they were in for quite the experience. Ibb and obb is a beautifully crafted game. It's definitely one of the best looking games I've ever seen. Most of the time I really appreciate when games go for a super edgy and dark look, but ibb and obb is a soft colorful game. It's abstract where as other games try to be realistic. But sometimes realistic works exceptionally well, like take for instance Mechaniarium! But back to ibb and obb. It tells you what to do without any words! There aren't even any cut scenes or thought bubbles or arrows pointing you into any direction! You just have to go from right to left like Mario Bros. 1... I think that was done really well, because it gives you time to figure out a problem with your friend. Ibb and obb is a two player game, there is no one player, but I don't see how a one player would work all that well with this game. You can play alone but ibb is controlled by the arrow keys, while obb is controlled by the wasd keys. But the main focus of the game is team work and puzzle solving. "TEAM WORK?!?!" I know some of you are thinking "*SCOFFFS!*" But in all honesty it's best to play with a friend. This game has online multi player which is awesome! The goal of this 2D side scrolling (adventure?) platformer is to beat the krabs, a race of spikey beady milky white pupiless eyed black sea urchin looking creatures. To defeat them you must use the power of 2 dimensions, I mean literally two separate dimensions split apart by a line in the center of the screen.  The top half being right side up, while the bottom half being upside down. Portals spread through out the world of ibb and obb allow you to pass through them so you can journey between dimensions or should I say "PLAINS". The game is split up into 5 worlds, or lands, or chapters, whatever...having 3 levels in each of them. Every world introduces a new game mechanic or enemy type. The game gradually gets harder with you soon over coming incredibly challenging puzzles and strategies for taking out krabs. Some crawl, some, bounce, some fly, some will follow you and I swear you will hate those followers, I like to call them kreepers, or kapers, whatever. To defeat a krab you must hit it's weak spot that is right bellow it or above it depending on where the krab is, on another dimension. Sometimes when a level gets to a big challenge the music will get slower and more melodic. That's another thing I have to mention the music is some of the best music in general I've ever heard!!! This game may seem like a colorful, cute game for all ages, but there are some parts of the game that feel...a little...unsettling to say the least. It's not until the last world in the game where things start to not feel right. Everything is all sharp and jagged and the music is creepy. Krabs are EVERYWHERE, and this may be my imagination but, it seems that you're not welcome at all in this strange part of the game. The last level has down right SCARY music. If you want to know more about these songs just look up on youtube ibb and obb krabs. For the down right scary song look up ibb and obb krabs chased. Anyways, back to the reveiw. If the game wasn't challenging enough there are also secret levels and achievements. That will push you to the brink of insanity! But at the end of every level you are greeted with a dancing trio who just want to party and celebrate ibb and obb's success. There are crystals hidden in every level and hidden inside krabs that add to your overall score and how good the victory/ party theme will be at the end of every level. Plus there are trading cards for all of the gate keepers. The guys who let you into the secret levels. Let's not forget about ubb the secret third character who's controlled by the hbnm keys. WARNING, he only appears in local co-op or single player where you and a friend share a key board, you might need a third buddy for ubb. My only complaint is that once you get ubb I wish you could permanently have him and can select him as a third player on the main menu screen. But then all the levels would have to be reconstructed into a three player game... Oh well! Another complaint I have is I wish you could have better communication with the other player in online co-op. For example, if you type something in with the keyboard and then press enter you'd have a little green or pink speech bubble appear over ibb or obbs' head. The bubble would be the color of ibb or obb, or ubb. It would hover over their head and follow them around until you press delete, which will get rid of the bubble. This game is an amazing experience from start to finish. I highly recommend this game to everyone. At least just give the first level a try. GG Sparp Weed, GG.
(Sparp Weed is the company that made ibb and obb.)

The game is great but it is very, very difficult if you choose to play a faction that has 4 stars or more, with the exception of the elves, since they just get hammered by lizardmen. This is a very well-thought out and fun grand strategy game for this time of price, in fact, it's a steal. Be aware though, not all factions are playable in story-mode YET, due to lack of localization in English in the game. There are indeed several problems that plague the game. However, I had tons of fun despite that. There's a nice little option to auto-battle or take control of the battle yourself, I usually almost always take control because I simply find the battles fun to watch. There is indeed an ending for all factions and perhaps an (alternative?) ending. So far, it took me a 10 hours to complete a campaign when I was rushing. Although, be aware, due to lack of localization, there are only a limited amount of playable story campaigns. But! You CAN STILL PLAY all factions EXCEPT [Crime] due to it being a Demon Lord-like faction.
You could say that this is similar to Japanese Isekai Light Novels or whatever due to the very well-thought out storyboard and background. If you're looking for a fun strategy game with good story, then buy it! Only if you don't mind 2D graphics. The art is indeed wonderful though, to compensate for the pixelated graphics in battle.
If you want to deeply invest your time in a 'grand strategy game' then this is for you! Usually it'll take 30 or so hours to complete a SINGLE campaign, and there are ALOT of factions in this game. From the dragon-rider factions to the 'Corrupted Empire' to the 'Aethesitic-Religion-in-the-Dessert' hell, they even included Lizardmen factions and FROG FACTIONS!
Each faction has their own dedicated units, from healers to ranged units to close combat to stationary units to cavalries, etc but to add onto that, each one has their own teir as well. For example, an 'Enlistee' can be promoted to a 'Soldier' once he hits level 10. An Enlistee starts out as level 1 and only costs 100 funds, however, a Soldier which is level 10, would cost 1000 funds. Of course, there are exceptions of more powerful 'Enlistees' in each faction such as the Reinhalt Empire's.
If you're not into RTS games then might as well play this game Turn-Based style! Yes, you can leave the fighting to the AI and have it skip the actual battle. Though, to RTS players, what's the fun in that? Different strokes for different blokes, this game allows for different types of play-styles and strategies. It's quite similar to the Total War series, albeit ONLY slightly. I believe if you had a blast with the Total War series and want a refreshing, quick-play. Then this game is definitely for you.
A bit of a warning, at first, you'll be COMPLETELY overwhelmed by the information when you actually start playing, that's why there's a tutorial, please play that! This game's map is quite large and since it is quite large, there are often tons of factions that surround you and want to stab you in the back. As I've said, this game is indeed difficult but not too difficult that SAVE-AND-LOAD can't fix! Screwed up trying to defend your city? Welp, load and retry, try a different strat and use the abilities of your troops much more efficiently! Yes, there are abilities in this game and there are a ton. Buffs, special magic, lasers from dragons and such exist in this world. Mowing down infantry with a single dragon laser breath is absolutely euphoric. If you feel a bit lonely then why not try Diplomacy?
A weak point in this game is its diplomacy. Everyone wants to kill each other and want your stuff, your land and your women. Thankfully, the AI isn't so bad that it disregards the alliance pact it forms. But, when it boils down to trying to make friends and/or enemies, it's just about funds. There's no such thing as 'negotiating' just give them gold and they'll♥♥♥♥♥♥off elsewhere. You can't engage in a talk with faction leaders either, which deeply disappointed me.
However, don't let this turn you away! This is a grand startegy game in the end and what's more fun than conquering stuff? In the end, this game is a small 3$ game but plays like a 15$ game should and is weeeelll worth the price. It isn't some triple AAA game and you should look elsewhere if you're looking for a Civilization copy. If you lower your expections by a bit, you'll be greatly shocked at how fun this game can be.

Master Levels for Doom II was ID Software's answer to the plethora of unauthorized level packs being sold for their popular game. Intent on outdoing the guys behind DZone, ID Software got some of the best amateur level designs to craft official levels as an expansion for Doom II. They also compiled over 1,800 WADs on a CD to give the DZone guys a run for their money.
While those 1,800 levels aren't included, the 21 that make up the "Master Levels" are fairly good. Not every level is a winner (and some are just down right cruel), but it's a fairly competent collection of levels for anyone who has mastered the base game.
The biggest issue is that "Master Levels" includes a lot of ridiculous enemy counts. Some levels have upwards of 250 enemies and keys hidden behind secrets. It creates an atmosphere where you can easily get lost or overwhelmed. A few times, I had no idea where to progress because my map didn't show anything else. I went to YouTube and found the answer to be obtuse beyond reason.
That could also fit the description of how to find the hidden level (taking an invulnerability sphere and making an Arch-vile blast you). It turns what is normally a fun hunt into a frustrating exercise in patience. The AI isn't exactly smart in Doom, so trying to manipulate it in ways that it wasn't developed for just sucks.
Then we get to how some levels are pathetically easy. A few of the WADs have spaced out battle zones that do little more than pad out the length of the level. If you constantly sprint (and why wouldn't you?), there doesn't really exist a reason to have such large landmasses.
Sprinting is also key to finding a lot of items. A yellow key may be perched on what looks like an unreachable pedestal, but you really just need to travel a few rooms over and run like a wild man out the window. It's just annoying to see the same tricks repeated so many times.
As for the Steam release, it's a bit of a mess. The game doesn't run any worse than Doom II or the other DOSBox ports, but it's strange to set up. There isn't a front loaded menu and trying to play them in any coherent order can be quite the ordeal. There are some extra mods for source ports that allow you to freely select each WAD (and the Eternity Engine has built-in support for Master Levels), but it's not as straight forward as launching ZDoom with the other main games.
There is also no way to individually buy Master Levels on Steam. You have to get it in the Doom Classic Complete pack. While that is, admittedly, a good deal, it is a bit annoying. If you happened to only buy one of the main games or skipped out on, say, Final Doom, you're stuck rebuying them all.
For that reason alone, I would say Master Levels for Doom II isn't worth it. The Doom enthusiast will already have the Complete collection on Steam, but casual users can just stick with Doom I and II.

"Master Levels for DOOM II" is an expansion from "DOOM II: Hell on Earth". You should get this for free after purchasing DOOM II. Master Levels contains 20 highly difficult levels which sit at the same level as the "Thy Flesh Consumed" episode of Ultimate Doom, and some are even harder.
It begins with a DOS-style menu which is complicated to use at the start if you haven't operated a DOS-related app like this. Oh and by the way, works with Windows 10 as I'm running the game on it perfectly. You come to the list of .wad files which are all the maps for the game. Follow the in-app instructions and you'll do fine. And if you ever want to quit, go back to the DOS menu while on a level and hit Esc.
For each level, there is usually a description or plot involved with it. You can also go to the level settings to alter the difficulty and even change monster-related events. Such as No Monsters and the conditions for Nightmare Mode. I suggest starting each level off on No Monsters Mode to learn the layout of the level and get puzzles without getting trampled by the monsters within.
I have cleared all 20 levels myself a while ago, however on ITYTD, and would say that the level design and difficulty are quite the thrill. I really love DOOM and I have gained enough experience to find several of these levels a breeze. But there were a few that were pretty ridiculous. The hardest one in my opinion is "Mephisto's Mausoleum" with many revenants squirming around outdoors and indoors, as well as multiple mancubi and barons of hell to defeat. Even the "Icon of Sin" makes a comeback.
I'm pretty sure Master Levels supports custom DOOM levels in the form of .wad files. I have just found a DOOM level editor and I'm pretty sure you can implement new .wad files onto wherever you have installed Master Levels. If my rumor of custom levels is true, then that makes the game a lot more awesome for me.
This is an excellent game to play after DOOM II, which I've cleared as well. You can "master" DOOM with these master levels with all kinds of new twisted combos of monsters and gimmicks. It's totally a pass for me as DOOM is my most favorite FPS franchise!

ibb & obb is a delightful co-op puzzle platformer for 2 (players) that plays around with gravity. The puzzles are well thought out and paced very well. The controls are very basic, all you can do in ibb & obb is move left, right, and jump. Despite this, the devs have managed to include a decent mix of gameplay mechanics that are never overused. ibb & obb feels fresh the whole way through and it never feels as if any part of it is overly repetitive or drawn out. It can be challenging at times, but the solution is almost always clear (the introduction of bubbles -if you play you'll know when you see- is a little bit unclear), and always rewarding to beat.
If playing through multiple levels at once, it seemlessly ends one level with a scoreboard display on an in-game sign as you run right(literally, the direction right -->) through to the next level. The downside of this is that it is unclear when it autosaved, or indeed if it was saving progress at all. Don't worry though, because it turns out the game saves at the end of each level and the "restart in limbo" option goes to a level select area where you can start where ever you want.
