To sum the game in one sentance.  It feels like Anime Risk.
There is more to it than that with unit leveling and real-time strategy combat like the total war games taking away the RNG of Risk.
With such a cheap price it is certainly worth the purchase, just expect to be frustrated with some of the UI and Dialog.  It takes a bit to get used to the controls, interacting with the units, the map and the AI behaviour.  If you want to experience the game's Lore, set everything to automated and spectate everything you can.  Other wise you will miss out on a lot of character conversation during the battles.
Of course, the game is only partially translated and the voice overs are all in japanese and some of the lore is missing until localized.  But hey, it is $3.00 which is pretty good even with missing content.
As a strategy game... it is not the smoothest.  Walls block your view and units can have a hard time pathing with obstacles around them.  Unit commands are going to take some adjustments, there are some hotkeys that help manage units and you can create new groups adding to the default two Vanguard and Rearguard.  Adding new groups is something you need to do if you do not want your calvary acting like front line units.  Middle mouse button pauses the game btw.  Take that opportunity to sort everything out.
The groups you make are saved but apply to every following battle including those of other armies other armies, you have to change them every time you use a different army since they are not compatible.
The command grouping is pretty 'bleh' but things play out well enough without a polished alternative.
Understanding what is happening to your units is a little difficult as well, you can track all unit HP and can see damage numbers.  Some character abilities are pretty obvious and very dangerous; however, I'm still scratching my head about why 1/4 of my army died instantly when attacking the elves in their territory.  I am pretty sure they dumped their special abilites, which I missed seeing because we are fighting in a dense forrest with numbers and status effects popping up all over our units.
I have done a lot of early games to get a feel of the initial game; however, I do not know how the game plays out in the later turns.  It feels like snowballing can happen.  But of course with some pretty big abilities, terrain modifiers, defensive positions, squad limits on different maps, etc it can be very easy for a prepared defense to beat a snow ball force.

give this game a chance. it's cheap. it has charm. it's a labour of love, clearly. it's a unique kind of strategy game - not perfect, a bit unpolished, but it makes up for that in charm.
it makes me feel nostalgic for an era i wasn't around for. if you have no trouble adapting to japanese indie games, you'll appreciate it. i really appreciate the sort of chrono trigger era drawings, even if they seem to conflict a bit with the style of the world map and battle scenes - at the same time, all those styles are things i really like. something about the disjointed retro, 16-bitness with the 32 bit quality art is frankly kind of charming.
if the screenshots put you off because you think it looks awkward - it's a unique kind of 4x-ish game. it gets me out of most of the things that 4x games do wrong for me. it doesn't feel like you're wasting turns just sort of moving about random squares and waiting your turn. and instead of just "put these troops against  these troops and let the cpu figure it out", you have a sort of rts with rpg elements and micromanagement battle interface. i love that.
lots of things about this game are clunky. it's a big time mod of a japanese freeware game that was never translated to english. the interface is almost like a sega saturn windows port in some ways, you drag and drop troops into territory you want to invade. but there's a lot of really nice stuff, strategy wise, to play around with here, and it has enough unique hooks and controls and random rpg elements that i'm really, really into it. you can micromanage the way your troops attack in battles, you can make them all attack specific points to choke things off - at the same time, coming to grips with this system is hard. the tutorial explains how to control the game but gives you very little guidance on what you need to do to actually win battles.
that's a problem - but the charm of the game, the cheap price, and the appeal strategy games like this have for me means i'm willing to overcome it. it's like 3 bucks. come on. i'm into this.

Now that I have over 75 hours logged in my main save, it might be time to write a review.
For a long time before finding the Atelier series, I had been looking for a game like this. Atelier Firis is essentially a turn-based JRPG with a character-focused, mostly slice-of-life plot, but the real draw is the huge focus on gathering materials and using them to create your own items and equipment. While some JRPGs have you just buy items and gear from stores (with a lot of items not being worth it) and use different level up or skill systems to make things interesting, the Atelier games let you feel like you're making the tools you need to succeed. This entry (the 18th main game in the series, from what I hear) really does a great job of making crafting items easy to learn but still have depth for those who choose to master the system. Two instances of the same item will rarely be the same, so you have to make sure you make the right choices when crafting if you want to do well.
The story of the game won't be too exciting if you want a strong plot-driven narrative, but if you can grow attached to the characters it can still be engaging. The first part of the game involves the lead, Firis Mistlud, learning to use alchemy and being given a year to pass the Alchemy Exam, which takes place in a city far from her home. Should she succeed, she then continues to adventure to try to find her calling in life. This is where the story (and game) really open up, as each companion has their own story arc and ending and many named NPCs have their own sideplots. While some characters take longer to develop than others, they all have at least a few interesting things about them to make the sideplots worth exploring.
From a gameplay standpoint, Atelier Firis is an open-world game that encourages exploring each part of the large maps. While there is a chokepoint about halfway through the world map that requires a questline to open and not every area is available until after the Alchemy Exam, you'll still have more than enough ground to cover and explore. There's also a fast travel feature within maps, and after the exam you can complete a quest chain in order to get a way to warp to almost any area in the game from rest spots. There is a time limit for the first part of the game, but you are given plenty of time to do everything that must be done pre-exam with some time to spare. Even if you fail, you can load the bad ending save to get the same benefits as a New Game+ clear, which includes a few features that makes surviving the time limit and doing pre-exam questlines even easier.
Aside from gathering items from the environment and making items from them, the game features combat with monsters as a big part of finding the best materials and completing some quest chains. The battles are played with a turn-based system that changes turn order based on stats, actions, and buffs/debuffs. While normal attacks and skills are available for each character (and can become powerful in the late game), the early and mid game will put a huge emphasis on item use. While only Firis and the alchemist party members can use a lot of items, everyone has access to some types of items and they are powerful for a huge part of the game (even into the endgame, if you craft them right). Making sure you have a good set of attack and healing items is essential before getting into any fights, because Firis is not a front-line fighter and there's only so much the rest of the team can do without item support. There's also an interesting system where a meter depicts how well your team is working together (which increases when you do damage to enemies) that can be expended to protect Firis from attacks or filled to unlock limit break-esque attacks. The game also has anti-grinding measures to force you to move into harder areas if you want to level up quickly, so you have to make sure to be improving your items and gear whenever you can to prepare for the next region. Items are also useful outside of battles, as they can be used to gather materials (such as bombing a rock) or alter the environment.
A few minor negative points do come up, though not enough to make me dislike the game. One problem I had early on is that fast travel between areas is not available until after the exam, which means a lot of walking when backtracking for materials (since in-map shortcut points are almost never near exits to areas). Another issue is the poor requirements for some recipes in the recipe idea unlock system (which gives you recipes based on what you do). Some items have absurd requirements, giving an otherwise cool system idea a bad reputation. It also doesn't help that some recipes get glitched if you complete certain quests too early, preventing 100% completion without doing a New Game+. The last, and probably least, of the issues is that I keep being annoyed by how "Atelier" is pronounced in the English voice track. The original French word sounds sort of like "a-tel-ee-ay", the Spanish cognate should sound something like "a-tel-ee-er". The English voice track for this game uses the made-up (as far as I can tell) pronunciation "at-lee-ur", which ignores the first "e" in the word. A small issue in the grand scheme of things, but with the Japanese word being closer to proper French ("a-to-ree-ay"), it gets a bit strange when the English actors are made to mispronounce a word.
Overall, Atelier Firis is a great game and, in my opinion, a good way to be introduced to the series. It has inspired me to seek out previous games in the series (particularly the game it's a sequel to, Atelier Sophie) to have further crafting adventures. If you're interested in a JRPG that gives items and crafting a big focus and tells a character-driven coming of age story, Atelier Firis might be a good fit for you.

Everyone not affiliated with Ludosity,

My wife, my 14, 7, and 6 year old children and I have been playing Card City Nights for a couple of weeks now.  Your game was unreasonably low priced, so I picked up 5 copies.
The kids picked up on it really quickly and loved it.  I knew it was a special game when I saw the card and interface design not get in the way of the superb play mechanic.  Its simplicity 3x3 grid and card interaction leads to a surprising amount of strategy.  We're talking enjoyable strategy...you know...the feeling of KNOWING I should have put that other card in the deck or KNOWING that I should have played those 3 cards in a different order.  When I lost games against the AI, it made sense.  When I won, there was absolutely always a reason for it and a reward to follow - a new booster pack or some money (used to buy cards to round off your pool of cards).
There is quite a bit of quality humor in the game from dialogue with AI opponents to flavor card text.  I couldn't stop playing.  Do I have the best card(s) - not yet.  Do I have enough of that card or that type of booster - not yet.
The game doesn't get old or feel played out, much like MTG, but at a MUCH cheaper price point. Not as hard to learn and held our interest at least as well.  There are no microtransaction here.  None.
My family and I appreciate you and your efforts on this one Ludosity.  I am in the process of checking out your other games.  Good luck in your future endeavors and let me know if there's anything we can do for you to return the favor!

I already didn't recommend Any other DooM release on Steam with the same review Copy-pasted because of the same problems. But this one deserves its own review.
A little statement first. As already mentioned in my other DooM reviews the 0/10 rate is related to the Steam Release. Consider that I grew up with doom, I was 6 years old when the shareware was being widespread all over the world, and still nowadays I own The original DooM, DooM II and The Ultimate Collection DooM 95 (With Ultimate DooM, DooM II And Final DooM). All of this to state I know and Love the game I grew up with. Despite all this I regret to NOT Recommend this RELEASE (Not THE GAME, mind you). On a Side note: all the DooM chapters have been released on Steam like this, so I'm not recommending Any other chapter, specifically The Ultimate DooM, Final DooM And DooM II: Hell On Earth. My same Review will be posted in all those releases because of the same flaws.
This Master Levels For DooM II release is supposed to have a total of 21 maps (including the "Teeth" Secret level) AND 1830 amateur custom levels. What does this release have? 21 Maps... Don't tell me the 1830 maps would weight too much, wad files have a ridiculous size. Anyways, to play the 21 maps you'll have to stick with an outdated and sometimes stuttering version of dosbox running the game with the already mentioned and useless "modern controls". Too bad that now you can't select a classic control system. Top of the Tops you still have to use that outdated, NON-user friendly ridiculous text-interface to select the map to play with. Meaning you don't get to play the 21 maps one after the other, but you have to select which map replace the original DooM II map. So this means you will get to play again some DooM II levels (21, replacing 32). And that's not the worst part. The maps have the "replacing slot locked" and most of them replace the same slot... BUT WHY?!?!? And if this wasn't enough You are FORCED to use the "Modern Interface" set as default in the other DooM Steam releases. But here you can't revert to the Classic interface. Definitley the worst release Ever. Fortunately this is a bonus pack for those brave or squanderer enough to buy these horrible releases. I'll just copy-paste the cons of the other releases, which still apply on this one. It's not worth a total rewrite...

An MMO shooter, free-to-play once you buy the game. If you miss Tabula Rasa, this is a pretty good substitute, and probably dodges some of the mistakes that led to TR's downfall. It's primarily PvE, and the enemies don't change much--it's mostly running around from arkfall to arkfall to volge siege to arkfall, with the occasional mission or random event, and the enemies are pretty much limited to mutants, hellbugs, raiders, 99ers (cyborgs), volge (a hostile alien race), and Dark Matter (remnants of an elite military unit), but they provide enough of a challenge to keep you on your toes. It probably doesn't have a lot of replay value though--there are no classes, so once you max out a character, you can start another as a different race, but there's nothing really different to do, and the differences between races are purely cosmetic (and playing as a different race requires a DLC).
There's a cash shop, but by no means required--it's not pay-to-win, though a couple of inventory upgrades are a big help, as is one of the cash shop vehicles.

I am not ashamed to admit I put 50+ hours into this game. If you look past the two-dimensional ladies and heavy sexual themes, you end with a simple yet addicting puzzle game with great presentation thrown on top. This western parody of a Japanese eroge game is rich with "plot" but the story premise is quite simple. Accompanied by a pink-haired love fairy, you embark on a sexual conquest to bang all the hot, single locals in your area.
The colorful, anime-inspired character models and backgrounds give Japanese eroge games a run for their money. The voice acting is great with hilarious, laugh out loud dialogue ("Thanks for the sex homie.") Each woman you encounter have their own personality, interests, and caters towards a specific *ahem* fetish. The soundtrack is well-balanced with catchy, upbeat bangers and peaceful bgm fitting to the game's various locales.
An average day consists of meeting up with a woman, giving her gifts, ask/answer each other questions, take her out on a date, and then move onto the next one. The actual date is the puzzle game with match 3 mechanics, similar to Bejeweled and Puzzle Quests, where you must generate enough attraction for a successful date in a limited amount of turns. Simple but there are date gifts you can use and certain tokens to consider that could make or break your date, so there's some strategy involved.
Eventually after a few successful dates, you can take the ladies to your bedroom for some sexy time which is underwhelming as a whole. I'll admit it's fairly repetitive and can easily burn out those who are not into the puzzle gameplay. But there are unlockable hairstyles, outfits, artwork, and dates which grant some replayability. Would've been nice if there are more cutscenes expanding the universe and characters outside of the first day.

It's like Total War, Dragon Force(yes, the classic Saturn Game) and Romance of the Three Kingdoms all got together and birthed a hybrid child.
You take control of one of the 12 factions of the world and vie your way to complete dominance, through Diplomacy, JRPG-style cutscenes and recruiting hundreds of individual generals, each with their own stats, levels and skills.
Battles are done in RTS style, in a way reminiscent of the Total War series. There's a lot of depth in the way you mix and match units, generals, skills and formations. The battles can become very large in scale, chaos and mayhem ensuing, with armored knights charging into infantry and mages slinging spells of destruction from behind. There are sieges in the game, and its entertaining to formulate a strategy and watching it unfold as your soldiers storm the castles.
This is a game I dreamt of playing as a child -it fulfills a lot of what I wanted to see in a fantasy wargame back then- but the game isn't without its faults. A better UI would have gone a long way and better graphic and resoution options are much desired.

I just love how this game came about. A Japanese dude made an empire war game. Another guy loved it so much he made his own module for it that eventually became this, and he loved so much he worked with the original creator to get that thing released here. This is like some guy's fantasy setting Dynasty Warriors Empires CAW roster, complete with backstories for various kingdoms, gone professional! He lived the dream!
As for the actual game, the DW Empires comparison is pretty apt. You have a fairly simple kingdom management game where a wide variety of factions, a full suite of the Japanese-take-on-Western fantasy setting characters, elves, imperials, knights, frog people, demons, each with unique hero units all voice acted by Japanese voice actors, are all locked in a map and jockeying to steal cities from each other. As near as I can tell, there is no tech tree, each turn you can just buy troops or invade, with a smidge of diplomacy bribes on the side. Battles are top down, real time, Total War style. Not a lot of strategy but you can try to micromanage your casters and archers if it makes you feel more tactical. The entire thing captures the immersion of working for a kingdom in DW Empires, as well as the repeatable war-gamey ness of it. Also taken from Empires is the ability to be a wandering general... but you literally have no options in this mode except to attempt to take on a neutral kingdom by yourself to rebuild a kingdom or sign on with another kingdom and get brought along on battles like another unit. It's not an addition worth considering, especially compared to what Rot3K and the Empires games offer in officer play.
Simming of battles is available, as well as letting the CPU do your turns, or just watching the entire game play out under CPU control.
To top it off, some of the factions (Hopefully all eventually, if the game gets a decent following to justify having it translated) have story segments to go along with the campaign. You can play any faction, but only a couple have their story events translated. They don't get in the way of the main war game though.
For the art and setting alone, this is worth your 3bux easily. The gameplay itself is pretty simple, but the addictiveness of it gets obvious as you play it. And you might find yourself wishing you had some mod tools to make your own crazy kingdoms as you get into it. I recommend this for anyone who has enjoyed Dynasty Warriors Empires type games and want to see that same sensibility applied to a more Total War-esque framework.
EDIT: As I've played more, I can see more of the strategy form. For the tactical battles, there are quite a few magic skills between the various units, but apart from the "expend all your summons and blast/heal/buff" I don't see that there is much need for strategy in the actual battles. Those good at the game might see what I don't.
In the strategic map, the game resembles a massive mexican standoff. Units that have recruited or attacked cannot be march to support defense, and can only defend if directly attacked. This means that unless you can be sure you are leaving only one province open when you make a move (Nearly impossible), you have to balance your main squads and your reserve squads ready to back up the main force when you get counter-attacked. Letting the enemy bisect your kingdom means they can easily prevent your heroes from escaping, forcing them to return to wandering.
Most kingdoms are between two or three mortal enemies, with a few more belligerents who cannot be bribed on far sides of the map, so gaining ground without immediately losing it is very hard. In this sense, it is not like Dynasty Warriors Empires where nothing can slow your march to unification except maybe a Lu Bu cheese combo.
In addition, Troops themselves level up, over time a bit when not fighting, and more in a successful fight. Troop levels are your main source of power beyond bringing sheer numbers to bear. If you have a troop of a certain level threshold you can actually pay more to hire troops close to that level rather than get level 1 scrubs again.
EDIT2: These campaigns are not quick things. Taking down your enemies is like nailing jello to a wall and it is a lot of work to try to crest the hill into dominance late game and then take down your opponents. I imagine for strategy gamers this is just fine but the length of these games to me makes it a little tougher to replay.

Started off with a 4-star difficulty nation on normal. Instantly hooked after I figured out how everything works. This game is 3$, and it's well worth it. If you have the money, buy it!
EDIT: After playing a little more, I thought I'd cover what I've decided are the best difficulties. There are 4 difficulties.
Easy - Self explanitory, there are no negatives to the players, and no boost to the AI.
Normal - Same as easy, except player has Fog of War (recommend this in the beginning).
Hard - Same as normal, except AI now have access to advanced units, instead of just the player. As the campaign goes on, via training, recruitment, and battle, the AI's troops will upgrade.
Luna(lunar? don't remember the exact term) - I really like this one, a lot. Basically, you can only control your main squad/general. So, you get control over your general plus his/her/it's units. You have the ability to recruit vassals for more units/squads. You get to do this as you  rank up and recieve money via battles (plunder/spoils). If you go to a territory without the faction leader/higher ranking general, you can invade territories and command any squads that are in the territory you're attacking from. The  Faction leader (AI) can command you to attack territories. You'll often find yourself with just your squad and half a squad (4 units) attacking a fortress, yea good luck.
All in all, I'm really digging this game, I'll add more as I play.

This is a beautiful, well-crafted game.
The controls and game-mechanics are introduced organically through gameplay, without so much as a word of instruction, which is definitely no easy feat and probably the thing I think is most amazing about this game.
The puzzles are sufficiently difficult that when you finally get that light-bulb moment, the rush cannot be topped, but equally they're not unfair or excessively punishing.
The music, sound design and art style are minimalistic and stylish, but neverthless manage to convey a lot of emotion about how you should feel in a given level.
Working together with your friend to solve the puzzles often involves "signing" - when you move your mouse it draws a line in your character's colour across the screen where the cursor is, that the other player can see. This is a simple yet powerful system for letting your partner know what you're thinking and what you'd like them to do. However, sometimes its just a tiny bit too simplistic and a built-in text or voice chat would have been nice, even if its only used occassionally to express the more complex plans.
If I had to name a bad point, its that the game is essentially multiplayer-only. It is possible to play the game on your own, by controlling both ibb & obb yourself, but this quickly becomes an impossible multitasking demand. Its an unfair gripe though, because the game's whole point is about working together with a friend to solve the puzzles: don't buy if you don't have a friend to play with, otherwise, I can't recommend this game enough.

That's not to say that Brothers doesn't have gameplay. In fact, it introduces a rather wonderful control system: one that seems weird at first, but will soon make you wonder why nobody thought of it before. As the title suggests, this game has two lead characters - but you'll control both of them simultaneously. Using the controller's dual analogue sticks, the left stick becomes "big brother" and the right stick is for "little brother", while the respective triggers become the "use" key for each boy.
The sons must find a herbal cure for their father's illness by undertaking a quest through a Tolkeinesque world, and along the way they'll help and be helped by the denizens of the countryside. You could easily walk past most of these opportunities without consequence, but it's always worth having a good look around a character/animal of interest to see what you can do.
It's a lovely-looking game, with the appearance of a living painting of a north European fairy tale. It's mercifully free of any UI or HUD, and if you're a screenshot hound like me then you'll be merrily jabbing at the F12 key and making new desktop backgrounds in every new scene. The music is nicely used, but perhaps the best thing about the sound is the complete lack of recognisable language and yet the clarity of communication. You won't know what anybody is saying, but you'll *know*!

The world is quite huge, I prefer this open world format in comparison to the old world map format but dang, there needs to be a lot of UI improvement like having a world map you can access anytime.
The ditching of items is a chore too.
Other than those gripes, story is ok, design is HNNNNNGGG!! level of cute, the exam idea is cool, the whole traveling tent is cool, though give us more storage space please, this is a game about items...

How Atelier Firis could turn to be the last Atelier game I play.
In my long history with Atelier games I never was disappointed by any of them until Firis, and they never were so ambitious as Firis is, but not this, or lack of polish, or not the best port are reasons for my disappointment.
So what's good about Firis:
1.it's the open world in nature, for the first time in the Atelier game
2. Complexity of alchemy is a notch down from Sophie, but in general alchemy feels better in Firis.
3. Character endings are back
4. The world is nice and monster design is great.
5. It's a huge game
6. learning alchemy and taking an actual exam of it is an interesting idea.
7. Many interesting characters with their stories.
8. Chain quests
what's not so good:
1. Localization is poor
2. Quest descriptions for many quests are wrong past the first step
3. A game is way too demanding on hardware and runs poorly
4. There are some glitches.
the ugly:
1. No real fast travel for 30-40 hours, depends on how fast you get there.
2. Even when you get fast travel, it is limited, as there are parts of the world that allow no fast travel, and these aren't small locations, also filled with dangerous monsters (that can wipe out even strong party) without ability to save your game, of course.
3. Sophie had an interesting system of unlocking alchemy recipes, which Firis ditched in favour of guessing what you should do and how many times to unlock what, yes guessing.
4. Alchemy results in Firis are strongly dependent on quality, yet you can't register a single item in this game (just let it sink in). What means creating the same items ad nauseam over and over again, what takes extra hours upon hours of playtime for no reason.
5. ridiculously small initial storage space available to you (you easily get it filled in first three-four locations) and you have no ability to sell anything for a long time after that. It never becomes sufficient too.
6. Many character events are pure guesswork too, and not something that is obvious, or even logical or easy to guess because of lack of options, nothing of the sort.
7. the game that can't be fully finished without of use of a guide (and that's not a few things but a whole lot of them), is not a well designed game in my book.
so those seven reasons are that make me think that Firis can be my last atelier game. I can't tolerate even one of those, all of them? overkill.
This is an end of era. I still have a hope that Gust will get some feedback and won't repeat all numerous mistakes they made with Firis.
I only recommend this game because it has redeeming qualities, but if you wanna a real good Atelier game, you should play Atelier Sophie instead.

Coming straight from Atelier Sophie was a mistake. The two games are very similar, they even share a fair few characters, only this game gives you a timelimit. The advantages Firis has over Sophie is: better graphics, larger areas and more cute girls.

A short gem -- the kind of game that sticks with you months after you play it.
Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is a game that pretty much cannot be played without a controller. I've heard it's possible with a keyboard/mouse combination but I can't imagine it working very well. You control the two brothers - one older, one younger - simultaneously using both sticks of a controller. Initially you'll be running into walls and struggling to progress, but it pretty quickly becomes relatively second nature, although I will admit to a few straggling control issues late into the game. Hey - it's hard to get used to!
The game centers around two brothers' search for medicine for their dying father. They have to trek across a fantastic and fairly desolate world, encountering a number of unexplained, fantastic things. The world is built in such a way as to really engender a sense of curiosity and wonder at the things you find, while never quite explaining everything. The absolutely gorgeous art direction, model design and texture work certainly help bring this fantastical world about.
The game isn't particularly difficult, with most of the puzzles never surpassing the "early stages of Ico" level of challenge. However, you really get the sense that this game would be totally without puzzles or gameplay if the designers could figure out a way to actually make it playable in such a state. Exploring the world, getting to know the various creatures you meet and engendering a relationship with the brothers themselves is obviously the focus of the game. It plays more as an exceptionally well-created art piece: beautiful, thought provoking and very, very structured.
It's worth noting that the end of the game is handled so outstandingly well that it will make you wonder why more games aren't as emotionally provoking as Brothers. There's no question that this game really elevates the platform, at least in terms of raw emotional throughput, beyond what is normally considered possible in videogames today.
In short: Buy Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons. It's outstanding. You'll finish it in a couple hours but it will stay with you far longer than most 40+ hour games.

I've played all the PS3 Atelier games. Sophie was a bit of a disappointment for me. I didn't like the way it handled time and combat. But Firis makes up for all of it. It feels like the day/night cycles they experimented with in Sophie finally came to fruition with Firis. The battles are fun again and it feels like you're in control.
The world feels HUGE! This is by far the biggest Atelier game based on map size alone. The maps feel well designed and you can go exploring them for hours.
Firis as a character is really cute and fun. They took a page out of Arland and brought back Sophie as your teacher. And they do a good job of making Sophie feel like an alchemist master.
There are some issues with the PC port. 2D art assets, lighting, shadows, framerate dips in certain areas. Hopefully they get fixed by patches or at least get workarounds by fans. Only the shadows really bothers me as it's really noticeable during cutscenes.
Overall, Firis is shaping up to be one of my favorite Ateliers. It feels like they went all out with the game and map design. I would like to see future Atelier titles continue on this path.

I played this game when it first came out, and spent years playing it. I played Oblivion but spent less time playing it and even less time playing Skyrim. (Skyrim was a bitter disapointment for me I'm sorry to say but better than Oblivion and Im still trying hard to get into it - Im not giving up that easily).
Yes Oblivion and Skyrim look better and the character movement doesnt look like they sh*t their pants. Yes I love the way archery works in these two games and even how melee combat looks (hence looks, not works). But goddamn did they take away vital elements of the game. The rpg and quest/storytelling in these two games are watered down and ultimately disapointing.
Yes, Morrowinds graphics are dated. Yes, you run around like you sh*t your pants.....Running speed is slow (at the beginning). If you are fresh to this game you will suck at combat (fatigue and weapon skill actually matters in this game). You will bump into enemies that you may not be able to defeat and may have to run away (get that eh, bet you never came accross that concept before). NPCs will dislike you. You will start with nothing. Your character is not special (at least in the beginning).
But these are some of the things (after a little patience and time) that I love about this game;
-You can steal from the vaults of the three Great Houses of Morrowind (Im not talking about little trinkets either, and its no easy feat).
-Become as powerful as a God (Many people have complained about this - but they never took into consideration that you actually fight Gods.)
-Playing as a mage is amazing in this game. Yes you can craft your own spells, yes you can create powerful enchantments, yes you will become powerful in time. Yes you will break the game (but in a good way and its also ironic when you consider the main questline).
-The other titles, Oblivion and Skyrim are missing some of the features that Morrowind has which makes me cherish this game more.
-The game is hard, its unforgiving, it will punish you when you make a mistake or do not prepare enough. Want to visit the area beyond the ghost gate at level 1? Go ahead, you can try but ill guarantee you wont last five minutes in there - no I dont mean hanging around at the door at the gate for five, I mean actually venturing out there....(You will struggle to actually get to the fence/gate itself, likely get hunted down by cliff racers). But if you ever make it, its a real reward - just like everything else in the game. I also felt the later titles failed in this respect, I didnt really feel intimidated or concerned that I might get my a** kicked.
-You cant become Arch-Mage at level 1 or with no magic skills at all. This ruined my experience with the later series. You need to actually be a mage to be arch mage, actually need to master some magic skills. Again, when you get there, rewarding.
-You dont get quests like
that insult your intelligence. The story telling and lore in this game are unmatched.
-The main quest is epic.
-The bloodmoon and tribunal (Solstheim and Mournhold) expansions are amazing.
-The atmosphere and music is great. (Skyrim is great in this way too).
-Stats. Yes stats, this is vital. It reduces the mindless hack and slash and encourages thoughtful decisions before entering combat. It gives you more options and choice on how to approach certain situations and opponents.
This game is not for the impatient. Its not for the individual that wants to switch on the game and start a new character slaying monsters left, right and center. Its not for the gamer that needs quest markers because they cannot be bothered to pay attention to what they are actually doing (your character will die otherwise).
But I promise you if you are patient, you will be hooked. If you give this game time you will understand what all the fuss is about. Oh and one last thing its not nostalgia talking (okay maybe a little), Oblivion and Skyrim have as much depth as a puddle compared to this game.

TL;DR: For those nights when you're saving up for the next Steam Sale and don't want to spend your money on booster packs in Hearthstone.
Easy to pick up, simple playstyle, quirky nods at pop culture and a TCG game that doesn't have you busting out your wallet every five minutes. There's no mindless grind either. Plenty of playtime with a variety of AI opponents. Game has a pretty active dev team. Good value.

This turned out to be a reeeeally fun game. It's a CCG set in a modern world small town with a cute story wrapped around it. You collect booster packs via duelling NPCs in the game, buy individual cards from the in-game store with gold coins that you get as you duel or explore, and form decks using one of a few varying strategies to finish the story and defeat all your opponents. I read other reviews that said defence decks were great, I used an offensive/disabler deck that worked well from start to end too. It's not grindy at all, you can easily play start to end without sitting around and grinding certain cards or something, though you can if you want to as well.
But there are a number of strategies you can employ to build your deck around, which is a neat concept, though there's little advantage in not maxing out the size of your deck, and the AI can be spotty in places, though it's not entirely horrible. The card combining system I found to be a little wonky too, although I didn't play with it fully.
Love the art, dig the character writing, and the music is fun and addictive and on both Spotify and Steam, apparently.
It took me about 8-10h of casual playing to finish the game, the rest of the time it was just sitting idle behind some other games, which is why the gameplay time is a little inflated.

Defiance puts you right into the Sci-Fi world of futuristic Earth, a now terraformed planet where you adopt the role of an Ark hunter. The game shares some similarities with the TV show on SyFy, in which both were created to run along side by side of each other, even with the same actor's doing the voice overs from the show.
A buy to play MMO where there is no subscription fee, albeit season passes get released for new content which you would need to buy, and there is a cash shop for cosmetic items, however, it is not thrown in your face like some games, nor is it pay to win and there's a rather large selection of clothes and vehicles which you can obtain yourself ingame.
Weapons do the same damage from the start, so a new player won't be at a massive disadvantage although weapons themselves level up and you aquire them with stats which do get better as you progress.
Compared to a traditional RPG MMO, the world isn't that large if you'd compare it to an old game such as World of Warcraft or Eve Online, however, it is still pretty darn big, and by no means is it the smallest MMO out there.
The game has some-what of an arcade feel to it, but that's primarily because it runs alongside the console versions, in fact, plonking you in the very same server. However, this isn't all bad as it does work fairly smoothly for gameplay. It's a game you can pick up, play and put down again. While you can grind contracts (Kill X amount of this, collect X amount of that) where some update per day and others per week, you won't feel left in the dust by older players, though some people might like being vastly ahead of the newer players, or at least feel as though they've progressed their character that they can feel proud of it and can flex their E-peen, it is by no means a drawback to the game.
The weaponry feels good, as does the combat as a whole. Shooting the bugs with your loud booming LMG, or getting dual head shots with the 2 shot burst sniper rifle feels very satisfying.
However, all this does come with a price, and the UI is rather limited. There isn't much chat going on in the zones, despite there being a large amount of people, mainly because of the console gamers, and it is very clear that it is a console port primarily designed for a controller rather than a PC game.
Lastly, I should mention the Arks that appear, since this is what the game is about. For those of you familiar with Rift, it's a bit like that (but with super fast cars and quads to get to each, rather than your typical pink donky with gold plated blinkers) and often these can get quite crowded. Loot is awared to you by how much you contributed, but you don't need to be high up in the scoreboard, in fact, you can turn up and heal one person and get awarded the max amount, though you won't be getting drops from the mobs obviously.
All in all, it is a very fun game. It has quite a bit of replay value, and might even appeal to those who enjoy MMO's but don't have the time to spend all day and night raiding.
Graphics = 7/10. The game is by no means ugly, but there is no wow factor.
Sounds = 7.5/10. Some of the weaponry really pumps your ear drums, but it's lacking any real ambience to pull you in
Music = 8.5/10 There are some good tracks, albeit they can be repeated a bit to much
Longevity = 7.5/10 I would sum this up in my own words as an "MMO Lite" sort of game. You can always pick it up and have some fun, you'd never get left behind but on the other foot, that doesn't give you incentive that you MUST log in otherwise you'd miss out, which in my opinion, is rather a low and dirty strategy from developers who do this, but sometimes, it's fun to be addicted.
Price = 9.5/10. This is very very good value for money. Especially when on sale!
Overall 7.8/10 I want to give this higher, I really do, but I don't feel it QUITE deserves an 8, but I don't think it deserves a 7.5 either.  78% still feels like I am doing the game injustice, as I'd highly recommend this game to anyone.

One of the most enjoyable co-op experiences I've had. Great puzzles, beautiful art style, cute characters, good music. Get a whole lot of mileage out of a handful of simple gameplay mechanics. You'll find yourself screaming in frustration,  shouting and pumping your fist in triumph, erupting in cathartic laughter as it finally seems you and your friend will accomplish the intricate, difficult procedure you've spent so long figuring out and attempting, only to see your friend make a stupid mistake and ruin everything at the last second.
The game only lets you communicate with your online parter by drawing blobby, imprecise lines onscreen. This could be seen as a drawback, but in fact it becomes its own meta-puzzle: how do I explain this detailed series of actions that will involve precise timing, without using any words? You come to develop a rudimentary syntax; you start saying yes and no by moving back and forth and jumping up and down, respectively, or you draw frantic scribbles on the screen to indicate frustration. It's so much more satisfying to solve puzzles this way; you really feel like you've accomplished something beyond the game itself. Of course there are also those infuriating moments when you give up trying to use the in-game language and resort to Steam chat, or even make a phone call and talk through it in real time. And then there are transcendent moments when you and your partner both know exactly what to do without attempting any communication at all.
It's also great fun to be a jerk and push your partner over cliffs or into enemies.
If I have only one criticism it's that if you're playing with more than one friend (say, one online and one IRL) there's no reliable way to keep track of which levels you've finished with each friend. Like, I beat the game with friend A while I was only a few levels in with friend B, and then I'd start up the game with friend B and some of the puzzles would start to seem mighty familiar, and I couldn't be sure if it was only because I'd already played them with friend A, or because I'd also already played them with friend B. You can reset ALL of your progress, which would have made it easier to kow where I was with friend B if I'd started with them AFTER beating the game with friend A, but I had two games going at the same time so deleting my progress with friend A would have deleted the friend B's progress as well, and it wouldn't have been fair to friend A, either, if we ever decided we wanted to go back and try to get all the crystals on certain levels without replaying all the others. The option for separate play "sessions" could have solved this (I always thought having three save slots in the Zelda games was overkill, but now I see the reasoning behind it). But, lengthy complaint notwithstanding, this is really a minor problem.
I was lucky enough to get this in a double pack as part of a bundle, but It's definitely worth the full price.

I am a WWII fanatic and I downloaded this game on a recommendation from a friend.  I will have to say, it is one of my favorite games right now.  It is chocked full of content and the game has very fun and very frustrating moments.  They have thought of many aspects of keeping your bomber in the air, completing the mission and bringing everyone home safely.  There are a few things that I wish they would change and a couple of additions that I think would great increase the survivability of the bomber.
Pros:
-Managing the crew during a mission is challenging, yet very fun and rewarding when you complete the objectives and make it home safely.
-The realism of failing systems, fuel shortages on long missions, the ability to lose crew members during flights and having crew members move about the aircraft to complete the different tasks is rewarding in its own way.
-Always having to return to base after a mission also provides that realism aspect of making it home safely.
Cons:
-The amount of money you receive from missions is limited and requires that you either choose priority to upgrade your bomber or outfit your crew.  You do not receive enough money to do both between missions
-The guns run out of ammo, way too quickly.  Please allow the ammo feed ability for all turrets, not just the tail gunner.  This would greatly reduce the amount of workload on you, while trying to keep your guns firing when swarmed by enemy fighters.
-You can install four turrets on the aircraft, but you can only have three gunners assigned to the base aircraft.  You can have other crew members man the turret, however, their aim is horrible, unless they reach level 5 and can gain the additional gunner skill.  I have only been able to reach level 5 with one crew member, as mine always get killed before reaching that high.
-The xp gained during each mission is very low and takes way to long to level your crew members.
Suggestions:
-Please allow for more crew members in the base bomber - at least one additional gunner to man all four turrets.
-Please add additional aircraft, such as the B-17, which has two waist gunner positions and two pilots.  This would allow for one pilot to leave the flight deck to assist with other duties on the aircraft.  With one pilot, they cannot leave the flight deck without the aircraft crashing.  If the pilot is killed or injured during the flight, the aircraft crashes without any ability to recover.
-Please provide more money and xp per mission.
Great game overall!!  Highly suggest it to anyone!!  Keep up the good work!!

Don't do it - it's addictive, but hugely flawed as a game. With an offensive deck you have three ways of winning: reduce the enemy health (9% of the time), wear them down till they run out of cards (1%) or disable their cards until they run out of viable placements (90%). This last strategy is so effective that the game ceases to be fun - whatever cards the opponent has, they're not going to be able to use them. It's not an AI problem, the AI is fairly good - the problem is that there are too many ways of getting a 2-card attack while the computer opponent is lining up the normally required 3 cards. Usually if you can disable the card in the middle of their board they will end up not having any moves they can make, and you just win. It's a fundamental flaw with the game design. And the writing is full of that annoying "zany" American humour that also ruined Psychonauts for me. I thought I was enjoying this at the time, but having completed it, I regret it sadly.

I got this game from the Humble Bundle store when it was heavily discounted and was excited to play it because I've always loved card games. I was satisfied with my gameplay experience.
The aesthetics are nice - the artstyle is cute and charming. There is a large variety of cards to collect and use, each with its own unique picture and text flavor. The sounds and music are decent, however, I quickly muted the latter in favor of my own. You can buy different game boards to place your cards on during matches, and your opponents will often have their own boards that are distinct from the default one. The story is highly reminiscent of a hybrid between Pokemon and Yu-Gi-Oh - you must obtain 8 legendary cards to qualify for a hefty gold prize, playing against an assortment of different characters along the way.
Controls are super simple and consist of mouse clicks. There is a helpful tutorial in the beginning that will show you most of the things you need to know, however, I found that some aspects of the game have to be discovered through play. For example, many possible strategies will be more salient to you when you've encountered them in a match - like using mainly defence cards to outlast/fatigue your opponent. The learning curve is minimal to moderate depending on your experience with trading card games. You may have to do a bit of grinding at times to farm enough cards/money to build better decks. A big thing I didn't like about this game is how you cannot just scrap decks (you can have 6 built at a time) to start from scratch - you have to manually click and drag 25 cards from your "deck list" to your "total cards list" one-at-a-time.
Gameplay consists of placing a single card from your hand of 5 onto a gameboard every turn - the board can hold a maximum of 9 cards, and filling it will cause you to lose the following turn. You will also start to take increasing damage every turn if you run out of cards. Cards have a certain number of differently-oriented arrows along the border. You must chain combos by matching up arrows between cards. Each card has an icon on it (a shield, sword, circle, or healing cross). Once you have matched at least 3 icons together (usually meaning 3 cards; they cannot all be circle icons), you will trigger an action. Shields provide you with +1 health/defence per icon, swords do +1 damage per defence icon, circles are neutral icons, and healing crosses will reactivate cards.
When you chain together an attack action, you can either attack your opponent's health, or one of his/her cards. Attacking a card (regardless of damage) will cause it to be deactivated, preventing it from being used to chain arrows. They will stay on the board, and accumulating too many disabled cards may result in you filling up your board with 9 cards, resulting a loss on your next turn. To revive cards, you must chain together healing icons. These cards are also useful because it will immediately remove all cards that are linked to it (possibly saving you from filling up your board with useless cards). Since cards with healing icons always have at least 2 icons, this means you can usually revive a card using only 2 cards (versus your usual 3 card set). Later, as you unlock more cards, you will encounter cards that may have 2 shield, sword, or circle icons.
Many cards will have an extra effect - for example, "placement" effect cards will trigger something (deal 1 damage to your opponent, gain +1 HP, or lose 1 card from your deck) once they are placed on the board. Other cards may rotate 180 degrees or move horizontally every turn, allowing you to pull off creative strategies and synergies. An effect you will frequently see is attack/defence/revive combos, which are effects triggered when using certain actions with that card. For example, a card may have an attack combo that removes a target card - using that card in an attack action will allow you to remove any card that has been played. Note, however, that chaining this card with different icon types (ex: shield) and using it to perform a different action (ex: increasing your HP) will not trigger the attack combo effect. Rarer cards will have multiple effects, and many cards with significant effects (ex: deal an extra +1 damage) will have a trade-off to balance things (card starts off deactivated, or it deals 1 damage to the owner whenever it is disabled).
Matches may be a best of 1, 3, or 5. At the end of every match, you will usually be given a booster pack with 5 cards of random rarity and/or some gold. You can sell cards at the mall for gold, and also purchase new ones. You may sometimes have to beat opponents before unlocking more difficult ones (including bosses that will give you a legendary card for beating them).
Overall, the game plays fairly well and is a nice time-filler for anyone interested in the trading card genre. The arrow-connect style of play is also a nice change from your typical Magic TCG/Yu-Gi-Oh style of placing monsters/characters to down to fight each other. Matches are usually very quick - easily one of the quickest trading card game I've encountered. If you enjoy playing with cards, then you should definitely give this a try.
Recommend!

This is a cool little single player CCG (i.e., it's all campaign play vs AI). The gameplay is vaguely similar to the Triple Triad minigame from Final Fantasy VIII, but with more cards and depth. Although there aren't as many fiendish combos as you'd get in a top CCG like Magic, there's still scope here to build decks based on damage, milling, denial, etc. The only negative is that you start off slowly with some crappy cards, and it takes a while for deckbuilding to become a serious option. The setting, art, and music are really fun so hopefully that gets you through the initial bit until the fiendish gameplay kicks in. I think this is a bargain at full price, and there's more like 18 hours of game here than the 8 hours they advertise. It also has mighty card battles in a gay bar and a haunted house, so tabletop gamers will feel right at home.

- Music is catchy. Sometimes the cheerfulness is a bit annoying if you're doing some mass crafting but otherwise it's not bad.
- Crafting is interesting. You'll experiment a lot trying to create the perfect bomb or potion!
Dislike:
- Some gameplay choices are pretty stupid.
- When delivering items to NPCs the game'll ask confirmation but it defaults to no. Press it accidentaly and it'll unselect all items, making a pain if you were choosing certain ones to deliver.
- Selling items is a chore as each NPC will only buy certain items which means you might have to travel to other cities.

As a long-time Atelier-series fan, I found this game quite enjoyable. I would like to share some pros and cons of this game.
Pros:
1. Huge map. Lots of quests. The content really worths its price tag.
2. As always, well-designed characters (with some stereotypes).
3. I heard scary stories regarding bugs in the earlier version but I found no bug so far in current version after 40+ hrs of play. There is one region that I saw slight drop in frame refresh rates on my system (i7 + GTX960) but nothing critical.
4. Japanese interface and subtitle - maybe not so important for most users on Steam, but I should say this is a huge step forward for the major Japanese game publisher on Steam. I really don't understand why the major Japanese publishers exclude Japanese interface / subtitle support in the list of languages. What's the point? Why only Japanese? Even though they included audio?
Cons:
1. Lack of transportation despite huge map - There is a landmark feature that you can jump between important locations within a regional map. Moreover, after the license exam, you can synthesize a flying broomstick that travels fast and flies over lake & river (...and also easy to ride & perfect for cleaning). However, there should be a way to make inter-region travel more efficiently, by single button press. It's not something new. There has been a feature like that in the past releases. But in this one, they made that huge world map, but there's no way to "warp" from one region to another, which I thought nonsense. Please let me know if any of you found the way. (Edit: It turns out there is a way. But I won't write detail since it will be a spoiler. Basically, you can create a flying ship and you can jump across regions. Still, you can only jump from the fireplaces)
2. Missing mass-production shop - This was one important aspect of the modern atelier series releases. I wonder why they removed it. Or maybe it's hidden somewhere?
In conclusion, I strongly recommend this game to all Atelier-series & JRPG fans. I wish I could recommend to everyone, but this game series requires some special characteristics from users who can do following:
1. You don't get upset even if your party at max level dies in single attack by an enemy boss.
2. You are ready to do seemingly tedius, repetitive work again and again to make the best bomb, armo, and accesories.
3. You become happy when you beat the enemy boss from #1 after countless trials of #2.
4. You become happier when you break the max damage record in a single bombing to the boss from #1.
5. You feel relieved when you found the most efficient way to complete all tasks and beat all bosses within shortest amount of days.

Take everything you know and love about the Atelier games, and combine that with an open world over ten times the size of the previous games. The result is Atelier Firis, one of the most ambitious and largest Atelier games to date.
Atelier Firis is the 18th game in the long running Atelier series, and the second game in the Mysterious trilogy. Firis, an energetic girl, hopes to take and pass the alchemist's license exam in order to fulfill her dream of traveling outside. Atelier Firis is by far the largest Atelier world in the entire series. In the previous installment, Atelier Sophie, the main character, Sophie, lives in Kirchen Bell. Sophie explores various fields around Kirchen Bell to harvest materials, and once she finishes gathering materials, she returns to her atelier back in Kirchen Bell. Now, in Atelier Firis, your atelier travels with you in the form of a tent! Gathering materials and exploring the world has never been easier.
Some notable differences from Atelier Sophie include the return of a time limit from older Atelier games. For Firis to gain her freedom outside, she is given a month to complete a few assignments to prove her ability to survive outside. After she leaves her hometown, Firis has one more generous time limit of a year to take and pass the license exam. After passing the license exam, the time limit is lifted and you are free to do whatever you please. Another notable difference is the revamp of the energy system. In Atelier Sophie, moving around the world map would use up some energy, also known as LP. In Atelier Firis, in addition to moving around the world, performing actions such as gathering materials and fishing will use up LP. Depending on the clothing and terrain of the area Firis explores, LP loss may increase. For example, not wearing proper clothing in the cold will accelerate LP loss.
The difficulty and battle system in Atelier Firis has changed since Atelier Sophie. Instead of selecting actions for all characters at once in one turn, each character performs actions on their turn, allowing for more complex strategies to be used. The obnoxious offensive and defensive battle stances have been removed and replaced with the new Chain Link gauge. As characters attack enemies, this gauge slowly rises. Once full, characters can perform powerful attacks and unleash their ultimate abilities, which can determine the win or loss of a battle.
The alchemy system has been improved since Atelier Sophie. Cauldrons have been removed and catalysts have been introduced. Each catalyst contains lines and patterns in the synthesis grid that give bonuses once the lines or patterns are filled. Some of the bonuses include increased final item quality and new transferrable traits to the final item.
New Game + has been added in Atelier Firis, allowing some progress such as character equipment and money to be carried over from a completed save into a new game. New Game + also unlocks some extra perks, such as the Very Hard difficulty balanced for New Game +.
Overall, Atelier Firis is a step up from previous Atelier games, and is my new favorite Atelier game in the series. The large open world and the extensive alchemy system keeps the game fun and exciting to play.

While the idea behind the game is very original (Use a twin-stick controller, where each stick controls one of the two characters), I found the execution lacking. I've had the main characters occasionally getting stuck behind geometry for no apparent reason and I've experienced some graphical bugs (you can find them on my profile) where there is a complete black figure a some kind of standin, which kind of acts like a spoiler of what is to come. I liked some parts of the game that felt really original, like where you walk in the night through a forest with wolves lurking or the giant battlefield (giving you credits for whose devs, I found those really cool), but those were my only two real highlights. The game clearly tries to win hearts over with the story and it's unique controls, but it just didn't cut it for me.
The game features some puzzles, but most of them are really basic. There are only a handfull that actually feel like it's emphasizing the whole cooperation of the two brothers which I like (navigating a long pipe through obstacles was one of them), and I really liked those. But that's about it.
For a game that is driven by it's story, I experienced quite some immersion breakers. These are caused by the graphical bugs I mentioned earlier, but also the fact that the two main characters must poses super human strength for most of the acrobatic feats they pull off. Pulling yourself up is one thing, but launching yourself in the same way for more than a length worth of distance... yeah... right...
Personally, I feel more things could have been done with a game like this. More puzzles that emphasize cooperation like you would in a normal world would really help. Also letting the smaller brother walk and climb just a little slower than the taller one would also have helped with immersion. And losing the super human strength and instead keep them just human would also really help a lot.
For it's price, I find it a bit steep. You might want to wait for a sale, as you can finish the game in about 2,5 hours, more if you want to get all the achievements. But if you don't happen to own a controller, let this game pass. I don't think it's worth it to buy a controller just to play this game (although I can recommend buying one nontheless ;) ).

Many years ago I played an Xbox Live Indie game called Red Box Reality: Fading Memories. It wasn’t anything special, but it was notable for the way it pitted your brain against itself. With one analogue stick you had to move a cursor around collecting blue orbs, with the other you had to simultaneously move a different cursor around blocking red orbs. Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons is kind of the puzzle-platformer version of that.
You control 2 brothers, an elder and a younger, one on each analogue stick, and each with their own action button. The boys father is deathly ill, and as he’s their only remaining parent they set off on a treacherous journey to find the cure. This means lots of one character opening a gate for the other, both pulling things, but also character specific stuff such as the younger brother being able to fit through gaps while the older is the one strong enough to pull levers.
The game world looks superb, it’s fairytale like in both look and tone. As you progress from your village the landscape changes dramatically, you’ll see caves and mines, dark forests, waterways, giant castles, all sorts of stuff. Considering one of the criticisms of the game would be how short it is (it took me around 3 hours I think), they do pack quite a lot in there for you to see, it kind of feels like you’ve travelled half the world rather than the county.
The problem with reviewing Brothers is that for me to tell you what’s great about it I would have to spoil stuff. There’s some moments towards the end of the game where gameplay ties to narrative beautifully, but it relies on the previous couple of hours of play to work, it relies on specific moments in fact, even acknowledging them in this form feels like I’m sailing close to the wind. It’s almost like this review is for people who have already played the game.
Brothers isn’t without its problems though, there’s a couple of bugs here and there, nothing game-breaking in my play-through, but I did have a moment where a character was handed an item but was clearly stood in the wrong place, the scene played out with the item just floating in the air, bobbing around and eventually walking off on its own.
The bigger issues are in the puzzle design. There’s maybe only 4 puzzles worth the name in Brothers, there’s lots of activating things, turning things, pulling things, but nothing that needs you to stop and think for a second bar a handful of sections. That in and of itself isn’t a problem, you’re controlling 2 characters at the same time, that is giving your brain a bit of a workout, and truth be told it was only approaching the end of the game I really noticed the lack of challenge. Towards the end I was going and activating things because they were in my path, it was where I needed to go, it was the only thing that could be interacted with, then I’d get an animation, an obstacle would be moved and the brothers would celebrate, but I didn’t even know the obstruction was there.
Once you get to the end it’s that sort of linearity that stops Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons from being truly special. But by “truly special” I mean “amongst the best games I’ve ever played” special, because it’s comfortably one of the better games I’ve played this year even if it is a bit content light. So, I feel like I’ve undersold it in this review, it’s not quite To The Moon, but it is an experience that will stay with you and you’ll want to talk about once you’ve beaten it, it’s well worth your time

Requires a Controller to Play
This game relys heavily on atmosphere to tell the story.  There is no dialogue outside of some vocalizations from the characters, but the music and the settings of each scene tell an emotional and engaging tale.  The overall setup reminds me of Journey, so if you are familiar with how that game tells it's tale, it is similar here.
The gameplay mechanics, primarily the use of each analog stick controlling one of the two brothers, are used frequently for simple platforming and puzzle solving.  These are not too difficult, often varied and unique to each situation the characters find themselves in, and almost always intuitive to solve.
It is a short, but highly memorable adventure that is worth playing if you are looking to get engaged into a story.

It is not often that I give MMO titles more than a passing cringe and brief denouncement. Most that I have had the misfortune to play - made tolerable only by the presence of close friends - have hardly measured up to even my most basic standards that I believe a video game should hold to. Most carry dreadful gameplay, uninspired mechanics, pay-to-win or pay-to-play service models, and more grinding than a hamburger factory.
To begin, the game's story - whether it is the fault of the developer or the writers behind the associated SyFy show of the same name - is one of the most forgettable I have ever seen. Dull characters, awkward dialogue, and uninspired motives mix together with a setting that isn't sure of what it wants to be. The game's background tries to be dystopian, it tries to be post-apocalyptic fiction, it tries to carry a science-fiction tone, and it tries to have some form of political intrigue. It fails to do any of this well. My most well-maintained memory was not of any gripping plot point or atmospheric element, but upon hearing an "alien" denounce humanity despite appearing quite human himself.

After taking leave for roughly five or six months, I've returned to find the following section of my review invalidated by updates that have greatly shifted the game towards traditional RPG leveling mechanics. Further still, additional changes have made the game scale to nearby players, forcing low level players to fight enemies balanced for substantially better equipped and leveled players.
In absence of a reverse of these changes - a doubtful prospect - or a much better refining of them, I cannot call Defiance much more than a mediocre MMORPG disguised as a third person shooter. All that I had seen as enjoyable from the game is slowly disappearing in front of me and both friends I play the game with have offered little disagreement.
What the game does well, however averagely it might do so, is break free from RPG tradition. Rather than having a linear progression of character potency, it instead features a mostly flat power curve. Players upgrade their character through primarily context-sensitive perks rather than direct boosts to their statistics, such as increased headshot damage when crouching. Weapon statistics remain the same throughout the entire game, meaning no weapon - save the slightly underpowered starting equipment - ever truly falls away as obsolete. Skilled shooter veterans fresh from the tutorial have a genuine chance to outperform senior players should they simply have greater skills.
Further, levels gained and the perks unlocked are done so in a relatively novel fashion. Rather than linear skill trees or railroaded classes, any player can take on any role with enough time invested into their character. Players unlock perks and the four main powers by following the EGO grid, which begins from one of the four powers - cloak, decoy, overcharge, and blur - that the player selects at the midpoint of the tutorial. Adjacent perks or even powers themselves can then be unlocked from any of those already earned, each of which can be upgraded twice - four times for powers - to better tailor the player towards a specific role. The player can then equip a limited number of these perks in one of their loadout templates, allowing them to have many varied equipment and skillsets allowing them quick adaptation to any combat situation.
As much as Defiance attempts to escape its MMO roots,  it is still an MMO through and through. Enemies appear from practically nowhere and are delivered directly on top of the player, rather than arriving naturally. Missions, sieges, and other events - while the latter two are interesting in their random nature - appear and pass by without consequence or any effect on the world itself. Enemy variety and the overall challenge presented leave something to be desired for the more skilled of players. Vehicle interaction is minimal; they offer few advantages in actual combat and disappear to the player's inventory quickly if left unattended.
In conclusion, I cannot call Defiance much more than a bargain bin game as much as it may prove to be my favorite MMO of all time - which isn't much of an achievement. Had it been the current retail standard of $50 at the time I acquired it, I would have laughed at the price and pleaded for the friend that gifted it to me to spend her money elsewhere. At $10, however, I believe it is worth the price of admission and I have definitely had my share of fun. Buyer beware, however; the game features no singleplayer and the death of its developer will take the game plunging down with it.

Also one must grind missions to level up and upgrade the bomber as not to be overwhelmed if one progresses to fast.
I managed to finish the campaign with only two alt-F4's (which were due to sending the pilot to rearm by mistake and thus crashing my craft). But the satisfaction of a job well done, the cute grimness of my crew, the feeling of saving dire situations  where my bomber is burning, crew is bleeding out, cirquits are popping, enemy aces are strafing, and just staying cool and meticulously fixing the problems with a cool head and finally landing on friendly soil is just so rewarding.
This game is compared to FTL, which I also adore, and there is a likeness in spirit. But Bomber Crew is original. It is also a good simulation of what it is, albeit with unrealistic gamey solutions. Having a fully trained and geared crew flying at high altitude over flak and searchlights on route to critical targets deep in enemy controlled europe is such a cosy and tense feeling I keep coming back just to be in its simplistically atmospheric world.
Highly recommended.
(Also, very glad to hear that it was a success and more content is on its way)

Many hours have I spent in Morrowind, and I still find myself unable to fully complete the game even aroud 100 hours in. Vvardenfell just makes me keep coming back with its diverse cultures, peoples, *cough cough* FALSE *cough cough* gods, history, and places to explore.
The soundtrack is very memorable and just outstanding, especially the main theme. Jermey Soule is really incredible at what he does and it shows here, and especially in Oblivion. The story is very engaging and good. Not only is there much more perspective from the antagonists than there is in Oblivion or Skyrim there is also just a much better sense of achievement when you do complete it for the first time. At the end you do truly feel like a god and true Nerevarine born again to stand with your people on Vvardenfell against threats abound. I mean you get to meet and talk to the very last dwarf on Tamriel which is really interesting. Also Azura's pretty cool I guess too, thanks Azura.
Vvardenfell might seem pretty small at first, but trust me it is not. Underneath the guise of it is a land full of monsterous creatures, dangerous weather climates induced by the volcano, countless interesting Dwemer ruins and Daedric shrines, bandit mines and cities that all feel completely different from each other. The great houses all have their ins and outs and all are interesting, especially the Telvanni who use giant mushrooms as places to live, which is really unique from any other game.
Armor designs are very good, and while they may not be as colorful or as detailed in texture, they have unique styles which differ from the other games in the series. The expansions are also simply awesome, with one being a slight continuation of the main story expanding upon the Tribunal, and the other being able to explore the harsh environment of Solstheim to the north-west all while dealing with Hircine and his werewolf followers.
Now gameplay...
Obviously Morrowind differs from a lot of other games, and it has not aged terribly well. Movement is slow at the start, you miss a lot at the start with your low skills in Agility and your particular weaponry, pretty much everyone hates you because you're an outlander and such, etc. But if you can manage to get past some of those flaws of the game, then it will only get better and better. Practically a whole new game opens up after that and it is really some of the most fun I have had in a game ever, exploring Vvardenfell and such, seeing and doing everything there is to see and do. Only a few hours of slightly unfun gameplay to acting like a normal human being and eventually become a god-like being afterwards.
There also is no leveled loot or enemies, which further adds to the sense of progression and accomplishment you get when you get past a certain obstacle you couldn't get past before. You really do have to let the game open up in order to enjoy it later, because those first few hours really are the hardest parts of the experience. Don't be afraid to look up guides and tips on how to enjoy it at the beginning, because I also hated this game too but as I played it more and started to get into it I began to see what everybody was raving about, what really is the game and how it is just so much fun.
Thanks old 2002 Bethesda, you really did a good job on this.

A Tale of Two Sons is all about the journey, and wow what a journey it is. The game is all about controlling two brothers at the same time, questing to find medicine to save their father from a terrible illness. You use the left and right analogs and triggers to manipulate their movements and actions. Each brother has a unique personality that complements a unique set of skills, and it's a lot of fun figuring out puzzles based on the character of each brother.
It's a game filled with puzzles and adventure and whose world welcomes you, not through a known spoken tongue, but by a common language that speaks to the heart, shared through a beautiful cinematic experience. The visuals and soundtrack are amazing, immersing you in everything from a humble town filled with busy people, to environments such as a a valley of dead warrior giants or a snowy town filled with inhabitants frozen in time.
Brothers - A Tales of Two Sons is an indie game that is a must-buy (and it's relatively cheap to boot). You can use a keybaord to play, but a controller is recommended.
