1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

I admire Gust for delivering a product outside of their comfort zone. However, even though the open world is the most exciting new addition, it also tends to bring the most problems with it. Atelier Firis will surly impress fans of the franchise, but could feel dated to modern RPG fans.
While still keeping its staple formula alive by maintaining the aspects of material gathering, simplistic turn-based battles, and alchemy, Atelier Firis is further improved by tweaking them in ways that’ll invite newcomers with open arms while keeping returning fans happy. While visually the game is a little rough, the sheer amount of things you can do and hours you’ll subsequently expend is endless. Atelier Firis: The Alchemist and the Mysterious Journey is a light-hearted and enjoyable JRPG where you can put your alchemy skills to the test.
These are really minor complaints, though, when stacked against the fact that Atelier Firis took me back to the innocence and joy in those Arland games that got me interested in the series in the first place. Most importantly, given that this is the first time that he’s helmed the creative side of an Atelier title, Shinichi Yoshiike has proven himself to be a confident and safe pair of hands to shape the series into the future. As such, I expect that this series will continue to remain my favourite among the more traditional JRPG franchises out there.
Despite its relatively flat cast, the game is a rather enjoyable experience that will feel well-rounded to fans of the series. The large map offers far more exploration opportunities than previous games did, which may help compensate for a pretty lackluster battle system. Smaller tweaks that combine older gameplay mechanics with some of the newer features from more recent titles like Atelier Sophie make Atelier Firis feel particularly special.
While still keeping its staple formula alive by maintaining the aspects of material gathering, simplistic turn-based battles, and alchemy, Atelier Firis is further improved by tweaking them in ways that’ll invite newcomers with open arms while keeping returning fans happy. While visually the game is a little rough, the sheer amount of things you can do and hours you’ll subsequently expend is endless. Atelier Firis: The Alchemist and the Mysterious Journey is a light-hearted and enjoyable JRPG where you can put your alchemy skills to the test.
This title certainly takes an interesting new turn in the franchise, improving some of its shortcomings, but not all of them. Still, a very good RPG Atelier fans should try.
Presentation(4)
The game world is stylized very well. The character models are incredibly detailed, the world is very large and diverse, much more than the last Atelier game, making it very fun to explore.
Gameplay(4)
While the battle system could be improved upon, synthesizing items is still a treat in this game. Throughout the game, players will have to explore, gather, collect recipes, and synthesize items together.
Lasting Appeal(4.5)
One might find themselves wanting to come back for more, even after beating the main game. There is so much to do that you might have to remind yourself to eat! The game sports multiple endings to encourage continued play, and the mix of the timed and untimed systems give everybody something to enjoy.
Final Verdict 4.3/5
Atelier Firis: The Alchemist of the Mysterious Journey is a game that can be played and enjoyed by both fans of the series, newcomers, and even people who would otherwise not consider it. It may not be a complete return to form for the series, but It does a great job of mixing both modern and classic Atelier games. I believe that it ranks slightly higher than the last entry.The presentation of the game is strong as well, with easy to navigate menus and plenty of shortcuts. The graphics are anime-chic, and definitely won’t wow you, but don’t let you down either. Perhaps most enjoyable is the music, and again this game allows you to use music from other titles in the Atelier family in place of the defaults.

Here are my observations. To be fair, I am not skilled enough to break open any logs or anything to know what is happening or why, but with the tools I have at hand this is what I saw.
Session 1:
1. The animations on menu items do not run at a smooth framerate. The particles kind of just jump around every couple of seconds.
2. At startup, the game loads my CPU up to 80% on all 8 threads and drops down to 5-10% and doesn't move from there. There is no meaningful change in CPU temperature.
3. GPU utilization floats between 50% and 60%, frame buffer sits around 30%, memory usage at 10% but the video engine does not appear to be used at all. It sits at a constant 0%, as if I haven't left the desktop. However there is no meaningful change in GPU temperature, either.
4. The game looks like absolute trash at 1080p. Like, it looks worse than Atelier Totori on the VITA (the best at-hand comparison I have). There are jagged edges, hard shadows and artefacts everywhere. Even facial features are somewhat blurry and mouths look jagged.
5. The 2D assets appear to be low resolution. They are not sharpened at all. I've seen anime at 480p with sharper 2D drawings for splashes than this game has.
Session 2:
1. The draw distance on this game is terrible, with distant objects flickering in and out of view depending on how you move around.
2. It seems to run at a stable framerate, but that could just be how far overspec I am for this game.
Still no meaningful jumps in CPU or GPU temperature.
Session 3:
1. 'Atlier' TRIGGERING INTENSIFIES!!
2. Following a comment from Kite on another thread, did some looking at light sources in the game and it looks like it has forced-on occlusion culling and still eats resources it in absolutely no way should require even if it didn't have occlusion culling on.
CPU loaded up to 100% across all eight threads for no discernible reason, temperature hit 58C. GPU temperature jumped up to 61C, with no obvious reason for that either. Normal CPU temperature for me is 32C and GPU is 44C.
I think that unless Koei Tecmo (and/or GUST) acknowledge and attempt to fix it themselves, this'll be yet another refund. This game eats system resources on a scale that Witcher 3 on ultra settings does not. I refuse to accept this kind of delivered product, no matter what platform I'm on but especially not on PC, and not at this price point. This is not a finished product. It's a mess.

tl;dr a 21 map expansion for DOOM II with exclusive levels created by renowned mappers in the community, they're pretty fun and it's worth picking up.
Tired of companies releasing shovelware CDs full of random WADs straight off idgames without giving iD a share of the revenue, iD contracted some of the best and most well known mappers in the DOOM community to make maps for iD's own official map pack.
This resulted in the 1995 release Master Levels for DOOM II.
The pack contains 20 single level wads (TEETH.WAD has a secret level, bringing the map count up to 21), almost an entire campaign worth of new levels.
Master Levels comes with a text mode frontend called Doom-It for launching individual wads in the collection.
Some parts of the original release were not included with the Digital version, such as Maximum Doom, which was a collection of 3201 random amateur maps downloaded off idgames. As you might expect these generally suffered in quality and had problems like some maps being DOOM 1 maps that were hastily ported to DOOM 2, which tended to break balance and cause additional problems. Some of the maps weren't even for DOOM but rather Heretic. However some of the maps were originally intended for Master Levels but didn't make it into the collection.
Other parts that weren't included were a poster, and id STUFF, a bunch of encrypted software that could be unlocked via phone order.
My thoughts on DOOM itself and the quality of the release here are the same as my other DOOM review.
Overall the quality of the map pack is great. The extra levels are a lot of fun and freshen up the DOOM experience.
A quick note, if you plan to play these using a modern ZDoom-compatible source port, check out
by Zippy, which is a replacement for Doom-It and allows you to launch the levels directly from the game.

Doom's Master Level is expansion pack for Doom 2, released in 1995. Actually, it is a small collection of fan-levels picked by Id Software. It uses interface, that will allow you to choose setting and level you want to play, without you having to mess with command line like people had to do when they wanted to play mods for original Doom games. Steam version of this comes free with any purchase of Doom 2 there. At least this is what I heard.
As usual, Steam version was screwed up as far as configuring DosBox goes. But at least interface works fine. As usual, you will have to change conf file in game directory, where you change "ddraw" line to "opengl" so DosBox will not lag hard. As usual, Setup was not included, and you will have to configure cfg file by hand, editing numbers in. As usual, it's Soundblaster by default when it comes to sound.
Collection includes around 20 levels made by fans of Doom. You will get to read info too in in-game interface. As you expect, none of them add anything new, not even new textures, aside from starry sky background. And it's quite a mixed bag. It has bad levels like Teeth, which is bad case of "FPS Elevator level", you got great levels like Black Tower, which is challenging and makes you feel like you are navigating through the tower. You got some levels that you can get through quickly, while most take some time. For sure you will have to pistol-start each level, as they aren't linked to each other. Which is nice, to me at least.
Didn't try mutliplayer there, not sure if supposed to work. Not messing with those ancient stuff myself. You can always pull wad file from game directory to use in Zandronum source port if you want to play some cooperative or survival on those levels.

A classic. No words can describe how great this classic and timeless adventure is as you journey through the land of Vvardenfell exploring a vast but differentiating landscape.

THE ELDER SCROLLS III: MORROWIND
(Please remember that while I do like this game a lot, I am not going to be biased. Also, this game is NOT nostalgic to me, I've only had it for a few years)
Morrowind is roleplaying game, released way back in 2002. Even thought it's pretty old, it's still a very fun game with tons of content, with or without the DLCs and mods. Morrowind's graphics aren't quite as good as it's successors, but aren't outdated enough to make the game ugly. The music is also pretty decent. Morrowind also has a large amount of weapons. Spears, Axes, Daggers, Swords, Claymores, Warhammers, Maces, Staves, Clubs, and more. Unlike the other TES games, Morrowind has 3 kinds of armor; Light, Heavy and Medium. Another thing Morrowind did was get rid of/put together a ton of skills Daggerfall introduced (e.g: Language skills, Swimming, Running, Jumping, etc...), making it much simpler. The story is also very unique. I'm not going to spoil this 15 year old game, but it is much more different than the old "Save the princess from the evil creature" cliche.
There are a few good mechanics that Morrowind inherited from it's predecessor.  Spellmaking and Enchanting are very useful for mages, the latter even being good for other classes too. Morrowind also introduced Alchemy, letting players
create potions and poisons (although unlike the later games, you cannot use poisons on weapons). Unlike in Daggerfall, where delving through a single dungeon could take hours, Morrowind's dungeons are much simpler and smaller (though this can be a bad thing depending on your opinion), so doing a quest that involves a dungeon doesn't take you too long. Magic is also different from Oblivion and Skyrim. You can levitate, teleport and much more!
The region of Vvardenfell itself is very creative. It has ashlands, HUGE mushrooms, a volcano, grasslands, and much more.
The factions in Morrowind are very diverse. There are many (the Imperial Cult, Imperial Legion, Houses Hlaalu, Redoran and Telvanni, the Mages/Fighters guild, etc...). Another thing that isn't in Skyrim and Oblivion is how other factions react to you. Let's say if you join the mages guild, members of the House Telvanni will NOT like you at all. Also, while you can join multiple factions, you can only join one House. Once you become a member, you can't join any of the two other houses. There is also a program called Construction set that lets you create or edit things in the game. This program is how mods are made.
Another mechanic that wasn't really in Arena and Daggerfall is voices. Although most dialogue isn't voiced, some things are (e.g: an npc welcoming you, or threatening you in battle). Morrowind also has a great amount of creatures- from rats, guars, alits, and nixhounds to clannfears, dremora, bonelords and WAY more, and this is just vanilla. The two DLCs (Tribunal and Bloodmoon) add even MORE content, including creatures, locations, weapons, and more. The journal system is also another thing I like about this game. Unlike in Oblivion and Skyrim, you won't just see a quest marker on your map. You have to actually go into your journal, and read for directions. However, this is another thing that can also be bad depending on your opinion. The game also has very rich lore.
Now we get to the cons, the bad things about this game. First is fighting. Unlike it's successors, aiming your weapon at the enemy and attacking won't always hit them. Even if you see that the sword or arrow is clearly touching them, it doesn't actually hit them. In this game, hitting enemies depends on your skill with that weapon. And since you start off usually with lower skills, you are going to be "missing" a lot. The animations are also pretty stiff, so you might want to get a mod for that. There are also a lot of bugs that can be rather annoying.
Vanilla Morrowind also has no followers (although some quests will have a NPC follow you), which kind of sucks. Another thing that can be a pro or con depending on your opinion, is that every creature and npc, even the ones neccessary for quests, can be killed. Unlike in Oblivion/Skyrim, the victim won't just get up again. They are actually dead. You fail the quest. When it comes to those NPCs that are neccessary for the main quest, they will still die, but once they do so, you will see a message box pop up, telling you how you have doomed the world, and that the only way to restore the prophecy is to load another save, or you can just keep playing in this doomed world. This also means you can kill literally every NPC, including the god Vivec. Also the NPCs don't really do anything. They just walk around a little. They don't even go in their houses when it gets dark.
Although there are some beautiful spots in Vvardenfell, a lot of Vvardenfell is bleak and grey looking, which can definitely   make the game less appealing to some people. There is also the fact that the only time the game autosaves is when you wait/sleep. So you may want to save more often.
My rating: 7.9/10
Morrowind is not perfect, but it has tons of content and for those who can get past the outdated fighting mechanic, the bugs and glitches and the dreary visuals, you will definitely find a fun game. Of course, no matter how many people love this game, it isn't for everyone.
Thank you for reading.

One of the most stirring and beautiful games that I've played in a long time.  The overall theme reminds me greatly of Ico, though it definitely has a personality of its own.  The game itself is rather short (~2 -3 hours,) but it leaves its mark, for me personally, as a game that I'm proud to have experienced.
Overall difficulty is low, though you still may die from time to time.  The controls are almost a character of their own.  They can get a bit confusing, but they ultimately make sense, and requiring a dual analog controller adds to the overall experience greatly, to include storytelling.
Also, interestingly enough, you can complete the game and gain no achievements.  All of them are for completely optional endeavors.  I like that.
I will recommend this to anyone who doesn't mind using a controller.  This is also the perfect game to invite a SO or family member to watch you play, regardless of their interest in gaming.  I already know which game I'll be gifting to friends in the near future.  Hint:  it's this one.

I bought the game on sale expecting an easy finish, unchallenging straightforward quests, and linear achievements (as I am fond of achievements). At first, I was impressed by the environment, the stellar character interactions without language translation, as well as the teamwork existing between the brothers. Throughout the game, as the cooperation of the brothers are 'tested' even more, the player feels a deep connection between the two, as if one cannot exist without the other, and symbolisms in the game made the game just that much more richer. The quest for the tree of life is a fair trade, and although there were many bugs I encountered throughout the game, I persisted to endure the journey as it was only a few chapters long. I cannot spoil the end, but the trade for me was the character development, as you see a flick of a 'switch' for the brothers, and that was the most AMAZING ending I have ever witnessed in my history of adventure games.
I give this game 9/10. I encountered two bugs that made me stuck for ages and that should cost 0.5 points each, and the rest were FLAWLESS. I am willing to trade my goal for achievements for the character development of this game, even wouldn't mind replaying some levels at all. But trust me, the breathtaking ending is worth your time and money!
Forget the reviews, forget the naysayers, Defiance is definitely worth a try. Despite some technical faults, the game is awesome and I would recommend it to anyone into MMO's, especially newcomers.

Port Review
There are good things and bad things about this port.  I decided to lean to the negative side because the graphics do not justify the high requirements for this game. Also there are PS4 graphical features missing. I'll reevaluate this review if KT/Gust ever releases a patch to address some issues. If you don't have a PC that exceeds recommend requirements and have a PS4 then the PS4 is a better option even though it has frame-drops as well.
Pros:
- Variable frame-rate. If you have a high refresh-rate monitor and a very powerful video card you can play this game above 60 fps.
- Synthesis does not have performance issue present in Atelier Sophie.  However, load is so low during Synthesis that powerful video cards may trigger power saving mode and drop below 60fps.  Workaround for Nvidia cards is to set "Power Management Mode" to "Prefer Maximum Performance" in Nvidia Control Panel.
- Supports 1440p and 4k resolutions.
Cons:
- Really demanding game.  The system requirements for this game are no joke and won't get you 1080p60fps.  For 1080p60 you're looking at a RX 470/GTX 1060 and can still have drops in areas with lots of effects/shadows.
- No Ambient Occlusion.  It exists in PS4 version.  Workaround is you can add it by using Reshade with MXAO shader, however will make game even more demanding.
- Missing Lighting that is present in the PS4 version.
- Low resolution 2D art assets. PS4 has higher resolution 2d assets. Update: Fixed in patch 1.0.0.13
- Blocky character outlines make it looks like there is a lot of aliasing. Reshade SMAA doesn't work to remove them because they are too large to detect.
- Shadows that disappear when source object moves off screen.
- Some flickering textures.
- Shadows that hit characters look broken.
- No AA options. FXAA can be forced in video card control panel or SMAA with Reshade/sweetFx.
- Only supports 5 different 16:9 resolutions.
Prologue using Reshade on high end video card.

- Portable Atelier!
- Sophie and Plachta
- Animations on the characters feel very, very smooth
- Far more open worldy than Sophie resulting in less time spent at loading screens
- Fast travel on the map
- Fast loading times (installed on SSD)
- PS3 controller support
- Lack of graphical settings: You get resolution, screen mode selection (windowed, fullscreen etc) and shadow quality. That's it.
- Performance issues. Bad. Just bad. GTX980 can't maintain solid 60 FPS at 1920x1080 all the time. Some areas just run at below 40-50 fps, and in some fights you might experience fps drops as well.
- Unable to run at 4k with stable 60 fps like with Sophie
- Shadows are flickering all over the place and disappearing randomly
If you want a smooth gaming experience from this title. Wait till performance issues have been fixed.

Take command of an RAF Lancaster bomber, with a diverse crew of differing strengths and backgrounds, as they fly across the English Channel to give a proper walloping upon the Jerries. Lots of bombing raids, a few supply drops, some (very lucrative) aerial recon photography, and lots of gunplay as the gunners knock enemy flighters out of the sky. But watch out for those Luftwaffe aces, whose sole mission is to knock you out of the sky.
Keep in mind that this is a game with a lot of grinding, and often with the same few missions available. This is for your benefit, and moreso for your crew and aircraft, because your crew can become more skilled and the bomber more powerful. And each segment of the campaign has a critical mission based on real-life RAF bombing missions like the Dambuster Raid. When the Aces are defeated, you get a nice chunk of change. But sometimes, even when you complete the mission, your plane might not be able to make it back to base and your only hope is for the survivability factors of both your bomber and your crew. High-level surviving crewmembers are worth more than their weight in quid. But dollars to donuts, this is a jolly good game which I recommend.

If you played the handheld Yu-gi-oh titles on GBA or DS, you man find this game entertaining in the same vein with much less complexity, less difficulty, and less grinding.
The formula for this game is as follows: Fight one of a few opponents, unlock new area with new opponents, repeat until you reach the end of the game.  Some opponents give you a booster pack upon winning, most give you money to buy single cards of.  Some areas you unlock let you recycle or combine cards for new cards.  Some areas make you battle in sequence without changing your deck, and some battles are best of 3 or 5.  Similar to Yu-Gi-Oh handhelds, but with a lot less blockading your progression than in those games and no grinding a fight 10-20 times to unlock a pack.
Game mechanics are fairly simple and fluid, but you may find yourself a little disappointed if you are used to MTG or Yu-gi-oh.  There aren't too many special tricks the player can do without a bit of grinding, meaning most times you will have a fairly rounded generic deck against themed decks.  This means a lot of fights will go to deck-outs since you will be even against other mixed decks, unable to break your opponent's defensive decks, and you don't encounter a truly difficult aggressive deck until midway through the game.  Taking this, I somewhat luckily found a card-mix recipe early that produced a strong milling card (Business Casual Man).  I made two of them a and sailed through most of the game easily with a mixed-mill deck, only adjusting my deck for 3 fights to be more defensive.  Only the mid-point aggressive boss and last boss required multiple tries to beat.
I ended the main game with a 56 W / 9 L score, and only battled a few optional fight-for-booster opponents multiple times.
There is optional postgame content against some difficult opponents, and you can complete a full collection if you are so inclined.
There is unfortunately no multiplayer, but I imagine the difficulty there lies in the problem of deck archetypes.  A strong burn / aggro deck is incredibly difficult to fight unless you have a defensive or disruptive deck, defensive-mill decks destroy any delay or mixed, etc.  It would come entirely down to archetype advantages determining who would win.
All in all, for $4 retail I'd say its not at all a bad game.  I got this game in a bundle, and I think its on iOS for $2.  If you see it at 50% off and want a casual game that's well-designed enough to appeal to gamers, then I'd say go for it.

Card City Nights is a lighthearted and simple card game.  It reminds me a bit of the Final Fantasy 8 card mini-game.  You and your opponent place cards on a 3x3 grid.  You link your cards together via connecting arrows and, depending on the card effects and icons, can either attack your opponent''s health, disable their cards, increase your own health, or revive your own cards (for the most part.)  You build your own card deck and unlock new cards as you go.  The AI is pretty mediocre.  It's enjoyable enough, but really would need another couple game mechanics and a better AI to really shine.
(Minor spoiler) The biggest negative I have against the game comes at the very end - the final boss is deliberately unfair.  They even say straight up that they don't have to follow the same rules as you do.  Just because the game's AI is♥♥♥♥♥♥doesn't mean that it's fair to balance it by straight up cheating.

This game is a work of art!
Plainly put, the graphics and story vibe the whole thing gives is a charming, casual feel - like you're going out to town for some friendly fun, which so happens to mean card games in this context. There is good humor and design in the art and characteres and presentation; it really draws you in by virtue of being friendly.
About the game itself? Masterpiece. This kind of card game is hard to come by - that is, a game that is played casually, with simple rules, but has an underlying complexity when determining strategy. It seems simply at first, and you'll steamroll the first few guys who are pretty aimless, but when the tricks start to come out, you can't help but be personally challenged! I was actually disappointed because I hoped for more development and more difficult tricks on the opponent's side to make things more interesting, but not because it bored me so much as it would keep me playing longer! As an added touch, it's the only card game I've ever seen where the players sit side-by-side instead of facing each other when they play.
Buy it? I already have it, but I would buy it at full price, even if the cost was doubled or so. No regrets here, at all.
It may not be the best as far as card games go but for £2.79? This game is incredibly fun and deserving of more recognition.

For a free game, it's very entertaining, and certainly worth trying if you are okay with making a separate account. The customization is impressive, graphics detailed, and performance generally good. Many parts of this game make it unique, but still has the classic MMORPG theme to it, making players of that genre already familiar with the gameplay. My complaints are that, while the game is certainly not Pay-To-Win, every indent and corner seems to have a slot for accepting money. They have implemented almost every form of premium goodies I can think of. This includes crates, skins, furniture, items, and equipment. There's even a cap to the amount of money you can have on hand, and you need to pay real money to access the extra. I do agree that the developers have put an astonishing amount of work and detail into the game, and the company should receive payment for it's work, but the game almost begs for it. If you can ignore the features added solely for sinking money, then I would definitely recommend giving this a go.
Oh, and the Bee-themed enemies are super annoying.

Open the lootbox and find out! What's upgrading the characters do? Why, increase their base health and damage, of course!
Since this is a mobile game, there's shoddy "matchmaking", meaning that whomever happens to be in the queue will be thrown together. Meaning Mr. I-Just-Downloaded-This will be playing against Mr. I-Don't-Know-What-A-Real-Game-Is-Like-So-I-Threw-Scrouge-Mc-Duck's-Entire-Fortune-At-This-Title.
Did I mention that lootboxes are essentially pay to open and make your character have statistical advantages?
Naturally, because this a mobile game, the experience of gameplay is secondary to all of those sweet lootboxes you'll open, so it's required in the EULA that while playing you will maintain a minimum ping of 100ms at all times with increasing spikes at random. And you can't jump. Or crouch. You can just WASD and sprint, and the game will decide if you vault over chest high walls or do a Mirror's Edge/Titanfall/Generic Action Game wallrun. And every character is a bulletsponge who can easily take over half a clip from an assault rifle to the face before expiring.

username: I Sware Im Not A W33b
text:
Core gameplay mechanics- Movement is extremely sluggish, the autoclimbing works on mobile but sucks on pc, and the animations look silly. Gunplay is terrible as the guns in this game have zero recoil and all handle and feel the same.
Gameplay balancing- It's pretty clear that the guys over at gameloft have absolutely no idea on how to balance a game. Ronen, a melee oriented agent has a crazy healthpool, insane damage, and the ability to dash. Dashing takes away all skill from a melee character, as you no longer need to close the distance, you can just sprint and press a button to dash forwards. To top it all off he has a super or ultimate that allows him to deflect bullets (instead they deal damage to the shooter). His ultimate also has one of the shortest cool downs in the game, so he will be constantly deflecting bullets during a match. (I am only at gold rank in this game, so I am assuming that at higher levels there will be more Ronens and other potentially broken agents)
P2W-  You get 3 free agents to start with. However it will take absurd amount of grinding to actually get another agent. The good agents in this game range from 7500-15000 korpens. As a reference I currently have over 3000 korpens (I have not spent any korpens at all, and I top frag almost every match). Modern Combat also has a upgrade system, where you can level up your agents to make them statically more powerful. This system needs to reworked as players can use real world money to level their agents, giving them a pretty significant advantage.
Closing words- To the average pc gamer, I tell you to steer clear from this mess, the core mechanics are not impressive at all and gameloft does not care about game balance. This is a pretty typical example of a lazy freemium game, it was created with intent to generate revenue rather than actually making a good product.
Advice to f2p gamers- There are a plethora of good f2p games out here in 2018, wether it be on steam or on their own websites. Low spec gamers should be fine in the f2p market as most games here are not graphically demanding.

Movement feels really floaty and you may as well have no control while in the air, so landing on trucks from long distances is basically impossible without a lot of luck. There are a few fun levels in the game, but you have to go through so many annoying or downright maddening levels in between to reach them. This game is not like Super Hexagon where it's difficult but fair, it throws cheap tricks at you constantly and relies heavily on random physics to create artificial difficulty.

There is so much to love about this game. Even in its simplicity it just sucks you in and keeps you playing for hours. You really get invested in the creatures you create and early decisions have long lasting effects with such a wide variety that replayablity is endless.
I have one major gripe with this game. There is no option for autosave. Now because of the size of the save files, it takes a few seconds to save, so I get why it was designed without autosave in mind but for the amount of complaining players have done since its release, this game should've been updated with an autosave feature as an option. The reason this bothers me so much, is because the game will occasionally crash.
The way the game plays tends to make you forget to frequently save. Between designing your cells, later your creatures, tribes and buildings and playing with them in between, you click on a "Save and Exit" button when you finish your design but this saves your creature, not your game. And you are not able to load that creature again when you go back to an old save. I originally had this review as a do not recommend, but with some tweaking the crashes have been brought to a minimum and the amount of fun this game has to offer is just out of this world.
Some players may be put off by the early stages and just want to put their creatures into the Space Stage of the game, but I feel that misses the point of Spore. While Spore offers you a "Creature Creator" that lets you design your creatures before you play with them, I prefer to create my creatures in the game using their history and experience to unlock DNA parts and giving them long lasting traits which result from your earliest decisions. You also get to share your creations and if logged on to the game, you will see the creatures of other players in your game as well. Overall I have to recommend this game.

NGD Studios does a great job bringing Adventure Time to the video game world with this epic hack ‘n slash adventure. Adventure Time: Finn and Jake’s Epic Quest is a fantastic game that mixes the great elements from RPGs with the awesome level schemes of ToeJam & Earl.
Adventure Time: Finn and Jake’s Epic Quest takes you out of the Land of Ooo and throws you into a new world that splits Ooo into floating islands. You play as Finn and Jake as they find themselves in a video game, which they use to explain all the weird elements. BMO has gone missing and it’s up to you to bring him back, but where is he? As you progress through the game you receive clues that help you find your lost comrade. In order to solve the mystery you must find artifacts scattered throughout the worlds, and eventually you will find the key.
The campaign is split across four worlds, which you can either run through quickly or if you take your time exploring every corner. Each world has six levels and a boss, which you must use different tactics to defeat. The first world is the Witch’s Garden (if you remember the show this is where Jake loses his powers for an episode because he stole a donut), Ice Kingdom, Fire Kingdom, and Land of the Dead. The levels have various minions which are all from the show, and you will fight bosses that are all characters who Finn and Jake got into scruffs with.
The game takes elements from hack ‘n slash titles and mixes it with that of ToeJam & Earl. In fact this game is almost exactly like Toe Jam and Earl except you can attack enemies. You find pages of the Enchiridion which you can use producing some sort of result either positive or negative. You can pay Princess Bubblegum to identify the pages, which if you ever find again it will remain identified (unless you use a page randomizer). Your character has a maximum level of 15, and every three levels you gain a new weapon. The weapons make your character stronger and grant them with special abilities. Jake is the powerhouse and Finn is for speed. As you progress throughout the game you will find keys which you can use to unlock chests, and you must search for artifacts. Similar to ToeJam & Earl you will be informed which levels artifacts are on so you don’t need to search every level. You can fall of the edges of the world which allows you to return to previous levels meaning you can go backwards in the campaign. Although unlike ToeJam & Earl you can only fall one level at a time, and the campaign seems to save the previous levels enemies so if you go back the levels are empty. The Enchiridion offers about thirty pages: two have negative results, three help you get across gorges, two of them give money, one of them gives health items, and the rest provide you with some sort of buff. Overall there are not too many pages, but you will enjoy them if you use them.
Adventure Time: Finn and Jake’s Epic Quest is a brilliant game that brings together elements of traditional Hack ‘n Slash and combines it with the greatness of ToeJam & Earl. I would not be amazed if the developers made this as a tribute to ToeJam & Earl. The game has four different bosses, loads of different enemies, crazy amounts of Enchiridion pages that give you special abilities, 24 levels (28 if you include boss fights), and quests that keep you going. If you like adventure games, RPGs, and Hack ‘n Slash this is the game for you.
Pros:
+Long campaign with 28 total levels, including boss fights.
+Loads of Enchiridion pages which allow you to essentially cast special spells.
+Fifteen levels, which allow you to become stronger.
+A funny story that brings Adventure Time to life.
+Great voice acting and awesome music.
+Four crazy boss fights that require you to use various tactics and strategies.
+Two different characters which you can switch through using different abilities.
+Decent graphics
Cons:
-The game can get rather repetitive; you definitely will want to take a break from it every now and then.
-When you fall off a level it puts you right at the end of the previous level.
-The audio volume settings are in the same page as the graphics settings (if you change the audio volume it also reapplies the graphic settings).
-There could be more Enchiridion pages, the book seems kind of bland at times and most of the pages seem to accomplish the same thing.
-There isn’t that much voice acting involved, there is very little conversation between any of the characters.
-Even on hard this game is ridiculously easy.

Most people might say this game is perfect in every single way, except in the combat mechanics.
That's where I disagree. This game has a 'chance to hit' based on your level in certain skills and magics. That's what a classic rpg was supposed to be, if you didn't dedicate to a build, or just didn't do a good job in making a build then you will find that combat in this game to be challenging and unpolished.
In Morrowind you create your character down to special traits. You create your very own person (you can even create your own skill class) and form your very own play style.  When the game starts you are given a simple task to go to this place, talk to this person. On your way there you will find various different paths in any direction you please, you can literally do whatever you want.
Morrowind will not spoon feed you! There are no quest markers, map or compass markers. You must find your own way in the game. You are forced to pay attention to details, and think for yourself. You must remember fictional names for things in a fictional language. You will get distracted constantly and lose your way. The guards are not pushovers, they will destroy you if you break the law, and the citizens will too. Everyone in the game hates you and will treat you like an outsider until you gain enough reknown status. This makes navigating in the game challenging and forces you to work on your relations with them. The npcs are not pushovers either, you will find in early stages of the game that there are OP characters in the game, they will destroy you Dark Souls style, and make you want to come back for them and exact your revenge.
You aren't playing a story that was written for you, you are playing YOUR story. This is an element that modern rpgs lack.
Bethesda will never be the same. This game is the perfect rpg, an rpg in it's purest form. As a die hard TES fan I hold this game in high regard, and it's my absolute favorite of the series.

This is a collection of 21 (including one secret) custom levels for
made by the fan community and originally released in late 1995. Be warned: the quality and difficulty of the levels vary, and they're usually not up to the par set by the Doom community's best-known works. This is more of a snapshot of Doom history than anything, taking then-contemporary 'masters' of Doom level creation and showcasing their talent.
The retail version of the Master Levels (as in the pre-Steam version) also contained 'Maximum Doom', about 1,830 amateur custom levels indiscriminately downloaded from the internet. It was iD's response to the shovelware discs containing thousands of Doom levels of extremely varying quality that were floating around at the time. You can read about it
and download it
if you
want to.
The Steam version comes with a level select program running in DOSBox, but you also receive the individual map files themselves. I would recommend loading these in a sourceport such as Chocolate Doom or ZDoom for a significantly improved playing experience. If you're using a ZDoom program, you could also use
. Some of them don't start on MAP01, so you may have to use a cheat code or the aforementioned map to switch levels.
Since you can only buy the Master Levels in a bundle with the other classic Doom games, I'd only really recommend this for Doom enthusiasts.

- a fun little jaunt by Tim Willits (a Strife level designer) through a Doom 2 style techbase in MAP01 style, except with tougher monsters.
- probably the best argument against playing these in alphabetical order. This one throws you straight into the deep end with lots of teleporting monsters, dangerous enclosed spaces and frankly frustrating progression. I will remind you that there is no shame in saving every once in a while on levels like these. Still pretty well-made and features notably tasteful usage of Hell marble textures.
- another slightly less challenging level from the same creator of BLACKTWR, Sverre Kvernmo. Devious but not too unforgiving, with the exception of the end area. Not as visually striking as BLACKTWR.
- another great MAP01 replacement by Willits. I'd say it's above ATTACK in terms of quality: it's bigger, badder and nicer-looking.
- appropriately named, this level has its moments but doesn't quite pack a punch altogether.
- punishing without feeling too frustrating, this night-sky techbase is a good challenge with interesting design.
- another fun and varied one with a surprise ending. Bit on the short side though.
- more frustrating than the last couple of levels, but still a solid entry.
- another distinctive nighttime level bigger than the last several entries, and a satisfying experience overall, especially the secrets.
- has some decent combat and great texturing/aesthetic layout, but perhaps a little too clever for its own good. I had to consult a walkthrough in order to figure out how to progress.
- perhaps the best argument against randomly selecting levels to play, at least if you pick this one first. Sverre decided to take the gloves off and prove he was serious about his difficult arena battles with lots of revenants and other projectile monsters, and a final boss fight that's actually
if you used all your rockets on the baddies that came before. It pulls the rug out from under you repeatedly, but it's oh so good to finally beat.
- this one throws the unexpected at you as well, but is more even-handed about it. It's also one of the larger maps in the collection, which is nice. The techbase-ish look is fairly appealing here too.
- tricky but kind of fun, like the little brother of the previous level.
- nicely constructed (if a little plain) and challenging but fair.
- apart from the Doom 2 enemies, this wouldn't feel out of place in an E1 throwback WAD. It's certainly an interesting one.
- a frustrating but memorable trek in a brick underground.
- Sverre saved the best for last apparently, judging by the powerful enemies in close quarters and ambush after ambush. Likely the hardest level in this entire collection. Also contains another (secret) level that flew under the radar.
- probably the second or third hardest level, after TEETH. Lot of tricks and traps here right out the gate, but with enough goodies to survive if you can manage to grab them. Pretty satisfying though.

Machinarium is a 2d point and click game developed by Amanita Design (renonwed for botanicula). You play as a robot named Josef who has to explore the city, helping other robots and stopping a plot by a malicious gang. The basic concept of the game is like old adventure games where you have to click on items on the screen to collect stuff and then use items to solve puzzles in one area before moving onto the next.
The Good
- Graphics have alot of detail
- Long play time
- Good plot
- Good atmosphere that draws you into the world
- Nice soundtrack
- Plenty of puzzles to solve
- Solution to puzzles available through completing minigame
The Bad
- Some puzzles don't give enough clues on how to solve them, so you may be forced to look at walkthroughs to complete the game.
- I found that moving josef around seemed a bit slow and would've liked it to be faster, especially when navigating different areas.
- If you move to a new area, you need to complete the minigame again to unlock the puzzle solutions for the previous area when you go back.

I really like playing this game! Defiance is now a free to play game so no investment other than your time is needed to play and enjoy this game.  I initially purchased Defiance while looking for something new to play with my family.  I did not have any expectations for this game and had never seen the Scify TV series, but I was surprised to see that even my wife liked it and she normally will not play a shooter, even if it is an MMORPG.
Defiance has a lot of good design features with it like dungeon/pvp grouping tools as well as a limitless questing network.  The game uses a feature for looting similar to Rift, also a TRION Worlds game, in that you do not have to be grouped to receive loot from a kill.  The game uses Rift's rift (outdoor raid) feature but calls them ark falls.  The game also uses a system that allows players to play with others at any level and still receive xp and loot.  This is a double side coin that can make game play feel very repetitive.
The leveling prgress in the game are not your typical 1-50 levels.  In defiance you level to 5000, although I do not believe it takes any longer than the more traditional level design of 1-50.  With your levels you get points to develope your character's talents/trates/perks. Unlike other MMORPGs, Definace does little to specialize classes/races.  Other than the Castithan race which gets to use a dagger/sword melee weapon, there is nothing special about picking the race or class at the beginning of the game.
Defiance's lore runs hand in hand with the popular TV series on the Syfy network.  The game and TV show writters/developers work with each other to make sure what one does, the other does as well. They even went as far a putting in a gamer's character into the show after holding a contest to pick the lucky gamer.
I really like the control and gameplay.  The loots system is great.  When doing an event or quest the item rewards are based on your level, not the zone.  The grouping system works very well for PvE and PvP.  The game is interwoven with the TV series.
Graphically, the character models could look better.  The game engine is last gen.  Because the NPCs adjust to the level appropriate for the gamer so to speak, the game feels repetitive even when completing new quests. And last, there is no class specialization or specialized class missions so there is no value in leveling more than one character which limits replay value.
Do I recommend it?  Absolutely!  It is a fun game that is now free to play so you have nothing to lose but the time investment of trying something new.

Bomber Crew was that game that we never realized we wanted until we got it. Games like this keep the game industry interesting, even if only for a moment.

This game was so much more than I expected it to be..
I remember first seeing this on the steam storefront and thinking it was just some simple, cutesy cartoon game with a WW2-ish skin on it where you just make sure ur little plane gets back in one piece without running out of fuel. Oh boy was I wrong.
Bomber Crew is the most unforgiving and (somewhat) realistic simulation of flying a bombing mission with a tin can bomber that might as well be made of paper. Each mission poses a very serious risk to your little cartoon crew, as the wrong choices in crew equipment and aircraft modifications can mean life or death depending on the mission. Fly a variety of bombing missions, carefuly traverse through formidable clouds of flak explosions, perform high altitude bombing runs while frantically sending crew about the fuselage to keep the cannons firing and the equipment operating. Make the right moves and you just might make it back to base.. albeit in a heavily perforated cheese grater that was once  a brand new Lancaster MK II bomber. My only real complaint with the game is the lost potential of having your bomber take part in realistically massive bombing raids into Germany with a sea of fellow bombers, though the map size is not necessarily condusive to such a massive scale attack. The game has so much potential and I'm surprised other devs haven't tried to create a similar game with a much more realistic design.
I guarantee you wont be able to put this game down after 2 missions. I highly recommend you buy this game!

For a game released in 2002 I would give this a thumbs up. I have played it many times before spending 80 hours plus each time on the non steam version and each time I had a blast. I even did a play through on the Oblivion mod version called Morroblivion. Other than graphics and combat mechanics it just didn't have the same feel as the original. I have also used the graphical overhaul mod which was great even with the couple of bugs it had.
The best part about this game is you actually feel like you are going on an adventure every time you leave Balmora. The only form of fast travel is silt striders and the mages guild teleporters. When you get a quest they tell you follow the river from this city until you find a bridge then find a way over the mountains to the west. I cannot tell you how many times I have got lost looking for an objective or went the wrong way and stumbled across something really cool. Like the guy who falls out of the sky and dies and drops acrobatics scrolls that fortify acrobatics 1000 points. If you use them you jump up in the sky so high you can't see anything because the games settings don't let you see that far and when you come down you die unless you use another one before you hit the ground. I enjoy this because most medieval games have satellites with gps capability and will direct you exactly where you need to go. After a while it just feels like you are playing the game just to play it. With Morrowind you never know exactly what you will run into unless you have already beat it 100%. I have wasted so much time exploring this game and I still have not explored everything. Each time I have new ideas how I want to play and even though the steam version doesn't show it I have played the disc version of this game for probably 500 hours and plan to put another 80 or so in this time around.
I see a lot of people say things like this “game is so overrated” or “the combat mechanics suck.” You have to remember this game is 15 years old and of course it is not going to have the same features that modern games have. I think that is what makes it so good. When you level up it doesn't just feel like you gained some stats but your guy actually got a little stronger. The skills and attributes are meaningful for example higher acrobatics means you can jump higher, higher speed means you can run faster. Modern games are all about leveling up to just do more damage or survive longer and Morrowind does that as well. The dice roll can be pretty annoying at times with enchanting for example, use a powerful 60,000 gold value soul gem and your enchantment fails, but with the PC version you can either mod away the annoying parts or just open the console and give yourself a way higher enchanting skill. I have not seen any “paid mods” unless people are talking about the construction set not being included but all of the best mods were free long before they did that anyways and are still free.
I would give this game a solid 10/10 when comparing it to other games of that generation. This game is a classic and is still worth more than the asking price of 14.99 at the time of this post.

Card City Nights does multiple jobs and it does them all very well. First off, it serves a satire of other TCG shows and games. If you've played the Pokemon TCG game for the gameboy color, you will notice the parallels. Parallels which are twisted into a funny, lighthearted experience. At the same time it is a crossover of many of Ludosity's different titles. If you're like me, the only character is recognized was the protagonist of Ittle Dew, a game I still haven't played (for now).  The game developers did not let this stop them from making the experience enjoyable, and made the rather smart decision of making said characters alternate versions that reflect the original form's personality and behavior but belong exclusively to that world. The visual designs have also been updated to maximize the effect. And as a result, the cards you collect become more enjoyable, as you draw the parallels between the characters of Card City Nights and the characters of the original games. And speaking of cards, the actual game is a nice, casual experience. The developers were able to take a rather simple concept for a card game, and still make it enjoyable. The music is wonderful as well. It is a light treat for the ears that doesn't provide any distractions that might ruin your cool strategies. My one complaint is that the game is only single player, but the games build up as a casual adventure doesn't really allow for that. I would recommend this game if you love TCGs and/or are looking for a casual experience. I also recommend you experience with different decks and go for all of the achievements. With only 8 achievements, it is very easy to obtain 100% completion for this game. Happy dueling, and may the 8 Legendaries fall into your hands!

This is THE PRIME of classic western CRPGs. This game obviously has it's flaws, but it can still be enjoyed rather easily.
This game does not have the grandest or most interesting beginning. You are a nameless prisoner, and are left to determine your character through the narrative. After getting off of a boat in the territory of Vvardenfell, filing some paperwork, and getting some orders to deliver a package to someone in Balmora. After this, you are on your own. This can be slightly overwheming and confusing in the beginning, but this game pulls off the "figure it out yourself" quest style well.
I won't tell too much about the main story, but it is around 60 hours long and is very well done. Alongside the main story, you have the many diverse guilds to join (this game has the most guilds of all of the modern TES games) and the countless hours of side quests available. THIS GAME HAS NO QUEST MARKERS. this is important to know if you are coming from Oblivion or Skyrim, as you won't be given exactly where you have to go and have to rely on somewhat vague hints to find our way around. Probably the only negative to this game's questing is the journal system. With the Tribunal DLC (which is included in this game) the journal saw some slight improvements. The journal is somewhat difficult to navigate, but besides that, this game's questing is fantastic.
This game does not play very differently than the next game in the series, Oblivion. The most noticable difference is the combat. The diceroll-based combat system is probably the most common point of complaint with this game's gameplay. Rather than the combat being based on if your weapon hits or not, it is based off of perecents and stats. In the beginning of the game, the combat can be especially annoying since you will miss most of your swings with your low level combat skills. After a few hours of playing and leveling up your combat skills along the way, the combat becomes much more bearable. THE COMBAT IS NOT THAT BAD. JUST DON'T GIVE UP ON IT. This game also has no fast travel system like it's sequels, so you will be walking or buying rides everywhere.
The world in Morrowind masterfully designed. Unlike it's sequels, it has a very alien and unearthly aesthetic to the whole place, and I LOVE IT. The games after it in the series could easily pass as real world places. This games map is the smallest of the modern TES games, but it feels huge due to the slow movement speed.
I'd recommend this game to anyone who thinks the modern TES games lack depth, or anyone who wants a great western CRPG. This game is worth it's normal price of 15 USD, and the sale price of 7.49 USD is an absolute steal.
Best Elder Scrolls game, period. So much more polish than Oblivion, and so much more fun to play than Skyrim. There is limitless possiblilities, and the main questline feels like a mere afterthought.

I was just feeling bad about leaving a bad review for Fallout 4 due to the Creation Club drama. Even though what Bethesda is doing right now cannot be justified, my review really comes from a place of caring because I love pretty much  everything about all of their games, even the often poorly regarded Fallout 4. As I'm playing through Morrowind right now, I thought: "Why not use my recent experience to talk about what I love about these games?"
This game has so much effort put into it. Through books, NPCs or simply by observing the game world, you can really see how the game world works. Everything feels genuine and your status as outlander in the province of Morrowind gives you a justified outsider's view through which to learn all this. The Dunmer are one of the most fleshed out civilisations in fiction full-stop, instead of being the usual "like humans but X" or "like Y human culture but they have scales". You really feel a part of the world, even with the janky graphics and numerous glitches.
The RPG mechanics are also very expansive. It's not very complicated in the grand scheme of things, but you can really have fun with it if you figure out the fine details. Stuff like the "Fortify Intelligence Singularity" and the Elder Scrolls' trademark spellmaking system allow the player to break the game as much or as little as you like: it just depends on what you want out of the game.
The quests are also quite interesting. While not on the level of Oblivion and Skyrim in terms of personality, a lot of the challenge in Morrowind quests lie outside the combat, with the player being given several options to complete quests using different skills suited to whatever playstyle/character archetypes you like.
There's also the more typical Bethesda stuff like the beautiful open world and mods, but unless you've been living under a rock, you probably already knew that. Yes, there's bugs. There's terrible in-game directions and terrible collision problems. The combat can really suck, with damage sponge enemies and more than a few unfair deaths at the hands of dumb enemies who singlemindedly charge at you like lemmings. The world is tiny relative to other Bethesda titles. One of the cities is the same building copy-pasted several times (Vivec) with one of those buildings by itself making up yet another city (Molag Mar). The SFX can get pretty awful with the broken-record enemy damage noises and the ear-destroying rainfall sound. But beneath all those problems (most of them fixable by mods anyway) are hundreds of hours to be enjoyed.
I would recommend Morrowind to anyone who has enjoyed Oblivion and Skyrim. I started with Oblivion and I got into Morrowind no problem. Play with no mods the first time, it's better that way. Unless you're installing bugfixes. Don't forget to steal the Limeware Platter.
And for crying out loud, stop leaving bad reviews on Morrowind because of the Creation Club. Save your protest reviews for SKSE and Fallout 4, they're the ones that are getting paid mods in the first place and Bethesda needs a good reminder of what they've done right in the past just as much as what they're doing wrong right now.

My first introduction to Elder Scrolls III was back in 2003, one of my best friend's older brother had it for PC and was kind enough to let his younger brother his friend (me) play around with it. I've never felt a more relaxing sound as this home screen and the music.  Enough anecedotal BS though, I just wanted to provide backstory as I have a heavy nostalgia bias. I've only had it on steam for a while but I've played the game on Original Xbox and retail disc for PC for 15 years or so.
(My personal beliefs on what makes a game good or bad is of course subjective if you disagree that's totally fine!)
What's Great!
-No hand holding introductory sequence. You leave the boat make your PC and are released into the world. This makes new character runs so nice as you don't have to go through annoying starter dungeons like in Oblivion or Skyrim for that matter.  Even Daggerfall had one as well.
-Magic is varied and has many amazing spells that were never used again like Levitate!
-Ranged isn't just bows, you had throwing weapons and crossbows!
-Fast Travel at fixed points so you slow down and take in the world's beauty and music.
-Weapons have their own skill line. Knowing how to use an Axe doesn't mean you know how to use a sword.  I strongly dislike the degradation into one handed or two handed. Also Spears!
-Did I mention the music! Oh my the music is so soothing and makes me feel at ease, my favorite soundtrack to a video game of all time.
-Quest's don't have a stupid waypoint constantly showing you your objective. This kills my enjoyment of the quest I'm doing and make's them too easy.
-Combat makes more sense than in other games to me.  In perspective, if you run up to a man with a dagger and you've used a dagger maybe twice in your life to open a letter you will have a higher chance of stabbing yourself then doing damage to an opponent.  Visually it's hard to grasp how you swung and "connected" but didn't hit but if you use something you know how to weild it's rarely an issue.
-Main Quest is obtainable even if you screw up the normal route by accident.
-Armor is sectioned into light medium and heavy PLUS unarmoured skill line
-Unarmed is super cool as it drains fatigue and you can knock enemies out, then you can kill them (I've beat the game with unarmed as my main damage skill excluding using certain story tools)
-Lot's of factions all needing certain skill sets to attain!
-Sorry the PC is not an all doing god, so you can rarely become the Arch Mage, Fighter's Guild Champion, High Priest of the Tribunal etc, you have to attain certain attribute levels and skill levels to rank up in a faction. You may not of the ability to get all of those but that also encourages you to make other characters and play styles.
-ETC. I can go on and on but let me warn you of the bad things.
Not so Great
-Bugs with some skills and quests which requires mods to fix normally.
-Cliff Racers may haunt your dreams.  I can recognize that sound effect anytime it's used, seriously those things have always spooked me.
-Sound effects can be a little borked, play with the settings to see what works for you.
-Character creator is pretty dated and the models are kind of bad.
-Diseases are downright brutal especially blight related ones, ALWAYS bring blight curing things or you'll find yourself screwed.
-If you mess with the law too much you can get a death warrant. It makes sense but it can make doing things a hassle.
-Not having any magic can become a hassle in some areas.
-Not an easy game to pick up and very old values may leave younger players feeling confused.  It's very close to a tabletop rpg's character set-up and non nerds don't usually enjoy that sort of thing. (thankfully I'm a mega-nerd.)
That's about the gist of it, I could include more in both sections but it would be unending.
tl,dr ;
A great but dated game for classic Rpg fans with amazing scenery and music.

Card City Nights is a fun and challenging single player grid base card game. In the game you play as a kid who just found out about a new card game that has become real popular. By playing with some kids you find out about 8 Legendary cards that if all collected let you face the card king. The gameplay is a 3-3 grid per player where you place cards with arrows any try to connect them for combo effects. There are 4 different types of cards Attack (damage/disable), Defense (heal), Revive (recover disable) and Neutral (any). Comboing cards and using special effects makes the game a blast. You can build your deck however you want and there are a lot of ways to beak opponents such as milling, (removing cards from deck) or board crowding (filling up opponents board). Every deck has its weakness and even the best player is vulnerable. The cards themselves are past games the developer has done and its adds nice style and character to the game. The price for the game itself is a steal at 4 dollars due to the game lasting 12+ hours. Overall if you have any interest in card games or want to see a new version of Triple Triad pick up this game now!

This expansion for Doom II is only available through Doom Classic Complete, which I highly recommend. The Doom series was a popular series in the 90s and has had another game recently: Doom II. The expansion pack consists of 20 "WADs", with one WAD containing a secret level [the first screenshot on the store page]. Think of this as a bonus, as steam has yet to sell this separately.
This game runs via the acclaimed emulator DOSBOX, and you will find a copy of the application in the Steam directory. You will be able to select WADs via the Doom-It interface, where you can select one of the 20 levels. The WADs are extremely well designed and my personal favourites are TEETH and MANOR. However, this game is certainly not for everyone.
Try the Doom I shareware on DOSGames using DOSBox before you make a purchase. If you don't like the limitations from the original DOS version, you can copy the WADs into a source port's directory [such as ZDoom and PrBoomPlus] and you can play it from there. They introduce new High Definition graphics and add jumping and aiming abilities.
I cannot give this a score as it is not identifiable as a standalone title; you will need Doom II to play this so that is why Steam doesn't sell it separately. Overall, this is a great modification for Doom II. If you want to use other mods on Doom 2, you will need to use this command on DOSBox Doom2.exe -file [Mod].wad.

TL;DR:  Worth picking up if you find it on sale.
This game pleasantly surprised me.  I managed to pick it up on Steam Summer Sale for 50% off.  It gets -slightly- repetitive while levelling, but no where near as much as most MMO / Grindfests.  It mixes MMO / 3rd-Person Shooter exceptionally well, and it doesn't try to force you to work with people (you can run through the entire storyline solo).  It's multiplayer offers several different modes of PvP combat, Co-Op missions, and a Rift-Like system called "Arks".  You are an Ark-Hunter, after all, and choosing to  help your fellow players in these big (sometimes massive) battles is rewarding both visually and inventorily.
Also, Vehicles!  In an mmo.  Summonable, like mounts, but vehicles!  And they act properly like vehicles.  That's almost a miracle.
All of that said, this game is still pretty easy to put down.  Despite everything I like about it, I don't think I would be nearly as happy with the game if I had paid full price.  For everything it does that is unique, there are 2 other things copy and pasted from previous MMO's.  I suppose that's to be expected.
The characters can be a little dry at times, but the storyline is solid.  Character creation is GREAT for a FPS, and Lacking for an MMO.
Buy it if it's on sale.  It's worth it.  I don't recommend paying full price.

Very beautiful adventure game with a fantastic artstyle. Splendid graphics contributing to render an extraordinary universe. The whole "city" where the action takes place is astonishing, full of details and surprises. You can easily get totally immersed in it.

All puzzles are of good value : those found in mini-games as well as those you have to solve with your character to progress in the story, getting to the next scene etc..

I'm Not Recommending "Machinarium."  My reasons exactly follow all the other negative reviews here.  On the plus side, nice graphics and sound.  On the negative side, almost every puzzle is a point-and-click hunt for arbitrary, non-sensical solutions.  There's absolutely no way to do these puzzles without a walkthrough since there's no way to know what you're supposed to do until after you've done it.  A puzzle game should let you figure things out based on environmental clues and themes -- not just by randomly trying things you click on until something happens.  This is nothing but a nice-looking and nice-sounding PITA.

Growing up I had a couple of domino sets designed to set up and knock down. My friend and I would set them up, knock 'em down, gather all sorts of stuff to incorporate into our runs. I still have my sets and my kids enjoy playing with them, but not as much as I did.
Enter Domino Sky. A video game where you can set 'em up and knock 'em down, but without the mess. This is a puzzle game where you have a set number of dominoes you can place. You must hit each of the checkpoints in the level before a star will light up. Hit that star (after it is lit) and you advance to the next level. There is also a freeform area where you can set-up whatever you want and knock it down.
The puzzles aren't too difficult in theory. There are new things that are introduced to spice it up: rotating and moving platforms, large blue "dominoes" you have to hit hard, orange platforms you can't build on, but need to find a way around. There are even some levels in space where the dominoes don't fall and continue on without any resistance.
As I said, the puzzles aren't too difficult in theory. In reality, the physics engine for this game sucks. Set up some dominoes, knock them down 10 times and they will not fall the exact same way any of the 10 times. I think they fall differently based on the camera view but not certain. There is one puzzle with some conveyors and not only do the dominoes fall differently, I noticed they move at different speeds on the conveyor. In the several puzzles that timing and placement matters, this becomes a frustrating exercise of trial and error with a huge helping of luck. Not fun.
The other issue is you can only place dominoes on the surface. There is no stacking of dominoes on top of each other to create pyramids or other neat structures. In free form mode, all you have is a large flat area. You can't add any of the "fun" structures from the puzzles to create your own designs.
I find this game very hard to recommend.

This trading card battle game is the perfect game for me. It emphasizes positioning with the various card abilities. The cards are on a 9x9 grid (like tic tac toe), and you can win by full out assault, by making your opponent run out of spots to place cards, or by making your opponent discard to zero cards. The AI is terrible in the beginning, letting you experiment with different strategies. By the time the game increases in difficulty, you will have some legendary and rare cards to deal with it.
The downsides are that the game only has a story mode (no multiplayer). The art style may turn people off too, but I like the charm of the characters and cartoon nature of it. The company that makes this game makes apps too, but I've never played any of them, so I don't recognize any of the characters.
This charming, strategic card game is $4, and you will easily get your monies worth. I highly recommend this game.

I wasn't sure what to think about this game when I picked it up, but for the price of $3.99, I figured at the worst, I wouldn't be out anything much more than my pride...  I've been an avid player of CCGs for a number of years and I've seen some great ones and some terrible ones, both in physical and in digital formats.  This is one of the better ones.  I wouldn't say it's a great CCG, but it's definitely not the worst, nor is it even close to being so.  It's quite good.
The game's mechanic of connecting points at the sides and corners of the cards took me a little getting used to as it's different to what I'm used to as far as making attacks, but once I figured out how to effectively build a deck, it's fun.
Speaking of deck building, one awesome feature of this game is that it's a one-time purchase.  You buy it and you get access to all of the cards in the game via gameplay (either by winning them, getting them in booster packs, or buying them with in-game currency).  None of that "buy the game for $20 and then pay $1 for boosters" crap.  This game knows that's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and it deosn't play that way.  It loves you and understands that your money is valuable to you.
The artwork is a little "meh", but it's whimsical at teh same time.  I've never played the game that it's based on, Ittle Dew, but maybe that's part of the charm that I don't get because of that.  The humor in the game is clean and chuckleworthy.  The game has in-game strategy help via talking to the characters in the game.  Unfortunately, the in-game characters are the only ones that you'll meet as there is no multiplayer support.  My only real complaint here is this, but, it's a BIG one.  This game is fun but after you beat it (which takes all of about 8-12 hours, from what I hear).  My only other complaint is that there's no cloud saves.  If this could happen, I might buy the mobile version to play on the go.  Fix both these issues, and you've got a classic...
From what I've played so far, this game is quickly becoming a new favorite of mine.  If you like CCGs, whimsy, and good clean fun, try this one on for size.     7/10

I was just feeling bad about leaving a bad review for Fallout 4 due to the Creation Club drama. Even though what Bethesda is doing right now cannot be justified, my review really comes from a place of caring because I love pretty much  everything about all of their games, even the often poorly regarded Fallout 4. As I'm playing through Morrowind right now, I thought: "Why not use my recent experience to talk about what I love about these games?"
This game has so much effort put into it. Through books, NPCs or simply by observing the game world, you can really see how the game world works. Everything feels genuine and your status as outlander in the province of Morrowind gives you a justified outsider's view through which to learn all this. The Dunmer are one of the most fleshed out civilisations in fiction full-stop, instead of being the usual "like humans but X" or "like Y human culture but they have scales". You really feel a part of the world, even with the janky graphics and numerous glitches.
The RPG mechanics are also very expansive. It's not very complicated in the grand scheme of things, but you can really have fun with it if you figure out the fine details. Stuff like the "Fortify Intelligence Singularity" and the Elder Scrolls' trademark spellmaking system allow the player to break the game as much or as little as you like: it just depends on what you want out of the game.
The quests are also quite interesting. While not on the level of Oblivion and Skyrim in terms of personality, a lot of the challenge in Morrowind quests lie outside the combat, with the player being given several options to complete quests using different skills suited to whatever playstyle/character archetypes you like.
There's also the more typical Bethesda stuff like the beautiful open world and mods, but unless you've been living under a rock, you probably already knew that. Yes, there's bugs. There's terrible in-game directions and terrible collision problems. The combat can really suck, with damage sponge enemies and more than a few unfair deaths at the hands of dumb enemies who singlemindedly charge at you like lemmings. The world is tiny relative to other Bethesda titles. One of the cities is the same building copy-pasted several times (Vivec) with one of those buildings by itself making up yet another city (Molag Mar). The SFX can get pretty awful with the broken-record enemy damage noises and the ear-destroying rainfall sound. But beneath all those problems (most of them fixable by mods anyway) are hundreds of hours to be enjoyed.
I would recommend Morrowind to anyone who has enjoyed Oblivion and Skyrim. I started with Oblivion and I got into Morrowind no problem. Play with no mods the first time, it's better that way. Unless you're installing bugfixes. Don't forget to steal the Limeware Platter.
And for crying out loud, stop leaving bad reviews on Morrowind because of the Creation Club. Save your protest reviews for SKSE and Fallout 4, they're the ones that are getting paid mods in the first place and Bethesda needs a good reminder of what they've done right in the past just as much as what they're doing wrong right now.
