My first introduction to Elder Scrolls III was back in 2003, one of my best friend's older brother had it for PC and was kind enough to let his younger brother his friend (me) play around with it. I've never felt a more relaxing sound as this home screen and the music.  Enough anecedotal BS though, I just wanted to provide backstory as I have a heavy nostalgia bias. I've only had it on steam for a while but I've played the game on Original Xbox and retail disc for PC for 15 years or so.
(My personal beliefs on what makes a game good or bad is of course subjective if you disagree that's totally fine!)
What's Great!
-No hand holding introductory sequence. You leave the boat make your PC and are released into the world. This makes new character runs so nice as you don't have to go through annoying starter dungeons like in Oblivion or Skyrim for that matter.  Even Daggerfall had one as well.
-Magic is varied and has many amazing spells that were never used again like Levitate!
-Ranged isn't just bows, you had throwing weapons and crossbows!
-Fast Travel at fixed points so you slow down and take in the world's beauty and music.
-Weapons have their own skill line. Knowing how to use an Axe doesn't mean you know how to use a sword.  I strongly dislike the degradation into one handed or two handed. Also Spears!
-Did I mention the music! Oh my the music is so soothing and makes me feel at ease, my favorite soundtrack to a video game of all time.
-Quest's don't have a stupid waypoint constantly showing you your objective. This kills my enjoyment of the quest I'm doing and make's them too easy.
-Combat makes more sense than in other games to me.  In perspective, if you run up to a man with a dagger and you've used a dagger maybe twice in your life to open a letter you will have a higher chance of stabbing yourself then doing damage to an opponent.  Visually it's hard to grasp how you swung and "connected" but didn't hit but if you use something you know how to weild it's rarely an issue.
-Main Quest is obtainable even if you screw up the normal route by accident.
-Armor is sectioned into light medium and heavy PLUS unarmoured skill line
-Unarmed is super cool as it drains fatigue and you can knock enemies out, then you can kill them (I've beat the game with unarmed as my main damage skill excluding using certain story tools)
-Lot's of factions all needing certain skill sets to attain!
-Sorry the PC is not an all doing god, so you can rarely become the Arch Mage, Fighter's Guild Champion, High Priest of the Tribunal etc, you have to attain certain attribute levels and skill levels to rank up in a faction. You may not of the ability to get all of those but that also encourages you to make other characters and play styles.
-ETC. I can go on and on but let me warn you of the bad things.
Not so Great
-Bugs with some skills and quests which requires mods to fix normally.
-Cliff Racers may haunt your dreams.  I can recognize that sound effect anytime it's used, seriously those things have always spooked me.
-Sound effects can be a little borked, play with the settings to see what works for you.
-Character creator is pretty dated and the models are kind of bad.
-Diseases are downright brutal especially blight related ones, ALWAYS bring blight curing things or you'll find yourself screwed.
-If you mess with the law too much you can get a death warrant. It makes sense but it can make doing things a hassle.
-Not having any magic can become a hassle in some areas.
-Not an easy game to pick up and very old values may leave younger players feeling confused.  It's very close to a tabletop rpg's character set-up and non nerds don't usually enjoy that sort of thing. (thankfully I'm a mega-nerd.)
That's about the gist of it, I could include more in both sections but it would be unending.
tl,dr ;
A great but dated game for classic Rpg fans with amazing scenery and music.

Most of my time in this game was spent on the Xbox version back in the day. Got it recently for PC and decided to install some mods to increase my experience and was left with a game that still stands up incredibly well today. Lore, dialogue, dungeon crawling and exploration galore. The game doesn't really hold your hand and you're left to find your own way to your objectives with whatever clues you have in your journal, which is a breath of fresh air. Combine that with the most in-depth magic system in almost any game ever and an amazing storyline (especially for someone who hasn't experienced it before) and you've got one of my favorite RPG games ever made. Plus it's too old for Bethesda to try and ruin with paid mods! :D
If you're a fan of Oblivion pick it up. If you're a fan of Skyrim and don't plan on dedicating some time into becoming intricate with the combat and leveling system then I might skip this one in favor of a more modern, simple action-RPG. Take it slow and immerse yourself in the world and prepare for something great.
Also, if you have a decent PC do yourself a favor and install MSGO (Morrowind Sound and Graphics Overhaul) to improve pretty much every aspect of how this game looks. It comes with an installer that takes care of pretty much everything for you and is totally worth it, whether coming into this game new or returning after a while. It's a collection of mods that just makes the world that much better.

Sadly, I cannot reccomend this game based on the publisher Bethesda's recent actions. Their huge push for the incredibly anticonsumer addition of paid mods into their game is frankly somewhat sickening. Worse yet, if the Creation Club succeeds, other companies will try it too, and it'll become the next microtransactions. I will no longer be buying any Bethesda games, and I encourage you to do the same.

This game was so overly hyped and ended up being a complete mess of promises and limitations of its time.
I love the concept of the game and I can't say that I did not enjoy it but there is just something wrong about how the game was finished. The gameplay is horribly sluggish and many of the things you do feel either tedious or just plain boring.
The game is split into 5 different phases of different qualities. . .
1. Cell stage (Or whatever it was called)
I really think that this stage was done well and in an interesting fashion. The gameplay might be a bit on the simple side and they dont really explain how to do a few tricks in order to get things right the first time. The way you design your creature does ACTUALLY change how you need to play and some tweaking in the size of your twisted mess of a creature can actually benefit you. I think this was a good stage but somewhat too simplified (most likely due to the target audience) and I would have liked seeing much more parts that fit different playstyles. Its good and to be honest its one of the best parts of the game.
2. Creature stage (I think)
The best part some say.
In order to be a fair review I must say that the limitations of computers only a few years ago was huge compared to what we have today (and in the future). This means that many things in the game were "fresh" and very unexplored.
This is the stage that most people wish was longer and to be the bulk of the game and to that I say "Sure!" because a game about evolution should focus mainly on evolution. This part of the game is filled with a lot of exploration that ends up being tedious or interesting. You always spawn near other creatures that are pretty easy to befriend or exterminate which is kind of boring but a good way to learn and kick things off.
You progress by finding parts and gathering more DNA points by killing, befriending and even eating eggs (Few people know this) and to be honest its kind of stale. What I would have loved to see would be a system that evolves as you play. The very interesting creature editor should instead be replaced with an information screen that allows you only to nudge things in a certain direction. Instead of tearing off limbs and replacing them with new ones constantly as you get more and more upgrades the game developers should have made it so that the player has to guide the evolution of their creature. I am NOT saying that the creature editor should be removed by any means (Its interesting) but something just feels so "off" about it. My worm like creature had trouble had trouble chasing enemies who were fleeing but what if I tried to nudge evolution to give my worm the ability to spit poison? Lay traps? I know this is very difficult to do and most likely impossible when the game was developed but its just an idea. . .
I could probably ramble about this for hours and most likely nothing of this makes any sense so I'm going to avoid talking much more about this stage. In summary this was a decent experience if not a bit watered down with clunky mechanics. The evolution theme is slightly backwards in this stage and many things have most likely been pulled out of the game due to time constraints, budget and technology.
3. Tribal stage
I for some reason used to like this stage but a more recent experience of this stage got me thinking. . . WHY is this here? This stage does little good and feels a lot like tedious filler. No longer you have control over how your creature is shaped but now you control how they dress. It feels lazy and the whole thing feels really rushed. There could have been a chance to show people how society first began to form. The invention of new tools and better tools is completely simplified as you start with all you really need. More tools and weapons come with progression but they dont really make much of a difference. You just gather a lot of food by killing, foraging, stealing, fishing and collecting eggs from the friends you might have made during the creature stage or the animals you tame during tribal stage. After collecting food you create as many you can and equip them all with either weapons or instruments. Go to some other tribe and do♥♥♥♥♥♥to them until you get rewarded. Head back and do the same thing over and over again until you've won. The social way of winning is slightly more difficult and that is by a VERY slight margin because it only requires you to split up your tribe into different groups of instruments. I really liked this before but now I only feel like this was rushed and doomed from the start.
4. City/Global stage
I must say that I LOVED this stage when I was younger. You get to design vehicles, houses, factories, entertainment facilities and you also get to micromanage your forces while balancing the cities you own for funds, vehicle slots, defenses and how happy your people get to be. The city designing feels a bit lazy sometimes and it lacks like many other things enough complexity to make it very worthwhile to fiddle with for longer amounts of time. The vehicle designing is pretty lazy and you can pretty much do anything you want as long as you got at least 10-20% power in each category.
The beginning is mostly a scramble for claiming as many resource nodes as possible and then attacking weaker neighbours with the support of your better budget. Diplomacy is rather dull and you can just rush everyone once you get a foothold. Attacking a city en masse with your massive ROFLSTOMP army is pretty much the way to go. You most often forget about your abilities that you've gaind from earlier in the game and you either focus on naval/land forces or the way I did it which is the lazy way and just swarm the enemy with huge amounts of aircraft. You'll lose a lot of money doing this but by now you should have enough money to do whatever you want.
This feels a bit lazy and perhaps more thought should have been put into HOW civilizations work. Most likely ideologies are out of the question due to the fact that its hard to not get someone rilled up but more complexity in warfare/religion/trading could have done so much more. Events that cause modifiers could challenge the player with more interesting tasks to be taken on. Resources shouldn't be just "cash" but things like metals that could enhance your defense or oil that makes your vehicles faster. Spending money on research for new items should have been something put into the game and maybe making the cities much more difficult to take out. Im sure I've missed many things here but as usual its hard to share everything without getting lost in ideas. This stage was rushed and severely watered down.
5. Space!
This is the largest stage which is kind of infinite and if you ask me it's the most tedious, frustrating and confusing stage in the game. This stage caused so much discussion from the players who either despised it or worshipped it and its clear why.
First you go through a tutorial full of incredibly annoying instructions and controls that make you feel ill. After this you get to do a lot of boring quests and such before you're finally truly free. You're often stuck from getting new things due to financial problems or a lack of certain items you need to make things go smoothly. The terraforming is pretty funny but held back by the abysmal storage space you have on your ship which forces you to go back and forth between planets or even stars to grab that one shrub that you need or that one herbivore you need to feed the carnivore that you now have to throw out to make space for the herbivore. Colouring the planets can be fun but it feels really annoying to be held back by so many things. Interaction between other species is dull, economy is tedious and just everything is tedious. Its huge and had so much potential but failed.
Do you buy this game? Only if you like the idea or want to learn more game design. If not. . . Leave it alone.

Fantastic fun!
Saw this game on sale, which prompted me to watch the show, which hooked me and got me to buy the game for my girlfriend and I, and we have been playing non stop for the week since we got it.
First, the separate stories for the show and the game are interesting on their own. Then you add episodic missions with some of the same decent characters from the show and events that explain other events, such as where Nolan gets a particular artifact, and in one mission you technically save the city of Defiance. The game also has a nice long story line mostly independent of the show, fascinating in its own right. The game and show stand on their own no question, but if you follow both they cross over in fantastic ways and further illuminate the world.
Controls and combat are solid, what you would expect from a typical 3rd person action shooter, notably with unlimited dodge rolls but without a cover mechanic. The progression is also very nice, with a wide variety of weapons with not much difference between them, instead progressing by skill and based on how you can mod the weapons and how the weapons and mods synergize. There are also 4 core abilities and a plethora of "perks" to unlock, upgrade, and slot. You choose 1 scifi ability and 3+ perks, unlocking slots over time. One of the best features is you can set up different loadouts, with weapon, ability, perk, and even outfit and vehicle choices set per loadout. It is fairly quick to switch loadouts, and you can in combat (pve), though there is no hotkey to switch yet.
The game is an mmo and has the necessary elements, clans, chat, friends, etc, but is light on other elements. You can only have a single mission at a time, though they are more engrossing than typical mmo quests by far; it will not cross your mind a second time. The chat is minimalist, but they have announced an overhaul. It is, in a way, a barebones mmo, but a very excellent coop 3rd person action shooter. Yes, there are also some bugs, but none of them terrible now, they are almost always easily ignored.

A physics-based domino puzzle game. It's somewhat fun for a bit, but it wears off pretty quickly.

A game that takes a really simple concept and tries to build on it over a number of levels. The most fun part of this game is the fact that you get a quite good simulater of domino physics. The problem is, there isn't much depth the game can add to those physics, and so if they aren't constantly adding new mechanics to the game the levels feel repetitive are are a bit too easy. Also the controls were a bit clunky.
I enjoyed it for a good 20 minutes, but it's really hard to make knocking down long chains of dominoes interesting after you've done it 5 or 6 times, although if you do enjoy that process of planning out your domino trains there's certainly plenty of levels for you to enjoy.

Achievements: All standard and possible.  They're given simply for beating levels.  There's no achievements associated with the last two levels, though.
Pros/Cons:
+ Surprisingly good controls.  Mouse wheel is for rotation.  WASD moves the camera.  Space/shift raises and lowers.  It's all very fluid.
+ Oddly satisfying gameplay.  There's nothing quite like toppling over a line of dominoes without having to pick them back up.
+ Unlockable patterns for the dominoes.
+ Free play mode.
+ Fun mechanics (ramps, balls, etc.)
+ The domino limit per each level is rather lenient, allowing for a casual challenge.
- I experienced some issues with the framerate dropping every so often-- not enough to discourage me from playing, but still annoying.
- Sometimes the physics were a little janky.  For example, I'd fail a level then retry(with no changes) and somehow win.
- Restarting a level after a failed attempt would sometimes leave a stray domino that I'd deleted earlier.
- Some levels seemed entirely based on luck.
- You cannot stack dominoes.
Overall:
Domino Sky was surprisingly fun.  For $3.99, I got ~3 hours of gameplay out of it.  It's not a bad priced given that I did not mess around too much with the free play mode.  Physics puzzlers are always a blast-- especially when the levels are so satisfying to figure out and complete.  Though my troubles with stutters and overall jankiness was frustrating, they didn't quite hinder my enjoyment of this game.  I liked this one.  I'd recommend it.

Mixed review: Domino Sky is a physics puzzle game where you arrange, well, dominoes to hit some specific marks on the map. The game has soothing classical music and casual play style. However, all the levels I have played so far only have 1 goal (to hit different markers), so it becomes quite dull after some levels. If Domino Sky could offer more in gameplay (game modes, background, or maybe even a story tied into the levels) then it would be a better game.

Haunt the House: Terrortown is going to a children's waterpark on a bored day.
Now, let me explain. Haunt the House: Terrortown is a love project by the Super Flash Brothers, and an expansion to the free flash game "Haunt the House".
The link is here, if you want to play it. It's very much a sequel of that game, with a larger budget and a 15 dollar price tag. This very much shows. There are 4 levels to scare every guest out of the building (done by haunting the various objects) with the cutesy animations from the actions of each possessed item. The animations and graphics, which are the prime focus of the game, are wonderfully done and every action looks beautiful. Seeing what each thing does is truly a treat and the driving force of most of your haunting. The gameplay is great too. As I've said, you go to a building and you haunt the other items to use their actions to scare people. The more you scare, the more the buildings Atmosphere level goes up, which allows you to unlock more actions. Each level has it's own individual Atmosphere level, so you have to work to scare on each individual one. This gameplay, although rather simple, is great and fun to play with until the very short game ends.
It's like a children's waterpark: It looks cute and great, the waterslides are fun, but the thrill of going on them only lasts for the time you're sliding down the ride. But when you are, it is a joy of a ride. Play this game whenever you're bored, the pricetag isn't too large compared to most games out there, and it's a joy of an experience. Just don't expect anything complex and elaborate that you can sink your teeth into. This is very much a game for the visual.

A really nicely done card game that I picked up during the Humble Bundle. The initial mechanics sorta remind me of Final Fantasy 8's side card game, but there's a lot of strategy and detail under the surface here. Going after your opponents health versus going after your opponents field is a key factor into this: each strategy is viable and you may have to change it depending on the opponent. Each opponent feels unique enough, and it does feel like a real mind game against them. Those who love strategy will love this game.
For more first impressions and gameplay footage:

Reminiscent of older card-centric adventure games, Card City Nights carries you through a self-aware and contrived adventure to collect eight unique pieces from different bosses, and to challenge a final boss for a defined reward. The card game itself is fun and varied, and leaves many opportunities for customising one's own deck. While a direct and offensive tactic can be used to beat most opponents, each uses different strategies that can seriously complicate such an approach, making it optimal to research tactics and learn more about the individual card synergies.
There is no penalty for losing and always a reward for winning, so it's very much so a gentle game for those who may be unfamiliar with battling card games in general, making it playable and appealing for new or veteran players alike.
The music is enjoyable and adds flavour to the already living world, and the artwork is unforgettable and appealing, in that "trying hard to look like it isn't trying hard" way. The palette choices and composition are aesthetically pleasing and give the world a setting all its own, despite borrowing elements from many other games that the developers have made. The default gender for the player character and most npcs is female, with most characters being confident and punkish, breaking the common representation of female characters in video games as passive, mousey, and largely helpless.
I loved this game every moment that I played it, and though it can be frustrating to find an opponent who is difficult to beat, that just requires more familiarity and effort with your deck. It's seriously a steal at its price.

If you've ever enjoyed anything like Magic: The Gathering or any other CCGs, then you may want to give this title a look.  It has a ruleset that is fresh and different from other card games I have played.  It is very simple and easy to grasp, but after you start in a little bit you will see there is a ton of viable strategies for deck building and you can come up with some really interesting combos.  As you play different people in the game you will be rewarded with booster packs with random cards in it that allow you to expand your library and tinker around with your strategy.  Different opponents give you packs from different sets and I found it really fun to see what else I might get with repeated battles.
The AI  starts off really horribly stupid, but this is fine since you start with a limited starter deck, and the difficulty slowly increases as it gives you time to build a library and contruct different decks for different situations.  The story is super silly and light-hearted.
The only downfall is that there is no multiplayer.  I would love to play my decks I've built against a friend online.  I'm half tempted to find a way to make these cards in real life to play as I think it would be a fun game with friends.
Even without multiplayer I think that Card City Nights is worth the purchase.  At only $4 it certainly was worth it for me.
Fairly unique, great player progression, quirky characters, diverse strategy and gameplay that's simple to understand and still gives a challenge or two.  I love this game.  I love mustaches.

I am incredibly surprised at how much I enjoyed this game. I'll try to keep this short, and to the point, first of all because I don't want to waste your time, but mostly because it is currently 6 AM, and I've been up all night finishing this game. Anyway, to get started:
MUSIC: Let me tell you, this soundtrack is great. It's catchy, and I find the tunes stuck in my head after I close the game.
GRAPHICS: Unique, cartoony, and easy on the eyes. The artwork on the cards is great, too, of course.
STORY: Although others are saying that the story is forgettable, I'd have to disagree. Although not the best around, it's compelling, and is easy to get into. Essentially, you're the new guy/girl/vegetable in town, and as you explore the city, you meet zany characters, get yourself a rival, and play tons of cardgames. Your goal is essentially to defeat the 8 people who each have a legendary card. If you win, you get the cards, and if you collect all 8 of them, then you are allowed to fight against the Card King, the greatest card player in the city, and claim one million coins. There is also a little more content to explore after defeating the King, like fighting the former legendary card holders looking for a rematch, or facing off the Card Gods, who are four great card players, who use illegal cards.
GAMEPLAY: The battling system is very unique, and lots of fun. To simply sum it up, each card has a different symbol (attack, shield, healing, neutral) which do different things. Attack does damage, shield heals your health (a maximum of 10, by the way), Healing can revive a knocked-out card (which get knocks out by taking damage), and neutral mixes with anything. The catch, however, is that each card has arrows, which you must use to connect the various cards to group together a total of 3 symbols. If one symbol is more dominant of the others, then your combo will go to that automatically, but if there is a tie, you get to choose what symbol you want to activate (Ex. Your card combo has 2 attack and 1 shield, then you will have to do damage to your opponent; Ex. Your card combo has 1 attack, 1 shield, and 1 neutral, then you get to choose to either attack for 1 damage, or heal yourself for 1).
Others:
+You get to play as a carrot, with a fedora. 10/10
+Ludicrously low price. 11 hours of fun, for 4 bucks? That's what I call value.
-One of the worst final bossfights ever. It's tough as hell, and not very rewarding, but the content that becomes available afterwards (the cards gods, and rematches) is a pretty good reason not to give up.
Overall, this game is really great. Really a hidden gem. To be repetetive, I was really pleasantly surprised at this. Anyway, that's just my 2 cents. I think I'll go get some rest.

Why can't games be like the good ole days where you rank up depending on how much you play the game and your skill level????

I'm always getting shot around corners and sometimes my bullets don't connect to my opponent even though im 100% sure i was aiming at them. The game is definitely worth the price (since it has been reduced so drastically), but I don't think spending the extra money for the Deluxe Edition is worth it. It's literally a red suit that looks (personal opinion) stupid, a rocket launcher (that you find for free and with better stats later), a shield (same as the rocket launcher) and a coloured quad bike you can't get anywhere else (oh noes! Not like you can get a free, faster quad bike later on, or a free dune buggy, or just buy a car). The only thing worthwhile on the Deluxe Edition are the boosts, but even then, they aren't necessary at all.
Why do I think the game itself is worth it? Well, I'll give both sides:
Good:
*Runs very smoothly in combat (even when it seems laggy I've never had a problem hitting my target)
*The graphics are decent (they're not Crisis but they aren't Minecraft either)
*The game is genuinelly a lot of fun!...at first
*Arkfalls are a lot of fun to go to (at first anyways), too bad some of the cool co-op mission bosses aren't available in the main game
*Clothing; all the clothing you can buy in the store for real money (do you like microtransactions) can be acquired for free (in different colours bearing in mind, so they may look better or worse) by completing challenges or missions
*Leveling and progression system; there's a lot less of a difference between a EGO 5000 character and a EGO 50 character than most MMOs... the only differences I can think of off the top of my head are: more chance for nano effects on weapons (fire, syphon health, electricity, etc.), more bonuses on weapons (e.g. x1.25 mag size); access to more co-op missions (last one unlocks at around 500 EGO anyway at the time this was originally written); more perks on the EGO Grid (skill tree) and more clothing unlocked (through the missions/challenges). There's probably some I missed, but health, shield capacity and weapon damage only very, very slightly scale with your level, so in terms of health and raw damage, there isn't much difference between the two characters
Neutral:
*I've never played PvP so I can't give my personal opinion, but according to the forums, it is heavily biased for certain weapons/EGO powers (meaning it could be difficult to use others effectively unless you know what you're doing) and it has been ignored for a long time and could use new features
Bad:
*Crappy launcher for patches. On PS3 I've spent 2 hours patching, only for it to come up with a failure and start from the beginning... 3 times! On PC though I don't think I had many problems, but maybe I was just lucky
*Fake patch notes... maybe they've stopped it now, but they seem to like to put old news into the patch notes to buff them out a bit, when in reality they've changed very little
*Can you say 'repetitive'? Because that's what this game is after a long time playing... I guess every game does this, but the co-op missions are repetitive (no randomisation in any way, even with enemy spawns), the little random events (don't know the proper name, where you'll find a derelict vehicle on the road or a hellbug nest or some other small event) are repetitive (after a while, especially when your EGO calls out to you repeatedly to check them out), driving around the world is repetitive (more on that next), the whole damn thing just feels like a bit of a grind once the new game sheen has worn off...
*Driving feels empty... oh I don't mean the physics, which are a load of crap (wanna drive through that wooden fence in your truck? NOPE! Wanna drive over this rock? NOPE! You get stuck on the rock/smash right into it and lose all your speed. This happens on everything you touch, at least you can drive through other players or this'd be a major griefing tactic). I mean just driving around the world makes you feel like you're playing a singleplayer game rather than an MMO. The chat is barely ever used (and for good reason too, in its current state it is bad, though it's meant to be getting fixed with the 7th Legion DLC patch) and players either don't load their appearance (this has been updated with a slider in the options menu, which allows you to always see the appearance) or just don't load at all, so you very rarely see anybody driving around that isn't at a fast travel point...
*The DLC is pretty poor so far, the Raptor vehicle is terrible and the arena is just that; a PvE arena that loses its magic after a couple of tries. The new Charge Blade is cool though, fun to use (if a bit suicidal) but you need to know which enemies you shouldn't attack or you'll get creamed :P Arkbreaker was... good for the free player, but not so good for the people that buy the DLC; all you really get for buying the DLC is the ability to call down Arkfalls; the thing is, most of the time, if you wait for 5 minutes somebody else will call it down anyway.

Incredibly frustrating, extremely fun.
You have doubtless seen many reviews of ibb and obb praising its cuteness (it is cute) and clever puzzles (they are clever) and the high requirement for solid teamwork (it does require very solid teamwork) and seen the recommendation that it is "good to play with a girlfriend or kids".
Use caution with the last.  Seriously, this is an excellent game, but it is a rough introduction to puzzle platforming once you get to the later levels--many of the puzzles require nearly flawless timing, and that's generally fine because you don't go back too far and the reset is fast, but those new to gaming will be sorely tested.  I have to give the devs a great deal of credit for tuning some of the puzzles to a razor's edge of perfection, and we found many sections where we knew what to do and came to the conclusion that it was impossible before seeking a walkthrough and discovering we had the right solution--we just weren't good enough and needed more practice.  I myself am OK with that (I love games like VVVVV), but my partner, who loved the game as it started, reached a point of "this just isn't fun now."  We have one more level, and I do hope we finish it.
So I love it, and do recommend it as an excellent coop puzzle platformer, but I would exert much caution using it as someone's first introduction to gaming.

Not too long ago, a friend was making his own VisualBasic B-29 simulator. It was a board game version of this and I really liked the idea.
Fast forward a year, now I've got the Lancaster version.
The amount of concentration and crew management needed to git gud at this game is unreal. I clicked like I was on crack and STILL had a guy die on me. Could that guy have lived if I didn't load him down with flak jackets and electrical boots so we could fly above cloud cover? Should I have made the gunner fight defensively so we got some breathing room? Did we have enough room to boost the engines? Should I have done all three in the space of two seconds? Sometimes it almost feels like you have to be god, but it's a game where you simulate flying a canvas tube full of guns with virtually zero protection.
When you manage to limp back to base, one engine going, empty fuel tank, a dead gunner or two and land almost by luck, you feel like you really achieved something, because to get that sorry piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥back to the airstrip takes a lot of concentration. About halfway, the game turns in to a bullet hell simulator, so be aware the difficulty will ratchet up, and the dead crew will pile up.
You feel bad when those crewman die too. Some of them had been with you for 20 missions, but this one time, they just couldn't get to a parachute in time or you ran out of first aid supplies and had to watch them bleed out while you tried to gun it home. That's tough.
The special abilities fit really well and come as a breath of fresh air. Auto tag helped me concentrate on getting the bombardier ready while gunners engaged. Focus got rid of those two planes harrasing my flank. Emergency dive got me the ♥♥♥♥ out of that hornet's nest so I could at least reload a gun and get a navigation update. Call for spitfires didn't seem to do much.

I really tried to like this game.
I love the idea of command points and player generals on a persistent map. Having one sided battles when your faction is losing the war is a great aspect that really puts the pressure on.
Where the game falls apart is the simplistic twitch style combat. Either the hitboxes glitch a lot or a bullet can be a dud. You can double tap someone in the chest and their reaction will be to maintain perfect aim and spray everything in front of them and if they slightly graze your elbow you die. Dem hit boxes.
Everyone is a superhero. Not only do they absorb bullets without flinching but they all make Usain Bolt look slow and have a 7 foot vertical jump. The vehicles are also comically fast with the Willys MB pulling 10's through the grass.
One of the best selling features for me is the refreshingly brutal free targeting system. This is one feature the game certainly got right. If you like to be smart and use the terrain to surprise your enemies then you will appreciate the layout of the maps as well. Seeing them before they see you is what it is all about. Do not expect this game to highlight your targets for you. You have to use your eyebals. =D
As great as I find the lack of help while aiming it conflicts with the twitch style Team Fortress gameplay and hilarious rag doll physics somehow. All the interesting tactics the environment affords are wasted when your enemy eats your bullets with their face while one shotting you in the leg.
It does seem to be a true free to play game. You can grind your way through the game to get the same goodies you can buy with a real job so it gets points for that as well.
Overall I had some laughs. I doubt I will keep playing myself but I would recommend the game and even throwing them a few dollars so you can buy a sub machine gun.

One of the greatest games I have ever played.
The story puts you on Vvardenfell, an island you last saw in the first game, Arena, in the middle of a prophecy that must be fulfilled, and it's a beautiful island as well.
The story is amazing, so much detail was put into the lore and how the prophecy was meant to be fulfilled, as well as many numerous side quests to do, even serving the daedric princes, or joining a faction like the Imperial cult, although sadly Sithis may not be served like in Daggerfall.
The environment is absolutely stunning, even for its time, you will find little islands, ash covered desert wastelands, humid swamps, prime grazing lands, even a frozen island to the northwest. Many creatures also inhabit the land, some are peaceful, some hostile, especially those cliff racers, we all know the struggle of cliff racers... slaughterfish are also not healthy for swimmers. In a nutshell, I have 311 screenshots at the making of this review, nature was meant to be enjoyed.
Expanding on the lore, this game has an amazing backstory, every single town, person, god, faction, all have their own backstories which are found in books spread throughout, every little thing has a backstory and a typically detailed lore, especially the very important characters like Vivec. Bethesda does not shy away from creative lore, and for this game, they made it a second life level of detail in the freedom you have and the backstories behind everything.
One impressive point this game has is the immense freedom you have, you can ignore the main story altogether, finish it, or even kill characters who are essential to the story, you can explore, be a petty criminal, as long as you can imagine it, you can do it, you have all the freedom in the world and it is amazingly fun.
This game deserves more than a 10/10, so many childhood memories, amazing lore that beats most real world novels, unlimited options on how to live your life, amazing environment, great cities to explore, Vivec City is one of the largest cities I have ever explored in a single game, and I hope everyone would enjoy such a great game

This is a fantastic deck construction game.  You fight battles on a 3 x 3 grid that each player has.  The cards contain either attack, neutral, defense, or revive symbols or a combination of them.  Each card has arrows pointing to cardinal directions around the card.  Some cards have more arrow directions than others.  Some cards have special abilities as well.  You must play cards to link the arrows until you have three symbols matched in which case the majority symbol action is taken and the activated cards are removed.  Reduce your opponent from 7 starting health to 0.
All the cards are contained in the game with nothing more to buy.  You fight card battles to win more cards.  Building your deck(s) with the right arrow and symbol combinations and then playing them to their maximum potential is very strategic and addicting.  This game has been a blast to play.

I've played dozens of card battle games digitally and in cardboard, and have to say Card City Nights is a unique entry in this huge genre. The theme is street based with awesome purposely poorly drawn Papa the Rapa or DDR characters, so it's a comedy. If you're looking for a good fun card collecting game, but either don't want Multiplayer, or don't mind Singleplayer;
this may be the game for you.
There's something just enjoyable about managing your decks, of which in this game you can have 7 decks, and can even choose the image (from an in-game selection) for the deck holder.
Since you have a max card limit for your deck, you're always trying to find 'better' cards for it, but also cards
that synergize with your other cards.. which has to do with the 'grid building gameplay.'
Basically every card can line up with other cards, only in certain ways, depicted by arrows on the cards.
You want to build a deck where it's more possible to draw cards that can link together.
(when linked cards provide bonuses, such as attack, defense, and heal)
Though linear, this game isn't quite as linear as I first thought it would be.
There is freedom in choosing the locations you travel to and who you choose to dual against.
And as you dual better opponents, more locations and opponents become available,
essentially having you work your way up the 'chain.'
Many opponents you can re-fight pretty much as often as you like, but the booster packs you win off them usually
become 'stale.' Meaning you keep getting the same cards so there's no way to build a better deck by vs-ing the same
old opponents.
This isn't a negative, I'm just stating it.
One thing I did find strange though, is there's no penalty for losing, at least from what I recall.
(it's been about a month since I've played and I've just started getting into the game from scratch again.)
Would be nice for some sort of 'Hardcore' mode where you lose something from losing, cards or something.
There's a nice degree of humour in the game.. I've never played the developers other games such as The Little Dew.
But from what I can tell it isn't necessary to have experience in that lore.
Humour such as; early on you'll be dualing with cards titled 'Stick' which is a weapon that's just a stick.
There is a decent variety of decks, as you progress.
With the early decks being comprised of 'sticks' and 'old men.'

If you look up mediocre, you may notice that it refers you to also see Finn & Jake's Epic Quest.
Very little variety between levels, uninspired combat with endless damage sponges, and some of the blandest music I've heard in a game in a very long time. A semi-confusing UI and lack of any sort of multiplayer sours the game even further, although those are the least of it's problems.

This game is so close to being really good, but a couple of really irritating (and easily fixable) problems stop me from recommending it.
Firstly, there's too much repetition, especially with the levels being as big as they are. Moving through a level facing the same enemies over and over wouldn't be too bad if the levels were smaller, but they can be huge and chock full of bad guys, which makes taking them out really tiresome. Plus, with the levels being as big as they are it's easy to get lost, and the minimap just doesn't cut it without a zoom feature.
Another issue is the poorly implemented Enchiridion system. There's not much point limiting the amount of page slots you get if most of the pages are pretty much useless anyway. Only a few of them are actually worth using more than once. This combined with the fact that activating a page often removes your ability to attack, forcing you to run around in circles aimlessly until it wears off, make it an upgrade system that doesn't feel like an upgrade.
Having to go through the previous level again after falling off ledges is ridiculously frustrating. There's no point to it except punishing the player for being careless, which could easily have been accomplished by simply starting the current level again. As it is, it just feels like overkill.
Overall the game isn't bad, but its lack of anything bar killing enemies and collecting pages makes it feel kind of sparse. Maybe if the devs add some extra features/content this would be more satsifying. Having said that, it's definitely not a

One of the best Co-Op puzzle games I think I've played in a long time.
Many games have come out for two (or more) players to try to solve puzzles together, but fall into one of a few traps:

-One player too easily can take over, directing the other player(s) to the solution or simply doing it all themself, while waiting for the others to catch up, or making the others feel the puzzle is being spoiled for them.
-The game forces each player into a specialized role which means they each have a specific job to do, and whoever is better/faster at the game is left waiting for others to figure things out. (Which makes it feel like everyone is playing their own solo game together, but separately.)
-The game tries to force individual problem solving by limiting or not giving any ways for the players to communicate.
Ibb & Obb does a good job of not falling into any of these traps through thoughtful puzzles and unique style and gameplay.
The gameplay and style are truly unique, both in terms of design and visuals/music.
A very lovely game that is challenging without being too hard, and has plenty of content without being a grind nor too short.

It isn't that this platform puzzle-adventure game is difficult. It isn't very difficult. It's just that all of my friends are into playing other types of games apparently. They play RTS (real time strategy) and other things. Oh well but that's the way it goes. It can be hard to find someone who is as good as you are at a game and ALSO wants to play it with you at the same time that you do. As this game depends on cooperation (most of this game's puzzles require a high-degree of cooperation) you need to play this with someone who is as competent at the game as you are and despite how cute this game looks, there are some fairly mind-bending puzzles in this game, but that's also a good part of this game's charm.
The music in this game is excellent. The sound is good and cute. The graphics are cute. The game runs really, really well. The controls are, if you are a platform gamer, intuitive. But you MUST find someone else who thinks the controls are intuitive as well. Your mother who only plays complex scrabble-type word games and who has never managed to win a super mario brothers game won't be good enough at this and so the game will be sort of frustrating. This really is one of those games, like the cooperative mode of portal 2, where you should ideally be playing with someone you know really well and who is at least as good at the game as you are.

I'm gonna be straight here. This game is F2P and eventually turns into a huge grindfest, and higher tier content is literally the same levels over and over, with stronger enemies to tweak the difficulty. I don't play as often since I don't have a subscription, and new content comes out too fast for me to keep up. Even so, I recommend that people try this game out, and here's why.
While making my first character, I found something identical to Spawn's mask, and immediately knew what I had to do. I combined certain gear pieces and colors to make him look exactly like Spawn, and later on, I discovered you can upgrade gear but keep any cosmetic look you've previously found. You can also pick up to three colors to apply to each separate piece in whichever way you want. The customization, even at the very start, is INSANELY generous. I chose fire as my power and selected dual pistols as my weapons, and this dude tanks enemies like a boss. People laugh at a tank using guns but they stop when I pistol-whip them in the face and light their head on fire. I can use chains to zip-line around the city, or I can just fly, because I'm freaking Spawn.
Besides being able to make whatever kind of crazy superhuman you can think of, the gameplay itself is actually pretty complex. This isn't a typical MMO with boring auto-attack and stacks of toolbars filled with useless spells. You get 6 slots for your powers, and you have to choose them wisely. You use your two mouse buttons to perform a variety of physical combos, and by alternating between clicking and holding, you can pull off some crazy attacks. I like that this game actually punishes you for thinking an R1 spam will give you a win. Even normal enemies will respond by blocking and interrupt you, unless you know how to counter in time. It's seriously a fun combat system that kept me wanting to make new characters to explore other powers and weapon movesets.
So, despite this game turning into a grindfest, I think the customization and intricate combat is what makes me feel so attached. I loved making new characters, and ended up buying nearly one of each power spread across hero and villain sides. I've seen a lot of content, both free and premium, and gotta say it's really a blast during the beginning. It's only much later in the game, when you get to max level and raise your gear rating to around 100, that the grind begins to take its toll. Most players will have decided long before then if the game interests them.

Its not the worst game of this type; y'know, the kind that sells off the success of the brand. There's plenty of references to the show, at least, and they are integrated with moderate success through the decision to make them affect gameplay rather than just be a collectibale on the side.
The mechanics are, for the most part, bad. A fairly simple combat system with lots of walking in-between. Would have benefitted greatly from a more comprehensive map possibly accessible from the pause menu. All the collecting is meaningless; money and silver keys only get you enchiridion pages which are already in abundance and the combat is, again, so simple that the pages aren't really all that useful.
There's been a lot of fuss over how much support the devs have shown after release. Well, cool your boots; its been like four days since release and, frankly, the game is so riddled with bugs it shouldn't have been released so prematurely. This is all the more embarrassing when you consider its a re-release of an, otherwise, free game.
All in all, the reasonable pricetag makes up for a lot of its shortcomings, and, for the fans, being able to interact with the Adventure Time universe outside of the show is great. But, ultimately, its not as good as the show, or other videogames, so maybe consider investing your time in those instead.

This is pretty much the most incredible game I've ever played, period. It simply cannot be recommended enough. I'm actually writing a recommendation for it immediately after finishing it, because it's just that good.
The controls are amazing and fun, and they're often incredibly well used. There's no "Press E to Perform Complex Action" here. For example, you actually have to rotate the analog sticks to have your brothers spin a crank. The game's not completely unchallenging, but most of the focus is on overcoming and executing it rather than the usual annoying, long, drawn-out search for a solution to figure out the puzzle.
The story is just absolutely wonderous, and without comparison to anything I've ever played in a game, or encountered pretty much anywhere, ever. It's fun, funny, and heartwarming at times; thrilling at others; and at points staggeringly sorrowful. I spent the entire end of the game crying, and I'm about to start again. This is also the first and probably only time I've ever found myself crying over a game mechanic, - it was just that amazingly touching. (You'll see what I mean at the end, I refuse to be more specific for fear of spoiling it.)
This is the only time I've regretted buying a game on sale - I honestly wish I'd bought it for full price, just in the hopes of making it that much more likely I'd see another game even close to this good.

If you've played a game made by Amanita Design, you know their style can be a bit... quirky.
But don't let the unconventional nature of the art and music throw you off.  This game is brilliant.  It does what games should do: it shows, rather than tells.  From the items you acquire, to the implementation of those items, to the puzzles themselves, the games walks the edge between complexity and transparancy.  Sure, there are a few stumpers, but the game does an excellent job of helping you along if you need it.  There is also a healthy mixture of puzzles sprinkled throughout the traditional point-and-click adventure style.
And the world that this game builds is wonderful.  The musician troupe, the pipe wrench dubstep, the adorable robots and the city they inhabit—I was drawn into the world and didn't want to leave when it was over.  A thoroughly satisfying experience that did not leave me wanting.  I heartily recommend this game, both for the playing experience and for the implementation of good game design.

I'm not a fan of point & click adventures, but I fell in love with Machinarium almost instantly. The atmosphere is incredibly thick, thanks to the sublime music and unique dirty/washed out visuals. Overall, the game is very artsy, in a good way.
The puzzles are never too obtuse and if you're stuck, you can always get help from the game, which actually features a full hand-drawn walkthrough, as a last resort. Apart from traditional item collection and usage, you'll spend a lot of time solving varied puzzles, very similar to what you'd find in Prof. Layton. Highly recommended.

While there is a wee bit of pixel hunting here and there and some puzzles lack explanation, the game doesn't suffer any from it and is a wonderful gaming experience recommended to anyone who appreciates adventure games.

Another instant classic from Amanita Design.
This point-and-click adventure is full of personality. Without ever really telling you anything, it conveys a story that's both cute, surprisingly deep, oddly satisfying and dark. Through it's beautifully drawn screens it manages to build a world that feels alive. There's always some interesting thing to look at.
The only thing I can think of is that some of the puzzles you'll come across are a bit too obscure. Getting stuck can definitely get a bit frustrating. The amount of backtracking you have to at some points also makes it difficult to discern exactly
you need to do
.
While Machinarium may not be among my favorites of the genre, it's definitely quite a gem. Despite some mildly annoying moments, I had a lot of fun playing through it.

Card City Nights is a charming little deck-building card game. The gameplay involves battling against AI opponents by slotting cards into a 3x3 grid to form combinations that translate into various actions. At first, a single, balanced deck suffices and your matchups are fairly easy, but as you follow the story (which, without feeling intrusive, guides you around town to increasingly challenging opponents) and meet foes with different kinds of decks and playstyles, you begin to realize that you have to adapt your own card choices and strategies accordingly.
I think it was this subtle sense of progression and the variety that a change in deck could bring that kept me hooked on what at first seemed like a very simple (albeit fun) game. Your options for deck-building improve as you play, since each time you defeat a foe, you're rewarded with cards that are then added to your library. The characters you meet are quirky, offbeat, and humorous, and I appreciated how many times you could talk to them without their flavor-text dialogue repeating. Replayability is high: new opponents emerge and existing opponents improve after you finish the story; you can continue to earn cards and fine-tune your decks; and the story was always secondary anyway. The game settles into a nice balance where you think just enough that your victories feel satisfying, but it's never so hard as to be frustrating.
I got Card City Nights dirt cheap as a part of a Humble Bundle, and I feel like I underpaid.

This game is a weird mix of cartoon graphics, and a deep mix of historical accuracies you wouldn't expect. It plays like a strategic/arcade game. And you'll suck at it and be really frustrated at first.  You'll probably suck in the middle, and maybe a little at the end, but you'll discover later that a combination of better gear, better training, and just smarter play on your part, makes the missions a little less hairy. Flying at high altitudes when you get warmer clothing to avoid flak guns and a lots of fighters help, a lot. Using custom waypoints can keep you out of trouble, as well. Nothing will keep you safe, but it will help.
I've found after playing three different crews about 30 missions each that if you advance too fast in the campaign missions, it becomes pretty hard in the mid to end game.  Don't be afraid to take some easier missions to build up some cash while you get better at prioritizing tasks in the bomber.  After a lot of hours of play time, you'll get pretty good at deciding when to do to what.
The most important thing is not to let untagged fighters sneak up any where near your bomber and start pounding it from below or behind.
This game has a lot of replay potential.  Beating the game is the goal, but you'll have just as much fun starting a new crew and seeing how they develop.  I normally like more strategic games, but this game is a lot of fun for sessions that don't have to drag out for multiple hours of play.  This game also strikes a wonderful balance between being light hearted, but still making your heart race in the middle of combat.  You'll probably get pretty attached to your bomber crews, as well.
To be honest, at first I didn't really like the game.  But the more I played it, and the better I got at it, it really became addicting.  I give this game a big thumbs up.  It's not like quite like anything I've ever played, in a good way.

You move each individual finger, starting with the pinky with A,S,D,F, and and the Space Bar(thumb). You can also grab by pressing Mouse 1. This closes all the fingers and the thumb at the same time. Thank you comments section for reminding me about Mouse 1.
To move an entire arm up or down you spin the scroll wheel on your mouse.
To  move an entire arm forward or back you just move the mouse forward or back.
To rotate the wrist you hold down one of the mouse buttons then start moving the mouse left or right. The wrist only rotates on a simple R axis.
To move the whole arm left or right you move the mouse left or right without holding a mouse button.
In order to switch hands you press shift. You can only move one hand at a time and the other hand stays where you left it, even if you are holding something (nice feature). If you bump into something with one hand while the other hand is holding it (think loading a magaazine into a gun) then it will move slightly. This is incredibly frustrating as you try again and again while your other hand moves ever so slightly with each try.
There is a button to switch your control from each individual hand to your head or your feet. The head works just fine but switching to feet does absolutely nothing at the time of this review.*
I hope this review has been helpful. Also, don't try to make a review while intoxicated.

I would NOT recommend Spore. As fun as the game looks, you will be bored of it within the span of the couple of hours and the expansions do nothing to aid this problem. Initially, the game looks fun and you see a lot of people online having a good time with this game, but it isn't as enjoyable as it looks. Looking at the creature creator on its own, the options may appear diverse, but they really aren't. You don't have many options and are restricted heavily on what a playable creature can and can't have. To make anything cool, you'll have to cheat a LOT and, even then, you won't be able to play the creature you've made. Getting into the actual game play, I can sum it all up in one word: repetitive. All you do is gather and charm your way though the different stages which range from green puke landscape to technicolor puke landscape. There is no real challenge and I managed to get through the creature stage in under an hour on my first playthrough. That being the biggest thing advertised in the entire game, speed isn't good. There really is NOTHING to do aside from charm, hunt and move nest every so often. The tribal stage is the same way save for the fact that it's top-down and you have to keep everyone alive and yourselves on good standing with the other tribes (also a very simple and repetitive task.) Finally, the space stage is as boring and annoying as if you were to sit at the menu screen of  Sonic '06 for five hours. Make of that what you will. In all, Spore isn't worth it. Save your money for something like "Subnautica" or "The Isle."

Have you ever wondered how it is to be a ghost, without actually embracing your end? Luckily you do not have to even experience cruel fate of Patrick Swayze either, just try playing Haunt the House: Terrortown.
A product, which originates from flash game project made by SFB Games, may not give us chills and make our hearts shiver in terror, but that does not mean it cannot offer us a decent level of entertainment. HtH :T is an action game, where you play as an (un?)friendly ghost. When you take the first glance of the game, you will notice its humble and simple 2D graphic, which resembles the style of Detective Grimoire.  With that approach game does not try to be scary, but instead is presented with pleasant and frivolous outlook. Soundtracks only contributes more to the not-so-horrific atmosphere of the game, and it certnaly has a charm.
Your main goal is, what a shocker… to scare people in town. The place, where our ghastly adventure begins is separated into 4 areas : hospital, museum, theatre and ship. Because our ghost is possibly too cute to actually scare anyone, he has to posses objects and animate them in front of unwelcomed  meddlesome citizens. Whole mechanic is very simple – you use arrow keys to float with our dainty blob of ectoplasm and with w,s,a,d keys you perform certain actions on objects installed in every area. Each scare builds our energy, which allows us to perform even more terrifying frights. Ghost Master anyone? You have to be careful though, being too scary may badly influence our rating, because our victims may decide to simply end their lifes. Whole gameplay is very simple and you just cannot dislike ghost characters and their silly moans, design of levels and general humour HtH:T has.
However the game contains a serious flaw: main problem is the lack of an actual content. Whole adventure may actually be finished in around an hour and two additional levels do not mend this issue completely. The another problem is the AI of our unfortunate victims. They sometimes can run back and forth without sense if we terrorize them too much, which may prevent us from getting a good grade for our haunting.
This leads to the conclusion, that product may fit better as an mobile app, that you play while riding a bus or during lecture, than actual Steam game. I can recommend it, but please be aware of its limited possibilities.

Brothers is good. You should play it. This game reminds me a lot of the recent, inventive Papo y Yo, although it's not as good as Papo... is. What's unique about this game is the main mechanic of controlling both brothers at the same time to solve environmental puzzles, each with one analog (you want to play this game with a controller). It became difficult keeping which brother was controlled with which one when they're both moving around at the same time in different directions on different parts of the screen. There are some good uses of this unique and fun play style that I felt could have been fleshed out more. I'm sure a sequel would realize this potential more fully. The biggest problem I had with this game is having to constantly hold down the trigger button for the brothers to keep performing an action and it tired out my fingers after a while. Masterclass.  This is not a game designed to be fun, it simply takes you on an adventure in a way that allows you to establish a connection and relationship between a number of characters in a story told by gestures, vague vocal exchanges and the environment.
The textures, lighting, shading, camera angles, environment design and interactions are pristine.  Despite some people describing this game as having puzzles, the solutions are so easy to intuit that they're mostly intended to be flavoring for the adventure rather than work your brain.  They're clearly trying to tell a story as smoothly as possible, not throw roadblocks at you.
The only issues I had were a single bug that a restart fixed and there was an important voice recording that lacked a level of emotion necessary for the scene.  The voice overs in general were kind of generic, though satisfactory and not distracting for most of the contexts they're used in as no words are spoken.  It's not as much of an issue until emotion is important in a scene and the voices don't convey that.
Overall, the game is very tastefully creative.  The creativity doesn't blow your mind so much as it impresses you that they invested the effort to bring you that experience.  There are subtle surprising progressions as things go from run-of-the-mill to wild over the course of the game.  Take ICO (minus the flaws), smash it together with some vague Journey inspiration, give it charming visuals, a touch of Tomb Raider and maybe throw in the occasional overlooks from Assassin's Creed by way of benches you sit on and you have Brothers.
As most of the story is told through brief interactions, it's probably best to interact with each thing in the game using each brother to see as much of their personalities as possible.
I laughed a few times, though it's not trying too hard to be funny.  Cranked the music in a few spots, but the music doesn't steal the show.  It's a linear game telling an extremely simple story that takes a short 3 hours to complete, so there's no need to rush through it.  It works with keyboard, but a gamepad is worth using.
Similar to Journey, it is probably best to play it in one or two sittings, keeping the entire experience fresh in your mind until the end.
This game is a work of art.  Sit back, relax and let brothers sweep you away into a emotionally engaging tale.  (It is only 4-5 hours long so check it out damn it)

Working with award winning Swedish director Josef Fares, Starbreeze Studios presents us with a downloadable story-driven adventure game. Question is can the influence of a movie director provide a fulfilling narrative and satisfying gameplay without sacrificing one or the other? Let's take a look.
The premise is simple. Two brothers must find an specific object located on a map in order to cure their father of a life threatening illness. Whilst the plot itself is pretty barebones, all the subtle nuances make up for it. From the different ways the brothers interact with objects to the interchanges between them both “Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons” is firmly under the implication that actions speak louder than words, which is further accentuated by the characters speaking in gibberish which relies a lot on body language to get the exact emotion or exchange across. Thankfully the game gets this right and later on in the game hits some truly dark and morose moments that’s sure to make most people choke up slightly.
The gameplay provides what can best be described as a single player co-op experience. You control both characters with each individual stick and triggers which can be difficult to wrap your head around at first but once the player is accustomed to the play style then it becomes a unique scenario where the gameplay works in tandem with the story so that these brothers feel more connected. This is especially used well in the later sections when the tone shifts and segments are given much more weight and power. Visually the game holds up great with its simple painted story book style to create some impressive looking scenes, the only drawback is that the animations can sometimes be a little jerky which is only a minor blemish on an otherwise stellar visual package. The only other major issue is the game’s length which only provides about 2-3 hours of playtime which could be a turn off for some. However this shorter length makes the game keep a steady pace and avoids any filler that could have otherwise bogged down the experience so it’s a decent payoff.
Some may want to hold off until the game is cheaper but be assured that it’s definitely worth recommending. By providing a grim fairytale and unique gameplay Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons creates a memorable, albeit brief experience that is sure to stick with you.

I had never heard of this game, but I stumbled across it while searching for online co-op games to play with a friend.  I don't ordinarily write reviews, but I like this game so much that I wanted to spread the word.
The basics:
In Ibb & Obb, you are in a world that has an unusual form of gravity.  If you look at the screenshots, you can see that there is a line that roughly divides the playfield into a top and bottom.  When you are above this line, gravity works how you would expect.  When you are below it, you "fall" up, towards the line.  (In other words, you're always attracted to the line.)  You can only switch sides at the various gates in the level (the particle-y lines in the pictures).  ORdinarily these gates are white, but some gates are red or green.  Anyone can go through a white gate, but only the character that matches the color of the gate can pass through the red and green ones.
The challenge comes from cooperating with your partner to solve the puzzles.  This often requires making clever use of your momentum when switching from one side to the other.  As you can see in the video, enemies can be killed on one side of the line, but the player on the other side has to collect the gems.
What I like:
This game is gorgeous.  I find the colors to be very satisfying, and I find the overall art style to be very pleasant.  Obviously not everyone may agree, but I want to really commend the developers for making such a stylish game.
Same thing for the music.  Pretty much as soon as the game started, I thought, "Wow, this music is great."  I never really stopped thinking that.
The gameplay is also fun.  The puzzles start off fairly simply to introduce you to the mechanics, then start to become a little trickier.  This is especially true once you realize that there are optional gems floating around in some places - getting these requires more thought than simply figuring out how to beat the level.  So far, the puzzles are hard enough that you feel satisfied when you beat them, but not so hard that you ever get frustrated.
I'd also like to mention the way this game is packaged.  You can buy a single copy, and it would be a fair price, but for slightly more money you can buy a double pack and gift a copy to a friend.  This game is definitely meant to be played with a friend, and the devs make it very easy to do that by so strongly incentivizing the double pack.
What I don't like:
Honestly, I don't have any complaints so far.  I've really been enjoying this game.
What I don't know:
I'm not sure how long the game is.  That information might be available, but I haven't really checked.  Given how reasonably priced the game is, especially with a double pack, I don't feel like it would have to be super long for me to get my money's worth.  I'll update this if I end up beating it in 15 minutes the next time I play, but I haven't even seen all the areas highlighted in the screenshots, so I don't expect that to happen.
Conclusion:
I highly recommend this game.  It's beautiful, fun, and clever.  I only wish that I'd heard about it sooner!

Russpuppy, it’s good to have you back on Steamified. This is the second of the developer-publisher’s games that we’ve been fortunate enough to spotlight so far this year. The first was The Deletion which we featured very early on (January 7th). Where The Deletion was a fast paced minimalist puzzle-platformer Domino Sky is a much slower paced strategic game where the objective is to drop dominos into a lovely cascade in order to complete puzzles.
I love the game. I was one of those kids who used to pull out my dominos to put them on the kitchen table, the living room carpet or any surface that I could possibly find to see how many dominos I could get to cascade down. Some of my most cherished childhood memories were doing spending hours doing this with friends. It was one game that I was pretty darn good at. Winning came relatively easy but I truly did love seeing how artistic friends could be with their dominos. Therefore you could say that I’ve been waiting for such a game to come out for a long, long time. And with Russpuppy’s excellence of execution they didn’t disappoint me. Sure, it could be a little more polished but the game does what it sets out to do. I love the different challenges and that the achievements tied to them are spaced out that you have to work for the next one and the next one until you’ve completed the game which I am dead set going to do at some point. The physics are also pretty much close to perfection which is absolutely an important facet of the game.
If I had to nitpick on the game a little it would be that the camera is a little frustrating. I would have liked it to have been a little more mobile and easy to move than what it is. But it does move it’s just a little bit of a struggle at times to get it where you want it to be. Other than that I have no complaints at all with the game. There’s more than a sufficient amount of levels for a sub-$5 game and you also have free build mode for those who want to be artistic and build something spectacular.
If I could offer something a little unnecessary but a wishlist item for the title it would have been nice to see a little game of dominos implemented into the game. Perhaps unnecessary but it would have been a really sweet touch.
The game has been Steamified with trading cards and achievements.
A hearty and childlike recommendation. Thanks Russpuppy.

Great game that really puts you on edge as you deal with one problem after the next. The hulll of the plane being carved out as you take damage is fantastic. The audio work is excellently done. I do enjoy customizing each of my crew, even if the navigator and radio operator dont really have useful, unique gear. It gives you the sense that you can customize each person to perfectly suit what you need them for. I like that losing your airplane is only a temporary set back instead of a game ender. The level system definitely makes you want to keep your crew alive as long as possible to get those good skills.
I like the idea of the slow down time function. I don't actually use that function but I enjoy the little reward I get for not using it.
The game could use steam workshop for sharing customized hull art or decals or even crew uniforms. More mission types or different aircraft would also be fun to see since mixing up the aircraft stations would provide a difficullty change. Maybe something like a side heavy fighter campaign? (Smaller plane, crew and more combat oriented missions instead of bombing runs.) Maybe having the player decide what bombs to take would also add some more difficulty, especially if you make them have to account for the weight of the bombs  and have that dynamically effect fuel range (which is not implemented from what I can tell.)
My few complaints so far are:
- Alarms for unmanned stations should be more noticable. With so much occuring on screen, it is hard to notice when you remove a pilot from the chair.
- The mission briefing could be better. It should include obvious things (if they would be known to the player)  like the number of targets, the forecast, the time of day your mission will fly at (or a selction if the mission allows it).

ADDICTING! The missions can seem a litte repeative in a way but all the options and upgrades really keep you going to the next. I would love to see some DLC of more bombers or maybe a pacific theater.

When I got this game I was expecting for it to be amazing.... and boy did it deliver. This is definitely my game of the year 2013!
I actually don't know which aspect of the game I liked more - the unique gameplay or the wonderful story and the way it's presented to the player.
On the surface it looks like a regular puzzle platformer, but the thing that sets it apart form other games is the fact that you control each of the brothers individually. And that's the thing that makes some of the latter puzzles challenging, since technically they alle are pretty simple. Controlling two characters simultaneously is an odd thing to do. Another amazing aspect of this game is the fact that throughout the game not a single word was spoken to either explain a gameplay mechanic or to progress the story, and jet it was easy to understand what was going on and what the game wanted me to do.
Both visuals and sound of this game create wonderful atmosphere that compliments the emotional story at all times. I wouldn't say the games graphic are anything special, but it by no means an ugly game. Pretty much all environments are nicely crafted and few places are down right gorgeous.
This reminds me that I have to look up the soundtrack of Brothers, because some of it's tracks are still stuck in my head.
But I must also warn you of few things that may put a frown on your face. The game was designed with a controller in mind, which is a non issue if you have an access to such a thing, but as far as I know most PC gamesrs do not have them. Keyboard controls work, and you can definitely play the game, but it feels much more organic when it's played with a controller. It also isn't the longest of games. I bet it in about three hours. Which for this kind of a game is just perfect I think, but I also bought it at a discounted price(50%) and at full price I would have probably been a little disappointed. But as it stand it was worth every cent I spent on it.
TL;DR
Buy it you dummy! It's amazing!

While this game does many things very well, there are a couple that really bothered me.
Pros
The game has a very cute and minimalist aesthetic that I enjoyed.
The puzzles have a pretty good difficulty curve, with progressively more challenging puzzles.
I also liked how the game exhibited new mechanics. There are virtually no words throughout the game, and the game does a nice job of showing you how to do something before you do it (at least for the beginning puzzles).
Neutral
The controls felt a bit off at first. The jump felt a little too floaty. But after about 10 minutes, it wasn't hard to adjust to it.
Cons
While I said that the difficulty curve is fine overall, much of the latter part relies too heavily on being able to precisely time and coordinate movements between your partner with little room for error. If you or your partner mess up, you'll have to retry.
My main gripe however, which will probably sound pretty inconsequential, is the fact that the game doesn't exactly excel. The game does things well, but not really well enough to stand out. It makes nice use of it's gravity-changing doorways, so they don't feel tacked on, but unfortunately, there's not much else to set it apart, and with so many indie puzzle platformers, you really need to do so.
