I started downloading this game with visions of a sprawling medieval land, where I was free to forge my own path. As I watched gigabytes tick away, I dreamed of my homestead. I knew it would be hard, but I was ready for the challenge.
Boy, was I disappointed. I started playing the game as a "fledgling." During that time, nobody could attack me and I couldn't attack them. I used the time to gather resources. I found a bank, made some deposits. I was disappointed immediately that the only quests in the game were the tutorials, which were an absolute mess, but I kept going. I bought armor, managed to craft a few things but kept feeling like the work was going to far outweigh the fun had in-game. The graphics were sub-par, the UI was reminiscent of Ultima Online's, terribly outdated, the servers were fairly laggy at times, the controls themselves were less than responsive, the items in-game were somewhat cryptic and disjointed and the help system looked like someone just put some filler text in and moved on.
A messaged popped up, "You are no longer a fledgling!" "Woo-hoo," I thought, "Now it's time to conquer." No such luck. Within a minute of getting my upgraded status, I was murdered. I figured, "Oh, well. It's a survival game. I like those." I shook off the fact that I lost all my inventory and set to respawning. I found the priest, told him to bring my back and was on my way. I grabbed only what I needed this time and decided to flee to a quieter area. Just outside of town, I was murdered again. This happened over and over. I gave up for the day.
I came back to the game the next day and set out, only to accidentally target what was apparently someone's pig. The game punished me and the guard killed me. I set out again. I found a quiet area, it was nice. I was murdered again. I was way out this time, far from a priest. I asked the game to send me to the priest, which takes 60 seconds. I patiently waited, "20 seconds... 10 seconds." To my dismay, the game popped up with its message that I had been transported, but, guess what? I hadn't been. I tried again, "I'm not walking that far." Same thing happened.
I started hoofing it only to come across priest after priest that would only service their guild, with no distinction between the ones I could use and couldn't. This meant walking endlessly, going to priest after priest, just hoping. I thought, "I could make a new character. That would be easier." If it's easier to create a new character in a game, and go through the leveling process again, than to simply respawn, it has problems. That realization brought me full circle and I gladly exited. Of course, it made me wait 10 seconds. I ALT+F4'd just to show them I wasn't going to be their plaything anymore.
The concept of the game is great, but it is poorly executed, poorly supported and lacks direction. This feels like a college project, not a game meant for production. For anyone wanting to proceed, despite these words of warning, I only say to you, "I bet you're going to be disappointed."
UPDATE - 10/3/2015
------------------------------
I still wanted to like this game after my review so I popped back in to give it my full effort before I uninstalled it. I was pleased to find that my spawn issue was corrected (probably due to the server reboot occurring when I logged on) and I set off to a new town. I found that town less "murdery" and was able to setup a haul near a banker as to quickly deposit my funds. Although the murders came less frequently, they were still of great impact. Unless you want to run back and forth constantly, you need to amass a decent amount of resources to make the time worth the effort. The murders wipe out tens of minutes of work and are really disheartening.
Now, don't get me wrong; I know it's a survival game, but it shouldn't also be work. A murder shouldn't necessarily come with less impact, but should definitely be less frequent. There needs to be a greater penalty for murders, just as is the case in the real world. They provide guards, but that doesn't introduce any real preventive measure, and players are apparently allowed one murder of an innocent before the murdered player can call guards (I'm not sure of the cooldown). I understand what they're going for, but, unless there is some sort of policing when it comes to other players ruining others' experience with the game, these types of reviews will keep coming.
So, unfortunately, I still can't recommend the game. What would it take for me to change my mind? Stricter penalties for murdering other players, such as a jail period that equates to actual time lost in-game. I'm sure the problem would decrease drastically. The survival aspect would still be intact, but players would be able to somewhat comfortably navigate the world. If you want to create a pure survival game, then do that, developers, but if you want to create a game players will come back to and can take pride in what they've accomplished, make the question of their survival one that can be answered, not one led by the whims of a murder bound five-year-old with an itchy finger.
Developers: Make this Moral Online by doing what any responsible government does: protect its citizens. I won't uninstall the game just yet. I'll ensure I continue to check release notes for these types of changes. If I see a similar dynamic has been introduced, I'll come back and give it another go, consider a subscription and, of course, update my review. The game has potential, and I would love to see it all come together, but I must admit, I won't be holding out hope considering how long the game has been in development. Please, consider the value of a wider player base. Simply satisfying the relatively small group of existing subscribers isn't the best route for funding your development.

If you want to 'live' out something akin to a stategic conquest game where youget to fight and order soldiers, which is immensely addicting and a whole lot of fun, then get this game. It has some flaws, yes, and the graphics are dated, but a lot of this can be fixed thanks to the amazing modding community which has created so many solid mods. There are complete era and map changes, that come with their own gameplay dynamics (and the existent gameplay dynamics are very fun). The game IS an RPG, and while I wouldn't compare it to Oblivion or Skyrim for example, because it's not complete open world exploration (which is a bit of a shame). It is, however, something that gives you real choice. You can choose to fight for an allegiance or kingdom, or work your way up as a vassal with a fief (a property such as a town, village or castle) and gradually collect more as you fight for them, and this creates a sense of drama between actually trying to get the fiefs (which is difficult as there is almost a fight for them). In that way, you can try to incriminate lords who might want it, losing honour but increasing your chances. You fight in your area against other people with your party. That's just one way to play it however - you can find an heir or claimant to the throne who wishes to claim the throne of a certain nation, and then work with them, and then later betray their trust or continue to work with them. A lot of human greed and human nature falls into it. You can either get greedy or choose to be honourable and fair - and there are consequences and benefits of all of this. I feel that there are some imbalances with this game. You can use a ool known as 'TweakMB' to tweak the game to your likings, but just remember not to overdo it because the game might get too easy and boring (but really, play how you want to). The game can be a lot of trouble and stressful on harder difficulties. I started at an easy difficulty and found a lot of challenge at the beginning, then found it progressively easier (but still somewhat challenging).
The game requires some time investment to know how it works, but when that's all done? Good luck on getting potentially hundreds of hours of your life consumed (although I wonder what else you could be doing that could be better than the hours you spend here).

This is a terrific game. I haven't played the Japanese Mystery Dungeon games this takes it's inspiration from. I guess I've been missing out.
Voyage to Farland is a turn-based roguelike. It's very bare bones. There are no classes, skills, stats, gold or shops. You are just your level, hit points, and whatever you pick up in the dungeon. In exchange for all that Voyage to Farland focuses more on consumable item abilities. The items you find control enemy pacing, placement, movement, etc. There is very little direct damage. Gameplay is focused on tactics, exploration, and inventory management.
There is a good variety of enemies, enough to keep things interesting. The enemies all have leveled up versions, Sometimes they will level up during a fight when they kill one of your companions, or when you trick them into killing one of their allies.
The items are where this game really shines. The variety isn't huge, but it is all useful. No clogging up your inventory with useless junk to sell later. There is just enough so that you can learn what it does, and how to use it effectively. Then you can finally stop dying repeatedly, and watching your companions be butchered by monsters.
I definitely recommend it to any roguelike fan.

Let's get it out of the way right off the bat. Yes, it's ugly as sin. I could say "at least it's not pixel art" but that's just damning with faint praise. And the music is even worse.
But this captures the heart of Mystery Dungeon style games so well.
For those who don't know what that means, Mystery Dungeon is a brand of Japanese roguelikes dungeon crawlers (You may have seen the Shiren, Pokemon, or Etrian flavors). What makes them stand out is how simple they are compared to the western brand of roguelike. There are not six fiddly stats and 40 rings, scrolls, and wands to manage nor are there 40 fiddly tricks to have to cover like keeping a wand of fire to scribble galadriel at opportune moments. You do not have to memorize 40 pages of spoilers and have "blessed +2 gray dragon scale mail" tattooed on your forearm.
In exchange for all that, the genre focuses more on gamey style abilities. The wands and abilities you find control enemy pacing, placement, movement, etc. And when there is a horde of monsters bearing down on you with a monster that can paralyze you and another that can drain your levels, your brain will be tested just like the best of roguelikes.
So what MD offers is something more innately intuitive and accessible than the overwrought and overfiddly roguelikes you may be accustomed to, but one still quite difficult. If the western flavor is an enormous wargame run by steely-eyed grognards with fearsome neckbeards ready to debate tactics from the galactic wars of the far future to the Civil War, MD is closer to chess.
Voyage to Farland is almost a straight reskin of the DS Shiren game. Every ability, every trick is there, with its own spin on balancing. If you can get past the atrocious art style, you will find an excellent homage to a roguelike flavor that just is not well-represented on PC. Complete with Shiren's love of secrets and inventory management, but with different enemy design, pacing, and balancing, it is a wonderful homage from a fellow who is clearly as moved by Shiren as I am.

It's a cute little Collectible Card Game (CCG) from the developers of Muri, Magicka: Wizards of the Square Tablet, and Ittle Dew. The game features characters and art styling from Ittle Dew, which may mean it is set in the same world. The goal is to defeat the opponent by either draining their defense to 0 through attacks or forced card draws (the opponent looses defense when they are out of cards and are given random cards) or forcing the opponent to fill their 9x9 card board with cards, leaving them with no way to complete combos. Card combos are made by linking three symbols from cards  in a almost tic-tac-toe fashion, where each card has an arrow pointing to where it can be connected. Combos include attack to damage defense or disable enemy cards, defense to restore your defense, revive to enable disabled cards and neutral to act as filler for other combos. Some cards have different effects, such as multiple symbols so it only needs a second card instead of a third, or rotating player or enemy cards.
It's a cute little card game that's quite casual, and most importantly, inexpensive at full retail.  I found the character design and interactions to be rather charming and definitely a more laid back exprience than Magic or Hearthstone.  I don't feel like this is a must play by any means, but it is a good CCG that in the worst case scenario, won't hurt your wallet much.

The cards are all based on characters from Ludosity's earlier games, but you don't need to be familiar with them (I wasn't). I guess that being familiar with them would make it easier to guess what cards to combine to get new ones, but there's a guide for that here on Steam. I'll start by saying this game flew under my radar (see what I did there?). I did not hear any reviews of this game in the usual YouTube gaming channels I visit; I only saw it featured in the Store page and it already caught my attention.
Bomber Crew really scratched that itch I had for "mindless" grinding for better skills and upgrades, while paired with the challenge of surviving through every mission and threat thrown at your hard-earned build. In a way, it's like a more colorful FTL-meets-XCOM in real-time (that's right, turn off bullet time, folks). The repeatable missions were perfect for getting more coins and unlocking crew and plane upgrades, as they gave me more time to assess if I'm already prepared for the next campaign mission. Permadeath was also the icing on the cake; you can really feel it when you lose one or two crew members, now imagine the horror when you helplessly watch your bomber crash due to its heavy damage.
The only complaint I have (that I'm sure will be addressed soon) is the difficulty of clicking items in the front equipment rack. Since the Radio Op and Navigator are hogging that small space, I usually could not reach the first aid or extinguisher there during critical times. Hopefully the developers can consider putting an option to zoom more inside the interior of each fuselage section of the plane during flight, just like how it zooms in the hangar while upgrading them.
Other recommendations I have would be:
1. Uploading your custom livery without having to draw it on the canvas. I suck at drawing pixel art.
2. Custom controls and hotkeys. I've been used to left-clicking to select units then right-clicking them to do an assigned action. While there are default hotkeys for selecting crew, I wish it could be assigned freely to frequently used units (such as assigning "1" to the bomber or engineer instead of the pilot).
With that said, yes I recommend this game a lot, especially since the developers are planning to release more content really soon (yay!). They deserve two-thumbs up for this one-of-a-kind gem, and I am excited to see what else they have in store!

A charming and quirky game about the crew of a WW2 RAF bomber. Full of promise, but has some major, unforgivable flaws:
1. The control scheme is awful. Crew members aree not automated and must be told to do absolutely everything. Sometimes this requires several people to be told to do several things at once, but due to fiddly controls, exaggerated time movement and incredibly unobliging camera angles, this usually ends badly.
2. Some missions simply cannot be successfully completed. Not because they're difficult, not because my tactics are bad, but simply because the plane doesn't carry enough fuel to get there and back.
These issues are clearly oversights of design, and could be easily remedied with a patch aimed at addressing them. If such a patch is released, this will end up being a very enjoyable, and highly-reccomendable (if somewhat shallow and arcadey) game, but for the time being I can not and will not reccomend anything with such fundamental flaws.

Actually pretty fun!  I could write way too much criticism of this match 3 dating sim, enough to embarass myself and prevent and future public office holding, so I'll just say that it's good.

TL;DR at the bottom
You've seen your favourite YouTubers play it, you've heard your friends talk about it, you've read websites' moral outrage pieces about it, it's none other than HuniePop!
At it's core, HuniePop is two things, a decent dating sim and an insanely challenging and fun match-3 game, even more so if you go for the game's achievements as they force you to approach the game from a different angle.
On the Dating sim part, you walk around your town, flirting with all the girls, giving them gifts, food, drinks, answering their questions and asking them out on dates. It's not particularly deep, but the full voice acting makes it really engaging(if you dislike the voice acting, there's a "beep" voice setting that makes all the characters talk à-la early Phoenix Wright games).
Now, for the match-3 part...it's amazing. That's really the only way I can summarise it. As opposed to most match-3 where you can only move any piece up, down, left or right by 1 space, this game throws that out the window to allow for more strategy. Instead, you can take any token and move it anywhere along the row or column that it's in. This allows you to play more strategically.
Say you want to move a token to make a 3 match by moving it the right. You COULD do that, but say at the end of the row, there's also a token you need to move all the way to the left to set up another move after this one. You can take that token and move it all the way to the left, while moving the token for the match-3 into place, effectively making the match-3 and setting up your next move, all with only one move (of course, to move a token like this, a match must be made somewhere on the board, else the token will just snap back to where it was).
The goal of the match-3 game is to reach a certain score before running out of moves. Doing so will result in a successful date, and failing to do so will reward you with snark or anger from the girl and a failed date. Now, it's also not just that simple. There's a few things that can change the outcome. The first is the Broken Heart token. Just like the other tokens, this token can make match-3 or higher matches. However, these are the only tokens you won't want to match. Matching them removes a certain percentage of your current score (each piece = 12%, and each piece in the match multiplying the %. i.e. match-3=46%). You can however remove these pieces safely or reduce the percentage. Let's discuss reducing the percentage first.
There are traits that you can upgrade with Hunie (earned by talking to the girls/giving them gifts/drinks) that affect how your dates will go. You can increase any of the 4 main stats (Flirtation, Talent, Romance and Sexuality) which will cause matches of those tokens to give more points, Passion, which will increase your max passion level when matching heart shaped tokens (which acts as a point multiplier), sensitivity, which reduces the percentage that broken hearts remove from your score when matched, Charisma which increases the points you get from matches overall and luck which increases how often you'll get a power token (causes the match you use it in to generate more points). If you use these wisely, as each girl likes a different stat more than the others (and one she likes the least), you can perform well in the match-3 games.
Finally, there are date gifts, items you can give the girls during the dates that change the date dynamic or cause some sort of effect on the board. One example of each would be the Leopard Print Pumps that cause any match-4 or higher to grant an additional move or the Stuffed Bear that changes every Broken Heart token on the board into a passion token. Of course, you can't just use these items whenever. There's a another mechanic in place that regulates them and that would be sentiment. Get enough sentiment by matching sentiment tokens (shaped like tears) and you can use a date gift, each having a different sentiment value.
Now, as for the game's other part...the nudity. While the Steam version comes censored by default, you can uncensor it easily by following the instructions from the developer himself in this thread from the game's discussion forum:
Now, let's go over some other elements of the game.
The music is really well done. They always fit the locations where they play. Be it the park, a casino or a water park, they're all nice to listen to. My ONLY qualm with the music is that you can hear the point where the music loops in certain tracks.
The visuals are very appealing (and I don't just mean the bedroom scenes). All the environments are well designed and really put you into the location. The HUD and menus are also very appealing to the eye, as they never seem too cluttered or hard to navigate. Finally, the girls. Well, that's probably gonna be subjective to you ;)
The controls are pretty much what you'd expect. Nothing huge. Just use your mouse (or trackpad) to navigate the menus and move the tokens during the dates.
The replayability of the game certainly exists. With all the different date items combinations you can attempt, as well as the achievements that challenge you to play the game differently, the game has a lot of replayability. The end game has some replayability issues as the final end game difficulty dates mainly just require you to abuse the most useful item in the game to finish it, but otherwise, replayability is not an issue with this game.
Now, a few minor complaints.
Sometimes during dates, you'll complete a match with a Borken Heart token underneath  the cleared tokens and two Broken Hearts will spawn from the top, causing a Broken heart match that was largely out of your control. It's rare enough, but it's still frustrating when it happens.
The luck trait is very subjective in how good it is. Personally, if I could redo my 100% profile, I would undo maxing it as a maxed luck stat gives 100% power token from a 5-match, 80% from a 4-match and a 20% chance from a 3-match. I personally dislike having the 3-match with a chance of spawning a power token. It can screw you over sometimes if you're trying to line up a match. I would personally cap the luck stat off at 5-match 100% and 4-match 50% (which is the third upgrade) if I were to do another 100% profile.
Going for 100%, you have to ask every girl for all their info. However, you can't ask them directly. You have to wait for them to ask you if there's anything you want to ask. This can be particularly frustrating sometimes if you're only missing one piece of info for 1 girl and the game won't let you ask about it. However, this will only really be an issue if you go for 100%.
However, with everything said and done, I cannot recommend this game enough. If you want a good dating sim with a match-3 puzzle system that's deeper than most, this game is definitely for you.
Now, for a TL;DR:
Pros:
-A deep match-3 system
-Music
-Visuals
-Controls
-Replayability
Cons:
-Some tracks can be heard looping
-Broken Hearts will sometimes screw you over when it's not your fault
-The Luck trait should be upgraded with caution
-100%ing all girls info can take a while
Very Recommended.

"Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons" is my Game of the Year for 2013. 2013 is the year I started to move away from "AAA" games and start looking at indie games. I've played a few great ones, but "Brothers" transcends the gaming medium into an experience you would expect from a television series or a feature film.
The most obvious thing about "Brothers' is the control scheme. You have not played a game like this before. One controller (and you do need a controller, though a keyboard can be used, despite what the store page says) controls both brothers. Stick moves, trigger is a context-based "use" button. Left for older, right for younger. It makes sense, and it works 99% of the time. The only trouble is when they cross over (you'll want to keep the older brother left of the younger brother) but that's easy to fix, stop them both and start with one, then add the other. You might notice my Steam avatar is from Rockband; the same technique is useful there as well when playing guitar or drums. Start with one beat, then add the others one at a time.
Most of the puzzles are fairly basic. When you realize that a ladder out of reach means the older brother has to hoist the younger brother up, you'll use that a few more times. However, the game doesn't feel redundant. It does challenge you in new and different ways, but the mechanics are all generally the same. Pretty much, once you get the hang of it, the puzzles seem to come second nature, which is necessary for this game to work the way it does. You aren't meant to get hung up on puzzles; rather, you may fail a couple times, but once you have that "A-ha!" moment and realize what you need to do—it just clicks.
The story is all kinds of wonderful and amazing. There are things about it I just can't talk about. It's like a film, you don't want to give away what happens in the second half, or the last two-thirds. Most of these scenes, I'm sure, will come out in the next few months, as more and more people play it. The ending will be given away. It was actually spoiled for me, or at least a part of it. I still found it incredibly moving. There's this thing that happens, and I just couldn't believe the game made me do that. And then afterwards. It's been about 6 hours and my mind is still being blown when I think about it.
$15 for a 3.5 hour game (that's about what it took me) seems high, but it's worth every cent. It will probably go on sale, but this is one you will want to play before all your friends. Because hearing about those incredibly moving parts, wouldn't be the same as actually experiencing them. Don't cheat yourself.

Clustertruck is a first-person view platformer with a very fun, yet simple objective, jump from truck to truck until you eventually reach the end of a level. Though lacking in a few features most FPV games usually have, this game is fun and will eventually enthrall you. Its graphics, controls, and appearance may initially appear to be bland and simplistic, but you'll eventually realize how a lot was done with so little.
CT is a game that's purely about gameplay, there's no story here at all and while that may dissuade some from playing this game, I had no problem with that at all. CT's control scheme is simple to the point where you won't be using more than 5 buttons in the whole game. It's possible to play (while using an xbox 360 controller) just using the left thumbstick and the A button, but some special abilities will eventually require the use of one or two more additional buttons.
As I previously mentioned, the main goal of this game is to advance through each of the 90 levels by jumping from truck to truck. The final level also features an unexpected "surprise" that isn't encountered elsewhere in the game. The levels are all separated into 9 unique worlds with their own separate environment specific traps, obstacles, and music to keep things fresh. (It's refreshing to play through a game where you aren't forced to listen to a limited number of tracks being endlessly repeated) An example of the levels/environments uniqueness would be the hell themed environment where you have to avoid lava, a forest environment with loads of green landscape, trees (they won't get in your way), and even a futuristic looking environment.
On the subject of the levels/environments, it's also worth mentioning that this game has holiday specific levels. These holiday specific levels are great, but I assume they only unlock during the time the holiday is celebrated. Being that it's October, I could only play through the Halloween levels, but I couldn't play through the Christmas levels. I wanted to play them almost immediately after having beaten the Halloween levels because it's more or less extra content and these holiday specific levels offered unique traps/obstacles.
I'd also like to mention that touching obstacles, traps, the ground, and generally anything other than the trucks will lead to an instant death. For that reason alone, you'll want to always jump onto the roof of each truck, it's usually the most secure way to get through a level. Should your jump not have been good enough, there's also the chance to grab onto the back of a truck. There are a few instances in which you can touch something else as a way to maneuver through the level, but this is usually a rare occurrence.
I've previously mentioned that this game is simplistic in more ways than one, but the game is designed in such a way that it'll eventually become much harder. The trucks will vary in speed/distance from each other, the different levels/environments will offer traps to make things more difficult, and the precision required to make even the simplest jump will at times lead to you having to replay through a level. The game's possibilities will also come off as a double-edged sword. You can stick to playing it safe through this game by jumping to nearby trucks, but you'll also have the possibility to skip over trucks by use of long distance jumping and if used correctly, you'll also be able to group together jumps so it feels like one giant interconnected, fluid motion. This in particular feels really cool to do and it'll allow you to get through the levels even faster.
For the most part, the levels can be beaten in one or two tries, but a few towards the middle/end of this game will require multiple attempts. It's usually the very specific levels/environments that require the most effort to get through. Even though you'll have to repeat these later levels multiple times, the respawns are almost instantaneous and the levels aren't too long (some levels can literally be beaten in a matter of seconds), it won't really bother you that much if/when you die a lot.
Honestly, there wasn't that much I didn't enjoy about this game. What I found to be bothersome didn't ruin the game at all, but I felt there were some things that I felt could've been different/improved upon to make this game even better than it is. One thing that's almost immediately noticed is that your character (if you can even call it that) in this game is more or less an invisible entity. Arms, legs, or even a combination of both would've been useful. It's funny that you play as a shapeless figure, but sometimes your movements felt stiff. As a result of lacking any discernible shape, landing precise/correctly timed jumps can be a bit troublesome when you first start playing through this game.
Even after I got the hang of this game, landing jumps were still a hassle to deal with, especially when I had to land on a moving truck from a long distance. In this game jumps have to be measured by sight, but things would've been much easier if you had a cross hairs or something to aim your jumps with. A special ability eventually gives you something like cross hairs, but it's not available by default and you have to accumulate points before you're able to unlock it.
The game has quite a few special abilities that you can choose to use/unlock, but you can only equip two at the same time. A few of them are the ability to freeze time for a brief moment, a double jump, and a grappling hook. Honestly, some of the special abilities didn't feel quite special. A specific example would be how the double jump works in this game. Your default first jump is very high, but if you unlock and use the double jump, it's not as good as the initial jump, it'll more or less grant you a brief moment of hang time in the air. There's a very particular way to jump off of the back of a truck that'll allow you to jump really high, which is much more helpful than the double jump, but it's difficult to use. You can go through most of the game without having to use these special abilities and it won't horribly affect your enjoyment of this game. There will be some levels that'll require additional assistance in the form of the special abilities, but the number of them is very few.
Besides those problems, I also felt that some of the game's levels lacked direction. For the most part, the levels are linear and they'll always require you to go forward. You'll eventually reach a point where that isn't the case and you'll have to eventually turn backwards to advance or even descend to lower parts of the level. My problem with this is that it isn't easy to figure this out and it'll require a few deaths until you figure out what you need to do. Others may find this problematic because the game offers bonus points for beating a level in one attempt.
Despite having a fun main campaign that consists of 90 levels and additional holiday levels, CT is a short game. I didn't try to rush through the game and I still managed to beat it in three hours. Not only did it take me three hours, I was able to beat two thirds of the game in one night. Maybe it's because I found the game to be that entertaining, but my experience with this game went by too quickly. There are some gamers out there that will enjoy the game due to being able to quickly play through the game and move onto something else, but at the same time there'll be others out there that really like getting the most bang out of their buck.
To conclude, I highly enjoyed CT and I could see myself coming back at a later time to play the Christmas levels. CT is proof why many more people should pay more attention to indie gaming. It takes a simple formula, but still manages to create a fun and unique experience. I most definitely recommend this game.

Let first open this review off with this. Whilst I do ultimately recommend this game I feel it has plenty of issues which I'll go into.
This game was so close to being this generations 'Toejam & Earl' so very close. For those of you that don't know Toejam & Earl is a game that came out on the sega genesis/megadrive way way back in 1990... or around about then. Regardless it went on to become one of my favourite games of all time and was a favorite between me and my friends when we fancied some co-op action.
So when I found out this game was clearly inspired by Toejam & Earl I was over the moon and very excited. So much so that it coloured my early judgement of the game quite heavily and made me have more positive thoughts at the time than I perhaps should've.
So Finn & Jake's Epic Quest is game where Finn and Jake go around a world (broken up into 6 levles + a boss battle) looking for the portal to the next one. In order to progress though some maps have artifacts (ship pieces for those familiar with Toejam & Earl) which must also be found along with the portal in order to progress. Other similarities to ToeJam & Earl include power ups which are a complete mystery until used which can (more often than not) give a benefit or (unfourtenetly rarely) a disadvantage... this includes the elusive Radomizer which made Toejam & Earl such an unforgiving game.
Which is my first problem with this game... it's not nearly difficult enough. In Toejam & Earl the predictable nature of the enermies was completely forgivable because every last one of them was a genuine threat but in this game the enermies become moslty a means to grind out levels. All of them are completely avoidable and aren't particuarly fun to fight in large number and whilst the combat isn't bad, it feels okay and in groups can be mildly challenging, it becomes pretty tedious with only one apparent combo being present in the game 3 hours and 4 worlds in. Therefore the enermies become a meaningless obstacle which are just there for coin. Which is another issue... you never 'need' money... another thing about Toejam & Earl is money was scarce and it'd cost way more than you'd ever aquire to get everything you'd want on a single map. Here the enermies are easy enough to vanquish without the aid of powerups with the powerups only speeding up the time it takes to kill things and are only every needed when you need to fly or float to specific areas.... the powerups are fun though and the is a lot of variety on offer. But asides from the Randomizer and 'Knife Storm' I saw no powerups which reminded me of 'Total Bummer' or 'Rocket Skates' on Toejam & Earl... in other words just go nuts and dont worry about any ill effects you'll be able to get them all identified again anyways because it's so cheap to do so.
Also the is no co-op, this is a galreing omission from a game thats inspired by a game that is known for it's innovative co-op mode where players where able to individually explore other areas of map but other stages entirely... the tag system from toejam & earl is here but no co-op.
But on it's own merits it's still a decent game for the price, it looks good enough, the gameplay provides a nice distraction in small bursts and you get quite a lot for your money. (I reckon 5hours if you try to complete everything and level up your character) and it's a solid homage to one of my favorite games of all time. It's not bad for a licenced game and is worth the asking price but those looking for a true spiritual succesor to Toejam & Earl this isn't it. It's so close to being a very nice modernized version of it but it falls short of truely capturing what the game great and instead is just a fairly enjoyable romp for a small fee.

While this game does many things very well, there are a couple that really bothered me.
Pros
The game has a very cute and minimalist aesthetic that I enjoyed.
The puzzles have a pretty good difficulty curve, with progressively more challenging puzzles.
I also liked how the game exhibited new mechanics. There are virtually no words throughout the game, and the game does a nice job of showing you how to do something before you do it (at least for the beginning puzzles).
Neutral
The controls felt a bit off at first. The jump felt a little too floaty. But after about 10 minutes, it wasn't hard to adjust to it.
Cons
While I said that the difficulty curve is fine overall, much of the latter part relies too heavily on being able to precisely time and coordinate movements between your partner with little room for error. If you or your partner mess up, you'll have to retry.
My main gripe however, which will probably sound pretty inconsequential, is the fact that the game doesn't exactly excel. The game does things well, but not really well enough to stand out. It makes nice use of it's gravity-changing doorways, so they don't feel tacked on, but unfortunately, there's not much else to set it apart, and with so many indie puzzle platformers, you really need to do so.

Machinarium is a terrific point-and-click adventure game. The animation style is really unique and cool, especially after the latest update which updated the graphics to be higher quality and smoother overall. The music is terrific, and complements the animation style to give a lot of character to each scene. It does a wonderful job portraying each character and telling a narrative without using any words at all.
The puzzles and scenes in the game are well crafted and are fun to figure out. The gameplay is smooth, and I was pleasantly suprised with the responsiveness of the minigames in particular. The puzzles themselves were a good difficulty, but there were a few scenes where I found it a challenge to figure out what to do. However, built into the game is a tip and walkthrough system by which you can get a tip at any time and by completing a small minigame you can get a pictoral walkthrough of the entire current stage (screen). This allows for you to figure out the solution to scenes when you're completely stuck without having to resort to external walkthroughs, which in my experience end up spoiling more of the game for you than you intend.
The only thing that I found that I didn't like about the game was the fact that upon entering a new stage (any time you walk through a door or up stairs or something) the application's volume resets itself. I was unable to initially find any volume controls and used the computer's volume mixer to turn it down as with my setup it was a tad loud. However, the volume would periodically reset to a louder level, which made this ineffective and I ended up playing the game with loud sound (which, given how good the music and sounds were, wasn't that bad). After I completed the game I did accidentally find the volume controls, nested in a menu under 'Help' at the bottom of the main screen, so this was in part my own fault. Most settings for the game are under that 'Help' label, which I wouldn't have guessed without clicking on it.
From a completionists standpoint, the achievements are all tied to progression, and if you complete the game you will earn them all without having to go out of your way at all, which is nice.
Overall, the game is very clever and I highly recommend it to anyone who even slightly enjoys point-and-click games.

Surprisingly addictive.
This is one of those rare games where I knew I wanted to get 100% completion rate on it.
For those of you familiar with the Final Fantasies of the early 2000s, this game is a lot like the card mini game tetra master from FF8, FF9, or FF11.
If you've played Ittle Dew, you'll see some familiar characters here.
Basically gameplay takes place on 2 grids, one for you and one for your opponent, where you place the various cards you've collected. Each card has a set of directional arrows, and making a combo of at least 3 cards by connecting the arrows scores some points against the opponent.
There are offensive, defensive, and healing card types, as well as neutral card types which usually have some sort of ability when you place them in combo chains.
The goal is to reduce your opponent's points to 0 before they do the same for yours. Either that or force your opponent to fill up all 9 spaces on their grid and they won't be able to place any more cards and will lose.
It's a simple premise, but quite addicting trying to collect all the cards and win as many matches as you can with the decks you build.

I think I first played this game near enough to when it came out as a disc copy: And I still love it! Ignore the '0.3 hours' in game - It's more than a 100 on here, not sure why it isn't registering it properly..
Spore is an evolution based game, situated in 5 main stages. In each stage there is a general 'goal', be it become more intelligent, increase your species technology, or outright go to space and become a galactic crime organisation.. Either way, the stages can get a little repetative, but with the vast array of possibilities with the creature customisation, it can feel quite fresh each time (all be it quick once you get the hang of it).
The final stage is, in my opinion, good fun for about 10 - 20 hours before it starts to get a little too samey. And I wasn't a fan of the expansion so didn't gain anything from that either, but it is definitely worth a good shot once! With millions of stars to visit (or whatever incredibly large number) you'll never be able to see them all, so extend your empire as far and wide as you can and see where you get too! :) There's quite a few fun things to aim for, and even if you go all out 'economic' to begin with, there's nothing stopping you taking planets by force later down the line.
So, yes, the game has some problems.. Either way, the odd crash to desktop and terrain glitch during Creature Stage isn't the end of the world, and so long as you save now and then you won't loose anything (should you hit problems) - Personally, I've somehow managed to never have a single problem! GO ME :D But in general, there aren't any major gameplay problems as such.
Good, fun, long lasting game! Maybe not the most prettiest game out there (compared to more recent games) but it's still pretty! And, as said previously, with all the customisation options available you can make some pretty interesting stuff. You'll generally have a unique creature, even if you don't try. 8/10 for me :)

Spore is everything I've ever wanted in a game. I grew up on Civilization and Sim City and Spore takes everything those games have to offer and expands it to...everything. There are RPG elements of strategic leveling systems, resource collection, multiple forms of "combat" including a well-supported pacifist playstyle. There is empire building, war, diplomacy and all of it is on huge scales. I also appreciate the impressive in-game customizability which really helped me sink even deeper into each playthrough.
My only complaint is that I would start playing, look up after a few minutes and realize that six hours had passed.

I enjoyed this game. I recommend buying the DLC for it as well though, because the Galactic Adventures DLC adds a lot. You could do without the other one though, but you might as well get it too if you have the money.
(read no further if you don't want to know what happens as you progress.)
You start off on a planet of your choosing. From here you get to start off as a microscopic creature where you can evolve over time by either eating what I assume is algae, or other creatures. From this, paths branch off. You evolve into a mindless animal, who either tries to make friends with other creatures, fights others, or both. Then you evolve again into a tribe, where the same principles apply.  The only sad part is that you can't choose to be an underground civilization, or one that dwells in trees, underwater or on top of mountains. You can choose to give your creature wings though, if you'd like them to "fly". It's sort of just gliding, due to the fact that you can only flap your wings about 5 times or something like that.
The next stage of evolution brings you to city life, where you can either choose to dominate other nations economically, religiously, or through war. Once you've dominated all of the other nations, you advance yet again to the space stage. It's basically the same thing all over again, but in space with spaceships. That's not just it though. In space you get a variety of different missions in which you can colonize planets, eradicate diseased creatures, and even elevate tribal civilizatons!
That's not just it though. You get to create basically everything from your creature (which you can change until you get the later stages), to the buildings in which they live and work. Not only that, but you get to create their land vehicles, air vehicles, and boats. Then once you get to the space stage you get to create the spaceship model that your whole empire uses.
If you want to play smart during the city and space stages, you can micromanage some of your cities to gain more income. Income is used to purchase vehicles during the city stage, and upgrades for your ship during the space stage. You get simple money during the city stage, but in the space stage, cities produce spice. You can sell the spices that are produced for a lot of money, if you can find the right person to sell them to.
Your goal is to reach the center of the galaxy, for who knows what might be there? But many obstacles stand in your way. Deal with them how you wish, because there are multiple ways to get there. Make friends, or dominate others to bring your rule to the whole galaxy. It's up to you. Just remember that everyone needs allies, or just really big guns.
Lastly. The game is really monotonous in my opinion. But I like those sorts of games. If you're not a fan of monotonous tasks then you might not be a fan of this game in particular.
Despite my annoyances with this game, I still enjoyed it a lot. Especially the missions that the DLC had to offer. I'd give this game a solid 7/10

I'll start by saying this game flew under my radar (see what I did there?). I did not hear any reviews of this game in the usual YouTube gaming channels I visit; I only saw it featured in the Store page and it already caught my attention.
Bomber Crew really scratched that itch I had for "mindless" grinding for better skills and upgrades, while paired with the challenge of surviving through every mission and threat thrown at your hard-earned build. In a way, it's like a more colorful FTL-meets-XCOM in real-time (that's right, turn off bullet time, folks). The repeatable missions were perfect for getting more coins and unlocking crew and plane upgrades, as they gave me more time to assess if I'm already prepared for the next campaign mission. Permadeath was also the icing on the cake; you can really feel it when you lose one or two crew members, now imagine the horror when you helplessly watch your bomber crash due to its heavy damage.
The only complaint I have (that I'm sure will be addressed soon) is the difficulty of clicking items in the front equipment rack. Since the Radio Op and Navigator are hogging that small space, I usually could not reach the first aid or extinguisher there during critical times. Hopefully the developers can consider putting an option to zoom more inside the interior of each fuselage section of the plane during flight, just like how it zooms in the hangar while upgrading them.
Other recommendations I have would be:
1. Uploading your custom livery without having to draw it on the canvas. I suck at drawing pixel art.
2. Custom controls and hotkeys. I've been used to left-clicking to select units then right-clicking them to do an assigned action. While there are default hotkeys for selecting crew, I wish it could be assigned freely to frequently used units (such as assigning "1" to the bomber or engineer instead of the pilot).
With that said, yes I recommend this game a lot, especially since the developers are planning to release more content really soon (yay!). They deserve two-thumbs up for this one-of-a-kind gem, and I am excited to see what else they have in store!

Bomber Crew gives you the chance to handpick and manage airmen flying a British Avro Lancaster during World War 2.  Although the graphics fall into the "cute" category, this game pulls no punches when it comes to difficulty and if you fail to address issues and dangers when they pop up your crew can quickly end up dead in a burning crater somewhere in occupied Europe.  Speaking of loss, once you lose a member of your crew, either by being captured or killed, they are gone for good and you must recruit someone new to take their place.  This makes losing veterans especially hard, but it is all part of the challenge.
In order to survive you will need to invest in training for your crew and upgrades for your aircraft with money that you earn from completing missions.  As you get further into your career the Luftwaffe will send more advance fighters to deal with you and some of the later missions can be pure chaos with the amout of flak and fighters trying to kill you.  Although this game can be very frustrating at times, at its core it is very fun and super satisfying when you are able to limp your bomber home with half of the fuselage shot away and missing two engines.

As a big fan of this game's Flash counterpart, Haunt the House, I was excited to experience this game, even with the understanding that it would not be much different than its predecessor. I'm sorry to say that even with this in mind, I did not find the game very worth it.
Pros: The graphics have improved slightly. While I personally prefer the more cartoony, flat look of the original, the HD revamp is nothing too jarring and is welcome. The game runs faster (most of the time - see below), and scares are as satisfying as ever (when they work - again, see below). The expanse of levels and new content is entertaining, as is the inclusion of characters that you can intentionally kill to unlock as ghosts.
Neutral: The controls are tighter. In almost all cases, this should fit in under one of the Pros for a game, but the lack of floatiness sort of detracts from the atmosphere, though this is mostly nit-picky. With the larger levels, it is necessary to be more mobile, and the ghost has been given a speed boost to compensate for this. However, with trying to precisely possess a specific object where multiple are clumped together, this sometimes becomes more of an inhibitor than something that is beneficial.
Cons: The game freezes and crashes at random, typically during the redesigned Flash-version level. AI has taken a few too many hits to the head, and sometimes your victims will stare directly at a top-tier scare with no effect, stand still or run in place, or go from being perfectly calm to jumping out of the nearest window for no reason at all. This is a significant downgrade from the original game which, while suffering from this issue, did so at a much lesser degree. Scaring all of the people from the house/train/mansion/etc. becomes more of a game of luck rather than one of tactically using your environment to your advantage. Most importantly, the game is far too short - I've completed much of it in an hour, and it seems that the only thing prolonging it are the built-in achievements, some of which are rather random (possess one particular object and use one particular scare) and others which are obvious (hit a Terrifying atmosphere).
Thanks to a sale, I managed to purchase this game for 99 cents. If you are a die-hard fan of the original Flash game, you can certainly pull some enjoyment from this title, but I would very much advise against doing so at full price. Be prepared for a game that may provide only a few hours of entertainment with many moments of frustration inbetween.

In my view, you'll enjoy this game more if you like the feeling of the character and animation. Everything is in place for this to be a great game, but I found it kind of hard to get into it. I don't know how to edit my other review and I wanted to articulate why I am thinking about giving up finishing it. After the five in a row puzzle, which I somehow beat on accident, I am beginning to lose interest. I am not sure why. I think it has to do with just playing Myst and Riven through from start to finish, and feeling that those games were 10/10 quality, then returning to this after starting it before those. The story and feeling of the worlds in the Myst universe is really cool, unobtrusive, and feels good. At first I was blown away by Machinarium when I first picked it up. It seemed super intuitive and cool, but after coming back to it I feel irritated by the loud music, slow movement, and actually the general feeling of the world. This is subjective, and it's really just me, no doubt. I just don't really like the world itself. I don't feel like exploring it. There is no real dialogue, which is cool actually, it's just that everything is a bit... twee... for my tastes. The art style is beautiful. Everything is exquisitely tasteful. And honestly, I do really like it on some level. It's like a story book. But I think that's why I don't really feel drawn into it. That coupled with the counterintuitive movement at times, and I don't like the feeling of the puzzles. It's just not fun to me. I don't like clicking on everything. I don't like not being able to click something unless I'm next to it. The movement is too slow. I can't get into it. I don't know what the character is trying to accomplish because there is no real story to begin with. The world itself feels arbitrary. It's well designed but for now I'm taking a break from it because it's getting annoying.

I've been addicted to this game for the last week.
It is a mix of collectable card games like Yu Gi Oh or M:TG. However, unlike most CCGs, you do not have to BUY the booster packs either through in game currency or real money. You earn them through the gameplay which is a major bonus to me.
The story is better than you would expect from a game of this genre as well. If you choose to, you can find that every person you come across has several (sometimes more than a dozen) different things they will say to you. And what they say will change depending on whether or not you have defeated them yet.
The actual gameplay is quite balanced. As you get stronger, so does the opponents. And there are many different strategies you must use. Going all out offense will work sometimes, but some characters are built to counter with good defense and the ability to disable your best cards at just the right times. You must choose your deck wisely depending on your opponent. This depth is part of what makes this game so fun.
The art style may turn some people off but I think it's very endearing and original. I don't know any of the indie games that this takes it's characters from but it's cartoonish and quirky and simple and it fits the overall mood of the game.
The best part of the whole game however must be the music. Everything from the menu screen, to the various places you visit, to the battles have music that is perfect for the situation. It's soothing and it's energizing at the same time. This, along with the humor of the game, and the visual styling make this a game you will never want to put down.
Although I have not beaten it yet, I know from reading around that the game has more things to accomplish even after you defeat the 'final boss'. So replay value is strong here too.

The card 'mechanics' put me off. Connecting cards on a 3x3 grid into 3 combos? No thanks, I'm outta here and back to MTG.
Seriously, as a strategic card player you'll look at your hand and those connector locations on your cards and just sigh. Might be fun if you're not used to card games and like to wait for that one puzzle piece (literally!) to appear.
A way better game than Yu-gi-oh now that they have all those op cards. This game is so balanced that there isn't a forbidden list

I enjoyed this game. I recommend buying the DLC for it as well though, because the Galactic Adventures DLC adds a lot. You could do without the other one though, but you might as well get it too if you have the money.
(read no further if you don't want to know what happens as you progress.)
You start off on a planet of your choosing. From here you get to start off as a microscopic creature where you can evolve over time by either eating what I assume is algae, or other creatures. From this, paths branch off. You evolve into a mindless animal, who either tries to make friends with other creatures, fights others, or both. Then you evolve again into a tribe, where the same principles apply.  The only sad part is that you can't choose to be an underground civilization, or one that dwells in trees, underwater or on top of mountains. You can choose to give your creature wings though, if you'd like them to "fly". It's sort of just gliding, due to the fact that you can only flap your wings about 5 times or something like that.
The next stage of evolution brings you to city life, where you can either choose to dominate other nations economically, religiously, or through war. Once you've dominated all of the other nations, you advance yet again to the space stage. It's basically the same thing all over again, but in space with spaceships. That's not just it though. In space you get a variety of different missions in which you can colonize planets, eradicate diseased creatures, and even elevate tribal civilizatons!
That's not just it though. You get to create basically everything from your creature (which you can change until you get the later stages), to the buildings in which they live and work. Not only that, but you get to create their land vehicles, air vehicles, and boats. Then once you get to the space stage you get to create the spaceship model that your whole empire uses.
If you want to play smart during the city and space stages, you can micromanage some of your cities to gain more income. Income is used to purchase vehicles during the city stage, and upgrades for your ship during the space stage. You get simple money during the city stage, but in the space stage, cities produce spice. You can sell the spices that are produced for a lot of money, if you can find the right person to sell them to.
Your goal is to reach the center of the galaxy, for who knows what might be there? But many obstacles stand in your way. Deal with them how you wish, because there are multiple ways to get there. Make friends, or dominate others to bring your rule to the whole galaxy. It's up to you. Just remember that everyone needs allies, or just really big guns.
Lastly. The game is really monotonous in my opinion. But I like those sorts of games. If you're not a fan of monotonous tasks then you might not be a fan of this game in particular.
Despite my annoyances with this game, I still enjoyed it a lot. Especially the missions that the DLC had to offer. I'd give this game a solid 7/10

I cannot, in good taste, recommend Spore to any gamer. The concept of the game is truly a novel one: create and let thrive your very own alien species, and guide them from being single-celled organisms wading in a tide pool to establishing an empire that spans the galaxy. But this concept is executed in such a poor fashion, that all of the potential fun is sucked out of the experience.
What bugs me about this game is how it plays, with all other aspects being at least decent. The graphics don't assault your eyes, and what story exists in the game is a believable scenario in which a sentient species grows. But the way that this story and graphics are presented is flawed in many ways.
First of all, the game is broken up into stages. Normally, stages in a game are usually fine, as the stages provide the player with a sense of progression; however, Spore fails to grasp the very concept of progression. Progression is the movement of the gameplay along with the in-game story, according to the actions of the player. Spore, on the other hand, has a progression system that consists of completely changing up the style of play after the player hits a certain in-game limit.
Take the "transition" from the Creature stage to the Tribe stage. Before the Tribe stage, the game consisted of you controlling a single member of your species, interacting with other animal and plant species, usually in the form of eating those species. As your creature progresses along the path towards growth and sentience before the Tribe stage, your species unlocks more and more ways to interact with the other animals, such as the ability to sing or pose to make allies with other animals, or powerful natural weapons with which the player can use to commit mass genocide. But after the Creature stage ends when your creatures become fully sentient, the gameplay style completely changes. Gone are the gradual upgrades to your singular creature, and instead are replaced by an RTS game that feels akin to a watered-down version of Age of Empires.
This type of abrupt change in the fundamental mechanics of the game are commonplace in Spore. As such, the game never feels truly deep, as a good game should. Each stage feels as if it could easily be its own game if fleshed out a bit more. But as it is, Spore only feels like a knee-deep kiddie pool of potentially good ideas that were weakly threaded together and released for no less than 20 dollars.

In
you play a ghost who tries to scare people away from each of the four locations this game offers. You win when the last person has fled the location.
To scare the guests into fleeing the place, you can possess various objects dotted around each location and using them when a person comes within its range. Using possessed objects near people causes a meter to fill, which in turn grants more ways to spook people per possessed object.
The art style is nice and there are a lot of possessable objects the player can use. I like how some of the haunts are references, like a book getting pierced by a fang (Harry Potter) or an object damaging an enemy RPG style, including the HP in damage it did.
However, the game unfortunately turns into a bore to play. At a certain moment you've seen all the haunts each possessed object can do, but the people have not all cleared out yet. So you need to chase them out, usually
. When they get scared however, they might actually run towards the haunted object instead of fleeing from it, so trying to steer them to the exit will prove to be hit or miss. Thus trying to chase them one by one from the location with objects you've already used alot turns the game in a chore, however charming the atmosphere.
Moreover, every level works in this same manner: possess objects and scare the guests away. There are no new mechanics being introduced during the gameplay and the only increase in difficulty comes from increasing the number of people your ghost is to scare away.
Last but not least, people rather often got stuck on objects and only started moving again after a good scare. This is a small bug though.
In conclusion I can't recommend this game, despite its charm.

DC Universe Online is a GREAT free-to-play MMORPG! It has loads of content(for PvP & PvE), lots of dungeons, raids and the PvP is balanced and has a few maps as well - which are quite cool. The character creation is so detailed and awesome as well. Overall this game is the BEST free-to-play MMORPG - if it weren't for the game's restrictions. If you are a free-to-play player you might not like these restrictions, but I'm okay with them. Such as a maximum of 1500(or 2000 if you buy smth. from the cash shop for at least 500 SC(that's 5€) credits for every character - and that's not much, also you have a lot less Broker, Banker and Inventory slots(again if you have spend at least 500 SC in the cash shop, you will receive a lot of Banker and Inventory slots for FREE, just because you have spent 500 SC - overall in the shop). If it weren't for that and many other restrictions I would give this game a 10/10, but since the developers hardly listen to their player base and there are some restrictions in the game(for end-game content) - I would rate this game 8/10.
P.S. Restriction to the end-game content aren't all that much(they are CONCERNING PvE PLAYERS ONLY):
- PvE: You can do 3/4 out of all the episodes per type of dungeons/raids(1/2/4/8 man), which means you can go up to Tier 3/4 if you are a free-to-play player, if you are a member OR have bought some/all of the DLCs then you progress to the most powerful Tier(currently 7 - May, 2015).
- PvP: While in Arenas/Legends there are absolutely no restrictions! Even if you are a free-to-play player you can earn the BEST gear in-game for PvP(you can't buy it from the Cash Shop)!
I am sure this may not appeal to all people, but just give the game a try! Believe me, as both a PvP and PvE addicted player I can tell you - this game is worth your time! Even if you are a hardcore PvE player just try the game and I am certain that you will most likely enjoy it!

You want a game with a compelling narrative?  This is a game with a compelling narrative.  You want a game with effective and unique atmosphere?  This is a game with effective and unique atmosphere.  You want a game with FXAA antialiasing, ambient occlusion and depth of field?  Err...   This is a game with cliff racers.
Let's start with a little honesty: TES3 has failed to age gracefully in many ways.  The graphics are badly outdated, and while there's a mod pack available to improve the graphics it is — for god knows what reason — not compatible with the Steam release of Morrowind GOTY.  Traditional RPG elements figure heavily into the play mechanics, including semi-random chance to hit or block in combat, or to cast a spell without it fizzling, or to mix a potion or enchant an item, etc.  On one hand it adds challenge, but on the other hand it can be irritating to continually miss a mud crab because your short blade skill is low.  The economy features some enormous disparities, which sort of makes sense when you consider how many NPCs could realistically afford to purchase the ensnared soul of a powerful demon, but it's problematic when you actually want to sell one.  The UI was designed by Bethesda — I don't think I need to say anything more about that.
Okay, there's really too much to talk about here, both positive and negative.  Also, coffee is lacking, so I'll summarize very briefly.

While Oblivion and Skyrim are both great games, I feel that they lack the sort of magic that Morrowind has. The island of Vvardenfell has so much to explore and so many hidden secrets that after a couple hours of playing, you realize just how big the world around you is. In the newer elder scrolls games, you figure out everything pretty quickly but in Morrowind even after almost 100 hours of gameplay so far, there is still alot mystery to the world and still many, many places I haven't yet explored. Oblivion and Skyrim are the typical medival and nordic fantasy setting and are both quite cliche, not to say that they are bad, but Morrowind Is so crazy and different from any other rpg game I have played. I'll never forget the first time I ventured into the ashlands in the center of the island and a ash storm started, engulfing everything in a massive, dark cloud of dust. I couldn't see more than 10 feet in front of me and had no idea where I was. Eventually after following a road through the middle of nowhere, I made it to the village of Ald'ruhn where I found an inn to stay at for the night. One of the best things about this game has to be the exploration. There is such a sense of wonder in this game from the giant mushroom trees that the Telvanni live in, to the lowland swamps of the bitter coast to the center of the red mountain inside the ghost fence, everything is so weird and magical. On top of that, Morrowind has so much more customization than either Oblivion or Skyrim did. Whether you like creating your own spells, or being able to wear multiple layers of clothes, or the many, many different types of armor and weapons that the game has, there is always something to do, and something to be mastered. The guilds in morrowind are great. They all have very good quest lines so far, and none of the quests are copy and paste garbage. Skyrim and Oblivion cut out many of the guilds that morrowind had. Morrowind has the fighters guild, the mages guild, the imperal cult, the imperial legion, the temple, the thieves guild, the morag tong, the vampire clans, (and probably more), and also three great houses to choose to become a member of, including House Redoran, House Hlallu, and House Telvanni. All of these, along with a great main story (the best main story of any elder scrolls game imo) add up to hundreds of hours of awesome stuff to do, things to explore, and memories to be had in this amazing game! At this point, at around 100 hours, I have literally, only scratched the surface of what there is to do in this game. I have only finished a small amount of the main story, I have done maybe 1/3 to 1/4th of the mages guild and fighters guild quests, and I haven't even started the Morag Tong, the Theives Guild, The Imperial Cult, the Imperial Legion, The temple, or even joined any of the great houses yet. Heck, I haven't even started the Bloodmoon expansion on the island of Solstheim or the Tribunal expansion in the city of Mournhold, both of which I know contain at least a hundred more hours on their own. This game can be harder for some new players to get into, but if you take a few hours to just play it, you will be hooked. Although the graphics are outdated and the combat can be weird, there is a great modding community for this game so pretty much any problem you have this game can be modded away! Currently, I am playing this game with Morrowind Sounds and Graphics Overhaul Mod and it makes the game look WAY BETTER with huge draw distances, high resolution textures, and better looking trees, grass, lighting, shaders, weather, and water. This game is MASSIVE and NOT in a bad way. There are insane amounts of things to complete in this game, all of which is high quality and interesting, which in my book is a good thing because this is, in my opinion, one of the greatest games of all time!!!

I had never heard of Bomber Crew until a guy I worked with started streaming it. The game has a truly endeering graphical style that makes all the characters look like cel shaded
figurines with a little hit of pixel art. The simple flat textures and bright bold colors really does make the game pop visually, even when you're flying through grey murkey cloud the view is vibrant and interesting. This also makes playing dress up with your crew extra satifying, and sometimes what is the mechanically best item of clothing is not the one that looks the most cool.

The pinnacle of this is the ability to customise your plane with a collection of different decals on different locations but also gives you a number of custom slots where you can manually doodle your own little pixelated creations and take to the sky in a look of your very own. My only real complaint about the visuals is that enemy fighter planes all cast very similar sillhouettes and while dealing with all planes are usually very similar there have been plenty of situations where I really wish I had a better idea of how whatever that thing in the distance is about to strafe me.
Bomber Crew seems to take a lot from spaceship roguelike
in it's notion of having one enviroment that evolves over the course of the game as you take it to different places, and having said environment be something your crew can move about in real time putting a real focus on people and time management, but instead of a journey from a beginning to an end it more takes it's lead from the
series in that you run repeated missions, upgrading and maintaining your plane and crew between flights, gaining new skills and getting bigger guns.
This progression is metered by 2 currencies. Money and Intel. Money is used to buy stuff, stuff for your plane, stuff for your crew it is earned and spent. Intel is basically a hard cap on your progression sort of like exp for your whole group accruing as you complete missions and unlocking higher tiers of weapons, clothing and systems for your plane that you can then spend the afformentioned money on.
Missions are simple affairs and essentially all have the same goal
. There are variations on the themes and sometimes special rules are applied such as having to drop bombs from specific altitudes, or  doing it in time limits or targets that hide etc etc. But as a rule you're going to be dropping a bomb on something and going home. Yet here I am nearly 20 hours in and this notion has yet to get boring. Ironically, being a bomber crew, dropping the bomb is the thing that occupies your thoughts the least. The real trick and challenge is staying alive on the way there and the way back as ever more deadly squadrons of armed luftwaffe fighters zero in on your plane and attempt to shred it with their guns. Early levels are usually a case of making sure the guns stay manned and you remember to grab some more ammo from the box when a gun runs dry. Towards the end, they become manic scrambles as you fire certain special skills at just the right moment, juggle different types of ammo and literally put the ship back together as it falls apart.
You manage 7 crew members who are distributed through 6 classes (you get 2 gunners). They all have skills that you are constantly using, they feel organic and never feel like busywork. There is something truly special about trying to get your rear gunner to switch to armor piercing ammo while your mechanic clings onto the wing desperately trying to get a starboard engine to start working again while the guy in the bomb sights at the front of the plane waits for the crosshairs to line up on whatever needs to die. The crew gain experience and skill up inbetween missions too each new skill offering up new lines of survival in ever more hostile skies. You can also kit them out in various things that will increase their individual survivability. While you might find yourself kitting everybody out the same at the beginning, by the end each one will have crafted outfits that lets them do their job the most efficiently.
Now this game has permadeath for your crew, if you lose one, you hire another and level them up again. However, one thing that truly sets
apart is that whereas a lot of games use the mechanic of losing characters and hiring new ones (XCOM, Darkest Dungeon etc). This game doesn't play on the disposability of your crew. The mission is the most important thing but your crew is a close second. Planes can be replaced in a matter of minutes depending on your funds. Crews can't, this adds a whole extra set of stat management for your crew in terms of their survivability. If your plane goes down and you didn't drive it into the ground like a screaming burning tent peg each crew member that wasn't already dead has a chance to both survive and be recovered. This chance is governed by multiple things. There are upgrades for your plane and crew that can improve your chances of survival different situations as well as a finite amount of parachutes. Losing your whole crew is truly devastating and this adds some real tension.
So despite all this, the game does fall down. Towards the endgame the balance loses it's god damn mind. Missions are simply categorized into Low Risk, Medium Risk, High Risk and Very High Risk and unsurprisingly the harder missions become available as you progress.
The jump from High Risk to Very High Risk is so huge that it becomes near impossible to play the game as intended. High Risk missions will involve you having to run a tight ship, and you will pay the price if you don't run at a solid effeciency but it is doable. Very High Risk missions are literally a case of
(those who can be bothered to not reload, I salute you). Your first playthough may wipe out a squadron before it's unleashed a bullet and you glide onwards unscratched, or your gunners take an extra
to kill the squadron, they managed to open their guns and now one of your engines is on fire another one needs to be repaired now and your oxygen system just shorted out and you will not have it fixed before more planes kill you.
The last 2 story missions truly are a slog and you will often find yourself being lucky a lot more than you will find yourself being skillful, which kind of stings after spending so much time getting to know the plane and your crew and their timings. All of a sudden all you can do is fire a bunch of skills and hope for the best, the rest is out of your hands and if something goes wrong, problems compound, you won't be able to fix them faster than you have more things go wrong and sometimes it can take 10 minutes to get to where you need to be. It's frustrating and exhausting.
Despite this I can't get enough of this game. The journey is worth it despite the destination. Each mission will give you skin of your teeth survival and excellent adventures of blowing stuff up. There is always something new to learn, be it skill synergy or new unexpected ways calamity can befall you. After 20 hours there is still no greater feeling than seeing your runway emerge from the mist as your plane limps home full of holes, with one engine, one landing gear and the corpse of your radio operator who got shot over the channel.
If you like FTL but wish you could be a little more involved and read few less multiple choice story options this game will keep you grinning for a long while.
