This is a game I was interested in for a while. After looking at the description it reminded me of not only one of my favorite games as a kid, but one of my favorite games of all time, Pokemon Trading Card Game for the Gameboy Color. IMO PKMN TCG was better than 80% of all of the Pokemon games ever made. It had a really fun battle mechanic, fun characters, fun sidequests that you would expect to be in a JRPG (i.e. doing certain things or trading to get rare cards), it was actually challenging unlike the standard Pokemon games (hurrdurr rock beats paper, idiot) and it had a lot of depth for both a seemingly simplistic Gameboy game AND as a Pokemon game.
First Impression: I could tell from the previews that this game had a fun and cartoony art style and characters, so I knew not to expect hyper realistic GRAFIX going in, and I didn't mind, the cartoony art style and the weird characters not only compliment each other, but the setting was appropriate for a "TCRPG" (Trading Card Role Playing Game). The setting wasn't overly dramatic and it wasn't some♥♥♥♥♥♥eating "deep" social commentary that hipster indie devs like to throw into their games for no reason.
The gameplay is simple enough, point and click adventure-y stuff with trading card battles (which are also point and click). I played this on a Microsoft Surface Pro so it was pretty easy to play. If you're using a desktop and mouse, it might be slightly more annoying due to having to move the mouse all over and having to plant yourself in front of your computer. If you have a laptop that doesn't have a touch screen or you don't have a traditional mouse to use with it I'd really recommend looking into buying the Android port of this game, this is a game that really plays best with a touch screen and it's also more relaxing to play in bed or in your spare time as things can get dull just sitting in front of a computer since this game doesn't feature much variation in how it plays.
The game was easy enough to control, but let's talk about the core of the game, the TCG. At first the TCG was kind of confusing, you place cards on a grid and they have to connect with arrows and all this♥♥♥♥♥♥ I pretty much won my first couple of games by luck because I really didn't understand the strategies well enough to do anything coherent. However, by the time you're ready to fight your first "boss" you should be able to have a general understanding of the main deck strategies and card types. The game does a pretty decent job of teaching you how to play and adapt to increasing opponent difficulty.
Now to pick out the criticisms I had about the game. This section should be a little less macular degenerating. I'm just going to pick out some things that I personally disliked about the game, you might agree or disagree, I don't really care. Just remember that I have somewhat overly high standards.
- Cards scale in strength and effectiveness.
This isn't something that I personally think makes the game bad, but when it comes to TCGs, I really dislike this. Basically, you start off with both you and your opponents using a bunch of weak, stupid cards that can barely pull off any kind of high damage or chain combo. However, the more you progress into the game, the stronger the cards get. What this means is that as the game goes on, cards that you used before can go from being the bread and butter of your deck to being completely outclassed and obsolete. Now, going back to Pokemon, imagine that when you go to fight your first gym leader you have a team of 3 weak pokemon. Now, at the time, they might be able to beat the first boss, but if you were to go directly to the next gym leader without any kind of interim training, you would get completely rekt. Now, imagine instead of training your pokemon to get stronger, you just catch a bunch of stronger pokemon and just throw your old pokemon into the trash. Theoretically this is a viable strategy, but it takes away most of the fun of pokemon games, being able to train your pokemon from being a bunch of bowl-cut, glasses-wearing noobs into a team of Hulk Hogan American heroes. Back to CCN, as the game goes on both you and your opponents keep getting newer and stronger cards. The strategies you use might stay the same and similar enemy deck types might stay the same, but now your cards are just slightly stronger. Now, for something like Final Fantasy this is an acceptable formula, but the thing that makes TCGs fun is the degree of strategic complexity. Would you rather keep playing against new enemies with unique decks and strategies or would you rather just keep fighting the same guys over and over but each one being slightly stronger than the last? The "Card Gods" at the end of the game have some of the most clever and difficult strategies out of anyone in the entire game, but there's only 4 of them and that's after you wade through the huge river of regurgitated goons that serve as checkpoints throughout the game. IMO, a good TCG should have as many "viable" cards as possible. If we're talking about something on as large of a scale as YuGiOh then of course there are going to be old cards that can't even hold a candle to some of the newer, crazier cards, but CCN is a game that can be beat in <10 hours and probably has less than 200 cards. If they spent more time creating efficient cards instead of just making tiers of cards then I think the game could have been a lot more complex and fun.
- The TCG system is too basic.
I honestly think that you can beat the entire game using the starter deck and maybe a couple of early cards. I know I just spent like 2 years talking about cards becoming obsolete and useless, but the thing is that the actual base TCG features overly simple mechanics combined with simple enemy AI. There are 3 main strategies; pure damage (attacking an enemy directly), preventing them from placing cards (blocking up their board) and making them run out of cards. It might be harder to do with weak cards, but once you devise a strategy based on one of the above methods of winning then it's possible to just go through the enire game with the same cards and either rushing the enemy's HP or blocking up their board. I mean, this obviously wasn't designed to be a game with some huge, competitive meta game, but with the number of opponents you have to fight and the fact that you can beat them using the same strategy (there might be like 3 or 4 enemies that require a different approach), the game can feel pretty repetitive.
-The game doesn't have a lot of content
It's a short game, <10 hours, but the biggest problem is that the game is too formulaic. There's 8 bosses, each occupying a certain area and following the formula of wiping out their goons and then eventually fighting them. It was fun the first and even the 2nd time, but by the 4th (not to mention the 8th) time it got old really fast. The only thing that drives you forward is seeing both the new cards and new characters (and wanting to beat the game, obviously). I really loved the characters though, despite this being my first game from this dev and CCN featuring a lot of cameos of their other game characters. The only thing that even comes close to variation is the little hidden coins mini-game. Each area has coins hidden in the scenery which I thought was fun.
Overall thoughts: In the end, I enjoyed the game a lot. I liked the characters, the setting, the gameplay (for the most part) and the "style." It was just enjoyable overall. I bought the game for $2 (regular price is like $4) and i think for that price it's a pretty good game, but with the lack of content and how easy most of the game is I'd say to go for the Android version (which is $2 and controls better with a touch screen). It's a good TCRPG, but not very complex, might be fun for kids or any fan of TCGs such as myself.

Defiance is an interesting mixed bag of an MMO. It is an instanced based one time cost game, like Guild Wars. So there's no fee, although there are some very light micro transactions. The neat thing is its actually a very fun third person shooter, which is just plain fun to play. There are also vehicles which help you traverse the landscape in addution to fast travel points. Basically there are no classes, and there is no real point of starting additional characters, other than asthetics. The skill system is a web of 4 Powers surrounded by various perks which give mild benefits. You can only have one Power active at a time. The world is relatively large, but not massive.
Of course the game has the tie in with the TV show, which I find mediocre at best. There are temporary episodic missions that tie into characters from the show (but not Defiance itself), otherwise the standard game does not tie in at all, it just takes place in the same world. The strangest thing about the whole game, is that you never venture to Defiance at all, which is in St. Louis, the entire game takes place around what was San Francisco, no where even close. Why the game is called Defiance at all, really only makes sense from a marketing perspective.
It is a good deal of fun, Even just offroading through the world and running over scavengers is a good time.  Generally each mission tends to decend into a you vs the waves of the horde scenario. Which is fun, albeit not a lot of depth there. The story is very forgettable, and you're about as attached to the characters as that saltine on the floor over there.

Absolutely loved it ever since I started playing it. It's not ground braking in any way but something makes it seem special to me. Even to this day I keep playing this game sometimes for an hour or two.
My first introduction to this game was when I was around 11 years old. I was absolutely stunned by the fact that you can basically create anything in this game, and not only create it but you could also place that thing in it's own world. It may not seem a big thing today but back then when I wasn't bothered about a game's graphics this game could chain me in front of the screen for hours.
I still enjoy creating my own worlds and placing my own creatures in it, the outcome is always something different. You can play this game no matter of what mood you are in, it doesn't get you frustrated. The game is fairly easy even on high difficulty but the challenge isn't lying in the gameplay but in your creativity.
This game really challenges your imagination, for example in my very first hours in the game was spent in creating weird creatures with sausage limbs, it wasn't so good but I reached the space stage with that and started a new game and every time I started a new game my creatures started looking better than my previous ones. You can't see your improvement in creativity in one playthrought but after ten or even a hundred planets you can see how much you improved from the start.
Spore is much more than a game in my opinion because it doesn't just challenge your reflexes and distracts you from the outter world but also challenges you creativity and by doing that it also improves it. Of course there are plenty of games that requires you to be creative but at that time spore was nearly the only one I knew about. Not saying you're gonna be an engineer but you'll definitely be more creative after investing some hours into this great game.

I've been playing games since the Commodore 64, probably played over a hundred of the most highly regarded games by now, and Mount & Blade: Warband is one of my all-time favorites. It has the best real-time melee combat system ever, more comparable to games like Street Fighter than Elder Scrolls. This combat system is a foundation for a deep role-playing/strategy sandbox game, as armies of hundreds of characters fight each other in real time, with charging cavalry and archers raining down death from castle walls.
The game certainly has flaws.
1. The battlefields have a border, but the game designers chose to make it invisible, which means that you'll often die because you accidentally ran into an insible border.
2. The combat is computed differently for battles in which the player is not participating; a simplistic algorithm is used for sake of performance, which means that you cannot use your knowledge of the troops to choose the best defenders for your castles when you're not there, but must figure out how to game the simplistic algorithm. This eventually ruined the game for me, but until then, it was great. I am hoping for a version of Mount & Blade with these two issues fixed.

I actually first got a hard copy of this game some years ago, and now I purchased it on Steam just to write this review because the game totally deserves it.
Yes, this is one of those hands down 10/10 games!
If you need a bit more convincing I can say that Machinarium is one of the best examples of the point&click genre. It does everything right - art, puzzles, story, atmosphere, sound.
You may or may not like this particular art style, but you will not fail to notice that an incredible amount of love and thought has been put into it. Everything is beautifully hand drawn and is aesthetically consistent throughout. The music and sound is also peculiar, but perfectly fitting to the game creating an absolutely unique atmosphere.
Puzzles - are very varied and cleverly executed. There is a good mix of fairly simple puzzles and quite tricky ones which will definitely challenge your wits. But if tricky puzzles is not exactly your suit the game has a cleverly built in hint system to help you along. And again, I was very impressed by the sheer variety of different puzzles - they don't feel stale or token at all. The puzzles are perfectly placed and balanced with the story.
Story. Well, it is a cute story about a cute robot who wants to save his girlfriend and maybe something more to boot. It has no written or spoken dialogue - all communication is done in animated picures, which again lends to the excellent atmosphere of the game. From time to time the main hero has short flashbacks, which explain the backstory, but overall it doesn't require any long exposition. The story is simple, but touching.
Well, Long story short this game gets top marks on all accounts. A must have for anyone who likes point&click genre, or consider themselves a connosiour of games as a form of art, or just wants to add a jewel to their games collection.

I'm a late adopter of TES series - started from Skyrim and gradually descended to Morrowind.
I'm safe to say that this is the best RPG I've ever had the chance to play.
Yes, the NPCs  appearances are three slight modifications of a brick with a frowny face drawn on it - not sure how much of an innovation it was in 2002, but right now, well, it doesn't look too impressive.
Yes, all dialogue is conducted through text, and yes, reading it all to the letter will save you not once or twice, but multiple times through the game.
The combat system could obviously be better. Hell, it couldn't have been worse. Getting the best weapon in the game and watching the exact same animation of the exact same attack for the rest of eternity... slip through your enemy without any effect because invisible dice rolled in his favour isn't fun, simple as that.
The game itself can sometimes render itself unplayable. Modding and player-made patches fix that, but only to an extent. If you are willing to spend a few moments setting it up correctly and familiarizing yourself with its weirdnesses, you won't ever run into anything critical, though.
But... Wait, I'm ACTUALLY role-playing here? No magical map which teleports me anywhere I want? No hovering arrows above quest targets? NPCs vital to quests are not made immortal just so I have absolutely no way to actually fail a task? Characters actually refuse helping me if they don't like me, without some plot-dictated excuse for why they do? Much like Daggerfall, this is a world you can live in - it rewards wit and punishes the modern-game approach of "pick up whatever the heck is under that arrow and bring it to whoever that guy with a map marker is" heavily. If you don't prepare for your quest, you die. If you don't listen to directions you are given, you'll end up in a swamp with no idea of how to get anywhere. If you kill the wrong dude crucial to the main story, the main story is over.
Exactly what I like. Let me play the game! Don't hold my hand through every challenge you put before me, or every victory will feel hollow and childish. Maybe I only killed a bunch of crabs for some farmer lady, but at least I can say I did it all on my own - without magical arrows guiding me through.
Pick this game up if you want a real RPG and can look past blocky faces and  outdated combat. Pick this game up if you can't look past these, but can dedicate some time to carefully fixing such issues through mods. This is likely to be worth your time - and money.

The game is not bad. I played it for 10 hours.
As a sniper/assault rifle.
The quests are a bit samey, but ok as they are at least in different areas each time.
It is nice that as a sniper, I can 1 hit kill with head shots.
But I notice your guns never seem to get any more powerful, but enemies progressively take more shots. When I stopped, those e-rep people took 4 head shots to put down, that excessive when there is like 20 of them shooting at you. Or an entire clip from the assault rifle per bad guy. That's extremely excessive for a shooting game.
And cover is useless, that's a big flaw. You can pretty easily be shot through cover, and you can't shoot from cover. Your shot often seems to just hit the cover in front of you.
So I end up just standing in the open shooting everything, then running to cover and hoping my shields recharge before the bad guys are on me.
But then grenades and bazookas ruin that strategy. So I end up "extracting" over and over.
It would be nice if this game had greater numbers, but less required shots to put them down. And make cover actually work properly.
Simple fixes but they would improve the game immensely.
Also, I have trouble paying for the game. We know they have already had lay offs, how much longer is this company going to survive? How much longer will this game survive? I am a casual player, some time on weekends only and only in the fall and spring. And maybe an hour each night. So I want the game to last long enough for me to play it fully and get my value for the money, and I don't think I will be able to.
Think of it like a broken Mass Effect, a cover shooter where cover doesn't work, guns don't get stronger, enemies don't understand cover and the RPG elements are minimal at best.
On the plus side, the combat is way better than say, star trek online ground combat.

Modern Combat Versus is a first-person shooter game, with two gamemodes. The two being capture and "kill confirmed". This is a great game, considering it is seemingly a mobile port. Nonetheless, here are some pros and cons.
Pros:
- OP against mobile players
- Fun game to pass time
- Simple game with simple controls
Cons:
- Pay2Win (in regards to classes)
- Endless popups to buy things
- No group play (for now)
- No chat
- The OP classes take a while to unlock
- The game can get boring after a while
- It is a mobile port, so controls are very simple
- No crouching, secondary weapons, knives, etc. (anything you are used to using in other FPS games)
- The "abilities" of different classes can be very imbalanced
Overall, I recommend the game, even though this is a mobile port and has a pay2win feel to it, but don't expect top-notch gameplay and controls.

I certainly liked the original Haunt the House, so finding a way to throw money at it made me feel good. Also, with 4 full areas (But can you really call Terrortown just 1 full area?) it's worth putting money into. The game retains its charm and humor from its flash days, and has even more polish than before. Really, it's exactly what you'd expect: A vastly expanded and polished version of the original Haunt the House, already one of the best, most addicting, and polished flash games I've ever played.
However, I do have a couple of complaints with this game. First of all, the controls. This game controls very similarly to the original, but there's one small change: You can't perform spooks with the arrow keys, which are performed with the WASD keys. (Also, I just realized--this game has individual names for every spook action, another almost unnessecary layer of polish.) If the game's going to use the arrow keys and the WASD keys, there should be an option to switch between arrow keys only and WASD keys only. Also, the people you're supposed to scare get scared way too easily, and in combination with them moving a bit slower(?) it makes it fairly easy to overdo it.
Though, those complaints all come from playing the original game for like 5 years. It's still a very good game, and even if you can't buy it or feel it's not worth the money, you still have no excuse not to play the original Haunt the House on places like Kizi and Armor Games.

Ibb & Obb is a gravity-based puzzle-platformer.
Which isn't to say you manually adjust gravity, as with some games, but that the entire game is composed of things like 'slow fall bubbles', trampolines, looped falling (where you drop from the sky after falling off the bottom of the screen), and reverse-gravity wells.
Despite fairly simple concepts, the puzzles quickly move from charming and cute and simple, to demanding and clever.
Unlike twitch/reflex platformers, once you actually figure out the trick to a puzzle, you're good to move on, which makes this a game more about testing your wit, than your reflexes- though timing is certainly important, as well.
Ibb & Obb is one of the best co-op experiences I've had in a while, and I can certainly recommend it-
Though there's some things I unfortunately have to point out.
||PROS||
* Co-op only play guarantees an experience built with co-op in mind at all facets.
* Puzzles are based around clever reuses of a small set of objects, presented in more and more complex ways, thus creating a steadily progressing experience where you build off what you've learned from your previous successes, rather than having to start each puzzle from scratch.
* Ibb & Obb (the two player-controlled characters in the game) are different sizes. This can have some interesting effects on gameplay, and is actually crucial to later puzzles. It's a nice twist that keeps each co-op partner feeling distinct in their roles. Similarly, the use of color-coded barriers limits which character can progress at points, creating interesting 'how do we both progress' puzzles.
* Looped falling can be surprisingly hilarious
* You can 'bend the system' by attempting crazy mid-air combos, such as trying to jump off your partner as they loop-fall. This can sometimes provide alternative ways to solve puzzles, for players that enjoy precision-reflex approaches over puzzle approaches. But really, it'll take quite a few attempts to do- though it's quite satisfying when you manage it.
* Charming atmosphere, and the most adorable little interactables- that you can actually push into enemies to cause the enemies to change course, or bounce onto enemy killing buttons, or just kick around like soccer balls, sometimes to absolutely hilarious effect. Great little tidbit for more creative puzzle solving, and just general palate cleansing.
* The ability to aim for a perfect score, by gathering all the enemy-kill score drops, for the more dedicated completionists.
||NEUTRAL||
* Secret stages are brutal and difficult to intuit, and may be best skipped by all but the most dedicated mental gymnasts.
* This game gets hard. It looks like it's designed for kids, but most kids won't have the patience to complete this kid of game [and if you know one that does, give them a cookie, they're awesome].  This is definitely a game for the patient and the people who really like working through problems until they understand them.
If you're into really puzzle-oriented games, enjoy teamwork, and physics manipulation, you're going to probably like this game. If your expectations run toward something more- or less- active in involvement, you may not.
* Similarly, puzzles will require several attempts to figure out, and at the time we played, all the walkthroughs were for the console version (which has different stages, see Cons below). Plus side, every time we got stuck and needed an assist, it was us overthinking a puzzle, so there's that. :)
Still, patience is a virtue- and one you may need to rely on for this game.
Then again, you'll still die less, hate yourself less, and feel far less frustrated than with twitch/reflex platformers, so there's that~
* Relatively short. 6 to 7 hours without the last level (see Cons), but that's mostly due to repetition in figuring out each puzzle. The core content is probably 2-3 hours in length, assuming a run-through where you know what you're doing.
(Secret levels will of course extend this time a bit further, if you choose to do them.)
||CONS||
* The last level is broken on the PC port- or rather, several levels got reimagined for the PC port (which is kinda cool) but the reimagining of the last level caused it to be incompletable (which is kinda not cool).
The game plays fine up to that point, so if you're able to view the end of the game being a level sooner, you'll be fine-
If you're a completionist, this screw-up may drive you up a wall.
* No mid-level save points, so you're forced to complete a stage to make progression in it.
[Each puzzle section within a stage does have its own respawn point, however.]
Plus side, once you know the puzzles, you can breeze through if you need to leave and restart- still, this feels like an unfortunate and arbitrary exclusion.
* Likewise, this game seems to have low replay value, given that non-campaign-level challenges (ie, secret levels) are all extreme in challenge, and all puzzles in the game are fairly easy to complete once you know how to do them.
This is a bit of a difficult game to describe, but if you like undertaking a mental challenge with a partner, and neither of you are the type to get agitated when you get stuck, then it's a fantastic game I recommend highly.
As always with co-operation games of this nature, if either person gets easily stressed, expect eventual argument and rage-quitting.
Despite that phrasing, it's not an especially frustrating game (in MY opinion), since everything CAN be figured out through rethinking and continously retesting your approach to a puzzle.
Still, it's a bit niche in its challenge, a bit curious in how certain things (like secret levels) are approached, and, of course, the last level cannot be played.
So..
I tentatively give it a 4/5.
Seriously, if it sounds at all good to you, give it a shot- and if it sounds at all not good to you, don't. ~.^

ibb & obb is a 2-player puzzle platformer best played on the couch with a steam controller.  Most levels are easy enough to beat but tricky enough to keep you interested.  There's almost no mechanical skill to the game; it's all about wrapping your head around simple puzzles based around the idea that gravity pulls you toward the centre (instead of the bottom) of the screen.
If you want a fun co-op platformer, ibb & obb is the game.

Very few games do co-op right. Some have little to no co-op interaction, and the players might as well be playing alone. Some have "shared lives" where the less experienced player feels like they're dragging down the team. Ibb & Obb has the best co-op mechanics of the many, many cooperative games I've played.
Ibb & Obb is a puzzle platformer. Both players are needed to solve every puzzle, meaning a player is never left out or dragged behind. Sometimes the puzzles require that the players fill specific roles--Ibb. the green guy, is allowed through green portals and Obb, the red guy, is allowed through red portals. The developers cleverly alternate the use of these portals to ensure that no one player always takes the active role in each puzzle.
My sole criticism is that Ibb & Obb doesn't have in-game communcation to match the intricacy of its puzzles. Players can only draw colored lines in the air, but they are fairly short and fade quickly. This problem disappears if you're playing couch co-op or are using a mic.
The puzzles are excellent and make clever use of teamwork and physics.
The graphics and visuals are very pleasing.
The soundtrack is amazing and certainly worth owning as well.
Ibb & Obb is among the best of the indie, co-op, puzzle-platform, and artsy genres. If you've got a co-op buddy, this game is definitely worth your time.

So, let's start out with the obvious: play this game.
Machinarium has the trifecta of art, story, and gameplay. Within this game you play as a clever, loyal robot. He faces a new problem on every screen, and you solve these puzzles to progress him further along in his goals. As you go along, idling in different areas makes him reminiscence about his life and how he ended up where he did. This provides the backstory, and then the current story speaks for itself; there's no words in this game, but it tells a powerful story with expressions and sound.
The art is fantastic. Every single panel is detailed and quirky, expressing volumes about the world this takes place in, the culture the robot is a part of, and even about the next steps of the puzzle line you face. Interactable objects all look like they belong, because no screen is perfectly static or poorly toned. The game is immersive and it's easy to forget that you're playing a simple point and click. The soundtrack is refreshing, unique no matter which screen you are on, and the variety of sound effects is higher then many other point and click games. This is an incredibly attractive, well put-together game.
Finally, mechanics and puzzles. The game received an update in mid 2017, making it's controls and character movement far smoother then the original flash player allowed. I replayed the game at that time, curious about it's new achievements (which are all story based, you'll get them naturally as you solve the harder puzzles). I was stunned at how different it felt, as while I loved it before, it felt far more in line with recent games and slightly decreases the amount of time it takes to complete the whole story. Controlling the little robot is easy, with every click responsive and the correct icons coming up for interaction whenever it's possible.
Usually I include a 'cons' section, but for the life of me I can't think of any when it comes to this game. This was one of the first point and clicks I ever played and I've come back to it a few times over the years, because I enjoyed it that much, even after finding so many other games out there. I've made over a dozen friends sit down and play this, so they could enjoy the puzzles and the story too. While a couple can take a few tries, the answers needed for each segment are completely logical. It's easy to tell when you need a certain item, and once you get that item, it's not frustrating or difficult to figure out what to do with it. The readability of this game is excellent.
Please consider playing Machinarium. It's a story that will stay with you, with an enchantingly grimy little world, and you won't find yourself pulling out your hair or bored from this game. The sounds and music of this game will find their way into your everyday life.

Morrowind.  Possibly the single best RPG experience of all time.
For one of the earliest RPGs able to be played in semi-modern 3D graphics, this game accomplishes so much.  If you're thinking about buying this game, there's one main point I'd like to get across.  Unlike other games, your success in Morrowind is based around your CHARACTER'S skills, not your own.  Hence the term "Role-Playing Game."  As the player, you don't exist to master the game, you exist to help your character become whatever you made them to be.  I suppose you could say that you play the role of fate: you guide your character along a path of your choosing.  If you want a fighting game, try something else, but if you're looking for a true RPG experience, you can't go wrong with Morrowind.
Also, with the new community project, TES3MP, the game is now very playable in multiplayer.  Even more reason to give it a shot.

Probably the best of the TES franchise to date gameplaywise. Graphics are dated, hop ever to the nexus and grab some graphics mods, they're needed (landscape isn't too bad, characters... are painful). Story is arguably the most well done of the series to date (far better than the joke that was Skyrim's). Guild quests are a little weaker than the later games, mostly due to the engine (which had it's limits).
Pro's:
Story. Good combo of specific quests and more general ones,
World. The island of Vardenfel (main game) is very well done. Mournhold (Tribunal expansion) is also well done, Solstheim a bit less so, attempting to make it seem barren worked a bit too well.
Moddability (the first TES game that modders really got into, there are some good ones)
Mournhold, city of light, city of magic
More that just the 4 main factions of the later games.
Con's:
Old engine
Dated graphics (although mods can help with these)
Expect to be dumped into the world with little to go on (which does make sense story wise, but still...)
No purchasable houses, either grab a mod, or kill someone and claim thier house
Mixed:
No quest markers, and your journal is cronological. Don't expect your hand to be held for quests.
Classic style TES stats/skills, advancing in skills automatically gives a pre-set perk every 25 levels. A lot more skills though
No fast travel (although there is the mages guild travel network, boats, silt striders and 3 varieties of teleport spells/scrolls). Get used to walking to where you need to go, then tele'ing back
No passive mana regen, difficult to be a pure mage. Birthsigns/races from mods can take care of this though if desired.

The game is loads of fun. Highlights:
* Pick your crew, name them, and pick their secondary skill as they level up in order to assemble a crack team of badasses
* Watch your veterans unlock convenient abilities such as auto-tagging enemy planes detected by radar (Radio Op) or laying down the ever useful Focus fire (Gunners)
* Listen to the radio chatter from enemy aces as they taunt you a second time and then run away like cowards. COWARDS, I SAY!
* ... shoot down said enemy aces for sweet, sweet revenge
* Drop bombs on stuff. While putting out fires. And tagging navigation waypoints. And reloading turrets. And repairing the hydraulics because oh god the turrets can't turn and WE'RE ALL GONNA DIE
* Limp home. Thank cheezus that you still have all your landing gear. Watch your plane proceed to lurch over to one side on landing anyways when one of the wheels collapses. Have a mini heart attack. Breath a sigh of relief when nothing explodes and your crew is okay
Criticisms:
* A "Return to Stations" button would be nice. For example, if you shuffle around crew so someone can go heal, then they won't return to their station upon recovery. Having a single button to send people back to their regular stations would be nice for that.
* I don't actually have any idea what the crew "traits" do.  My Bombardier is an amateur photographer. Does this mean she gets the improvements to taking recon photos a few levels earlier or something? I don't know. As far as I can tell it's flavor...?
* Complaint I haven't experienced but have heard a few times: all engines shot out means immediate nosedive. Have these pilots never heard of gliding?
Tips:
* DO NOT LAND USING LEAN FUEL. Maybe it's just me, but I have rougher landings if my Mechanic is still using the Lean fuel mix on landing. Having them stand up and sit back down disables the ability and puts it on cooldown, fixing the problem.
* Your top turret and rear turret are your bread and butter. Upgrade them first. The front guns don't get nearly as many shots at enemies, and the ventral turret underneath sees almost no action at Low altitude which is where you'll spend your early missions.
I'm still noobing it up so I'm sure there are way more tips out there.

Very few games do co-op right. Some have little to no co-op interaction, and the players might as well be playing alone. Some have "shared lives" where the less experienced player feels like they're dragging down the team. Ibb & Obb has the best co-op mechanics of the many, many cooperative games I've played.
Ibb & Obb is a puzzle platformer. Both players are needed to solve every puzzle, meaning a player is never left out or dragged behind. Sometimes the puzzles require that the players fill specific roles--Ibb. the green guy, is allowed through green portals and Obb, the red guy, is allowed through red portals. The developers cleverly alternate the use of these portals to ensure that no one player always takes the active role in each puzzle.
My sole criticism is that Ibb & Obb doesn't have in-game communcation to match the intricacy of its puzzles. Players can only draw colored lines in the air, but they are fairly short and fade quickly. This problem disappears if you're playing couch co-op or are using a mic.
The puzzles are excellent and make clever use of teamwork and physics.
The graphics and visuals are very pleasing.
The soundtrack is amazing and certainly worth owning as well.
Ibb & Obb is among the best of the indie, co-op, puzzle-platform, and artsy genres. If you've got a co-op buddy, this game is definitely worth your time.

I just bought this game yesterday, and already I've played it for 7 hours so far! So yes, I have to recommend this game for those who like casual puzzle games, solitaire games, or trading card games. The game has very pleasant cartoon-style imagery and pleasant-enough music and sound. The interface is easy to come to grips with, and the tutorial mode is reasonably effective in teaching you the basic gameplay mechanics. The story is pleasant and involving enough, providing the motivation to keep playing further.
If you’ve noticed, the key word I’m using to describe “Card City Nights” is “pleasant.”  The basic card-game mechanic is challenging and fun, and I’m motivated to keep playing until I beat the game.
If you like “casual” games like “Bejewelled” or “Solitaire” or other such games, I think you’ll like this one, although it’s a bit more complicated due to the “card collecting” motif. “Card City Nights” is certainly a worthy game for anyone who likes casual games or “collectible card” games.

Card City Nights gets a 9/10.
This hilarious and brilliantly executed game tickled the pleasure centers in my brain like virtually nothing else that I've experienced. There are few things as fun as opening packs of cards, and this game throws enough your way as to make you positively addicted. The game's main flaw (it is rather short) is also its saving grace, as I'm sure I wouldn't have been able to tear myself away from the screen unless I had already accomplished everything within the first day!
Pros:
- Innovative, fun, and clever gameplay. It may appear simple at first, but there is surprising depth.
- You get to open tons of booster packs and form a huge card collection. How sweet is that! Also, there's no in-game purchases or anything like that. My hat is off to you, Ludosity, for having some moral fiber, especially within a genre of game that seems to feature some of the most rampant abuse of "pay-to-win."
- Super lighthearted and dumb characters, cards, and locations. The aesthetic quality of the art is great!
- Really nice music. I'm a musician and producer, and I really enjoyed the tunes. Game music is often tired and boring, but not here.
-Crafting and recycling system which allows you to get rid of excess cards that you don't want, and discover new cards!
Cons:
- Somewhat short game. I've played a total of 7 hours, and done all the fights and achievements. To be fair, I went through very quickly, playing a very fast "RDW" style burn-to-the-face deck. I'm fairly experienced with CCGs, so I was able to be pretty efficient. Also, this was before the balance patch, so that particular style of play is a bit harder now.
- General card and deck management is kind of annoying. It can be a bit of a pain to constantly have to scroll through your collection, especially once you open a few hundred boosters. Additionally, when you're buying and selling cards, it's difficult to know how many of each you actually own, because cards that are currently in decks can't be sold.
- Rehab expenses are pretty high if you want to stop playing Card City Nights for good.

The game is filled with an array of warm colours, gorgeous lighting and an absolutely HUGE sense of scale. Playing as the two brothers in such a lonely yet amazing set of environments, you feel absolutely dwarfed by the sheer scale of it all. This is saying a lot - but I'm going as far as to say this visually looks more impressive than Okami, which if you've played you'll know is one of the best looking games despite its age.
Coupled with a superb, chilling soundtrack and a completely unique single-player co-op gameplay style; this is seriously the perfect game. Two hours in and I swear this is game of the year material, if not one of the best games I've ever played if it continues the way it's started.

(I am reviewing this based on my past experience and not of the current status of the game, but it shouldn't be too far off. Maybe SOE being bought out changed a few things.)
-TL;DR is at the bottom-
Short and simple; The gameplay is nice, there's quite a nice customization with the clothing and gear in terms of the appearance (Color schemes are in a 3-color palette, it sucks). The Character Creation itself is moderate. There's a lot of choices to pick, but it's more of a "quantity over quality" type of deal. The faces are almost all similar with some actual unique choices. There's nothing like "face-width/height/depth sliders" to get a truly unique feel.
Dialogue in the game has it's moments and is overall good, but rarely anything too memorable. You can have your character use every weapon type (except the shield. You gotta pay for that, why?) in the game if you so desire. The powers are also pretty unique in their own ways, but you basically only have access to HALF of what you could choose without paying. (I mean to say choices, not the skills/abilities in the powers themselves) The PvP feels very... fast-paced? You could end up on your♥♥♥♥♥before you even realize it even though the Combat is a bit stiff, but fun. I guess it's balanced, I haven't been involved in PvP enough to get a good, true feel for it. In my experiences though, I was able to turn the tables on a superior enemy when I played the tactics game.
They have open-world PvP in the form of: duels, certain areas in the worlds pertaining to a type of gamemode, and your queue-type arena PvP gamemodes. This game is very wide-open, it has its little info-bits to find scattered throughout the worlds too and some unique things to find, like Batman or Harley Quinn in Gotham City. There's Gotham City and Metropolis for you to explore and go around, there's no level-restrictions in where you can go either. There's certain-level enemies scattered about in the world. A level 10 Hero/Villain can go run into level 1~99 enemies and be completely owned or get pretty much nothing from lower-level enemies.
Yes, there's a Hero and Villain faction. Each has their own storylines even though they technically go through the same areas. It's basically like parallel universes. P2W elements? Well... From personal experience, I don't believe I encountered anything that was too overwhelming. ALTHOUGH, PAYWALLS... EVERYWHERE... Do you want to save up your monies to go a shopping spree? Well... ♥♥♥♥ YOU! :D GIVE US MONEY SO YOU CAN HAVE MORE THAN 1,500 of the in-game currency on hand! What about if you end up getting more money than the limit? It goes into a "credit" type of bank that you CANNOT ACCESS unless you pay for the MEMBERSHIP. With the Membership, the credits are accessed as if you had it on hand, that's it. And let me tell you, 1.5k currency IS NOTHING with the prices of items and gears when you get deeper into the game. Buying one item can take up half of that 1.5k.
There's also a "base/hideout" you get for free whenever you progress through the game, ALTHOUGH... YEP, YOU GUESSED IT... ANOTHER PAYWALL... Assuming you want to get the most out of your home. There's features that are RIGHT THERE, but NOPE... "PAY FOR THE DLC OR ♥♥♥♥ YOU!" *sigh* There's also other worlds that you can go to, but... yeah. More DLC to BUY... Even when the portal to the DLC world is RIGHT THERE in the Watch Tower or the Villain's lair (I honestly forgot the name). You can get "rare" and powerful gears in the respective Hero/Villain HQs if you participate in PvP and other ways, might take a while, but still. Though... They might be meant for PvP... but I do remember some gears that work all-round.
TL;DR Gameplay/Combat is nice, Character Creation of appearance/personality is a bit bland overall, but the gears/armors/weapons you can equip make up for it despite the color scheme being rather dumb... PvP seems balanced, though no restrictions on levels for who can play. ♥♥♥♥ Sony for all the damn paywalls everywhere, hopefully the game gets turned around with the change of hands. The game feels a bit gutted with all the DLC in your face. Overall, the game is alright. If the paywalls, outrageous DLC and restrictions get taken out, the game would be a solid 83/100. From my own experience, it's a 71/100. "Play the game for yourself" kind of deal. It's still a "free" game after all.

From Disney's cutesy version of "Alice in Wonderland", to Tim Burton's gothic and creepy adaptation, we all have had some type of contact with Lewis Caroll's "Alice's Adventures in Wonderland", and Alicemare is just another worthy addition to this list.
Alicemare's themes are heavily leaning on creepy, and the cute artstyle can take quick turns to the dark and negative. The story is the game's strongest point. It's quite compelling and has the flavor of some other "fairy tale gone dark" games like Kingdom Hearts. Yes, that might sound like a strange comparison, but starting from the amnesia ridden protagonist, through the booming orchestral musical soundtrack, to the addition to references to other fairytales (Snow White and Hansel & Gretel, to name a few..) and the discussion on "what's one's soul contain?", it really seems the two games are rather similar.
Alicemare is quite short and light on features, though, and while it uses an RPG engine, there's no combat or character progression. There is an inventory and it purely serves the purpose of the completion of puzzles. The game does have multiple endings though, so the story can be seen from multiple angles.

This game is cute, has great music and challenging puzzles. And you play it in cooperation with a buddy. What's not to like?
The puzzles are challenging not only in regard to their solution. They often require both players to perfectly execute several steps in a row, with very little room for error. This can mean that you have already figured out the solution and make it halfway there but then you misstep: Start over. Then, your friend is too fast: Start over. Then, you jump a little too early:  Start over. Then, your friend hits an enemy: You know the drill. Solving a puzzle can get quite tedious.
Another issue is savegames: One level took us up to an hour (in the later stages), depending both of how well we could crack the puzzle logic and execute the steps. During that, the game saved our progress just fine; if we failed a puzzle, we'd only be back at its beginning. But whenever we had to quit before finishing the level (or had a desync or just didn't feel like trying the same puzzle for the umpteenth time), the next time, we'd have to restart the whole level from the beginning.
Finally, playing it with a friend across the ocean, we found that in-game voice chat was delayed by a few seconds. Maybe it doesn't happen with less of a distance between you and your co-player. For us, it didn't help, what with some puzzles needing near-perfect timing. Towards the end, we thought about using an external solution like Raidcall, but it never came to that.
Overall, the game can get quite frustrating.
Before this, we played Portal 2, which did a better job of e.g. the savegame issue by having many smaller levels, so if you had to quit at some point, you wouldn't have to replay as much as in this game. And there, when you already knew the steps leading up to where you'd left off, they were usually pretty easy to reproduce. If you're looking for a fun coop puzzler, I'd rather recommend Portal 2.

Resident evil is one of the biggest named horror games. It used the idea of tank like controls and preset camera angles to add fear to the player of limited control and the unkown of what is ahead to be faced in the next camera angle. Does all of this make resident evil a good game as of today? I will be reviewing the game on a pro/ con style and end with my final conclusion.
Pro:
The mansion and atmosphere is brillian. Large mansion like locations are excellent for a horror atmosphere because of how large it is and how closed end the hallways are. Added to that the game does an amazing job with sound effects like thunder and lightning in a few areas which helps aid the spooky nature that the game holds.
The spooky moments that occure in the game are handled very well. Some moments that are ment to be spooky are simply sound effects followed by a adrinaline rushing music much like the moments when zombies open doors or when zombies break through windows. It is not easy to explain how well it is done but it is far better scares than the generic jumpscares that plague a lot of current generation games. Scares like these plays on the players mind.
The game is full of replay value. That is a huge plus for the game as to how it has two seperate character stories which has some minor differences but enough that nets more than one playthrough. On top of that there is many endings depending on what characters survive till the end, many new modes which challenges the player like the real survival mode, and finally unlockable weapons with infinite ammo which are a major reward for those who can speedrun the game.
Characters are very good. Each character besides their models looking good also have great dialogue. It is not super worth mention besides the point how originally when the game first came out somewhere in the 1990's had very cheesy dialogue which is ok in my book but how it improved with both the remake on gamecube and the remaster on pc, those changes are very much in need of acknowledgement.
The saferoom music is a classic. Really that is it, the music is very soft and comforting, ment to inspire hope in a situation of fear or dispare. Definently worth a listen.
ChrimsonHeads are very creepy. A new type of zombie never before seen in any other resident evil game exists in this one game, known as chrimson heads. They are mutated zombies that were killed and not burned. If left unburnt they take the time to mutate into these red zombies with sharp claws and run pretty fast. This is a warning to any future player to burn the bodies of dead zombies so they dont turn into chrimson heads.
Con:
The initial first time player would be confused to what difficulty to choose. There options are very vague with slight hints as to what they are likely to be getting into. This is just a nitpick.
Also when one dangerous zombie is unlocked, it is very scripted. When I say that I mean that he shows up in only a few set locations but he will always be there once that character is unlocked. There is no chances that he will show up in those set spot, he will be there everytime and that can be very frustrating making those locations where this zombie hangs around just a drag to visit. There really should be a percentage chance that he will show up in those set locations but within 3 to 4 playthroughs he always showed up in those same locations everytime.
Conclusion:
There are so many good things about this remake of a classic game. It adds and fine tunes what made the original so successful without changing anything too much to allienate the game from fans of both the series and the original. There is some negatives and one if forgot to say was how in the later end of the game has more instant death situations which feels a tad unfair compaired the early moments in the game. That can be a tad annoying to experience 4 instant death moments within about a 20 minute time frame. That aside the game is amazing and I would reccomend it, definently worth a try and with practice and preparations any situation can be overcomed.

Ever wanted to anxiously hop from truck to truck while taking a scenic route through Hell? Here's your chance.
Clustertruck is definitely something I haven't seen before. The concept it simple: hop around on trucks until you get to the end of the level. However there is a batshit amount of traps, tricky designs, or just play hard setups that you have to navigate through. The difficulty of the levels can be a bit inconsistent, as I feel sometimes I play through the first 7 levels of a world and think it's been a horrible time, and then the 8th level is pathetically easy. It doesn't have a very solid progression in that sense. But it's not something that's going to ruin your experience.
The controls are a bit slippery which can be frustrating sometimes, and the levels where you need to use the RS to change your view can be a nightmare, mostly because it makes your movement very awkward and doesn't flow as well as I think it *should*.
My other complaint is that the longer you play through the game, the more levels become inconsistent with their gameplay. By that I mean trucks will start moving around in a more random fashion, making it hard to have a consistent plan on how you tackle a level, somewhat akin to how Hotline Miami had this same problem. Sure, it makes you think on your feet a little bit more, but I personally would rather have a set timeline of what's going to happen so I can stop swearing at the TV screen and calling a bunch of trucks '♥♥♥♥ing♥♥♥♥♥♥♥'
Overall, it's a really fun game to pick up and play every once in a while, flaws and all. There's also leaderboards to try and gain global acclaim, as well as bonus abilities to change it up a bit. (Get double jump and your life will be a thousand times easier)

I've been wanting to review Machinarium anyway, but amazingly it was just updated a matter of days ago. This little treasure from Amanita Design has been brought fully into the present with modern resolution support, controller options, and a pretty hilarious bug that makes it run super fast if you try to G-Sync it. Despite that last bit this update has wiped out any criticism I could have leveled at the game for feeling dated or being clunky, leaving only the clunky charms of its trash robot inhabitants to recommend to you without reservation.
Machinarium is the tale of a little robot in a junkyard. He isn't WALL-Eing the place up, he was dumped out here and it's up to you to find out why. A quick jaunt across the wastes finds him in a towering mechanical city of similarly junky, quirky robots all needing your help. Somewhere in the great beeping metropolis is a secret that only you can uncover, and a plot that only you can unravel to save its clanking inhabitants.
Doing this is sure to be one of the most adorable gaming experiences of your life. Your little robo-buddy toddles along on two baton-like legs, snakes his little grabbers out to nab things, drops items into his flip-top maw, and takes in the world with the most precious, gormless stare you can imagine. Just having him on the screen will put a smile on your face, and when he starts tooling around in carts and tumbling off of ladders you really can't help but sensibly chuckle. The other denizens of the city are no less charming, with uptight patrol bots stomping around, mechanical street bands tooting on old pieces of pipe, and clockwork bugs humming happily through the alleys.
It's a living game world in a way that so many other titles can't seem to capture, and it's ironic that it's accomplished entirely with robots. Much like Primordia every robot has their own distinct character but here, it is expressed entirely without words. As with all Amanita games the only language you'll here is perky gibberish, leaving characters to communicate through wild gesticulation and the occasional thought bubble. It's the little details in the art and animation that make it work so well, all the way down to your robot's eyes narrowing when enacting small revenge on a tormentor, or the way he adjusts his metal plates when left idle long enough. And more than anything this helps the story, which has some emotional twists that are heightened by the players emoting their little metal hearts out for.
As excellent as the look and feel is, we can't forget the puzzling. Machinarium, much like other Amanita games, only allows limited ranges of movement on most screens. While this opens up more later in the game it can feel limiting, but the trade-off is that it becomes easier to find what you need to interact with and how to interact with it. Almost as a concession to this point, your robot can stretch or shrink his height to reach out-of-the-way items or blend in with taller or shorter robots, a gimmick used to full effect throughout the entire game. You won't be finding a ton of items, either, so combined with the limited movement and interaction points this should be a pretty simple game for anyone to get through.
Your journey in this mechanical wonderland shouldn't take more than two hours, but those are two hours just loaded with humor and charm. The sketchy art style itself is a joy to behold, with rich details in every surface and object. A subdued soundtrack accompanies the look in a way that gives more texture to the troubled city, offsetting some of the silliness with a reminder that not all is well in the mysterious metropolis. And with the recent updates, any concerns about compatibility or accessibility have been entirely wiped away. With so many fully-realized elements, Machinarium is a clear classic of the point-and-click genre, one that makes an excellent entry point for newcomers or a charming diversion for veterans alike.

If you are unaware, this is a trading card game, so you do have to like this genre of games. I don’t like TCGs IRL but I do tend to like them on a PC, and I really enjoyed this game. So if this is in your wheelhouse, buy this game immediately!
This is a great fun game, what indie games are all about. The graphics are average, there is no voice work, the music is repetitive (though not terrible for an indie like this), the conversation is in the cheesy tongue-in-cheek variety but none of that matters, nor detracts from the fun. I understand this is also an Android tablet game, and it does have that feel, but not in any kind of bad way. Just that it feels like I could easily play it on one of my tabs and get the same enjoyment.
The card system is very simple but well thought out and complete. With 187 or so cards well designed around specific ideas, there is room to make several kinds of successful decks. The balance (as of 5/22) is pretty good. I found a deck attacking the opponent’s number of cards was the most challenging to make work right and an attack deck the easiest, so the balance does tip a bit to the attack and defense based cards.
I have 10 hours in, I got to 100% completion and I enjoyed every minute. My 10 hours would probably be around 20 if you grind. However, I don’t like to grind and the devs give you an easy way to avoid that without throwing the game off with cheats. Your card library is in a text file that you can edit to add more copies of cards you already earned (and add new cards as well, if you are so inclined). So you don’t need to go through hours of battling to gain booster packs or gold, and just do the duels you want while using in-game tools (card recycler, card mixer) to expand the kinds of cards you have quicker. I really appreciated this!
Even at my 10 hours and at the non-sale price, I would say you get great fun for your buck. The only thing I would like to see in a sequel is multiplayer. Other than that, more cards for more deck ideas and the ability to import/use our deck and library. Whatever you guys do, I’m in for any sequel you make.

Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is not merely a game, it's a masterpiece of modern gaming and storytelling with the use of a made up language. Considering it's a fairly short title (about 3 hours long), which might put some people off it is surprisingly worth it's value. Brothers presents you astonishing visuals along with one of the best soundtracks I've ever heard in a game. Brothers doesn't really tell you a story like most games out there, it shows you the story by using a made up language, as I mentioned above, you are not presented with a certain and linear story but the way each brother interacts and uses body language to express himself gives you a good feeling of what's going on. Another thing I love about this game is how the developers decided to show you that these two brothers are inseparable, you control each one with a different stick on the controller but yet each puzzle or obstacle cannot be exceeded by using a single brother, one brother needs the other in order to survive... Besides this, everything else I have to say is abunch of spoilers and things that would ruin the way you would experience this game for the first time. I have nothing else to say other than, please buy the game, if not by paying full price atleast try to get it once it's on sale (like I did), we need more games like this, I need more games like this. Definitely one of my favourite games of all time, taking the top 1 place on best storytelling for me and bringing The Walking Dead to top 2.

Well, well, well - Alicemare, a game I played when it came out back in 2013; yep folks, you heard me. And it wasn't even the "original" (japanese) version, as other people translated this free-to-play game. For free. Without needing 3 euros for a translation that's not as accurate as the others.
Before I, actually, continue this very obvious rant, let me say something else: It's not a horrible game at all.
Yes, not even three hours long, but filled with nice music and a story that's not explained until the actual end of this short journey in a weird place, filled to the brim with dangerous things and riddles, that prove to be just as life-threatening if you get them wrong. More importantly, it seems to be different fairytales put together in one strange world, and taking a new outlook on old things, such as Hansel (Rick) being a mere illusion made up by Gretel (Letty) or instead of killing Snow White (Stella) with a poisoned apple, the entire town has said fate with the exception of her. But then again, isn't that all just a dream? Yes, the game may lack some explanation, especially as to what XXXX could be, and what we - as Allen - have been robbed of, and if the Cheshire Cat is even speaking the truth when it tells us that he was it who took our memories, or was it the incident that got described later on in Davids dairy? We don't know, that's for sure - and we probably will never know, after Miwashiba stated that there was no intention to go back to this game, or making games at all, which is quite sad. I enjoyed the artstyle a lot back then, I still do, and it all looks very clean and neat, even when it isn't.
Except for that there isn't much too say about this, as I've probably mentioned a spoiler or two already, and taking away all the fun wouldn't be nice. However, as much as I love this game, it's not worth the money you could be spending on something else and I'm not going to change my mind about that; though, the review is gonna be a rather positive one (as I do still recommend playing it, but buying it DOES seem like a waste of money if you can get it for free), you would be better off if you don't buy it.

Ever desired to be a ghost to spook some unsuspecting people? To drive house owners out of their house? No need to wait, Haunt the House: Terrortown may satisy your need.
Haunt the House: Terrortown has you play a ghost throughout all of it's levels to drive the people out of the building. There are different ghosts in each level, several in the level Terrortown due to the scale, which are designed accordingly to the level. This also goes for the items within each area, if it's a museum theme, there will be objects to fit into it. An added plus is the personalized scares between each type of item. Not including duplicate items that appear across all levels, each new item has it's own spook. Depending on the item, it can also have between 1-3 available spooks that will have to be unlocked by the atmosphere meter, which fills the more you spook people, and along with this, people will run out. The AI, however, can be frusturating as it dashes to go in the opposite direction of the exit consistently. They will eventually go to the exit as you scare them constantly, but this can be annoying especially if it is the last person on the map.
Haunt the House: Terrortown will crash when first playing it. This does force you to close the game in the middle of playing a level. Fortunately, Haunt the House has a saving system that saves quite often. You can continue the level from where you left off, with only the objects returning to their original places and the people walking around contently.
The soundtrack has the same theme throughout each levels without annoying the player. With how much the player does, and the individual sounds each spook has, it is easily forgotten. While the artwork is one of the selling points, which is why I bought it, as the cute art style shines.
The replay value depends on the player. If you are an achievement hunter, there are achievements that are rather difficult to complete.
+ Cute art and animations
+ The unique spooks with every type of item
+ Effective, simple controls
- Short
- The AI can be frusturating
- Crashing is common when first playing
Haunt the House: Terrortown is short, but it does bring enjoyment in those empty afternoons. I do recommend playing this, but grabbing it during a sale, if possible, is also recommended. However, be aware screenshots may be hard to understand where the action is.
This game will teach you one thing: being a ghost can be insanely fun.

I initially played this game before checking out the earlier works of Ludosity, and I loved it. After having played Ittle Dew, I love this game much more! What we have here is a card game adventure packed with charm and humour in a quirky setting with quirky characters. If you're curious about the mechanics, I suggest having a look at people playing on YouTube. It's very simple to learn how to play. Slightly less simple is the deck building, which will require a little trial and error if, like me, you're not accustomed to games that require building your own decks. And once you get in the swing of things, the card game is legitimately fun.
Everything else around said card game is just window dressing, but at least it's nice window dressing. The characters make fun of various archetypes, both in real life and in fiction, and have lovely hand-drawn avatars to match. Their dialogue is frequently amusing, if not actually funny, and generally well-conceived. These characters are certainly not going to be your reason for playing the game, but they are a welcome addition.
That being said, the card game's fun and the window dressing's charm eventually run dry, and the game (which is surprisingly lengthy) somewhat overstays its welcome. But, for $4, you won't feel cheated, as there are several hours of solid fun to be had.

I didn't have the chance to play this game while growing up, and admittedly, i was a bit spoiled by the more intuitively handled controls of Skyrim. It took me a while to really start to enjoy Morrowind. But once I did? I've been finding the adventures fun, and Morrowind itself to be an incredible place to explore. Just the size of it may initially seem a daunting task to explore, especially if your character is one with low Athletics and Speed skills at first, and you realize there is technically no real fast travel system other than the Mages Guild teleporters, a few ship captains, and the Silt Striders, who only take you to certain places. I love the variety of weapons and weapon skills, and while I feel that the process of actually casting a spell could have been a bit simpler, the magic system in general is pretty nice. Plus, I like that the Argonians and Khajiit are digitigrade (Just a small preference, I prefer my anthropomorphic animals to be a little more accurate in leg shape). The dungeons are structured better, they actually feel like ruins or temples or what-have-you, and overall the story is far superior to that of Skyrim, in my opinion. It doesn't look quite as "pretty" as Skyrim, but this is a mix of gameplay, graphics, and story that I feel is more properly handled, at least for its time.
I only have two issues, the DLC and the Save system.  With the DLC, they did not include all of them when putting Morrowind on Steam, there were 8 other DLC missing from the package, and I had to hunt them down on the Nexus to get my hands on them. As for the save system...well, you have to go into the game's files to delete it manuaally, but but it doesn't remove the character from the Cloud, so there is no real way to permanently delete a character you weren't satisfied with, at least not that I've found yet.
Other than that, I'm looking forward to playing more of this and exploring even more of the great island of Vvardenfell, as well as creating more solid or contrived builds as they strike my fancy.

After playing this for a bit I gave the show a try, only up to episode 4 as by the time of writing this only 4 episodes are out & so far it’s so cliché that even calling it cliché seems redundant. Nothing about the show is unique in anyway. It’s like they bought the How To Make A Sci-Fi Show Like Every Other One For Dummies. Yet it’s oddly cool, oddly interesting & oddly enjoyable even though it borrows from oh so many places that it’s more like a fan fiction than a real show. The game you ask? The game is exactly the same. The voice acting is bad, the story is cliché, the quests all involve you going somewhere & holding E on a few things & nothing about it is unique in any way.
So why am I recommending it? Well like the show for as less than average as it is I found it oddly enjoyable, the combat never got old even though I rarely replaced my weapons since I almost always got worse loot than the items I already had & that’s pretty much what carried it. Well that & the fact that it’s the least-social MMO I’ve ever played, never forced me to look for a group & is completely solo-able. That is an experience I’ve NEVER had with an MMO & to me is a good thing as I want a vast open world RPG in my MMO not a lets stand around for hours looking for a group or grinding just to progress. Yeah this is another recommendation where I ♥♥♥♥♥ about it more than praise but if the 70 hours of playtime is anything to go by you can bet that I by no means hated it & rather enjoyed it. Not going to win a spot in a top games of the year list but it’s enjoyable for what it is. Now I think I’m going to start the episode missions.

You want a point-and-click game that's less talk and more actual puzzles!

The real triumph of Machinarium is that it stacks puzzles within puzzles. You go through the typical point-and-click rigmarole of combining the thing-a-ma-bob with the doodad... and next thing you know you're rotating lights to get green ones in the centre or trying to illuminate a whole grid; very much like those 90's hand-held tactile puzzles or electronic gizmos that chewed up 6 AA batteries. Those classic spatial/shape-oriented puzzles which you seldom see anymore. It's this fun and varied array of puzzles weaved into the main game which keeps things fresh, interesting and each area very much unique. For a game to not only give you great puzzles, but a complete compendium of different types is downright superb! Whilst the space invaders and 'debugging' game seemed a bit unnecessary, but the rest are pretty damn good. You probably get around 6 hours for the playthrough, but it's 6 hours of solid head-scratching.
The design is also sublime with its gorgeous hand-crafted artwork. For the desolate industrial setting, there's a wonderful warmth that runs through the game as you fix the problems of the charming denizens* and communicate with nothing more than cartoony dialogue bubbles. How Machinarium manages to be touching, melancholic and light-humoured all in one is nothing short of exceptional. The end is a bit abrupt, but by no means disappointing.
All in all, a tough, rewarding puzzler with a cracking variety of enjoyable challenges.
*Except the tic-tac-toe bot. He can go do one. I swear the game took pity on me and handed me an easy victory after watching me lose several times in a row...

Card City Nights is a Cardplaying Adventure. You play as a new citizen of a city located on a little island. The interesting part is that everybody on this little island is into this wierd card game. So you also begin to play it. So you soon find out that there are the so-called legendary-cards and now your task is to get all this cards before your rival does. Sounds like POKEMON ? Yeah actually it's the exact same thing but with cards. So how does this card game work? Every player has a 3x3 square board.Every turn you can place a card in one of this nine squares. If you can connect 3 cards with eachother(like tic tac toe) the will do a certain action. There are  3 actions you can do:
-Attack: Attack the opponents HP or disable an opponents card
-Defend: Increase your HP
-Heal: Enable a disabled card.
So that are the basic rules of the card game. You will battle tons of people and every enemy has an other deck of cards and stratagy. You get new cards in form of booster decks  by defeating other players. And that's the whole geme in a nutshell.
The only complaint I have is that there is no online multiplayer but the single player is long and entertaining enough.
Oh and I forgot that the game has an awesome OST. So if you buy the game buy the OST to^^
A great cardgame with an awesome soundtrack.

Grrrrrrrrreat game! Finished the entire story (which includes post-game events) in roughly 15 hours. Story follows the courageous attempt of "SpacePirate", aiming to be the best card player in the city. Comparable to Pokemon games, in a way. Rather than collecting gym leader badges to reach the elite four, you're collecting legendary cards to battle the Card King.
Game is fairly straight forward, though not as casual as it may seem. You travel from location to location in seek of information for legendary cards. Each victory earns you gold and a booster pack which may contain a common, special or rare card. There's a variety of different booster packs, which further adds to the gameplay and replay value if you intend on building your deck around a specific type or card. Legendary cards pack unique abilities, further adding to the variety of options available. You can also buy or merge cards to create your ideal deck - Whether that be an all out offensive deck (which is what I used), defensive, deck burner, healer, focused on a combination deck, or various other combinations. Storage space of 6 decks, with minimum 25 and maximum 40 cards.
Gameplay is also fairly straight forward, though the battle phase is not like your average trading card game where each card has an attack and defence point, but rather connecting card arrows to form an attack, defence, heal, and so on. Victory is earned by either depleting the opponent defence points, burning their deck, or forcing them into filling up their playing board by stunning cards or hoping they can't match anything. Very formidable opponents late game, including some challenges early on when trying to understand the type of deck you want to build and the cards to include in this construction.
Visuals are both charming and delightful. Several cards and characters, from my understanding, are characters from the Ludocity franchises - Including Ittle Dew. No complication in terms of settings and adjustment. The game in general is very accessible and user-friendly. Soundtrack is a mixture of beautiful jazz and hip-hop.
Overall: A very charming and delightful card game topped off by a remarkable soundtrack. Definitely recommended, especially for that asking price! :]
