Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is a beautiful top-down puzzle adventure developed by Swedish developer Starbreeze Studios, who are better known for rather action-heavy games such as Riddick, The Darkness, Syndicate or Payback, so it's definitely a surprise that their first non-shooter game ended up being such a lovingly crafted piece of work.
The game tells the moving story of two brothers who set out on a journey across the lands to find a cure for their ailing father. While this is a pretty average story, it is presented with so much strength and emotion that it is really hard not to get touched by it. Even more so due the fact that there is no 'real' voice acting in the game apart from bits and pieces in a made-up language, so every bit of feeling and emotion the game tries to convey is is entirely transported through the fantastic soundtrack, the level design and the character acting.
Although the game is based on the PC-friendly Unreal Engine, it doesn't really provide many graphics options aside from brightness, resolution and VSync, but that shouldn't hold you off because the game looks absolutely stunning regardless.
The level design is fairly linear, so there is usually just one path to get from A to B, but the varying enviroments are packed with so much detail and love that it is a real pleasure to the eye to just wander around and explore all the tiny details Starbreeze has left in the game, such as a squirrel climbing a tree or bunnies hopping around. You can also sit down on any of the various benches in the levels to get a scenic view of some special spots. Absolutely fantastic.
An innovation that I haven't seen in any other game yet are the gameplay mechanics as you control both brothers at once, each brother with one thumb stick on your control, so it's basically like playing a two-player co-op game - but alone. This feels extremely weird at first and will definitely put your coordination and multitasking skills to the test, but the further you get into the game the more you get used to it.
The puzzles in the game make use of this mechanic in various ways and while the puzzle solutions as such generally are fairly obvious, solving them by controlling both brothers at once provides the actual challenge.
PSA: Despite the fact that the store page mentions 'Notice: Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons requires a controller to play', the game can be played with a keyboard just fine and the launcher also lets you rebind the keys (by default you control one brother with WASD and the other one with the arrow keys). I definitely recommend playing the game with a controller, though, as this simply feels better with a game like this.
With roughly 3.5 to 4 hours the game isn't exceptionally long by most people's standard, but it has so much depth and emotion that I consider it worth it every single cent if it manages to leave me with both sadness and satisfaction upon finishing it. If I had known what a strong game this is, I wouldn't have hesitated to pre-order it.
Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is a shiny gem among the games released this year and needs all the attention it can get. Especially these days where games rarely tell such an emotional story - or any story at all.

It's crazy how attached you get to your crew. I didn't know what to expect from the crew of the Jerry Jumper, but I was surprised. In just 3 hours, a bumble of 7 rookie crewman with no real redeeming traits have become a bumble of 7 rookie crewman who have done more heroic deeds than I can imagine. I plan on updating this review as I continue, but here's some highlights.
Sergeant Elizabeth Wright climbed out onto the wing during an air assault by 109s, lead by Ace Pilot Felix Feder. Successfully fixed Engine 2 and just in time to fix the hydraulics.
On the same mission, Sergeants Stewart and McKenzie gunned down ~18 enemy aircraft despite heavy fire. Wright delivered ammunition which let them have a constant barrage of fire. Felix Feder escaped, but took heavy damage.
Sergeant Davies dropped a full payload on a motor factory in Belgium, and then instantly switched over to his nose turret, shooting down a 109.
Sergeant Wright took over Stewart's top turret after heavy fire nearly killed the gunner. Wright shot down a 109 and most likely damaged others, while McKenzie and Davies supported from the rear and nose.
Sergeant Hunter, the pilot, despite being wounded on practically every mission the Jerry Jumper went on, brought all of his crewman back intact.
And that's it for now, but there will be more. Next up - Operation Chariot.
(first edit)
Alrighty. So, I just completed Operation Chariot, and it was a little shotty. We survived, so thats a bonus, however we came a little too close to being shot out of the sky.
During our approach to bomb out coastal gun emplacements, multiple squadrons of Bf.109s engaged and just strafed the pilot, Sergeant Hunter, continuously. By the time the last gun emplacement was knocked out, he was under half health. Once the operation was a success and the port was destroyed, we broke off and headed for medium altitude to avoid anti-air. However, the Luftwaffe had other plans, and 3 more squadrons of 109s broke through the clouds to engage. This time, they strafed Hunter some more, bringing his already dwindling health lower, and also heavily wounding Sergeant Wright, who was delivering ammo to Stewart. Luckily though, McKenzie and Stewart were able to focus fire, and knocked out the 109s with relative ease. We made it back in one piece, but it was a close call.
I believe the next critical mission is Operation Hydra, however there is some work that needs to be done with the crew and the bomber before we go on a long range operation like that.
(edit 2)
Well, something exciting has just happened while I was training my crew for Hydra. On their 16th mission, the crew of the Jerry Jumper successfully shot down Fighter Ace Felix Feder. This is the 4th time Felix Feder has engaged the bomber over the course of their missions, and the past 3 times he escaped. This time, top gunner Stewart, with the new Mark 3 turret, ignited Felix Feder's engine with a burst, which sent him spiralling down into the English Channel, before exploding on contact. Today is a glorious day for the crew! But there is no time to celebrate, for there is a war to be fought.
Next: Operation Hydra!

There's 4 map/level in this game, the original map on flash game and new one, the map design is creative and each of them unique.
Grapich and art are cute and colorful, the animation is also quite nice.
Love the soundtrack, i still humming the tune till now since 2011, the character/ghost sound effect is also nice (love that ghost boo sounds)
Beside the nostalgia, this game is really enjoyable and fun to play even with friends/family, i played this game with my family and compete who's the fastest one to complete the map, the game is also quite hilarious.

Firstly, it's manaless, which means that you do not require any farming of resources to play a card, and secondly, you create combos to attack and defend yourself, using the arrows drawn on the cards. At the same time, it has good drawings for each of the cards, most of which are characters from Ludosity's earlier works. For a price of $3.99, it is a must buy. Great replayability, as you constantly want to improve your end-game stats. It does not have any in-app purchases, which means you are not troubled by any future payments for additional content in the game. However, it lacks constant game updates, which means that the game content stays stagnant for a significant amount of time. Also, it is a single player game, this makes it impossible to challenge human players who have newer decks, further incresing our gaming experience. So we can only play with A.I. opponents. This makes the game frustrating to play. At the same time, this game does not deserve a TCG tag, because you don't get to trade cards with other players in the game.

This game has a delightful sense of irreverency to it, speaking as someone who's played a fair amount of trading card games and a fair amount of TCG video game adaptations. Rather than going for a complicated ruleset, the base rules are straightforward, but there's just enough variety in the cards available to allow for a number of strategic options in deckbuilding, and the excellent soundtrack helps the game's upbeat feeling. The difficulty curve is just about perfect if you hate getting "stuck" in games, as well... only in one or two places did I ever feel I wasn't quite "getting it."
There's also some fanservice here, as the characters/cards are mostly from the company's other games, but it's unobtrusive enough that those unfamiliar won't find it distracting. (Of course, if you're me, you will squeal in astonished joy the first time you see an Iji or General Kor card.) Those seeking a great story should look elsewhere; although the characters feel well fleshed out and the writing is clever, more emphasis is put on gameplay than worldbuilding or plot, which I feel serves the game well. The card game mechanics form a solid core, and nearly everything present here is in service of that.
In conclusion, this game is a definite recommendation from me. It won't change your life, it won't suck away weeks of your time, and it won't provide anything truly revolutionary that you'll measure other games up against for years to come... but what it will do is provide a solid, fun experience for relatively little money. There's some great value here. Give the game a try; it's fun stuff.

Summary: A very simplisitc game that seems to be targeted towards casuals, and even they may have trouble enjoying the game.
The basic gameplay is this: The two players play on separate 3x3 boards. Each draws cards from their decks and place them on the board, one per turn. The cards have arrows pointing in anywhere from 0 to 6 directions. Linking 3 or more to make a combo is your primary method of attack and defense. You can do damage to the player or disable their cards on the board. The advantage of disabling cards is they can no longer link together, though they can be healed. You win if you can drop their life to zero or their field fills up and they can no longer place cards. If a player runs out of cards, they don't immediately lose, but damage is dealt to them each turn by the board.
There's very little strategy involved. You fill your deck with cards that will link together easily. Beating enemies is mostly luck based, since they tend to have weird and unpredictable cards, like ones that randomly rotate or move cards. The winning strategy is often just to disable as many cards as possible without regard to health.
Overall, veteran gamers will find this simplistic and boring, while casual players with not be especially enthralled.

This is the first mythical fantasy-world game that I have played that feels as if it's making no effort at all to explain its world to the player. Instead, "Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons" simply welcomes the player with open arms, without a single instance of contrived exposition, backstory, or narration. Quite the opposite, in fact, since the entire game plays out without a single word uttered in a real-world language – the game's language is made-up.
The game plays out as a surprisingly grand adventure for two brothers who must travel to the metaphorical ends of the world to seek a cure for their ailing father. The story is very simple, yet it remains terribly engrossing and powerful without a single dull moment, in no small part because of how much depth and empathy the characters have and how much well-thought-out splendor and grandeur the environments have.
This game world is the sort of game world that I would absolutely love to visit. It has incredible potential for being dangerous, sure, but its sheer beauty and variety are riveting enough to make the dangers seem worth it. What's more is that no single part of the world feels disconnected from the rest. Each location feels sensibly connected to each other location, all while offering plenty in the way of location-based storytelling. That is, you will learn a LOT about this world simply by walking around and observing.
From a gameplay perspective, what makes this game so unique is that the player controls both brothers at all times using the two separate joysticks on a controller. (A controller is required to play at all.) It's a little weird to get used to for the first half-hour or so, but it eventually becomes very fluid and intuitive as the game continually introduces new platforming and puzzle-solving mechanics, all of which are immensely creative and perform flawlessly.
Truly, this is an adventure game in the most distilled sense of the word, and I cannot recommend it enough. My playtime clocked in at 3 hours and 15 minutes.

Bug Fixes
FIXED >> * When you restore functionality to each secondary radio tower (KTAM East, West, South) you fall from the sky after the cutscene.

* Sometimes, shots that should be missed, hit.

* Textures. They look okay for mid-HD range, but not high-end HD (1080p+) range where they can have washed out edges, etc.

Things to add

This game was initially  overhyped, but beneath the surface is something totally worthwhile, if somewhat simplistic. However, simple isn't always bad in games, and quite often some ofthe most addicting games are quite simple (Candy Crush) or have some simple elements (sneaking around  clueless NPCs in Skyrim). Spore is not Candy Crush, however it certainly isn't Skyrim either.

Spore has an amazing creation engine that is in an of itself completely fun to  use. Growing up I used to joke about there one day being game that was  nothing more than the create a character function, where that WAS the game. Spore is not that game. Even with the parts pack it will give you at best one more page or less of pieces to mess around with. (Yet to this day EA has no qualms about still charging $19.99 for even its worst  reviewed Sims 3 expansions.) Spore could have been better but this was before Minecraft sold for an enormous sum and the industry took note of how much life you can breathe into a piece of software by allowing people real creative  control. I'm sure at the time EA was more worried about "Sporn" and other issues they didn't want to spend their time managing to preserve the game,  and the company's, brand image.

Spore though presents some amazing possibilities, and also functions in some ways as a statement on life  itself, from the single celled on up. No matter how big and complex we get, we still seem to encounter some of the same essential problems.

I do recommend Spore, but even more so I recommend EA make a sequel. Spore only requires 4gb of space, a modern AAA game will usually require 15 times that. There is a lot of room for expansion here, and profit, if EA is willing to construct a sequel that allows their engine to more fully serve people's creative impulses.

One of the most climatic horror game I had ever played.
It is a masterpiece in the following levels: game design, game mechanics, level design, atmosphere, sound design, OST, horror element, etc. Limited and consumable saves, which you can use ONLY at designated locations –This added so much to the horror element to the game, it can't be stressed enough. This, like many other mechanics in the game, linked the gameplay with the setting, in the way that not only do you feel scared of the spooky monsters and the mansion, but you also feel scared that you might lose a lot of progress if you screw up, which makes the feeling of fear much more REAL. It also adds an element of risk, in that if you screw up, you'll have to start from the last save, which could be a big chunk of lost time. The feeling of relief you get when you arrive at a save room after playing for half an hour without saving would not exist without this. "Should I save now, or should I carry this save ribbon and save at the next save room? I don't wanna use ribbons that I might need later". This also applies to some of the following points: -Limited inventory space – This ties in to the choice thing I was talking about. It makes you take crucial decisions and it forces you to try to predict what you will need in the future. Do you need an extra space, or is that green herb worth taking? In that case, for example, you'll have to decide between: Consume a bullet, or take the risk of getting close to the zombie and try to run past him without taking damage. Which one is more valuable: The bullet, or your safety?

Ever since the classic Ghost Master gave players the power to scare idiot homeowners out of their dwellings, I've been eager to see more games about being the haunter rather than the hauntee. Poltergeist: A Pixellated Horror was another fine offering, if a little simple. Now we have Haunt the House, possibly the most polished of the haunting simulators yet, but still not as deep as you might be hoping.
You take on the role of the cutest ghost in the entire world (seriously look at him) as he works to scare away every mortal in sight. You're going to need more than his adorably pitiful ooOOoo though, which is why you can possess just about every object in the game. Once you have taken over a chair or lamp or dresser or whatever, you get some new options to terrify those in the vicinity. Most objects can move or make some little sound, but once you raise the overall terror level in the building (shown in a big, helpful bar at the bottom) you can unlock new moves with certain objects like projecting apparitions and breaking things.
Starting out, the gameplay appears dead simple. You find the largest gathering of people, possess something, mash your spook button until everyone flees, then repeat. After a some time with your ghostly bud you'll come to discover there's a little more nuance to it than that. People recover their composure after escaping a spook, so chasing down specific victims and chain-haunting them is far more effective for getting them out of the house. You can also corral terrified residents to windows which they will gladly leap from to save you the wait for them to reach the door. Not all spooks are equal, either, as the ones that can be unleashed rapid-fire can send people into a tizzy before they can escape.
The base scenario, Terror Town, features an open map with four locations to haunt. There's also the mansion from the original Flash game, a holiday map, and a train with three cars. Most areas have 20 to 30 people to run off, along with some secrets to find like fatalities you can cause and objects with special spooks. That should be enough to keep you busy for an hour, but beyond that... I can't really say. You're scored on the efficiency of your haunting and there are achievements to turn up, though if neither of those interest you then this is going to be a short game.
I will say that I can't get enough of the bold, cartoony look Haunt the House revels in. Possessed objects do all sorts of ridiculous and adorable things, from tables dancing to portholes becoming eldritch portals. Your victims are all wide-eyed caricatures with giant expressions and silly screams. The sound design sells a lot of it, in fact, with equally adorable honks and swishes for the spooks and an old-tymey cinema soundtrack. It looks great, sounds great, and plays great (especially with a controller), it'll just be over before you know it. But if you like terrifying virtual people as much as I do, it's a good time while it lasts.

Machinarium was, I believe, the second game I owned on Steam. Now I have 1000 games but Machinarium still holds a place in my heart. As Amanita's first full-length game, it has its flaws - Save-game issues, originally had no achievements, now it has achievements but they don't unlock. Slow, unskippable walking animations. The seemingly unescapable "click the exact pixel" puzzles. In spite of all that, Machinarium has undeniable charm and style. Beautiful art, one of my favourite video game soundtracks. Clever puzzles to accompany a gorgeous game. I think everyone should finish Machinarium at least once, which is saying something considering how many flaws I was able to list.
For what Machinarium does right, it excels at.

I bought this game when I only had a Netbook available to play games on. Had it on my wishlist since release and it's extremely cheap in comparison with some other games, so I just thought "Why not?" and bought it. After starting the game you choose a character and give yourself a name. You're new in town and how else could it be, the whole town is crazy for card battles. The main goal of the game is to collect all legendary cards by beating the owners of those cards and finally beat the Card King. On your way you get to see lots of crazy looking, humorous characters and get to hear some nice chilling-jazzy tunes.
What I really like about this game is, that it's extremely fast and easy to learn, yet fun to manage your deck and finally use it in a card battle. To explain it very roughly, most Cards have arrows on them or some special effects and you just have to connect them on a 3x3 board to create combos using Cards that sum up to at least 3 Icons. Cards have one of four Icons on them, Attack, Defense, Revive and Neutral. Using attack Cards you can either attack your opponent and he'll loose "defense" (just like Health Points) or disable one of your opponent cards, so he can't use 'em until he revives them using Revive Cards. Using Defense Cards will fill up your defense until you reach the maximum of 10 defense. Neutral Cards can come in handy when connecting Cards. You win a game when your opponent can't place a card on his 3x3 Board or he runs out of defense. Most opponents give you a card booster as a reward and you can also buy or fuse cards. I haven't spent much time collecting Cards, I just went on with the Cards I owned and updated my deck now and then, mostly only changing the legendary Card or replacing one or two Cards from my deck with Cards I got from a Booster.
While - at least in my opinion - you should never judge a game on how long it is (you don't pay 10 $ for a visit to the cinema and regret it because the movie was only 2 hours long, right?), Card City Nights entertained me for about 11 hours until I've beaten the whole game and got all the Achievements, which is quite long for a game that price. Instead a game should be judged by how fun it was to play and I really had fun playing it. I definitely recommend this game. It's fun, it's cheap, it has Steam Trading Cards and Steam Achievements. So: Why not?

Card City Nights is another fun game like Ittle Dew, but it suffers from the same problem, it is too short. And while there are all sorts of cards to collect, I feel it doesnt have the replay value of Ittle Dew. But on the other hand this game is still fun and its gives you some more after you beat Ittle Dew and you get all the cards and beat all the dungeons. My final verdict is pick this game up if you have the money, but a little advice from me is pick this up with Ittle Dew, and then it won't seem like too short of an experience.

Morrowind is clearly an old, dated game.  That's no surprise.  Games of this type are usually coasting on nostalgia; only known as a "legendary title" because of childhood memories or its quality for its time.
Morrowind is no such title, with a few exceptions.  These are most notably combat and user-friendliness (a complete lack of instruction on how combat actually works).  However, combat can be greatly improved using mods, and guides exist to teach you about the game.
If you're a fan of the Elder Scrolls series, and intend to use mods, this is worth the buy.  If you're not willing to mod it, maybe get it on sale.
In short, it's a great game even now.

The un-nerevarine amount of hours I have put into this game before it was released on Steam, plus the hours amassed on a computer without internet, simply are not captured in the recorded time of my account.  And to me, this is, quite simple, the best game ever created.
The best example of why this is so is a comparison, between Morrowind and Skyrim, of how you are treated when joining the Mage's Guild/College of Winterhold.  Skyrim: "Oh, so you're Dragonborn, slayer of Alduin, Listener of the Morag Tong, etc.?  Great.  Here's how you magic and, oh look, a magic ball and you say that a sorcerer appeared to you alone saying it will destroy the world and you're the only one who can prevent it?  Okay, better go do that."  Morrowind: "Oh, so you're Nerevarine, Knight of the Imperial Dragon, and Councilor of the Great House Hlaalu?  Okay, well, I'm engaged in some critical research on alchemy, so why don't you bring me a ceramic bowl.  Oh, and here's 5 shiny gold pieces to help you buy one."
Next, you can create a character that is bad.  In Skyrim all skills level you up, so if you have a poor character concept, simply changing in mid-game has little impact on continuing.  In Morrowind, if you screw up character creation, you can more or less forget about surviving even on easiest mode.
My favorite bit comes down to none of the factions have quest lines dealing with the potential destruction of the world.  The Mage's Guild has you collecting guild dues and buying ceramic bowls.  The Temple and Imperial Cult send you off to cure people of diseases or collect small amounts of gold as alms.
Other plusses are the minor details like merchants refusing to dealing with you if you are carrying illegal drugs.  It feels like a functional world.
Oh, and there's a strip club.

The pinnacle of Resident Evil perfected.  Resident Evil Remastered took what remake done back in 2002 and makes it even better making this version the best version to play.
What can I say? The game looks stunningly gorgeous 17 years on, playing this game 120fps versus 30fps makes it feel like an entirely new game.  It plays so smoothly, the jump scares still to this day make me jump and the hunters will always give me an uneasy feeling bypassing them as I open the door across the hallway.
This is technically the first game of the series (Resident Evil 0 is a prequel to this game so that's why I'd say this is the first main game in the series).  It's one of the best if not the best in my humble opinion.  Everything just works, the pacing from travelling through the tight corridors of the mansion, not knowing what's going to be around the next corner to little wooden hut out in the middle of nowhere where you meet what only can be described as an abomination living there.  The game just makes you feel uneasy from start to finish as everything is out to kill you and you never feel completely safe.  Your only respite is a save room and even then you have to eventually leave it to zombie invested corridors attempting to dodge most of them to save precious ammo on bigger more powerful enemies.
That is another thing this game does really well, it forces you to conserve your ammo which in doing so makes the game that much scarier as you have to attempt to dodge enemies in tight spaces without dying.  I can't tell you how many times I've been on red caution/danger health wise and just dodged enough to make it to a save room to collect a health item from the item chest and heal.
Combine this with great voice acting (MUCH MUCH better than the original game which came out in 1996 on the PSX) and interesting characters and you really feel for your team whenever you meet them throughout the storyline.
You have a choice whether to play as Jill Valentine or Chris Redfield.  Each character has both pro's and negatives (Chris can run faster and has a lighter by default whilst Jill cannot run as quick but to compensate has a lockpick by default alongside being able to do other things Chris cannot).  Jill also has 2 more item slots than Chris does, has access to the grenade launcher which chris does not, has access to a lockpick which means she doesn't have to collect small keys to open doors like Chris does and finally is a lot more knowledgable on certain areas than Chris is which makes puzzle solving and one particular boss fight much easier.  For each character the gameplay is the same in terms of story progression, you need the same keys to open the same doors and the same objects to unlock the same items etc. but your interactions with your fellow Stars members are different and ultimately the game feels much different which gives the player an excuse to play through the game at least twice over, once with Jill and once with Chris.
This game for me gets a perfect score of 10/10 as I simply cannot fault this game whatsoever.  Some may say that it's too short but isn't that subjective? It has perfect pacing, engaging enemies, a great cast of believable heroes and villains and AWESOME boss fights and an incredible backstory to what exactly happened in the mansion and beyond.
One thing I will mention however to make this game just a little better is to install two mods:
1) Door skip mod - this mod allows the player to completely bypass/skip the door-loading animations thus saving a lot of time overall.
2) Resident Evil real time graphics mod - this mod allows the player to change the in-game graphics how they see fit, either by removing bloom, changing various colour filters, fog etc. I feel this mod is essential because it makes the game look much better by removing elements which either a) obstruct the player from actually seeing what's in the background and b) Removing harsh lighting that comes from bloom

I told my 3 gunners to focus on their aim and had my most experienced gunner switch to incendiary rounds. Unfortunatley for me, while I was doing this the German ace was lining up on my tail. He procceded to unload a looong burst of incendiary ammo into the tail gunner, setting the tail gun position, and my tail gunner, on fire. As the tail gunner ran, burning, towards the middle of the bomber, my engineer grabed a fire extinguisher and began sprinting for the tail. My 2 remaining gunners were struggling to handle the swarm of hostile fighters and the Spitfires were similiarly overwhelmed, we were taking fire from multiple directions in the air as well as flak from the ground. After putting out the fire in the tail, my engineer swaped his extinguisher for a med kit and went to revive my tail gunner who had collapsed by the ammo box for the turret machine guns which my top turret gunner had just come down for more ammo. The German ace decided to make another pass at this moment and caught all 3 crewmen with a full burst, downing the engineeer and top gunner and badly injuring the newly revived tail gunner AND setting the tail gun on fire, again. So while my tail gunner went to put out the new fire, my radio op grabed a med kit and ran to revive my engineer. This entire time the other German fighters were tearing my bomber apart, the only positive was that I was now at mid level altitude, which put me out of range of the AA. About this time several German fighters hit me simultaneously and downed my tail gunner and the radio op who was nearly finished reviving the engineer. The only crewman still up and about were now my pilot, navigator and bombardier. For his final run the German ace decided to put the nails in my crews' coffins and blew off my tail taking the tail gunner who had collapsed at his position with it. My bomber proceeded to steadily lose altitude until ultimately crashing into occupied France. I returned to base to find out the fates of my downed crewmen, my navigator made it home no problem (thank you survival gear!) by some miracle the radio op and engineer survived both being downed and crashing and were somehow able to return home, my pilot, gunners and bombardier were not so lucky.
The perma death of these crewmen and the inferiority of my replacement bomber may have put me into a now unwinnable situation in the campaign, that said I am very eager to startover and try again.
So if you like FTL and are looking for a similar challenging experience, give Bomber Crew a try.

It's Spore that I have to thank for shaping my love for Science and Sci-fi. It was 2008, October 22 when I received Spore for my 7th birthday. It was on a basic disc install and I remember spending the whole week playing this game. I didn't know a thing about the game. I saw the cover, thinking it was some kid's adventure game, for a second I was confused as to why my parents would buy me such a game. One with colorful monsters and fancy worlds. I installed it onto by Windows Vista. This is the story.
You begin the game as a lonely little cell, struggling for survival in the harsh waters of an unknown world. You choose to be a hunter carnivore or a defensive herbivore. As you survive, you birth more of yourselves. This is when the creative element of Spore came to be. Being able to choose how you look. From color of your skin, to the amount of fins on your body, to the razor-sharp spikes around you. After some time, your little creature grows into a sentient being.
And so your creature evolves from a little fish organism into an animal, as you live in the lands shared by other creatures, some beasts and others friends. You continue to evolve until you reach a point of where you learn to use tools. Spears and torches have become the norm. Other tribes come, all are different life forms but all of a similar intelligence. You have to choose which you befriend, and which you fight to the death. Sometime after all these tribe wars, your tribe becomes a civilization. One that thrives from an economy, military or religion. This is actually my favorite part because it's fun to play Civ 6 with aliens (not the same as Civ beyond earth). Once all the countries on this world have been taken over by you, whether it was from annexing, destruction or religious manipulation. Your Civilization becomes a cosmic superpower. One that trades, battles and discovers other alien races, all with different personalities and goals. But beware of the center, because for some, technology has gone too far, so you must not let that corruption destroy galactic friendship for omnipotent power. One that is evil.
But there is one massive problem with the game. EA has ♥♥♥♥ed this game up for me and almost every other fan. It has removed the one feature that kept it alive after 100 hours of game time and that is the community. When galactic adventures first came out, the game was awesome. More than it already was. But it relied on the community, otherwise there would  be no more galactic adventures. But now you can no longer download community adventures. And this is what the game is now. Less than 80 hours of EA created bullcrap. Nothing new to the table. If you are a returning fan like me, don’t waste money on it. its best to keep the memories alive in your head than to ruin them with EA horror. But if you have never played Spore, please buy it. It may not be as large as it used to be but its still fun.

I was playing this game outside of steam for quite an extended period of time so my actual playtime is a lot more than the ~90 hours stated there.
Let me just start by saying that this game isn't pay-to-win, unless winning is building anything of considerable size, which some would say is what this game is about (lol). If you are like me, playing this game to hang with friends or just strolling through other people's creations then, you'll be alright, it won't cost you much. However, suppose you want to create something and wouldn't want to spend hours after hours mining material, then I suppose you might need to chip in some real cash. Of course, the choice is all yours, so is this pay-to-win? Again, it's on you to decide whether it is or not.
The community (excluding devs and mods, cause that's a topic for future paragraph) of this game is one of the most friendliest that I've ever seen. A lot them are willing to take the initiative to help newcomers adopt into the game. Just scroll around the official forum, you pretty much get all the help you want (and more) there.
The game updates pretty often as well, which while others may see as a good thing, to me, it is not quite so. Devs have been pumping out more and more cosmetics like hats, pets and other what-have-you's that the game is straying more and more away from its 3d platformer + sandbox roots to become some sort of a trading simulator (just look at the amount of buying and selling that clog the hollas).
(Sigh) mods... Where do I begin? On one hand, I've made quite a few friends who are mods themselves and on the other, I've got a few friends of mine that leave this game because of their run-ins with mods. So... Make of it as how you see fit.
Lastly, like all great religion, there's quite a bit of fanatics that live and die by this game (and its dev/mod team)... So... Just be careful of what you say and to whom you say those things because there are ears behind every cubic walls.
All in all, I'm half and half on recommending this game, the moment I'm writing this, I feel quite ok about this but perhaps an hour later, the sentiment will change.

This is one of these strange, slightly-surreal-with-a-bit-of-horror Japanese adventure-not-RPG-despite-the-engine games, similar to Yume Nikki or Ib. Yes, I know I need to cut down on the dashes.
The title (a combination of Alice and nightmare, nothing to do with horses, for better or worse) is slightly misleading, since there aren't actually many elements taken from Alice (mostly the White Rabbit and the Cheshire Cat), but on the other hand the inspirations from classic fairytales (Little Red Riding Hood, Hansel and Gretel, etc) are numerous. Yes, I know I also need to cut down on the brackets.
The story takes place in some kind of institution for children with "issues" (not exactly an orphanage, nor a hospital, but something along these lines), which quickly becomes entangled with a nightmarish world with a fairytale flair. While not relying on jumpscares or an overly unsettling atmosphere, it kinda reminded me of Silent Hill, if Silent Hill was written with children in mind that is.
Visually, although I found the mapping average, the color tones really reinforced the atmosphere. Not as well as it was done in
(the second game from Miwashiba), but still pretty well.
The gameplay is mostly composed of puzzles and riddles, some of them being fairly well-known (like that river where you have to ferry across a wolf, a sheep, and some kind of extremely rare and precious lettuce without any being eaten by their natural predator). If you have an affinity for logic and math you'll breeze through, if not, well, there's still bruteforcing or walkthroughs.
This was originally a free game, which is still available for free in English on
. You can check it there if you're interested, although I recommend buying it on Steam to show support for the dev if you liked it (in that case be sure to check
as well). The Steam version is mostly the same, though it comes with the usual features like achievements or cards.
+ Interesting twist on classic fairytales
+ Great atmosphere
+ Multiple endings
- Pixel hunting now and then
- Some puzzles can be hard to grasp
7/10 If you like the kind of games I laboriously described in my first paragraph, try this one, it's one of the good ones. Yes, I know this succession of "one"s is hardly proper English.

Great for people who like old school, slow, very strict RPGs. But, if you're coming at Morrowind even from simply playing Oblivion, you're out of luck. I'd rather play D&D than Morrowind. Not a bad game, just not my cup of tea. But for sure recommended for those who like the old school era of RPGs.

Morrowind is up to this day one, if not the best Open World RPG ever developed. Back when most games were tiny at best, it featured a gigantic map with countless secrets, dungeons and completely unique quests, not having to get 10 of that or kill 20 of something different. It was deep, complex, unique and back then looked absolutely beautiful, had (and has) a timeless soundtrack, probably the best main storyline of any Elder Scrolls game so far and the longest as well as most complex guild questlines (spanning 30 or more quests for each guild alone, which send you all around the entire continent many times over, compared to the measly rough dozen in Oblivion and Skyrim which are mostly each contained to one area and are not necessarily building on top of each other.)
Morrowind is also the only game featuring the Morag Tong, a guild so secret that many players couldn't even find it with directions back then and which is probably the coolest guild ever featuring in an Elder Scrolls title (a thieves + assassin guild which is literally not allowed to use violence but has to manipulate npcs into killing each other or suiciding or has to steal things without being detected.)
The whole game was and still is peerlessly brilliant and I personally have been waiting the last couple of years for Skywind, A Morrowind total conversion based on the Skyrim engine to get finished and go public. Probably my most awaited mod of the entire decade.
Morrowind can not only be recommended, it is gaming history at its finest, not only being a milestone of gaming and a beacon of nostalgia, but also still to this day an extremely well balanced and fun game to not only play, but delve into for weeks on end.

You know Overwatch? Y'know, that indie hit from Blizzard Entertainment. Kinda a big deal.
This is a very dumbed down version of that.
You pick a character (You start with two of the most boring characters I've ever played in an FPS: Sad 76 and Hockey Player), and then you play King of the Hill or Kill Confirmed matches. The only things you can do is sprint, shoot, aim down sights, and your ability which charges extremely fast. Vaulting and wall jumping is done automatically.
Most fights boil down to players awkwardly strafing side to side while hoping they shoot the other person more, or their ability is ready. It is frankly one of the most boring FPS experiences I've ever had, mobile or otherwise.
Don't worry, though! It's made worse by a progression system that requires you to open loot boxes for Agent XP, which you can use to upgrade your existing characters, chosen at random. The very first box I received that wasn't a tutorial box requires you to wait an hour until it can be opened, and you can only open one at a time. This means upgrading characters (Which improves several important statistics) will take a very, very long time...Unless you're willing to part with some real life cash to purchase Diamonds.
Diamonds allow you to buy everything instantly, including loot boxes. This means if you're willing to pay a decent amount of money, you can have more characters, and more character upgrades than someone who's trying to grind it out. The in-game currency currently does next to nothing to my knowledge: You earn so little of it that unlocking a new Agent will seemingly take weeks.
It's an extremely boring game topped off with an extremely manipulative and unfair pay to win system. Don't even bother when Paladins exists...Even when Paladins has it's fair share of issues.
Also, hey, did you know Overwatch is on sale right now? You can get it for like $20. Just get that instead, man.

Great game. I laughed, I cried, I did both at the same time cause I didn't lower the landing gear...
Note: We need Runner Duck (this games developer) and Subset Games (the group that made FTL) to get together and make a game baby.

In short:
Casual B-17 Flying Fortress having people from Kerbal Space Program with a dose of FTL. Since Steam doesn't have a neutral rating, I'll recommend it.
In more detail:
The premise is you lead a UK bomber crew in WW2. Some people dislike the overly cartoonish presentation, but I'm fine with it. I think it serves it's purpose of reminding the player this is not a simulation. The best example is even in the last days of WW2 you'll be attacked by enemy fighter planes.
The presentation and the gameplay were the two most catching things for me. While you play the tutorial missions, you're thinking, yea, this is a chill game, just like the visuals. Then, when you run your 2nd or 3rd mission, still learning the ropes, you hit the learning curve like a brick wall. You can upgrade your plane, your crew, you unlock skills, kinda rogue-lite. To progress in time in WW2, you finish some special missions. And then, the first issues start to show.
You'll get hooked by the gameplay, the possibilities and get crushed many times. Especially when meeting enemy aces. It's big time fun, when you hectically try to bomb the target, while you're attacked by enemy fighters and at the same time your engineer informs you that the fuel tanks are leaking. The game boils down to decision making under stress. At least in after 3-4 hours playing it looks like so.
Then, after a dozen failures, things are starting to come more clear. You don't advance the campaign, until you build your skills and plane enough. This is for me the major issue with the game. In the 90s, games were much more spartan and this would fit in that timeframe. But in the meantime people got used to many things. You'll have to find a sweet spot between grinding to a fully equipped plane and crew, and dying in 10 seconds, because you're too weak. I got the hang of the game by now, but I still couldn't beat some missions, with not a good enough start. There are certainly some skill involved, but less than it seems at start.
So the "easy" way would be to grind your way through the game. But then, where's the fun? If you grind too much, most of the missions will become a cakewalk, so you get bored. If you don't grind at all, you'll be fine, and in a single mission lose everything. If you progressed to a further point in the campaign, recovery will be a pain where sunshine doesn't go in. For the later missions, an almost fully upgraded plane and skills are almost mandatory, otherwise it will be a lesson in frustration.
So, all this sounds too negative, but when you start getting used to the gameplay after a couple of hours, it's awesome. When the difficulty is spot on and you almost always have something to do. The missions vary between roughly 5 to 30 minutes in lenght. 30 being the rare ones. My favorite was (not really spoilers, because its a generic mission) to bomb some Flaks in Austria. I traveled the whole map avoiding enemy positions. After bombing vice versa. Of course there were fights, but when I arrived back to good old UK, it really felt like an adventure.
So, my conclusion is, if you ever played B-17 Flying Fortress and liked it, you'll probably like this too, but after a while Bomber Crew will seem too simplistic. Adding overpowered enemies won't convince you of the opposite. So if you play it enough, you'll probably want to return to B-17. To the majority who didn't play that game, if you don't expect realism and are okay with some frustration, you'll have an awesome experience with Bomber Crew most of the time.
A very good game in all aspects, though it is almost impossible to fly at anything above low altitude until your navigator is lvl.8. Which takes a while.

A fantastic mix of FTL and mysims.
It doesn't sound like it would work but it does. The game starts off introducing simple mechanics and an underpowered bomber with a crew that has no gear. As you play through missions you get unlock a variety of upgrades that you have to choose from. You are constantly reaching for better armor or guns to buy, and it's so appealing to push through a couple more missions just to get that .50 cal that you know will shred through enemy aircraft. There is also a depth in gameplay that keeps you entertained and makes you feel like you can always do better.
The art style is clearly set, and never breaks away from its own design. All of the characters are chibi, the colors are bright, and there is a 40's feel to everything. Every aspect of this game is dripping with character, its hard to narrow down what best describes its feel. From the soft radio playing at the base, the upbeat vocabulary of the captain that gives you missions, to the the constant hum of your bombers engines. There is something deeply pleasing about all of it and I am constantly finding myself play for hours longer then I ment to.

- polished beyond necessity,
master has several, key lighting and 3D environment tweaks along with improved sound design for engulfing the player in its claustrophobic setting.
Shinji Mikami truly remasters old, familiar territory. Ripples sent by this title have emanated well beyond its natural life which began in 2002 as the GameCube version, and just as true today, is the epitome of fan service. More importantly, it improves the formula to provide new and engaging mechanics over the original 1998 version. HD
master is best enjoyed after a few playthroughs of the original or Director's Cut version in order to absorb the mansion's fecundity as the series' centerpiece.
How many modern, full-priced horror games focus on replayability
the addition of DLC? HD
master pulls it off with one location and sports several unlockables for the completionist, no additional fees included which is almost sacrilege in this day and age when DLC reigns supreme. Replayability depends on player fortitude for doing puzzles over and over to which they know the solutions and, if the player enjoys the game, their appetite for a challenge through new modes of play.
Arguably the best of the series,
make and this remastered version fare well visually among today's horror titles. However, limitations placed on player movement, inventory management, and visible area is likely to be among the game's most noted criticisms. Several playthroughs, while ideal, is not guaranteed. The game is
to feel constricting at the player's expense. Liberation is only gained momentarily from the acquisition of ammunition. To
make's benefit,
make balances gameplay and story-driven action through the time-tested design of the mansion. Exploration opens up after a certain point; plot structure, rising action, and difficulty overlap to keep experience intact.
(TL;DR): Fan service with solid design and replayability, Capcom proves you can teach an old Cerberus new tricks.

Very fun game if you enjoy the sorts of games that start you from scratch. You literally start from a microorganism and carry through to a galaxy-conquering civilized species.
The process is a bit odd since the journey involves successive stages that have fundamentally different game dynamics. The "cell" and "creature" stages have no time dynamic or death penalty, for instance, while the rest of the game stages play a lot more like an RTS. Plus the game will enable you to move to the next stage well before you've optimized your creature to move on, so you have to gauge how important bonus optimization is to you.
The graphics quality is much lower-quality by today's games, but the creature design (and then vehicle and building design) options are VERY well optimized to allow you to do diverse things with how your critters and their culture appear. As a big fan of character customization this is a huge plus for me and was easily one of the game experiences that functions that served as the biggest time sink.
The issues I had were:
1. The repetitiveness of the space stage. It's the endgame and the longest section of the game, but it plays out the same way with little variation despite different abilities and randomized star systems and other space empires. Once getting my captains to the max "rank" with a species I generally stopped and started over to make a new creature. Otherwise it's just kill the ones that want war, manage the ones that don't, fix disasters in time, keep expanding and collecting spices to sell... over and over and over across a HUGE sandbox.
2. Despite the great variety in creature designs available, each creature component has a specific bonus to it, so if a feature looks totally cool on your critter, it may nevertheless have the least bonus along its line of features. Thus I ended up with critters that all used mostly the same features (and a huge amount of them) despite not really looking the best, even if it was a fun challenge to distribute them differently across a new body shape each time. It's true that by space stage those bonuses are mostly irrelevant, but it means a harder time getting through the tribal stage if you don't max the bonuses and even in the space stage if you do combat ground missions before you've got weapons.
3. It's structured at every stage with the same old strategy game dynamic where some civs/tribes/organisms/space empires are OK with you, others just going to go to war with you no matter how stupid it would be for them. I'm kinda bored with that dynamic by now, even if it's not really something to frown upon since it's so quintessential to the genre. Spore is certainly not a poor adaptation of the dynamic, though it's a lot more simplistic than, say, Civ 5. The fun in this game is mostly just the organism.
4. Despite some pretty mature themes in terms of devouring/destroying other creatures/civs the ground missions feel like they were designed for a 6-yr-old. Doesn't mean they didn't have their charm, but... meh. I tried to avoid that content so as not to tire of the game, but it's at the cost of sacrificing a means of pleasing allies. Arguably the non-violent methods in the creature stage is also pretty kidstuff, but it's also a creative approach, so... *shrugs*
I also had issues with the counterintiutiveness of development choices trying to steer the development toward a particular outcome, but ultimately I found it a fun challenge to get what I was after, and overall the game is really enjoyable, particularly as a sandbox in the space stage where you can explore and find the HUGE amount of critters (both native to the game and uploaded by fellow Spore players).
It's also the only space-travel game I've ever played where the galaxy layout was truly 3D so that stars that
closer may actually be farther away due to verticality. Really appreciated that aspect. The sheer number of star systems and opponent/ally empires compelled me to maintain a written list as I went along so as not to be so lost in the vastness that I couldn't remember where I get the best trade deals for various items or determine from where battles against me were being waged.
If you can handle some scaling back of graphics quality and enjoy adding an element of goofiness to your game of cosmic conquest and domination, Spore is worth checking out.

Native is fun, but you're going to want to play this with total conversion mods. If you're just starting off stick with Native, until you get a good hang of it, because most conversion mods can be and will be brutal.
For mods I recommend:
-Prophesy of Pendor: One of the more difficult mods, but one of the most well done, and full with new things to do.
-Perisno: This is more of a Fantasy mod with dwarves and elves (That are playable), but sadly doesn't have as much content as other mods, but this is still my favorite conversion I've played so far.
-The Last Days of The Third Age- If you're a Tolkien fan, like I am. This is a must, very well done and Lore-friendly. Play as Orcs to Man to Elves. You also get to see some of your favorite characters from the books. The only problem I have with this mod is, it takes time to get a really good army going or anything really, but I still love this mod, and I love killing Trolls.
-Warsword Conquest: A Fantasy Warhammer mod with every faction you could ask for, not as fleshed as the others mentioned above sadly.
I recommend giving this game a try, I promise you won't regret it. If you don't get this, you should try Bannerlord, when it comes out.

I have to say, this game was my first love of the elder scrolls universe, and to this day playing it brings me feelings of Nostalgia. Though the graphics haven't aged well, I remember how complex it was for the time that it came out. It was the first game I recall playing that wasn't linear, and had an entire map to explore at my leisure. I also feel that out of the most recent Elder Scrolls games, this one ties in the RPG mechanics the best and gives you the most options. The Speech skill is utilized the best in this game, The list of spells is the best, the Variety of weapons and armor. It is so easy to love this game. While the combat hasn't aged well, the story is fantastic and you can mod to fix the combat if nessicary.

I definitely think you should get this game. By far my favourite Elder Scrolls game,  although you may not think it from the hours I've played this compared to Skyrim. That's because I used the OpenMW mod, and I'd advise you to do the same, as it fixes most of the game's bugs and updates it to run better and look nicer.
But this game is so deep and packed with lore I don't even know where to start. I heavily recommend this game to any fans of Elder Scrolls, or just fantasy/RPGs in general. It's a bit annoying at first, but once you get the hang of it, it is so very satisfying.

PROS:
+Good Graphics
+Gunplay feels amazing
+Every character (except Kult, atm) can be bought through ingame currency that you get by playing
+When you have an xbox360 controller plugged in the UI changes to the xbox360 buttons
+Horizontal FOV slide from 60 to 120
+AntiAliasing x2, x4 and x8
+ScreenScale slide, which i'm assuming is ResolutionScale
+Leagues, i think it's important in a PVP fps game
+Leaderboard
+Dedicated clan chat
+Achievements that give the player normal currency and premium currency
+Events, like login 3 days in a row to unlock a character for free
CONS:
-EXTREMELY PAY TO WIN, you get xp for the characters through LOOTBOXES, and guess what, by leveling the characters you get MORE HEALTH and DAMAGE
-LOOTBOXES TAKE TIME TO OPEN, i have a lootbox that takes EIGHT HOURS to open, and YOU CAN PAY TO OPEN INSTANTLY, and i can bet there's lootboxes that take way more than that to open, also, you can only open one at a time
- Frames Per Second are REALLY inconsistent, at first i thought the game was stuck at 30fps, but then it jumped to 60 fps mid-game, changing resolution to the lowest and then to my native resolution again got me back to 60fps for a few minutes, but soon it dropped to 30fps again, the devs MUST look into performance
-AD POP-UPS during menus, like in-game advertisements for you to buy other characters when you go from one menu to another, really annoying
-Inconsistent UI navigation, sometimes you have to scroll by holding the menus with the left mouse button and moving the mouse up and down, like a mobile game, sometimes you can use the scroll wheel, when the game window loses focus the buttons (like back, shop or agents) stop working and i have to press them 5 or 6 times for themt o work, sometimes i have to go back one menu and go forward again to click on a button that wasn't working
-When you have an xbox360 controller plugged in the UI changes to xbox360 buttons, YOU CAN'T TURN THIS OFF and these won't go away even if you're using a mouse and keyboard to play
-Poor PC settings, Graphics: Low, High, Ultra
-AntiAliasing x2, x4 and x8, great, what kind? MSAA? FXAA? SMAA? TXAA? it goes up to x8 so guess not.
COMMENT
The devs must realize they can't milk the PC market like they do with the mobile market, lootboxes can't contain xp for characters, we should win xp through playing the character not paying money, we could spend our money on skins if we chose to, not on speeding up the process of opening a lootbox.
Would i recommend this game to everyone? NO!
I would only recommend it to people who don't mind playing against Pay to Win players, and people who like to spend 100€ at a time on premium currency for the BEST VALUE(tm) OR people who just don't mind losing a lot and waiting hours for their lootboxes to open.
4/10 could be a 8/10 if the devs stripped the pay to win mechanics, made the lootboxes more cosmetic, fixed the performance issues and added more graphical settings.

I remember when Machinarium first came out. What an exciting introduction to the genre for those who had never experienced older point and clicks! This robot-filled adventure game has charming art and animations, stellar music and sound effects and an endearing story that put a smile on my face. It’s an earlier offering from Amanita Design (2009) and now the studio has a number of other games available to continue your adventuring, games that also rely on visuals rather than writing things out in language. Those other games can wait though, as you should not expect to finish Machinarium in a single sitting. It offers a fair number of challenges to work through. The puzzles are varied from environmental to mini games, each one well-designed, enjoyable and engaging, and reward correct inputs such that you are satisfied when you figure them out.
As the game begins, the player is introduced to the controls (primarily clicking 'within reach of the robot') and user interface, including the inventory/hints bar at the top and settings bar at the bottom of your playable area. These are minimized or hidden unless you move your cursive all the way to the edge of the playable area, such that they do not interfere in immersion or enjoyment of the game environment. The hint feature shows a single graphical representation of an aspect that needs to be solved about the current room your character is in (or as the game calls it, the current level). If there is nothing to solve in that room, the hint's lightbulb will appear grayed out and not be clickable. Even if the lightbulb is grayed out, you can still access the walkthrough pages through a book next to the hints button, which opens a mini game best described as a key flying through a cave shooting pellets at spiders. Once you have evaded all stalagmites, stalactites and shot through the arachnids, your key will fly into the keyhole and a page of the prophecy will be revealed! Each page offers graphical cues as to what you might be missing. For some puzzles, the walkthrough page just shows you exactly what moves are necessary to solve it. These walkthrough pages are fairly comprehensive, although, as noted, you have to be in the correct room/level in order to get the prompts for what to you need do next.
Minor Complaints on Controls and Bugs
-------------------
The game is primarily operated with the mouse, although you can use the keyboard for some of the mini games, like in the arcade. Machinarium runs in Adobe Flash, so right click functionality is limited to opening the typical flash settings menu. This created a mild frustration for me, as I am used to right clicking to release/disengage a held inventory item or to discontinue an action I had started. It was a very mild inconvenience. In terms of game settings, you are given only a generalized control over the whole game's volume (no one-click mute, nor can you change the music volume independently of the sound effects). In addition to the full screen toggle, there's an option in settings to switch to 80% zoom from 100%. However, I encountered a few bugs with this setting:
Recommendations
-------------------
To reflect on some of the artistic work put in by the developers, I recommend re-playing or revisiting levels after you’ve solved them and looking at the walkthrough pages. In addition to the clues being nicely sketched and showing a synopsis of the actions you take, there is some concept art on the left leaf of each page.
For a similarly language-devoid point-and-click adventure, but with more horror/adult themes (i.e., clowns, dogs urinating, firey scenes), check out Dropsy.

This is a game that, when it's good, it's really good. It's just that those moments are too few and too brief. Beating a level can be exhilirating, and the outrageous speed at which everything happens makes Clustertruck feel like a roller coaster that's falling apart (and I mean that in a good way). But ultimately, for every one of those fantastic, high-adrenaline moments, there's a dozen other moments where things get infuriating. You don't have enough control of your movements in mid-air, and the first-person perspective, along with a fairly narrow FOV, makes it all but impossible sometimes to avoid crashing into an obstacle or falling to your death. Honestly, I could look past the sometimes unreliable controls and the limited perspective if the game was just more forgiving - make it so that instead of killing you instantly if you touch a tree or a wall, you can use those environmental objects to your advantage, jumping off of them or running along them. Never has wall-running seemed more appropriate for a game that doesn't have it. This game could be incredibly fun if the devs focused less on punishing difficulty and more on the feeling of freedom and power you have when jumping from truck to truck at high speeds. But no, every time I get a glimpse of joy and fun out of this game, the game makes me start the level over when I brush against a tree branch.

So, I forget where I first read about this game. Probably somewhere in the vijagame jouranlisms.  I really liked the visual aesthetic and the idea of a puzzle platformer built not just with co-op in mind, but built entirely around co-op as a necessary central mechanic.  I ended up playing the first level and a half solo just to get a feel for the game, and came away with the impression that it was going to be a cute, clever, but ultimately soft experience.
That was quite some time ago.  Recently got into it seriously with a friend, and damn, my initial impression was proven wrong.  This game is certainly cute but it is anything but soft.  ibb & obb will challenge your brain meat.  The semi-hidden bonus stages especially; they gave us several excellent opporutnities to flex our brain muscle and were always very satisfying to solve.  Considering all your character can do is move and jump, it's amazing the depth of puzzles they're able to create with concepts like maintaining or building momentum or manipulating which direction gravity pulls your character.
The only basic mechanic you have other than moving and jumping is a little colorful bubble trail thing you can create with either the mouse or the right stick, if you're using a controller.  It's the only communication tool you have in-game, and I was impressed with how much information we were able to convey to each other using this simple, visual medium.  Of course sometimes we had to open a chat window to talk deeper strategy, but still it's an elegant solution for the issue of communication between players that fits in with the game's minimalist approach to it's mechanics and aesthetic.
I only have a couple negative points to share. The game starts out slow as you learn the mechanics and builds up the complexity on a pretty satisfying curve, but there are a couple challenges that boil down to basically challenges to your manual dexterity rather than your abilty to problem solve, and those are never as satsifying.  Secondly, we played online and towards the end experienced some pretty bad lag, which the game was not always good at mitigating.  We ended up with some weird lag artifacts like random enemies spawning in locations they shouldn't that only damaged one of the two players, or multiple copies of either ibb or obb respawning at once, or just really long wait times to respawn after death. Generally play was smooth and honestly you have to expect some problems when you play online over a crappy connection, but when the lag got particularly bad, the game had more trouble with it than I was expecting.
It's a relatively short game but there's so few games out there that are anything like it, and those few hours are densely packed.  ibb & obb is pure gameplay; there's no text or any exposition of any kind anywhere in the game.  If you dig platformers and puzzlers and various combinations thereof, and you've got a friend with similar interests, there are certainly less engaging ways you could split $14.  love that the "Best Friends Forevr" double-pack only costs two dollars more than one copy on its own.  If you buy the two-pack and split the cost with a friend, you're both basically getting the game 40% off.  That's how strongly the developer believes in their vision of a 2-player co-op puzzle platformer.

I picked up this game recently hopeful that it would be a fun little bomber strategy/sim but I _completely_ underestimated this title.
Its core gameplay is effectively a crew management simulation, a casual flight sim, a bombing-run simulator and  a situational awareness test all in one... And at the same time!
The crew management aspect of Bomber Crew very much reminded me of FTL; you have to move your crew around to respond to challenges mid-flight in order to keep things on track. Move to another station, repair things, reload guns, assist wounded crew etc.
The other major place you'll be focusing on is whats going on around you... I have to say the developers have struck the perfect balance here because the situational awareness required to play this game is ALMOST overwhelming... Almost. Its like, Riiiight on that line, which is what makes it challenging, but not too frustrating... It just takes focus. You'll be lining up a bomb run, reloading a gun, looking around for and tagging incoming hostiles... all at the same time and just get it all done before you fly over the target! This might not be the best time to bring this to your attention, but your engine is on fire... Did you forget to close the bomb bay doors? that'll cost ya!
As this is also a casual flight sim, you are also in control of your plane, albeit to a limited capacity. Through utilizing each of your crew's abilities, individual aspects of your plane (including flight behaviour) can be influenced. Additional skills and abilities are unlocked which give you more control and effectiveness (if those members of your crew earning them survive to do so.)
The strategy aspect of Bomber Crew is primarily in choosing how to spend your rewards on the most prudent upgrades after each mission so as to keep your crew out of harms way (or at least as best as possible anyhow). Keep that roll going and you just might win the war!
I'm very confident this game will become a classic. It really is exceptionally fun to play, at least it is for me!

Let me first state that not all games are created easy, not all games that look cute are designed to be casual, and if you want a simple, stress-free game about a bomber crew, navigate away from this page immediately. It may show only 14 hours as my time played, but i have played all the critical missions, bombed Hitler, have all the bomber upgrades, and a fully skilled and equipped crew. This game is deceptively simple in it's design, bomb targets, shoot attacking planes, repair damage, land. Your skills WILL be tested when you find your outer right engine on fire, your fuel tank leaking, the ventral turret is out of ammo, you're approaching the bombing target, and your radar operator just announced that a new wave of fighters is coming, while your filght engineer is ressurecting your tail gunner (yes, this is entirely possible).I have never been on he edge of my seat as compared to this game, I have never felt so stressed playing a game (minus that stupid civ 5 game with ghandi) than playing bomber crew. and I loved it. I loved the challenge of playing without slow mode and figuring out how I was going to survive an onslaught of bf-109's and fw-190's. I loved having to activate focus on my tail gunner before the me-262 launched his rocket attack. I loved pretending i was a dam buster flooding the ruhr valley. I loved avoiding radar to bomb a high value target. And I loved having to watch my crew helplessly plummet out of the sky after bombing Hitler and realizing their sacrifice meant the war was won. I loved this game, it was what I was hoping for in a bomber game, a game that truly characterized the 71% death rate of bomber crews in WW2, thats what I found in this game.

There is, undeniably, a large element of this game which encourages the user to try and have sex with as many different women as possible, getting sent images of them in various states of undress along the way - all by showing your prowess at match-3.
The match-3 on its own, though, is one of the most competent, well-balanced match-3 games you will play: instead of swapping adjacent gems a la Zookeeper/Bejewelled, you can move a gem anywhere along either its horizontal or vertical axis. You can take bonus items with you into each level, and you have limited moves in which to reach a score total. Different girls have different preferences for colours; and you can upgrade different colours before each match-3 session based on how well conversations with the girls have gone, and which gifts you have spent the money on and given the girls. In isolation, the game itself is a very, very solid puzzler requiring tactics and load-out management.
There are some pretty easy clichés within the girls themselves - and even the game calls itself out for casual racism at several points. The game's scripts is far from charming or nuanced, and once you have taken a woman to bed, the way the game is set up means that talking to that woman again gets you no further reward: but I feel that I am offering up more sophisticated criticism of the wrapping of the game itself than it warrants - this is Strip Poker for the 64-pit generation, nothing more, nothing less: except it is a very, very good puzzler.

I picked up Card City Nights when it was on sale for $2.00, and after having played it I am happy to say that it is easily worth its full price of $4.00 if not more. Card City Nights is a lot of fun and combines the elements of card collecting and battling.
Pros:
The three things that I would say set this game apart from other card games would be the card battle system, the graphics and the fact that earning a new booster pack is as simple as defeating an opponent (no cash shop). The battle system is similar to card battling in Final Fantasy VIII but with various factors that allow you to create decks with different win conditions (Attack, Defense, Board Control. The graphics are skillfully done and keep the game feeling fun.
Cons:
The main con for me was that the game is somewhat short. At casual playspeed it took me 8 hours to beat the game. I had so much fun that I was sad to beat it. If there was more content to this game I could see people easily spending $20+ for it. As far as other cons, the only thing that comes to are some minor UI problems that the developers have been quickly fixing.
Overall this game is a hidden treasure and I highly recommend it to any strategy/card game lovers.

Charming, short, and sweet game with hints of atmospheric horror that asks you to think about the origins of evil in an interesting way: Is it what is born out of an absesnse of love, or just something that's innate inside people who snap and do terrible things?
The story is about creepy children being just that, and revolves around some exagerrated tales of losses and what they force people to rationalize while in mourning, using the story of Alice in Wonderland as a jumping off point. There's some decent replayability since after you finish one ending of the game, the point at which the endings diverge is easy to find your way back to (easier still with a handy save), and curiousity will get the best of you trying to get each ending's Achievement.
Alicemare's main mechanic is a few simple puzzles and riddles that advance your character through each of his companion's questlines, called Worlds, that are supposed to be journeys through their hearts that reveal their dark secrets and what motivates their quirky behavior at face. The puzzles aren't punishingly difficult, and all you'll need to feel a sense of satisfaction in this game is to pay a bit of attention to the character speech screens and cutscenes. The little bit of frustration that you will feel comes from needing to check [spam the Z key to see if there are any relevant items around you] absolutely everything, or make multiple trips through hallways and several rooms in order to speak to different NPC's to obtain items or complete mini-quests. It is still a game at the end of the day, so there's some annoying grind to get to the meat of it.
Value for the price is fantastic, particularly because Alicemare and LiEat, the other game from this developer, are always on some kind of sale.
It's cheap, (fairly) easy, and plays fast- why wouldn't you get it?
