Alright, time to share my early thoughts on DC Universe Online...
At the time of posting this review, I have about 9 hours played time.
I'll just get straight to the point:
Pros:
+Good introduction!
+Amazing character customization.
+Splendid combat, it's interesting and there are many many possibilities and combo's.
+Very interesting and cool class system. As I said, character customization is top-notch and the "classes" you can pick from have great variation and combined with movement types (flight, super speed, acrobatic, skimming) and weapon types it's a lot of fun with many possibilities.
+Good feel to the overall game, nice world (though it seems quite small so far, but I've only just started)
+Fun, at least so far. Questing isn't too grindy, though, being an MMO, it kind of is.
+Hideouts and League Halls! Seriously, so badass! Dream come true! Honestly, this is what most MMO's need. The guild system in this game (called Leagues) is pretty good so far, and the league gets a big♥♥♥♥♥♥hideout called a League Hall wherein there are statues of players with the highest rankings at one thing or the other. Big♥♥♥♥♥Golden statues. The hideout thing is like a personal base, and it's pretty interesting so far.
+Flying. (movement types in general, damn, awesome!) (Also wings!)
+Good controller support. I only play this game with controller, it works great.
That's a lot of pro's, and I'm sure I could think of more if I tried... but here come the cons:
-It's incredibly obviously commercial. Of course, it's a game, and an MMO at that, but dAmN! I've played Neverwinter but this... Alright so basically there's a huge amount of
-Microtransactions and
-DLC's. Also you often find out you can't do stuf because
-You often get asked to pay for stuff to get that stuff, such as acces to the "Lair", an upgraded better version of the hideout.
-The community.. Honestly, I haven't had much contact with the community yet, and that generally means that they're either passive or just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. I haven't really met a lot of people - as in, talked to them - they generally seem rather passive, chatting in an instance seems pretty much out of the question too.
-Instances? Well, this is basically because the first time I did a multiplayer scenario (4 players) I got in a group with a level 100 character, and they were all DPS specced. I don't know about the other types of scenarios but this was just not fun, for obvious reasons.
-Still an MMO, so yes, some grinding. But it isn't as annoying.
-Disconnections. For some reason, I get these rather frequently and I hear other people do as well.
-Kinda pay to win, not too sure. But the limit to character slots (without buying more or subscribing) does annoy me
So basically, it's a pretty damn good game. I give the developers a lot of credit. If you would think away all the microtransactions and money business, it's a true feat. As it is an MMO, it requires a lot of money to keep up - so I don't blame them. It's just too bad that monthly fees have made way for such extensive commercialism. If you want to enjoy this game to the fullest, I suppose you'll have to get some membership. I don't know, I am not really planning on getting one yet, at least not untill I reach the end game.
That was my impression so far, give it a try. It's fun, but, it's a F2P MMO. Don't forget that.

MCV is alright, but it doesn't do anything new or interesting. It is a mobile port, and unlike some ports that turned out well this one still feels like it. I don't find the gameplay horrible, but it is very basic and uninspired. The only options you have are movement with sprint (jump and wallrun use the same key as sprint), aim, shoot, reload, and an ability dependent on your character. There's neither voice nor basic text chat so you have no way of communicating with your team (or telling the person who killed you about your relations with their mother).
Aside from the gameplay, the game uses the lootbox mechanic to award currency (used to buy characters) and experience (used to upgrade). Each lootbox may take several hours to open unless you spend premium currency to speed it up. Upgrades to characters offer straight stat bonuses, increasing damage, health, etc. leading to gameplay that is potentially very unbalanced, rewarding purchases and time played more than skill.
TL;DR - probably should have stayed a mobile game.

This game has been elevated to one of my all time favorite games.
The super tense and stressful moments are often followed by hilarity. That combination brings about such relief and feelings of joy and acomplishment that you barely notice how fast your heart is still beating.
The game has some great mechanics where you get to select your crew, choose upgrades on your plane and outfit your crew.  There is never enough money to spend to get everything you want, and what you choose can affect your in-flight strategy.
The main game is taking your bomber on various missions during WW2, but don't think of this game as a true simulation.  Rather, the developers mix in several mechanics that keep you busy and stressed out during a mission.  There are always too many things that you need your attention, and that is what causes the stress.  But don't worry, it is a very good, fun stress, and like I said above, laughter often follows as you try to direct your poor crew around the plane and navigate the plane and make bombing runs.
It sounds like such a simple thing, and perhaps it is, but the combination together, all randomly timed while getting shot at creates such a beautiful game that I think any fan of any genre could enjoy this game.
The only negative I found was that you cannot remap controls in-game, but it does have a launcher where you can custimize the controls outside of the game, so it isn't a huge deal.  The controls are rather simple as it is and I don't feel the need to want to remap any of them.

Alicemare:
~~~~~~~~~

Sadness will probably be at its deepest when you lose a parent or other family member who means so much to you, especially at a young age.  It can be so devastating as to trigger a loss of memory as a side effect. This is exactly what happened to the young Allen, and now he finds himself in a facility with four other children, all of whom have their own story to tell!
Alicemare is a pixel art / adventure/ exploration game where you play Allen, who ends up in an establishment with four other children who have had their own specific experiences.
In Alicemare, Allen has to recover five keys from five worlds for a character named the White Rabbit.  Each of these worlds is related to the children who are living in the facility, including yourself. You will meet another couple of characters; one will be the teacher and the other will be the Cheshire cat, who pop up here and there for guidance.
As you play the game, you will have to resolve puzzles and riddles. The puzzles are fairly straight forward but some of the riddles are quite challenging, and you will need to reflect for a while to successfully decrypt them.
It’s a fairly short game; you’ll probably finish it within four hours. I really like the pixel artwork, the story, and also the soundtrack, which is superb. In terms of the controls, you have to play with the keyboard. In my opinion, the level designs could have been better and I would like to see more puzzles and riddles.
Positive:
~~~~~~
-	Great pixel artwork and soundtrack
-	Good Story
-	Good price point
-	Several endings
-	Achievements and trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Levels designs could have been better
-	Fairly short game
Alicemare has an interesting story to tell. Give it a try!

Lovely card game with simple rules. Nice graphics, very good music and oddball humor.
It took me about 8 hours to complete so you'll definitely get bang for your buck.
As a possible negative point, I made it through the game with a modified starter deck where I kept swapping in the better cards. I don't think there was really an option at any point to completely throw out my deck and start a completely different one. It is possible but I would need to grind quite a bit for booster packs.

I bought this game expecting a basic card game with a small story to keep people playing. It turns out there's more to the card game mechanics than it would seem at first glance. Card City Nights gives you a 3x3 grid to play cards on, and asks you to make combos by joining groups of two or three cards together to perform certain actions. Cards connect to each other only in certain ways, so making sure you've got the right cards in your deck and knowing when to deploy them is crucial. Later you'll discover different ways to interact with cards, including rotating, moving and disabling cards, lending additional depth to the game.
Beating the game itself is relatively straightforward, though certain opponents will exploit weaknesses in your strategy, forcing you to take a second look at your deck. The real fun parts lie in trying to get the achievements, which really get you to closely examine the cards available to you and think about how you can combine them to achieve goals that seemed impossible at the start of the game.
Outside the basic gameplay, the art style's pretty neat (though it's an acquired taste) and the music is pretty addictive. The story is really just there to lend some structure to the card battles, but the recurring cast of characters are at least endearing and goofy. Overall, I was surprised by how much I liked this game. Definitely worth the four bucks.

Quite a lot of fun for its price. I got it in the initial sale, and it's one of the more satisfying $3 I've ever spent on a game.
The card game itself could probably use some more balancing, but since you only play against AIs which are not always the smartest about how they play (and seem to all cheat a bit about what is in their hands), it's hard to say how things would work out between humans. As it stands, it seems like pure attack decks (with only a small amount of defence/revival in the form of cards with special properties) are unreasonably good compared to practically anything else. Part of that is that players only have 7 life and that maxes out at 10, beyond which more defence won't help, and the attacking player will also have the option to disable the defensive player's cards about as quickly as they can attempt to form combos. With a decent attack deck, you can easily deal a consistent 4-6 damage every 3 turns, with an occasional burst that's even higher if you get a nice hand. (It's possible to win on turn 3 before your opponent has a chance to even do anything.)
I think it would be reasonable to increase the starting defence and to increase or remove the cap.
I beat the game the first time through with an infinite win/loss ratio using essentially the same strategy the whole way, augmenting my deck with cards as I obtained them. But despite the fact that it's on the easy side in absolute terms it's still a lot of fun to play. It could use a New Game Plus sort of option, and it would also be nice if after you won the game, the bosses and other characters would all play cards, rather than just the few characters which offer booster packs.

As typical, I wrote out a long review for this game, tried multiple times to post it without success, threw away the review only for Steam to start working again.
I don't feel like typing out my review again, but I'll summarize it.
This game is still as enjoyable as it was on GameCube, but with better graphics and cutscene quality. If you've never played Resident Evil, going back to the first one is probably a daunting task - the tank controls combined with the ugly outdated look of PSX polygons do not age well - so this is a great alternative. You can even download a mod that inputs the cheesy voices from the original, if you're interested in hearing this infamous voice acting.
I don't remember this being in the GameCube version, though I haven't played that since I was in high school circa 2003, but the PC version offers gamers a more "modern" movement style, with the character moving in the direction you press, as opposed to the tank controls that are an entirely different monster.
There are a few detractors to this game. Firstly, because the game still uses the dynamic, cinematic angles for every room and environment, the modern movement style can clash with this, particularly in dynamic angles that are polar opposites of each other. The result is the player running back and forth between angles, with their delayed reaction creating this seemingly infinite loop. It doesn't happen as much with the tank controls, and I can't describe it in any better detail that also doesn't get more confusing, so I'll simply say that it can result in unnecessary damage if an enemy happens to be there, but overall isn't worth forgoing the game. The second detraction to this game is some of the older style concepts they kept, by this I mean primarily the inventory system and the save system. Since I started playing these games with Resident Evil 2, the limited inventory space doesn't bother me, but it can result in a ton of backtracking if you are missing an item you need to progress forward, and have to return to the item box to grab it. The save system requires ink ribbons to save at typewriters. Sometimes, you'll advance in the mansion far, and think "I should save," but there were times where I just didn't have the patience to backtrack or deviate from the course, go through 3 or 4 door loading animations, switch out items in the item box, save at the typewriter, switch back items into inventory, go through 3 or 4 door loading animations and finally arrive back to where I was to continue advancing. I get it, it's the old school Resident Evil experience, but it is tedious to do this, and the consequences of dying without saving means doing a lot of stuff over again, including watching doors opening.
Still, despite these things, the game has been touched up and polished enough to keep it as fresh as it was when it was launched for GameCube back in 2002. It's recommended for RE fans and newbies to the series alike. Though, a word of caution: if you took an interest in Resident Evil due to watching gameplay or trailers of Resident Evil 4, 5 or 6, this is a VERY different game.

This is the Elder Scrolls game that started the road to Skyrim. This isn't a bad game, I'm just going to get through that first. I wouldn't necessarily call it good, but looking at it as if it were 2002, I think it is okay. Of course it isn't going to be as good as Oblivion or Skyrim (because of hardware limitations), but if you want a nice, old RPG game then you are set.
The graphics are pretty good for 2002, and the world design is pretty interesting. There are some cool areas and towns.
The controls are pretty good, WASD to move, click to attack, your normal stuff. You control pretty well, compared to some games I have played where it feels like you're running on ice all the time.
I'm not a huge fan of the combat. From what I can tell, you swing at your enemy and hope that your accuracy is good enough to hit it. But sometimes you'll end up swinging many times, but no damage is done. This ruins the stealth combat a lot, if you want to be able to fight, you pretty much have to go for combat skills when creating your character.
That is another feature, character creation. You can choose a species, gender, look, name, etc. You can choose a class, or make your own class. It isn't as diverse as it is in the later games, but it is acceptable for 2002.
The animation is pretty goofy, I like watching the walking animation for Khajjits. Not a bad thing, I just think it is kinda funny. Same goes for the voice acting. It has that quirky, old PC game voice acting. Cheesy, but acceptable.
There are some cool quests, but I think the ones in Oblivion and Skyrim were more creative.
If you are looking specifically for an old RPG, then this will definitely work for you. However, if you are looking for a better experience when it comes to an RPG or an Elder Scrolls game, I would recommend Oblivion, preferably Skyrim.

TL;DR:
A genre-defining PCA (Point and Click Adventure) with a lot of innovative features (like the in-game hint system), gorgeous hand-drawn scenery, some of the best music in the genre, and lots of tricky but very fun puzzles beyond finding what to click on.  It has a solid story, likeable  characters and is sure to become a favorite if you like the PCA genre.
Graphics:          8/10 (Sub-hd resolution, but everything is gorgeously drawn/animated. VERY talented artist(s)!)
Sound:            10/10 (The music is phenomenal, accenting the mood and "feel" of the scenarios. Voicing is not required, as there is nothing to voice!)
Interface:         9/10 (Fully art'ed menus, an innovative hint system that is completely artistic, and the puzzles are easy to use.)
Story:               8/10 (All the characters have a development arc of sorts, even the "C" listers! Touching, memorable and really sets the mood, combined with the artwork and music.)
Length:            8/10 (Took me about 12 hours to get through the game my first time. Not an endurance marathon, but long enough to do what it needed and short enough to remember everything.)
Difficulty:         7/10 (Scored without using the hint system. There are a few moments where you wonder where to go next, a hallmark of PCAs, and some of the non-PCA puzzles can be quite challenging! Very few puzzles can't be solved using brute-force methods.)
Overall:            9/10 (This is one of the finest examples of an innovative, modern PCA. It's long enough for ye old-skoolers, short enough for the newbies, tough enough for veterans yet the inbuilt hint system will greatly help newcomers to the genre. BUY THIS, YOU WILL LOVE IT!)

Micro. Manage. Don't let the cartoonish style of this game fool you into thinking it will be easy in any way shape or form. You will lose your crew. You will lose your plane. It happens, and in my opinion it's what makes this game such a gem. I feel like this game is as difficult as you make it.
If you've ever played games like X-Com or FTL you'll know not to get too attached to members of your crew or your squad, and this game is no different. After doing countless missions with your trusty, high level crew member, you'll look into your bomber to see them burning alive while nobody else is helping them because you've been too busy worrying about the countless jets on your tail. It happens, and it sucks. You level them up, give them good gear, and they die. It's frustrating. But, to be honest, it's what keeps me coming back to this game. My memorial wall has about 60 names on it now at time of writing after about 60 missions played. You just have to get used to it, and as morbid as it sounds, learn to love it. The game provides you with a lot of options that affect your survival rates and it's fun to experiment and use them to save vital members of your crew or attempt to save your aircraft as a whole, like the pilot instructing everyone to grab a parachute and jump out to fend for themselves in enemy territory, or trying to emergency land in the sea on the way back home (Pack some survival equipment!). The game doesn't completely punish you for losing your plane or your crew either, as the crew and plane you recieve as a replacment will be only slightly worse than the one you lost, meaning that while there is an incentive to preserve your bomber and her crew, the game is not over if they do die. And you will continue to progress despite losing everything.
Bomber Crew manages to stay interesting despite having a very similar pattern to each mission through the upgrade system and the crew levelling system. At the start of the game your aircraft is very barebones. Your crew don't have any particularly interesting skills. After a few missions,however, you'll start to have enough money and exp to get those sweet sweet upgrades. Survival equipment, new gun turrets, better systems, new engines, more first aid kits, parachute racks, bigger fuel tanks, armoured hull upgrades, etc. All the while your crew are levelling up and unlocking new abilities, like new maneuvres for your pilot, your radioman being able to tag targets or call in spitfire support, new ammunition types or accuracy boosts for your gunners, first aid abilities, navigating by the stars, the list goes on. Experimenting with different combinations of crew abilities, flight paths and equipment loadouts help keep the game fresh on every mission and give you a target to work towards. If you see you need more money for a new turret with 4 guns instead of 2, it makes you want to go play another mission and go get that upgrade, or that new skill, or that new cap for your pilot, etc.
The missions themselves are dynamic and keep you on your toes. It is not always as simple as flying to the target, dropping your bombs, and flying back again. The developers have crafted an engaging series of missions and targets to add a unique replayability to this game, from using bouncing bombs to destroy dams, to supporting the D-Day landings or helping bring supplies into the french resistance, while doing some optional photo recon detours, or perhaps rescuing a downed pilot from the sea, the game keeps delivering and keeps the player interested in what is happening in the air and on the ground. It's satisfying to see the war progress as you fly deeper and deeper into occupied Europe with each mission, and more pleasing still when you finally shoot down that German Ace pilot that has been bothering you for the last few missions and return to Britain with more money to upgrade your trusty bomber and get back in the air again to do it some more.
If you hate losing characters in a game don't bother playing this one. For everyone else, I cannot recommend this game enough. The controls are easy to learn, the gameplay is frantic and a lot of fun, the historical aspect is spot on, the graphics are brilliant and somehow this game manages to make it fun to watch your whole crew crash into the ground in a ball of flame, to the extent that you'd do it all again in a heartbeat. For £15 it is criminal to not give this gem a try, and the developers seem very invested in improving this game as much as they can, unlike some.

I wish everyone a merry Christmas, but that´s not the full purpose of this review.
I discovered SPORE in 2012, more than 4 years ago and I can still enjoy it like I did then. This game isn´t only one of my all-time favourites, but my secondly most played game of all time as well. As you can see on my playtime, SPORE is absolutely massive and I don´t regret any minute I spent on it, not even those 2,880+ I had already collected on Origin. I am thankful this is now also available on Steam, but unfortunately EA games are simply not made to be here, EA doesn´t give a **** to their Steam-community.
Whom do I recommend SPORE to?
(All following aspects are listed in order of importance)
Explorers: First spot, definately. If you love to spend your time on uncovering secrets, this game is perfect. Especially the last stage has tons of things waiting to be discovered by YOU. If you aren´t an explorer, don´t be afraid, this one is OPTIONAL, you can "complete" SPORE without finding all secrets as well.
Creative: Very close to the previous type. The designers feature nearly INFINITE possibilities. There´s almost nothing you can´t create, your imagination is the only limit. More than 400 Creature-, 500 Vehicle- and 600 Building-parts to use, modifacation of those and no set placements allow an unbelievable ammount of possible combinations. In fact there is no object looking like another one.
"God-wannabes": Write your own story from the very beginning. Start as nothing but a little cell, the most simple lifeform, evolve to an intelligent group leader and rise to the lord af the largest empire in the entire universe.
Mess-Around: Everything said. Build ugly monsters and use them to kill everybody, edit the surface of planets, transform water into lava, highjack your friends, wipe out innocent creatures... The only limit is your free time :D
Challengers: Who said this game was going to be easy to finish? In fact it´s impossible, the last stage is endless... And trust me, if there´s one thing you have to try to understand, it´s (Spoilers Ahead) reaching the galactic core and wiping out the Grox... I wish you fun at exterminating around 2000 star systems...
Children: I know this has a teen-rating, but seriously, nobody would be mad about a six-year old playing this. Of course you can literally take out the entire universe without showing mercy, but the brutality is way to low to be frightening to anyone... Come on, the animation isn´t even realistic...
Non-EA-haters: I am afraid, but that´s the point I have to admit. The only thing I dislike this game for, but only the Steam version. EA doesn´t let Steam-users connect to their servers, so all online-features are disables for us. Bad thing that you can´t share your creatures or download other´s epic content, but this review won´t change either. EA isn´t ready for Steam yet and won´t ever be. I think singleplayer fun can annihulate this point, but the condition is bad, that´s sure.
Do I recommend Spore to anyone else?
I am not sure about this one, to be honest. This might be considered too kid-friendly for some adults and too boring for action-gamers.
This review is intended to be funny, just as SPORE is. In fact I want to say that you shouldn´t miss this, SPORE is just a game everyone should at least know. Please, get it in a sale. I do not force you to play this for as long as I did. Since there are no achievements you can also get rid of this within a daytime. I am still really surprised by this, SPORE just marked the simulator-genre, it´s still the one and only god simulator. I know there aren´t even many, but those few won´t ever reach this.
Why do I say "get it in a sale" when it seems like I am amazed enough to pay it fully?
Because I didn´t either. Spore without online support isn´t just worth it. Get the Origin version if you don´t mind. saving your progress for this is important and sharing creations keeps the community alive. SPORE is an amazing game, but the publisher isn´t a great one.

This game feels like an amazingly original horror ride. The grotesque atmosphere of the mansion, enemies, and puzzles really jump out at you. I found myself creeping around corners and camera angles to eventually peel sight of the shadow creeping down the hallway. If you want a great horror game to start out with, this is the one. It takes a lot of time to go around finding clues and matching them to certain areas, and while this did occur, I found myself looking up a few hints. Just for time sake. But it all falls together once you are able to find key locations and items, leaving you with a feel of accomplishment and wonder about what comes next. If you've seen later Resident Evil games where they seem like a bunch of crappy 3rd person zombie shoot-em' ups, this completely isn't that. It does have 3rd person shooting but the game doesn't rely on that to carry through. More so clue solving. The combat is kinda clunky since it's an old game but I got used to it after a little bit. If Horror is one you favorite genres of games, I highly suggest this product, bringing mystery, suspense, and gore. Unfortunately, the 2nd game isn't up on Steam, but if and when it does, you'll find me at the front of the line.

Resident Evil's return to form before the 2017's RE7 came in the guise of the GameCube remake with a fresh coat of paint.
A lot could be said about Resident Evil, one of the most iconic horror video game series of all time. This remake of a remake (or remaster, rather) is the de facto best version of the original game. The game includes high resolution textures and supports modern controls, so there is no need to play with the old school tank controls.
The game features couple of difficulty settings and gives you the ability to play either as Chris or Jill. This changes the story and cutscenes, but only slightly. Each charachter has their own starting gear (for example, Chris has a lighter, but Jill has a pistol), and there is even something rather new for this HD remaster. A feature which was previously only present in the GameCube remake is present here as well, namely Crimsonheads. Killed zombies have the potential to resurrect themselves later on as deadly and fast crimsonheads which are really tough to kill. This feature is a great add on the already great game. The courtyard sections with Lisa Trevor are here, too. The HD remaster manages to retain its atmosphere right till the end, proving that the first game in the series is also one the best to date.
Veterans of the original game are able to run through the game with ease in a couple of hours, but for newcomers the game may take anywhere between 8-15 hours.
Pros:
+ A fresh, new look for the best version of the iconic horror series' first offering
+ An incentive to play the game twice: Jill and Chris
+ Added features from the GameCube remake
+ Modernized control-scheme for those who want it
Cons:
- None
Resident Evil HD Remaster is a must-buy for the horror aficionados and Re fans.

Having grown up with such single player card games as the Pokemon TCG and Yu-Gi-Oh: The Sacred Cards, I was instantly drawn to this game. And I enjoyed it. That isn't to say the game is perfect. It has a number of flaws, some inherent to being a single player card game, and others that are the problem with the game itself. I'll list the pros, cons, and things that are more up to a person's taste.
Pros:
-Unique gameplay. Unlike a regular card game like MTG, this game is played on a 3x3 board and the cards have arrows on them. You must connect cards using the arrows and then use them for attack or defense (depending on the card symbols). I can't really think of a game that has utilized this style of gameplay, and the fresh take on the rather traditional style of card games is a nice break from the games that are more in the style of MTG.
-References galore. If you played any of this dev's previous games, you'll probably get a heap of enjoyment out of all the references made.
-Deck progression. I guess that's a good term for this. Traditional card games you usually end up just buying a number of cards, and you have a solid deck right off the bat. I enjoy the progression of a single player card game, replacing worse cards for better cards as you continue to play the game.
-Cost. I purchased this for $2. Regular price is $4. You'll probably see it going on sale during the Summer/Winter sale for $1. I'm basing this review off the $2 price point. You won't be getting a full card game for $2 (not unless you're insanely good at Hearthstone's Arena). I bought it with money I made selling Steam Trading Cards.
Cons:
-Very Easy. I didn't lose a single best of three or best of five. Even the final boss I beat with three wins in a row. They very much need to ramp up the AI. They make some very silly plays that have the put a card in a location where they are unable to connect to anything.
-Weak story. To be fair, who expected a good story from a card game? Still, it's a con.
-No multiplayer. For a $4 indie title, this isn't much of a surprise. I personally don't care, as I was looking for more of a single player experience, but plenty of people will definitely find this to be a black mark against the title.
-Lack of variety. The card effects basically boil down to: attack, defense, disable, revive, rotate, remove, move. While the connect three mechanic helps make up for this overall, it does prevent the game from being more enjoyable. I like me some crazy card effects.
Up to Personal Taste:
-Art style. I'm neutral to the art style. That's generally how I am for most games. Look at the screenshots and decide for yourself if the art style is going to throw you off.
-Humor. The game seems to be trying to go for some humor. I chuckled once, and that was it. However, I didn't find the humor to be intrusive to the experience.
Btw, game took me 11 hours to beat. In my opinion, that's a solid amount of time for $2.
Anybody who enjoyed the old Pokemon TCG game or the Yu-gi-oh Single-Player games, I'd very much recommend getting this. To people who enjoy card games, I'd suggest giving this a shot. The price is low enough that it really won't hurt to give it a try. I had fun with it, which is why I'm giving it the good old thumbs up.
Hope this helps with your purchasing decision! :D

The idea behind Haunt the House is so incredibly genius that it's hard to believe there aren't more games like it. You're a ghost trying to scare off the living. You manipulate things in the environment to freak people out until they run away screaming. Many of the classic basic horror movie props are involved (mysteriously swinging light fixtures!) but there are also surprises and enjoyably unexpected results.
The graphics are cute and creepy in a way that's distinctly different from nearly every other cute and creepy game. The stylized design reminds me of antique marionettes from old childrens' books - cute enough to make the horrible aspects less disturbing, but weird enough to remind you that you're not playing a goofy kids' cartoon. I enjoyed making little kids scream and cry WAY too much.
Unfortunately, the idea is so good that you can't help wishing they'd taken it farther. I'm reminded of Jaws - another genius "why aren't there more games like this?" idea that ended up as a good but not great game. I'm also thinking of Spelunky, and how all the different elements sometimes come together to produce hilarious/catastrophic occurences. If Haunt the House had more potental for those kinds of "perfect storm" random interactions, you could play it forever and see something different each time.
So it takes a short time to see and do all of HtH. Even with the additional levels, I pretty much finished everything but the completist acheivements in a couple of casual hours. On one hand, there's nothing wrong with that - it's a great casual game that isn't loaded down with unecessary filler. I'd much rather have devs do a small game perfectly than try and fail to make it bigger than it needs to be. On the other hand, I was left wanting more... that awesome idea just begs for more.
So I liked Haunt the House, it's one of those great little games that I know I'll pick up and play every once in a while. But a bigger Haunt the House - with more complex and unpredictable environmental interactions - could easily be one of my favorite games ever. Will anyone make this happen?

Alice_mare is a bit of a classic game for me when thinking about RPGMaker type games, it was one of the first few I played when RPGMaker games blew up about 4 years ago. And it still holds up to this day. Playing through all the endings, getting all the acheivments, I had fun all over again.

I hate to give this game a bad review as it has a lot of potential, however there are a lot of gameplay mechanics that need some major adjustment before I can give it a good review.
Leveling system - Just like any other first person shooter, this game has a leveling system. Basically the more bad guys you kill, the more XP you get which levels you up. Seems pretty standard right? Well, it should be, but the problem lies in the fact that there are only four maps which you can play before you unlock new game modes. Without buying a "veteran" package, leveling up to unlock those game modes takes quite a while and playing the same four maps over and over and over again get really repetitive really quick. It feels like the devs are forcing players to spend real money to gain access to the "veteran" status, which grants double XP in matches and in turn unlocks new game modes and maps quicker.
Team balance - Matches don't start when the lobby is full. Once a certain number of spots have been filled the match starts. This usually happens when 3 or 4 players are on each team and once you get in game, the teams don't fill evenly, due to the fact that there are three factions in the game - US forces, German forces and Russian forces. You find matches based on which faction you're currently playing as, and the teams can become lopsided very quickly when more of one faction join a match than another. I've seen matches were there are 10-15 US forces and 4-5 German or Russian forces and the US forces are usually able to gain the upper hand at the beginning of the match, and the rest of the match is a one-sided battle making the game either really easy or really frustrating depending on what side you're on.
The grind - In addition to the leveling system there are badges for unlocking pretty much everything in the game. Want to unlock a vehicle? You're going to need to spend a lot of time driving or riding a bike around to level up your "driving" badge to gain access to the lowest tier vehicle unlock. Want to unlock a LMG like the M1919? You're going to need to grind your "Infantry Assault" badge, then your "LMG" badge to unlock it. If you don't like grinding away in matches to unlock literally everything, this game isn't for you.
Movement - It's clunky. Shooting can be frustrating, especially at long ranges. Keyboard controls need a lot of work and there isn't much in the way of key bindings.
Graphics - I generally don't bash on graphics, but the level design and textures need a lot of work. Some weapon models look cheap and glossy, textures are low resolution and the environments aren't great. I'd expect more from a game like this.
Al-in-all, this game has a lot of potential, but the devs are going to need to do a lot of work to make this game more enjoyable for the majority of people currently playing as well as future players.

Picture a fantastical world filled with characters and creatures reminiscent of any number of fairy tales and classic literature, but with unique interpretations and a strong Scandanavian influence. Now tell a story in that world. You can write a book, you can make a movie, or you can make a game. Many would design that game to ape the movie, or fill your screen with exposition like a book.
What the designers have done is something truly genius. They have interpreted this story in a way that can only be done when your input drives the story along. But that is admittedly nothing new. What is new, to me, is the manner that they've tied those inputs directly to your emotions and psyche. The buttons are given emotional weight, which is wholly new to me. By the end of the game, you will have experienced joy, humor, fear, and most poigniantly, sadness. All of which are intrinsically tied to your controller.
And sadness you will experience. This game's story will call back those movies of your childhood that they don't really seem to make any more. I want to call it a children's story, but not in the modern sense. This is a children's story where the power of life and death are on full display. Not the logical certainty and cold cynicism of adulthood, but the mythical proportions of those subjects. You will learn that life is not fair. It is scary, screwed up, and full of disappointments. But you will also learn that it is full of promise and a beauty that begs to be explored. If you are picturing a children's movie from the 80's wherein muppets were involved, then you're not far wrong from the general nature of this story.
As for the gameplay itself, there aren't many surprises, but it is in the presentation that it finds its feet. Press left trigger to pull a lever. Got it. Hold left trigger and rotate the joystick to rotate a winch. Okay. Press left trigger to wave a torch. Yawn. Oh, wait, you're in the middle of dark forest, and you were woken up in the middle of the night. Malignant eyes stare at you from the edge of your torchlight, and there is a growl that sends shivers down your spine. You must protect your younger brother, and at the same time you must hide behind your big brother, not daring to leave the circle of light. At the same time you are both vulnerable, and protective. Now press. that. left. trigger.
There are also some fairly clever puzzles, and the payoff for some of them is very rewarding. You are generally completely overmatched by your enemies, so combat is done through stealth, trickery, and intelligence, again, much like the aforementioned movies. Outwitting ogres who can crush you into a fine paste has never been pulled off so well in a game before.
In conclusion, this is a game that is not to be missed. I have no doubt that developers have taken note, and there will be more games like this down the road. I firmly believe that this is the genesis of a new type of storytelling which will only develop into bigger and better things in the future. So get a controller, set aside a three hour block, and play this game from beginning to end. Screw achievements, discard your preconceptions, and just experience the game. You will not be disappointed.

I near on never write reviews. Bomber Crew is going to be one of those exceptions. I'm a Youtuber/Streamer and I picked this game up cause it looked like my sort of jam - 25 hours and several streams later my audience was in love with it and I had found my favourite game this year.
Everything about it is perfect - with the exception of the difficulty at times (but they have literally just updated that, so hey! that's not a thing anymore). You care about both the crew and bomber, and the upgrades make it possible to focus on one or the other - going for a rich bomber run at risk to the crew, or a highly skilled crew run where you just ditch the bomber every time. The best part of it all is how involved you feel with the characters - XCOM style. This is doubly so thanks to the physics engine - people stumble, fall out of the plane, move slowly and so on as the plane does manuevers - it feels like real people desperately running around a plane, not like a simple "move manuever".
The best part of the game is the lack of a pause button, but the introduction of the new limited slow time mechanic. Personally I loathe the idea of using it - which is why you get a bonus at the end if you don't. If you do, it's very well thought out. A pause mechanic would remove the frantic juggling of priorities and things to pay attention to that makes up the core of the game, and instead you can slow time for a limited time - but you still need to be quick about actually issuing the orders you want.
This, comboed with the hot-keys update, make this my favourite game of the year. Prepare to get attatched to your crew and watch them die horribly.
My favourite part was that only very rarely did I feel I was beaten by a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t situation or enemy. 99% of my crashes, deaths or ccrew wipes were followed by me going &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥... If only I had done <blank>" and then adapting next time and succeeding. I love it.

Probably the first time I finish a game in one sitting. Although it's only 2-3 hours of gameplay, but that's just enough for this kind of thing. Great example of storytelling through gameplay. Very well-directed in that regard. A little corny sometimes, but that's just charming. The puzzles are very easy, but it would probably harm the pacing if it was more difficult, with trial and error. Excellent.

Quite an enjoyable game with a very moving story told in a unique way.
Firstly, you *need* a twin stick controller to play this - you *might* be able to kludge your way through with the keyboard, but you really don't want to. If you don't have one, go in to the City and buy an XBox 360 controller right now - I'll wait.... OK, you have one? Good.
Now, I love a game with a good story, but let's be honest - in most games the story and gameplay are somewhat disconnected from each other and could just as easily be presented as two separate pieces of art. Heck, there are some games that would have done better to throw away one (or two!) of those pieces altogether!
This game is different - the story and the gameplay are both perfectly intertwined. Sure, it still has cutscenes, but the story is largely conveyed while you control the brothers throughout their journey. This game has managed to figure out how to use the unique properties of a video game to tell it's story, rather than relying on techniques from movies or novels like every other game.
There is also, no speach - well, at least not English. The characters do use body language and speak some kind of made up language to effectively convey emotion and meaning, without distracting from the story or journey at hand. If you have ever played The Sims or The Singles it's similar to the spoken "language" in those games.
The story is very moving - I don't really want to spoil anything, especially as the game is not all that long and I couldn't do anywhere near as good a job as the game itself does. The basic premise is that the two brothers have to go on a journey far beyond their village, past troll mines and Giant's cities to find a tree that produces a healing exiler to cure their sick father (or so I gather - no English, remember?). I won't say anything more - you need to play it.
The gameplay is also pretty unique - at it's heart it's really a puzzle platformer where you have to use the strengths and weaknesses of each brother  to manipulate levers to move obstacles to allow both to progress on your journey. None of the puzzles are particularly difficult, but they are still satisfying and there is enough variety that the gameplay never outstays it's welcome.
What makes the gameplay unique is that you control both brothers *simultaneousely* with both of the sticks on the controller. This can lead to a bit of brain♥♥♥♥ at times - often coping with that that was more difficult than the puzzles themselves, but it doesn't take long to get used to and is never a serious problem (so long as you remember which button is which brother when you need to let go of a ledge).

Morrowind is a phenomenal game, but it is hard to put a finger on why.  It is not nostalgia -- I played Morrowind after Oblivion and Skyrim, so I had no nostalgia to look back on.  Part of it is the feeling of being in a strange world, with unique buildings, creatures, and cultures; a world very different from ours.  Part of it is the real sense of progression.  Your character starts out often struggling to kill a mudcrab or a rat, but one hundred hours of gameplay later hovers effortlessly above the landscape, easily destroying any creature foolish enough to cross you.  Part of it is the sheer variety of quests offered by the sheer variety of factions you can join, so there is always something interesting to do.  But it is hard to put into words exactly why you will set out in this dated game with a clunky UI and not want to stop for hours.

The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind is one of my favorite games of all time, and not for nostalgic reasons.
Here's why.
A little back story, my first introduction to The Elder Scrolls franchise was in 2007 when I played Oblivion for the first time on a heavily modded save file, and I didn't play too much because I didn't want to hog his computer. Prior to the release of Skyrim, I bought myself a copy on Xbox 360 and I loved every second of it. Oblivion remains my favorite, and I completely recommend everybody at leasts checks it out.
I then bought Skyrim the December following its release in 2011, same story. Absoultely loved it. Not as much as Oblivion, but I do find myself being able to hold a single character on Skyrim for much longer.
I finally bought myself Morrowind the following Christmas alongside Oblivion again, to start my PC gaming collection. Now, I had an awful PC and I was really hoping to play Oblivion, but Morrowind was the only of the 2 that could run. Without a guide, I immersed myself in the rich and diverse land of Morrowind.
I was amazed at the roots that eventually came to be Skyrim. I was a little terrified to have no fast travel at first, but as I came to figure out how to travel and interact with the map, I came to really appreciate Vvardenfell or its beauty. There were so many more stories to tell in Vvardenfell. On top of it all, I felt like my character had to earn her place in the world rather than have the world scale with me.
My arbitrary rating system for these 3 games is Oblivion > Morrowind > Skyrim. Morrowind is a game that once you take the time to learn becomes a beautiful experience worth checking out.

It's not bad. It's not great. It's just kinda there.
To explain: I had fun with it for a few days. Sure, some of the items are locked behind paywalls, although you can earn paid content over an enormous amount of time. Took me around a week to earn enough currency for a 10x10 room. The community is full of children/childish adults, but I was able to just lock myself away in my castle and avoid them.
This is a crafting/building type game, so here are some of the features of the process, divided into pros and cons.
Pros:
-You start out with a decent sized plot of land, deep enough to dig down, and wide enough that you don't feel constricted inside your free little home.
-You can build incredibly tall structures before you hit the invisible ceiling. I never got that high other than the test I did, but I'll get to that later.
-Blocks are easy to place.
-Water acts as a block you can swim through, allowing for intersting structures and pathways.
-Storage seems like it might be a pain initially, but chests are amazingly easy to craft with basic materials. I never felt like I was running out of room in my inventory, unlike most MMOs.
-You can lock your realm so that people can't wreck your fun.
Cons:
-Levelling starts out incredibly fast, but by level 10, it's so grindy that you forget level-ups were a thing.
-Levels are the way you learn new crafting methods. If you aren't the right level, you can't even make some of the basic tables.
-Level perks are limited to a choice of one of three per level. Even if you manage to grind past 10, you aren't assured that you'll get the right skill. Have fun getting to level 12!
-ROOFING. UGH ROOFING. You can craft a spray that makes roofing invisible when you walk under it, but that spray requires one of those lovely crafting stations locked behind level 15ish. And the spray is crazy expensive, even if you have the materials to make it. This stopped me while I was building my ridiculous mountain cavern, because there was no way that I was ever making enough spray for the whole mountain.
-Did I mention the community was terrible?
To conclude, the game is just average. It could be fun to play with friends for a little bit, but you'll probably tire of it after a week or so. Honestly, if I could, I would just give this a neutral grade. Although at this point, I have to not recommend this game, just because of the large amount of things that impeded my progress. It's the the kind of game I want to like, but until at least a few features are fixed, it's just going to gather dust. The only thing keeping on the fence is the fact that it's a free game, so I can only complain so much.

The nightmarish game of my childhood, I remember sitting next to my sister while she was playing the game on a PS1. I have a vivid picture of the first time I seen the zombie in this game that caused me nightmares for days. I could not believe when I found out Capcom had made a HD remaster of this masterpiece.
As an adult the first thing that caught my attention was the environment I found myself to play, a vintage mansion that I already knew I'd spend hours revisiting during the progress of the game, I've learned the locations of each room like my backpocket while desperately looking for a key or solution to a puzzle. That brings me to the puzzles of the game, I can't express how well done they are especially the Bee Puzzle which felt quite simple at first but the audio and setting that accompanied the puzzle made me forget my surroundings. The audio in this game is well designed because every time you visit an important location the music is drastically different to the regular audio, as the game progress and things get done, each time a new soundtrack plays the feeling of going forward is so well adapted in the players brain that I could call it a magic at times.
I found the combat system to be in par to the original, at first I found it stiff and hard to adjust but with time I was able to pull off some nice headshots (much easier with controller). The one thing I didn't like about this game is the camera angles and how it affects the keyboard while moving from one angle to another, my character would change the direction of his movement if I pressed the same button on different angle, therefore, each time there's a new angle a 'go forward' button could be any of the WASD keys.
The graphics are well done, each item of interest nicely highlighted in comparison to the background and monsters are easily distinctive. The music is absoultely fantastic, I found myself to be in trance while doing puzzles. Cinematics were ok at best, let's not forget this is a remaster so I didn't expect 21st century cut-scences. Story is well done although it didn't caught my attention all that much, I tend to forget different characters names and their significance except Albert Wesker because he was in the movie adaptation of the Resident Evil. The overall content of the game was fluid, I didn't find much items that were very situational or locations that would be non-significant in any way. The controls are fairly difficult to adapt but overall I'd say the game shouldn't be rated negatively solely based on one aspect. The gameplay is very compelling and after several hours - surprisingly, fluid.
I certainly advice you to go pick yourself a steam copy of this game, as it might be just the best Resident Evil game to ever come out.

I've played Magic the Gathering, SolForge and Hearthstone to mention a few so when I spotted this cheap little indie game I got curious and had to check it out.
The story in short is that you're a card player and are out to gether the 8 Legendary cards in order to face the Card King. It's simple but charming and along the way you run into a nice cast of fun characters to battle against and earn cards, gold and sometimes even new boards from.
I found the rules really easy to understand and the discovery of new cards very enjoyable. An autosave function after every match or change of environment means that you can quit and continue later at any point in the game.
There are also other functions where you can combine some cards into new ones as well as trading in cards you don't need for boosters.
The graphics were quite charming and some of the illustrations made me laugh a few times.
On the downside I'd say that the game was a bit easy and I wouldn't mind a filter option in the alchemy lab.
All in all, with lots of cards to collect and being able to continue even after finishing the game I say that this is a really good casual card game that I had a lot of fun playing. In addition to that it's also very cheap!

One thing thats sets this game apart from conventinal TCGs is that each gard has arrows on then that point to other cards on a 3 x 3 grid. and in order to make moves agains your opponent, you need to match the right cards (and there are many cards in the game, and the matches can be a miriad of combinations, so this is a lot easier then you think) in order to Attack opponents HP, increace you own HP, Disable your opponents cards to render them useless, or "revive" your disabled cards.
The game world is small with a point-and-click navigation. there are no animations in this game (save for a water effect around the island) But that dosent contract from the game at all. A very casual and really unknown game this is. I stumbled upon it on the Halloween Sale and it looked like it could be fun. You have a meter which indicates the atmosphere of the situation and it goes up by scaring people. Alright bois, time for my review of this time-wasting masterpiece. Let me get the flaws out first: Sadly there is only one map, and only 3 teams you can choose from: Russians, Americans, Germans, and Muslims. The Coreans are coming soon. So: You can choose from these 4 teams which ones are going to fight, 2 per match. There are up to 4 players per team, either player-led or computer-led. Once you select the teams, you will spawn, together with everybody else, on a random point of the map. You have no weapons, so you should avoid the bullets and try to find some laying on the ground. Three weapons are currently in the game: a Shotgun, a Land Mine and a Machine gun. If I'm honest, I think the shotgun is currently the best weapon. Why? There are only 8 directions in which you can face the enemy, and a spread shot does well for the occasion. Also because bullets 1-shot people. Which is good when you are surrounded by enemies. The Land Mine is exactly what is is in real life, you have 3 land mines you can put anywhere you want. It's very sneaky, since it may confuse you whether it's a pickup or an already placed mine. The machine gun, instead, shoots a straight bullet, of course faster than the shotgun's. There is also a tank, which oneshots people at point blank range, since it squishes them, and has missiles to launch, which are basically bullets with larger hitboxes, slower movement and an explosion radius. Once your tank loses all of it's health, you'll die. Yeah, I didn't understand this one either. You're supposed to get out of the tank before it dies, I guess. You can find out how to do it in the controls menu. Each weapon, including the tank and except for the Land Mine, has about 5 shots. The game trailer already showcased the Trump feature, which is basically a computer-led tank that has short ranged lasers instead of the missiles. I think the game is fun. Sure, some more weapons and features could be implemented, but as of now it's a real good time waster. I'd also like to take my time to enlist some features i'd like to see in the game:
1) When picking a team, I'd like to be able to decide a playermodel. You know, there are more people on the team selection menu instead of one soldier. I'd like to be able to play as them.
2) New Weapons!
3) Please put Italians in the game... I'm a bit patriotic, y'see...
4) British and French pls!
5) MOAR TRUMP VOICE LINES
That's it. I'd like to see them in the game. I hope I've been helpful. Well, all story short, if you didn't want to read all that, it's basically a good game to play when you have nothing to do or you want to have fun with friendzos.

I want to give this game a good rating, I honestly do, but I also honestly cannot, because it does not deserve it.
The credit system is my main issue with this game for a few reasons:
-The game has completely become pay-to-win
-It takes days upon weeks to unlock and obtain the weapons and gear you want
-You're spending more time than you should to have a good time
(Before reading, this is based on a Rank 5 soldier's income and gameplay.)
The credit system is based on an hourly salary that honestly makes no sense.  At Rank 5 a soldier makes 10,500 credits per hour of combat time, that means you are in a match and fighting (note: you must be within fighting range for this to count, you cannot be idle at the edge of a map or traveling to the battlefield), therefore you must spend an hour of combat time to obtain 10,500 credits.  Most late-game guns are 120,000+ credits, and if in most matches you only make 1-5,000 credits, that means it takes 24 (if you're lucky and get 5,000 credits every match, which most do not) to 120 hours of gameplay to purchase one gun, and this does not include the time it takes to unlock the ability to purchase said gun, which is even longer.
The credit system needs to be buffed, preferably to double the salary so every 30 minutes of combat time you make 10,500 credits, so every hour you make twice that amount.  This would be reasonable and make it easier for people who aren't spending real money on the game to unlock the equipment they would like.
This system is so game-breaking for me so I have to give this game a 6/10.
I recommend this game only to those who are patient and can handle a lot of unnecessary ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t from its pay-to-win money system.

I near on never write reviews. Bomber Crew is going to be one of those exceptions. I'm a Youtuber/Streamer and I picked this game up cause it looked like my sort of jam - 25 hours and several streams later my audience was in love with it and I had found my favourite game this year.
Everything about it is perfect - with the exception of the difficulty at times (but they have literally just updated that, so hey! that's not a thing anymore). You care about both the crew and bomber, and the upgrades make it possible to focus on one or the other - going for a rich bomber run at risk to the crew, or a highly skilled crew run where you just ditch the bomber every time. The best part of it all is how involved you feel with the characters - XCOM style. This is doubly so thanks to the physics engine - people stumble, fall out of the plane, move slowly and so on as the plane does manuevers - it feels like real people desperately running around a plane, not like a simple "move manuever".
The best part of the game is the lack of a pause button, but the introduction of the new limited slow time mechanic. Personally I loathe the idea of using it - which is why you get a bonus at the end if you don't. If you do, it's very well thought out. A pause mechanic would remove the frantic juggling of priorities and things to pay attention to that makes up the core of the game, and instead you can slow time for a limited time - but you still need to be quick about actually issuing the orders you want.
This, comboed with the hot-keys update, make this my favourite game of the year. Prepare to get attatched to your crew and watch them die horribly.
My favourite part was that only very rarely did I feel I was beaten by a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t situation or enemy. 99% of my crashes, deaths or ccrew wipes were followed by me going &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥... If only I had done <blank>" and then adapting next time and succeeding. I love it.

Its hard to pick out exactly what qualities make bomber crew so good, mainly because there's so many of them!
Many review sites are comparing this to FTL, which is in some ways true as it is also a game about micromanaging individual crew members aboard a single aircraft. As much as I enjoyed FTL I find that I enjoy this more because its easier to get attached to your crewmembers, you see them wandering up and down and they 'feel' like they have more of a personality.
This game pits you against the forces of the enemy (ze germans) in multiple missions striking at their heart through a mini campaign that seems simple yet is so long and difficult. You choose between varying missions with a lower reward to bump your crews skills, to more and more difficult ones facing extra challenges and ace enemies to make the mission more difficult.
Combine this with an economy system that really pushes you to make hard choices with regards to upgrading your bomber, do you add more guns or better armour? Better engines of that nice fire extinguisher system? The choice is yours but will it be the right one?
I've had no issues with bugs in this game, The graphics might not appeal to everyone but the simplicity and art style keeps it that step away from the horrifying reality of what actually happened to these bombers during WW2. Its important to remember that back in the day the real lifespan of these bombers and their 7 man crew was roughly 2 1/2 weeks. I think the game does a great job of being fun to play and realistic just enough to never devalue the sacrafice people made in these aircraft.
All in all, a great game for a great price and a truly niche idea. Well worth every penny.

Picture a fantastical world filled with characters and creatures reminiscent of any number of fairy tales and classic literature, but with unique interpretations and a strong Scandanavian influence. Now tell a story in that world. You can write a book, you can make a movie, or you can make a game. Many would design that game to ape the movie, or fill your screen with exposition like a book.
What the designers have done is something truly genius. They have interpreted this story in a way that can only be done when your input drives the story along. But that is admittedly nothing new. What is new, to me, is the manner that they've tied those inputs directly to your emotions and psyche. The buttons are given emotional weight, which is wholly new to me. By the end of the game, you will have experienced joy, humor, fear, and most poigniantly, sadness. All of which are intrinsically tied to your controller.
And sadness you will experience. This game's story will call back those movies of your childhood that they don't really seem to make any more. I want to call it a children's story, but not in the modern sense. This is a children's story where the power of life and death are on full display. Not the logical certainty and cold cynicism of adulthood, but the mythical proportions of those subjects. You will learn that life is not fair. It is scary, screwed up, and full of disappointments. But you will also learn that it is full of promise and a beauty that begs to be explored. If you are picturing a children's movie from the 80's wherein muppets were involved, then you're not far wrong from the general nature of this story.
As for the gameplay itself, there aren't many surprises, but it is in the presentation that it finds its feet. Press left trigger to pull a lever. Got it. Hold left trigger and rotate the joystick to rotate a winch. Okay. Press left trigger to wave a torch. Yawn. Oh, wait, you're in the middle of dark forest, and you were woken up in the middle of the night. Malignant eyes stare at you from the edge of your torchlight, and there is a growl that sends shivers down your spine. You must protect your younger brother, and at the same time you must hide behind your big brother, not daring to leave the circle of light. At the same time you are both vulnerable, and protective. Now press. that. left. trigger.
There are also some fairly clever puzzles, and the payoff for some of them is very rewarding. You are generally completely overmatched by your enemies, so combat is done through stealth, trickery, and intelligence, again, much like the aforementioned movies. Outwitting ogres who can crush you into a fine paste has never been pulled off so well in a game before.
In conclusion, this is a game that is not to be missed. I have no doubt that developers have taken note, and there will be more games like this down the road. I firmly believe that this is the genesis of a new type of storytelling which will only develop into bigger and better things in the future. So get a controller, set aside a three hour block, and play this game from beginning to end. Screw achievements, discard your preconceptions, and just experience the game. You will not be disappointed.

Quite an enjoyable game with a very moving story told in a unique way.
Firstly, you *need* a twin stick controller to play this - you *might* be able to kludge your way through with the keyboard, but you really don't want to. If you don't have one, go in to the City and buy an XBox 360 controller right now - I'll wait.... OK, you have one? Good.
Now, I love a game with a good story, but let's be honest - in most games the story and gameplay are somewhat disconnected from each other and could just as easily be presented as two separate pieces of art. Heck, there are some games that would have done better to throw away one (or two!) of those pieces altogether!
This game is different - the story and the gameplay are both perfectly intertwined. Sure, it still has cutscenes, but the story is largely conveyed while you control the brothers throughout their journey. This game has managed to figure out how to use the unique properties of a video game to tell it's story, rather than relying on techniques from movies or novels like every other game.
There is also, no speach - well, at least not English. The characters do use body language and speak some kind of made up language to effectively convey emotion and meaning, without distracting from the story or journey at hand. If you have ever played The Sims or The Singles it's similar to the spoken "language" in those games.
The story is very moving - I don't really want to spoil anything, especially as the game is not all that long and I couldn't do anywhere near as good a job as the game itself does. The basic premise is that the two brothers have to go on a journey far beyond their village, past troll mines and Giant's cities to find a tree that produces a healing exiler to cure their sick father (or so I gather - no English, remember?). I won't say anything more - you need to play it.
The gameplay is also pretty unique - at it's heart it's really a puzzle platformer where you have to use the strengths and weaknesses of each brother  to manipulate levers to move obstacles to allow both to progress on your journey. While the original may have aged considerably unlike its sequels & later games that share the same name, REmake–as called by many fans–updates pretty much everything about the original game as well as adding new content and slight changes to what was already there.
Playing with a keyboard or a controller is entirely up to preference as they're both very much playable with this game. Keyboard and mouse controls are rebindable but you can only change controller buttons through pre-set control schemes like Type A, Type B, etc.
The plot starts off simply with a special forces team searching for another team that went missing. Killer dogs come around and the team escape to a nearby mansion and then the game begins.
Before all that, you can choose to start the game off as either Jill Valentine or Chris Redfield. Each have different stats and you go through the story almost the same exact way solving the same exact puzzles.
Most of the game takes place inside a mansion full of claustrophobic areas. Every room you see is accessible at some point. It's a very non-linear game where progress involves solving puzzles in order to unlock areas to get items to unlock more doors to solve more puzzles and so on and so on. The entire game really is just one big puzzle box. The puzzles themselves aren't at all difficult and finding solutions is one way it encourages you to explore around to see where what item may go and such, but this also means there's a lot of backtracking involved whether a puzzle solution needs you to go to the same places again or you're just lost.
If you're pressed on gathering every item a room has, you can check the map to see if the room you're currently in still has items laying around somewhere.
Both a flaw & charm of this game are the fixed camera angles and tank controls.
The camera angles are meant to only show you what the developers want to show you (or hide from you), which can lead to some great "horror" moments that aren't necessarily
From a gameplay aspect, it can often be an incredible nuisance – for example, the enemy may be right in front of you but the camera just won't show it until you move to where the camera angle changes to view that general direction.
The tank controls encourage the slow pacing of the game. Trouble with that is you can't move & shoot, the speed when moving backwards is limited to only walking speed (which is already slow), and doing a quick turn-around can feel like ages during critical moments. You can use "Alternate" controls, which allows you to move around more fluidly like in most other 3D character action games such as Devil May Cry, but it's not really natural for this game as the camera will always change when moving around, thus forcing you to constantly reorient your analog stick or change the key you're using to move. If you're on a controller, using "Alternate" is only changed for the left analog stick, meaning you can use both tank controls with the D-pad and "alternate" controls with the left stick simultaneously.
Additionally, you can only aim straight ahead (neutral), upwards, and downwards, but precision isn't necessarily needed so long as your weapon is pointed in their general direction. There's an auto-aim to rely on anyway that aims towards an enemy when they're within the character's 360-degree sight.
All the backgrounds in-game are pre-rendered with very little 3D models actually being on-screen. The environment sometimes look blurry since all they ever did for this port was upscale the backgrounds as well as the FMVs. Regardless, the atmosphere portrayed and the 3D models on top are convincingly fitting with even the lighting and reflections having been focused on.
The music & sounds accentuate with the dark atmosphere. When there's a lack of either, it can make good on that "fear of the unknown" feeling.
Being strong on the
aspect in this survival horror game, resources are very limited – even saving is limited to the amount of a certain item you have. You've got to manage your resources and learn when and when not to waste bullets and health items. Your inventory is also very small, guaranteeing the need to leave some items where they are and making return trips to item boxes constantly to store unneeded items. All item boxes in the game are unrealistically, but conveniently, connected, so you can store items into one box in one location and find the same items in another box in another location. The difficulty chosen when you start the game also determines how many items will be in the playthrough as well as how many enemies there will be. There's only Very Easy, Easy, and Normal, though on a first run they're hidden as "Like climbing a mountain", "Like going on a hike", and "Like taking a walk". You get Hard mode after you beat the game once.
The most basic of zombies are often serious threats and can drain your ammo and health items fast if you're careless thanks to the slow pacing, the claustrophobic maps, and limited resources. Damage dealt is pretty random; one zombie may take up to 10 shots to kill with a basic handgun while the same zombie re-loaded from the same save file may take just 5. The same go for enemy damage against you, at least for the weaker attacks. Even headshots–which are actually just instant-kill shots as visualized by a head explosion–are incredibly random unless it's with a shotgun, up close, and aimed upwards, but even then that method is just "most likely" to grant a proper headshot. You can't aim up at the head, shoot with a handgun, and expect an instant or even faster kill. Even if you do manage to kill a zombie, it can come back as a stronger, faster version of itself usually after a certain amount of time passes unless you burn the "dead" zombie or get lucky with a headshot. You can't burn every zombie out there either as even the resources that allow you to do so are very limited.
The entirety of the mansion is designed so that you're creating your own routes, relying on you to know what paths are at least safe enough to backtrack through & not waste resources on, leaving it up to you to see what enemies you should just leave alone. Progress throughout the game can however trigger certain events in places you've run back & forth through several times, thus keeping up surprises in already familiar locations.
All that and more in mind, the entire game is all about surviving. There's action, but taking the action-route is obviously not always going to help.
The entire game is only really difficult on the first run and with little to no outside help whatsoever. A first-time playthrough may take up to 10 hours, but once you get to know how the game works and find out where items and even enemies are located, the "horror" is pretty much gone and the difficulty is tremendously lowered, making future playthroughs possibly take up half or even less than that of the first run, even if you decide to run through the game again with a different character.
You can unlock a couple of bonus weapons if you finish the game fast enough and a few extra costumes for finishing the game multiple times. You can also unlock a couple of bonus game modes that may make the game considerably tougher.
Some events only trigger if you do–or don't do–certain actions, like getting the infamous "sandwich" cutscene only if you didn't find a certain item by that point.
There are 6 endings for each character. They're pretty much the same for each other and are all pretty underwhelming.
You can't really treat this as a proper action game at all as there are too many random elements to consider even if you decide to treat it as such. It's a brilliantly flawed game with excellent level design, atmosphere, and survival gameplay.
