I've known about the Resident Evil games for a while, but never really cared to try any of them, partly because I'm a huge pansy. However, when this remastered version of the supposed best game in the series went on sale not too long ago, I decided to give it a buy and try. Would this REmake REmaster be too much for a colossal wuss like myself? Was I ever too spooked to venture deeper into the Spencer Mansion?
Nah, REmake isn't that scary. Though the frights are very well done, I rarely ever jumped or let out a "WOAH!" in terror. Regardless of the fear factor, it's a phenomenal game.
The story of Resident Evil takes place in the year 1998. Mysterious murders have been happening around the outskirts of a city I'd imagine the mascot would be that famous Mario 3 powerup. The local police department then sends in it's squad of dots in the night sky to investigate, but they're ambushed by doggos and are forced to enter the survival horror by exploring a spooky mansion filled with plentiful puzzles... and even more plentiful zombies.
Before the game starts however, you have to pick one of two characters to play as, which affects your abilities and the events in the game. Chris is the default option, but despite having a bit more health, is generally harder to play as than Jill due to less inventory space. Nevertheless, I went with Chris on my first playthrough. One thing I noted is that the difficulty selection is a bit... confusing. The top difficulty seems like the hardest, but is actually the Normal difficulty while the latter two are Easy and Very Easy. Just though I'd point that out for those who wish or wish not to play as intended.
The game itself plays like... Resident Evil. The fixed camera angles give RE a stylish presentation and really adds to the fear of an enemy showing up. You know what else adds to the spook scale? The tank controls! Even the most basic flesh-eaters are a lot more intimidating when you can't spin around them like a toddler at Disneyland (though you can do so if you choose the "alternate" controls, assuming you hate a challenge). Once you get used to it, movement is never too bothersome, especially since RE is rather slow-paced. While a fair amount of skill is needed to avoid earning a ticket to Heck™, no lightning-fast reflexes or uber-precise actions are ever required due to the slow speed of the gameplay. Be patient, think carefully, don't waste what few bullets you're given. Speaking of which, RE is a
horror game, so resources are scarce. Nothing is worse than the feeling of running low on healing items, shotgun shells, or saves. Yes, freaking SAVE POINTS are a resource; a punishment for save scumming scum. But fret not, as those with enough perseverance and caution will surely find themselves in the slightly rusted copper-plated halls of VICTORY! Though when you do make it to the end of the game, you're not even close to conquering it. There's plenty of unlockables and extra modes that give RE excellent replayability. This is a 4-10 hour game, but I can easily see some people spending dozens or possibly even hundreds of hours mastering it and doing everything there is to do.
Overall, I'd say Resident Evil is the masterpiece I've been told it is. It's dread-drenched atmosphere, mercilessly intelligent design, and thrilling gameplay make it a must-have, maybe even for even those who usually dislike the Survival Horror genre. Whether it be during a sale or at full price, few will regret such a grand purchase.

Defiance is an MMO with a difference, and that difference is not that it has a TV show tie-in. The big difference is that it's actually a solid game despite being an MMO.
From that statement, you can probably tell that I have not been much of a fan of MMOs in the past. From "World of Warcraft" to "Conan" to "Rift", I have found MMO gameplay to be repetitive (which is fine) but not engaging (which is not fine) and the storytelling sub-par (the exception being BioWar's "Star Wars: The Old Republic", but even that was pretty pants), and that the presence of randoms within my gameworld turned out to be detrimental rather than enhancing. Even worse is that all MMOs seem to basically play like "World of Warcraft", so there is little competitive advantage to be found from one MMO to another; you may as well just play "World of Warcraft", being the biggest and arguably the best of the bunch thanks to more than a decade of continuous development.
[ASIDE: I should say that I really want to like MMOs, especially MMORPGs, but I just haven't enjoyed them for the above reasons. They may be great MMOs, but, for me, they have failed to be fun and engaging games. I have typically given up around Level 40 in most MMOs, which is purely coincidence. I have had several friends of mine who play "World of Warcraft" say words to the effect that they agree the majority of the game is awful as you "level up", but that the end-game is great if you can persevere...but that argument just doesn't hold water for me; I refuse to be punished for 40 hours on the off chance I finally enjoy what follows.]
Enter "Defiance", an MMO that tries to be a decent third-person action game and an MMO. And you know what? It succeeds. "Defiance" has more in common with games like "Mass Effect" and "Halo" than it does any MMO I can think of. Those comparisons probably tell you all you need to know about the shooter gameplay, so I won't labour the point; suffice to say, it is a solid shooter. And it is a shooter. It is not an RPG-style MMO; there is no character progression to speak of--weapons come in classes, such as Pistol, SMG, Assault Rifle and so on, but the stats of each class does not change as you level up with EGO powers and perks (think biotics from "Mass Effect"), and the rarer loot-drop weapons you collect only ever add between 1% and 5% here or there to weapon stats.
The "Defiance" PVP offering most closely resembles the "Battlefield" series, albeit a very arcade-like version thereof. The net result of the weapon system described above, though, is that new players can readily compete directly with old-hand players. There is no "I'm a Level 35, so I can kick your puny Level 30♥♥♥♥♥..but that guy is a Level 40, so I'm ♥♥♥♥ed" moment in this game, which is something I really like.
I have now completed the first major mission arc, and I am really enjoying the storytelling -- much more than any other MMO, with the possible exception of "Star Wars: The Old Republic". The writing is decent without being great, and the characters are crafted to "acceptable" levels.
My biggest gripe is the dearth of real story content after the first campaign. Months later and we have yet to see any real "meat" to continue your story. That annoys me as I was enjoying the Halo-style storytelling to this point, and Trion has very much dropped the ball by not giving me more.
This was supposed to be a quick review, so I'll wrap up with this: Defiance is a solid third-person shooter with limited RPG elements...if you don't expect it to be anything more than that, you can have a lot of fun with it. If you're looking for something to take over from WoW, though, this is not that game.
Subjective Assessment: 7/10

Haunt the House started out, as I understand it, as a browser-based minigame, which you can still find and play if you want to get a general feel for it. Controls on the Steam PC version are slightly different, but not terribly so.
The Steam version is essentially a collection of minigames, with not a terrrible amount of variation, but enough that each is distinct. The goal is always the same: creep people out enough that they leave your residence.
The Mansion
The browser game is, essentially, the Mansion. It plays pretty much the same, and you play the cute little inverted teardrop "Oooooh" ghost. This one I occasionally will just let float off somewhere and press the possession button a few times just to hear it's cute little ghost noises. The moans don't seem to really affect people so much as actually possessing things and creeping folk out. Some things don't seem as effective at scaring in the Steam version, such as the hand-plates. In the browser version, claws breaking through wall-mounted plates would be enough to send people to jumping out the windows, but here it often is only mildly frightening, and is less likely to induce panic.
The Holidays/North Pole
The little ghost that inhabits this area has the sniffles, and will sneeze when possession button is pressed apart from objects. This area has fewer strict rooms, and has a general holiday vibe (if you hadn't guessed). It isn't that much different from the mansion in terms of environment, but it still definitely has some interesting things going on.
Terrortown
In Terrortown iteself, you return to the "Ooooh" ghost...sort of. You start out in the bell tower and float around scaring people out of a total of four locations: a hospital, a museum, a cruise ship, and a theatre. You will find a total of nine people whom you cannot scare. These people you kill off, in essence, and once they are dead they will haunt the bells, and you can play as them instead of "Ooooh", though I am reasonably certain everything does the exact same things, so it's really more like if you want to be a nurse ghost, now's your chance.
Ghost train
Despite the fact that this level features a CARNIVAL on a TRAIN, this is, I believe, the only level where you cannot cause someone to commit suicide. At least, no one did when I played it. The dynamics here are unique: there are three cars, featuring a haunted house, a carousel, and a fun house. Each car has a different atmosphere, but people can walk through all the cars. The goal is to get everyone off the fun house car at the back of the train, This is a bit different than previous levels, because in, say, Terrortown, people did not come back into a vacated house; they just left, and stayed out. Here, though, you could have someone get chased out of the haunted house, go all the way to the fun house, and wander back, screaming the whole way.
Oh yes, and that ghost is a steam-shaped poultergeist, dubbed, the "Nyaaaah" ghost.
In conclusion, if you want a basic idea of what this game is like before you buy it, play the browser version first; it's a nice little preview, and should give you a pretty good idea whether you'll like this or not.

Pretty Fun title, with a tight and precise loop of gameplay.
Though the core of the game is "compromise".
A fire in the rear of the plane:
Do you get a gunner to put it out, risking having to not answer attacking fighters?
Or
Do you run your Engineer to the back, risking the fire growing instead?
The lack of a pause makes every decision critical, every pause fatal.
A slow plane, a fast game.
Things I've found exploitable:
You can farm missions until you get aces on low risk missions, literally only having to fight the ace is much easier; maybe have the ace come in a flight if there are no other fighters.
You can farm missions without bothering with the non-optional missions until you have high level equipment early game; maybe unlock equipment with intel AND stage.

First things first, the game has its issues. Once you hit lategame the amount that the game throws at you is absurd, to the point that on main missions you WILL be returning home a skeleton, if at all. However, I honestly did enjoy the difficulty, although I do recommend you look at some tips on the forums. Perhaps some balances lategame are needed (Like limited fuel on rocket planes, and ammo on planes in general)
If you enjoy an intense challenge, I highly recommend this game. There are some times where you'll be thinking "How the hell am I going to make it out of this" - and sometimes you'll be right, you won't make it out. If you enjoy the permadeath aspect, you can let it take its course and see how your crew survives - do you bail out, emergency land, crashland? Your choice.
I personally don't have the will nor the time to deal with losing an entire crew, and chose instead to just savescum and quit the game if I know I'm going down. The massive loss upon losing a plane was recently fixed however, as you now get a plane that is upgraded as it should be to the current stage in the game, and I hear that crew members will also be higher skilled later in the game. Will be going through the game a second time, this time with no savescumming (barring glitches/stupid mistakes on my part)
Which brings me to the next part: Glitches. There aren't many of them, but the one big one I encountered is levelbreaking. Apparently if you call in Spitfires on certain missions, your gunners will switch to firing blanks... good luck getting home when your gunners aren't able to shoot down anything.
Finally, if you're looking for an actual simulator, this isn't for you. You're flying a bomber that is magically able to fly missing half its wings, control its roll without ailerons, your crew can repair an entire engine in-flight by climbing onto the wing, etc. However, don't let this discourage you as I am a historical enthusiast and stlil had a blast with the game. The damage modeling is beautiful (you might survive one pass from a fighter to your gunner as the plane's armor eats it up, but once you have holes the shells eat right into your crew)

This is a solid if not very casual collectible card game. Cards are placed in a 3x3 grid and when the arrows are aligned between enough cards they cause an effect. There's a few options on how to win: lower an opponent's health to zero from attacks or from taking damage when their deck runs out (a way to win with mill-type decks). Another option is to disable their cards, forcing their grid to fill up. If they can't play a card, they lose.
It's this third option that turns out to be the easiest to exploit, making the game extremely easy. I enjoy the game but without tougher AI this will only get a single playthrough from me. However, I will enjoy the ride.

For the price this game packs quite a bit of entertainment. Its really charming and the card game itself is really fun. In the beginning of the game the foes you will face are dumb as rocks, but thats on purpose and the game even jokes about that fact. Your "rival", Little Dude, is probably the first somewhat challenging opponent.
The game is a lot of fun and is almost a hybrid puzzle/card game. Its a simple game to learn though and after my first match I felt I had a solid idea of how to play the game effectively. The tutorial is very good at explaining how the game works.
I think every win earns you a booster pack of 5 cards. The cards vary quite a bit and have lots of different effects. You can also have up to 6 custom decks.
So far I've gotten a little over 2 hours of enjoyment out of this game and I plan to play it to completion, which I hear is around 14 hours based on someone elses review. For $4 (or $2 if you bought it in the first week like I did) this game is an excellent deal and well worth the money.

Years later, I found it on steam, and played it again, hesitant to see if it stood the test of time. I was pleased however to discover that it more than stands up against it, in fact it shoos it away.
Pros:
- Fun, easy gameplay
- Cute soundtrack and noises
- Scaring the♥♥♥♥♥♥♥out of people with a teddy bear you haunted
Cons:
The only downside that comes to mind is the fact that the game is much more suited towards left handed players than right. Traditionally, games use the wsad key map for movement, and leave the directional keys alone. As such it's almost an industry standard. However this game uses the wsad keys for interaction purposes, and the directional keys are used for movement.
Aside from that, its a charming game that's worth the purchase!

This seemingly simple little indie game is so much more than I expected!
I have been having an absolute blast playing this game with my friend. It's a similar experience to what we had playing Portal 2 co-op, occasionally hurting our brains trying to solve a puzzle and then facepalming when it becomes blatantly obvious (after you've spent 15 mins trying to solve it of course). ibb & obb actually has us both in tears a few times, just dying with laughter as we repeatedly fail jumps and die to the Studio Ghibli-esque wandering soots.
The graphics are PHENOMENAL - the simplicity of it all works so well and the vibrant colours make me so happy. Even the darker levels were executed so well and add to the game: You have just enough vision so that it doesn't hinder you playing (like so many other games where you can't see 2 inches in front of your face) and it's fun not being able to see the soots. Nothing like a spikey lil surprise to make your day eh?
Not gonna lie, I normally rage a bit while playing platformer/repeatedly dying games. Like I said earlier I've had the exact opposite happen..I cry with laughter when we keep dying. The whole atmosphere of the game is very zen-like and relaxing, and the gameplay is just so fun (lots of wooshing and sounds are made while flying through the sky) that I haven't raged or gotten annoyed whatsoever..which is great. :)
Can't recommend this game highly enough. What're you waiting for go grab a friend! And if you don't have any friends...you should rent one for a day just so you can play this game. It'll be worth it, I promise.

Frustratingly difficult. Given the campaign indicator, which suggests I am still right at the very first 10% of the game, the difficulty curve is incredibly steep at the early stages and is making me simply quit in frustration and go do something else - a dangerous place to put your players. Chances are I will lose interest pretty quickly at this rate. It's not even a skill thing - the game simply presents the player with 6 highly critical tasks to perform during a mission, with no reaction or thinking time and a control scheme that makes it very hard to issue the orders quickly and effectively.
Reload this! Put that fire out! Fix this! Navigate there, and tell your gunners you want them to shoot planes down, now that bit's broken so fix that as well, while that guy's almost dead and that guy needs to switch over to be on bomb aim! It's just too much; it's frustrating. If you're a dab hand at multitasking and can operate several control systems simultaneously, and are a very quick aim with a mouse on a screen control, then you'll probably get on OK.
It's a shame, because it's polished and cute, humorous, and the upgrade chains are logical and pretty easy to understand. But the level of play interaction required, as opposed to a degree of autonomy employed by the characters ("Hey, gunner, if you're out of ammo why don't you just go get some anyway? Why do you need me to tell you to go get some?") puts me right off.
It's a shame the Steam rating system doesn't allow a middle-of-the-road rating, I can't really give this a thumbs-down but it's not a perfect thumbs-up either. Playability suffers a little, for me. But... it's not a bad game, no.

classic rpg. when games were tough, required reading and thinking. this title in my favorite game franchise was made to be very close experience to what old school table-top roleplaying games had to offer, where your skills combined with luck and decisions were the main thing leading you through the game. for example, when you swing your sword trying to hit enemy, it depends on your skill level, type of weapon, weapon stats, some luck, etc. whether you will hit the evemy at all, or if you will, how many damage will it take, etc. this applies to all other aspects of gameplay. another example is places you go, quests etc. there is no map pointer showing you where to go, so your destinations are decided purely by you reading the quest details, asking around where that place is, and asking for directions how to get there. so, in short, no holding hand while you play. so, many new gamers see all these things as "broken" mechanics, when in fact, the game is designed to give you tabletop rpg experience, its meant to be like that, that not every hit registers, that not every spell casting is successful, that sometimes you dont know exactly where you need to go, etc.
now for the eyecandy effect, yes, vanilla game does look outdated in 2017. BUT, all you need is 1 single mod. it's called morrowind graphic and sound overhaul. it is actually compilation of mods. with that, game feels and looks AMAZING (check my morrowind screenshots if youre interested). it contains huge collectiond of, not only graphic and sound upgrades, but many many gameplay and bug fixes.
i will recommend this game for any hardcore rpg gamers, even those who enjoy only tabletop rpg games, as it is designed from that model. it is one of my favorite titles in rpg world, and it brings memories of how good games used to be over 1.5 decade ago. and i repeat again, dont get frustrated at how gameplay is right at the beginning, give it a chance, you will get used to things after one hour of gameplay, dont go in expecting dumbed down gameplay from skyrim, or even oblivion. not that i dont like those games, shyrim, oblivion and morrowind are my top 3 rpg games, and whole elder scrolls is my favorite franchise ever. im just saying its much harder and much less forgiving.

(I recently Purchased it from steam but I already have 150+ hours in Morrowind)
(No Nostalgia What so Ever)
Introduction and Combat Mexhanics:-
Morrowind in my opinion the best elder scrolls game (though not my favorite). What I love the most about it is the world and how unique it is and how it feels bigger that you. You start the game as nobody, you have to painfully work your way to earn a reputation. This game is not easy, and while you may be turned off by difficulty, finishing questlines is so Satisfying that you get the urge to replay it. Out of all the modern Elder Scrolls, this is the most RPG like in the series. As for the combat system, it's outdated and extremly difficult, however for players like me who praise difficulty, that doesn't really take away from the experience. As for the magic system, I can say it's one of the best in all RPGs, mainly because of the spellmaking ability (also in oblivion though not quite as good), with spellmaking different effects can be added together to form spells that are extremly helpful for a grand number of situations. However, the system is quite exploitable, giving you the ability to create extremly overpowered spells in the late game.
Exploitability:-
Morrowind is a game the is extremely exploitable, so much so that you can get a daedric weapon from the start even though you aren't supposed to. As mentioned earlier the spellmaking system can get you to OP status with the right spells, which isn't that bad actually. In fact, one of the reasons I like Morrowind is the tricks that you learn to get better, and exploits for me are tricks that are used to improve yourself. And even with the exploitability of Morrowind it's still difficult.
The World:-
Morrowind, unlike future Elder Scrolls games, has a de-leveled world, Meaning the world doesn't shape around the player's level. which means before you can fight bosses you need to prepare and get to the right level to be powerful enough to stand a chance. And that creates a sense that you're in an actual world with people living it. At the start of the game you are an outsider trash, some people will outright reject talking to you. You have to finish quests to get a reputation for yourself. And these quests need you to join guilds.
Guilds:-
Guilds in Morrowind are a strong point for the game, however they feel a bit stale. To join a guild, you need to meet the minimum requirements of that quild, and each time you advance the requirements for the next rank are higher. This is both a good thing and a bad thing, On one side that makes guilds more realistic so doing a few quests won't suddenly get you to guildmaster, but on the other hand some of these requirements need a ton of grinding to meet which sometime takes the fun out. As for the quests, you start by doing tasks that are expected of a low ranking member of that faction, however as you progress you get quests that are more personal to the quest giver. And reaching the rank of guildmaster gives you a lot of respect from the members of that guild and a few reputation points for yourself. There are 7 main factions but for me the Imperial Legion and the mages guild were the most fun.
The Atmosphere:-
Morrowind takes place on Vvardenfell, an island in the province of morrowind. Vvardenfell has flora that is unique to it. While Exploring you will find large mushrooms and ashlands. The cities are truly large and have shops that the player may never need, further showing that the world isn't revolving around you. In ym opinion the atmoshpere is Probably one of the strongest pros of Morrowind. And the soundtrack is just Perfect, this is one of Jeremy Soule's best work. The soundtrack gives you an Epic feeling that makes you want to explore the game even more.
(SPOILERS ALERT)
The story and the dlc:- The story in Morrowind revolves arount you discovering that you are the reincarnation of the dead dunmer leader Lord Indoril Nerevar. Most of the plot is you completing the Nerevarine Prophecy which leads up to you fighting the leader of the dead Sixth House, Dagoth Ur. The story in Morrowind is probably the best in the entire Elder Scrolls series (which really isn't an achievment considering they all had mediocre stories). As for Tribunal, the first dlc, it takes you to mournhold, the city of Almalexia. After a darkbrotherhood assassin comes after you to travel to Mournhold to discover who sent the assassin after you. The dlc didn't really offer much and for the most part felt like a burden instead of an adventure, However the ending is kinda fun and has great rewards for sword users (Basically every build I do is a Sword User). As for the Bloodmoon expantion. The story revolves around you travelling to solesthiem and Discovering the Causes of the mysterious Happenings there. The dlc is a ton of fun and intoduces a new faction, The East Empire Company, which in my Opinion is the best faction in Morrowind.
(SPOILERS OVER)
Mods:-
Morrowind is an old game with mechanics that some would call outdated, however one thing that I didn't mintion is Mods. Mods can make morrowind Playable and takes it to the standards you would expect from an AAA game in 2017. Most of the cons the I Mentioned Earlier can be fixed with Mods in fact.
Conclusion:-
Morrowind is a great game that unfortunatly aged badly, However if you are willing to install a few mods and are willing to Bear the difficulty of the game. You will have a Blast and one of the best Adventures in the Elder Scrolls Series. If you only Played Skyrim, I suggest you Play Oblivion first and then Morrowind.
Rating:-
Story - 8.5
Guilds - 8.5
Magic - 9.5
Combat - 7
World - 9
RolePlaying - 8.5
Overall - 8.5

I'd never played a Resident Evil game before this one, and the Survival horror genre in general was alien to me. A few weeks back, I watched a friend of mine play the game during one of his livestreams, and I decided to check it out. It was only a few bucks in the current Humble Bundle, so even if it had not been for me, it wouldn't have emptied my bank account. Can't hurt to give it a try, right ?
Well I guess it can hurt. My wallet, to be precise, because after playing this game, I'm looking forward to playing the rest of the series and the upcoming RE2 HD remake ! I found much to love in this HD remake of the very first game in the series, so much so that I ended up 100%ing it, which I don't do for just any game. It's filled with content that will make you go back and play it again and again and again !
Resident Evil, also called Biohazard in some countries, is a Survival Horror game in which you play as either Chris Redfield or Jill Valentine, two members of a special task force known as S.T.A.R.S., as they explore a mysterious mansion and its surroundings and try to uncover the fate of their lost teammates. The game plays like a third person shooter, but the camera is always in fixed angles chosen by the developers. You must solve puzzles to acquire keys, items and weapons in order to open more rooms and progress through the mansion. The hallways are filled with zombies, but resources are extremely scarce so you'll have to decide whether to shoot, or to run.
This HD port for the current generation was a great way for me to discover the series, even if the regular asking price of 20 bucks is a little high. Wait for a sale or for it to show up in a bundle, but if you find it or less than 10 bucks, it's well worth it. I recommend this to both fans of horror games and total newcomers like me, it's a game worth experiencing at least once in your life.

Resident Evil HD REMASTER
Release Date: March 2002 (Gamecube), January 2015 (PC)
Strengths:
-Originality
-Beautiful graphics (game is an eye candy)
-Great story
-Puzzles
-Great sound (especially weapons) and voice acting
-Has Jill :)
Limitations:
-Some sections are frustrating e.g. doors opening only one side and you have to take a long walk around.
-You have to watch door open and close animation all the time :p and there are lot of doors !
-Camera view in the game can't be controlled manually and auto change in camera view can be frustrating at some places.
-The game is pretty short.
-Requires lot of patience to play and complete which may not be liked by some gamers.
Conclusion:
Resident Evil HD REMASTER (also known as Resident Evil 1 Remake  or Biohazard)  is the 2002 remake of the first resident evil game launched by capcom in March 1996. This game is known in the gaming industry as one of the pioneering games that defined the survival horror genre and the game that started it all. It hit a record of over 8.5 million worldwide sales when it was initially released for PS2 and is considered one of the greatest video games of all time which is still evident from its present fan base and from the fact that almost every RE title is an immediate hit. But what makes this game so special? Simply because there is no other game quite like it and has no equal (Silent Hill is good but as good as RE). This goes for all the resident evil series games. The most strong point of the game is its story and direction. Japanese directors are great in horror as well as emotional drama and this reflects perfectly in RE HD Remaster. You play as either Jill or Chris who are the members of Special Tactics and Rescue Service (S.T.A.R.S.) a special unit of the Racoon City Police Department. You are deployed in a Mansion where your objective is to investigate the strange incidents related to bio-weapon development. You are given very limited supply of bullets and medical aids which have to be used wisely or you are dead. Enemies include zombies, mutants, mutated animals and plants. There are booby traps as well.In order to proceed in the story you have to solve numerous puzzles and obtain various items like keys, objects, gems etc. to unlock doors.  I really like mid boggling games and is one of the reasons I've liked RE games especially the older ones. Plus it features combination with modern firearms with great sound and effects (like zombie heads blown off in a single shot :) ). I started off playing it like any RE game but there was a part of the story that was really touching and emotional which I had never expected (I wouldn't discuss it as it'd be a spoiler).  Shinji Mikami did a great job there. Still thinking whether its worth that expensive price tag? Hell yeah ! Every penny !

Machinarium is a treasure of a game that I bought a good number of years ago (long before I got Steam) and fell in love with. I adore the charming, scratchy, hand-drawn artwork, the rich soundtrack, and all the care and love that obviously went into this grungy robot world. I'm especially fond of all the little creature robots, like the very first one you meet, who wants a stuffed doll out of its reach in return for the favour of finding your missing leg for you. There are so many cute, silly, and/or interesting details scattered throughout the game. Sometimes it is slow or clunky to get around, so depending on your temperament, you might find your patience tested. But there's plenty of scenery to absorb and admire while you're waiting for your little robot to move from one side of the screen to another for the third time, haha!
The puzzles can be incredibly challenging at times, but there's a hint in each area, and there is always a detailed in-game walkthrough for the current area available to you in the top right corner (after completing a small mini game, which seems pretty fair). Sometimes that doesn't always help though, especially when there's an item in another area that you need, so thankfully there's plenty of walkthroughs floating around out there on the internet. I'm a fan of how tough the puzzles tend to be, and I find it rewarding to manage to figure them out on my own...but some of them are just downright difficult or obscure. But even if you're not a fan of puzzles, and you find yourself looking at a walkthrough every five minutes, I still think this is a really nice game to play through for the story, art, and music!
There do seem to be some strange glitches that I don't recall running into in the standalone version I had on my old laptop (it's been years though, so I can't be sure), but nothing that completely hindered gameplay. Strange instances where one event starts playing before the previous one ends, and you'll briefly end up with duplicates of characters or items on screen...or items may spontaneously reset to previous positions. I did run into an issue where an item I needed suddenly disappeared entirely, but upon saving and reloading, it was back in my inventory. The game is short and simple enough that I don't think this is a huge issue in the long run, and I only ran into the issue twice in my recent playthrough, but I'd say it can be startling, especially if you're on your first run ever and just got through a very difficult puzzle.
These little issues are just that though: little issues. Machinarium is probably one of my top favourite games to be honest. It feels very special to me. All of its parts: the art, the music, the designs, the personalities, they all combine into a very unique and memorable game. (Though waiting six or seven (I think) years wiped my memory of the specifics of the puzzles, so I got to really wrestle my way through them once more, heheh.) Well worth buying again on Steam for me! (Especially since I got it in the Amanita Bundle: I'm really looking forward to starting up Samorost 3!)

I've never been one to write Reviews, but here goes.
DCUO is very polarizing, it seems. Some people claim there is a good, loving community always available to help. Some say it's an acidic community that leaves people feeling insulted. Personally, it depends on when you log in. To be honest, while MMO's are frequently about community, so much of this game could be played alone for the Super-Hero experience.
The game is, very much Free. While high-end content requires DLC expansions, you can play from Level 1 to Level 30 (Max) without much care. If you want to play certain powers, then yeah, you have to buy something - but despite a lot of claims, these powers aren't the powers you "Pay-to-Win" for. It's no different than when other MMO's release new classes. The builds are broken. There are exploits, but after a patch or two, the power levels match up again, and it becomes about skill once more.
As far as the Combat goes, it has a Rock-Paper-Scissors feel quite often. Melee breaks Range. Range breaks Block. Block breaks Melee. While annoying at first, it allows you to know that you should always be able to escape an otherwise inescapable combo by just knowing what breaks what. Melee Character wailing on you? Block it. Dual Pistol Character kiting you at range? Hold Melee and get a lunge in (every Fighting style has a lunge of some kind).
That's another thing about the game that's rather nice. The fact you get to place the Fighting style of your choice, with the Power style of your choice allows you to create a custom "Class". And with each Power having two different trees, the variety increases more. A Bow/Nature (Flora) will play a lot different than a Martial Arts/Nature(Fauna), even though they are both essentially "Nature" Classed.
So... yeah. All in all, try it. It's free. It only costs you some Bandwidth and Disk Space. If you don't like it, Uninstall for a free "Refund".

This game hasn't been updated for quite a while, however, the developers have at least kept in touch. This game offers around 10 hours of gameplay for quite cheap. The soundtrack is great, and the battle system is unique. The AI can be beat by using one stategy for the entire game, however, it is still quite entertaining to do so with different combinations. Also, this game, despite the tags, is NOT a TCG. Anyone who tags this as one doesn't know what that stands for. There is NO  trading, thus, it is not a TRADING card game.

(Need a tl;dr? Just go buy the freaking game.)
I would like to start out by saying that I have a lot of experience with TCG's. I played Magic: The Gathering for a while, and I liked it but I was never in love with it. The game that I really fell in love with was Yugioh- which, from about 2010 to early 2012, was the best card game of all time, no holds barred, perfect pacing, for most of those formats well balanced, all playstyles were represented, and most importantly a deep, deep, deep, DEEP card pool that constantly rewarded me for scrolling through lists of cards, pointing at a random one with weird subtext and saying "I'm gonna make a deck around that one!" But eventually, konami ruined everything, the game sped up until it was too fast, the power crept up until I couldn't build a creative deck and survive against anyone competent for more than a turn or two, and the community got even worse. The state that it was in was much akin to the happy accidents of "Super Smash Bros. Melee" or "Marvel vs. Capcom 2" in that they probably didn't actually think about how the things they added affected the meta game, but eventually it somehow turned out fantastic. I'm saying all of this because Card City Nights reminds me of this era of yugioh. Very different gameplay, yes, but I'm not talking about the gameplay. There are two very important things that this game gets very right and other digital tcg's get very very wrong: card collection and deck building.
When you play hearthstone, and even scrolls (despite mojang having no motive to do so since it already costs 20 bucks), you might notice that you get like, 1-2 packs a day. Even if you get really good at drafting in hearthstone, you get a good pack or two every hour- if you're really, really good and really, really lucky. Card city nights, on the other hand, gives you a pack like every 5 minutes. And then gives you the option to use your extra cards to get more packs. And then gives you a fusion system to get more cards. And gives you a large singles shop. Seriously, collecting all the cards available to you in their maximum usable quantities seems so doable in this game, whereas every other online tcg asks me to grind for weeks or months just to finish my damn deck!
Perhaps the best part of the fact that Card City Nights gives you so many cards, is that the deck building involves a lot of creativity and strategy and is just overall fantastic. Deckbuilding in other games seems very one-dimensional compared to Card City Nights... Cards fit together in unique ways, and not only do you have to think about your strategy and what each card is contributing to your strategy and the synergies between them and all of that stuff, but you have to think about the synergy between their arrows, think about the combos you could make with this deck... it adds a lot of depth to deck building. I'm not entirely sure if it was intentional or a byproduct of the gameplay, but either way I love it. Other than that, for a game I spent $2 on, the card pool is impressive (with an implication of more cards coming at the end) and the cards are designed well, giving some good strategies and combinations to build decks around without enforcing them as cards that need to be used together.
So all this should come together to be a great card game, right? Well, this review unfortunately ends in tragedy, as Card City Nights lacks a key component to this equation- multiplayer. It practically ruins everything I've just said. I can build all these great decks and collect all these cards and it won't mean anything in the end, because there's no ultimate test of my deck against another and there's no one who cares about my innovation when it's all within a relatively easy single player game. However, it's not a stretch to say that, in the event that online is patched in, and more cards are released, and the game is balanced a bit for competitive play, this could become the best tcg on the market.
It has a good base and a fun singleplayer, even if it lacks some fundamental elements necessary for it to become really great. It's worth the price of admission, and it could eventually be worth 100 times that if the game's potential is explored. In the end I still had a great time with it, even if it never becomes more than it is.

It's hard not to recommend this game at a $4 retail price, however I still have to.
This game does have it's own unique system of presenting a card game, using a 9 grid board with cards that can have one or more of the 8 direction arrows. You then place cards on the board and match these direction arrows up to make "combos". A potentially fun concept but it really struggles in its execution.
A lot of different arrow combinations means you are going to struggle early in the game when you don't have a good number of cards to draw from. This is a problem because that moment when you place the cards perfect and get a nice combo together, you get that warm fuzzy feeling and it is the primary draw of a game like this. Those moments however, will be few and far between in the early going. This leaves the user with a sense of confusion and lack of will to keep trying to better their decks.
I may perhaps have a higher standard of TCGs, as I'm a long time player of games like Magic, 7th Sea, and others. You may find some enjoyment here that I could not, especially if you are willing to tough it out in the early going.  If not however, you will be very disappointed in the games fun factor.

Honestly, my recommendation is drawn straight down the middle on Brothers.
On one hand, it tells a unique story through gameplay and gameplay alone, and always varies up each and every encounter in the story. While the world is nicely populated with different environments, the digital scenery is nothing more than a backdrop for the gameplay. You play as both Orange and Blue (their real names are simlish and thereforehard to pronounce), with each brother being controlled by either an analog stick or wasd/up-down-left-right on your keyboard. The mechanics are a bit jarring at first, but the game's puzzles are surprisingly intuitive and you will be zipping through the obstacles like a pro in under an hour. The camaraderie of the brothers comes through as you see them working together to solve puzzles, help people and defeat bad guys, and they're fun to watch in play, even if they control oddly. In this regard, Brothers is one of the few games that does storytelling through its gameplay and its gameplay alone - no "Thomas Was Alone" or "Bastion" narration, no brain dump curscenes, what you play is what you get.
On the other hand, it is a game where the controller is the crutch of the storytelling. You will want to punch the wall if you play with the keyboard - the game is built around this mechanic where only the triggers and the analog sticks are used in gameplay. Using WASD while holding the CTRL or SHIFT key is probably the equivalent of Twister for your fingers, and I recommend you find a compatible controller for playing. That said, the game's use of the controller's rumble feature in a post-climactic scene is extremely powerful, and the game's mandatory requirement of a controller will be absolutely worth it.
Brothers is a game that knows who it wants to target - it targets the indie game fan, the core gamer looking for something new, and it is definitely a niche product that may not please the crowd. It tells a simple story, and fortunately it does it in an interesting and entertaining manner.
As such, I recommend this game, but only under the condition that you a) Buy a controller for this fascinating experiment, and b) Are looking for an alternative to your "hardcore" gaming diet.

There does not appear to be a widescreen option; the game seems visually optimized for a rather small 4:3 display, which strikes me as very odd, as 16:9 has been the PC industry standard for damn near a decade now. There's no borderless window mode, fullscreen mode is locked at a painfully low monitor resolution, and windowed mode only allows several preset window sizes. If this were a port of a mobile game I would understand, but it was apparently designed with Unity specifically for Windows/OS X/Linux, so I'm not sure what gives. Oh well. Still looks halfway decent.

Firstly, to set the record for anyone who doesn't know - THIS GAME IS NOT IN BETA. Cash Shop that asks for extreme amounts of dollar are not in Beta. Secondly, EARLY ACCESS, false claim as well.
As for the game itself, it handles strongly with its mechanics, with dense shrubbery and forestry, fog effects, explosions, exhaust from your vehicle, etc. Vehicle play is strong, and can be an experience to have.
Unfortunately, downfalls within the game are its weapons and imbalance spread across SMGs, MGs, Vehicles, and so on.
The "grind" as it is called, is a strong, and long one, especially if you're not winning battles. This will severly hamper your progression to get vehicles, weapons, and rank, which is highly discouraging, demoralizing, and utterly redundant, which would completely ruin gameplay.
The Germans are the most frequently populated faction, with the United States as the second, and Soviet Union (USSR) as the third. This basically sets the theatre as the Germans (usually) winning the "War". There is strong faction bias within the game, and Germany sets the table by having more armor choices, bigger playerbase, and so on. If you intend on playing other factions frequently, such as the U.S. and USSR, prepare for underpopulated games lacking in infantry and other types of ground/air support, which severly hampers your ability to either defend or attack on two fronts (for some assault maps).
Some parts of the playerbase are highly toxic, featuring racism, sexism, discrimination, hate speech, and more, to extreme levels. Others play the game in an "extreme hardcore" style, by trying to win the battle in any means through spawn camping, "vehicle rushing" to eliminate friendly armor, and using weapons that are much more competitive than the ones you start with from each faction (e.g. Sniper Rifles (with scopes), automatic rifles and SMGs).
In addition to that, a starting player will be solely equipped with their initial rifle and a grenade, lacking essentials like a melee weapon (for hand-to-hand combat) and Anti-Tank/Anti-Vehicle (for combatting armor and vehicles alike), and for some maps, a vehicle (because bicycles and "civilian" trucks do not spawn everywhere), which puts one at a disadvantage in the battlefield, making the player less versatile, less mobile, and less adaptable to the current combat scenario.
I have picked up and dropped this game frequently to see how it has aged, and, truly has gotten better since its raw release, but still contains complete mishaps like the playerbase, faction imbalance, amongst other problems.

You're probably here because you played one of the other Elder scrolls games and wonder, "Is Morrowind worth it?" The short answer is: Yes. This game is vastly different from the sequals of it in many ways, from flight spells, to spears and halbirds, and the skills and armors avalable. Its actually possible to use the unarmored skill to make cloths a viable option.
Positives of Morrowind:
-Spell crafting system greatly simalar to oblivions
-Enchanting system that is the best i've ever seen
-Vast world with many, MANY things to do
-Music that will remind one of Skyrim, and is well done.
-Unique spells not found in other games, like the aforementioned levitation spell
-Class system that is more in depth than Oblivions, with Major, minor, and Misc. skills, along with greater racial differences and powers. This allows more role play and immersion.
-Different and cool factions to join, like the Imperial legion, imperial cult, fighters guild, mages guild, thieves guild, the three vampiric clans, the tribunal temple and probably more. The fighters guild alone took me 25 hours to get to Guildmaster, and i left 10 or so quest behind
-Probably many more, but this keep this short.
Negatives of morrowind:
-2002 graphics cause a less than desired world and character aesthetic. Still, not horrid.
-Combat system isnt as fluid as oblivions or skyrims, but some like it. Mainly due to its flexibility or, how broken it can be, especially if you stack effects.
-Steep learning curve
-no compass or objective marker, one must follow directions.
-buggy as all balls, my save got corrupted and then uncorrupted in two days, not to mention the pathing system.
--nearly all problems with Morrowind can be fixed with mods, so there really isnt any reeason not to buy it and install any mod you like, like skywind to fix the combat, or the unofficial patch to fix the rampent bugs. Maybe even a graphics overhaul to make the game not look like a painted potato.
Overall, Morrowind is a classic definatley worth getting, with a great many differences to the other games, giving it a unique experiance unlike any other RPG before, or after it. A true Masterpiece.

Rating: 9/10
Genre: Third Person survival horror
The Good:
+ The pre-rendered backgrounds still look gorgeous which really add to the haunting atmosphere
+ Solving puzzles, exploring, opening new shortcuts around the mansion feels very satisfying. The mansion is well designed even though certain rooms/areas make no sense.
+ Combat feels rewarding, headshot a zombie with a shotgun feels great in addition to every other weapon
+ Multiple gameplay modes, real survivor, invisible enemies etc. that add to the replay factor
+ A choice between camera relative and character relative (tank) controls. Though the game was designed around character relative controls, those that never grew up with this game will find greater comfort with camera relative controls.
+ A choice between two playable characters, each one has a different variation on the story and outcomes. The choices you make within the game also affect cutscenes and boss battles later.
+ A Mod that removes door opening animations, though some purists will argue against this
The Average:
+/- Voice acting is hilariously bad but its also part of the charm
+/- Certain background textures look blurry
+/- Certain camera angles can be confusing
+/- Highly recommended that you use a controller
Conclusion:
This game is about managing your resources given a limited inventory space, i.e do you shoot the zombie or conserve your ammo for a later time?  Do you use a health item to free up more inventory space or do you run back to an item box to store your goods? Decisions like this when you first play the game is what makes this so rewarding.
This is one of my favorite survival horror games of all time. Playing it for the first time on Gamecube way back when was a joy and having the ability to replay it on steam is even better.

Spore has always been a fantastic game for me, my brother, sister, even our friends to create wacky creatures and enjoy the content at which Spore provided, I don't know anyone who dislikes this game! I will admit, once you get to the space stage there's nothing much going on other than the infamous ("Grox") or whatever.. Here are some of our thoughts on how Spore could have been improved overall as a game:
* Bigger planets and better customization of nests, villages, towns, etc.
* Weather effects on the planet, if you're in a snowy plains your creature could potentially freeze to death if it hasn't evolved to such a degree making life on your planet a treacherously hazardous one indeed!
* A lot more customizability, it's one of the biggest things keeping Spore alive to date and we all agree we wish there was more to the whole customization of it all so we could create our amazing potential top of the food chain ruler of the Galaxy.
* More to the whole space stage, you work so hard to get to it and you're not even a quater of the way finished.. the space stage is so long, tedious, and perpetual a lot more customizability and content could really go into improving it. Perhaps something like orbital space cannons that defend the planet you place them around; having alien ships drop off tanks and troops to overall make the invading of another planet more interesting; the mining of planets and stars for steady cash flow to fund your endeavors in this empire of yours and beyond! Having to do all the work to make money while also defending and invading planets over time especially with as many as you encounter and in the distance you encounter them in simply put becomes ludicrous insanly fast.. like come on, defend yourselves for once! The player shouldn't always be required to save a planet from some kind of mythical disaste only they can stop apparently.
* The ability to forge numbers in your army to send armies of troops to invade/defend planets for you without you having to even leave the star system you're currently in.
* Have freight shipments go to and collect your resources for you automatically based on the number of freight ships you have available.
Well those were some of the ideas we discussed.. overall, game's worth a play in my opinion and was a fantastic game for its generation. ;)

Machinarium is not a cult classic, but I think it deserves to become one. Why? Because everything it does it does
.
The plot is overly simple – you play as a little robot in a world of robots, and your goal is to stop local criminals from bombing the main tower. No one has any spoken dialogue, but as you play you'll quickly realize that, unlike most adventure games, in Machinarium the story doesn't matter at all. Instead it focuses on the quirky world around you, and believe me, there is
to see. The little dog which can be lured by machine oil, the living wrench with an attachment to his radio, the (literal) fan who wants you to solve his riddles… Or how about a robotic church? But what really makes it all work is Machinarium’s beautiful art style. It’s incredibly charming in its uniqueness, and at the same time each screen (and I do mean each one of them) is so detailed it could be used as a wallpaper.
The game is pretty short, but don’t be fooled thinking it’s also easy. If you’re not a fan of puzzles, then, sad as it might be, Machinarium is not for you – solving puzzles is what you’ll be doing most of the time, and some of them (especially mini games) are pretty hard. There is an in-game solution for almost everything, but you’ll have to play another mini game to get that. But if this type of gameplay doesn’t turn you off, or if you even enjoy racking your brains, then you should absolutely buy Machinarium – I promise that you won’t be disappointed.

Alicemare is an adventure fortunately with very little adventure game logic. Adventure game logic is the primary reason that I generally tend to dislike adventure games. You play Allen (though you'll spend half the game being called Alice). You're at some kind of boarding school(?) where you hang out with other problem children with horrors in their pasts. Apparently this "Nightmare Syndrome" is killing people in their sleep. You... somehow... find a way to enter the dream world. Then you adventure game it up to solve puzzles. As you solve these puzzles, you are rewarded with little cutscenes that tell you the backstory to the other children at this boarding school. It's a good design choice for character exposition because instead of an exposition dump you get to live the life through the child's eyes. Almost makes you feel sorry for the kids, as they all have somewhat uncomfortable backgrounds. But hey, the game has "Horror" as a tag, so ya get what you saw on tin, amirite?
There's a white rabbit and a cheshire cat but that's really about where the similarities with "Alice in Wonderland" end, after the name.
Honestly, I don't like the execution. The art for some of the maps feels a little too "RPG Maker-esque" if that makes sense. Not only that, but some of the maps themselves feel a little too "RPG Maker-esque". I remember there was this one time where I had to walk through an entire maze which was pretty much copy/pasted rock sprites. I would've been more satisfied with a solid looking wall. The guy did LiEat as well and there was a maze section in the game that could've been handled better too. But if I recall correctly, that was something like a series of wooden floors with a black background and glowing lights. It had more ambience than this.
The game is filled with little puzzles. There was a literal copy/paste of the Wolf-Lamb-Cabbage bridge puzzle. There were a couple of math puzzles. A murder mystery with very little mystery. A spot-the-difference game, can you believe it? I think of these as gimmicks that serve only as barriers between me and story progress. The adventure game puzzles were a better way to progress.
Let's see, since I know the guy's past work LiEat, allow me to compare the two. First - the characters in LiEat were far more interesting. I think if you contrast Alicemare to LiEat, you get a game that's about a setting rather than about characters. In my opinion, LiEat is the far superior one. While the battles were kind of a waste of time, I feel like the characters and story are better explored in LiEat than they are in Alicemare. On top of that, the deduction game was a better way to move me between set-pieces than a stupid spot-the-difference game. LiEat had more interesting characters overall.
The game is short, and I'll edge on the side of the recommend because it does have its appeal. The art direction and music are well done. I guess My problem is that the story just feels so weak and even at the end I wasn't satisfied. Maybe a sequel will come out, as it did with LiEat. The characters are forgettable, possibly because they were flat characters upon introduction with the purpose of being fleshed out during gameplay. But nothing really stands out. There's nothing that says "Yes, this character had this happen to them and that's why they're a massive tosser". There's just "I am a tosser and this happened in my past".
Overall, I give it a pass but only just.

ibb & obb is a co-op puzzle game that unfortunately
for regular play. There is a local co-op mode where you technically can control both characters at the same time but unless you want to stress yourself out multi-tasking, this puzzle game should be played with two people.
The game shares quite some elements with Portal, with the similar portals and the momentum building, as well as the co-op aspect. If you enjoy co-op puzzles like in Portal 2, it's likely you'll enjoy ibb & obb as well.
You play as ibb & obb, traversing a land with two parallel dimensions, and solving puzzles with the help of one another and with some familiar portal physics. In this game, there are colored portals, and only either ibb & obb can go through them depending on the color. This means you two have to cooperate and synergise to get to places that are inaccessible alone.
The game has a minimalistic art style which looks really sleek and works really well. This is accompanied by an awesome soundtrack which further enhances the atmosphere of the ibb & obb world. ibb & obb are also really adorable with their wide-eyed walking blob forms.
The difficult scales really well as the game progresses, from simple and easy-to-understand puzzles, to insanely complex and challenging ones. There are a lot of timing and execution-centered puzzles as well, which might be bad thing depending on your preferences.
When I played with my friend, there were some minor bugs such as the camera following one character and completely ignoring the other character (only if you manage to glitch it out), but this only happened once or twice.
Overall, I would definitely recommend this game to those who enjoy 2D puzzle games in general. It's a seriously awesome co-op game to get together with a friend to play, but do be prepared for quite a bit of raging at the execution-based puzzles!

I'm sort of split on this game. In the end I really like it and I had a lot of fun with it on pc and ps3. I dropped a ton of hours into it on ps3 and decided to get the pc version with my friends so we can all play since they didn't have a ps3. The main problem with this game game is that it's a lot of fun with friends, but single player is really lacking. I'm going to strip the Resident Evil tag off this game for a minute and just explore what the game itself contains without a franchise looming over it's expectations.
You choose from six operatives, each with unique abilities. Throughout the game you can purchase new weapons or upgrades for each characters abilities. This adds some replayability but the game itself seems like it was flawed on release. I may seem to be harsh on this game but in the end I will say why I recommend it still, I just feel you should have the full knowledge of what to expect. For my example, I'll just give a run of how a level normally goes.
First off, let's say you want to play online campaign. You will select join game, then after a few minutes you will get thrown into single player since no one plays this game anymore. If you are lucky, you will find a room with just one other person or two. Either way, the level starts, you select a character. The first thing you'll notice is the awkward controls. I highly recommend a controller for this game as the keyboard is very difficult to get used to for this pc port.
What you may learn also after getting the controls somewhat down is that enemies have switched roles with you. The zombies themselves are easy enough since you can 1 hit kill them with grapples and special attacks, but instead of the player being a bullet sponge and the enemies being made of paper, enemies can take rounds to the face and shrug them off like you were shooting spitballs. Meanwhile one bullet to your body and your health depletes more than half. You can do a 1 hit kill move if you get close enough, but getting that close is near impossible without taking a round to the face and dying. This is definately a game where you have to learn to take things slow. It can get fustrating for new players or people used to a more fast paced action experience. I guess you could consider it somewhat tactical, but simple cover based shooting is hardly a comparison to true tactics. I don't mind the challenge too much but that's just me.
As for bugs, they exist and you may encounter them. They aren't as frequent as a Bethesda game, but they happen. One time a boss was supposed to appear but never did, forcing me to quit the level. Another time I was supposed to activate a garage door to open it, but the prompt never showed up so we all had to quit on that as well. It's not horrible, as I said they happen rarely, but it's still something that shouldn't of been overlooked in development.
Speaking of development, this game is unfinished. There is a character named Spectre you can play as. At one point in the story line, you have the ability to activate a computer to shut down all generators. He is the only character capable of doing this (it's not very useful since you can just shoot the generators) but this implies that Capcom had intentions of having certain character only interactions with the environment throughout certain levels. No other option exists in the game for any character so it was obviously cut from the game. This kinda sucks as it makes characters less unique. On a side note, if you get the expansion dlc levels where you play as the BSA team, this idea is implemented. So Capcom did probably have intentions to have this in the base game but cut it.
Graphics wise, its ok. For me it works fine but I know my friends had a hard time running this game. The optimization isn't the best so for lower end computers it can get very sluggish. Sound wise the game is fine as well. Guns make gun noises, zombies moan, your character makes sounds when shot; the usual. Nothing exceptionally fancy.
So far it may seem I've been bashing the game. But there is some things I like. For one, the characters are cool. Their whole persona is let's work together just to get things done. There is no romance, no true friendship, just business. Sadly there personality isn't dipped into much, usually only side comments being made that make their personality, which I feel is appropriate because there not supposed to be the chatty friendly type. Also I'm a sucker for co-op orientated games. If you actually utilize a characters abilities you can pull off some fun gameplay. One of you can go invisible and sneak behind the enemy while one cover fires. You can human shield a zombie, while your teammate throws a sticky bomb onto it, then you throw the zombie into a group of enemies and watch them explode. You can make your own fun somewhat, but as I stated in my first paragraph, this requires human players as A.I. bots don't do any of this. Lastly the gameplay can be interesting. You can human shield an enemy, kick him down to his knees and choose to shoot his head or shoot his stomache to cause him to bleed (bleeding makes it so zombies quickly rush to you and attack, useful for distractions), there is an array of weapons to use like rifles, smgs, shotguns, machine guns, and sniper rifles, and finally special abilites. It would take forever to list special abilites in detail but a few worth noting is one character can disguise as the enemy and roam freely behind enemy lines causing havoc. Another can shoot the zombie virus into a non undead enemy and turn him into a zombie. or shoot an infected enemy to control it. One character even has the support role, where she can shoot darts that buffs teammates.
There is a versus mode online where it's pvp, but to be honest, it's horrible. People abuse cheap mechanics and there isn't much to it. The game is mostly about the co-op storyline element, and the pvp was slapped on because every game now days needs some pvp gameplay.
In the end I do recommend this game. I stated early that I took the Resident Evil tag off this game and judged it without that title. If you look at it from that perspective, it's not a horrible game, it's not polished, but its cooperative content can make you have fun with it. If you add the franchse tag back onto it, I think it lets us know Capcom was trying a new idea. It didn't go perfect, but it was a nice idea.  I enjoy the characters, the atmosphere, the challenge, and if you get the DLC, the game is much better since Capcom took there actual time with that. Either way if you can get a group of three friends to get this game on sale with you, it can be a lot of fun regardless if you are into Resident Evil or not.
tldr, get on sale with three friends. It's not the best game of it's kind but its unique in itself and can offer some fun gameplay if you take advantage of what the game gives you.

Slant Six Games tried, but they were not up to the task to create an interesting and compelling third-person shooter with Operation Raccoon City. The classes, weapons, and their unlock system are great, but the stages are boring and the campaign has no real story.
Operation Raccoon City has become quite infamous since its release as the worst Resident Evil game ever made. While it is far from the truth, it is also undeniable that ORC has enormous issues.
The first big problem is that the campaign is criminally short: the par time on its seven missions is barely three and a half hours (granted, the Echo Six DLCs double its length). It has to rely on an unlock system for replay value, where you can grind XP to buy dozens of weapons and skills for each individual character class. This system is common in shooters, but few of them have ORC’s balance. Every class brings a unique set of special skills (although only a handful of them are useful in single-player), and the weapons—except for some infamous DLC additions—cater to many play styles.
Still, good mechanics mean nothing when the level design boils down to copying the same room repeatedly on each stage. Combat is even worse: when we are not fending off the same zombie horde, we participate in generic third-person cover-based shooting against even more generic human soldiers.
Not even the story tries to justify our endless quest for the next set of chest-high walls, because apart from the mission briefing and debriefing screens, there is no plot. The original selling point, promising us the chance to hunt down some famous RE characters thanks to ORC’s non-canon status, is a lie as well. All we get is a 30-second encounter and one large shootout at the very end. Not only it feels like being cheated, but it also shows how lazy the writing got, also reflecting ORC's overall quality.

Card City Nights is a card collecting and battling game where you build a deck to defeat enemies, collect randomized card boosters, and improve your deck to take on tougher enemies. This genre of game is one of my favorites, as were Magic: the Gathering: Shandalar and Pokemon Trading Card Game for Game Boy Color. So few of these games are made nowadays that really, I'll take whatever I can get, so when I saw this game on sale for $2, I jumped on it.
In the card game, you place cards on a 3x3 grid. Link arrows on the cards to make combos, which can lock down your opponents cards, release your own, boost your life total, or hurt your opponent. You win by reducing your opponent to 0 or by making them unable to play by filling up their grid or depleting their deck. The nice thing is that the game is fairly elegant, and most of the game's strategies involve using relatively simple cards. The strategy in deck building comes from putting together a good theme and making sure you can get the arrows to line up properly. There are a lot of card with powerful abilities that are rendered near useless because they only have one arrow.
As for the rest of the game, it's clear that this game was meant to celebrate this developer's previous titles. The only one of those games I had played (or heard of) previously was the fairly good Zelda clone, Ittle Dew, so I got a few of the self-referential jokes. Even if you're not in on the references, though, and I doubt you will be, this game has a lot of goofy humor, between the bizarre characters and funny backgrounds. I thought the music in this game was fine, with the exception of one or two tracks thay annoyed me. The art style is very cartoony and drawn in very thick lines, and I think the graphics work well enough. I would have liked a few more choices for your avatar, though.
Overall, Card City Nights is a pretty solid card game and an amazing bargain at $4. If you enjoy collectible card games, then this is definitely worth picking up and playing for a few hours.

I picked this game up because I love trading card games. I've played a lot of YU-GI-OH back in the day and quite a lot of Magic the gathering and I'm familiar with a few other TCG's like Pokémon and Duelmonsters and this game is really cheap. I'll admit right away that I didn't really like the game because this card game is not my cup of tea but I can imagine there are a lot of TCG fans out there that will like it.
The game pretty much is a card game, you battle opponents, gain boosterpacks to change your deck  and earn money to buy cards so you can take on stronger opponents. The game does have a storyline, all I know about it is that you have to collect the 8 legendary cards by defeating the holders of those cards so you can take on the champion of the game, but it's a card game so no need for a fancy story there anyway.
Its kinda hard to explain how the card game works so it might be better looking up some gameplay videos but I'm gonna try anyway. Both players start with 7 shields (hp). You win the game if your opponent drops to 0 shields or if he can't play anymore cards. The playingfield consists of 3 by 3 spaces where you can play your cards, the goal is to create a combo of 3 cards and that will trigger a certain effect based on the types of the cards used in the combo which I'll explain later on. You must play one card a turn and you cannot remove any of the cards on the playingfield so if you donnot make combinations you'll run out of spaces and lose the game.
There are 4 types of cards: defensive, offensive, revive and neutral. If you make a combination using 3 defensive cards you gain 3 shields, if you make a combination using 3 offensive cards you can deal 3 damage to the shields of your opponent or disable one of his cards on the playingfield, if a card is disabled it cannot be used for combinations and it just stays on the playingfield. Use a combination of 3 revive cards and you can re-enable a disabled card and neutral cards don't have any effect and are just used for making combinations. The way combinations are made is rather interesting. You can combine all 4 types of cards in the combinations, for example you can use 2 offensive cards and 1 defensive card in a combination, but ony one effect can happen based on the most cards of a single type within the combination so that means this combo does damage but does not give you additional shields and because there are only 2 offensive cards in the combo it only does 2 damage. The position of the cards on the playingfield also plays a role, the playingfield consists of 3 by 3 spaces and there are arrows on every card indicating in what directions they can make combo's, for example you place a card in the centre of the playingfield and it has 2 arrows, 1 pointing up and 1 pointing left. That means it can only make a combination with cards placed above or on the left of this card if however that card also has an arrow pointing towards it. I hope that kind of explained how the game works.
The reason why I give the game a recomendation is because the card game is solid and I cannot deny that. Because it wasn't my cup of tea doesn't mean I cannot recomend it to others especially because it's cheap and solid. I won't give it a rating though because I would give it a low rating because there wasn't much fun to be had for me personally and I rate games based on the fun factor. If you like TCG's you should definitely try it because there is a fair chance you will like it and it's only 4 bucks (if not on sale). They're practicly giving it away.

I knew and admired Amanita Design ever since the first Samorost webgame, and Samorost 2 was a great sequel, so when they came out with Machinarium, their first full-length game, I expected nothing less than something great.
But what I discovered was far above all my expectations. With seemingly simple tools in a 2d world, Czech artist Jakub Dvorský and his team create a live, beautiful and magically strange world with so much detail you'll want to explore every pixel of it, and you will be well rewarded to do so.
Characters are colourful and charming, interactions are fun, puzzles interesting, animations fluid, each location is wonderfully detailed, and a touching little story is told without a single spelled word. Great sound design adds layers to the atmosphere, and the music... Well, the music just sticks with you. To this day, every time I turn on the OST by Tomáš Dvořák I still get those magical chills.
This game is a 100% proof that videogame design is/can/should be an art.
PS> very enjoyable with a girlfriend, wife or kids.

.
