I better start off with this: I was recommended to play this by TotalBiscuit, as I had seen his 'WTF is' before I played the game. He said that this game might be the best game ever made in his opinion, and I started the game with that in mind.
Now, as to whether or not this is the best game ever made, I will let that be up to you, but I can say that I don't think it's the best game ever made.
It was a really nice movie.
Yea thats pretty much my opinion  There isn't a whole lot of actual gameplay in the game, it is mostly running from point A to B, get up this cliff, get over this bridge. And the gameplay that was there, could be a bit confusing, because you had to control two characters at once. It was pretty easy to get past, and the times I got confused wasn't really enough to pull me out off the game.
I think this game could be defined as a story driven puzzle game, although the puzzles wasn't all that hard, and more often than not, they were very simple. I didn't really encounter a puzzle that really had me think, and all of them was pretty much obvious. The gameplay of this title is in my opinion the weakest part of this game, and it is pretty weak. If the story and world hadn't been there I would say it was a pretty bad game.
Speaking of the world. I got sort of a Zeno Clash vibe from the world, because it had the same way of having wierd animals, trolls, and oversized buildings lying around. It had sort of the same psychedelic dream setting, although not anyway near as weird as Zeno Clash. I really liked the setting, and the game uses a system with some benches that function as vistas as you sit on them, to show off the world.
The world definitely had a lot of wackiness to it, and the chapters where sort of themed, as you pass through the different areas.
The graphics wasn't anything good, and it was obvious to see that the game is optimised for xbox (although I have heard it shouldn't run all that well on xbox). Textures weren't all that high quality, but that didn't really matter as the art style is a cartoonish style. Although it came for xbox first, the pc port, if it even is a port, is pretty good. I had a steady 60 fps all the way through, and not a single lag spike.
As for the controls I personally played with a controller, which seems to work the best as well  but I tried the keyboard controls and they seem to play just fine, so really don't HAVE to play with an xbox controller but it is recommended.
I saved the best for last: the story.
The story is definitely the strongest part of the game. The story is really good, and Starbreeze somehow managed to convey the whole thing without a single real word. All spoken language in the game is pretty much gibberish (it might be a real language, but you aren't expected to understand anything from it). Even though everything said is gibberish, it is really easy to understand the messages conveyed between the characters of the game. And there is absolutely no problems in understanding the story.
The story is very emotional, but it didn't make me cry, as it did TB (guess people really are different after all ;)). Although single manly tear at the ending.
So is this worth buying. In a way, you can think of as this: it is pretty much the price you would pay to go see a new movie in the theaters  so if you are looking for a great story, in a game Wahtzy could beat in 2 hours 33 minutes, this would be worth it. If you are looking for an actual game, I would say this isn't worth the full price, and if you aren't interested in story at all I would say you should pretty much just avoid it. As for replayability, I only managed to get a single achievement, so I guess there is a reason to play through it a second time.
TL;DR:
If you are looking for a movie length game with a great story then BUY IT.
If you are looking for a game to play, secondarily with a good story, then: Buy it when its on sale.
If you are looking a game, but aren't interested in story at all: AVOID.

Card City Nights might be the best adventure game about playing a card game since Pokemon Trading Card Game for the Gameboy Color.
I play a lot of games and most of them I don't play for very long. I am a casual player and don't have the patience for anything "hardcore" or otherwise overly time consuming. So I usually play fairly shallow "casual" games and then figure out what the mechanics are and get bored, or I try deeper games and then the difficult ramps up too high for casual play.
So far this has been a game which I keep going back to because the difficulty ramps up gradually, introducing interesting variations on the core mechanic. For instance, I built an attack-heavy deck and was coasting through most battles until I got to an opponent that had a better attack-oriented deck than mine. I was at an impasse, but then one of the characters recommended that I try going for disabling cards instead of dealing direct damage. Great suggestion! Now I'm thinking future opponents will try this strategy on me and I'm considering adding more revival-type cards to my deck. What I appreciate about this game is that it's got me thinking about strategies without going into hardcore deck building territory. However, it's not a shallow game like you find with, for instance, most mobile games. There's a story, characters, and a progression of mechanics so you're not just playing the same board over and over. It's the perfect mix of narrative and strategic depth with casual play.
I got this game on sale on a whim and now I wish there was a Kickstarter because I'd like to give them 10x what I paid so that they will make more games like this. I guess I will just go buy all their other games too! Good job you guys, you've made a fan.

I like card games, but as I prefer single-player, don't want to spend money on extra cards, prefer simplicity, and like to take my time, there aren't too many games that fit the bill... but Card City Nights does!
CCN's gameplay is straightforward, with cards having defensive, attack, or neutral effects, as well a number of arrows. You have 5 cards in your hand at one time, and take turns with your opponent to place a card done on a grid.  Create combos of 3 or more by connecting arrows between cards. Place them carefully, as when you run out of spaces you'll lose the round.  Since HP is capped at 10 and there are penalties for running out of cards, each round goes fairly fast and you won't get into stalemate situations.  It may not be as strategically deep as other card games where you have to manage resources etc., but it's easy to pick up, and fun.
In between card battles, you can organize your card decks, buy cards to augment your decks using virtual money (you can also get booster packs by battling, and there are no IAPs) and go around town to talk to other characters. The storyline is rather silly (but are you really playing a card game for the story?) and humourous.  The charmingly cartoony art fits the game well, as does the cheerful music.
My only drawback is that the AI appears to be on the easy side so far, but as I've not gotten too far yet this may be something that fixes itself later on.
Card City Nights may not be a super-challenging card game, but it's good for a breezy time of card-battling fun. For casual fans of the trading card genre, this could well hit the spot.
EDIT: as I've progressed, the game has indeed become a little more tricky. The developers have also released a patch that should make the AI stronger, so consider me a happy camper :)

One of the best and most addictive games I've played in ages. I was put off by the UI and graphical style somewhat when I first started, thinking, why waste the WW2 period by making things cartoony? But it grew on me, because while your soldiers may have large heads, they also die horrifically in plane crashes and get shot to bits and fall off the wings of the plane and burn to death and so on. The amount of gameplay you get for the price is more than worth it. There is a lot more content than I initially thought. I've put about 111 hours into the campaign since release, (probably ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t because I leave the game alt tabbed since it doesn't use many resources) and I still have not got all of the guns and other unlocks.
Like I said, while it may look simplified or cartoony, the landscape appears to be fairly accurate and planes customization and controls are fairly deep. Players must manage navigation, altitude, evasive maneuvers, fuel usage, boosting, radio and radar, ammo, repairs, operation of bomb bay doors, landing gears, reloading of guns as well as temperature and oxygen. Planes have many different categories of upgrades or sidegrades allowing you to attempt different tactics and plane configurations. Upgrades include things like armoring or lowering the weight of every individual section of the plane, (E.g. tail, mid rear, mid, wings, front, nose), as well as upgrading of guns, electric systems, hydraulic systems, equipment racks, engines, engine extinguishers, and survival devices.
Planes can also be cosmetically altered with a cool ingame drawing system that allows you to make your own decals. The drawing system could be a little better to be honest but it's still really cool that it's in the game. I love any time a game allows you to do something creative in the game world like Rust's painting system and this is similar. I would love it if you could import decals or images from online as well or if the drawing system simply was refined to look less scratchy/aliased. 6 or 7 Decals are also included by default and there are a decent variety of typical things of the era and I wish there were more but at this price, it's fine.
Soldiers can be customized as well in terms of equipment and name but sadly you cannot change their hair, hair color, facial hair, skin color, face or gender. So if you were planning on making your crew resemble your best friends or relatives or characters from movies and so on, well, you'll either have to intentionally allow them to die until you get the right one or wait until they add it.
If you don't want the details really, I guess I would summarize it as:
If you liked FTL, or X-Com, or any other tactical strategy game featuring permadeath of soldiers, and you like the WW2 setting you will love this game. If you like anything that people describe as a roguelite, you will probably have fun with this.
If you are looking for a good blend of relaxing but focused cruising gameplay spaced out by tense but satisfying battles, this is the game for you. If you like the feeling of stepping into a game and experiencing total chaos and then perservering through it to master it and finally experience everything working in order and efficiency, this is the game.

Cubic Castles is a better choice of the many Free to Play MMOs, but it has many things that rightfully turn serious MMO players away. The first of which being that this game is very light on RPG elements. There is a level system, and experience toward each next level is earned through small daily quests which usually involve mining for blocks and materials, or crafting certain items. With each new level up comes a perk to add to your character that improves your abilities slightly. That's... it.
Second reason is that you have no real goal, just do as you like. As any good sandbox game should have, you are given a starting world or "Realm" to customize with any blocks you have and make it your own. However, ever since this game started on Steam the population of this game became extremely crowded and it's hardly possible to make your Realm accessible because there's ♥♥♥♥ing castles everywhere in the overworld. So there is the potential possibility of not being able to access your own Realm at all if you were to start fresh within the couple months.
Lastly, this game is full of KIDS. Hundreds of thousands of kids. It wasn't when I first started this game when it launched on Steam. With all these kids comes many bad encounters if your focus in this game to build cool Realms or host your own store, you may have a tough time. You can easily be scammed. Thankfully over the many months this game has been alive, the developers have made transactions and trades between players much more safe.
Now, if you can look past these three main things, you may have a decent time playing Cubic Castles! Mining for materials isn't too bad, building is simple, crafting is smart and fairly complex, and there's always some entertaining things being said in the global chat. Although most people don't realize they're throwing away the in game currency every time they write "Hi :3" in the global chat, you have every right to point and laugh. Whether you wanna explore, build up a huge wealth, create obstacle courses, or run your own store, there's something for everyone. Just be friendly and take passion in your work.
Now then, I'll let you know that my partner Mario! and myself, Luigi!, are building a Super Mario Bros. themed obstacle course. It's still in constuction but will be done soon, so if you find us around in the near future, be sure to check it out.

Played this with mods and just couldn't get into it. That being said I respect it as a legendary game. I just think that it would be difficult for many people to get into for any number of reasons that you probably already know.
This is for people who want to really delve into lore and try to figure everything out on their own. It doesn't hold your hand. It takes committment and lots of time, which I don't have. It FEELS old, which it is. I was expecting this. When I played the game, my expectations were confirmed within a couple hours. I got it for under $5, so I won't complain. I was expecting what I got. I wouldn't recommend paying more than a few dollars just for the novelty of experiencing this old game and comparing it to their newer titles like Oblivion and Skyrim.
There is a cult of gamers who believe that old games are good BECAUSE they're old. They talk about how new games are so much crappier than old games (which they are for the most part), but I believe that Oblivion and Skyrim were actually PROGRESS. I know that they have less quests and there is far more handholding, but I actually have fun when I play them. I couldn't have fun in Morrowind. I just couldn't. The game wasn't difficult to figure out, it was just clunky and boring to me. The combat is ridiculously unsatisfying, with nearly every sword attack missing. This is an actual rng mechanic. Even with high agility I was still missing. It's simply not as realistic as their later games that include hitboxes. Yes, you have less quests in Skyrim, but the game is easy to get into... I already have a job and college, I don't want my game time to feel like a job, but that's just me.
It's a good game, but I couldn't possibly recommend it, especially with a price that seems to be going up by the second, with a greedy studio attempting to milk it for all it's worth. The people glorifying this game played it when they were kids and fell in love with it the way I fell in love with Oblivion when I was 16. In my opinion, this game is going to mostly have value as a nostalgic revisting of the past, and I wouldn't recommend most modern gamers spend money on picking this up.
Again Morrowind fanboys, this is simply my personal opinion.

The magic system is still the best thing ever made in a computer game. You can create the most sick items and spells ever. And If you have high level spells you can do the most awesome things ever. You feel more powerfull than in any other Elder Scroll game.

It's more difficult than Skyrim and Oblivion, but in those game its almost impossible to get stuck in the story.
The only part that is hard, is exploring and knowing your way around. Just learn where the high level enemies are, avoid those areas and just complete the first main quest. The game will give you some direction, money. After those first quests your character's stats will explode and the game will get very easy, very fast.

Machinarium was the
, so I like to look at it as the start of my adventure behind the computer screen.
I think I was around 13 at the time. We didn't have a console or gameboy at home and the only previous contact I had had with games happened when I went to my friend's place to play FIFA on his PS2. I remember there was only one computer in my place and it was my dad's work laptop. We barely ever touched it.
One day my father came home with a usb pen which he took from a colleague by mistake. It had this game inside (probably an illegal copy). After having finished it, my dad gave me and my younger sisters permission to use his laptop to play Machinarium. He even encouraged us to play it, sort of like when he tried to convince us to read good books. This on itself tells a lot about the game, considering how conservative my father used to be when it came to video games.
Anyway, from then on we started gathering in front of the computer screen every day to play the game one hour each time. It was everyone's favourite part of the day. Everyone looked forward to the time just before dinner when my father used to get home. He'd open the laptop, launch the game and we'd all get absorbed by these
, the
and the
. Eventually my mom joined in and soon this became something we'd do as a family every day (we're five). Can you imagine five people in front of a laptop playing a point-and-click game? Ye, it's as weird as it sounds.
The interesting part is my parents don't even like video games or technology in general. They are bookworms more than anything else and for instance they are heavily against my usage of the PC for entertainment. But somehow... somehow this game captivated them. Somehow they were able (more like eager) to spend an hour of their busy lives to take part in this adventure. And the fact that I was able to immerse myself in this
together with my parents and sisters, makes me look back at this time of my life with fondness and gratitude. Fondness towards the fact that this game united my family and brought us closer together. And gratitude towards my father for having introduced me to video games in the best way possible... through a game with an
,
, a
(one of the best soundtracks I've heard) and
. This game will always have a special place in my heart and I couldn't recommend it more.
PS: I eventually bought this game on Humble Bundle to support the devs but I haven't played it since.
PS2: It's funny that the trigger that started my video game adventure 6 years ago was pulled by my parents, who were so against this kind of stuff to start with. Little did they know...

A perfect love letter for Resident Evil (the ones set in Raccon City) fans!!!
I am such a fan, I finished Resident Evil 1-3 like dozens of times, so due to those countless hours sunk into those games I feel I have an authority to judge this curious instalment in RE saga.
First and foremost... THIS IS NOT ANOTHER CANON RESIDENT EVIL GAME! Get it into your thick skulls you crazy purists!
This is a cooperative action game set in the Resident Evil universe. You can say this game is LEFT 4 DEAD: RESIDENT EVIL EDITION as the game is very similar in many core aspect of the gameplay:
- 4-player coop (bots are available and fill in empty slots)
- you progress through map by doing objectives
- you got 1 main weapon (shotgun, assault rifles, sinper rifles, SMGs, light machine guns) and 1 sidearms (all kinds of pistols)
- you fight zombies and many other special infected
- if you get down, other players must revive you
Of course it is not a complete 100% L4D copy! There are differences, the only big one being Third Person Perspective opposed to first person perspective in L4D. Some other diferrences that make the game even better then L4D:
- characters in game have different skills and abilities, you gain experience to level up your chatacter
- you can choose a gun when you start the map
- aside from monster enemies, you alos fight armed human enemies
- every time you get hit by zombie/monsters there is a chance you will get infected, if you wont cure the infection before your health runs out, you will become a raging zombie that will viciously attack your companions
But like I said before, there are so many main aspects of the game that are in common with L4D, you should treat it as this kind of game and not a typical RE game.
But that dosent mean it cannot be a survival horror!!! Just switch to the hardest difficulty and enjoy a true survival horror where you must use ammunition, gernades and health items wisely if you want to survive.
That is what this game is, and it is briliant. You can feel that people who created this game loved the Resident Evil games. There are so many details, some bigger and some smaller, that are directly showing this love to the original RE. Calling this game a spin-off would be too much as events in this game are completely different when it comes to some important parts. So I would call it an alternative reality in RE canon, where the events of Raccoon City outbreak occur as they did, but the military and Umbrellas private army had bigger roles in this event.
There are two sides, the BAD, being Umbrella corps, ruthless guns for hire that do the dirty work and cover up Umbrellas involvement in the incident and the GOOD, being special military unit Echo-6, whose mission is to uncover evidence of Umbrellas fault.
During missons you encounter characters from original RE. As the good guys you help Jill and Carlos fight Nemezis or you help Sherry when she gets separated from Claire in the sewers, you also accompany Claire while she is looking for Sherry. As the bad guys you accompany Hunk as he is about to steal T-Virus from doctor Birkin and you escape Umbrella labs being chased by his mutated version. You encounter Nicolai from RE3 and you chase down Ada Wong only to receive later on an order to... assasinate LEON KENNEDY!
So like I said this a perfect love letter to RE games and it should be treated like that, it is not canon, it is a 'what if' version of events. And as huge RE fan I love it and I think creators did a wonderfull job.
There are plenty of guns in the game, and also every member of the team have different abilities that they can use.
There are also many (if not all) iconic monsters from RE 1-3. You have standard zombies, zombie dogs, but also Lurkers and even TYRANT! And of course that is not all.
Being able to play up to 4 players and cooperatively playing the missions is a great fun, honestly I liked it even more then Left 4 Dead.
But there is bitter taste in all this tastefull cake... the game has horrible performance, no matter how good PC you have it will still run like sh*t most of the times, it is not unplayable but it is certainly a pain to play very often. The controls are also not very good when it comes to PC standards so many people can have issue with that but I, myself got used to them and they didnt bother me very much after some time.
If only Capcom had invested into getting the game more optimized and removed the GFWL service and replaced it with Steamworks, it would be a perfect game. So sad that they abandoned this game cause it could've been a great game and I would look so much forward to a sequel set in the newer RE games' universe.

Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is a beautiful game that keeps you fully engaged and immersed throughout the entire experience. It took about 3 hours to complete and is it was worth every penny. The game definitely knows how to pull on your heart strings.

Modern videogames struggle with the idea of marrying gameplay to narrative. More often than not, modern game stories end up feeling very detached from the core gameplay elements, making the overall experience feel unbalanced. Brothers manages to avoid this pitfall, leading by example and making its control scheme an  entirely integral piece of the overall narrative. Rarely does Brothers ever rip control away from the player for a flashy cutscene. You're free to experience the game's world, full of breath takingly beautiful and surreal sights and positively gorgeous musical cues, at your own pace.
The size and scope of Brothers' adventure is astonishing in and of itself. There's an honest sense of childlike wonder and fairy tale adventure seeping out of every locale and setpiece the game offers, and you're often encouraged to take your time and let the world and characters around you breathe, as evidenced by all the game's achievements being tied to simply exploring the world. Without ever saying a comprehendable word in any language at all, Brothers is able to communicate all it needs to the player without ever resorting to dialog boxes or tutorials. The world around you and characters' interactions with one another always provides enough context for you to know what's going on or what you need to do next.
As trite and silly as it may seem to say, Brothers is one of the truest examples of how to create expressive and emotionally engaging interactive fiction without sacrificing either side of the equation. Wholeheartedly recommended.
As emotionally effecting as it is mechanically resonant, the grim fairytale of Brothers sits up there with Journey as one of the best story-driven games of this generation.

Mouse sensitivity in tagging mode is ridiculously high, even if turned all the way down. And field of view in tagging mode is extremely limited. As a result of those two factors, the challenge isn't so much about getting your crew to be in the right place as getting lucky with FOV and then having the patience to inch your mouse - almost millimeter your mouse, actually - to get your target in view.
On top of this, when you are trying to tell your people what to do they frequently are not responsive. Want your crew member to pick up a medical kit to save his dying friend? Well, that's no problem actually. But now that he's holding it, want him to actually go resuscitate his companion who is bleeding out? Good luck finding the exact right pixel for that with your super-sensitive mouse. By the time you do, chances are it's either too late, someone else is bleeding to death, or, worst of all, something else needs to be tagged.
Not a good game in its current iteration, unless trying to keep a spotlight on a tiny, steadily moving target with a hyper-jittery mouse appeals to you. I may try this game again with the newly-implemented "slow time" feature - the idea is cool and the art is great - but for now this one rates "refund before I miss my refund window."

A really fun little card game, if you are just looking for something small to burn a few hours on this could be your thing.

It's a very simple card game: Lay and link 3 cards in your 3x3 grid to do damage, bring up your defense, or revive cards disabled by your opponent, with the goal of bringing your opponent down to 0 defense or eliminating their ability to play a card. All the usual tricks and tropes of collectible card games appear within a new construct for the dueling players format. Fans of popular indie games will enjoy all the references the story and cards have, especially those familiar with Ittle Dew. Purely single-player for the moment, and the AI is on the easy side for those looking a challenge, but the game itself is relaxing, refreshing, and straightforward. Definitely worth picking up for card game fans and newbies.

I've only ever played Skyrim from the Elder Scrolls series and I always heard people say that Morrowind was the best of them.  I don't understand it.
The UI is terrible.  Ten minutes into the game, I had 5 overlapping menus bound to right click. You literally have to drag items into your inventory unless you want 200 pairs of common pants.
You move SLOWLY.  I can't begin to tell you how long it felt slogging from the first town to the first quest point.  Apparently you can get faster over time, but I'm not snailing my way through this game to find out.  Before I quit for good, I put in a console command to up my speed to 500 and that was ok.  I reccomend you do the same if you buy it.
Combat is wierd.  Bows are mostly nonfunctional, at least in the early game.  If you are trying to shoot someone more than 3m away, you have ~5% chance to hit them.  Most of my shots went way wide from where my reticule was.  The blades aren't any more reliable.  I think I stabbed myself more than the enemies.
The landscape is dull and uninteresting.  As far as I can tell, and after upping my speed to 10000 I can tell a lot,  The landscape is an endless mush of softly undulating grey with nothing really interesting about it.
The game is unstable.  In the 1.5 hours I played, it crashed 5 times.  The two times I exited to look for help, it crashed and I had to kill it from task manager.
This is a game from 2002 and it shows.  If you've got nostalgia for it, that's one thing.  If not, I'd advise you to stay away.

No matter how long of a review I write, it is very hard to capture what type of game this is. First thing first, it will be a slight adjustment if you are coming from the modern Elder Scrolls games. One example of this is the combat. Since "Hitting" enemies is on a dice roll, you have to get better in a certain catagory of weopon to be effetive with it. Say if you have a skill of 50 in long blade. You'll hit people pretty consistently. However, if you try to use short blades with a skill of 10, you'll be lucky to give someone a papercut. Another adjustment, that in my opinion is the biggest one, is the fast travel. To be more specific, the lack of fast travel. To get around, you have to either A) Walk B) Take a Silth Strider. For Skyrim players, it's just a carriage that goes to more cities  or C) Take a boat along the coastal cities. Lastly, the story. In my opinion, it is the best story out of the 3 Elder Scroll Games I've played. It both acts as a tour for your stay in Vvardenfell, and as a catalist to show your progress. It's exaclty what a Open world story should be. If you're a fan of both The Elder Scrolls and older RPG's, then I can't recommend this enough.

It's been years since I last played Morrowind. While I enjoyed Oblivion and logged hundreds of hours in Skyrim on multiple platforms, this recent reload of Morrowind makes me realize it is truely far and above the 4th and 5th entries to the series. A far better magic system and generally more depth to character development are big reasons why this game is so far ahead of the later titles. However, the biggest areas where Morrowind outshines the rest in my opinion are story, lore, and atmosphere. Additionally, if you are familiar with Skyrim and Oblivion, prepare for a learning curve. This is a real RPG, the newer titles are moving towards action/adventure titles with RPG elements. There are no quest markers here. You get a journal which is updated with character dialouge that is deep and packed with lore. The quests are satifying and while there are multiple ways to fast travel you really end up feeling immersed in the world in a very satifying way when knocking out quests which require reading directions from one place to the next in the journal. The only downside to playing this game in 2017 are the dated graphics but mods make it look like a new game.
With Morrowind Graphics Extender XE running, the game truely still looks pretty good despite how old it is. We should all thank the mod community for keeping this title alive because while the story is ageless and the RPG elements are deep and satifying, the vanilla graphics are showing their age. MGEXE really brings this game up to playable standards and it becomes immersive once more. Play around with the graphics extender and get the shaders set up as you like then set the draw distance out as far as your system can handle (it's taxing). Getting all this set up should only take 15 mins or so then you will be ready to enjoy the best title in the series in a way that we couldn't in the early 2000's.

Bomber Crew is deceivengly cutesy, but brutally hard. It requres careful management of your resources, from money to bomber health to crew efforts to stay alive. It is hard, harder still if you slip hard enough to lose your entire crew and the bomber... But it's also incredibly rewarding to see the homebase again after an incredibly hard mission and escaping by the skin of your teeth. It may be best to wait a bit on earliest campaign missions, because taking your bomber to a mission it's not ready for will most likely result in you seeing it, along with whoever's left alive of your crew, fall to their fiery doom.
However, if played adequately, the game is a lot of fun. The feeling of surviving after a hard mission can only be compared to FTL or similar games when everything looked set for you to die, and yet you were able to escape and survive against all odds. A bit of careful planning, along with some grinding, can also mean the difference between the life and deaths of your crew. Do you waste fuel on navigating around the flak? Do you climb over it, risking to freeze or suffocate your crew? Or do you power on though it, risking it taking your bomber apart? The bomber upgrades will certainly help.
However, the skill of the crew can (and will) mean all the difference. Where a level 5 pilot will be shot down, a level 10 pilot will pull the bomber through with minimal damage. While a low-level gunner can be overwhelmed by fighters, a level 8 one can shoot down entire enemy fighter patrols before they so much as shoot a single bullet in your direction. This goes for every single member of your crew. Keeping the crew alive is even more important than keeping the bomber, and the game certainly helps with that... In an unusual fashion. Many will find that over time, they develop attachment to their flying coffin and her crew, much like (again) in FTL, but spending far more time with them and customising your flying tin can results in that attachment being far greater... And makes the game all the more fun when you defy the odds and do the impossible. Or all the more sad if you see your crew, with whom you've flown many successful missions, plunging to their doom.
Oh, and the plane visual customisation options are a lot of fun.

For such a simplistic game, Bomber Crew does a great job of getting you invested. Invested in playing, invested in your plane that you've meticulously upgraded piece-by-piece, invested in your crew, who you've seen grow from level 1 and into a squad of epic badasses who slaughter every challenge in their way to victory.
At first glance, I was unsure if I should buy Bomber Crew. No real direct flight control, seems way too management style during missions, and eveything is timed to make you fail. But, after giving it a go, I gotta say this is one of the hidden Best Games of 2017. After getting the ability to place custom waypoints, you don't mind the lack of dircet control so much. And the game is really all about balance in your own playstyle. So managing your time and when you mark fighters, or grab more ammo, depends purely on your own playstyle.
There is a bit of grinding involved with repetitive missions, but there's randomness in each mission too. Do the enemies make a really accurate pass or do your gunners overmatch and take them down before they get a shot off? Do those shots hit your engine, causing fire, or your fuel tank, springing a leak? The game has a way of keeping you on your toes, even when your fly a sortie you've completed 20 times.
In closing, do I recommend this game? As much as I recommend breathing. Is this game perfect? No, it still has a few flaws (which 1st patch has improved many of them greatly!!). Seems like a great group of devs who are very attentive to their playerbase and have made (and are making) changes based on feedback, so break out your wallet and throw cash at your monitor until Bomber Crew is finished downloading. Seriously.

I'm not quite finished with the game, but the game seems fun so far.
This is a single-player card game where you build a deck and battle against other people to get booster packs or money for individual cards. The goal of duels is to either reduce your opponent to 0 health or to fill up your opponent's board. Combos are done by connecting at least three symbols through the arrows on the cards, and the highest type of symbol except for the empty symbol determines what kind of action you take from the combo, which is either attacking, gaining health back, or restoring one of your disabled cards. You can interact with your opponent's board mainly through disabling, which can be done by attacking the individual card, and rotating and removing their cards, which happens through specific card effects.
There are strictly better cards, but since there are varying card limits (5 of a common, 3 of a uncommon, 1 of a rare, and 1 legendary out of all legendaries), the inferior cards are sometimes still used to get the arrows needed to carry out combos. There's also a way to recycle excess cards.
AI starts out dumb, but their decks and intelligence increases as you play. So far I haven't lost yet (though I have had plenty of challenging matches), but the decks may become much harder.
My one nitpick is that attack symbols are very strong because they do two things: lowering your opponent's health and disabling their cards. Defense symbols only gain you life, which alone won't let you win the game, and the restoration symbols which are very situational when your opponent actually disables one of your cards. The cards with attack symbols aren't much worse than other cards, so they will tend to dominate your deck. I wonder if combining the defense symbol and the restoration symbol would have helped the depth of deck building.
Also, the settings menu can only be access through the world map, which is strange. You also need to double click on some icons.
A lot of the game resides in the deckbuilding and making sure the cards work with each other. The interactions are complex due to the directions for comboing on each card, as well as balancing the effects you need to survive against opponents. The dueling is fun and feels like a puzzle game in way.
Overall, if card games and puzzle games seem interesting to you, I recommend trying it out. The cost of the game won't set you back much either.

I would consider Cubic Castles a Voxel-Sandbox MMO, where unlike other sandbox oriented games you have a constant connection to the rest of the commuinty with online play. Players come from all over the world, and flags above each players name signify their regions. Besides building, Cubic Castle also offers Parkouring and P.V.P In player and devloper-made realms.
Quest are used to help new players get a familar understanding with the game, along with a little exp. While daily quest give you a little more initiative to play by rewarding you with 50c or Cubits (the In-game currency).
Crafting adds to the game, allowing you to build and create things you wouldn't find normally in mining realms; weapons, furniture, and new means to craft even newer things.
Want to make tons a Cubits? Why not open a player-owned shop and merch. Don't have time? Well the game also offers a In-game cash shop in which you can purchase clothes, pets, furniture, and yes cubits.
The Bad:
The community is very small and mostly compized of younger gamers, which makes it a little bit more difficult for older players to enjoy.
At the time of this review, the game does have a few slight bugs here and there.
The game is also lacking a few key features that would really hit home.
Conclusion:
The only way you're going to know if you like the game is just to play it! No one can tell you head nor tails if you have your own prespective. But, I will say the reviews for this game are on the mostly positive side and that speaks louder then any single review.
So in my opinion, yep! play it!

This game is great. It feels like it's suitable for all ages (I met a mother daughter duo playing, the mom mined for resources and the daughter sold them in her store). Cubic Castles fills a niche that I have not yet seen in a game. It's dynamic, as it fulfills many different playstyles. I personally like to mine, hoard and build a beautiful and unique realm. While others take part in the economy of the game and buy and sell items. There are also people who build realms to be tutorials, games, parkour courses, etc. This game is suitable for someone who doesn't want to spend a single dollar, and for someone who wants to invest some money in a new hobbie. Threre are PvP capabilities, but something I value about the game is that if you guard your belongings and are generally smart about trusting people, your things won't get raided like they would in games like Rust or ARK. This game also caters to different social gaming styles. You don't NEED to join a clan to succeed, but you can if you want to. Overall, I'd like to conclude that the game is balanced and considers most playstyles. They are constantly adding things to the game, but not taking things out that you like. My third review of this game... a lot has changed since I started playing the early access. First, I still think the American faction is slightly overpowered, by way of the M24 Chaffee, a 'light' tank that was used mostly in the Korean War (it's better than most heavy tanks), and the M1/M2 auto-carbine, also not widely distributed before the end of the war in Europe. Spawn camping is alot less of a problem than it was, with new protected spawning zones. The additional cover and map updates do help the overall feel of the game. I think a few static emplacements besides Anti-Air might provide for some interesting encounters; things like artillery or MGs. The new medic kits and new fighter craft are excellent improvements, which I applaud. I do wish there were buyable gun variants, such as the M44 for the Mosin-Nagant, just as there are buyable options to customize each gun. (This could also work for the M1 carbine; the M1/A1 and M2 could be sub-variants). Overall, I would rate this game as 7.8/10. It is usually quite fun, but can become quite frustrating.

I origionally gave this a thumbs down, but with hindsight that was a bit harse, but my complaint still holds true.
I didn't mind the lack of a pause and/or shortcut buttons (although hats off to Curve Digital for just releasing an update that fixes this), or the grind of almost going back to square one if you lost your plane. I have managed  to end up with a top notch crew and plane doing some really nasty missions and I was really enjoying that. I even enjoyed the hours I spend designing my own nose and wing art (takes real skill to squeeze something meaningfull into 64x64 pixels)
However where you use the Grand Slam bomb, which has to be dropped from high altitude, the game play has a really annoying flaw and you end up:
1. Flying to the far side of the map at high altitude navigating by the stars.
2. Reach the target, which is always under partial cloud cover.
3. Tag the target - fly over it, but don't drop the bomb as you can't see the target because of the clouds
4. Loose the target because of the clouds.
Now at this point the obvious thing would be to get your navigator to plot a reverse course allowing you to fly back and forth over the target area until a gap in the clouds allows you to spot the target again and drop the bomb. I really wouldn't mind if you had to do it a few times. However the navigator can't plot a custom waypoint if he doesn't know where he is (which he doesn't as he can't see the ground and by now it's day, so he can't see the stars). Therefore the way it works (unless someone can tell me otherwise) is:
5. Emergency dive to mid altitude, get shot at a lot, reaquire the target, turn around, start to climb to high altitude.
6. Loose sight of the target because of the clouds, don't drop the bomb and overfly it. You are now lost again and need to turn around
7. Repeat 5 & 6 until you run low on fuel, get shot out of the skies, or loose the will to live.
8. Fly at high altitude back to base (go make a cup of tea during this as nothing will happen), or like I do, just drop out of the mission.
Now I understand it's not meant to be totally realistic, but wasting half an hour of my life on something that just defies common sense is pointless.
I think this is a good game which has real potential, but it still needs some work.

*caveats: As of this writing, I've played ~10hrs with no attempt to rush the game & have watched other players complete it. The Halloween patch has just come out, correcting several things that would have otherwise been criticized here.
This is a very good idea of a game. It is a very exciting play. It also does a lot of things that may likely put you off it if you aren't prepared and willing to deal with them.
Let's address that list of "things that may likely put you off".
It is almost an Absurdist take on the WWII Bomber Command experience, from the doll-like characters to the solo-bomber-as-gunship-wins-the-war missions, and has a UI that apparently was intentionally designed to make it hard to do several basic gameplay functions reliably. Perhaps more jarring, dozens of details are included that are "just right" for historical verisimilitude and yet along side them are things that are plainly wrong and give the wrong impression of how it went. (ex: Wing walking for repairs is pretty much common in-game. In the real world, that was rare, deadly, and so commendable to even attempt that it was cause for an award of a VC.)
The Mission UI, from point-and-click to the tagging system (necessary for everything regarding navigation to targeting) to the camera, seems designed to do more wrong that right in the name of challenging gameplay. The Post-release Patch (OCT '17) fixed several issues and revealed clearly that fixes to some others were already in the game, but tagging is still tagging and the camera and mouse issues remain. If Mouse Accelleration in certain situations matters to you, for example, this game has it and you can't change it.
The game is learned by exploration of the mechanics. The sparse Tutorial elements teach only the basics, and give no clue as to the interactions of the later game mechanics. While "learning is fun" is generally a good idea in a game, doing so in a game with Ironman-Only play is just a way to fill the Memorial Wall with names before you ever get to the meat of the game. (You pretty much need to watch someone play who is further up the learning curve than you are to avoid that, but to avoid constant re-starting/re-building... let's just quietly mention that alt-F4 is your friend.)
The missions are as varied as the Devs could probably make them, and some of the "Critical" (campaign progression) missions in particular have twists, many many missions of the game are within a point or two of "the same". As a player, you could likely address these missions with a number of gameplay style choices... but in practice, there are just a couple of reliable ways to play them, and those ways are pretty prone to making the gameplay feel very same-same. There are also a couple of pretty obviously Scripted "random events" that happen during specific Critical Missions which fall into the "surprising, once" category of not really adding to the game.
There are a number of just mis-balanced or mis-designed things in the Equipment for the Bomber, which will be obvious the first glance you take at a spreadsheet of their in-game values. Crew Armour in particular has some obvious "do buy this; never buy that" cases.
Take-off Weight is the only thing that matters re: engines and load during missions, so long as 1 engine remains turning. The absence of any motivation to build the "fast bomber" (speed only changes during specific crew perk usage) means the game runs contrary to the historical case of late-war bombers shedding armament for bombload, range, and speed... but the game also posits a solo Bomber, not a formation or stream.
*Whew*
Still with me? Wondering why the hell the "I Recommend This Game" was pushed?
Well, the answer to that last is that Game Play Experience can trump a lot of other issues...
...and this game is a SUPERB play experience, in my opinion.
The frantic moments during action of a true point-and-click-and-don't-misclick tactical game are at times overwhelming, but you can learn to play well enough. (the OCT '17 patch also allows for limited amount of time-slow for more casual play, if you want that.)
The progression of your crew and your bomber is essential to later success. Crew skills in particular should be leveled before taking on "Critical Missions", which means some grinding of lower missions... but that's where you learn the player skills to go along with them. Those crew skills are the main way the game gives the player the feeling his crew is really getting powerful... and as you stack up Equipment on your Bomber late game it turns into a devastaing Fighter-Mauling-Machine. If that makes you smile, then this part is for you.
There is a Strategy Layer of sorts; mission choice needs to be sequenced to get certain Bonus effects running at the right time to have them available for "Critical Missions"; you need unlock various Equipment as well as buy them, so there are choices about gaining Intelligence (the unlock currency) and Money (the equip currency)...
...but the real cleverness happens at the Operational level. While on a mission, you can and must assess the enemy's current Air Defence posture. Recognizing Flak and RADAR zones before getting mangled by them; learning to be cautious and clever about navigating into and during action; knowing when to stick in and when to run, that last whether by altitude or distance. All pretty hard to keep in mind when you are heavily engaged.
Nothing ends your day faster than being out of Airspeed, Altitude and Ideas at the same time.
Get this game. Play it as an experience, not to "beat it" or for some completionist urge.
It really rewards learning to play it, and that's a compliment I rarely give games any more.

I want to begin this review by stating my entry point in TES universe was Skyrim...
Morrowind is the best RPG I have ever played. Even if you buy this game and only play through the main storyline, you will find something richer and deeper than almost anything else. The world is fully fleshed-out, unique, and strangely believable. The game had me *wanting* to read every book and scroll I laid my hands on.
Yes, the graphics are dated, but the world is still beautiful and full of character. The gameplay takes a little getting used to, with the RNG-like hit detection, however once you get used to it you will discover that there are a huge range of possibilities to explore.
The DLC's are also a fantastic addition. While Bloodmoon was a little ordinary, Tribunal gives you more of the amazing story you expect from Morrowind, and segues neatly into Oblivion and the end of the era.

This is my first review, so bear with me.
I'm coming up on the fifty hour mark on Morrowind, and feel I've got a pretty good feel for this game. Morrowind has a lot in common with the later Elder Scrolls games, but it definitely has a lot that makes it its own game.
Morrowind contains a vast game world that makes you feel weak and small. In the beginning, your character will crawl along at a slow pace. You will barely be able to kill a rat. And oh yeah, nearly every native of Morrowind will absolutely hate you.
Morrowind is an isolationist region that doesn't take nicely to "Outlanders." But as you rise up in any of several guilds or noble houses, you will accumulate fame and renown. Eventually, some citizens will begin to consider you a friend or ally, and the world grows a little less hostile.
The levelling system is immensely satisfying. Skills take time to grind, but the results are tangible. The level of customization is astonishing. Armor is divided into tiny units, allowing total control over the look of the player. Spells can be created to the player's customization, and enchantments allow any player to create powerful items.
After enough time, the player is effectively a god within the world, something not really found in later Elder Scrolls entries. You can leap halfway across Morrowind, render yourself invisible, control every living creature in your vicinity, summon undead servants, teleport, fly, and even (Spoiler alert) kill a few gods.
Overall, I love Morrowind. It's a little dated, but still offers plenty to amuse any fan of RPG's.

Chapter I is great.
Chapter II drags on forever but is still good.
Chapter III feels like a black hole that you just can't seem to escape as it goes on forever
Chapter IV plays like an MMO with pingpong quests galore, altho that's somewhat redeemed with a reasonably intriguing Lovecraftian "The Shadow Over Innsmouth"-esque story to it
Chapter V is oversaturated with combat, which most people will have grown tired of at this point in the game due to the clunky controls and uninteresting mechanics.
Then finally, the climax, the epilogue, where the choices come back to you, was very satisfying story-wise, but the constant combat that just keeps getting dragged on and on and on grows ridiculously tiresome; even more so with the unreliable autosaves that will have you lose 30-40 minutes of progress if you die (often by ridiculously frustrating reasons like stunlock + bleed spam)
If you're playing this game so that you know the lore for the 2nd and/or 3rd games, I would recommend that you either blaze through the main quests, or just read up on the story and fabricate a save for The Witcher 2 instead. Unless you're a huge fan or lore enthusiast, I would not recommend playing through the first game. Not in 2018 anymore, at least.

Motionless lips, flickering stillframes, jerky motion, and stale in-game cutscenes are just too cheesy. it's fortunate that the voice acting, overall writing, and sparse storyboards distract from this. Just what I love the most about this game (besides the hilarious marvel knockoffs made by the few remaining players) is how involved I felt in LEx Luthor and the Joker's campaigns. Few games give me a stroonger sense of evil in my character's actions than this. The very first mission Lex gives you is to bust up into a college campus and murder every cop/student you see except for the few you spare to turn into monsters.
The sense of involvement my character had in the setting was like maining an Undead in WoW right after Cata dropped and leveling through Silverpine Forest. You were in the middle of a war that you would become invested in and the major hitters of the game addressed you not as a faceless grunt or great general, but as a combatant just as involved as they were. In DCU, hero or villain, you will walk through Gotham and Metropolis and see craziness the result of every other person getting super powers and going ape with it. It really reminds me of
.

The first time I played this game was many years ago and was the absolute scariest♥♥♥♥♥♥ Granted I was still a child but I can assure you this game is dripping with as much atmosphere and terror now as it was then. At its core it holds up ridiculously well despite the original REmake being over a decade and a half old now. This game is one of the only two that come to mind when I think of a pure 10/10 game, the other being Resident Evil 4. Huh, another Resident Evil game that began life on the Gamecube is my favorite? Maybe my age is showing. Even so the only games that come to mind being MAYBE 10/10 are Metal Gear Solid 3: Snake Eater, Final Fantasy VI, and the original Legend of Zelda.
If you've never experienced this game or another Resident Evil in this style I certainly from the bottom of my heart recommend it, but with a big warning. This game though aged well is 100% a product of its time within its genre. Expect tank-like control of your character's movement (this can be switched on and off, but please play the classic style as the game was designed with it in mind and mastering it is incredibly satisfying), a sorta cheesy story, camera angles that are not controlled by you but are dependent on where you stand within a room to give an appropriate shot of the scene straight out of a horror movie, limited ability to save the game, and an overall great challenge.
With the risk of sounding like a backwards elitist I must say that this game is not for the faint of heart or those without an open mind who aren't ready to experience something like this. As I've just stated, death doesn't mean reloading a checkpoint, it means going straight back to the main menu and reloading a save. The number of saves that can make is limited by an in-game item known as an Ink Ribbon, which are used at typewriters scattered throughout the game. There are two different characters to play as with their own unique experience with one being able to carry more items at once for example, as well as story differences but between them is enough similarity to call beating the game with only one of the characters a full run of the game, which may last first-timers somewhere between 7 to 15 hours to pull off. Once you play through once though this time naturally gets shorter as you remember the layout of the mansion and where items are to be taken and placed, resulting in fast runs of about only 2 to 3 hours. In case you haven't caught on to what I'm trying to convey here, this game is gushing with replayability. Just this past week when I returned to the game for the first time in many years I played about 6 full playthroughs to get all of the steam achievements and even now I feel like it was well worth it.
For players who have already played REmake in some form or have at least played other classic RE games, this port of the game isn't perfect I'm afraid. The original game was clearly never intended for "HD" widescreen support and some textures look especially artificial compared to the original version of the game, some objects really standing awkwardly out against the pre-rendered background. The lighting also feels pallid, or flushed of color while I remember the original version of the game being a bit warmer and grittier. This could be imagined or a weird hang-up from experiencing the Silent Hill HD Collection. The biggest flaw I personally experienced was a laggy slow-down effect well below 30 fps seemingly at random, which I believe shouldn't happen for me seeing as my PC is capable of running a 60 fps tense battle in Overwatch at max settings. While I am by no means a stickler for muh fps below 30 is just bad, and the game itself slowing down is problematic. Especially considering the achievement/unlockables based on completion time where it's unclear to what extent the slow-down affects the in-game timer.
Whether this is your first Resident Evil game, you're looking to explore more of the series, or you just wanna return to this game on another form I have two last important things to say. The first is play with a controller (didn't try keyboard and mouse but I can only imagine how unnatural it must feel) and if it is convenient for you to just get a Gamecube and the 2002 Gamecube release of this game, do that instead of getting this version. If none of the problems I've explained in my previous paragraph bother you and you really want this version for the achievements/steam crap (like me) or the ease of access, then feel free to buy this version. I don't regret buying this version despite it being largely inferior to the Gamecube release.

First thing off, don't let the preview screenshots fool you into believing that game actually looks like that. Those screenshots are graphically enhanced... meaning the graphics in the game looks nothing like them.
I started playing this game a year ago, in April of 2015. I have had 730 hours in the game. I have written 2 previous reviews for this game. The first one was a negative one that I wrote after playing the game for 2 months, and spent 200 hours on it. The second review was a positive one after playing the game for 5 months and having spent 400 on it.
Now this is my third review of this game, and I am sad to have to change my overwhelming positive review to a negative one. This game has been slowly going down hill for the past 6 months/updates (since they have an update every month).
Though most of negative stuff I have to say comes from the update 4 months ago (the Adam's Build).
The main problem with this game has always been how the developers at Reto decide to "balance" things. The problem is so obvious to everyone on the forums except Reto to the point that we all joke about it. We call it "Reto Logic™".
The problem with "Reto Logic™" is that they make the most absurd and silly excuses and reasons to do the most crude, unpolished, illogical methods of attempting to balance the game.
For instance, tank drivers can't initiate a manual reload for their turret mounted coaxial machines guns, or autocannons if you have a Panzer II tank. Reto claims that this is done for game balance... but meanwhile all other vehicles' support machine guns can be reloaded at any given time... Even the support gunner machine gun on a tank can be reloaded... So instead of doing something more logical for the sake of balance like giving the tank driver a slower reload, they just completely disable the ability to reload at all... and the only way for you to reload is by wasting all your ammo in your current clip which not only gives away your position, but wastes extra time.
Another example is the American M1919 .30 Browning Machine Gun. Most players complain that the rangefinder (iron sight) on the gun is way to optically obstructive for the gun to be used effectively, and ask for it to be flipped down. Reto says no, tells us that the rangefinder blocking most of your screen is there for balance. So instead of balancing the gun statistically, they decide to basically blind the user instead.
Another example of "Reto Logic™", is instead of simply tweaking stats accordingly they basically decided in the past couple of months just to make every gun unusable. For instance they have been adding muzzle residue clouds to all automatic guns... this wouldn't be a problem at all if they were simply just small highly transparent aesthetic animations.... but no they are large, densely dark residue clouds that are equivalent to a black powder musket discharges that is enough to blind the user.
Not only did they add that. They added a conefire system. Now you may think that conefire means weapon or bullet spread... but no... it doesn't. Conefire is this stupid massive RNG weapon sway, that makes it look like your character's arm is made out of jello... where your character is constantly just moving his arms around in a large drunk wide random circular motion that prevents you from ever getting an accurate precise shot.
So this game went from a good skill based FPS game, to a drunk blind pray and spray RNG simulator all in one update.
And if that wasn't bad enough... The game has extremely poor lighting and sun glare effect. Not to mention black hole shadows.
Where the majority of the game's graphics has this dark grey filter over it which Reto said they added because of "Pixel Hunters", where people use to be able to see enemy soldiers so far off to the distance...  like 200 meters away where they appeared to be only a few pixels, and still managed to spot and kill them. So after adding this terrible grey soup filter to the game... most players a lot of times can't even see enemy soldiers at 10 or 20 meters in front of them.
Then add that on with the black hole shadows... where entire bright green, or whitish grey tanks can become almost invisible in plain sight when sitting in the shadows.
Then lets not forget the sun glare... the sun glare is unnaturally bright, and is static. It doesn't dynamically change intensity or shape at different viewing angles. Even when going into a shady spot where the sun isn't shinning on your character, you still get sun glare no matter what. Even if you're in a building with solid walls where the sun doesn't shine. The only time the sun glare goes away is if you have the sun at your back at an  angle of somewhere between 175 to 185 degree .
Also this game for the past entire year that I have been playing, they still hasn't fixed the firing sound and animation bug. Where most of shots fired by someone else makes no sound at all and has no muzzle flash. This is extremely detrimental bug to have in an FPS game because it is literally the difference between life and death. Where someone can be standing literally 2 meters away from you, trying to shoot you in the back, and you simply won't hear at all. They might shoot 20 rounds at you before you even hear the first shot sound. Or a magically invisible enemy tank sitting in the shadows 10 meters right in front of you can be shooting its cannon, and you will never even know its there.
So in short why do I not recommend this game? Because the developers at Reto do not have any idea how to balance the game. They use the most bizarre illogical unrefined hack slashed methods to balance the game, by simply removing basic game mechanic functionality, trying to blind players in every way possible, dumbing down the gunplay mechanics to the point where your aiming ability doesn't matter at all since whether you hit or not due to the fact that your soldier holds his gun as if he is drunk and has jello for arms and its pure RNG base.
This game has a lot more problems than just what I mentioned in this review, but this is the stuff that you will encounter first thing off when you start playing the game as an infantryman.
Also if you're considering becoming a tanker in this game... just remember, the higher the tier the tank is, the more expensive it is, the more easier it is to be killed, and the more inaccurate it's coaxial machine gun is. Yeah you read that right... the more expensive and better armored a tank is... the more it sucks and easier to be killed in. Because the bigger and more armored your tank is, the slower it moves, which just makes it easier for infantrymen with sticky grenades (hand held anti-tank nukes) to run up to you and instantly vaporize you as if you're sitting in a aluminium foil toy car.

This game challenges you not just to complete levels, but to master them. The super meat boy influence is clear, however this game adds the additional mechanic of a time limit and time-replenishing orbs that makes it unique. The movement is tight and responsive (which is expected for a difficult platformer) and there are tons of levels including bonus stages and a bonus world.
Make no mistake, the game is hard. Being a player of IWBTG fangames, which this game also takes influence from, I found myself beating the levels pretty quick, however if you truly wish to complete the game there are S times that you need to beat on every level, which are VERY demanding. They force you to think like a speedrunner, optimizing movement and finding the best path to save even a tenth of a second. Despite being a grind, it was a fun grind since every level was like a puzzle trying to find the shortest path. Thankfully, in order to get "112%" on every world, you only need an A rank on every stage which is fairly easy to do.
So do I recommend this game? Of course. It's fast-paced and satisfying to play. If you are not so good at platformers, you may want to watch a few videos before determining if it's for you. If you liked super meat boy or the end is nigh, the difficutly is around that level.

"ERRRM MY GLOB! THIS THING IS A MASTERPIECE!"
I put this game on my wishlist thinking 'Oh, I already have the other TES games... I might as well complete the collection, even if I'm not gonna play it- ever.'
But then my friend bought it off my wishlist and my entire view of TES was turned around. This game, even at 15 years old, presents a level of meaning and immersion that I have never seen in any video game: modern or classic. I hit 'New Game' and within the first 5 seconds of the intro video I was thinking to myself: "Oh. Oh yeah this is going to be GOOD."
I was met with a soundtrack like no other- containing dramatic music filled with excitement and boisterous music filled with gaity. My heart fluttered at this game. I couldn't play more than a day without tearing up 3 times at the beauty.
This game is a masterpiece, indeed.
It may be blurry.
It may be foggy.
It may be nearly impossible to land a swing until you're level 2.
But it is a masterpiece nonetheless.

It really breaks my heart to have to give this game a bad reveiw. There were clearly talented and passionate people behind it, but it just doesn't play well.
Here's an example that helps to describe one of my biggest issues.
-You've just broken out of your cell, and are currently in a crawl space under a room occupied by a guard, who is shooting a pellet gun of some sort at a target on the wall. You can get into the room via a manhole under the table. The guard has a large dish full of pellets on the table and a key on his belt.
You try to reach for the keys. You're not allowed to do that.
You try to reach for the pellets on the table. You're not allowed to do that.
you try to do both in the moment when the guard is aiming and has his attention elsewhere. You're not allowed to do that.
You slowly, slowly, slowly, shuffle your way back down the tunnel.
You try going back to your cell to see if there's anything you missed. the exit is wide open, but you're still not allowed back in.
You slowly, slowly, slowly, shuffle your way back down the tunnel.
You go back to the room with the guard. You notice that he tips back in his chair every time he goes to take a shot. You click on the chair, hoping to send him tumbling backwards. Nothing happens.
Enraged, you finally crack, and decide to use the walkthrough provided in-game.
You slowly, slowly, slowly scroll through the randomly-generated shooter level.
When you finally get the walkthrough! the answer was... to click on the guard's chair, knocking him over.
You enter an entirely new realm of anger when you realize that you were supposed to click on the guard's chair, you just didn't click on the bottom of the front left leg. This is the only game I've played where you could be right, but still be wrong.
That, and a lot of the artistic choices prevent the game from playing well as a point-and-click. Specifically, because none of the characters speak, there's no proper way to examine your environment besides looking at it. For example, in one scene, you have to dry some lichen on a lightbulb. However, the light was in a thick-looking glass housing with metal bands, nothing really indicated that it was hot. In any other P&CA, you could look at the light, and your character would say "It's hot." or something similar.
Also, the game's main means of movement is horrible. The robot is SO SLOW! the game also doesn't include any sort of automatic movement when iteracting with the environment. If you drag an item out of your inventory and click it on something in the environment, what do you expect from a P&CA? for your character to either say "that won't work" or to walk over and do something with the item. In this game, you have to click on where you want to go, then watch the robot slowly waddle over, then take the item out of your inventory and use it. It seems like a minor gripe, but when you've played other P&CAs it gets so obnoxious, like a child who won't eat if his sandwich isn't cut at a precisely 62.5 degree angle.
In short, this game doesn't want you to play good, it wants to look good.
I tell you, this game has the most rotten bad guys in all of video gamedom.  This is a quality title, although the memory of their depravity may leave scars on your psyche.

This, I would say, is an example of a good idea which is a bit too big for the package it came in.  But for what it's worth, it works.
Spore is a game where you guide a species' evolutionary history, from microbe to animal to civilization and beyond.  Using a tool called the creature/vehicle/building creator, one can evolve any number of weird and wonderful beasts, as well as fabricate a whole bunch of amazing structures and vehicles to spread throughout the galaxy.
On paper, the idea is amazing: essentially, you can craft the whole universe in your image!  One can observe civilizations battling for control of a planet, watch microorganisms swarm the seas, even make effigys of your victories!  The first 2/3 of the game is the strongest point, going from cell to civ.  Cell and Creature modes are both single-player modes, which help tie into the simplistic mechanics.  Then once you reach Tribal stage, it shifts to a simplified RTS, where you control a group, and then build to a planetary civilization.  It really feels like you're growing your own civilization from scratch, and as stated below, you get nigh-total artistic freedom with all of it.
The creator is easily the best part of the game: an editor machine which lets you create creatures, vehicles, buildings, and starships.  Total artistic freedom for your charactr and units, in other words.  And for folks like me, who make up animals and the like for fun, this is a wonderful tool!  And as an added bonus, sometimes your (and other people's) creations can spawn in the universe as AI, allowing you to meet your own creation free of your control!
In short, the creator, the editing powers, and the humor it's packaged in is a wonderful combination!
The main negative aspect is the scale of the idea itself, along with some execution.  Only the first 2/3 of the game are really engaging, going from cell to creature, tribe, civilization, and finally space.  While the pacing and gameplay mechanics from cell to civ is fluid and sensible, space mode is the weakest part of the game and really breaks the pacing.  Rather than sticking to the Simplified RTS gameplay like they had introduced earlier, it's a single-player mode where you play a lone captain travelling the verse.  While I understand why they did this, as it does empower you as one who can shape the galaxy in your image, I think sticking to an RTS formula and making it a dumbed-down version of Stellaris or Star Wars: Empire At War would've helped more.
What also would've helped is an ending.  I mean a real, legitimate ending.  As it is, space mode just drags on and on and never really goes anywhere after you lay your first colony and meet your first aliens.  You do get kind of an end when you reach the galactic core, but the game keeps going afterwards, so it never really does end.  So the end goal is
Spread your civilization?  Create things?
In the end, Spore gets alot right, but it also falls short in a big way.  Creature Creator is definitely worth the price of admission, and going from Cell to Civ is loads of fun.  On the other hand, Space Captain Mode is a bit of a deal-breaker, in some ways.  But if you're willing to look past that last bit, you can have alot of fun here.
My Rating:  7/10
Good Points:
- Cell Mode is an open-world Pac-Man game.  Loads of fun!
- Creature Mode is the 2nd best part.  Making and playing as your own animals is fun!
- Tribal Mode is a little off, but it works in bridging Creature and Civ Modes.
- Civilization Mode is awesome!  Controlling a nation, capturing cities, claming resources, and unifying the world!
- Being able to edit and change the galaxy to what you want is awesome!
- Living worlds with AI make it fun to watch the game play itself sometimes, and makes it feel alive!
- Creator Mode is the BEST best part!  Making all of the things!
Bad Points:
- Would have liked to create plants/sea creatures, but it's ok.
- Space Mode is the worst.  It's not an RTS when it really should be.
- The lack of a decent ending/goal is compounded by Space Mode's gameplay style.

This game is a masterpiece. It's cute, it's funny, it's beautiful, it's engaging, but most of all it's thoroughly entertaining.
It's so rare to come across a flawless game like this that I'm actually lost for words. There are literally no faults, just a list of things that were done well or adequately. There were no frivolous attempts at reinventing the wheel - saving works the old fashioned way, as does returning from the dead. I don't think level of perfection was an accident either. The game openly invites you to glare at it, to scrutinize, looking for clues, to scan every inch of the screen admiring the attention to detail. The features have been pared down to the very barebones required for function, leaving nothing to distract from the overall experience.
The main character and protagonist is a big standout for me. He's hilarious, adorable, and instantly likeable. Everything from his little dance to the way he "speaks" fills my heart with joy. It's not often that I find myself so attached to the player character, so I was pleasantly surprised by this.
The music and artwork/level design is simply beautiful. The OST was written by notable IDM artist, Floex, who was also responsible for the soundtrack to Samarost. These two game elements come together in perfect harmony to create a uniquely atmospheric world that gave me a limbic response I haven't felt since playing the Oddworld series.
The humour is organic, witty, and sometimes quite subtle. The game strikes a great balance between comedy and serious themes. When it's not being funny, the storyline explores loss, loneliness, depression, addiction, reunion, family, and various other themes with tact and sensitivity. There is never "too much" of any one emotion, so that the game remains enjoyable without straying into being overwhelming. This level of emotional balance is, in my opinion, unparalleled.
The storyline flows extremely well - there are no side quests, instead the game takes a seemingly meandering course through all characters and areas. Sometimes it can take a while to figure out a puzzle, while others are relatively straightforward. The nice thing about this is, the game works a bit like an IQ test in the sense that it will test your weaknesses as well as your strengths. It's puzzles run the gamut and no puzzle is repeated - some gamers will find a section hard, while others will find it easy. Your mileage will truly vary.
Finally, I want to add that after finishing this game I felt like my life had been enriched having played it. I felt like I was better off, like I had taken a cultural-tour holiday, or been to a museum. This game is wholesome and good for the soul. If none of the other things I've said have encouraged you to buy and play it, but you've been feeling a little blue lately, here's my advice:
Take one Machinarium and call me in the morning.

Brothers is an incredibly beautiful game, both visually and conceptually. The adventure you experience is so fantastic. The connection you gain to the brothers is so strong that I started to refer to myself as "we" when I was describing what I did in the game. The puzzles are usually a little too simple, but there's some challenge in learning to control both brothers at the same time.

A few recommendations. Play through the game in one sitting. It's only 2 hours long and it has the best impact if you take it all in at once. DO NOT USE THE KEYBOARD. Use a controller. The game doesn't feel right without it, you'll understand once you play it.
