Brothers A Tale Of Two Sons tells a beautiful story of two brothers looking for a cure for their ill father. Let me start by saying that the graphics are dead set gorgeous. The environments are beautifully realized, with a couple of excellent surprises (well, surprises might not be the proper word for it, but they're awesome nevertheless).
The sounds might not be as impressive, because all you'll hear is a bit of gibberish and it's up to you to interpret what's being said, explained or insinuated. It works, and in hindsight I think it was definitely the right choice to handle it this way.
Emotional is what I would call the story without spoiling anything. Brothers is already a short game (around 3 hours) so it's best if you experience the entire game yourself. I think Shelter and Journey are the games that best describe the experience you'll have playing Brothers.
One thing that will infuriate many people are the controls. They're not that terrible, but they're not good either. I like the fact you control each brother with a seperate analog stick, but once you move the little brother to the left side of the screen you'll most likely get all confused and start mixing things up. I know I did. I died several times because of this. Walking around usually works without too much trouble though, but once you have to start turning levers the controls are a bit vague.
Note that this was the only thing I disliked. The charming story (which I can relate to) and interesting, interactive, world make up for any mistakes made.

A truly wonderfull masterpiece of a game that manages to do something that many games haven't succeeded with: it manages to carry wide array of emotions via it's gameplay, and provides a methaphor of a brotherhood in a manner that only games are able to do it. Ironically, it's directed by a film director.

This game is better than you'd think. The control scheme seems a little difficult at first but over time the two characters feel like one. Luckily the puzzles don't require too much in terms of split-second coordination.
The story is simple but unfolds purely through the environment, the brothers don't even speak any known language. It's the story of two brothers struggling through a perilous journey to a mountain top to save their father, and right off the bat it makes it clear to you that it's going for your heart strings. Some might think that it's trying a little too hard at this and they'd have a fair point, but the presentation I think goes a long way.
The gameplay itself is mostly navigating the various environments using the two brothers slightly varied ability. Much like you'd expect, the older brother is braver and can handle the stronger stuff while the little brother needs more protecting but is faster and can climb things more easily. They both have different things they can do that you learn as you play, which I quite liked. Graphically the game is very good looking and has a great art style. They put various vistas around the world so you can get a good look at it too.
It's a short game, but I doubt you'll complain about that aspect. The gameplay elements fully flesh themselves out and don't leave you wanting more by the end. I will say that the end of the game does have a really interesting moment (that I won't spoil), and it's something that only a game with this particular gameplay mechanic would be able to do.
Overall the game is pretty interesting and I recommend giving it a go if you ever get the chance. It can be played in one or two sittings.

It's not the best game in existence and it's certainly not a brilliant Resident Evil game gameplay wise. But, having said that, it's not entirely awful. It's a pretty generic third person shooter (although I'll admit there are some nice features such as the blood rage stuff (which basically means you could cause severe blood loss from an individual which will attract zombies) and the fact that both human enemies and allies can be bitten and become infected, and there is also a decent amount of enemy variety and classes and special abilities to choose from), which bares the Resident Evil title and is based in the Resident Evil universe.
Additionally, it's not scary (which isn't suprising considering it's a TPS that gives you loads of weapons and ammo), but there were moments that made me jump enough or had enemies catch me by suprise to make me feel (slightly) on edge and as if I was actually heading through this zombie infested city.
I'm having some fun with it so far, hence the positive review, but it really isn't amazing. It's not worth full price, however. If you're a Resident Evil fan or just want another basic TPS to play I'd recommend giving it a go. But don't pay full price.
EDIT: At the end of the game there's a two choices than can be made, which I won't mention for spoiler reasons, and they both have decent cutscenes to follow, but the lead into the parts after that choice are insanely hollow. There are no cutscenes after that choice and it practically just throws you straight into that decision without any drama at all. Of course I didn't want it to be insanely over the top dramatic, but having literrally no dramatic introduction to that scene made it feel empty and pointless. Additionally, the only consequences of that decision are a (slightly) different ending boss fight and a different ending cutscene. It's a linear shooter so I'm not suprised, but it feels rather pointless.
That being said I did enjoy the game enough to give it a postive rating and I'm just going through the DLC Echo Six story now. I've not tried the multiplayer as I don't want to and I'd be suprised if anyone still played it.
Also, on a side note, the Crimson Heads look absolutely ridiculous in this installment xD
From what I've seen of Umbrella Corps. though... Well, in comparison to that, this game looks like someone at least did something right when they turned Resident Evil into a generic squad-based TPS.
EDIT: The Echo Six story has a much better finale than the USS story. A pretty cool, but repetitive final boss fight makes it go out with much more of a bang than the main game. In fact, I prefered most of the Echo Six DLC to the original game which makes the DLC feel like a cash grab that should've been in the base game. Unfortunately, the Echo Six story leaves the story with an unresolved cliffhanger, but it's not too annoying. Just feels like a set up for more DLC or a sequel, just in case they made the decision to do so. I'm pretty much done with the game now. I'm unlikely to play it much again. Not particulary interesting enough to make me play it again.

Card City Nights is one of those games that show up and, despite their price tag, have a lot of value in them.
You play as a new arrival in Card City, having won a house there. There's no description of this event but the game throws the hint right at the start if you know where to look. You get to pick your portrait and name and next thing you know you'll be battling your first few opponents. The story, because yes, there's a story, is barebones but this isn't a bad thing, quite the opposite. You want to win the Card City tournament because of reasons and get its prize but you need 8 legendary cards to even get to participate in it, so you must win those cards first. That's the whole story right there. It's nice to see a card game that doesn't take itself too serious and the story is a amusing distraction from the proceedings.
The game is incredibly simple to pick up, the tutorial is short but effective in telling you the principal mechanic of the game.
Essentially, the game plays out in two 3 by 3 grid, one for you and another for your opponent. The cards you use have arrows on them pointing in any of 8 different ways and one or more of 4 symbols attached to it (attack, defense, neutral, revive). You PLAY the cards by placing them on your grid but you USE them by matching arrows and symbols, making combos. You need at least 3 symbols linked by arrows to make a combo. Meanwhile, your opponent is trying to do the same. There's a little bit more nuance to this but that's THE game right there.
You mix and match the cards in the deck(s) to your style of play, since there are no "set" decks. You edit them in any way you like on up to 6 different decks, using the cards you get via randomized booster packs that you win after defeating certain opponents. The total number of cards in the game is healthy enough to actually require some tough decisions as to what cards to actually put in the deck.
The battles themselves can be won in few different ways. Two examples would be, you can attack your opponents defence, bring it to zero or disable his cards with those same attacks for a grid lock, where he has no legal move. Either way, you win (or your opponent does).
However, there is definitely some concern about balance. For example, you can have 3 uncommon cards and 5 common ones in a 40 card deck. In reality, while playing, you'll find that 3 uncommon  cards that are straight-up upgrades from common ones (as in, they have the same everything the common card has but with one extra bit, like an extra arrow and/or special ability) are much more worth having.
There's no real reason to keep common cards around because they will eventually just take up room from the more useful uncommon cards, unless you need A LOT of cards with arrows pointing the same way, which you won't, since it's counter-intuitive. And since uncommon become powerful on their own (like damaging the enemy just by placing them, for example), and booster packs are always available to be won, you can, with a little luck in the boosters while farming them, steamroll most opponents early on, if not for the entire duration. So this warants these two paragraphs.
The A.I. isn't particularly challenging but with more card variety, the possible moves it makes also increases, so it keeps you guessing the first or even the second time you battle a particular opponent, which is nice. There's no multiplayer, for those more inclined to battle humans, so this feature lacking is going to put off some people, which is understandable but it's not a major gripe, in my opinion, obviously.
In conclusion and to make a long story short, it's a casual card game that offers some solid gameplay with solid mechanics. It doesn't reinvent the wheel because it doesn't have to as far as card games are concerned but it stands out enough to warrant a look. And for it's price tag, it's a great steal. Buy it, play it, no real reason not to.

So heres my first impressions.
DISCLAIMER. I have never played the original resident evil (With the exception of about 5 minutes on my psp) and therefor have no nostalgic ties to it in anyway. I have played other resident evils with 4 being one of my favourite games of all time having completed it over 10 times across the PS2 and PC. I love the resident evil universe as a whole and also enjoy resident evil 6 so I am not one of those 'Oh you are stuck in the past resident evils only wanting them remade' bellends that review resident evils.
First of all something that NO review I have seen address or even mentioned. Jill has jiggle physics and they are quite obvious. Now I don't care if you give me outsits with boobs or whatever in them but when you are trying to give me an atmospheric experience expecially with horror jiggle physics just ruin it for me. There is no need for these to be in the game and it takes away from the experience personally and is a problem I have with dead or alive 5. These weren't in any other resident evil to my knowledge and adding them in has done nothing for the games immersion. You're going to tell me Jill, an agent working for the government is going to go to work in a bra that makes her boobs jiggle like she isnt wearing one from walking the pace of a snail.
Secondly The game being a 'remaster' is.. questionable since from the screenshots I saw I was expecting a fully 3D environment with fixed camera angles. However it feels more like a skybox still image background kind of effect with some 3d rendered models in it such as the characters and certain key items. This however doesn't take away from the atmosphere it creates which I can compare to the first time I played resident evil 4. It would have just been nice for these environments to be 3D.
Thirdly the camera angles are weird. Now I dont mind them being fixed at all and I dont mind it combined with the tank controls. However, I have played for about an hour and its already killed me twice since aiming snapped the fixed camera to a different position and walking down a hall while being chased by a zombie snapped the camera to another position and made me walk back down the hall into the zombie.
However. Despite all of this I would still recommend this game. The animations can be abit slow sometimes but do add to the immersion and the overall atmosphere is really well done. And learning the whole story of resident evil is very interesting and can see why alot of people are nostalgic about this game. There is clearly alot more to this game then where I have gotten up too and am looking forward to completing it. Let's get those out of the way first. I would consider myself a fan of the Resident Evil franchise. When I was young and couldn't afford a Playstation 1 or N64, I used to read the strategy guides and stare at the screenshots from Resident Evil 2 longingly. However, as someone who doesn't have nostalgia issues when it comes to dealing with games from "back in the day," I can look at this remaster of Resident Evil and say that there are some serious flaws in my opinion.
I found the game's plot and characters to be very lame and uninteresting. Dialog is extremely rare, because you are alone at least 95% of the game (excluding feral monsters), and what little dialog there is I found to be either bland or terribly delivered. They do not use the original lines, either, so much of the meme fodder fo the original game's release is gone (no "Jill sandwich," but a similar joke is said in its place, nowhere near as enjoyable, in my opinion). Each character is just sort of there, without any nuance, character arcs, or even playing into fun tropes or archetypes. If a character is going to be static, at least play up the archetype, writers. The story seems like it's supposed to be a bunch of big twists, but almost everything seems plainly stated in the hard-to-miss documents, long before each twist or plot development comes up.
The camera angles are fantastic...if this was just a movie or a set of screenshots. However, as a video game, the camera gets yanked all over the place. You could be running toward the screen, then the camera angle changes to a view off to one side...or the other side...or behind your character...or at a diagonal. The angles themselves look great, but the slightest touch to a keyboard button or gamebad directional button other than a single direction being held consistently will result in your character running all over the place in the wrong direction, which can sometime lead to instant death. I was about ready to chuck my mouse at a wall while trying to push a statue into an alcove in between two crushing walls, because I kept getting insta-killed when the camera angle on the puzzle reset button kept changing and having my character run back into danger despite me struggling with controlling it.
I'm no stranger to tank controls, and have no problem with those. I've beaten all the numbered Resident Evil games with those controls before, and they work well enough, even if I don't think they're necessarily ideal. However, the camera angles make maneuvering in Resident Evil something that I do not enjoy. The new control scheme offered in the PC version is nice, though arguably worse since pressing up while using the old controls won't send you the wrong direction if the camera angle changes while you're moving.
I've beaten this game at least twice before beating the PC version, but it had been a few years. Unless you know where all the items are and what items you need when, do

Aside from having a little more health and supposedly firing weapons a bit faster and possibly with more headshots than Jill, he seems to be inferior to her in virually every other way. Chris can't play the piano. Jill can. Chris can't mix chemicals. Jill can. Chris has to fight a boss that Jill can skip (no benefit for fighting it),and so on. OH. And he has 33% less inventory space that her. If you don't know exactly what you're doing, this is probably the biggest reason not to play Chris. 6 inventory slots SUCKS. It's rough all throughout the game, and requires tons of running back and forth from items to safe rooms to store my stuff. I was doing laps for 15-20 minutes straight, collecting stuff, and that's with me only carrying a pistol with no extra ammo at times.
This is the difference between making something that's just technologically good, and something artistically legit. The backgrounds in this game are gorgeous. Ten years from now, they will still be gorgeous.  The sound quality is nice, the music and sounds are creepy (the safe rooms have this lovely, haunting melody <3), and the game manages to be creepy even when I'm armed to the teeth. All my gripes about things before this topic...those are my issues with the game, but the atmosphere from the sights and sounds in this game are why I recommend it. These are so good that they gave me an overall good time despite those things I didn't like.

Then again, I wish a
of games would get the Resident Evil Remaster treatment. This is a good game, and I wish other games that have become dated and suffer for it could use this treatment. I was playing Soul  Reaver on Steam the other day, and everything looks so incredibly dated without "immortalizing" art style that graphical quality can't hamper. This, I would say, is an example of a good idea which is a bit too big for the package it came in.  But for what it's worth, it works.
Spore is a game where you guide a species' evolutionary history, from microbe to animal to civilization and beyond.  Using a tool called the creature/vehicle/building creator, one can evolve any number of weird and wonderful beasts, as well as fabricate a whole bunch of amazing structures and vehicles to spread throughout the galaxy.
On paper, the idea is amazing: essentially, you can craft the whole universe in your image!  One can observe civilizations battling for control of a planet, watch microorganisms swarm the seas, even make effigys of your victories!  The first 2/3 of the game is the strongest point, going from cell to civ.  Cell and Creature modes are both single-player modes, which help tie into the simplistic mechanics.  Then once you reach Tribal stage, it shifts to a simplified RTS, where you control a group, and then build to a planetary civilization.  It really feels like you're growing your own civilization from scratch, and as stated below, you get nigh-total artistic freedom with all of it.
The creator is easily the best part of the game: an editor machine which lets you create creatures, vehicles, buildings, and starships.  Total artistic freedom for your charactr and units, in other words.  And for folks like me, who make up animals and the like for fun, this is a wonderful tool!  And as an added bonus, sometimes your (and other people's) creations can spawn in the universe as AI, allowing you to meet your own creation free of your control!
In short, the creator, the editing powers, and the humor it's packaged in is a wonderful combination!
The main negative aspect is the scale of the idea itself, along with some execution.  Only the first 2/3 of the game are really engaging, going from cell to creature, tribe, civilization, and finally space.  While the pacing and gameplay mechanics from cell to civ is fluid and sensible, space mode is the weakest part of the game and really breaks the pacing.  Rather than sticking to the Simplified RTS gameplay like they had introduced earlier, it's a single-player mode where you play a lone captain travelling the verse.  While I understand why they did this, as it does empower you as one who can shape the galaxy in your image, I think sticking to an RTS formula and making it a dumbed-down version of Stellaris or Star Wars: Empire At War would've helped more.
What also would've helped is an ending.  I mean a real, legitimate ending.  As it is, space mode just drags on and on and never really goes anywhere after you lay your first colony and meet your first aliens.  You do get kind of an end when you reach the galactic core, but the game keeps going afterwards, so it never really does end.  So the end goal is
Spread your civilization?  Create things?
In the end, Spore gets alot right, but it also falls short in a big way.  Creature Creator is definitely worth the price of admission, and going from Cell to Civ is loads of fun.  On the other hand, Space Captain Mode is a bit of a deal-breaker, in some ways.  But if you're willing to look past that last bit, you can have alot of fun here.
My Rating:  7/10
Good Points:
- Cell Mode is an open-world Pac-Man game.  Loads of fun!
- Creature Mode is the 2nd best part.  Making and playing as your own animals is fun!
- Tribal Mode is a little off, but it works in bridging Creature and Civ Modes.
- Civilization Mode is awesome!  Controlling a nation, capturing cities, claming resources, and unifying the world!
- Being able to edit and change the galaxy to what you want is awesome!
- Living worlds with AI make it fun to watch the game play itself sometimes, and makes it feel alive!
- Creator Mode is the BEST best part!  Making all of the things!
Bad Points:
- Would have liked to create plants/sea creatures, but it's ok.
- Space Mode is the worst.  It's not an RTS when it really should be.
- The lack of a decent ending/goal is compounded by Space Mode's gameplay style.

It's great, it's amazing! I don't understand how I put off playing this game for so long.
If I could describe it it would be a mix of Civ and Total War (though not as niche).
Making your own empire is exiting, it never gets old. It's always a constant battle for territory and each war tells a story. Maybe you're desperately struggling to siege that one final castle from the Swadians, or maybe you want to get revenge on the Lord that just looted you village, it doesn't matter what your goals are, each choice unfolds a unique narrative and it makes this game great.
The multiplayer is amazing, with multiple modes and hundreds of players, multiplayer is bound to put a smile on your face.
The DLC is also great, Napoleonic Wars is a MP only expansion that brings you to the age of muskets where your shots are horribly inaccurate but give you a surge of adrenaline when you land that perfect shot.
Viking Conquest pushes your face in the mud and keeps pushing harder and harder until you can get a footing in the ranks of vikings, and I love it. While multiplayer for VC is very very small. The singleplayer portion is very hard at the beginning, but is very rewarding. It also adds a variety of features.
All in all this game is great and will greatly prepare you for the sequel: Bannerlord (cause contrary to popular belief, Warband is a standalone expansion for M&B). It'll keep you locked away in your room for hours on end and you'll never want to leave.
Oh, and did I mention there's mods?

A truly wonderfull masterpiece of a game that manages to do something that many games haven't succeeded with: it manages to carry wide array of emotions via it's gameplay, and provides a methaphor of a brotherhood in a manner that only games are able to do it. Ironically, it's directed by a film director.

This game is better than you'd think. The control scheme seems a little difficult at first but over time the two characters feel like one. Luckily the puzzles don't require too much in terms of split-second coordination.
The story is simple but unfolds purely through the environment, the brothers don't even speak any known language. It's the story of two brothers struggling through a perilous journey to a mountain top to save their father, and right off the bat it makes it clear to you that it's going for your heart strings. Some might think that it's trying a little too hard at this and they'd have a fair point, but the presentation I think goes a long way.
The gameplay itself is mostly navigating the various environments using the two brothers slightly varied ability. Much like you'd expect, the older brother is braver and can handle the stronger stuff while the little brother needs more protecting but is faster and can climb things more easily. They both have different things they can do that you learn as you play, which I quite liked. Graphically the game is very good looking and has a great art style. They put various vistas around the world so you can get a good look at it too.
It's a short game, but I doubt you'll complain about that aspect. The gameplay elements fully flesh themselves out and don't leave you wanting more by the end. I will say that the end of the game does have a really interesting moment (that I won't spoil), and it's something that only a game with this particular gameplay mechanic would be able to do.
Overall the game is pretty interesting and I recommend giving it a go if you ever get the chance. It can be played in one or two sittings.

Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons is an adventure title with a unique control scheme. Two boys set out to find a cure for their ailing father and take an adventure across a sweeping landscape to obtain it. Through villages, over frozen lakes, underneath mountains, saving people and creatures alike, Brothers is a game that achieves a cinematic edge to it while making sure the player is involved as much as possible. It's a small, heartfelt yet epic tale that never oversteps what it sets out to do. The brothers don't speak English (none of the characters do) so the entire story is told through the gameplay and what's happening onscreen. And while English is never spoken, you can understand the events going on well enough through their actions and how they talk.


I still stand by what I said. There are only a handful of games that have affected me as Brothers did and I enjoyed it all the more for it.
The game has the story and mechanics mix almost perfectly. You control both brothers with the two joysticks on your controller. Which at first wouldn't seem like a big deal, but it forms the basis of the rest of the game and the puzzles. It's a bit janky to control the brothers and can sometimes be a little more difficult than you would imagine. But you eventually get used to it and the game would be worse off without it. Controlling them
a controller, there isn't any way around that. What surprised me most was that you interact with many of the events in this story that I expect to be thrown into a cutscene. Which makes the emotional impact of some scenes all the harder.
Settings are limited due its console roots but overall the game looks rather good, even if it's not going to blow your socks off. There isn't any Steam Cloud (not that it's really necessary) and all the settings are managed in the launcher. All two of them (resolution & v-sync + keybindings). However, the game didn't have any framerate or crashing issues on my end.

This is a game worth the single playthrough you'll get from it. You'll get around 3 hours from the playthrough and it'll leave one hell of an impression. There are few games that leave such a mark in my mind and Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons is one of them. The unique control scheme and the game's insistence that the player be involved as much as possible is well done. I have few complaints with Brothers. This was my GOTY for 2013 and it was earned.
Welp, Game of the Year unless something amazing comes out of nowhere in much the same way that this did. Like To The Moon? Like Journey? Play this now in one sitting on a rainy afternoon.

Buy? Likely. I was convinced to buy this game thanks to TotalBiscuit - I didn't know this game existed until I saw his video. Is this a great showpiece of gaming that made me cry? Honestly, no. I didn't cry. Whether that's the fault of the game or if I'm too emotionally unresponsive is impossible for me to answer, but you do have a good story based puzzler with a clever mechanic of controlling two characters with a separate analogue stick and trigger. I don't think that the tale alone of a random father who is on his deathbed thanks to an undescribed condition as well as the ending is enough to make me cry - gaming has desensitized me to death.
There is some gameplay contrivance, such as why is there a funky, switch activated bridge just to get to one family's house? Puzzles are cleverly implemented in my opinion, but all are simple to solved - you'll rarely if ever be stumped. This game has plenty of photogenic moments as shown by my screenshot library, and this can be completed by most around 3 hours. It's arguably pretentious, but I don't think it's trying to force some abstract artistic or literary vision.
Brothers - AToTS looks like something Pixar could do if they weren't limited to doing purely "Disney friendly" content. I enjoyed the game, but I was not as moved as many people said - I will no longer let people's fawning over a story experience influence my buying habits.

GOTY 2013 for me. Just incredible. In the same realm among the likes of Journey and Limbo, this game knows how to tell an emotionally compelling story mechanically - in this case via logical and fitting puzzle solving and platforming and via an innovative 'one player co-op' control method. And who needs excessive and intrusive cutscenes and celebrity voice-acting?! THIS is how you tell a story in a videogame developers! No dialogue, just this gibberish and actions/expressions, it's so well done. Overall, excellent fairytale world setting, unique and slightly low-poly aesthetic though I think that's intentional, lovely chanting and voila soundtrack. We NEED more games like this, buy this, play this. Please. It is now one of my favourite games of ALL time, it's that exceptional.

Did you miss out on Journey? Have you wanted a game that will make you think about family relationships and how your hands work at the same time? Are you ready for a god damn ADVENTURE? Good, because this is your game!
Brothers gave me three hours of fascinating exploration, amazing detail and wonderfully fun puzzles. It's not hard in the slightest, but you still feel a sense of satisfaction out of each new setpiece that never overstays its welcome.

Initial impression:
Being a player of Magic the gathering I though that this game was going to be boring, however, due the low price and the Scot Piligrim art style I gave it a shot.
TL;DR:My thoughts were wrong, It's actually a pretty neat and nice game
Gameplay
***********
The gameplay it's really simple, the objective is to kill your opponent, you do it by placing and connecting cards that have different types in a 3x3 space.
Types of cards:
Attack: Hit the oponent or kill a Card in your opponent's board.
Defense: Give you life.
Resurrect: Resurrect a dead card.
Neutral: They don't do nothing, but these cards have multiple connection arrows allowing you to easly connect gaps.
in order to achieve different effects.
When 2 or 3 cards connect (Depending of the ammount of symbols of Attack, def, etc) they do the effect and dissappear.
You have to place a card mandatory each turn, so if you cannot place anymore you lose (Same for your opponent).
At first the game it's really easy since your opponents don't have combos and kill themself because they fill the grid, but after a while it becomes more challening.
Regarding progression, it seems that there are a lot of cards (Common, uncommon, rare and legendaries), you win booster packs by defeating other characters.
Art:
****
The art of the cards it's really cool, most of them are weird stuff (There's an avatar that's a Carrot with a hat). As stated before, the art style really looks like Scot Piligrim.

I'm impressed with the card game. It's charming, with very simple rules, while still requiring thoughtful tactics. It's not a hardcore trading card game, but it's not casual either. It's more of a distillation.
You have to "link" cards in a 3x3 grid to activate them, but specific cards can only link in certain directions (there are arrows on the cards... check out the screenshots). This mechanic allows the game to have very simply cards (there aren't really stats on cards) and still require thought.
It ticks nearly all the checkboxes, deck building, booster packs, good art direction and music.
It's set in a neat universe with some irreverently quirky characters. As rich as the universe is though, the story's a bit thin. You have to collect legendary cards from various "bosses" to enter an ultimate tournament and win a million coins. It's little more than a reason to be playing cards with every person you see... which isn't a bad thing at all.

I haven't played too much of it, but that doesn't mean I can't still give you my opinion! I really like it so far, and plan on putting a good bit more time into it. I'm gonna try to give you a good idea of the game becuase not too much is explained here or anywhere online so bear with me.
It's a very simple little card game wrapped in a Yu-Gi-Oh-esque adventure shell. You go through different locations battling people, getting more cards, getting new decks, all in an effort to get the 8 legendary cards and become super cool and powerful and make mad bank at a tournament.
The gameplay itself is simple. There's a world map that you click locations on to go there and interact with or battle people (also, click around the environment to find hidden coins!).  The card game puts a heavy emphasis on positioning. All the cards have arrows on them, and you want to put your cards together so their arrows point at eachother. Connect (usually) 3 arrows and you can make a combo to either do damage, increase your defense(HP) or other effects. That's it. You win when your opponent has no defense or can't play another card.  After you win, you generally get a pack of cards to build your deck with, and some money to buy more packs.  Your deck must be at least 25 cards, but they can be bigger.
I really like the story, well what little of it I've seen so far. It's basic, you know, get the best cards and be the best. That's good enough for me though, and it should satisfy anyone who grew up watcing shows about kids playing card games.  So far, it's bee pretty light-hearted, it's silly and kinda funny which I dig. The art style is childlike and well drawn in a good way, it fits the theme of the game very well. Now we move to the music, and goddamn do I love it. Seriously, I hope I can get the soundtrack, because it's probably my favorite part.
The last thing to mention is the price. It's 2 bucks right now. Yes, it's clearly a port of a tablet game. No, it doesn't have visual/sound options aside from a resolution changer and a window/fullscreen button. No, it does not have multiplayer. Let me bring this up again. IT'S 2 BUCKS. Even when it goes to full price at 4 bucks, it's still totally worth it. If you like card games, you should buy it. Even if you don't like card games, but cheap and charming games, buy it. Anyone can get into this, and you should get into it.

Summary: The game is quite good, but it's not perfect. There are minor hints at mobile heritage, but nothing that would stop anyone who might like a computerized card game from having plenty of fun.
Progress Disclosure: I finished the game and have every achievement. I didn't collect every card. That took about 14 hours. It could probably be done in 8-10 hours by someone hurrying.
Updates: It's over 2 months later, and this game is still getting free content additions.
The mechanics have clearly received attention and tuning; the basics work nicely on their own, and as more abilities are introduced they interact in interesting but not convoluted ways. The interface in general is good; however, it is full of tiny delays for animations and pointless confirmations of non-permanent actions. Combat animations can be set to anywhere between 100% and 200% speed in the options, at least.
The tutorial was good, even having heard and read nothing about the game except the store description before playing. The difficulty hasn't sharply spiked or stayed tutorial easy since; the AI can be observed getting steadily more competent in addition to having better cards. Most games are semi-close wins, and the occasional enemy provokes a new deck style. I have a win ratio around 5, and I doubt that's exceptional.
Deck size is allowed to vary between 25-40 and failing to draw causes damage, so milling is a somewhat viable strategy with the right cards.
There's an deterministic, seemingly associative 2-input alchemy system. The vast majority of combinations are disallowed, and this is indicated by dimming incompatible cards; there's still a pretty large space of recipes, though. A little experimentation produced some deck-worthy but not ridiculous cards. As an example, two Pancakes gives a pretty good milling card. I didn't find a guide, so I'll warn that in my experience combining a alchemy-created card and one of the ingredients used to craft it is allowed but just gets the created back, effectively throwing a card away.
There are 6 icon-identified deck slots; a card can be used in multiple decks. The deck building interface is passable if imperfect; it lacks bulk management options, and the sorting options are deficient. It could use a tweak to show more cards on a PC screen. Cards used in decks are hidden on store and alchemy menus (for good reason).
The art style is pleasant. The dialogue is mildly humorous overall and better in parts; the optional dialogues are pretty extensive, as well.
The achievements look to be quite doable, so it would probably be good for 100%ers. The non-trivial ones (10+ attack and 9 combo) are easy enough to manage once you have a 6+ arrow card and deliberately try.
As described, there are no hidden in-game currency, card, or booster purchases.
Accessibility: The game is fully turn-based with no time pressure ever. The interface doesn't require great precision, but it does require dragging. The interface is fully mouse-driven, except optionally entering your name. There are no vital sound-only cues. No lines are voiced; all dialogue is presented in text. Nothing relies purely on color for identification. As a non-expert, I see no problems.

Prologue
I know this is the remake... or the remaster of the 2003 remake to be precise, but i'm still going to talk about the 1996's original game since neither Steam nor pretty much any of the current digital distribution platforms offer the original PC ports of the RE trilogy (Which are the best versions by the way, though they're quite unknown to players) Which is a shame because it's really hard to acquire RE 1-3 for PC without getting an actual physical copy, but due to the rarity they tend to cost more than teenage wh*re's p*ssy. Luckily there's always Pira*e B@y, which i used as a kid when i first tried out RE.
My Introduction To BIOHAZARD
Resident Evil One... the game that started it all. Having been born just half a year after the release of the original, i didn't really have much of a chance to experience the 1996 masterpiece in its prime, but it didn't stop me from experiencing the series from the very original game first. I think it was back in 2006 when i first started fooling around with Pira*e Bay and torrents... so having been a loser whose only life was video games even back then, i started trying out older video games and one of these was the PS1 version of Resident Evil 1 on an emulator, but since our family's computer back then was a potato with carrots for cables, it couldn't emulate anything for♥♥♥♥♥♥ so i proceeded to download the PC version and luckily so, because even to this day, i HIGHLY prefer the PC versions of the classic RE trilogy.
My First Taste Of The Original 1996 Game
So, it was 2006, i had our family's ♥♥♥♥♥♥ computer ready for this supposedly classic horror game and i was about 12 years old back then and a huge ♥♥♥♥ing coward too. My family was always at work or away so i spent majority of my time at home alone, so i could pretty much watch or play whatever the ♥♥♥♥ i wanted to despite the Age Rating. I still remember the first time i launched RE1 and getting startled at the cheesy intro of Chris getting killed by a zombie. So my first playthrough stopped soon after the iconic ''Zombie Introduction CGI'' y'know the one with the clown looking zombie biting the S.T.A.R.S member's gory head off and then staring back at you. Yeah, i got scared of that and tapped ALT+F4 like a hyena. Afterwards, i had a ''short'' 2 week break from this back-then ''terrifying'' game, and then tried it again... i don't remember if i ever finished it as a kid, but i sure as hell sucked at it, but nonetheless it was and still is, a game that i love and RE1 will always have a special place in my black heart.
Review Of The 1996 Game
STORY - Cheesy as ♥♥♥♥ and iconically so. The voice acting especially, is something RE1 is known for and not in the good way. It's so bad that even the 12 year old me noticed that something was off about ''the way these guys talk'' (quoting my younger self ;P). The story itself has all sort of ret*rded sh*t going on like the fact that this supposedly highly trained S.T.A.R.S special rescue team consists of members that intentionally decide to split up all the time thinking it's the best idea in a HUGE mansion full of apparent cannibals (Read: Zombies) and other mutated monsters. Luckily you can, and many do view this original game as a horror comedy since the aforementioned voice acting really is hilariously bad (Which by the way originates from the fact that Capcom just hired some random people to do the voices purely based on their appearance 'cause they needed them for the live-action intro too)
GRAPHICS - For its time, the pre-rendered backgrounds albeit quite blurry, were still very beautiful and well received for their semi photo-realistic visuals and i myself greatly enjoy them. Basically this means that the environments are just pictures/photos instead of actual 3D models which allowed for much greater emphasis on detail and atmosphere back in the day. Though the characters and items are proper 3D models and therefore tend to stand out from the scenery a bit, but eh, that's just part of the old RE magic.
GAMEPLAY - Now this is where some newer fans and casual players have had trouble with. Resident Evil made use of the so called ''tank controls'' for a very long time, all the way from this to RE5 before Capcom decided to listen to the filthy casual crybabies who couldn't handle them and the bit of a challenge it brought along. So these tank controls basically mean that your character moves like a tank in the manner of needing to rotate the character with ''left'' and ''right'' buttons and from there on walking either forward or backwards with ''up'' and ''down'' buttons instead of instantly moving in the direction you press like in most video games.
Many of these complaining people don't realize that since the old RE games are viewed from constantly changing static angles as you move, so if your guy/gal instantly moved in the direction you're pressing, you would be constantly running in the wrong direction you didn't mean to since the camera angles change in relation to the direction your character is facing at. So the tank controls are necessary... well, the N64 port of RE2 and the modern remasters of REmake and Zero optionally feature modern controls, but like i said, it doesn't work very well.
Plus, the tank controls add weight and realism to your character's animations and the general ''feel'' of the game.

Ibb & Obb looks like it might be a good game to play with your young kid.  Simple graphics, relaxing soundtrack, cartoon atmosphere.  But it's actually pretty darn challenging for myself and my brother, who are in our early 20s.  The game requires a lot of 2D spatial critical thinking, and anyone younger than a teenager will probably have difficulty with the game.
Ibb & Obb is a bit different from most puzzle platformers because the primary object you use to overcome obstacles is your partner, instead of the usual items or abilities in your inventory.
When one of you dies, both of you die.  However, the dev was smart and makes you respawn almost immediately and very close to where you died.  This allows the game to keep its relaxed feel, and when you die, myself and my brother found ourselves laughing instead of getting frustrated, because there's no real penalty for dying.
Cool game and a good soundtrack make this a recommendation for me.  The only downside to the game is the simplistic graphics, but all the other "Pros" to the game outweight that single Con.

Really wanted to like this game, because the premise sounds really interesting, but in the end, it just doesn't live up to what it sets out to do.
+ Great premise
+ Fairly interesting story
+ Mostly good voiceacting
+ Responsive controls + FOV slider
- Mentally challenged AI
- Flat and boring levels
- First person platforming
- Loads of small unpolished bits
Probably not worth the full price.
The controls feel responsive enough, but getting stuck on some level geometry and ragdolls occasionaly messes with the flow of the game.
Took a few minutes to get used to the heavy scottish accent of the main character, but other than that, her voice acting is good. Most of the other voice acting is passable, but some is downright awful - the german soldiers for example.
They keep the feminist stuff on the down low at the start, the kids freaking out during the quake deathmatch when finding out the player's a girl was kind of funny, but everything after that felt really hamfisted. Boils down to "Hey guys! Us gamer girls have it so hard, eh? Eh?" It ends up reinforcing the stereotypes it's trying to fight, though it's not too dominating, so whatever, it's fine.
The levels never end up capturing the feel of the games they're based on. Most of them feel really copy-paste after a while and get confusing due to the uniform nature and lack of a minimap. The quake/doom levels are too large and open, feeling empty. The CoD levels could have been more linear, but end up being claustrophobic and too open at the same time. You're either stuck in a narrow hallway or have half of the wehrmacht zeroing in on you. The medieval levels felt the most natural and the halo levels looked the best. The AI is really stupid, and it shows. The zombies have DayZ levels of hit detection and are frustrating to fight. Most of the enemies just run at you and shoot. Most of the time the enemies are really easy to beat, but then the game turns up the difficulty and throws 10x more enemies with 5x stronger attacks at you. Near the end a new enemy type that can turn invisible shows up, instead of providing a new interesting challenge, they bumrush your ♥♥♥♥♥♥ while cloaked and  proceed to backrape you. The only really enjoyable part to play was the medieval level, as the skeletons encountered fit with the braindead AI and the shooting enemies didn't really move, and then the game throws some 30+ OP enemies at you and messes it all up.
The bosses follow the same pattern, first ones are just bullet sponges that are very easy to beat and then there's the flying saucer that has attacks you need to dodge, but the range of these attacks is hard to judge and seemingly inconsistent, making the fight annoying.
Player's health doesn't regen during level change, so you may be stuck with 5% health and no medkits anywhere to be seen. You may restart the level to fill the health, but you will lose all your weapons. You can also get stuck between some geometry.
There are short "virtual space" levels between the main ones and about halfway through they become frustrating as falling down from the platforming parts is instakill and the game is really inconsistent with checkpoints.
There are also some bits where british politics are brought into the dialogue, don't care about that personally, but seems like a good way to♥♥♥♥♥♥off a potentially large portion of your playerbase.
The game doesn't feel challenging, rather unfair at places. Playing on normal managed not to die until the final sewer section fighting against the zombie horde. Then the trend of swooping through most of the level and then constantly getting killed at a point where the game throws a huge number of enemies at you continues throughout the game.
If you're willing to get frustrated every time you have just begun to enjoy the game and rinse and repeat for some 4 hours, then it's for you. The deathmatch section, retro games and a few bits and pieces at other spots were fun enough so it's not fair to call this total shovelware, but it just doesn't live up to it's own premise.

I was quite disappointed during and after I finished the game.
I was told there would be a premise of hopping between game timelines, and although they do, I expected going from Duke-Nukem-3D era to modern. The game doesn't go back that far, starting near Quake era.
The weapon graphics don't change with the time period,  so your weapons are entirely unmodified throughout the game.
This leads to direct comparison of the quake-esque weapons with a Halo setting.
Despite that, the graphical differences are not very noticeable.
Modern is not an immensely HD texture, and the retro ones aren't polygonal messes (I think they should be).
The player character's voice is a Scottish woman, which didn't annoy me but could be annoying to some. She talks a lot.
The premise is interesting and develops throughout the game but ends on a cheap cliffhanger.
The most entertaining part of this game was using an MP40 from the mid-2000s WW2 era of games to fight Skyrim skeletons. That was a moment that put a smile on my face at just how silly it was.

This is an amazing game. The writing is very tight, good science fiction. The voice acting is top-notch (who doesn't want to listen to gamers curse like sailors with a Scottish accent?!)
The combat and level design can get rather repetitive, too many wide-open-space battles with weapons that don't have interesting differences. But this is made up for by great nostalgia references and some very quirky levels, like stomping around an RTS as a giant, first person pac-man, and a side-scrolling shmup.
Definitely recommend this game to anyone who enjoys classic FPS titles, great dialog, or female protagonists.

The game is written well enough to be interesting for people who are well into the RE games and for those that are new to them, with gameplay that's challenging enough on normal to be fun.
The game's place in the RE universe isn't strictly canonical/non-canonical, being a ~70% canon "what if?" scenario that is believable enough for the people that know the background material.
That said, it isn't a long game campaign wise, and some of the settings involved are a pain (Games For Windows Live being the top of that list), and is better suited to co-op play with friends than going it alone.
Getting it to work first try just doesn't happen - you have to program remove all Games For Windows Live stuff already on your computer, then reinstall it from the xbox webiste, then reinstall it through the game, then sign in...
...but once you've done that, it just works.
It's probably going to be more enjoyed by the kind of people that liked the Left for Dead games, in that its level progression is more forgiving while also having a better range of easier-harder difficulty settings (they feel pretty good for what they're labelled as), access to an extended arsenal that everybody can use but has to be unlocked (without the to-range guns being "stupid strong" - there are a few direct upgrades, but those are only minor, with the big changes also drastically affecting reload time, range etc in a negative trade-offf), and abilities.
The grenades system is familiar enough for those players, but the special grenades and one-use items are improved on - there are two characters for every class (one for one campaign, one for the other), and each of those gets two passive abilities that can be upgraded and chooses one from three active abilities that can be upgraded, resulting in easy to select varying gameplay per person and a largely range of 'special items', which can be used multiple times due to the recharge mechanic.
The health system is also better. There's the normal healing items that you can carry, which also heal any allies you're next to, and a virus mechanic that can turn your downed allies into an enemy (don't worry, even if you blow their legs off, you can still revive them good as new - and they get their base kit back!), and you can heal that or go on the run for a while if you don't have access to the right tools, but two classes are also set for dealing with it.
The big thing though is that you can just... revive people. You don't have prone time, but you don't need it, as you just get them back up ready to go pretty easily.
6.5-7/10 game for objectively, though it'll obviously score less with people that were never going to like the game.

You are tasked with controlling the pair of siblings in real time with opposite sides of the controller. If it sounds like it can get confusing, don't worry it does. But it is worth it. At its worst, it can feel like scratching your head and rubbing your stomach at the same time, but there are moments where there is a lot of subtext behind the button presses. Those are moments where Starbreeze manages to put real emotional impact in actually playing the game, not just watching it play out in a cut scene.
Just as brilliant as Limbo, Journey and all the other emotionally charged, short games of that ilk. Play it.

This game is simply marvellous. Until this very day I will never cease to regret stumbling upon Spore when I was around thirteen years old. By the time you launch the game, the whole galaxy spreads wide before your eyes, leaving you lost in thoughts of becoming a god - either a protector and overseer, or relentless emperor capable of slaughtering millions. The path is straight from the beginning - from a single cell to entire population - you are supposed to be perfect. Enough to survive the harsh enviroment of your home planet until you aim for the stars.
What I adore about this game is the creator. You are left with almost infinite amount of choices on how to portray your creatures. Every time I play, I come up with something new - and it always works. Thats why I enjoy the first two stages the most.
It's a bit of a pity there is a certain limitation on how many parts you can use in the gameplay though, that's always what I'm struggling a bit about. Also, sometimes the games look maybe more childish than necessary, I would love to see a more serious approach and maybe a free creation system next time - if there will ever be something that could work as a sequel to this gem.
So, let's sum it up. I'm almost 19 years old now, and I still love this game no matter what. Occasionally I find a little time to play, and get lost in this evolutional marvel. My world, my creations.
And hell, no way I care that this game is meant for kids - maybe because I've never ceased to be one deep inside.

I purchased The Witcher two reasons:
1.) It cost me less than 2 dollars.
2.) The storyline and gameplay were supposed to be superb.
I'll put the bottom line up front. It really isn't worth your time if you are looking for a good, deep and well acted story line. If you are in it for the scenery, then it does quite well, especially considering the age of the game.
This game has all the potential to be superb, but fell flat on its back instead. The lore and setting of the game is excellent, but the developers took absolutely zero advantage of developing into a rich, interactive environment. Instead, you are left to read about the lore in your journal, when you'd rather be living it out in the game. Its other crimes include shallow to non-existant character developement and quests involving no critical thinking or problem solving,
First I'll talk about the quests, both main and side. Side quests are simply step and fetch, and you as the messenger boy will have to ceaselessly run back and forth across the same wide areas over and over again to hack and slash X number of beasties and bring back Y items from their corpses. Really, that's the whole game. No thinking involved, and nothing to develope the personality of your character. The main story quests are no different in the fetch nature. You can summarize the entire game thus: Geralt runs to the swamp and gets X item for Character A, returns to Vazima. Geralt runs to the swamp and gets Y item for Character B, returns to Vazima. Do this for the entirety of the alphabet and you will have beaten the game. You won't have learned anything about your character, the background and lore of the game, nor any of the supposedly "main" cast of characters.
The cast of characters is interesting, but none of them are ever developed into anything meaningful, and they never feel necessary to the story, except as recepticals for the quest items which you bring them. The voice acting is shallow and the lines are often something you would imagine a 15 year old saying if he was trying to act the part in a midieval adlib play.
The game is also overly sexualized. Every single woman has boobs that they most certainly paid for, and you actually get collectable cards for every woman you choose to have sex with. Unless you are a 13 year old boy who just discovered his first swimsuit edition calendar, this is incredibly pathetic. Actually, it's disgusting, let's be honest.
The story only gets good in the Epilogue, when your character is chasing down his final enemy and you are presented with the choices you made along the way. Now, none of these supposed momentous choices actually change anything huge in the end. Neither do any of the choices aid or hinder you in any meaningful way come the final chapter. They simply get woven into the dialogue in a way that finally feels meaningful, even if the ending is about the same. If the whole game had been this way, it would have launched The Witcher from being "bad to mediocre" to a level of "enjoyable".
The final strike against this game is the fact that it is incredibly buggy. Oftentimes, combat is entirely unresponsive. Doesn't matter what you click, doesn't matter what spell you want to cast, you will stand like a lifeless dummy in front of your enemy as he takes chunks from your flesh. I encourage you to google the other bugs, but there are too many to list here. Crashes, items disappearing from your inventory, on and on and on.
The graphics are excellent for its age. The cities and landscapes are very well laid out, but you can't explore them the way you wish you could, or the way other games allow you to. Much of what you see is inaccessable, as you can't climb the smallest hill, jump down a river bank, most stairs have an invisible wall stopping you from climbing them, etc. There isn't much incentive to exploring unless you are just wanting to take a look at the graphics and layout. In other games, exploring every nook of the kingdom you are inhabiting is bound to lead you to some interesting sidequest or buried little treasure, there really isn't anything out there. Just grass and trees, and randomly spawning monsters who don't carry anything intriguing on them and are typically easy to kill.
Well that's it. The Witcher has great graphics for it's time, but a buggy and ineffective combat system, and  a story that falls on its rear in a hollow heap of blandness when it had every chance to be great.

I did complete my playthroughs of the original Witcher game prior to the release of the beast that is known as
. The Witcher game series is based on fantasy books originally released in Poland, and their story centers on Geralt of Rivia, a witcher, a man blessed, cursed, and tasked with killing supernatural creatures in a grim fantasy setting. For context and story, prior to playing
, I strongly recommend playing through both
and
.
Gameplay in
involves resolving quests, hunting for monsters, and battling foes along the way. Combat, for the most part, is swordplay, although physical combat is supplemented with magic in the form of witcher signs and alchemy to boost abilities. Some fights can be challenging, and being prepared (often meaning drinking the right potions for the right occasion) can make all the difference in the more difficult fights. Occasionally combat starts immediately following a cutscene, hence not allowing for the required preparation (which cannot be done while in combat). As such, liberal use of the save game feature comes in handy.
One of my pet peeves with the Witcher series as a role-playing game series is that your only option to play the game is as Geralt of Rivia. My bar for role-playing games is set by the various Bioware games (Dragon Age, Mass Effect). Sure, you can only play Mass Effect as Commander Shepard, but you do have the option to play as male or female and pursue good or evil paths. On top of that, Geralt is not exactly the nicest guy in the world. He can grow on you, and in the English version of the game, Doug Cockle's voice aligns perfectly with Geralt's cynical outlook. You also get plenty of opportunity to build your Geralt's abilities as you see fit by reinforcing his combat, magical, or alchemy skills.
The Witcher series takes place in dark, medieval setting with a healthy sprinkling of fantasy elements, ranging from dwarves and elves to monsters and the undead. The background story for the world is actually quite rich and deep, with political intrigue, various monarchs vying for power, and race relations bubbling to the brink of civil war. While Geralt operates within this context, he is not out to bring peace or be the hero who solves it all. In fact, he often takes the stance of staying out of the conflicts of men and just focusing on his monster killing business. The story that has clearly been going on long before the game even begins continues to evolve throughout the series.
Technically
is sound, although the graphics and production value in general continue to improve as the series goes on, culminating in the masterpiece that the third game is.  I do not recall encountering any major issues during my gameplay.
Yes. There are opportunities to make different decisions along the way. Also, a few of these decisions influence outcomes in the sequels.  I played the game both on Medium and Hard difficulty.

I have poor sight, so when the screen suddenly zooms

, this kind of zooming is unnecessary and only serves to irritate the player. An online game should use a set zoom (with the zoom level in the options). As it is, the constant stretching and shrinking, stretching and shrinking, stretching and shrinking makes me feel nauseous. Synchronization through vocal communication is important. The game provides no way to synchronize actions other than skill alone. It does not feature hand holding countdown timers through a button press nor gameplay elements favoring synchronization.
The directional controls feel like there is something uncanny about the acceleration rate, inertia and friction.
The above combined makes it so that several puzzle elements are frustrating because they are non deterministic. A slight variation in position or momentum will cause your character to move in various ways with a difficult to predict outcome, meaning that a puzzle section has to be attempted many many many times before any success, even if you already know how the puzzle is meant to be solved.
Some puzzles will require one specific player to execute one specific part of a puzzle. There are sometimes an urge to swap roles which can't be done.
It may be difficult to have two players stay engaged through the entire game. The overall longevity of the game is obfuscated because an entire chapter may have such frustrating puzzles we had to stop at the end of each chapter and resume days later.
There is frustrating difficulty but it doesn't feel "bad", it feels like it was intended to be this way.

Bedlam: One of the few games making me wish I could give a neutral recommendation rather than a strict yes or no.
To start things off I'd like to make it clear that Bedlam is best experienced if you have low expectations going into it however that's not to say that it is a bad game. This game, like all others has its flaws.
I received Bedlam from♥♥♥♥♥(Thanks for censoring G2_ steam) buying a few random keys with some left over money and took one look at the store page and said "This looks like a mess, probably another indie dev trying to make something cool but really just ending in a clusterf-" well, point made without having to incur steam's wrath. To a slight extent my initial thoughts were correct, this game is a complete (I suppose I'll say CF in place of the previous word) CF though not necessarily in a bad way.
Map design:
Overall the quality of maps is about average for what you could expect from a game this price, perhaps a bit better from personal experience. No two maps in Bedlam feel alike, sometimes it feels great but other times it is an utter nightmare. This game unfortunately suffers from poor map design where it matters most, objectives are confusing to find and at certain points within the game progression can be ground to a halt because the map was laid out poorly. That being said there is still an appreciable level of quality to them all, they all feel natural despite being confusing at times and generally end up being enjoyable to explore and take in, not on the level of Skyrim or similar but it has its own unique charm though despite this some of the levels can be downright infuriating, especially towards the end of the game.
Plot:
Bedlam's plot is simple yet sweet, Starting out with a blank slate in a white room, your only information being your character supposedly having some form of surgery performed on her only to wake up within a virtual world themed around numerous different video games from Quake to pacman. Your goal throughout the entire game is attempting to find a way out of the "gameverse" and back to your life though as it would be expected, you run across numerous roadblocks along the way. Grunts in quake to aliens in space invader or world war 2 German infantry. Along the way you are "assisted" vocally by numerous other individuals in the same predicament as yourself and eventually end up teaming up with another individual to attempt to take down the one behind the "gameverse" you exist in and earn your freedom once more. Though this story had potential it felt a bit bare bones, I realize this type of game would have a bit of a lackluster story line focusing more on gameplay however despite this it felt a bit weak with little explained to the player and ultimately being left on a cliffhanger with only our thoughts to figure out what may have happened beyond the end of the game.
Combat:
Combat in Bedlam is tolerable and at times enjoyable, if you can find a weapon you like and then ammo for said weapon however there is a large and somewhat disturbing power gap between early and late game weapons, carrying around tons of weapons to only end up needing 3 or 4 which is highly disappointing as the further into the game I got the more I wanted to use some of my older weapons, only to find that they were next to useless most of the time which to an extent falls into the mapping category, the enemies most certainly get stronger with time however the weapons suffer most because of range. Range will be your worst enemy in this game, enemies will often blend in with the scenery or snipe you from a distance assuming they haven't all rushed you like brain dead children with no sense of self preservation. In their defense though, they all have incredibly good accuracy to the point you're probably gonna get hit if you're not behind cover.
Performance:
For a game coming out when it did with graphics like these it's unfortunate to say Bedlam runs somewhat poorly, optimization was done poorly as throughout the game I would experience infrequent however quite noticeable hiccups and frame tanks when using certain weapons, the rather bad♥♥♥♥♥looking fire shooting sword received roughly halfway through the game would cause frame drops of 20+ frames when equipped no matter where I was. Some portions of the maps start to get a tad sluggish with high enemy counts though if your computer is above potato status these drops will be minimal at worst. Potato PCs should avoid this game if good framerates are a must.
Pros:
Interesting story
Amusing dialogue
Decent weapon variety
Adequate map design variation
Nostalgia
5-6 hours for a relatively low price.
Cons:
Poor optimization
At times confusing map layout
Little explanation of anything
Bullet hell. The unfair, hair pulling kind.
Power creep
Anticlimactic, overall pathetic "boss" fight ending on a cliffhanger.
Overall:
Bedlam is a decent little game for its price range, it has its moments where it's something than can be quite lovable. Even if a few minutes later is has you swearing at your monitor because the quality suddenly dropped. The game has noticeable flaws, more than it has strengths though if you can catch it on sale (or better yet, free) I'd suggest picking it up to give it a go. At worst you waste a few hours on an overly ambitious project from some Scots that evidently tried to make a good game but had some difficulties. This game is far from being great, unfortunately as I loved the concept but it is also not a bad game. Bedlam is one game truly deserving a mixed rating, such as it has now. Not everyone will find what they're looking for in Bedlam, some people will hate it and others (myself included) will attempt to love it for what it is, regardless of how flawed it happens to be.

Haunt the House: Terrortown is a very short yet charming little game backed by a very nifty art style.
-the art style is very nice and colorful
-funny sound design with quirky ghost sounds, amusing screams and nice soundtrack
-the overall gameplay is fun, making people scream and run away from your ghost and haunted objects really becomes a guilty pleasure
-tons of objects to haunt with 2/3 different scares each
-simple yet effective controls
-the game is VERY short,about an hour for both the main game+expansion, you'll get some more mileage if you decide to replay it to hunt achievements though
-not really any strategy involved, you can just spam an object's spooks and it'll do the trick as there's no need to diversify
-sometimes terrified people will run the wrong way rather than exiting the location, giving you extra work without reason as you scramble to terrify them again
Overall Haunt the House offers a very charming and quite amusing experience, it's just a shame that the game is so light on content and extremely easy.
I think that the 2$ sale price I got it for is a decent proposition overall, the game is fun enough,sports a really good art style after all and this is enough to give it a try if you think it'd be your thing.

Each game takes 10 turns; and, during these 10 turns, the opponents switch back and forth between different regions, while trying to earn as much victory coins as possible at the expense of the other players.

Awesome game! Unfortunately this port is pretty hom hum. It's not the worst port I've seen but it screams lazy. Like they didn't do anything to make this PC ready. In the option settings you only have 2 options and they are for sound...  I'm not playing on a tablet. I want resolution options, I want a fullscreen mode without having to ALT+ENTER, etc. The tutorial also does not load, its almost as if its trying to use flash like its a web browser game. The rules can't be broken, so there is no he said she said trying to interpret what something actually means between players. The art style and UI works really well for the game. Still the game holds its own despite all of the annoyances. So It's worth the money but I really hope the developers own up to some of these issues and fix them. If they do they will not only make their customers happy but also prove that their future titles will be supported. And that's a great thing us customers like to be aware of.

I played a lot lot of P&C games since my childhood being born in early 90s, so I kinda follow the genre ever since. And it took me time to get Machinarium, I wanted it!
But I must say the visual appeal has unfortunatly nothing to do with the content. The first hour of discovery is alright and pretty blowing. But as I went through "riddles" and repetitiv puzzles and minigames (which represent half of the game), I found Machinarium's limit. Not only some minigames are  either difficult and unfunny to solve (they have several levels you must enforce to progress), either pointlessly easy, like fillers. But the riddles are out of logic, even in this mysterious world.
The last decades have proven you can achieve to implement a sense of logic in an absurd story and lore. And Machinarium fails at it imho. You have to try every item on every interactiv npc/environnement to find your way through. It's a pixel-check game that reminds the darkest days of p&c.
Then, devs have put 2 "help" tool in-game, including the solution to riddles/puzzles. Besides the gentle will of helping the customer, it tells us that devs were totally aware of the absurdity and difficulty of their own riddles. And that is unprofessional. A p&c with solution in-game, this says a lot...
Lastly, the ergonomy is nowhere to be seen. In Machinarium you actually have to "go to" the item you wanna check, and only then, you can interact with it. Meanwhile most p&c do that simply by a single click on the item itself.

I recently replayed this after not playing a Resident Evil game for at least 10 years. This is the Gamecube remake which completely updated the graphics, added new areas and story and re-recorded the hilariously awful voice acting. This remaster makes it available for modern widescreen displays and resolutions without adding (any?) extras.
The graphics are a mix, characters generally look good but some of the backgrounds and objects are very murky looking.
The set up is simple and as close to a coherent story as the series ever managed. There have been murders in the forest and you must investigate as a member of the ‘Special’ police (S.T.A.R.S).
The mysterious mansion and claustrophobic environments that you investigate fit well with the exploring and puzzles that are really the heart of the game. The puzzles are fun to solve, they are not to cryptic but you will have to think where and how to use items. The homage to classic horror movies add suspense and tension. Jump scares are used sparingly and the sound design is wonderfully creepy.
My major criticism is that the inventory management becomes cumbersome if you are playing for the first time because it is so limited. You have to guess when you need certain objects or tediously back track to collect and store items. The door cutscenes can thankfully be disabled with a mod as they are really slow.
The game offers good replayability. The 2 characters have slightly different stories and a few item changes between them.
Overall this holds up well for an essentially 20 year old game and I would recommend it if you want a slower paced adventure game.
