A friend of mine suggested this game, and it's quite fun! Although, the game has numerous flaws which can get in the way of playing... Let me list some of the Pros and Cons and such:
Very Fun and Addictive!
Quite good structures and realms!
Very quick difficulty learning curve, meaning you'll get the hang of it quite quick!
You get 'Perks' once you level up, which range from Cosmetic stuff to helping features to mandatory features.
Realms are easy to find, although quite confusing as well due to their erratic placement on the World Map. This can pose a problem when trying to find free space for a Realm. (See Below)
When you die, you don't lose anything, and just get sent back to the warp or a checkpoint if you hit it.
Realms have a location of their own, so placing them anywhere doesn't matter for their appearances, excluding where they're located on the map. This can lead to oddities where a player was expecting something themed after where they placed their Realm, only to find a small Grassy Realm with some of the basics.
The Game sometimes abruptly disconnects, although that often doesn't do much but log you out. Even then, you can just log back in with ease.
If you're offline for too long, your Realm may end up back in your inventory as a Deed to free up space in the World Map. It works, although finding free spaces isn't easy. (See Below)
The game doesn't make an account for you automatically, so you'll have to click on the Question Mark box on the right of it to make one there.
I know this is a free game and it costs to keep it up, but you should really consider making some items craftable in some form or another or make them much more cheaper, as you'll have to mine tons and tons of blocks to get the amount of Cubits you need just to buy them! (Or just use your real money.. See below) Heck, even the stores operated by players have cheaper items, making the official Cubit store kind of redundant, provided you can find one that's on, of course. This brings me to my next con (I'll get back to the store later);
You'll have to click each and every block you want to mine, as apposed to simply holding down the button associated with mining in Minecraft. I think there should be like a fill tool for mining where your Qbee (Or Tool) will mine out blocks within a certain radius (5x5x5?) or something. And speaking of mining...
Well, it's not that bad, but sometimes when your Qbee is mining, they'll say "I can't reach that!" even though it looks like it can easily, which means you'll have to manually move your Qbee to get to the block you want to mine. This is especially problematic in tunnels with only 1 block to pass through in the Y range (Vertical), since your Qbee will say "I can't reach that!" If you want to go up or down a block unless there's an 'air block' above you. And sometimes, your Qbee just spazzes out with Slam Jumps for a while if it's a bit high up. Which makes me go to my next point...
Only a few blocks have Slam Jump compatibility (In that they'll do something if you Slam Jump on them), while the majority of others don't. Plus, it gets in the way in Parkour Maps, where if you Double Jump and accidentally press the Jump button again, your Qbee will Slam Jump all the way to the bottom of the map or where ever the last ground block was (Provided it lands on it), meaning you'll have to restart the map from the beginning or checkpoint. Plus, speaking of Parkour Maps, I had a bit of difficulty in one where the Camera was basically covered by some ground in certain positions, which lets me go on to my next point...
I know there's Fadey Foam, but I think that could be like an option for worlds if you want to force the ground to fade somewhere, or if the feature is turned off. Honestly, it's really irritating if you make a cavern, and then you have to mine all the way to the edge of the map (Unless you change the camera angle, but even then, it could still be covered by the foreground) just because the camera is blocked by the foreground. And speaking of the camera...

You only have a certain radius of moving the camera up and down, and you can't even zoom in or out (Well, sans the fact it kind of zooms out from the bottom of the screen when you open up your inventory), although it can go in a full 360° along the X axis (Horizontal).

I once wrote  loving review for this game, it was in 2012. Time is moving forward and yet the game does not. There was once a great amount of charm around this game, the road from 1 to max level was fast and colorful, and it was all based on quests. Yes, quests, filled with brilliant voice work and actually building up to the idea that Justice League will accept you as their member. Although there was a part of me that didn't really like this idea of levelling like a sidekick (after City of Heroes and Champions Online), but I was intrigued by the idea of what will open when you actually become a member. And then, after reaching max level, the problems started.
Let’s talk about the endgame structure. After reaching level 30 you get introduced to a new vertical levelling system – Combat Rating(CR). All the endgame content is divided into Tiers, and each tier requires a certain amount of CR. Each tier consists of a few Challenges (Solo missions), Duos (2-man content), Alerts (4-man content) and Raids (8-man content). From each of this activities you get random loot drops (once a day) and a certain amount of currency that you can use to buy better gear. The better the gear -> the higher the CR -> the higher the tier that is available to you.
So, let us continue. With introduction of new Raids and Alerts, the story still treated you like a sidekick. But that isn't really a problem. The problem was, that there wasn't an actual story behind any new content. Yes there are few Investigations/Briefings(game's variant of Data Logs), a few cutscenes and an "epic premise" behind the scenes, which you don't have an ability to enjoy. In all the modes you get a little glimpse at something epic. And that's it. They did try to implement daily story missions in some DLC's but the last fun ones were in "Home Turf", since then it was only getting more boring.
Now remember that to get further in that little story, you need to have an appropriate CR. But until reaching the needed CR to open a new tier of content and some development on the story, you're just replaying the same few alerts over and over, grinding as if you're in an Asian MMO (which are changing to the best lately). Without any variation. Until you reach a new tier you are just replaying the same few activities. And the sad part is, that they reuse the same content in every new DLC, you will see instances that were there even from the launch of the game. And every new zone that they actually create in the latest DLCs are suffering from a copy paste syndrome, where the starting zone is something new, but when you walk a few meters all you get is catacombs with one repeating section. I've heard an argument that maybe they do this so that PS3 will run it without problems, but come on, Defiance on X360 has more variety.
And that is the main point, comics are all about the story and characters, so was this game (from 1-30 levels). But in the end the focus shifted and instead of creating and implementing new campaigns, they create a few grind arenas. And after you reach that maximum CR there is nothing to do, except maybe feats that grant you some Skill Points, but you will need to replay the same content that you will probably hate.
One thing that you can actually praise the development team for is balancing and patching. Although this praise can be nullified, because when you see their live stream where, after this many years, they are proud that some Bosses are no longer turning instantly, but they do take their time, it is just preposterous. But they do balance the powers towards each other, although instead of creating different instances of your power in PVE and PVP, they meshed it up and occasionally PVP players will cry about something, which will lead to PVE nerf for that power and brake someone’s style of playing.
All in all, I do hope, that they will get back to their roots of creating stories and original content. Now that SOE has become somewhat independent, it can lead to great things or turning the money into a complete cash-grabber.

This game is a push.
I can't say I don't like it...but I don't exactly recommend it either.
The game has lots of personality.  The music and visuals are totally appropriate for the tone and subject matter.  And the idea of being a ghost to scare people out of *wherever* it is you happen to be is fun.  Each object has its own feel, and they did a decent job about not repeating object animations too much.
The controls are sufficient for the game -- though even on a game pad they still feel a little sluggish.  That's fine since you don't really need pinpoint precision to get your scare on.  I'd still recommend against playing on a keyboard.
The gameplay, itself, is incredibly shallow, which is sort of acceptable for about as long as it takes to see each possible scare each item can provide.  The major issue is that you'll have seen each and every scare, on each of the maps, long before you run out of people to scare away.  It becomes an exercise in tedium as you rinse and repeat the same (now) tired scares to people because there appears to be little rhyme or reason as to how long any person takes before they either toss themselves out of a window or finally run out of the map.  Achievements aren't tacked on, but do appear to require more than one playthrough if one is looking for a 100% completion -- and the game just doesn't have enough depth to be worth a second playthrough.
A special nod, here, to the frequency of terrified people who constantly run past the exit rather than leaving the map is in order.  By about the halfway point, their tendency to stay -- despite all the freakish stuff happening around and to them -- simultaneously felt like an artifical extension and also served to break what little immersion there was and drag me out of the game through sheer annoyance.
I'm not sure I can even recommend it for children.  While there's nothing really objectionable here (there's no blood, even with the small number of people who are required to suffer fatal "accidents" or the people whom you might drive to auto-defenestration), the gameplay just becomes shallow and repetitive too quickly and there's little-to-no replay value that might allow me to otherwise justify the purchase.
I would only recommend it as part of a larger bundle, which is how I got it.

Mixed feelings but fails short when faced with other established names such as the Baldur's Gate series.
I heard about all the good reviews of the Witcher series since the time it has come out but somehow I never got to playing it as I felt that a Polish game developer would not be able to create an experience on the level of Baldur's Gate / Icewind Dale / Prince of Persia / Assasin's Creed (Ezio) series. I got a copy of this game in a sale for about 1.5 EUR which after spending 30 hours in the game seems to be the fair price for this game. So let's some up the good and the bad
Good:
- Modding community that lets you upgrade the graphics so it doesn't look dated even though it is 10 years old
- Original battle system. Some people dislike it but I found it to be a nice & refreshing change in comparison with the mindless left clicking until everybody is dead
- Immersive environment with a really good music soundtrack that makes the running around bearable and a meditative experience. The poker mini-game is a great example of that
- No level scaling - The key reason why I never played the Morrowind series. What's the point in leveling and getting better if the monsters level with you? Seems like such a lazy and cheap thing to do that this game gets a big plus for not having it. If you are not ready and you ignore the side quests - you die... the way it should be.
Bad:
- Running, running & some more running. Geralt? They should've named him Forest Gump.. Remember that time in Icewind Dale where you had to backtrack back & forth through the same location 3 times in a row in order to progress the same story? Well.. Multiply that by 10 times over and add a TON of meaningless side quests which seem to have been directly copied verbatim from the Progress Quest mockery of a game. The last time I saw a quest asking you to fetch an NPC some wine / food / 5 troll heads / 5 bat wings etc etc was in World of Warcraft .. just before I stopped playing it for exactly that reason. If I wanted to fetch people food I would get a job at a pizza delivery.. not pay to play an RPG game.
- Story: Somewhere around Chapter 2 I got completely lost and uninterested by all the mess caused by 10+ new characters being introduced and some mystery you are supposed to solve (its been a few days and I don't even remember what was the mystery).. It could've been caused by the onslaught of 30+ secondary quests and running back & forth for hours in the same single map location. I am now in the beginning of Chapter 4 and I couldn't care less about the story or the main character or characters he meets... probably because it took me 30 hours to get so far and the side quests add little substance except to serve as a leveling / money making mechanism.
- Lifeless protagonist: I have no idea what the fuss about Geralt or the Witcher is.. He is probably the least charismatic or inspiring video character I've ever played. A womanizing drunk with zero emotions and a monotonous voice that will put you to sleep. He kills monsters for money that he later spends on hookers & booze... with some forced choices that make him pick one meaningless side over another ... waaat?... Probably has to do with the Eastern European origins of the game & lore. I prefer the western characters which tend to have more passionate & epic lives.
The only reason why I keep playing is because the game mechanics are pretty good (the running around is significantly lowered after Chapter 2&3) and I remain hopeful that things will get better in the Witcher 2 & 3 (so i've heard) where you can import your save. I also hate deleting a game I paid for before I finish it. Would I recommend it? Sure.. for 1.5 EUR its OK.. Also you might have a different preference to the main character being basically a jerk.
To hell with your memory loss, the true goal in this game is to get laid as often as possible.

**Edit at bottom when I completed The Witcher**
Notice my time played. I'd only recommend this game if you are a die hard fan, learn about the story, or to experience The Witcher universe in a more missing depth from what you didn't know from before.
I personally like getting caught up in story, which is the only reason why I can't wait to finish this bloody game so I can get more onto the more exciting and well known parts of the games triolgy. In short, the game is extremely *insert curse word* annoying.
It would make me feel better if I took a minute to rant about MY experiences, since I'm currently on Act 4 (Minor Spoilers).
Prologue
Exciting, makes you question about your character's missing past, has the common cliche situations which happen but no better way to start off the game. Overall is pretty enjoyable!
Act 1
The game's more linear open world aspect loses slight attraction due to the horrible Quest Tracker, which in all honesty took me awhile to figure out (until Act 2's horrible mess of confusion made me learn it). The Act required a slight force of play but the story was interesting and fun enough to pull through, the ending outcome of the Act is extremely satisfying, plus he says Pleb which was a hoot. Overall is a building progress!
Act 2
Remnants of the past Act's second wind is still alive, now inside new territory. Rather exciting and the thought of wonder was high for me, but dies down by the frequant back tracking, annoying Quest Tracking, and finky♥♥♥♥♥emotions and reactions character's have, not to mention sometimes it feels like the past 20 minutes of flopping around the place was completely worthless when you find out one line of dialogue which you thought wasn't important or missed ends up changing you from the goal you thought you we're following but guess again I suppose.
I kinda digged that little lady, Shani, only to have her get all♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off at me without possibly thinking of another reasonable option, which happens quite a bit with a few character's but I get it, their trying to make "big decisions" happen even though they praise you for helping them one second then its like off with his head the next. Overall this Act is my first notice of annoyance, the story, saved by the investigation is still rather interesting and keeps you hooked at certain moments if you follow along.
Act 3
To be honest, my most enjoyable moment from this Act was from having to find a guard in the city streets and respond from a password just to have him, like any other guards you encountered before go like, "What?! Ahaha I'm just kidding *Tells the responding password*." Overall though I was pretty annoyed at the Quest Tracking system and the constant back tracking which CONSTANTLY seemed to always envolve around 5 different character's where everything is related too which quickly became tiring once noticed. Only cool thing was meeting Adda from the beginning cinematic of the game, that's it.
Act  4
The Act I'm currently on from writing this review. I've lost all motivation and it seriously feels like I'm grinding the last level in World of Warcraft, plus I'm annoyed enough to write a review lol. I can't wait for this mess to be over. Although...a very exciting moment happened were I was able to visit the fields and pluck about 15 raseberrys for future health gainz in fights. Overall that has been my highlight since I don't even have patience with this game to craft potions anymore.
Honorable Mentions and Final Thoughts:
This is a good game, don't get me wrong but I wouldn't recommend it unless you have a strong reason for doing so. The improved visuals are quite nice, especially lighting and I was always found of the realism, or at least more than other titles. How when it would rain, citizens of a town would seek cover, the grime and heavy masonry feeling, how studded in the English language some were and so on.
Only thing I can really say is that it feels like I was wasting my time running back and forth to the same 5 character's in each different Act with nothing but news as a messanger, where just watching a summary YouTube video would be a lot more beneficial. Based on my experiences and way I encountered things with huge amounts of back tracking I'd stay away from this game unless you are a die hard fan, motivation to learn the story, or just to experience the past.
**Edit**
The final two Chapters of The Witcher offically made it worth my time strange enough after all the annoyance. I felt slightly sad once it was over based on how perfectly things were put together in Act 5, and how thing's concluded in the Epilogue. At this point Geralt felt a hint like Command Shepard, in different ways of course but a hero. The first notice of me actually having a feeling finally for the character's Triss, Abigail, Geralt, Jacques, Dandelion, and Adda all folded and came into play which was refreshing after the incredibly slow pace and disaster I had to go through for most of the game. It was nice and was art in play, these final Chapters.
I would change it to now I recommend the game AFTER completing but that's too unrealistic due to how people still have to sit through the 60 percent of head smashing material of utter annoyance, so my result still stands even though the ending is beautiful. I'm hooked and am excited to see what The Witcher 2 brings next to the Chapter!

TL;DR Get this game. You will not regret it if you love The Elder Scrolls. IMO the best game in the series.
Within 5 days of purchasing this game, I've already spent 55 hours on this. This game is amazing. No, I'm not saying this is the best game in the TES series purely due to nostalgia. This is my first time playing this.
The reason why, in my opinion, this game is the best in the series, is that you have more freedom than all other games, and that your actions have great impact on other people's opinions on your character. This greatly adds to the immersion. I didn't even know where to begin with the MAIN QUESTLINE. There are so many factions/guilds to join, quests to complete, dungeons and shrines to raid, spells to create, skills to train, invincible wood elves to run away from, stupid wood elves to laugh at, annoying wood elves to simply ignore... The possibilites are quite endless in this game (wood elves are quite the outliers.)
One of the downsides I can think of about this game, for some, would be the combat system. If you hit somebody with a melee weapon or an arrow/bolt, there is a large possibility it won't register. At least in the beginning of the game. The combat system is a dice roll; the higher you train your skills, the less you will miss with your weapons, and the more often your spells will cast. The other downside is the graphics (if you care about them, of course.) Being honest, the graphics haven't aged well. However, there are MANY mods to suit your graphics needs. However, they are also somewhat poorly optimized, so even powerful computers likely wouldn't be able to maintain a solid 60 FPS with a heavily graphics-modded game.
Overall, I give this game a 9.85/10.

If you are looking for a horror game that will challenge you, this is a good choice!
Obviously this game is a remake of the classic Resident evil Director's cut developed and published in 1996 by Capcom on PlayStation and then in 1997 on Saturn and Windows.
The story takes place in a manor house where you took refuge after fleeing blood-stained dogs.
Unfortunately, a member of your team disappeared, depending on which character you have chosen (Chris or Jill).
It is by searching for him or her, after hearing a shot of gun that you realize this place has dark secrets.
It is through this adventure, trying to escape from this hell, that you discover the secrets at the base of the existence of the universe of Resident evil.
Now let's see the pros and the cons!
Pros
+ If you have played the director's cut, you will feel the same atmosphere and feel nostalgic;
+ The fact that we can perceive a lot of phobias in this game, zombies, spiders, evil dogs, bees, snakes, sharks and more;
+ You can change the resolution (original or 16/9);
+ Beautiful graphic.
Cons
- Inventory management can be frustrating because you always have to go back to the safe to pick up or drop things;
- The game can be very difficult for some people because a lot of things are limited, so if you do not like to break your head, despite the levels of editable difficulty, I do not recommend it for you, this is not a soft game with a horror atmosphere.
So I hope this will help you ^^.
Thank you for reading.

ibb & obb might be the most adorable game I've ever seen.
Psychedelic colors swirl around the screen, weird geometric characters dance about, parties are thrown for no reason whatsoever; it's just so 'effing cute and I wanted so much to fall in love with it. But playing ibb & obb is like petting a dog and having it bite your fingers off. It's cuteness is equally matched if not exceeded by its degree of frustrating, nonsensical design decisions, to where my head began to hurt so much I'm not sure how I ever managed to complete the trek through hell that was somehow hiding below the delightful exterior.
Just to be entirely clear, ibb & obb is coop only, meaning you better have a friend ready and willing to brave its horrors with you before you even press start. And to this point there are some pretty cool ideas buried here, which force you to play cooperatively and make clever use of its main gravity inverting hook. There are two sides to every level, with each flipping your character over like you've cut a hole straight through to the other side of the world and gravity hasn't yet realized.
Using both characters in tandem is almost always required to allow both to progress, be it providing a step up onto a ledge or using momentum to carry each other through. It's a fantastic hook but its implementation here is unbelievably hamstrung and convoluted. The camera that has to contend with two characters often going in opposite directions bears much of the blame, often obscuring parts of the environment or even your character entirely as you fight against it to keep moving as it holds you back. The pretty environments come at the const of making levels difficult to even comprehend, often blending so well with platforms or bubbles I needed to float in that I often had no idea they were something I needed to interact with.
Puzzle designs, while on occasion genuinely brilliant, are often constructed such a ridiculous manner that numerous times throughout the game I thought we were breaking the game finding their solutions. So many moments are needlessly tedious and absurdly challenging, forcing literal split-second timing which its floaty, imprecise controls make cumbersome at the best of times and a living nightmare at its worst. Each new mechanic introduced only seems to worsen the already overburdened experience, leaving exasperated and fatigued before I was even halfway through. The abundance of network lag (which from what I've gathered is by no means an isolated issue) made parts of the game nearly impassible, as if the game was at last telling me to give up as my character ran wildly around at his own inclination.
The dissonance between ibb & obb's truly marvelous artwork and mellow soundtrack and it's reprehensible gameplay is probably one of the most shocking I've ever experienced. It's bewildering and depressing, and I'm still finding it hard to fathom how miserable an experience it was to play when it all seemed so wonderful from the outside.

Bedlam, the 'capital I' Indie FPS adapted from the novel of the same name, delivers a satisfying experience... and that's all that I could ask for.
In spite of the game description, Bedlam does not jump between genres. It stays firmly within the realm of old-school, fast FPS fragger as you progress through the various worlds inspired by other games and genres. This is actually quite nice in my opinion, as for one, I'm a fan of this style of gameplay, and it also keeps things a lot more uniform. It's also fitting, as your in game avatar is a cyborg from the fictional game 'Starfire', a parody of Quake 2. You move incredibly fast, carry a huge arsenal of weapons, which carry over between game worlds, and can gib individual enemy limbs based on where you shoot. All in all, gameplay is fun, although weapons can be a pain as multiple are bound to the same key, and you have to fully equip one before you can switch into another. Mouse movement is also not good, as with all Unity3D engine games, but it doesn't really matter as the game doesn't have any multiplayer component, and it's bearable for fragging the NPCs. On that note, I think Bedlam could've benefitted from having a deathmatch mode tagged on. It would have been interesting with the game's arsenal and sense of humour.
At around 6 hours, the game was pretty short, though it nonetheless gave the developers enough time to deliver the unique story. The writing was great. Quality on par with Monolith's FPS games (which I think would be an appropriate comparison). Presentation was a lot more rough, reflecting the game's indie nature. The fact that a lot of the dialogue occurred during scenes of heavy action also meant that a lot of the plot could be missed simply because you're too busy shooting. I won't say much about the actual plot, since I don't want to spoil it for anyone, but it feels like a doomsday Tron packed to the brim with video game references.
Gameplay wise, Bedlam's level design is predominantly linear, but many areas are very open, giving the player an abundance of tactical options. Item pickup locations are sadly very predictable. There's barely any of the classic maze design, & levels tended to get worse as the game progressed.
In spite of the flaws, or moreso the general lack of polish, Bedlam was an enjoyable shooter to play through. It was released around a time when these 'retro throwback' shooters were becoming more and more common place, culminating in 2016's DOOM reboot, which brought the old-school genre squarely back into the mainstream. Bedlam was one of the better games out of the Shadow Warriors, and Wracks made before then.

A quick disclaimer:
This is a no nostalgia review of Morrowind. My first introduction to TES was Skyrim, then Oblivion, then Morrowind, then Arena (bleh!). I plan to review the game in a critical fashion and lay out its strengths and flaws regardless of how it is remembered by the nostalgic reviewers. Also, I use minimal mods to enjoy a mostly vanilla experience, and my review is based on vanilla Morrowind (I only use Morrowind Code Patch).
Morrowind is a game from another era in gaming. Its graphics are absolutely hideous to our modern eyes (yes, even in 2002 when it was released. See Hitman 2:  Silent Assassin). It processes most things through dice rolls, even whether or not your axe swing lands, or if you cast your spells properly. These of course get better later on as you level up, but in the beginning it can be INFURIATING. The GUIs are very unintuitive:  even looting a chest or an enemy can be tedious, and don't even get me started on Alchemy! Leveling up is weird too... you get points and depending on how you use your skills, you get multipliers for those points to be spent in attributes. It just feels unnatural. And to top it all off, it's still buggy.
Then why do I recommend this game if I have such qualms with the above?
Morrowind is a game from another era in gaming. Vvardenfell is an island filled to the brim with mystery, weirdness, monstrosities, and side quests. There is an incredible amount of content packed into this game, and it was, in fact, originally going to be the entire province of Morrowind instead of just Vvardenfell! There are so many guilds and organizations the player can join, each with their own unique questline, plenty of random sidequests you simply find, and places to explore like Dwemer ruins and Daedric Shrines. Truth is, you'll never run out of things to do, and I haven't even mentioned the main questline (I haven't finished it, because I get so sidetracked by everything else).
But it is hard/different...
I had to look up a few guides just to learn how to play this game, because it does not help you one bit. You're dropped off in Seyda Neen and that is it. I was fumbling around trying to kill a mudcrab and didn't understand why I couldn't land a hit until I looked up a few guides on it. Oblivion and Skyrim spoiled me. But once you get the hang of how the game functions and keep in mind that things will get better as you increase your stats, you'll find that Morrowind is truly one of the best RPGs ever made despite its flaws.
I'll make some comments about specific aspects of the game here:
Magic
Magic in Morrowind, I think, is one of its strong suits. There are tons of different spells you can learn, and you can assign your favorites to hotkeys in a GUI by pressing F1. But the best part is once you buy a spell, you can then make spells at certain vendors who will give you a host of options to choose from. You can make Self spells (they affect you), Target spells (aim and fire!) or Touch spells (get up close and personal!), and then you can select how long the spell lasts, and how effective it is. The game then generates the price for the spell, how much Magicka it consumes, and your chances of casting it properly (pesky dice rolls). As of this review, I'm doing a play through as an absolute Mage, and this freedom with Magic is just phenomenal.
Melee Combat
Once you have increased your stats, you'll find that caving in someone’s face with an Orcish Warhammer can be quite... relaxing. Just push through the tedium in the beginning. The melee combat is not the best by any means (Skyrim did FAR better), but it is still fun and there are many different types of weapons (Something Skyrim did not do so well at) including Long Blades, Short Blades, Blunt Weapons, Axes, Spears, Bows, and even Crossbows. Most of these have to be leveled up individually, so it's best to pick one or two and never all of them in character creation.
Speaking of Character Creation
Another highpoint for Morrowind. If you fill out the papers in the beginning yourself, you can become a truly unique individual. By selecting skills to put in the Major category, you gain a ton of points in the beginning for those skills. The same goes for Minor skills, but to a lesser extent. Everything you don't pick is tossed into Misc. with only a paltry 5 points (you can use them, but you have a 5% chance of success!). Good thing Morrowind is good at this part, because it falls flat on its face on player appearance. I won't lie, it's disgraceful. You pick a race as always, but you only have a few different heads, hairstyles, and faces to choose from. Seriously, if/when you play it, you'll see what I mean.
Stealth Combat
I can't speak from experience on this subject so I won't say much. From what I've read online, most people think it's broken. If I do a sneaky character, I'll update this review with my own thoughts.
A Couple of Random Comments
- The GUI is trash. You actually have to tell the game to take all of the money from a chest of body, because maybe some weirdo out there only wants half... WTF. If I remember correctly this may have something to do with pickpocketing, but I could be wrong. But even if so, it makes no sense if you are not sneaking!
-Characters are extremely generic. Other than Therana of House Telvanni, most characters are completely uninteresting and you will likely not remember them. It also doesn't help that there are only a few voice-acted lines in the game that you hear OVER, AND OVER AGAIN.
-Levitation, Unlocking spells, Water Walking and Water Breathing spells? Sign me up!
-The fact that Fatigue affects your ability to cast spells is annoying to me, but from a balance perspective, I guess it's ok.
-CHARACTERS THAT GET STUCK IN A HALLWAY YOU NEED TO GET THROUGH! I hate that guy in the Ald-Ruhn Mages Guild! I want to send him to Oblivion!
-Vvardenfell is gigantic. There are so many things to explore outside of the cities, and quests to go on. Don’t underestimate this aged title, and have the Wiki bookmarked. You’re going to need it.
-The main quest is completely separate from everything else. You are not required to do any of it at any time. I still have not completed it among my many playthroughs.
-In the options, there is a difficulty slider. You can change the difficulty on the fly, and sometimes you need to make it harder later on so the game doesn’t get too easy.
-The game is very slow-paced. This can be a good or bad thing depending on your playstyle. If you love really digging into a game this is perfect. If you are looking for some instant gratification, this isn’t the best title.
Conclusion
Morrowind, despite its flaws and age, truly is a diamond in the modern rough. It is a labor of love, and you will, with patience, have a fantastic and memorable experience in this legendary title. I’ve avoided making too many comparisons to TES IV and V because it is a little unfair to do so as far as graphics go, but I believe Morrowind is the better RPG of all of them, while Skyrim is a more polished lite RPG. If you are a true, hardcore RPG lover, Morrowind is an ideal choice.
MODS!
To fix many problems, I recommend the Morrowind Code Patch. It doesn’t change much about the game other than fix some broken aspects. This is a must-have. You can get a Fair Magicka Regen mod if it annoys you that you don’t regen magicka. If the graphics offend you too much, you can try out the Morrowind Overhaul. Check out Nexus online for a host mods.

This game is the best remake I have ever come across though I'm a bit bias since I love Resident Evil since the original. If you hate tank controls and don't like the classic Resident Evil static camera angles then this is not the game for you. This is a remake of the original Resident Evil now in HD and it keeps true to the original games with controls, static camera angles, and everything else. Some people say these controls and camera angles are outdated these days but I find this system still holds the charm it had and always will be my preferred method of playing Resident Evil games. I still enjoy Resident Evil 4,5,6, ORC, and the other games with their methods of play but if a remake of 1,2,3, CVX, Outbreak, or any others with the classic set up was done I feel removing the tank controls and static cameras would change the entire experience and it just wouldn't feel as good as the originals.
So please Capcom use this game as the example to follow when making remakes of the older titles because this is how they should be done. If you ever remake Resident Evil 4,5,6, ect... that use over the shoulder then keep them over the shoulder, if you remake Resident Evil 2,3, CVX, ect... that use static cameras and tank controls then keep them that way.
I rate this game a 9.5/10 since it works perfectly on the PC as it done on any other system, it plays out just how a classic Resident Evil game should play, and still a very beautiful game graphically. I would recommend this game to anyone and everyone.

Are you looking for another fun puzzle game? As a fan of the genre myself, I can say I look often. This game stood out for it's art style, co-op, and simplicity.
When it comes to puzzle platformers, ibb & obb uses a recently popular mind-bending alteration on physics. Many of its peer platformers have also used dual or mirrored characters, but not quite in this same way. In those, you the player are able to control both. Here, each character must fend for himself, but also cooperate to succeed. It has taken cues from the co-op element of Portal, but is still self-contained.
While I typically don't enjoy platformers in the genre, this was an exception. Simplicity is key, and the developers executed it very well. It doesn't remain the same throughout, and there is clear progression in the art, but it's always minimal, clean, and fresh. The smooth dream-like artistry behind it, including the music, is excellent and I applaud it.
There is hardly any story, which is fine with this game, and what exists is only shown visually, and you are up to interpret it. It's not as integral, but makes for a neat dynamic if you think about it. I think this part could be developed further. While it's clean, and I like that, it's not overly progressed. It appears, and then goes nowhere. Because of this, it doesn't stick with you long after you play. It's good and lovely mental and cooperative exercise, but not much more.
The puzzle difficulty is variable, and you can choose to pursue more challenging ones that don't hinder you from the main drive. Co-op makes this a lot of fun, as you decipher these physics traps together. It's a good communication and team-building exercise also. It certainly delivers on mental puzzlers, and if you enjoy them, I recommend it to you.
It's a good fun game for friends / couples, requires teamwork, and puzzle solving together!

A Tale of Two Kingdoms is an indie adventure game created by Crystal Shard, the same studio that created the more commonly known Heroin's Quest: The Herald of Ragnarok.
The player takes the role of Maeldun Whiteblade, who is framed for the death of Theylinn's monarch, King Vortigern. With the help of his friends Branwyn and Taliesin the Bard, Maeldun has to stop a horde of invading goblins, clear his name, discover the true culprit, and gain the trust of the faeries of Thierna Na Oge.
This game originally came out in July 2007. I remember playing it in 2009, and my anti-virus program thought the game was malware. The version on Steam is a remastered version - all of the characters are now fully-voiced (which makes it a lot easier to understand the pronunciations of some names), and some characters have received visual upgrades to their portraits. Additionally, the game now has a playable prologue that explains the story setting, rather than a big info dump serving as an opening narration.
Perhaps the strongest point of the game is that there is no way to screw yourself out of winning (*cough* King's Quest 5 *cough*). While you CAN miss items and events that will lock you out from achieving the best ending, or a 100% rating, you can still complete the game. Furthermore, some puzzles can be completed through different methods or different items; the only downside to the latter is that, again, certain solutions will preclude you from getting the best outcome. The points system is divided into 2 categories: Wisdom and Honor. Solving puzzles will award you wisdom, while performing "noble" acts, such as helping out an NPC, will grant honor.
Similar to how Heroine's Quest draws its motifs from Norse mythology, A Tale of Two Kingdoms draws inspiration from Irish/Celtic mythology. The game world is vast; you can explore the majority of it at your own leisure, and run across many NPCs. A particular favorite of mine was the city of Carbonak; you see many game characters, guards and townsfolk strolling around its streets, entering buildings and going about their business. This is a stark contrast to so many games where cities either appear vacant, or are saturated with NPCs that just sit around all day and do nothing. It's little touches like this that give the game its charm.
Puzzles can vary from simple to complex, but a notable feature is that Maeldun can ask NPCs to "do" something for him. When this option is selected, the NPC in question can describe surroundings, or can let Maeldun borrow an item, assuming they trust him enough to do so.
While this game has many positives, it does have a few (if only minor) negatives. For starters, I didn't feel much empathy or emotion for Maeldun. He doesn't have much personality outside of asking a lot of questions, and his emotions are very rarely laid bare for anyone to see. Despite the fact that he's been falsely accused for regicide, it doesn't seem to faze him - he's pretty relaxed throughout the game's story. I didn't particularly "get" his supposed-lover, Branwyn, since she has about as much emotion as a cactus; she usually only talks about fighting the goblins and wanting to kick the crap out of Geraint, the captain of the late king's guard.
Secondly, there are a few frustrating puzzles that are arbitrary if anything. For example (think of this hint as a freebie), an item that you need as a "good luck charm" is a horseshoe. To get it, you have to go to Carbonak, go into the stables, physically move Maeldun into the stall on the right, and then click on said empty stall to pick up the horseshoe. There is no way of actually seeing the item in question, and the only time you might actually hear about it is if you go to the smithy and overhear the stable-boy telling the blacksmith that his horse kicked one of his shoes. Of course, this conversation only happens in chapter 3, and it doesn't fully explain the horseshoe's significance. Another vexing puzzle regards a wounded pigeon. This pigeon can show up in one of four screens, but if it spawns near the beach leading to Carbonak's gates, you will have difficulty finding it, since its gray feathers blend in with the rocks on the road.
Despite the above issues, A Tale of Two Kingdoms is one of the best adventure games I've played. Crystal Shard clearly knows what players want in an adventure game and what they don't. When they created the original game, they made it through their own toil and were not being paid a single cent. Players can easily see the amount of passion and soul the studio put into creating the game. I'm glad to see that indie developers can still stick out in a world that is saturated with AAA garbage, and I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys the adventure genre.
A classic!!

Knights, castles, and sword fights—medieval times have been universally fascinating and appealing almost as long as they have been in existence. A Tale of Two Kingdoms by developer Crystal Shard takes medieval gameplay to the hilt (pun intended), from the music to the dialogue to the setting design. A simple explore-and-combat game, it plays like a classic early video game, where you have to click on the different items in each scene and interact with them in a certain sequence in order to progress to the next chapter. This game may be old fashioned, but it is definitely not easy. You must always make use of your surroundings in each scene, and discovering the solution often requires you to think several steps ahead. These combinations of simplicity and complexity, the familiar and the unknown all contribute to A Tale of Two Kingdoms’ solid credentials as a great game.
As mentioned before, A Tale of Two Kingdoms challenges you to think ahead and solve problems completely on your own. The mouse does let you toggle between viewing objects and using objects, and so clicking on something to view it will probably reveal interesting information. However, it is up to you to piece together the multiple clues and discover the right way to achieve your objective. For example, one of the earlier challenges was to get past a bored guard in a castle chamber. I clicked on the kitchen on the far side of the room and was told that my character stole a bottle of liquor. From there, I easily guessed that I wanted to spike the guard’s drink in order to make him fall asleep so I could slip by. My go-to thought was to slyly place the bottle in a conspicuous place in the room so the guard could see it, but the game kept telling me that it was not wise to place the alcohol anywhere in the room. After almost a full hour, I finally realized that I needed to open one of the side doors in order to distract him, and then pour the liquor in his cup while he was distracted. As obvious as it seems in retrospect, this actually required a lot of creating thinking outside the box. I would definitely say that this game sharpens your critical thinking skills, which I do not often find with these types of games.
The other major aspect that I appreciated about this game was how genuine it was in terms of creating a true medieval ambiance. From the music, which sounded like it was composed centuries ago, to the beautifully detailed backgrounds of battlements and great dining halls, I felt fully immersed in the historical time and location. On the other hand, A Tale of Two Kingdoms also includes incredibly strong female characters, such as Branwyn, who is a fearless fighter and one of the protagonist’s main companions. Of all things, I am glad that gender norms in the game are not exactly the same as the traditional medieval beliefs that prevailed during that time. All in all, a surprisingly stimulating gameplay and impressively authentic game design keep A Tale of Two Kingdoms a relevant and enjoyable game today.

I'm going to assume that most people found this game after playing
. Compared to
,
has more focus on puzzles. There is no actual combat system in this game since the protagonist isn't really a fighter, so you have to use your quick wit to get yourself out of dangerous situations. This may prove challenging as you can find many items within the game and sometimes it takes a while to figure out which item you need to use.
Having said that, I think
is harder than
, mainly because you often find yourself wondering what to do next. The first 2 chapters are pretty straightforward, but after that the game allows you to explore and that's where things start to get more complicated. You will probably need 15-25 hours to finish your first playthrough.
To summarize the story in one sentence: you play as Maeldun Whiteblade, a man who is falsely accused of murdering the king, and you need to prove your innocence whilst saving the kingdom from a goblin attack.
is based on Celtic mythology and folklore. It has a more compelling story than
, but doesn't offer you different character classes to choose from. However, the game does offer different routes and endings (including Steam achievements), so it definitely has some replay value. It's really easy to miss some side quests and cutscenes the first time you play the game, too. If you're a completionist, you'll probably need to finish the game a few times to unlock all of the achievements.
I'm not going to say that one game is better than the other, because it depends on your preferences. If you like puzzles, but didn't like the combat in
, this game may be more to your liking. Both games combine exploration and puzzles with pixel graphics (and nostalgia, if you've played similar adventure games from years ago).
All in all, I can definitely recommend this game to anyone who likes the classic puzzle adventure games.

This is a tribute and throwback to the classic adventure games of last century. Unlike Heroine's Quest it is not also an 'affectionate parody' of the genre or the mythology it's based on. I bought it partly because I liked those games and it is fun to play that way again. I also bought it in part because I really enjoyed the free Heroine's Quest but I don't want to join yet more online services just to donate money.
While I enjoyed those old games, I wasn't very good at them and I played this using the walkthrough for the original edition of this game. It worked quite well but for some reason the developers took it down. At any rate, I didn't get the full effect of wandering around wondering what to do. The basis of these old-style adventure games was moving around and picking up or at least looking at anything more pixellated than the painted backgrounds. Then you would apply the various items to the puzzles you encountered and seeing what worked ... if you survived. This game doesn't have the hidden dangers the King's Quest series was infamous for. You can usually see danger coming. However, it can usually also see you, so you are barred from saving until you survive. You should save after anything important or that you just don't want to do again.
I quite enjoy this game. The Two Kingdoms of the title are the mortal kingdom of Theylinn and the Faerie Realm that co-exists with it. Theylinn has requested aid from your group to help against an army of goblins. Then Theylinn's king is assassinated and you are blamed. While the goblins and humans prepare for war, you investigate the murder and seek out the Faeries to resolve things diplomatically. I enjoy the theme of seeking peace. I love elves so I quite enjoyed dealing with the faeries and seeing their realm (although they rather exasperate the character you play). The game looks and sounds beautiful. The voice acting is quite good. The first chapter especially wouldn't have such diplomatic tension or sarcastic humour if just left to the writing.
The main thing I didn't like was the cutscene mechanic. If you look in the Achievements you will see that there are 20 to try and witness. Their purpose is partly to give you clues to the murder and partly to show that other characters are trying to affect the situation, even if only you advance the plot. However, getting the cutscenes is a combination of finding the right trigger and then, often, waiting for the cutscene to run by repeatedly entering and leaving a scene. If you didn't know they were a specific thing to look for you could easily miss about a third of them. For that matter, you can easily lose some potential later actions by simply solving puzzles 'too early', in chapter 4 rather than chapter 5, although you are more likely to lose story-only cutscenes.
I would recommend this. It might be a little short and a little random by modern standards, but it is more than just nostalgic fun.
edit: something I didn't mention originally: there are usually at least three options for about half the puzzles in the game. The achievements encourage thinking about alternate ways to do things.

Honestly, this is my favorite multi-tasker war simulator. The game centers around a bomber crew (of course) beginning missions in the Battle of Britain all the way to prepartion for D-Day. There is literally 0 story except the real events that occured, (such as the dam busters, which, was such a fun mission). The airmen (and yes, women) you find yourself with gives you a blank slate to decide their story. And because you can almost fully customize your plane (cannot change it...yet), you could be a Royal Australian Air Force bomber, or a Free Polish (or French) bomber, or my personal favorite,  an intelligence bomber with the Queen's Secret Service.
The randomly generated (race, moustache, and gender) makes it seem a little impersonal. While this makes me laugh when it made me question the legitimacy of having an almost full black female crew; the game still certainly lives up to realistic standards. That being said, while I can still make the trip from Paris to London with only one engine, the whole plane (based off an Avro Lancaster) is connected to subsystems such as hydraulics, electricity, and oxygen. In addition, you need to be following preset navigation plots (or even create your own), engaging hostile aircraft, not to even mention bombing, and don't forget your fuel gauge. All of this requires constant thought and can overwhelm even the most professional Starcraft II player.
When one thing explodes, do you want to wait for your engineer to finish fixing the engine on the wing, or do you want your gunner who is currently shooting at an enemy ace coming your way to fix oxygen so I can breath?
Speaking of enemy aces, I feel like they are lacking. Their personality is limited to quirky one-liners & "unique" outfits. That being said I love the enviornment and the multiple successful attempts at recreating airplanes during the era in Bomber's Crews' own style. The graphics are fun: not exactly new, but the contrast between WWII & a cartoony styled graphics is just too good to pass up.
The game does have some glitches, as most tend to do, this is mostly limited to random audio-switch ups during the changing of missions. Nothing truly game-breaking. The worst of these glitches, to show you how insignificant these are;  was I could see through my right rudder as if it was opaque despite being zoomed all the way out.
At higher levels, I kept on getting tools and additions that made my crew practically invincible if I played my cards right. This included selecting the right people to be cross-trained to be a first aid officer or another gunner. I felt I had too many tools for not enough situations. I have never once been shot down, and frankly, am too scared to try it. To be frank, I gave up on insulation because the only way I can get my crew to high altitude is if I bundle them up like they are going to Mt. Everestt (well, they are going higher after all). So I stayed in the medium/low altitude and despite having to deal with flak fire from time to time, I typically am able to take on entire squadrons all by myself.
Now it's time for a small guide on how to play this game (not really):
There's three ways to play this game
1. Act like you're gonna get shot down
Don't spend anything on engines, guns, or what have you, focus entirely on crew safety, dinghies, pigeons, parachutes EVERYWHERE. Buy life vests or survival vests
2. Act like you're never gonna get shot down
Flak jackets, guns, armor, gunners. The only thing worse than a tank is a flying tank.
3. Try to balance the two
Heyyy...did you know this game gives you the option to wear a life preserver, a survival vest, and a weighted (very heavy mind you) flak jacket...all at the same time?
Yea, I didn't either. Because only idiots try to balance survival, AND WINNING. I'll let you decide which is which.
Now time to talk to about navigating.
Oh boy I have a love-hate relationship with the navigation system in this game. You have to phsyically look at the direction you want to go, and wait about 3 seconds for it to confirm, if you don't do this, you continue going the direction you are currently going - forever (not really, you eventually turn around). However, once you get the option to do your own navigation, the game completely changes. Avoiding radar, taking alternative paths to objectives, practically avoiding 90% of the fighters. The only thing that limits your fun is your fuel (which you can luckily extend by some dumb tricks like "Leaning" it). I honestly stopped doing this because it ruined some of the fun, but it is an option if you feel your level is not good enough.
Pros:
Great style
Accurate plane models
Impressive level of detail in regards to the inner-workings of the plane
Good customization both character & aircraft(needs more planes)
A sizable map
You can basically do dead-reckoning as a navigator!!
Cons:
Replayability is a little lower than expected
Aces are annoying and tend to be ignored (except for the cash rewards)
The most minor glitches

This is like the Cuphead of Management games. Not only because it's difficult and extremely hectic, but also because the cutesy, Minecraft-esque artstyle and humor clashes HUGELY with the obscene amount of violence you'll see play itself out over the course of a playthrough.
So basically you're playing as a manager of an RAF Lancaster in World War II which means micromanaging your gunners, repairing stuff when♥♥♥♥♥♥eventually catches on fire or malfunctions, dropping bombs, taking pictures, and basically trying not to die while the Luftwaffe sends increasingly dangerous aircraft toward you, not to mention the flak.
If you've played any itteration of the XCOM games you should feel right at home since you gain research by completing tasks, which unlocks new and better gear, and money you can use to buy said gear. It's about managing your resources at the base, and getting your job done while trying not to die as you do your frankly dangerous missions against occupied Europe.
Does it have flaws? Yeah. The missions kinda become grind-y if you want to avoid being underlevelled for the times when they start sending Bf-110s and probably Me 262s, you're stuck playing the Avro Lancaster (which is a damn shame since RAF Bomber command did have other planes like the DH Hallifax and Exported B-17s), and you're basically at the mercy of your gunners being able to hit anything (especially at the start of a new playthrough), but overall it's a good game worth playing if you're up for punishingly difficult missions, shockingly horrifying deaths, and you're an XCOM masochist on a budget.

Let me start out with a somewhat positive. Versus. Can be fun for the competitive types out there. Pretty cool to play as RE2 and RE3 heroes and villains. Gamemodes aren't too bad. If you have a group of friends to consistently play with, you'll most likely have fun.
The game plays as a third-person shooter that has cover mechanics. I personally fell in love with these kinds of games since Gears of War (great cover system). Not here unfortunately. Cover mechanics are just out of wack. You can be in cover with half your damn body sticking out and it won't let you peek out for a shot! And of course you can still get hit. Sometimes you can't even peek out to shoot from cover. The positive is that they have one. It's like 60% broken, but they have one. As for your character movement, it is not smooth. There is a diving/dodge mechanic but it's not implemented in the best way either.
Gunplay is OK. Not impressive by any means. You can aim and shoot your target with mostly no problems so it passes the test with a bare minimum score. Unfortunately there are weird angles that won't allow you to hit your enemies, but will allow your (gun-wielding) enemies to hit you. Ridiculous.
Teammate AI - dumb as hell. No problem fighting regular zombies, but anything else (soldiers, bosses, hunters) it's like they're trying to get hurt. Enemy AI on the other hand, will wreck you. Even on normal difficulty. When fighting soldiers, the player character takes like 90% of the aggro. I mean♥♥♥♥♥♥ there's three other targets to choose from, wtf? And your teammate AI will barely do damage, while take a ton because they'll get in the crossfire. You're also going to hate getting knocked down, whether it be by and explosion, tyrant, hunter, whatever. I'm that kind of annoying person who only writes bad reviews (albeit constructively). It's not because I give everything bad reviews, but because I only ever feel the drive to write a review when I'm angry that sellers stole my money. I feel like I have to write a good review for Machinarium, though.
Knowing that this masterpiece will stay in my Steam account forever, for only £2.09 (70% sale) makes me a happy buyer.
It's an artistic game, and what an atmosphere it has, too. Out of all the games I've played in my lifetime, this might be the one most deserving of a 'puzzle game' categorisation. There are puzzles within puzzles. Basically, everything's a puzzle. There's a lot of backtracking to be done to solve certain puzzles, and that's why the game is of a decent length. There aren't many areas in the game, but each area is detailed with care, and most of the areas have to be revisited a number of times. I don't mind this, at all. I've grown to really like the areas in which this game is set, and I got really comfortable and confident with the map. I knew how to get where quite easily, and also, whenever I found or earned a new artefact, I tended to know just where to use it eg. which door it will open, even if that door is relatively far away.
The cartooney scrap metal theme, with robots mimicking human life was done brilliantly. It shows that the developers put a lot of time and care into that. Add that to the downtemp/IDM (I think?) soundtrack and you have a brilliant atmosphere.
It's also  worth noting that this game is rather funny. The humour was also something that the developers seem to have put a lot of thought into. Although the humour is generally subtle, it will make you laugh out loud if you like the right kind of humour for it, and not too common for it to get old.
One flaw I found in this game is that the puzzles are a bit too hard sometimes. As a person who's against ever using guides to beat games, even puzzle games, I'm not ashamed to admit that I did use guides on certain occasions here, and I never regretted it. Rather than thinking "Oh, no! It was that obvious all along!", I was more like, "How was I supposed to know that I should do THAT? I wish I checked a guide an hour ago!". Of course, there are also some puzzles in the game that don't require you to have to figure out what artefact you have to find where to open what, and more obvious puzzles that require skill (and hair-tearing), like doing actual puzzles on game machines to earn coins. These were genuinely really hard and required a lot of time (and similar stuff... people who beat the game will know what I'm talking about). I was not ashamed to use guides to beat these puzzles. I would never in a million years accept to try and do those by myself, they're not worth it.
Anyway, I don't want to end this review on a bad note, so I'll just end it by saying that I loved this game. It's different and great. If watching trailers and looking at pictures got you interested in buying this, then buy it! Chances are, it will exceed your expectations like it did mine! :)

I have finally found another video game that mixes anachronisms with pop culture references in a most pleasant manner. Darkest of Days was the first title within this narrow niche, that I got to play way back in 2010. Now it’s time for Bedlam to impress me with its humor and rather unique gameplay mechanics. The game I’m writing about today represents an excellent Steam debut for the developer in question. RedBedlam, is the name and they have every reason to be proud of their first project to be released and enjoyed on Steam.
Bedlam’s story is quite convoluted, so bare with me. Players control an interesting young Scottish woman, named Heather “Athena” Quinn. She’s got mouthful alright, so you better get used to more than a few swear words. Yet I can hardly blame her. You see, Athena (that’s her gamer tag) has been trapped in a strange digital world not so different from the Matrix, yet geared predominantly towards gaming. A nightmare world, in case you were wondering. Video games can be lots of fun, provided you can quit them any time you wish and resume your daily life and various activities. Heather can’t go back to her normal life. Not until she gets to the bottom of this mystery and surprise, surprise, civil war. Again.
And zombies are back! I knew I couldn’t swing a proverbial dead cat at my Steam collection before hitting a few undead. More than a few, in fact. I’m still glad Bedlam doesn’t limit its foe diversity to yet another rotten horde. You’ll get to battle so many types of baddies, that you’ll literally lose track of it all. And that’s precisely what Bedlam intends. Even the etymology of “bedlam” should have been a hint by itself. Confusion, indeed. But also a throwback to simpler gaming times and the classic shooters which defined PC gaming. Don’t expect Bedlam to refer to them by more than name, since the gameplay is emulated in a skillful manner as to avoid any potential copyright infringement.
Unity 5 Engine provides the graphics in Bedlam. No surprise and frankly, I wasn’t bothered at all and actually appreciated the fact that I can run the game maxed out, 4K res and stable 60 frames per second. You know what didn’t quite click? The fact that I had to endure several CTDs (crashes to desktop) in just a few hours of gameplay. Those crashes would usually occur during the transition between levels and not during the action in full swing. Still bothersome, since the CTD would force me to restart since the last checkpoint and hope that I shall be able to pass the level “unscathed” this time around. And no, there aren’t any personal hardware or OS incompatibilities that would hinder my progress. It’s the game’s fault and subsequently, the review rating had to reflect this.
The voice acting is top notch as far as I’m concerned. Been a while since my ears were treated with a thick Scottish accent and I could only appreciate the break from the norm. Don’t even get me started about that ghastly cliché with good guys = American accent & bad guys = British accent. The soundtrack is naturaly shifting along with the genre of the in-game section it represents. Arcade sounds for the PAC-MAN clone, as an example. You’ll be pleased by the end results and the developer has obviously cared enough about Bedlam to offers sounds most suiting for the visuals as the situation demanded.
At its core, Bedlam shall remain a fast-paced first person shooter no matter what genre classic it pays homage to. Whether we’re talking of clones for Quake, Medal of Honor, Return to Castle Wolfenstein, Elder Scrolls or even Space Invaders and the aforementioned PAC-MAN, Athena shall always blast her way from one point of the level to another while being constantly on the move. If only the AI in Bedlam would offer a worthy challenge though. They don’t, sadly. Most foes, no matter their size or weapon of choice, shall just mindlessly charge towards the player despite their option to accurately shoot from a safe distance.What the Artificial Intelligence seems to be lacking in quality, it tries to even the odds through the good ol’ strength in numbers.
Unbalanced difficulty, would be an exaggeration yet there were instances when I had to load from a previous save file, since I was getting swarmed from all sides by enemies which can be literal bullet sponges at the worst possible time. The saving grace for this particular issue, lies in the anachronistic situation I was mentioning earlier. How about shooting Nazis with the laser weaponry you still have from the previous Sci-Fi section? That really simplies the initial challenge, even if they send a few Panzers towrds you. That overpowered rocket launcher you were using earlier on to destroy robots, can be used just as effectively against WW2 tanks. The list of wacky examples can go on and on. This type of scenario coupled with the humorous dialogues and truckload of references to gaming or the ‘90s in general, is what appealed to me and certainly to many other players which grew up with the video games being emulated and evoked in Bedlam.
I managed to have fun with this title in spite of its stability shortcomings. It contains all the bells & whistles a Steam collector could wish for, along with a decent price tag as well. All I could sincerely hope for now, is a worthy sequel to it and far more examples of classic titles that have shaped the gaming industry and fan base forever.

I HIGHLY recommend it.
The game expands and improves the original game from 1996, adding new areas, new rooms in the mansion and gameplay elements not present in the original like new puzzles and enemies. It also expands the plot and connects it better with the other titles in the series like RE2. This is the definitive version of the classic Resident Evil experience, with an even better atmosphere.
Pros
-Classic Resident Evil improved
-Great replayability, two main protagonists that play differently, slightly different endings, different game modes, challenges to beat, unlockable costumes/weapons, awesomeness
-Very good atmosphere
-Better voice acting than the original (still a classic one, though)
Cons
-Insane rendering resolution that ignores your chosen screen resolution, may cause slowdown
-The controls take some time to get used to, the original controls are second nature to veterans but may feel awkward for newbies. Meanwhile the alternate controls may get in your way when the camera changes the angle (statue and moving walls puzzle, I'm looking at you)
The pros outhweight the cons by a large margin :)
You may have some slowdown if your pc doesn't meet recommended settings but you can easily find workarounds provided by the community that work 100%.
The new controls (alternate) can get in your way because the angle of the camera may change and that means you can easily walk into the arms of a zombie when you intended to run pass it.
The unlockables and extra modes are really fun and challenging to do, encouraging you to replay it in different ways. I got 100% of the achievements after 48 hours app.
I wouldn't recommend this if you don't like survival horror games or you're very afraid of spiders, otherwise this game is a MUST PLAY.

Newcomers be warned that this is nothing like RE5 or RE6. In this game you have to plan ahead. Unless you play on easy difficulties, you have little amunition and health items, so sometimes you have to avoid fights entirely. On a side note, the camera angles are fixed and sometimes I found myself walking on the opposite direction of where I wanted to go, due to the sudden transition. Other than that, I have no other issues with the game. I found zero bugs or glitches.
Summarizing, it's a classic survival horror game. If you like this kind of genre, pick it up. You won't regret it.

I definitely recommend this game. It's one of the best I have ever played. The thing is, a lot of people like to say it's bad because of the way its marketing is handled, but the way they do things is justified.
...to a certain extent. The DLC they release has licensed stories that go along with them, along with armors, feats, base items, etc... So, of course, I think it's just to have a limit for Free Players' levels.
However, I do think the game is in dire need of some changes. First off, my legs get broken every time I attack or get attacked. What's up with that? I can go to Crysis, and fight aliens with fast-paced combat, while keeping real-time momentum, and being able to keep my speed. Why the *foop* do you want to slow us down? I picked Superspeed as my first power, and as soon as I got to the Hive mission around level 9, I got sick of it.
*Acquires Super-speed*
*Does NOT use it in combat*
Then, I got the Last Laugh DLC, went into the Safehouses (as a hero) and Night Clubs (as a villain), and saw Superman and other flight-enabled iconics flying so fast in combat? Why weigh us down, Daybreak? Why? I think there's no need for this at all.
Anther thing I want to do is make a request, if you're reading this. I think it would be a good idea to make advanced mechanics for iconic powers and movement powers. See, some people play this game to be as close to their favorite super heroes and villains as they like. They even go around with names inspired by those people. As of now, people who use iconics at level CR 43+ are ridiculed, since this game is heavily reliant on teamwork, which isn't a bad thing, so, I think you should actually allow people who want to use these to be relevant in damage output, rather than having them stick with a loadout that everyone else uses, thereby making them have less of a fun time.
TL;DR:
This is an awesome game. Their DLC practices are justified, especially compared to games that sell you DLC that's already on the discs.
Please don't slow us down in battle, and please make advanced mechanics for Speed, Flight (as well as its re-skin, Skimming), Acrobatics and Iconic Powers. Make people who use iconic powers to actually be "stronger than a locomotive."
Anyway, thank you for this awesome game. As I said, I cannot love it enough, and would defend its DLC practices forever, but I do have my problems with it, 'cause no game is perfect. Thanks again, Daybreak.

Small World 2 is an easy to learn and quick to play digital version of the popular board game by Days of Wonder.  The object of the game is simple, be the player to gain the most coins by the end of the game, through occupying regions of the map and taking over opponent’s regions through conquests.
The rules of the game are simple and easy to learn and this digital rendition makes it easy to keep track of everything and prevent mistakes that can easily be made when playing the original board game.
Once the basics of the game have been grasped the skill comes in when deciding if it is worth paying coins for choosing a better race/ability combo, choosing which regions to occupy/conquer and when to send your race into decline and choose a new race.
The DLC’s add new race/ability cards creating new combinations to master and get used to.  At the moment, there are only a few DLC’s available and not all of the expansions available for the board game version have made it to the digital version as a DLC.
There are many ways to play:
- The AI of the game does seem a little unbalanced with dice rolls frequently failing for the player and constantly succeeding for the AI (way above what the statistical average should be).
- Unfortunately recently there does not seem to be a lot of players wanting to play online.  I have gone into the Online Waiting Area to find very few or no games at all available to join.  I have also had the game crash or freeze a few times when playing online with a private game between friends.
- Great for playing against family and friends when all on the same network.
- Tedious way to play but means that the game can be played on just one computer and with only one copy of the game.
Overall Small World 2 has made a successful port over to a digital version.  It has been sympathetically done, in line with the artwork and lore of the Small World board game.  There are one or two small issues with the game, but generally these do not detract from the convenience and speed that the digital version brings over the original board game.

If you have an hour or so to kill, Haunt the House: Terrortown is a really cute, breezy game where you play as a ghost trying to scare people out of buildings. The creators clearly had a lot of fun finding creative ways for you to "spook" people, as you possess different items, each with different scary abilities. The environments and character designs are really distinctive, too. In spite of how fast it goes, all the different item combinations -- as well as being able to play different ghosts you can unlock throughout the game -- allows for lots of replayability.

Firstly, you can try the prototype for this game at
(or another similar flash game site that the developers posted at). Once you've finished trying it out and are itching for 4 more zones (5 if you include the holiday expansion) of diverse furniture and props to possess for human-scaring purposes, then buy this game FRIGHT away!
Poor pun aside, Haunt the House: Terrortown is one of the smaller games that Steam has to offer, but an enjoyable experience nonetheless; you can finish your first playthrough in under an hour (faster if you rush it), and it serves well as an in-between game, something to download and install quick for to occupy your attention while travelling or waiting for something else to finish. If you've got an hour to spare, and want to spend it on a quick session of spooking, give Terrortown a try!
